12034-knights-of-malta-1523-1798:
R. Cohen's Knights of Malta, 1523 to 1798, late scholar of Wadham College, Oxford, won the Lothian Prize Essay for 1920 at the University of Oxford. Its first chapter covers the settlement at Malta from 1523 to 1565, from departure from Rhodes and residence in Italy to settlement in Malta in 1530.

Cohen describes the condition of the Mediterranean, the corsairs, Turkey, the fortification of Malta, the loss of the English langue. The enterprises of the Order, ending as Suleyman decides to attack. The essay treats the Knights Hospitaller as a military and religious order caught between empires, and its prize-winning form gives the history a clear, scholarly shape.
14414-lancashire-idylls-1898:
Marshall Mather wrote Lancashire Idylls in 1898, tales of the stern Puritan hill sects of Lancashire. Waugh and Brierley, Mather notes, saved moorland and factory life, but left the hill sects unsung. These idylls aim to recall their poetry and simplicity. The tales draw on a famous valley in the northeast of the county, and its own local speech. Mather writes with affection for chapel folk and their ways.

One idyll gives a mother and daughter in dialect, the girl doubting she is her mother's child in spirit. The mother answers that she loves her more now than when she was small, like a hill well that flows stronger in drought. A second scene shows a younger woman weeping out grief on an older woman's shoulder, till sleep brings peace. An old granny prays God to ease the heart. The idylls keep the speech, faith, and sorrow of the hills.
18265-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
One issue of the Scientific American Supplement, dated June 25, 1898, gathers short illustrated articles from many fields at once. Its table of contents lists tombs of the first Egyptian dynasty, the milestones of human progress, the Queen Regent and Alfonso XIII of Spain, and rose growing. Engineering, medicine, and biography sit side by side in the same number.

Other pieces take up the lock of the Dortmund-Ems Canal, the growth of the central electric station, steering gear on North German Lloyd steamers, and theories of sleep. Short engineering notes close the issue. A reader gets a snapshot of what counted as new and useful knowledge in the summer of 1898.
20393-a-short-history-of-english-printin:
Printing came to England in 1476, and this short history follows the craft through to 1898. It moves press by press and printer by printer. The writer based the account on personal study of the books and fragments each press produced.

For the earliest period, the book draws on detailed Sandars Lectures about the first printers' work. Originality, it notes, is out of the question for that age, so care and proof matter most. The history gives students of books a compact map of how English printing grew from Caxton's day to the modern trade.
20994-kilgorman-a-story-of-ireland-in-17:
Reed scorned tales that hid moral powder in jam, says the note that fronts Kilgorman. Such dosing, he held, spoils the jam and sickens the reader of the powder. Blood-and-thunder penny tales earn his scorn from the other flank as well.

Kilgorman tells of Ireland in 1798, the year of the great rising. Talbot Baines Reed sets a boy amid rebels, redcoats, and a land aflame. He aims for thrills with truth, not shocks for their own sake. The book shows a boys' writer at his most ambitious, facing a grim, real war with care and pace.
21225-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
Scientific American Supplement No. 1157, dated New York, March 5, 1898, gathers longer technical articles than the weekly paper could carry. Its table of contents runs from the requirements of a Palestine explorer to a biography of Emperor William II of Germany with his portrait. Heat in great tunnels and the causes of poverty follow.

Other articles cover liquid rheostats by H. S. Webb and the use of cables. Ocean currents and climate follow, plus a machine moulding process described in seven illustrations. Park making, tree measuring, and a Newfoundland passenger steamer round out the number. One issue preserves the range of 1898 applied science.
22701-the-blindman-s-world-1898:
Edward Bellamy wrote The Blindman's World, a short story of 1898 by the author of Looking Backward. Bellamy's tales often test a single strange idea, and this one begins with an astronomer's ruling passion. The narrator confesses that a specialty easily grows into an infatuation. His interest in Mars had grown well past the strictly scientific.

Through the telescope, he believes, Mars testifies as plainly as written words to a climate like our own across the gulf of space. From that conviction the story builds its quiet marvel, a vision of another world and what it proves about this one. Bellamy writes wonder in a plain, earnest voice. The story shows the utopian novelist working small: one man, one telescope, one overwhelming idea.
22702-an-echo-of-antietam-1898:
Edward Bellamy wrote An Echo of Antietam, a short story of 1898 set long after the Civil War battle whose name it bears. Bellamy, famous for his utopian novel Looking Backward, also wrote tender tales of ordinary people carrying old wounds. Here a soldier sits at a family table years after the guns stopped.

The soldier's cousin, the Rev. Morton, sits on one side of him. On the other sits Miss Bertha Morton, the kindly, middle-aged hostess of the occasion. A dinner among kin becomes the ground where a buried memory rises. Bellamy handles war's long shadow without battle scenes, through talk, reticence, and sudden feeling. The story is a small, humane pendant to the grand histories of Antietam.
22703-hooking-watermelons-1898:
Edward Bellamy wrote Hooking Watermelons, a short story of 1898 told in the dialect of country boys grown into unequal men. Bellamy is remembered for Looking Backward, but his short tales of New England life have their own following. This one turns on luck, envy, and the friend who rises in the world.

Bill, the narrator, insists that a former companion is on the make, and warns his listener not to forget it. Many's the time, he recalls, the two went swimming and hooking apples together as little chaps. The mild reproach in his voice does the story's work: early fairness promised equal fortunes, and life broke the bargain. Bellamy lets dialect carry both comedy and a quiet sting.
22704-to-whom-this-may-come-1898:
Edward Bellamy wrote To Whom This May Come, a short story of 1898 in which a traveler meets people whose speech he cannot unlock. Bellamy, the utopian novelist, liked puzzles of communication, and this tale is built on one. Shipwreck or stranding has set the narrator among strangers who will not, or cannot, talk with him.

Unwilling to wait for the strangers to speak first, he addresses them in English. He gets only deprecating smiles. He tries French, German, Italian, Spanish, Dutch, and Portuguese in turn, with no better result. Six languages fail him, and the mystery deepens. The story turns that failure into its engine, asking what passes between people when words will not. It is Bellamy in his speculative, wondering vein.
22705-a-summer-evening-s-dream-1898:
Edward Bellamy wrote A Summer Evening's Dream, a short story of 1898 steeped in the drowsiness of a country summer evening. Bellamy, famous for Looking Backward, could also write the slightest of sketches and make mood itself the event. Here nothing hurries, and that is the point.

The talk circles the art of the Plainfield yawn: a rite never to be hurried, but savored slowly and lazily, stage by long-drawn stage. City visitors, fretted and quick, know only the yawn of irritation. Lucy, the hostess figure, finishes her yawn and compliments her guests on theirs. The story is a small comedy of rest, written against the grain of an hurrying age.
22706-two-days-solitary-imprisonment-189:
Edward Bellamy wrote Two Days' Solitary Imprisonment, a short story of 1898 about how an innocent man tastes prison. Bellamy, the utopian thinker, distrusted easy judgments, and this tale starts with a story inside the story: an account of circumstantial evidence that very nearly hanged an innocent man.

Joseph, the listener, is struck by the victim's ordinariness. The man was respectable, inoffensive, much like Joseph himself. He probably never dreamed of danger from the law. That thought prepares his own brush with confinement, two days that test what a blameless man feels when the machine of justice closes on him. Bellamy writes suspense from respectability itself. The story questions how thin the wall is between the citizen and the cell.
22707-potts-s-painless-cure-1898:
Edward Bellamy wrote Potts's Painless Cure, a short story of 1898 with a comic title and a young man's deliberate heart. Bellamy, author of Looking Backward, filled his tales with gentle irony about the poses people strike. His hero here falls in love on purpose, as a matter of form.

The fall, the narrator says, was quite voluntary and deliberate. The young collegian fell in love on principle: it was the correct thing for a student of the humanities. It made him feel more grown and manly than smoking or drinking could. Even a stove-pipe hat and cane did less. From that pose, real feeling presumably ambushes him, as it does in Bellamy's courtship tales. The story mocks and forgives its hero in the same breath.
22708-a-positive-romance-1898:
Edward Bellamy wrote A Positive Romance, a short story of 1898 whose title plays on positivism, the philosophy of Auguste Comte. Bellamy's fiction often argued ideas through conversation, and this tale opens mid-argument about the worship of woman.

Talking about the adoration of woman, the narrator turns to his companion. Was it not that crack-brained Frenchman, Auguste Comte, who proposed just such a thing? He built it into his Religion of Humanity. The joke sets the story's terms, a romance argued as much as felt. Comte's system, with its priests and its goddess-like ideal of womanhood, gives Bellamy rich material for satire and sympathy both. The tale shows the utopian novelist at his most conversational.
22709-at-pinney-s-ranch-1898:
Edward Bellamy wrote At Pinney's Ranch, a short story of 1898 with a murder at its center. Bellamy is best known for Looking Backward, yet his tales range into crime and the western ranch country. Here suspicion fastens on a man named Lansing after another man, Flint, is found dead.

A couple of days before the murder, the two had exchanged blows on the street. With no other clue, people thought of Lansing, and Lansing knew it. He therefore stayed silent about a fact he would otherwise have sworn to at the inquest, fearing it might now imperil him. Silence under suspicion drives the story's tension. Bellamy builds a study of fear, evidence, and the danger of the obvious suspect.
22710-the-old-folks-party-1898:
Edward Bellamy wrote The Old Folks' Party, a short story of 1898 in which old friends talk of ghosts, and one guest turns the talk toward the future. Bellamy, who set his famous novel a century ahead, never lost his interest in what is to come. This fireside tale gives that interest a homely form.

Ghosts of the future, one speaker declares, are the only sort worth heeding. Visions of the past, he says, make a very unpractical kind of ghost lore beside visions of what is coming. The line could stand over Bellamy's whole career. Around such talk, the party of old folks measures past against prospect. The story is slight in plot and rich in the author's ruling idea: the future judges the present.
22711-a-love-story-reversed-1898:
Edward Bellamy wrote A Love Story Reversed, a short story of 1898 that opens by a fireside with two school friends, one newly married. Bellamy, the author of Looking Backward, wrote many tales of courtship seen from the woman's side, and the title promises his favorite trick: the usual positions exchanged.

Lucy Merritt, recently married, pays her first visit since the wedding to her roommate and bosom friend Maud. She sits on a hassock with her hands folded over her knees. She looks up at her friend with the air of a petitioner. The posture hints at the reversal to come, in which the married woman seeks, and the single one bestows. Bellamy tells it with his usual gentle irony about the rituals of love.
22712-lost-1898:
Edward Bellamy wrote Lost, a short story of 1898 about parted lovers and a journey timed by the seasons. Bellamy, famous for Looking Backward, set this tale between Bonn and a steamer, in the ache of a separation that spring makes crueler.

Had it been November, the narrator reflects, nature at least would have sympathized. Instead their parting fell in spring, when the sky brims with promise. That felt cruel. Everything blooms except the lovers' prospects. The title leaves its meaning open: lost love, lost chance, or a lost traveler. Bellamy writes the mood in his clear, wistful prose, trusting weather and season to carry the feeling.
22713-with-the-eyes-shut-1898:
Edward Bellamy wrote With the Eyes Shut, a short story of 1898 that begins on a train full of new wonders. Bellamy, the utopian novelist, loved technology's novelties, and his narrator marvels at the railway carriage around him like a man preparing to believe anything.

He had just been admiring the vestibuled cars, the electric lights and annunciators, the steam heat and air-brakes. After such wonders, almost any new railway convenience seemed likely. That mood of pleased belief sets up the tale's device, an experience had with the eyes shut that rivals sight itself. Bellamy plays with how new machines train the mind to accept marvels. The story is a light, curious pendant to his serious utopias.
22714-deserted-1898:
Edward Bellamy wrote Deserted, a short story of 1898 set under the hard, bright air of the desert West. Bellamy, author of Looking Backward, traveled in imagination as readily as in time, and this tale rests on looking: a woman trying, and failing, to put the desert into words.

Miss Dwyer scribbled two pages of description in her notebook that morning, then read them over, looked out of the window, and tore them up. The wonderfully fine, clear, brilliant air, she concludes, transfigures the landscape into something that must be seen and cannot be told. Around that failure of description, Bellamy builds his story of a place and a person left alone. The title does double work, as his titles like to do.
22715-the-cold-snap-1898:
Edward Bellamy wrote The Cold Snap, a short story of 1898 about a country household in the grip of the winter's bitterest day. Bellamy, the utopian novelist, grounded many tales in New England farm and village life, where weather is a public event and reputations rise on reading it rightly.

The narrator claims the honor of the coldest day of the season for his own household. In the country that counts for much, since weather wisdom earns real esteem. Everyone hastens to support the verdict with evidence. His mother reports that the frost never left the kitchen window nearest the stove all day, and that was a sign. Bellamy makes comedy and character out of thermometers, windows, and village pride in hardship.
22809-the-hermit-of-street-1898:
The Hermit of —— Street is a mystery story dated 1898, about a recluse in a great city and the new neighbor who watches his house. The catalog record names no author, and the street's name is left blank in the classic manner. City hermits were a newspaper staple of the age, and fiction fed on them.

I had never truly seen him, the narrator says, except in the sly way already related. And he had never seen me at all. The day after my arrival in the city, I noticed the large house in our rear. It was among the few mansions in that great city still keeping an old-style lawn. Naturally, I asked some questions about it. The answers unlock the hermit's history. The story mixes urban mystery with the pathos of a life withdrawn.
23168-a-ride-with-a-mad-horse-in-a-freig:
W. H. H. Murray drags himself through a battlefield in A Ride with a Mad Horse in a Freight-Car, dated 1898. Enemy fire passes a few feet over his head as he crawls. The work is slow and painful. Inch by inch he drags himself clear of the batteries' direct line, then creeps to the wood's edge and looks out over the green slope.

That crawl is only the approach to the title's ride, a Civil War episode in which a wounded man and a maddened horse share a freight car. Murray, famous for Adirondack tales, wrote war memory with a sportsman's eye for ground and weather. The excerpt's care with slopes and ranges shows it. Few magazine titles promise so exactly the ride they deliver.
24836-rodman-the-boatsteerer-and-other-s:
Louis Becke published Rodman the Boatsteerer and Other Stories in London in 1898. The title tale opens aboard the whaler Shawnee of New Bedford, cruising off Samoa after a year at sea with no luck. Captain Harvey Lucy, a man of violent temper, has already driven his crew to trouble, and the boatsteerer Rodman must steer through it.

Nineteen more tales follow, from Peruvian slavers and a Ponapean custom to a trader's wife and the escape of a slave girl who swims to an English ship. Becke writes from life in the Pacific trade, with salt detail and moral bite. The book suits readers who like sea stories where the islands, the ships, and the men all feel real.
25782-the-american-missionary-volume-52-:
The American Missionary Association publishes this quarterly for March 1898, volume fifty-two, number one, from Congregational Rooms on Fourth Avenue in New York, priced at fifty cents a year in advance. An editorial notes the magazine, now a quarterly, with a list of field workers.

Industrial work, both are right, and notes on five civilised tribes, China and the Chinese, and Alaska fill editorial pages. Field reports cover teachers' residences, the south, Orange Park in Florida, a Congregational church in Atlanta, and coloured ministers of the Black Belt in Alabama. Obituaries, receipts, jubilee shares, and women's state organisations close the issue.
25958-the-american-missionary-volume-52-:
The June 1898 American Missionary, volume fifty two, number two, reports the association's work in a year of war. Editorials note that success is costly, weigh war and its results, and mourn missionaries murdered among the colored peoples of Cuba. Southern news leads with samples and examples from Secretary A. F. Beard, then Straight University at New Orleans, Tougaloo, and Dorchester Academy.

Colored teachers in the South, a sketch of a Straight graduate, and notes on Indian uprisings and the California Chinese mission fill the middle pages. An obituary honors Rev. C. L. Woodworth, and long receipt lists name givers town by town, from Roxbury and Stoneham to Providence and Little Compton. The number is a plain monthly record of schools, missions, and giving.
26079-the-american-missionary-volume-52-:
The September 1898 issue of The American Missionary gathers the quarterly work of the American Missionary Association. Editorials weigh whether Cuba should be taken for Christ, the place of Black citizens in American life, and the new Louisiana constitution. Field notes report from schools and churches across the South. Talladega College in Alabama and Tillotson College in Texas get full reports.

Short notes follow missions in Georgia, North Carolina, Tennessee, and Mississippi, and the issue closes with receipts and the work of women's state groups. Christian Endeavor meetings, the S'Kokomish and Capon Springs conferences, and a missionary gospel section round out a number that shows the association's schools, churches, and fund-raising in one snapshot.
26106-u-s-patent-4-293-314-gelled-fuel-a:
Bertram O. Stull's United States patent 4,293,314, granted October 6, 1981 and assigned to the United States Navy, sets out a gelled fuel-air explosive method. The patent compares fuel candidates and finds 1,2-butylene oxide markedly better than ethylene oxide or propylene oxide for such devices.

Detonation limits are given for each fuel: ethylene oxide clouds from 3 to 100 percent by volume can detonate, against about 3.1 to 27.5 percent for propylene oxide. The claim rests on safety as well as power, with 1,2-butylene oxide put at about three times safer than propylene oxide under long exposure. Background, summary, and preferred embodiments lay out the method in full.
30684-the-boys-of-98:
James Otis writes The Boys of 98, stories of American history, copyrighted in 1898 and published in Boston by Dana Estes, illustrated by J. Steeple Davis and Frank T. Merrill with reproductions of photographs. Otis, author of Toby Tyler and The Boys of Fort Schuyler, lists eleven companion tales in the front matter.

Those tales include When We Destroyed the Gaspee, Boston Boys of 1775, When Dewey Came to Manila, and Off Santiago with Sampson. When Israel Putnam Served the King, The Signal Boys of 75, and Under the Liberty Tree follow. An illustration shows the charge at El Caney, and contents open with a battle-ship chapter. Otis writes spirited history tales for boys.
31711-the-life-of-william-ewart-gladston:
John Morley's third volume of his life of William Ewart Gladstone covers the years 1890 to 1898, though its contents also reach back to the parliament of 1880. Books within the volume treat the Irish revolution, Egypt, the Soudan, reform in 1884, the defeat of ministers in 1885, and the accession of Lord Salisbury.

Morley draws on Gladstone's own records, including his note of May 20 after forty-eight years of public life, meeting his twelfth parliament as chief minister amid a great and fervent crowd. Readers get the closing part of a major Victorian biography, following an old statesman through his last years of power.
4869-history-of-the-united-netherlands-1:
Turnhout in 1597 gives Maurice one of his clearest victories, and John Lothrop Motley follows the march, pursuit, and demolition of the Spanish army there. Improved military science and the moral effect of the battle matter as much as the surrender of the garrison, and the campaign then shifts to France, where Spaniards sack and burn Amiens.

De Rosny plans a reorganization of French finances amid jobbery and speculation, Philip repudiates his debts, and Jesuit persecution renews. A Polish envoy pleads at The Hague for reconciliation with Philip. Motley links battlefield reform to finance and diplomacy, showing a republic whose armies and credit grew together.
4870-history-of-the-united-netherlands-1:
As France moves toward peace with Spain in 1598, the Dutch States send a last mission to stop it, and John Lothrop Motley follows the envoys to Paris and London. The great advocate Barneveld leads the effort, Henry proposes elevating Maurice to sovereignty, and the envoys then face Elizabeth's demand for repayment of her advances.

A second embassy settles the final arrangement between queen and republic, after the envoys return from England with hard terms. Motley presents the mission as a test of Dutch independence: whether the republic could keep its allies without becoming their debtor. The volume closes an era of dependence with a bargain struck, not a victory won.
9622-lyrical-ballads-with-a-few-other-po:
William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge published Lyrical Ballads in London in 1798, a book that changed English poetry. Its advertisement calls the poems experiments, testing whether the plain speech of middle and lower folk suits poetic pleasure. Readers used to gaudy, empty phrase were warned they might feel strangeness at first. The book asks poetry to speak like conversation.

Poems inside include The Nightingale, The Foster-Mother's Tale, and other lyrics of common life and feeling. The plain style shocked some readers, then won the age. A reader gets the founding book of English Romantic verse, where humble subjects and natural speech became poetry's new ground.
a-new-race-phrenology-1898: A New Race Phrenology, dated 1898 and credited to Rachel Bevington Webber, is a short pamphlet of twenty-eight pages. Its title joins two late Victorian enthusiasms: phrenology, the reading of character from the head, and the idea of a coming new race of improved humanity. Webber also wrote on Bible phrenology in the same years. The pamphlet survives as a slight, curious specimen of phrenology's last phase, when the old head-reading science was being wedded to schemes of racial and spiritual improvement.
a-thief-in-the-night-a-book-of-raffles-a:
E. W. Hornung brings back Raffles, the gentleman thief, in stories told by his loyal friend Bunny. Bunny opens by promising the whole truth at last: Raffles was a villain, he admits, yet the glamour holds him still. The contents list Out of Paradise, The Chest of Silver, The Rest Cure, and The Criminologists' Club among nine tales.

Raffles and Bunny move between cricket fields, country houses, and London clubs, stealing with style and escaping by inches. One tale builds a trap to catch a cracksman; another turns on relics of Raffles himself. Hornung fills in blanks from their early days, and Bunny's divided loyalty gives the crime stories their lasting charm.
abramelin-mathers-1898:
S. L. MacGregor Mathers gave English readers the Abra-Melin book in 1898. He worked from an old French copy of a text said to date from 1458. The book claims to teach the sacred magic of Abra-Melin the Mage. Mathers led the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn.

A long course of prayer and pure living fills the plan. It leads to talks with a holy guardian angel and power over spirits. Later books of ritual magic drew hard on this one. Its strict demands and bold claims still start debate among readers of old grimoires.
arxiv-2509-00498:
Junjie Zhou, working with three co-authors, Xinpeng Li, Menglin Huang, and Shiyou Chen, addresses phonons, the vibrations of atoms in a solid, near defects, flaws in the crystal. Exact phonon work needs huge cells and costly first-principles math, while broad machine learning potentials, models that predict forces between atoms, are fast but not exact enough.

Zhou and his co-authors propose training one potential for one defect, using a small set of shifted large cells. Their defect phonons match the costly method on frequencies and related measures, and on light emission and carrier capture rates. The cost drops by more than ten times, opening studies of very large defect cells.
arxiv-2509-00798:
Changin Choi, with three co-authors, proposes PMSR for visual question answering. Some questions about images need outside knowledge beyond the picture. Existing retrieval-based approaches often search only once. They can gather too little knowledge that way. They also lack a way to revise reasoning that goes astray.

PMSR builds a structured reasoning path step by step. Queries draw on both the latest record and the whole path so far. They retrieve varied knowledge from mixed sources. Retrieved evidence is then merged into compact records. This loop refines reasoning in a controlled way. It also limits how errors spread through the chain. Tests span six diverse benchmarks. PMSR improves both retrieval recall and final answer accuracy throughout.
arxiv-2509-00898:
Matthew Welsh, writing alone, studies intersections in a quotient space built from three-by-three matrices. The matrices have determinant one, over integers and reals. He looks at translates of closed orbits of the positive diagonal subgroup. Those translates meet a maximal parabolic subgroup. The pattern of those meetings is his main object.

The meetings connect closely to roots of cubic congruences. The polynomials are monic and irreducible, with integer coefficients. Welsh shows the meetings are jointly equidistributed. That means they spread evenly across both subgroups. It follows that certain affine lattices are also jointly equidistributed. Those lattices are set by pairs of congruence roots. They correspond to ideals in the ring of integers. The methods parallel work on multidimensional Farey sequences.
arxiv-2509-00998:
Rachel Pries, writing alone, presents a manuscript on the Torelli locus and Newton polygons. It grew from a lecture series at the Arizona Winter School in 2024. The lectures were on abelian varieties. Abelian varieties generalize elliptic curves to higher dimensions. The Torelli locus sits inside their moduli space.

The manuscript covers two topics in turn. The first is the geometry of the Torelli locus. That locus consists of Jacobians of curves. The second is arithmetic invariants of such Jacobians in positive characteristic. Newton polygons are the key invariants there. They encode p-adic behavior of the varieties. The text serves as a descriptive guide linking curve geometry with arithmetic.
arxiv-2509-01098:
Judging tools that flag odd points in time series data, data recorded in time order, is itself a hard problem. Zhijie Zhong, with three co-authors, notes that present scores can lack sharpness, depend heavily on settings, shift under small noise, or cost too much to compute. They propose a new scoring method called CCE.

CCE measures both how sure a model is and how steady that surety is, at the level of the whole series and of single events. It uses Bayesian estimation, a way of stating uncertainty with probabilities. The team proves the score stays bounded and stable, runs in linear time, and they add RankEval, a shared benchmark for comparing such scores fairly.
arxiv-2509-01198:
Shrinking data to fewer dimensions can twist the geometry that later tasks rely on, such as which vectors sit at right angles. Eddi Weinwurm and Alexander Kovalenko propose a Relationship Preserving Loss, a training score that guards those traits. It compares relationship matrices, tables of pairwise links, between the raw data and their low-dimensional forms.

The loss trains neural networks to make nonlinear projections while keeping orthogonality and linear independence largely intact. Error bounds drawn from matrix perturbation theory support the method. Early tests suggest performance on later tasks holds up even as dimensions drop. Weinwurm and Kovalenko also list wider uses, from aligning data across domains to fairer and federated learning.
arxiv-2509-01298:
El Gordo is a pair of galaxy clusters caught mid-collision, and its layout tests what dark matter is made of. R. Valdarnini reviews a detailed simulation of that merger with self-interacting dark matter, where dark matter particles can scatter off each other. New results from weak lensing, the bending of light by mass, are added to the comparison.

The simulation reproduced the observed offsets between the clusters' mass parts, with a scattering strength near four to five square centimeters per gram. The two stellar parts also moved relative to each other along the line of sight at several hundred kilometers per second. Yet that scattering strength clashes with current upper bounds from other clusters. Valdarnini argues the particle scattering picture may be too simple for such violent mergers.
arxiv-2509-01498:
Medical image segmentation networks often need hand tuning for each new data set, and the popular nnU-Net framework automates most settings but not those inside the network itself. Chao Deng, Xiaosen Li, and Xiao Qin present MSA2-Net, a network whose convolution kernels resize themselves to suit each data set's fingerprint. That self-adaptive module is the core of their design.

The module sits in two places: a multi-scale convolution bridge that refines features passed across the network, cleaning out redundant data, and a multi-scale amalgamation decoder that rebuilds the segmentation map. By capturing both global and local features in the feature maps, the network aims to generalize better across scans. Deng and the co-authors argue that internal self-tuning, not just outer settings, is the missing step for robust medical segmentation.
arxiv-2509-01598:
String theory amplitudes can be written as integrals over punctured Riemann surfaces, and their structure mirrors a pattern called the double copy. Andrzej Pokraka, Lecheng Ren, and Carlos Rodriguez study a family of generalized hypergeometric integrals on surfaces of genus g, tied to multi-loop string amplitudes in a chiral splitting frame. Loop momenta, moduli, and all but one puncture are left un-integrated.

The team examines the twisted homology groups attached to these integrals and determines their intersection numbers. Those numbers let them write a double-copy formula for the complex, closed-string versions of the integrals. Numerical tools were built to check the findings, including recent Enriquez kernels for higher-genus polylogarithms. The work extends a powerful organizing principle of scattering amplitudes to higher genus.
arxiv-2509-01698:
Nadzieja Hodur, Monika Pilsniak, Magdalena Prorok, and Ingo Schiermeyer work on coloring problems for a restricted family of graphs. A graph coloring assigns colors to points so that linked points differ. The bull is a small shape made of a triangle with two short tails, and the claw is a point joined to three others. The authors study graphs that contain neither shape.

For three or more colors, they describe all colorable graphs in this family that hold a long ring. They also give full lists of the linked graphs that cannot be colored with four colors. A matching list covers graphs that also lack a five point ring and fail at five colors. The lists turn a hard check into a clear set of cases.
arxiv-2509-01798:
Antonio Ismael Cano-Marmol studies Hardy spaces in a setting where values do not commute, meaning order matters when they combine. These semicommutative Hardy spaces extend classic spaces used to study functions on a disk. He describes them through molecules, which are small building blocks that can rebuild any member of the space. That description is the core tool of the work.

With the molecule picture in hand, he bounds a class of singular integral operators named for Calderon and Zygmund. The operators take values in a semifinite von Neumann algebra, a broad noncommuting number system. The bounds hold from the space back into itself. Such bounds matter for harmonic analysis, the study of waves and signals, in quantum settings.
arxiv-2509-01898:
Zhipeng Weng leads five co-authors on sharpening heat images from drones when training examples are few. Large diffusion models, which build images by removing noise step by step, often overfit small drone infrared sets. Overfitting means memorizing training cases and failing on new ones. Their fix adds a Gaussian quantization step, which rounds features through a bell shaped code, to the learning of representations.

A monitor watches training for early signs of overfitting in large designs. The team also builds a multi source drone infrared bench for detection and rebuild tasks. Tests on that bench beat prior sharpening methods under tough conditions. Overfitting drops a lot while the large design stays intact. Code and data will be released publicly.
arxiv-2509-02098:
Paolo Barucca builds a maximum entropy theory for temporal networks with continuous timestamps. Temporal networks record directed interactions as they occur over time. Few studies model that timing directly in continuous time. His approach maximizes entropy under basic constraints to get the least biased network ensemble.

The ensemble splits neatly into global time processes times a static edge probability from a standard maximum entropy graph. That split yields closed form likelihoods plus degree, clustering, and motif expectations. Edge timing follows non-homogeneous Poisson processes whose rates come from path entropy optimization. Those processes beat plain Poisson timing on likelihood, while edge labels recover strength constraints. Links to Hawkes calibration, renewal theory, and graph networks are discussed.
arxiv-2509-02198:
Anum Afzal, Juraj Vladika, and Florian Matthes build FActBench, a benchmark for fine grained factuality checks of medical text from language models. Factuality is the most critical evaluation axis in specialized domains like medicine. Reliable fact checking tools also feed hallucination mitigation pipelines. Their bench covers four generation tasks and six leading models in the medical domain.

Two checking techniques are compared: chain of thought prompting, where the checker reasons step by step, and natural language inference, which judges entailment. Unanimous voting between the two correlates best with domain expert evaluation. The result guides builders of automated medical fact checkers. Public benchmarking of this kind helps track hallucination risk as models evolve.
arxiv-2509-02298:
Victor G. Kornilov and six co-authors report a 2025 astronomy paper on measuring shaky air inside a telescope dome, where trapped turbulence blurs star images. Their instrument, Domecam, watches how the light of a bright star flickers, recorded at a plane tied to a point below the telescope pupil.

Observations ran from 2022 to 2024 at a 2.5-meter telescope in the Caucasus mountains under varied weather. Checks against a standard turbulence sensor validated the device. By pairing Domecam readings with speckle images, the team converted dome turbulence power into expected image sharpness. They find dome air worsens typical sharpness noticeably. The result gives observatories a direct way to measure and fight a local source of blur.
arxiv-2509-02398:
Hui Wang and nine co-authors present a 2025 benchmark paper for text-to-audio generation, where models create sound from written prompts. Existing checks mostly grade sound quality, leaving robustness, fairness, and safety untested.

Their TTA-Bench grades models across seven dimensions, including accuracy, robustness, fairness, and toxicity. The prompt set holds nearly three thousand items built by automated and manual routes. Scoring mixes objective metrics with a large pool of human annotations from experts and general listeners. Ten leading models were run under the shared protocol, exposing strengths and gaps side by side. The authors release the data and tools openly, aiming to set a fuller standard for judging audio generators.
arxiv-2509-02498:
Hemanth Manikantan and seventeen co-authors wrote a 2025 instrumentation paper reviewing lessons from IXPE, a space mission that images X-ray polarisation, and planning its successor detectors. The mission proved the technique works but exposed limits in its readout chip and amplification stage.

The team is developing a three-dimensional photoelectron track polarimeter based on GridPix, a detector first built for axion searches. Tracking the full path of each photoelectron should sharpen polarisation measurements. Early proton beam tests at a Bonn cyclotron checked two things: that the new chip survives space-like radiation doses, and that the facility can run at low enough rates for controlled trials. Both checks passed, and ion-irradiation preparations continue.
arxiv-2509-03798:
M. Gatti and thirty-nine co-authors' 2025 research paper unveils the largest weak-lensing map yet of the late-time universe's mass. Weak lensing reads the slight bending of galaxy light by invisible matter, letting astronomers weigh cosmic structure directly. Their map combines the DECADE and Dark Energy Survey Year 3 datasets, covering thirteen thousand square degrees and 270 million galaxies.

Systematic tests against observing conditions like depth and atmospheric blurring find the map statistically clean of contamination. Such a wide, trustworthy mass map suits cosmology, cross-correlation studies, and hunting large-scale structure features. As a demonstration, the team detects cosmic filaments, the thread-like bridges between galaxy clusters, in the mass map directly, a first. Those filaments are validated by their association with clusters found through the Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect in Planck and ACT data, where hot gas distorts the cosmic background light.
arxiv-2509-03898:
Joining diffusion generative models with compressed sensing to speed up synthetic data generation is what Zhengyi Guo and three co-authors do in a 2025 research paper. Diffusion models produce high-quality samples but pay heavy training and inference costs in the original data space. Compressed sensing, which recovers signals from far fewer measurements than tradition demands, offers a way to shrink that space first.

Their approach compresses data into a latent space and trains the diffusion model there instead. Samples drawn in that space are then decoded back by a compressed sensing algorithm. Under stated sparsity assumptions, the combined method provably converges faster than plain diffusion training. The analysis also guides the best latent dimension, balancing compression against recoverability. Experiments span digits, medical images, climate images, and financial series used for stress testing. Across them, sample quality holds while the computational burden falls.
arxiv-2509-03998:
Zhizhong Huang and one co-author devote a 2025 mathematics paper to integral Diophantine approximation on algebraic varieties. It asks how closely points can be approached by rational or integral ones. The setting is a log pair, a variety with a boundary part, and attention fixes on integral points near a chosen rational point in that boundary.

An integral constant quantifies the best closeness near the fixed point. Two landmarks frame expectations: Siegel's theorem on integral points, and McKinnon's conjecture about rational constants. Guided by those, the authors conjecture that on weakly log Fano varieties, integral points near the fixed point must lie on rational curves. Those curves may have no more than two points at infinity, a strong shape limit. The conjecture is then checked for a number of examples. Confirming cases suggest local behaviour is governed by a small supply of special curves.
arxiv-2509-04298:
Yingxuan Li and two co-authors use computer-generated images to fix wrong labels in photo collections in a 2025 research paper. Categories that look alike, such as similar animal species, often get swapped by human labelers. That semantic noise poisons supervised training. Synthetic pictures from text-to-image models carry trustworthy labels, but their style differs from real photos and their variety is limited, so training on them directly helps only so much.

Instead, generated images serve as clean reference points for spotting and correcting mislabeled real ones. Accuracy rose across benchmark sets under many noise conditions. Combined with leading noise-resistant training methods, gains reached large margins on standard CIFAR and ImageNet subsets. The two approaches stack because they attack different weaknesses.
arxiv-2509-04498:
Krithi Shailya and three co-authors audit university advice from language models for bias in a 2025 research paper. Students increasingly ask chatbots where to study, and biased suggestions can quietly narrow their futures. Three open models, LLaMA-3.1-8B, Gemma-7B, and Mistral-7B, answered for 360 simulated profiles varying by gender, nationality, and wealth. Over twenty-five thousand recommendations were analyzed for geographic, demographic, and economic skew.

Institutions in the Global North were heavily favored, gender stereotypes surfaced in program suggestions, and the same universities repeated often. LLaMA-3.1 offered the widest diversity, naming hundreds of universities across dozens of countries, yet systemic disparities persisted. A new multi-dimensional fairness framework accompanies the findings.
arxiv-2509-04598:
Luciano N Grippo and two co-authors settle complexity questions for perfect edge domination in special graph families in a 2025 mathematics paper. An edge dominates itself and every edge touching it. A perfect edge dominating set leaves every outside edge dominated exactly once, a tidy covering condition. The authors first prove a hardness result for graphs admitting no efficient edge dominating set, an even tidier pattern. Deciding whether at least two perfect sets exist there is NP-complete, meaning no fast algorithm is expected.

For graphs avoiding the six-vertex path, they give a cubic-time algorithm finding a smallest perfect edge dominating set. The same engine adapts to weighted versions and even counts all such sets, keeping the same running time.
arxiv-2509-04698:
What happens to certain homology groups when two weights coincide? Kentaro Mikami and one co-author answer that question for the one-dimensional case in a 2025 mathematics note. The setting is vector fields and differential forms on Euclidean space, structures earlier work organised into Lie superalgebras with double weights.

Earlier results using the Euler vector field showed Betti numbers vanish except the last when the two weights differ. Mikami and Mizutani tackle the equal-weight case that question left open. Their note gives a complete answer for the Euclidean line, clarifying the super homology groups in that setting.
arxiv-2509-04798:
Controlling many qubits takes many controllers that must stay in exact step. Yilun Zhao, lead author with fourteen co-authors, propose a distributed quantum control design in a 2025 paper. Existing synchronisation strategies impose heavy performance penalties, and existing instruction sets are either too abstract or too detailed.

Their design has two parts. HISQ is a hardware-agnostic instruction set that decouples control language from quantum operation meaning. BISP is a booking-based synchronisation protocol that may reach zero-cycle overhead. Together they aim at one reconfigurable microarchitecture that supports varied control methods as qubit counts grow.
arxiv-2509-05198:
A standard benchmark for classifying three-dimensional point clouds has labelling flaws that hold models back. Mohammad Saeid, lead author with two co-authors, introduce a refined version of that benchmark in a 2025 computer vision paper. The original dataset suffers inconsistent labels, two-dimensional data, size mismatches, and weak class separation.

Their cleaned dataset, ModelNet-R, is designed as a more reliable testbed. They also propose Point-SkipNet, a lightweight graph-based network using efficient sampling, neighbourhood grouping, and skip connections. Models trained on the refined data improve significantly in their experiments. Point-SkipNet reaches leading accuracy with far fewer parameters than contemporary models.
arxiv-2509-05498:
Defenders can exploit attackers' mental blind spots, Ya-Ting Yang and Quanyan Zhu argue in a 2025 paper on cyber deception planning. Cognitive arbitrage means gaining advantage from superior awareness of how the other side thinks, including gaps in knowledge and biases like inattention or base-rate neglect.

Their two-level game models a strategic layer that designs deception for advanced persistent threat attackers, and an operational layer that carries out tactics. Game theory links the layers in one quantitative design. In simulations the defender's early edge fades with time, yet well-timed deception flipped the attacker's payoff from negative to positive value for the defence. It also raised total rewards by at least forty percent during execution.
arxiv-2509-05898:
Reading on screens that respond to eyes and hands rather than a trackpad is tested in a 2025 study by Omar Elgohary and one co-author. Multimodal interfaces are spreading in education and assistive technology, yet their effect on memory is understudied. The authors ask whether gaze plus gesture control helps or hurts retention.

Twelve participants read four articles through both a standard trackpad setup and an interface using eye movement and hand gestures to scroll, zoom, and reveal content. Retention was tested at once and again after a day, alongside workload and usability scales. Targeted retention matched the trackpad at first, but the multimodal version demanded more mental effort and seemed to fade faster over the day. The authors draw design lessons for learning tools that use richer input.
arxiv-2509-05998:
A q-deformed version of cosymplectic geometry is built in a 2025 paper by Melvin Leok and two co-authors. Cosymplectic manifolds blend symplectic geometry with a clock-like direction, suiting systems that evolve in time. The q-prefix signals a controlled twist of the usual structures, whose Hamiltonian dynamics the authors set out to develop.

On these manifolds they study Hamiltonian, gradient, and evolution vector fields, then prove Liouville-Arnold-type theorems, the classic results that make well-behaved systems solvable in closed form. A q-cosymplectic version of Marsden-Weinstein reduction, the standard tool for removing symmetry, follows. Worked examples in multitime dynamics, including fast-slow systems, illustrate the tools, and full proofs are included so readers need no other source.
arxiv-2509-06098:
The slowest of many searchers sets the finish time, and Talia Baravi and Eli Barkai work out that extreme statistic in a 2025 paper. Classical extreme-value theory gives a Gumbel law for the slowest first passage in a finite domain and a Fréchet law in an infinite one. Real systems sit between: many searchers in a large but finite space.

The authors take the thermodynamic limit, where searcher number and domain size grow together at fixed density, and solve for the extreme value explicitly. The solution recovers the two classical laws at high and low density and reveals new behavior between them. An extension to diffusion on fractal domains shows how two fractal dimensions steer the statistics, with the full moments and finite-density corrections supplied.
arxiv-2509-06398:
First dark matter searches with the MADMAX experiment are reported in a 2025 contribution by Fabrice Hubaut. MADMAX hunts halo axions, hypothetical dark matter particles, by converting them to photons in a strong magnetic field. Its booster, a stack of dielectric disks before a mirror, resonates the conversion across a target mass range near one hundred microelectronvolts, territory post-inflationary theories favor and no experiment has charted.

Small prototypes tested over three years validate the dielectric haloscope concept and already deliver strong searches for axions and dark photons. Hubaut presents the experiment's status, results so far, ongoing development, and remaining challenges on the road to the full instrument.
arxiv-2509-06498:
Fibonacci spirals in sunflower heads get a fresh mathematical explanation from Michael F. Staddon in a solo 2025 paper. Plant patterns of seeds and leaves, called phyllotaxis, are well known, but the real mechanism behind them is still unsettled. Many models can draw spirals without proving that nature uses them.

Staddon tests a Keller-Segel model, where a spreading chemical signal creates its own transport signal and can form local instabilities. The plant becomes a steadily growing disc whose center emits the signal. Depending on the balance between growth and source strength, the model yields Fibonacci spirals or alternating patterns. A stability analysis shows the pattern comes from instabilities growing alongside the plant itself, suggesting the model may describe several plant processes.
arxiv-2509-06598:
Locating sounds in ordinary stereo videos, and judging how far away they are, is tackled by Davide Berghi and one co-author in a 2025 audio-visual paper. The task mixes naming what made a sound, when it happened, and where it sits in three-dimensional space. Meaning is the hardest part to model, and multichannel recordings limit training data.

The authors enrich a standard system with pretrained models that link language to sound and to images. These embeddings feed a modified Conformer block built for cross-modal fusion. Tests on the DCASE 2025 development set separate each model's contribution, and the team also describes large synthetic audio and audio-visual datasets built for pretraining, expanded by swapping left and right channels. The full system, with ensembling and visual cleanup, placed second in its challenge track.
arxiv-2509-06698:
Skin-sweat sensing for wearables, without calibration, is the aim of a 2025 electronics paper led by Leidy Mabel Alvero-Gonzalez, with six co-authors. Electrodermal activity tracks stress and arousal through skin conductance, and continuous monitoring is in demand. A wearable front end must be sensitive, frugal with power, and easy to use on different people.

Their design, VCO-CARE, reads the skin signal through a voltage-controlled oscillator, a circuit whose frequency follows the measured conductance. Post-layout checks show very high sensitivity across the normal conductance range and a tiny relative error on fixed test resistances. Power use is only a few microwatts, and added noise stays low across the slow band where these signals live. The authors aim at wearables that adapt to many users with minimal fuss.
arxiv-2509-06798:
Driving data for rare road events is synthesized from real scenes by Zhengqing Chen and seven co-authors in a 2025 autonomous driving paper. Sensor simulation is essential because dangerous or unusual cases are hard to capture on real roads. Game-engine simulators lack diversity, while learning-based ones cover only narrow object types like vehicles and demand heavy multi-sensor data.

Their system, SynthDrive, follows a real-to-simulation-to-real path built on three-dimensional generation. It automates the mining of real assets, the generation of new ones, and the synthesis of rare-case driving data, aiming at objects beyond a single category. The abstract presents the pipeline as scalable and aimed at high-fidelity sensor data for perception training. Broad, automated asset generation is the key claim: rare scenarios can be manufactured in variety rather than waited for on the road.
arxiv-2509-07098:
Computer-using agents that copy a human demonstration instead of improvising are built by Yinheng Li and three co-authors in a 2025 artificial intelligence paper. Graphical interface agents have advanced quickly but still fail on complex tasks with novel interface elements, long action sequences, and personal workflows. One expert demonstration is the input here.

From that single demonstration, the Instruction Agent builds a step-by-step instruction list, then follows the user's intended path closely as it acts, avoiding improvisation errors. A verifier module judges the outcome of each action, and a backtracker handles surprises such as pop-up windows. On a set of OSWorld tasks that all top-ranked agents had failed, the system achieved a sixty percent success rate. The authors offer the design as a practical, extensible bridge toward reliable real-world interface automation.
arxiv-2509-07198:
Yiyue Chen and 3 co-authors present Fed-REACT in 2025, a federated learning framework for data that differs across users and changes over time. Federated learning trains a shared model across many devices without moving private data to one server. In practice, each client's data looks different and drifts, which drags down standard methods.

Fed-REACT works in two stages. First, each client learns a local model that extracts feature summaries from its own data. Then the server groups clients with similar summaries into clusters and trains a task model for each cluster. Theory backs the first stage, and tests on real datasets show better accuracy and robustness than standard approaches. The design suits settings like phones or hospitals, where data is private, varied, and always shifting.
arxiv-2509-07298:
Cataclysmic variables are star pairs where one star dumps matter onto a white dwarf, causing bright outbursts. D. A. H. Buckley and 10 co-authors simulate how the Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time will catch them, in a 2025 research paper. They run mock observations using a thin-disk picture of how these systems spread through the Galaxy.

The simulations suggest only a fifth of the most energetic dwarf nova outbursts will be caught during outburst. Polar-type systems, which swing widely in brightness, can be recovered fairly completely to faint levels over ten years. The team also estimates detection rates for micronovae, small fast bursts. Their results help astronomers plan follow-up observing for the flood of alerts the survey will produce each night.
arxiv-2509-07398: Seyed-Mohammad Bagheri, writing alone in 2025, proves results in logic about the affine part of some classic first-order theories. The results concern quantifier elimination, where each formula can be rewritten with no quantifiers such as 'for all' or 'there exists'. They also concern model-completeness, a close property that makes the models of a theory behave in a uniform way.
arxiv-2509-07498:
Factories still run on rigid, layered control charts drawn decades ago, and those charts block modern cloud tools. Hai Dinh-Tuan proposes an alternative, CRACI, in a 2025 research paper written alone. CRACI is a cloud-native reference architecture for the industrial compute continuum, the mix of factory devices, edge servers, and clouds. It replaces fixed hierarchies with a decoupled, event-driven design.

Data can then flow flexibly between levels instead of climbing a strict ladder. Trust, governance, observability, and lifecycle management are built in as founding pillars, not add-ons. Dinh-Tuan validates the design two ways. He compares it against established standards and models, and he reuses performance data from published smart manufacturing projects. Both checks suggest CRACI can support scalable, interoperable industrial systems better than the legacy models.
arxiv-2509-07598:
Lauri Alha, writing alone in 2025, introduces a family of self-inverse functions built from the dilogarithm. A self-inverse function undoes itself: applying it twice returns the starting value. The dilogarithm is a classic special function with a rich web of identities. Alha defines a fundamental form through an integral equal to a two-term combination of dilogarithms.

A wider family generalizes that form through two auxiliary parameters, called shape and scale factors, and the members are named gemini functions. They keep similar self-inverse and symmetric properties. Through new integration techniques, Alha proves a variety of dilogarithm identities and evaluations, covering ladders and two-term combinations. The framework is offered as a broad tool for deriving and applying such identities, an area where each new relation can unlock integrals elsewhere in analysis.
arxiv-2509-07898:
When particles collide at extreme energies, counting the produced hadrons reveals how the underlying interactions cascade. Krzysztof Kutak and Sándor Lökös compare quantum chromodynamics dipole cascade models in a 2025 research paper. These models picture a particle splitting into color dipoles that split again. The authors compare the classic one-dimensional Mueller model with newer versions.

A practical problem is that experiments define their measurement ranges differently. The authors propose entropy, computed from the average particle multiplicity, as a universal observable that sidesteps that ambiguity. They calculate entropy and multiplicity from each model and fit the parameters to proton-proton collision data. The generalized dipole model describes the data much better than the classic one. The result helps modelers of high-energy collisions choose tools that match real measurements.
arxiv-2509-08098:
I. Y. Dodin and 4 co-authors fix a classic failure of geometrical optics by changing coordinates, in a 2025 plasma physics paper. The ray method models waves cheaply in plasmas but predicts a false infinite amplitude at reflection points, exactly where accuracy matters. The singularity is an artefact of describing waves by position and wavevector.

Rewriting the theory in phase space with ray time as the coordinate and ray energy as its momentum removes the blow-up. A Weyl symbol calculus on the new space connects the formulation back to standard symbols. Reduced wave models steer fusion and space plasma simulations, so removing a spurious singularity at reflections improves every prediction that passes a turning point.
arxiv-2509-08198:
Carlos Rito and 2 co-authors use computer search to build a surface that theory had only promised, in a 2025 geometry paper. Their method hunts for members with many singular points inside families of surfaces. It is applied to Godeaux surfaces, a class known for tricky counts. The search pays off with clear, explicit cases.

One surface found has four singular points of two simple types. A branched cover of it, built from two cyclic groups, is smooth. It has the counts of a quadric surface but a different soul. Such fakes are called fake quadrics. With the appendix, this is the first explicit fake quadric ever built. Existence proofs now have coordinates to point at.
arxiv-2509-08798:
Henning Fernau and 1 co-author start the study of reconfiguring alliances in graphs in a 2025 paper. An alliance is a group of vertices that work together, for example to defend against outside attack. Reconfiguration asks if one alliance can be turned into another step by step.

Two alliances of the same size are given, along with a limit on sequence length. Moves include sliding, jumping, and adding or removing tokens. Most versions prove PSPACE-complete, a very hard class, though some need only logarithmic space. Parameterized results give fast methods for small combined parameters. The paper links the move regimes through a new monotonicity idea.
arxiv-2509-08998:
A classical inequality about convex shapes and their duals has a many-function generalization whose equality cases were recently pinned down for symmetric functions only. Thomas A. Courtade and Edric Wang remove that restriction in a 2025 research paper. The functional Blaschke-Santaló inequality compares a function with its Legendre dual. Two researchers had shown centered Gaussians saturate a broad family of such inequalities, assuming even test functions.

Using an entropic duality, Courtade and Wang give a short alternate proof of that result. The new proof needs no symmetry assumptions at all. As a payoff, they settle a conjectured inequality about Wasserstein barycenters, a way of averaging probability distributions. They also prove the matching statement for many convex bodies with no symmetry assumed. Shorter proofs that assume less tend to travel further, and this one tidies a corner where geometry, probability, and information theory meet.
arxiv-2509-09298:
Oh-Tae Jang and 2 co-authors present SlotSAR, a method to learn target traits in radar images, in a 2025 paper. Synthetic aperture radar gives sharp images, but terrain clutter and speckle noise fill them. Clutter can look like targets, which muddles the traits a model learns.

SlotSAR pulls target traits apart from background with no mask labels. High level semantic traits from a pretrained model join low level scattering traits from a wavelet net. A slot attention module merges both levels and sharpens each slot's identity. Tests show top scores on radar tasks while keeping fine structure. Past object centric methods trail on the same tasks.
arxiv-2509-09598:
César Barilla and 1 co-author ask how the climate lived through by ancestors shapes green attitudes today in a 2025 economics paper. Drawing on several modern surveys plus cultural records at the ethnic group level, they trace a U-shaped pattern. Descendants of groups from very steady homelands, and from very volatile ones, rate environmental stakes highly, while groups from middling climates rate them lowest.

Folklore and other cultural stories show the same curve, pointing to culture as the carrier across generations. The authors model attention to the environment as a costly choice made before conditions are known. Because people commit early, evolution only tunes beliefs through average gains and losses, leaving different groups with different lasting biases.
arxiv-2509-10298:
Laith Nayal and 2 co-authors harden image classifiers against adversarial attacks in this 2025 paper. Tiny, crafted changes to an image can fool deep networks and vision transformers, while many defenses cost too much computing or give no formal safety bound. Their method guides a training trick called stochastic depth, where layers are randomly skipped, using the network's Lipschitz constant as the guide.

Skip rates grow with depth, which regularizes the deepest layers most and trims computing cost. On CIFAR-10 with a small vision transformer, their custom schedule kept clean accuracy near the baseline. It also improved resistance to three standard attacks, from a simple gradient method to AutoAttack, while using far fewer operations than rival schedules.
arxiv-2509-10398:
Disorder usually ruins a crystal's neat physics. Arpan Manna and three co-authors report it creating a new phase instead. Their material is WTe2, in this 2025 paper. The compound is a type-II Weyl semimetal. It is normally nonmagnetic. In messier samples, the authors observe Kondo screening. There, magnetic moments get cloaked by surrounding electrons. The effect acts unevenly along different directions.

The measurements show resistance changes that depend on direction. They also show a Hall effect with no magnetic field applied. That effect grows stronger with disorder. A large second-harmonic Hall signal appears as well. The authors' reading is specific. Disorder-driven Kondo interactions pin the key energy level right at the Weyl nodes. That boosts curvature-driven transport effects. The claim recasts disorder as a knob. Turn it, and correlated topological behavior switches on.
arxiv-2509-10798:
Yijun Liu and six co-authors teach a language model to remember what matters in this 2025 paper. The topic is KV cache eviction. Long conversations force models to store ever more key-value memory. That eats memory and slows decoding. Eviction methods must choose what to forget. The usual trick judges importance with the last few tokens as queries. It overvalues local detail. Crucial global context can be dropped.

Their method, Judge Q, appends a short list of trainable soft tokens to the input. Only the embedding layer is tuned. The soft tokens learn to mimic what real decoded tokens will look for. They then grade the cache with a global eye. Tests used Llama and Mistral models. Benchmarks included LongBench, RULER, and needle-in-a-haystack tasks. Under the same memory budget, the method lost less performance than rival eviction schemes.
arxiv-2509-11098:
Mengke Wu and four co-authors wrote this 2025 human-computer interaction paper on why people often feel powerless in front of AI recommendation feeds. Users usually cannot see how their data shapes what they are shown, and they get few real ways to steer the system.

The team built a test interface with tools for managing data use, finding more varied content, and switching recommendation modes by context. In walkthroughs and interviews with nineteen participants, these features helped people read the signals behind their feeds, push back against unwanted guesses about them, and trust the system more. The authors also discuss how such controls can be made visible enough that people actually use them.
arxiv-2509-11298:
Madhava Gaikwad, writing alone, asks when two training objectives for language models are secretly the same in this 2025 paper. Such methods train models on human likes and dislikes. Many named objectives are sold as fresh improvements. Gaikwad built a tool called Opal to test them. Opal puts an objective into a standard form. It can also produce a case where two objectives truly differ.

Running Opal across the field showed a pattern. Many popular methods optimize the same goal under new dress. Batch handling can even make one pair of replies pull in different directions from batch to batch. A small set of deep features explains the truly distinct goals, the author finds. Most of the rest is re-dressing.
arxiv-2509-11398:
Anusha Sinha and 6 co-authors argue that testing AI systems for weaknesses should grow out of cyber red-teaming in this 2025 position paper. A red team plays the attacker so defenders can fix real flaws before real adversaries arrive. As companies adopt AI widely, that practice must adapt to systems that fail in unfamiliar ways.

The authors say cyber red teams, properly briefed on AI's new risks and unpatchable failure modes, can judge AI systems better than ad hoc testers. At the same time, AI testers gain from security practice: realistic adversary emulation, formal rules of engagement, and tooling that makes engagements repeatable. Merging the two crafts, they argue, builds a stronger security culture for both fields.
arxiv-2509-11498:
Zhuoxuan Ju and 3 co-authors present Georgetown University's entry to a shared task on discourse relation classification, in a 2025 system paper. The task asks software to label how text passages relate to each other, such as contrast or cause, across many languages.

Their system, DeDisCo, tests two designs: an encoder based on a multilingual model and a decoder approach using an open Qwen model. They augment training data for low-resource languages with material translated automatically from English. Extra linguistic features, inspired by earlier shared task entries, are also tried. The system reached a solid macro-accuracy score, and the paper interprets the results with an error analysis.
arxiv-2509-11798:
Rémi Schlama and five co-authors let a swarm search for the best reaction conditions. This 2025 chemistry paper treats reaction optimization in drug work. Many parameter mixes must be probed. The search must be fast, parallel, and sustainable.

Their algorithm is α-PSO. It augments classic particle swarm optimization with machine learning support. Candidate mixes drift and cluster like flocking birds. Unlike black-box predictors, its calls stay clear to follow. Each call ties to things a chemist can observe. A theory frame gauges how rough a reaction landscape is. Local Lipschitz constants do the gauging. Smooth hills split from cliffs of reactivity. Settings adapt to each landscape. On pharma benchmarks, the method matched Bayesian optimization. In two live campaigns, it found the best conditions faster.
arxiv-2509-11898:
Alexandru Ternar and four co-authors pull together what field studies say about AI tools in game making. This 2025 human-computer interaction paper notes a gap. Tools that create text, art, and code reshape how games are made. Pipelines and the wider trade both shift. Single studies of the upheaval rarely speak to each other.

Set search rules (PRISMA-S) were followed. Studies based on interviews and field notes, from 2020 to 2025, were gathered across major computing and games archives. Each was checked for quality. Ten studies passed the bar. They were combined by translating their concepts into one shared frame, step by step. Nine big themes emerged. Advice for practice accompanies them. Game makers and scholars get grounded guidance rather than hype.
arxiv-2509-11998:
Given several families of invertible matrices, can one pick a member from each so the product is the identity and nothing nonzero is fixed by all of them? William Crawley-Boevey and one co-author settle that question, the Deligne-Simpson problem, in a 2025 paper.

The first author had earlier conjectured an answer phrased through an associated root system, and one direction was already proved in joint work with Shaw. What remained was the reverse implication, and that is what this paper supplies. With both halves in place, the conjecture stands confirmed. A clean root-system criterion now decides when such a tuple of matrices exists. The result closes a problem at the crossroads of linear algebra and representation theory.
arxiv-2509-12098:
A tiny, hand-labeled benchmark puts a sharp question to named entity recognition: when a word like Hope could be a person or an idea, who reads the context better? Payam Latifi runs the pilot comparison solo in 2025 across six systems.

Three classic tools, NLTK, spaCy, and Stanza, face three general-purpose language models, Gemini, DeepSeek, and Qwen, on a dataset of about a hundred nineteen tokens spanning persons, locations, organizations, dates, and times. The language models generally win on context-sensitive names, with Gemini posting the best average score, while Stanza stays more consistent on structured tags like locations and dates. The models wobble on time expressions and multi-word organizations, leaving practical advice on which system suits which job.
arxiv-2509-12298:
Molecules in space form and break through vast reaction networks, and modelers need fast tools to follow the chemistry. Luke Keyte and one co-author release SIMBA in 2025, a Python package that evolves molecular abundances at a single point under set physical conditions.

The solver handles gas-phase reactions, grain-surface processes, and photochemistry, with heavy routines compiled just in time for speed. A graphical interface lets users sweep conditions quickly. In a demonstration on a photoevaporating flow, chaining many solver runs into a moving one-dimensional model showed water ice lasting far deeper into the flow than a static treatment would suggest.
arxiv-2509-12498:
Quantum field theory in the Euclidean setting rests on probability measures, and building them as limits of finite approximations is a foundational chore. In a solo 2025 paper, the first of a series, Svetoslav Zahariev constructs projective systems of measures for free scalar fields, the simplest case, in two different ways.

One construction is purely combinatorial and covers massless fields living on polyhedral cell complexes, spaces assembled from flat pieces. The second uses a discretized version of the field's covariance and handles massive fields on a compact curved manifold. Projective limits let the discrete systems converge to a continuum theory.
arxiv-2509-12798:
Nenad Petrovic, Lukasz Mazur and Alois Knoll test in 2025 whether large language models can help keep car software systems easy to change over time. Car systems mix many parts and strict rules, so updates, checks, and redesigns take long and cost much.

Three early case studies frame the work: help with updates and rule checks, checks that parts still fit each other, and hints for better system layouts. All three use a leading chat model as a proof of concept. The results point to real help for slow manual steps, while still at an early stage that needs more checks before wide use in cars.
arxiv-2509-12898:
Pedro P. Poblete and 6 co-authors study how uneven radiation shapes disks in binary star systems in a 2025 paper. Models of binary systems often simplify the radiation field, which is unlikely to capture complex asymmetric environments. A young binary has two light sources and a surrounding protoplanetary disk with substructures that affect how light travels.

The team ran three-dimensional hydrodynamical simulations coupled with a Monte Carlo radiative transfer code that computed disk temperatures on the fly. They explored different binary-disk orientations for an eccentric binary and simulated an outburst event with a drastic luminosity increase. Heating from the secondary star inflated the outer disk, raising its aspect ratio on the side facing the companion, more strongly in inclined cases. Results carry implications for disk evolution and chemistry.
arxiv-2509-13098:
Kyu Jung Bae, Arghyajit Datta and two co-authors match two cosmic gaps at once in 2025. EMPRESS data hints at a large electron neutrino gap. The baryon gap is tiny but firm. One source for both was missing.

A supersymmetric charge extension does both jobs. A heavy Higgs field rules the early cosmos. Its rare splits seed heavy neutrinos near the weak shift. Those splits make the baryon gap. Later full decay makes the large lepton gap. Only the normal mass order gives both signs right. Cosmic strings from the break may sing in future wave hunts.
arxiv-2509-13198:
Thanh Nguyen, Alexander Teytelboym and Shai Vardi design in 2025 fair lotteries for indivisible goods with no money. Course seats, food banks, and resettlement all need efficiency without envy. Past designs give one trait before or after the draw, not both.

Random token budgets plus market prices that clear in mean form the core. Prices guide every final draw. All efficient ranked outcomes arise this way, as lotteries over near-feasible efficient draws. Equal budgets give ranked envy freedom. Small budget sets give envy freedom up to one good. Large markets gain a near-efficient, hard-to-game build.
arxiv-2509-13398:
Stephan Troyer, Florian Fechtel and five co-authors cool two rocking modes of a nano rotor to their quantum ground state in 2025. Holding nano objects at the quantum limit opens new tests and sensors. Rocking motion adds rich acts beyond straight trapped motion.

Silica pairs and triples load by laser into an optical tweezer with steady repeat success. Coherent scatter in a fine cavity cools both rocking modes at once to very low counts. Joint cooling aligns rotors to a fixed axis with precision near the zero-point swing. Ground-state rocking is thus in hand for later quantum tests.
arxiv-2509-13498:
Diego Gonzalez-Hernandez, Caitlin Doughty and three co-authors constrain reionization history in 2025 from the Lyman-alpha forest power spectrum with neural emulators plus Hamiltonian sampling. Forest data at high redshift retains thermal and ionization marks of reionization. Forward models are costly to sample directly.

Five hundred low-resolution simulations with user-set histories form the training base. Spectra and covariances feed two emulators with sub-percent errors. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo then estimates parameters efficiently in a JAX frame. Mock tests recover true values reliably. Low resolution limits this run; richer models will sharpen real data constraints next.
arxiv-2509-13898:
Keith Ball, Károly J. Böröczky, and Assaf Naor prove approximate isoperimetry results for convex polytopes in a 2025 geometry paper. The isoperimetric quotient measures how efficiently a shape encloses volume relative to its surface, and spheres win outright. For polytopes, the question is how the best achievable quotient depends on dimension and on the number of facets or vertices.

For polytopes with a given number of facets, they bound the smallest possible quotient between constant multiples of one explicit formula. For symmetric polytopes with a given number of vertices, every such polytope has an affine image whose quotient is within a constant factor of a matching formula, and the bound is sharp. They also prove a weak form of the isomorphic reverse isoperimetric conjecture for polytopes with few facets.
arxiv-2509-14198:
Juan Diego Toscano and four co-authors give a firmer base in 2025 for a common trick in neural solvers of partial differential equations, which are equations for change across space and time. Solvers often focus effort where their error, called the residual, is large, but that choice has mostly rested on habit.

Their framework shows that each weighting choice matches a clear error goal. Weighting that grows fast targets the largest error anywhere, while plain weighting matches squared error. Seeing weighting as a choice of sampling points links it straight to error control. The authors report three gains: cleaner design across error measures, lower error from steadier loss estimates, and better training signals. Tests on operator learning, where a model learns whole solution patterns, showed large gains.
arxiv-2509-14298:
