Justin Lovelace and five co-authors introduce SpeechOp in 2025, a model that turns a text to speech system into a general speech processor. Speech to speech jobs such as cleaning noisy speech lack large training sets. Hungry generative models then distort words or voice identity.

SpeechOp adapts a pre trained speech synthesis model with a diffusion process in a latent space. It can carry out many speech tasks and combine them in new ways at run time. One pipeline uses a transcript from a speech recogniser to guide speech enhancement. Because it inherits rich speech knowledge, training is faster and output quality rises. The system even improved basic text to speech scores in the reported tests.
arxiv-2509-14498:
Alex Nguyen, David J. Schwab and Vudtiwat Ngampruetikorn show in 2025 that throwing away data features can improve a model, if the right features go. Lossy changes lose information by definition, yet pruning and augmentation often help generalisation in practice. The paradox needs a solvable case.

Their solvable model is high dimensional ridge regularised linear regression under data coarse graining. Borrowing renormalisation group ideas from physics, schemes discard features by relevance to the task. Prediction risk varies nonmonotonically with how much is discarded. Keeping high signal features while dropping low signal ones helps, while the reverse hurts. The analysis gives a clean rule: coarse grain away from relevance, never toward it.
arxiv-2509-14898:
Taha El Ghazi and Tatiana Starikovskaya detect repeating patterns in data streams that arrive once and cannot be stored, in a 2025 theoretical computer science paper. Real data is noisy, so repetitions come with mismatches, wildcards, and small edits. Their problem: given a long string, find shifts where the prefix and suffix of matching length are close under a chosen distance.

Earlier streaming work handled Hamming distance, which counts mismatched positions. The authors combine a compact Hamming-distance sketch with a structural description of near-matches between a pattern and a text. The combination yields a leaner streaming method for finding periods under Hamming distance. As a corollary, periods can also be detected when the string contains wildcards, symbols that match anything. The results tighten what streaming algorithms can certify about noisy repetitions.
arxiv-2509-15398:
Mohammad Adarbeh and Mohammad Saleh open a new topic in the algebra of semirings. A semiring is like a ring, but items cannot always be subtracted. Inside such a system, parts called subsemimodules can be studied for special traits. The pair define two new traits, named 1-absorbing prime and its weak form. Each trait sets a rule for when a product lands inside the part.

They prove many facts about the new traits. One key result gives a test for the trait using ideals and parts of the system. A like test covers the weak form for a class of well behaved parts. The paper lays ground work for later studies of these objects. It is aimed at algebra readers.
arxiv-2509-15498:
Zahra Aref and Narayan Mandayam give decision making transformers a kind of memory for each action. These models learn from past runs and pick actions in order. Standard attention, though, does not track how each action has fared over time. That gap makes long term learning about actions less sharp.

The pair borrow from a mind science model in which each choice gains or loses pull based on past outcomes. Their add on keeps a small account for each action, summing recent wins and losses. Smooth actions are routed through a compact codebook to find their account. The module is light and fits into an online version of the model. The aim is steadier learning from trial and error.
arxiv-2509-15998: Petra Schwer asks whether machines will one day solve every math problem, and what doing math really means. Her short essay also asks how mathematicians share their work with each other. She asks what math is beyond the solving of set problems. The piece is a personal attempt to answer those questions, written in plain terms for readers who wonder what the field is for.
arxiv-2509-16198:
Language models write single functions well, but building a whole software repository from a brief remains a hard test. Jane Luo and thirteen co-authors replace free-text planning with a Repository Planning Graph, a blueprint that maps features, files, data flow, and functions in one structure. Their system, ZeroRepo, plans, builds, and then writes code guided by that graph, with tests to check the result.

On a benchmark of six real projects, the system wrote far larger code bases than rival tools. It also covered more of each project and passed more tests. The graph plan scales well and helps agents find their way in large code.
arxiv-2509-16298:
Fuzzy logic needs implication rules, and new rules are often built from old ones by set recipes. Raquel Fernandez-Peralta and Juan Vicente Riera survey and extend one such recipe based on chains of functions. Their wider version draws on whole collections of implication rules and two growth functions, rather than one rule and one chain.

They work out when prized traits survive this building process and give clear conditions for it. Several older recipes, from swapping to threshold tricks, turn out to be special cases of the new frame. That unity reveals hidden kinship among methods that looked unrelated.
arxiv-2509-16398:
In homes and warehouses, people move objects all the time, so a robot that last saw a cup on the counter may find it gone. Francesco Argenziano and four co-authors argue that such moves follow habits that a model can learn. Their FlowMaps model, built on a flow matching method, predicts where an object is likely to be now, across space and time, with several plausible spots.

Tests give statistical support for the habit idea. Finding moved objects more often would cut task failures for service robots. Code for the model is shared in public, opening the way to richer uses.
arxiv-2509-16498:
Rasoul Abazari, working alone, offers a 2025 math paper that rebuilds a classic tool from statistics. In place of plain real numbers, the work uses positive elements from a special class of algebras. That swap lets distribution functions, which track how values spread out, take a more general form.

Distance distribution functions get close attention. With them, Abazari defines a kind of metric space where distance itself is given as a distribution. The paper checks basic traits of such spaces, such as their shape and fixed point results. Examples and uses for integral equations close the study.
arxiv-2509-16598:
Byeongho Yu, Changhun Lee, Jungyu Jin, and Eunhyeok Park aim to cut false claims from chat models in a 2025 paper. One prior trick contrasts a model's final answer with its early, half-formed guesses. The team found those early guesses too flat to help much. They build a sharper contrast by pruning the model itself.

Their method, PruneCD, trims parts of the model to make a weaker twin. The twin's output is then contrasted with the full model's output. That contrast steers decoding toward facts. Tests show steady gains in truthfulness. The extra cost at run time stays small. The approach could be added to many deployed models.
arxiv-2509-16898:
Jingming Yan and co-authors study the cost of finding local optima in contrastive learning in a 2025 theory paper. Contrastive methods place an anchor closer to a matching example than to a non-matching one. Training seeks a spot where small moves no longer help, a local optimum. The team ask whether any fast method can always find such a spot.

Their results say no, under standard complexity beliefs. Reductions show some cases force local search to take exponential time. That holds even for embeddings on a simple line. The work sets a hard limit on what training algorithms can promise for many contrastive problems.
arxiv-2509-16998:
Nishka Khendry, Christos Margadji, and Sebastian W. Pattinson design parts that robots can assemble in a 2025 paper. Design for assembly still leans on manual planning and rigid simulators. Those simulators assume a perfect world model, which factories rarely have. Their frame instead lets a language model design, check its own work, and adapt.

Self-verification sits at the core of the loop. Context-aware adaptation adjusts designs to the setting at hand. Human judges in paired comparisons favored this approach over rivals. The frame shows promise for messy, unstructured manufacturing. Robots that can assemble a part reliably need designs born with assembly in mind.
arxiv-2509-17298:
Xiao-Yue Xu, Chen Ding, and Wan-Su Bao wrote a 2025 arXiv paper on cleaning up measurement errors in quantum computing. Faulty readouts can spoil a run, so mitigation methods twist the measurement with random Pauli steps. That trick turns noise into a simple scale factor, but it can demand a huge number of sample circuits.

Their method, subsystem-balanced Pauli twirling, keeps the Pauli operators balanced on each measured subsystem. That balance wipes out the main error parts while using far fewer random circuits, with the gain largest for sparse observables. For heavy observables, a companion method rewrites them as light effective ones with shallow circuits. Noise from that rewrite is mitigated along with the native readout noise. The result is a path to trustworthy results on larger quantum machines without a sampling bill that explodes.
arxiv-2509-17698:
Michał Horodecki, Michał Studziński, and Marek Mozrzymas build matrix units for a quantum algebra step by step. Their 2025 arXiv paper treats the algebra of partially transposed permutation operators, a matrix form of the walled Brauer algebra. Such bases matter wherever symmetry governs quantum systems, from entanglement theory to representation theory.

Earlier constructions followed a nested Gelfand-Tsetlin pattern. The new basis instead adapts to the action of a product of two symmetric groups, one for each side of the wall. Built that way, the construction presents the algebra as a direct sum of ideals, a decomposition not previously given in full generality. A recursive scheme generates the irreducible matrix units in every ideal, for small systems and any local dimension. The authors apply the machinery to a problem in their field, showing the frame at work beyond pure algebra.
arxiv-2509-17798:
Feodor Svetlanov Konomaev, Mithuss Tharmalingam, and Kjetil M D Hals look for a heat sign of twist in a magnet. Their 2025 paper deals with kagome antiferromagnets, whose spins point in a set, non-straight pattern. The twist, or chirality, shows the hand of that pattern.

When the magnet meets a plain metal, heat can pump spin into the metal. The team finds that an in-plane spin flow shows up for just one twist state. A second flow, out of plane, shifts with field and differs by twist. Such heat tests could spot a twist switch as it happens.
arxiv-2509-17898:
Paul Hamelbeck and Johannes Schiffer certify how much a recurrent net can amplify input noise. Their 2025 paper deals with nets that read data in sequence, used in control tasks where safety counts. A Lipschitz bound caps that gain, so a proved bound gives a safety claim.

Their method, RNN-SDP, turns layer links into a convex maths task and solves it for a bound. Known input limits can be fed in to tighten the bound a bit. Tests on a fake tank system gave bounds close to measured ones. Start-state error stood out as a factor folk often underrate.
arxiv-2509-18098:
Saul Antonio Herrera-Gonzalez and 5 co-authors model graphene stuffed with extra atoms. Their 2025 paper deals with heavy doping by intercalation, where guest atoms slip between carbon sheets. That lift can push the electron sea toward a sharp peak, where linked phases may form.

Guest atoms also bond with carbon and settle into neat super-patterns. Those patterns fold the carbon bands and flatten them near key points. The team builds tight models with values drawn from a standard quantum method. Light response sums from the models mark clear signs of each pattern and bond type.
arxiv-2509-18298:
Some spaces in math are built from simpler pieces layered like a graph. Siddarth Kannan and Terry Dekun Song develop a counting method for such spaces in this 2025 paper. Their focus is moduli spaces, which sort geometric objects like curves and maps into families. The method tracks features that stay fixed under symmetry.

They apply the method to the Deligne-Mumford space, which sorts stable curves, and to a space of maps with a circle symmetry. New formulas come out in each case. A key tool enriches a classic counting polynomial from Pólya, tying it to a ring of wreath product functions. The team shows that ring can be read as a catalog of certain functor types. That view yields an action on ordinary symmetric functions, which drives the final formulas.
arxiv-2509-18598:
Superalgebras blend ordinary algebra with a sign rule, and their representation theory can be intricate. Lauren Grimley and Jonathan R. Kujawa prove a bridge between two such worlds in this 2025 paper. One side is the wreath product of a symmetric group with a superalgebra. The other side is a general linear Lie superalgebra, a matrix-like structure.

Their main result is an equivalence of categories between the supermodules of the two sides. It holds whenever a size parameter clears a stated bound tied to the other parameter. They also give an example showing that bound cannot be improved. Such equivalences let hard questions on one side be answered on the other. The result extends the classic Schur-Weyl pattern into the wreath product super setting. It is a structural result aimed at algebraists.
arxiv-2509-18898:
Blurry photos break the usual pipeline for building 3D scenes, which leans on sharp images to fix camera poses. Pengteng Li and six co-authors present DeblurSplat, a deblurring 3D method that skips that pipeline in this 2025 paper. It is built on 3D Gaussian splatting, a fast scene representation. An event camera, which senses change with extreme timing, joins the capture.

A pretrained stereo module supplies the starting point cloud straight from blurred images, so pose errors never enter. Event streams are then decoded into latent sharp images. Those images supervise the scene rebuild with fine detail. Across varied scenes, the method produced high-fidelity new views. It also rendered more efficiently than top rivals. The authors claim the first pose-free deblurring splatting method of its kind. Sharp 3D from shaky footage is the goal.
arxiv-2509-18998:
Cancer models that simulate how cells move carry many unknown parameters, and fitting them to data is hard. Christina Schenk and two co-authors compare four ways to calibrate such a model with Bayesian methods, which report a range of plausible values for each parameter. The data come from a real experiment on glioblastoma, an aggressive brain cancer, growing in tiny fluid channels.

The four approaches mix two choices: a direct parametric model or a fast surrogate stand-in, each with or without a term for the model's own flaws. Surrogates ran faster and predicted better, while the direct model gave more trustworthy parameter values. Adding a flaw term exposed where the model itself falls short. The comparisons offer practical guidance for anyone fitting complex biological models.
arxiv-2509-19398:
Federated learning across several edge servers can stall when one server becomes a bottleneck. Yun Ji and five co-authors exploit a quirk of real deployments: where two servers' coverage areas overlap, some clients can reach both. Their framework, FedOC, gives those overlapping clients two jobs. As relays, they forward models between neighboring servers in real time. As ordinary clients, they pick which server's model to start from, based on delivery time, quietly fusing information across regions.

Each round, clients train on the earliest model to arrive and return updates. Servers aggregate, relay the result onward, aggregate again with what arrives, and broadcast. No central coordinator is needed for models to spread across the whole system. Experiments show remarkable gains over existing methods. The design suits latency-sensitive edge settings where every round trip counts.
arxiv-2509-19698:
Neural networks that keep learning new tasks can quietly lose the ability to learn at all. Gunbir Singh Baveja, Alex Lewandowski, and Mark Schmidt study that stall through the lens of optimization. Common warning signs, such as curvature rank or gradient size, fail to predict the stall reliably. The authors derive two sharper indicators.

One indicator bounds gradient noise with batch size in view. The other tracks how wildly curvature swings. Merged, they set a per-layer cap on safe step size. A scheduler that respects the cap kept learning alive in their tests. Continual learning matters for systems that must adapt for years, from robots to recommendation engines. Knowing why trainability dies is the first step to preventing it.
arxiv-2509-19898:
Merging drone photos with ground photos builds rich three-dimensional scenes, but matching points across such unlike views is brutal. Jiangxue Yu and five co-authors bridge the gap with rendered in-between views. First, aerial images alone yield a sparse model through structure-from-motion. Then 3D Gaussian splatting renders new views from chosen standpoints.

A viewpoint selection method picks renders that step gradually from air toward ground. Matching features across those stepping stones is far easier than one giant leap. Perspective distortion, the core enemy, is tamed by degrees. City-scale modeling, heritage recording, and disaster mapping all mix air and ground imagery. Reliable matching is the hinge each of those uses swings on.
arxiv-2509-19998:
Deciding whether two group elements are the same up to conjugation is a basic test in group theory. Gemma Crowe and Islam Foniqi solve that conjugacy problem for twisted right-angled Artin groups, a family built from graphs with a twist. Their algorithm is implementable, not just existential. In certain cases it runs in linear time by reduction to a twisted problem in the untwisted family.

The groups are also shown to be biautomatic, which yields a second route to the same decision. Algorithms for conjugacy underpin proposed cryptographic uses of groups and basic classification work. Twisted variants widen the family where answers are known. The authors give both the machine and its guarantee. That pairing is what makes a decidability result usable.
arxiv-2509-20198:
Philipp Erler of TU Wien in Austria and three co-authors wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on visualizing huge terrain scans. Laser scans of whole countries can hold hundreds of billions of points. Just opening such a dataset normally needs hours or days of preprocessing to build detail structures. Their system, LidarScout, removes that wait entirely.

On opening, the system loads a sparse sample of points for an instant overview. It then builds hole-free height maps, starting where the user is looking. When the user zooms in, full-resolution data loads for that region only. Regions left behind drop their raw points but keep the improved height maps as a middle level of detail. The method renders terabytes of compressed data directly, with no preprocessing and no extra disk space. Code and data are publicly available.
arxiv-2509-20398:
Operating systems isolate programs from each other, and Sathvik Swaminathan shows a side door through that wall in a 2025 arXiv paper. When a program touches memory that is not currently mapped, a page fault occurs. The kernel pauses the program while the page is fetched, letting another run. That pause can carry a hidden signal.

Swaminathan builds a covert channel on those pauses. A malicious process encodes secret data in the timing and pattern of faults it triggers. A second process reads the signal, receiving data it should never see. The channel needs no timers and works regardless of hardware brand. Experiments reached a bit error rate under four percent. The work is a security warning: even fault handling, deep in the kernel, can leak information across isolation boundaries.
arxiv-2509-20498:
Even at infinite temperature, a chain of interacting electrons keeps quantum coherence. Catalin Pascu Moca and three co-authors document that persistence in a 2025 arXiv paper on the one-dimensional Hubbard model. Infinite temperature sounds like total disorder, the worst case for quantum effects. The authors compute the single-particle Green's function there with tensor network simulations in Liouville space.

A Chebyshev expansion method in the density matrix formalism gives matching access to spectral functions. Without interactions, their formulas are exact and benchmark the numerics. Turning interactions on splits the sharp spectral peak into two bands tied to hole and doublon excitations. A simple mean-field picture captures that split surprisingly well. At infinite interaction strength, a determinant formula takes over. The spectrum keeps a sharp cosine-like dispersion while excitations spread inside a sub-ballistic light cone.
arxiv-2509-20898:
Cosmologists disagree on how fast the universe expands today, a dispute called the Hubble tension. Tonghua Liu, Shuo Cao, and Jieci Wang probe whether the answer changes with distance in a 2025 paper accepted by Physical Review D. They avoid assuming any specific model of the universe.

The team combines baryon acoustic oscillation data from the DESI survey's second release with cosmic chronometer readings and the Pantheon Plus supernova sample. Gaussian process regression rebuilds the expansion history from the data alone. They extract the Hubble constant at five distinct redshifts, with full covariance between measurements included. If the inferred value drifts with redshift, that drift could point to hidden systematic errors rather than new physics.
arxiv-2509-21598:
Bacteria can compute: their gene networks process chemical inputs into expression patterns. Adrian Ratwatte and 4 co-authors turn that system into a library of maths solvers in a 2025 paper. Past biocomputing used engineered circuits with fixed logic and limited firmness. Their system uses native gene regulatory networks instead. A search algorithm finds functional sub networks for set tasks.

Tasks include identifying Fibonacci numbers and prime numbers, plus multiplication and Collatz step counts. Inputs are chemically encoded, and expression patterns give the outputs. Problem specific sub networks are tested by gene wise and collective perturbation. Lyapunov based firmness analysis evaluates robustness and reliability. Native transcriptional system, the results suggest, can perform diverse mathematical tasks. In short, cells can be read as small math tools that work with the rules of life.
arxiv-2509-21698:
Risk sections of corporate filings matter for oversight, yet no public benchmark tests topic discovery on them. Ying Li and Tiejun Ma present such a benchmark in a 2025 paper. GRAB contains millions of sentences from thousands of 10-K filings. Span grounded labels were produced without manual annotation. FinBERT attention, keyphrase signals, and taxonomy aware matching combine to label sentences.

A risk taxonomy anchors the labels: many terms map to fine grained types nested under five macro classes. Evaluation is reported at the macro level with fixed splits. Metrics include accuracy, macro F1, topic BERTScore, and an entropy based count of effective topics. Classical, embedding based, neural, and hybrid topic models can be compared reproducibly. Data, labels, and code are released.
arxiv-2509-21798:
Reward models grade the answers of large language models, and their grades steer how the models learn to behave. Hongbin Zhang and four co-authors ask whether those graders understand culture. Their 2025 paper builds a benchmark called CARB for the purpose. It covers ten cultures across four areas of cultural life, an area where test data has been scarce.

Grading the top reward models on CARB showed clear gaps in cultural awareness. Scores on the benchmark also tracked how well models did on later multilingual culture tasks. The team found that graders often lean on surface clues instead of real cultural understanding. To fix that, they propose a training method that makes the grader reason like a local. Tests show it cuts the surface-clue problem and improves culture-aware grading.
arxiv-2509-21898:
A model that learns class by class faces a hard problem: new lessons can erase old ones. Zihuan Qiu and six co-authors study that forgetting in this 2025 paper. Even strong methods for class incremental learning trail far behind a model trained with all past data at hand. The authors look at the geometry of that ideal model's solutions for a clue.

They find that ideal solutions stay linked to earlier task optima by straight paths of low loss. Their method, Increment Vector Transformation, uses that fact. During training it periodically moves the model to a reshaped solution that keeps those links alive. A cheap approximation built from diagonal Fisher information makes the move practical. The method plugs into existing systems, with or without stored examples. Across four image benchmarks it lifted strong baselines, in one case by a wide margin, and reduced forgetting.
arxiv-2509-22598:
Katsuhiko Hayashi and Hidetaka Kamigaito prove that a set of classic language classes can be split by a straight line. These classes, called subregular, sit below the regular languages and show up in the sound patterns of human speech. The pair show each such class is linearly separable when a language is coded by the checks that decide it. That trait, finite observability, means simple linear models can learn these classes.

Tests on made-up data confirmed perfect splits when the data held no noise. On real English word-form data, the learned traits matched known rules of the language. The authors argue these classes give a strict, clear base for modeling how natural language is built.
arxiv-2509-22998: Matthew B Hastings builds a sparse chain complex over the field with two elements that has no sparse lift to the integers. The complex has three degrees, so it matches the shape of a quantum code. A lift would rewrite the same structure with integer entries while keeping it sparse. Hastings shows no such lift exists for his example. The result answers a question raised in an earlier reference.
arxiv-2509-23098:
Zero-shot image segmentation leans on vision-language encoders, whose middle layers hide useful bias. Na Min An and 3 co-authors probe those layers for position and language effects. Final-layer embeddings favor global semantic match. That leaves vision codes weakly sensitive to position. Text codes also shift shape by language inside the shared space.

A path through mid-layer features builds a better spatial map. It raised segmentation scores on nine RefCOCO benchmarks. Mixing languages in mid-layer embeddings lifted grounding further, at extra compute cost. The same trick helped zero-shot text-to-image retrieval. The team urge more probing of representational bias.
arxiv-2509-23198:
A printed forehead patch that fools face recognition in the real world is the threat here. Andrey Kaznacheev and 4 co-authors built GaP under a strict black-box setting. Their greedy, query-light algorithm adds Gaussian blobs one by one. The symmetric gray pattern grows to maximally degrade identity match scores. Only similarity scores from a surrogate model guide the search.

Roughly ten thousand black-box queries to an ArcFace model shaped the patch. Attack success ran high in both digital and physical tests. The patch also fooled an unseen FaceNet model, which shows strong transfer. The team frame it as a practical, severe vulnerability.
arxiv-2509-23398:
Sixth-generation networks will be too varied and fast-changing for management by fixed rules. Tuğçe Bilen and Mehmet Özdem propose a knowledge-defined, twin-assisted architecture for that job. Digital twins mirror the physical network from live streams. The twins also forecast short-term state changes. A knowledge plane builds a graph view and drafts context-aware intents.

Graph neural reasoning supports the intent drafting. The management plane matches intents to pre-learned actions by semantic embedding, with no retraining. A closed loop refines forecasts, knowledge, and policies over time. Simulations show better response time and service agreement compliance. Intent matching accuracy also improved.
arxiv-2509-23798:
Splitting a beam of atoms by their internal spin opens a route to delicate phase measurements. Igor Kuzmenko and 2 co-authors propose such a beam splitter built on spin-dependent optical standing wave potentials. The device sorts the atoms while also letting users manipulate the spin state of the atoms in each output beam. That dual control is the paper's central claim, stated as a proposal.

The authors show one use: measuring the Aharonov-Casher phase of atoms in a constant, uniform electric field. Reading that phase would in turn give the strength of the field. The work is theoretical, presenting the design and its intended application.
arxiv-2509-23898:
Pruning a neural network by group sparsity is principled but clashes with the gradient descent everyone actually uses. Chris Kolb and 3 co-authors propose D-Gating, a differentiable stand-in for structured penalties. Each group of weights splits into a main vector and several scalar gates. The authors prove that any local minimum under D-Gating is also a local minimum of the non-smooth structured penalty problem.

They also show the gated objective converges at least exponentially fast to the penalized loss in the gradient flow limit. Learning starts dense and slides into sparsity on its own. Across vision, language, and tabular tasks, the method delivered strong performance-sparsity trade-offs.
arxiv-2509-24098:
Luc Ta compares two ways to build invariants, quantities that can tell three-dimensional spaces apart. One way uses groups, the classic algebraic tool. The other uses risandles, nonassociative structures brought in recently for this purpose, in analogy to the quandles used for knots.

Ta shows the two routes match at a deep level: the category of groups and the category of nonempty, faithful risandles are equivalent. He also defines a fundamental risandle for a space, which encodes the coloring invariants of Ishii, Nakamura, and Saito. For infinitely many spaces, the match lets one recover the fundamental group from the fundamental risandle, and the reverse as well.
arxiv-2509-24298:
What people say about their feelings may predict brain activity worse than what machines infer from watching the same scenes. Changde Du and 6 co-authors test that idea with millions of triplet judgments from AI models on thousands of emotional videos. The models picked the odd one out, and patterns in their choices formed a thirty-part emotion space.

That space proved readable and mostly organized feelings by category, blended with graded traits. The multimodal model's space predicted activity in human emotion networks best, beating a text-only model and even ratings from humans themselves. Sensory grounding, the authors argue, is key to concepts that match the brain.
arxiv-2509-24398:
Classic game theory assumes every player knows all strategies on the table, but real people differ in what they know. Feipeng Zhang and 3 co-authors study evolutionary hypergames, where players may hold different views of the strategy set. Their model uses three strategies, cooperation, defection, and loner, which dominate each other in a cycle like rock-paper-scissors.

Across well-mixed and spatial lattice populations, the team tracks how strategy sets themselves learn and evolve. Rich phases appear that classic dynamics miss: loner dominance, coexisting strategy sets, and mixes of cooperation with loner play. One clear finding stands out: stronger rationality markedly promotes cooperation.
arxiv-2509-24498:
Mini-games inside WeChat get cloned to rival platforms, and the JavaScript that runs them needs scrambling at industrial scale. Zhihao Li and 14 co-authors built JSProtect, a parallel obfuscation framework for that job. Existing tools were too slow, bloated the code hugely, or wrecked runtime speed on large codebases.

Its core algorithm analyzes scope in a parallel-aware way, splitting code for multi-core work and reusing short names to fight bloat. In tests it processed huge codebases in minutes with full semantic equivalence kept. Size growth stayed near a fifth, against over tenfold for baselines, and runtime stayed near native. Security held up against static tools and language models alike.
arxiv-2510-00098:
Marco Costa and three colleagues wrote this 2025 cosmology paper asking whether dark matter feels extra forces. Some sky surveys hint that cosmic structure grew more than the standard model predicts. A light particle carrying a force between dark matter particles might explain that extra growth. The team tested whether the simplest such models really do boost structure.

Their answer is no, and the reason lies in how the early universe fixes the model. Any faster clustering is cancelled by faster thinning of the dark matter background. Matching the microwave background data then forces more dark energy, which slows growth further. Heavy carrier particles make growth slower still, since they add matter that does not cluster. The paper warns that claims of boosted growth must reckon with these background effects first.
arxiv-2510-00298:
Changjie Lu and three colleagues published this 2025 paper on measuring medical image quality by the task at hand. A restored scan matters only insofar as a reader can act on it correctly. Classic scores judge pixel fidelity, not whether a lesion can be spotted. The authors test a newer quantity, predictive V-information, as a task-specific quality metric.

V-information measures how much usable information an image holds for a stated family of observers. Unlike ideal-observer measures, it credits only information a real, limited observer can exploit. The team applied it to a stylized magnetic resonance image restoration problem. The metric tracked the area under the ROC curve on binary detection tasks. It also kept discriminating in regimes where conventional metrics had already saturated. Since it extends naturally to multi-class tasks, the authors offer it as a complement to detection theory scores.
arxiv-2510-00398:
Dmitry Dolgopyat, Spencer Durham, and Minsung Kim wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on random walks over nilmanifolds. A nilmanifold is a compact space built from a nilpotent group, a structured kind of symmetry group. A random walk steps by random translations, and rapid mixing means it spreads to uniform quickly. The authors ask how typical that fast spreading is for such spaces.

They prove rapid mixing for almost all random walks generated by enough translations on any nilmanifold. Mild assumptions on the number of generators make the theorem run. For several classical families of nilmanifolds, just two generators already suffice. The result gives a partial answer to a standing question about how common rapid mixing is on homogeneous spaces. Mixing rates matter wherever random walks serve as algorithms or models of diffusion. This paper widens the map of spaces where fast mixing is the rule, not the exception.
arxiv-2510-00798:
Jahan and Neog compare three global parton distribution function sets in this 2025 arXiv paper on quantum chromodynamics. Parton distributions describe how a proton's momentum is shared among its quarks and gluons, and nearly every LHC prediction depends on them. Because the distributions are non-perturbative, they cannot be calculated directly and must be fitted to worldwide scattering data. Different fitting groups make different choices, so their sets disagree in informative places.

The authors evaluate gluon distributions and proton structure functions from CT14, MMHT2014, and NNPDF 4.0 across wide ranges of momentum fraction and energy scale. They discuss where the sets agree and where they diverge, especially for the gluon at small momentum fractions. Comparing fitted structure functions against measurements tests QCD itself at those scales. The authors stress that such comparisons keep LHC cross-section predictions honest, which matters for new-particle searches.
arxiv-2510-00898:
Balogh, Tajkov, Nemes-Incze, and Koltai model correlation-driven magnetism in multilayer graphene in this 2025 arXiv preprint. Graphene stacked in the rhombohedral ABC pattern hosts a magnetic ground state at charge neutrality, making it one of the simplest homes for strong electron correlations. The authors use a Hubbard model within a distance-dependent tight-binding framework to study how stacking and strain shape the magnetic moments across three to eight layers.

A single universal Hubbard U value reproduced the spin polarization predicted by costly hybrid density functional calculations for both ABC and hexagonal ABA stackings. Mixed stacks kept their magnetic structure robustly, with moments near an ABC-ABA interface recovering within about two layers. Pressure increased the moments by squeezing layers closer, while uniaxial stretching enlarged them and compression shrank them in their calculations.
arxiv-2510-01098:
Bordelon, Letey, and Pehlevan, at Harvard, derive scaling laws for in-context regression in this 2025 arXiv paper on transformer theory. In-context learning lets a transformer solve a new regression task from examples in its prompt, with no weight updates. How performance depends on width, depth, context length, and training time was unclear. The authors analyse a deep linear self-attention model in a limit where dimension, context, and width grow proportionally.

They solve three settings exactly: isotropic tasks, fixed structured covariance, and randomly rotated structured covariance. Depth helped only when context length was limited in the first two settings. In the rotated setting, depth improved performance significantly even at infinite context length. The solvable model yields exact risk asymptotics and power laws, and it predicts an optimal transformer shape for a given compute budget.
arxiv-2510-01198:
Mandelbrod and co-authors decide which little persuasion badges deserve space on eBay's most visited page. Signals are short text or visual snippets that add context to a listed item and nudge engagement. Each slot on the view-item page admits only certain candidates, so assignment is a ranking problem.

Two statistical modeling approaches were built to populate the page optimally. Both survived live A/B tests against the production system. The winning estimator lifted gross merchandise volume and organic revenue significantly. Engagement rose across the whole funnel, from first impressions to final purchases. Hundreds of millions of daily impressions make small lifts worth fortunes. Urgency and conversational snippets illustrate the signal styles in play. Retrospective learning from past outcomes drives one of the two models. Mid-funnel actions, like adding to cart, moved as well. Placement constraints keep the optimization honest at scale.
arxiv-2510-01298:
Demirel and co-authors generate synthetic cell images that respect real biology closely enough to stand in for experiments. Simulating how cells respond to drugs or gene edits could speed discovery enormously. Their diffusion model, MorphGen, produces the full set of fluorescent channels jointly instead of squashing them into ordinary color images.

An alignment loss ties the generator's internal features to a biological foundation model's embeddings. Organelle-level detail survives, which coarser generators sacrifice. Standard cell-profiling features confirmed the images behave like real ones. Image quality beat the previous best generator by a wide margin on the standard score. Six fluorescent channels are generated together in the final system. A large public drug-response dataset supplied the training scale. Multiple cell types and perturbations test controllability, not just realism. High-content assays are the expensive experiments being simulated. Biological faithfulness is graded, not assumed.
arxiv-2510-01498:
Ou and co-authors synthesize contrast-enhanced scans of aortic aneurysms from plain scans while segmenting the vessel in the same model pass. Contrast dye endangers kidneys, triggers allergies, and harms the environment, yet aneurysm assessment depends on enhanced imaging. Pipelines that generate then segment accumulate errors and ignore shared anatomy.

Their unified diffusion framework optimizes synthesis and segmentation jointly, end to end. Shared encoder and decoder parameters let the tasks teach each other. Semi-supervised training exploits scans whose labels are missing, a chronic clinical scarcity. An aorta-focused strategy with background fusion repairs misaligned training pairs. Lumen and thrombus segmentation ride inside the same diffusion process. No coarse initial mask is required, unlike earlier multitask models. Joint optimization beat the sequential pipeline on both tasks. Annotation scarcity is the clinical reality the training scheme respects. Contrast avoided is risk avoided.
arxiv-2510-01798:
Bernal-Arencibia and three co-authors improve automatic smoothing of noisy data in this 2025 paper. The Eilers-Whittaker smoother balances fidelity to data against curve smoothness through one parameter. Choosing that parameter by hand is impractical for large datasets. Common automatic rules, like leave-one-out cross-validation, stumble when the noise is correlated over time.

Their rule reads the spectral entropy of the residuals left after smoothing. They build an S-curve from distances in a plot comparing residual entropy with signal entropy. The parameter at the curve's absolute peak becomes their choice. On simulated data with known truth, the method beat cross-validation and the V-curve method. Its picks stayed closer to the error-minimizing parameter, even at high noise levels. Tests on varied experimental data supported the same conclusion. The procedure is simple and robust enough for everyday analysis pipelines.
arxiv-2510-02198:
Chalker and Hahn reduce chaotic quantum energy flow to a classical diffusion story in this 2025 physics paper. Their model is a minimal many-body system with spatial structure and local interactions, governed by one fixed Hamiltonian. In the tractable limit of large local Hilbert spaces and weak coupling between sites, exact results become possible. Energy dynamics there obey a classical master equation and spread diffusively.

The spectral form factor, a standard diagnostic of quantum chaos, comes out exactly from that same master equation's solution. For a two-site system, closed forms for the energy correlator and the form factor match numerical simulations almost perfectly. In longer chains, the universal linear ramp of chaotic level statistics emerges at late times. Earlier growth of the form factor splits into two distinct mechanisms, which the authors identify. Diffusion, a classical idea, turns out to organize the quantum spectrum itself.
arxiv-2510-02698:
Iyengar, Ma, and Walker prove that special modules exist for a large class of two dimensional local rings. Their 2025 algebra paper concerns Ulrich modules. Such modules sit at an extremal edge of module theory. Earlier work by the same authors found rings admitting none. Complete intersection domains of dimension two were the counterexamples. The new paper maps the positive side of the border. A large class of dimension two rings does admit them. Blow-up geometry at the closed point drives the proof. The existence statement comes with a sharp application.

Module lengths gain a universal lower bound. Any nonzero module of finite projective dimension is long enough. Its length at least matches the ring's multiplicity. Existence questions shape homological conjectures broadly. Dimension two is the testing ground where patterns emerge. The border between existence and failure is now clearer. Commutative algebra gains a firmer map of this terrain.
arxiv-2510-02798:
Ozaki introduces OptunaHub, a community platform that collects black-box optimization methods and benchmarks. His 2025 software paper serves the optimization community. Black-box methods power AutoML and materials informatics work. Research stays fragmented across separate domains today. OptunaHub centralizes methods behind unified Python APIs. A contributor registry packages methods for reuse. A web interface makes the catalog searchable. Anyone can publish a package to the hub. The code lives openly under the Optuna organization.

Users gain one shelf for methods and benchmarks. Contributors gain a broader audience for their work. Cross-domain borrowing becomes easier by design. The authors commit to growing the platform steadily. A virtuous cycle is the stated goal. Good packages attract users, who then contribute back. Shared infrastructure speeds fields that rarely talk. Optimization knowledge compounds when it stops hiding.
arxiv-2510-02898:
Bianchi and co-authors caption images one patch at a time. Zero-shot captioners describe images without paired training examples. Most of them read the whole image as one blob. That blocks captions for small or odd-shaped regions. Their framework, Patch-ioner, treats each image patch as a basic unit. Captions for any region are built by joining patch captions. No region-level labels are needed at any point.

The team checked which parts make latent captioners work. Dense visual features proved to be the key ingredient. Backbones like DINO supply those rich local features. One forward pass can then caption many regions at once. Tests covered dense captioning and region-set captioning. A new task, trace captioning, joined the list. Patch-ioner set the best scores on those regional tasks. The gap between local and global reading, though, clearly shrank.
arxiv-2510-03298:
Zheng and Fu present a 2025 arXiv paper on training language models across many small devices without draining them. Their method, CAFL-L, extends the common FedAvg approach used in federated learning. Phones and watches have tight limits on energy, memory, heat, and data transfer. Standard training often ignores those limits and fails on real hardware. CAFL-L treats each limit as a budget that training must respect at all times.

The system adjusts settings like batch size and frozen layers as budgets change. It also keeps the total training text steady, so learning stays stable. In tests with a small character level model, CAFL-L cut memory use by about a fifth compared with FedAvg. Data sent between devices fell by about ninety-five percent in the same tests, while accuracy stayed close. That trade could make on-device learning far more practical for everyday gadgets.
arxiv-2510-03598:
Mantzaris presents a 2025 arXiv paper testing whether the Hierarchical Reasoning Model, a recurrent reasoner, can classify images without data augmentation. The model pairs a slow planning module with a fast execution module and trains with deep supervision. He ran it on MNIST digits and on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 photo sets under raw conditions. A two stage convolutional network served as the baseline under the training recipe.

On MNIST the reasoning model scored about ninety eight percent, close to the baseline. On CIFAR-10 it reached sixty five percent while the convolutional net reached about seventy seven percent and trained thirty times faster per pass. On CIFAR-100 it memorized the training set but scored under thirty percent on images. The baseline managed about forty five percent there. Optimization stayed healthy, so the gap reflects missing bias, not failed training. Reasoning architectures need vision structure before they can replace convolutional designs.
arxiv-2510-03698:
Arana and Stehlík present a 2025 arXiv paper characterizing when the Lovász complex of a graph forms a surface. The Lovász complex, a relative of the neighborhood complex, carries a two fold symmetry. Quadrangulations are graphs drawn on surfaces so every face has four sides. The authors link the two notions: under assumptions, the complex is a surface exactly when the graph quadrangulates the complex's quotient space, with every four cycle bounding a face.

That equivalence yields a classification of Lovász complexes for quadrangulations. As an application, the paper revisits a result about chromatic numbers of quadrangulations by Archdeacon and Mohar and Seymour. The new statement is stronger, phrased through the Z2 index of the complex. Topological bounds on coloring are powerful but mysterious to graph theorists. Pinning down the case gives the theory a foothold. Classification results tell which graphs realize which surfaces.
arxiv-2510-03998:
Yu and Zagula present this 2025 arXiv paper on fairer grading for group projects in computer science classes. Group projects teach teamwork and real development skills, but grading each student's contribution fairly is notoriously hard. Equal grades reward free riders, while peer reviews carry bias and social pressure. The authors build a semi-automated system that judges both the project and each member's effort from objective records.

The system mines code repositories and communication logs, then applies machine learning models to score contributions. It plugs into platforms like GitHub that classes already use. Modules handle project evaluation, contribution analysis, and final grade computation. A pilot run in a senior-level course matched instructor judgments closely. Students reported higher satisfaction, and instructors spent less effort on grading. The authors discuss ethical concerns and plan support for non-code contributions. Their design aims for grades that are transparent, explainable, and fair.
arxiv-2510-04198:
Singh and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on single-photon emitters formed where a one-atom-thick semiconductor meets semiconductor nanowires. Monolayer tungsten diselenide hosts localized quantum emitters created by strain, making them candidates for on-demand single-photon sources. Pick-and-place transfer lets researchers marry such emitters to photonic structures. The team transferred a WSe2 monolayer onto horizontally aligned indium phosphide nanowires and studied the resulting hybrid.

Photoluminescence measurements revealed multiple narrow, bright emission peaks in the deep-red to near-infrared range, roughly seven hundred fifteen to seven hundred eighty-five nanometers. Photon correlation measurements dipped far below the classical threshold, confirming strong antibunching and good single-photon purity. Emitters could be placed on the top facet for optimal coupling into photonic circuits. Integrated quantum photonics needs exactly such deterministic, couplable light sources.
arxiv-2510-04298:
Zhu and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on a first-principles simulation framework for interpreting Thomson scattering signals from inertial confinement fusion plasmas. Thomson scattering infers plasma conditions from light scattered by electrons, but driven ion waves and imperfect experimental geometry complicate the spectrum. The authors use particle-in-cell simulations to calculate ion acoustic features with high resolution in angle and frequency under representative fusion conditions. Their approach follows the plasma dynamics directly rather than relying only on an assumed density spectrum.

In the super-thermal collective regime, agreement requires plasma modes whose wave vectors match the probe and collection beams. More surprisingly, significant signals persist under imperfect matching, contrary to the conventional expectation that the spectrum simply tracks density fluctuations. The authors attribute the extra signal to a beating wave created when the probe interacts with driven density modulations.
arxiv-2510-04398:
Buyun Liang and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on tricking AI chat models into making up false claims. Older attacks often stuff prompts with gibberish or change what the prompt means. Such tricks say little about how false claims arise in normal use. The team built SECA, an attack that rewrites a prompt in a way that keeps its meaning and reads smoothly. The goal is to find realistic prompts that still push a model into error.

SECA treats the search as a constrained puzzle over possible wordings of the prompt. A search method that needs no access to model internals finds good rewrites while respecting the limits. In tests on open ended quiz questions, SECA caused false answers far more often than rival methods. It did so with almost no breaks of its own meaning and coherence rules.
arxiv-2510-04498:
Qiao Wang and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on a story game that teaches English. Learners of a second language gain words fastest when reading feels like play, not drill. Fixed story games cannot adapt to a learner level or interests, though. The team built GenQuest, a text adventure whose story is generated live by a large language model. Players steer the plot through choices, in a choose your own adventure style.

Branching decision points and story milestones keep the tale coherent while the player drives it. The text is tailored to each learner level of proficiency as the game runs. A vocabulary assistant explains any word, phrase, or sentence the player clicks, in context. A five day pilot with university learners of English in China showed gains in vocabulary. Students also rated the game as useful and easy to use. The study suggests such stories can support language learning.
arxiv-2510-04598:
Pierre Louis Giscard, Omid Faizy, and Christian Bonhomme wrote this 2025 paper on new frames for computing quantum evolution. The evolution operator of a quantum system solves a differential equation that resists treatment. Series expansions give approximations, and their error shrinks with each order. A change of frame can speed that shrinking, but frames gain only modestly. The team defines frames, and studies one called the biframe above all.

In the biframe, the system evolution is viewed as an equal blend of two standard frames at once. Every series expansion then converges quadratically faster than in frames, at the same cost per order. An error that fell like a power now falls like that power squared. The biframe is one member of an infinite family the paper constructs. Stronger members accelerate more, yet they cost more to set up at the start. Users thus trade setup effort against run time gains.
arxiv-2510-04798:
Mengjia He wrote this 2025 paper on speeding up the design of control pulses for quantum spins. Magnetic resonance tools steer spins with shaped radio pulses, and finding good pulses is an optimization problem. The standard solver, GRAPE, computes gradients well but slows down on realistic models with many spins. He combines tools into a method called FEMMA. The finite element method rewrites the spin evolution equation as a linear system by treating time steps like space.

Gradients then come out more than ten times faster than with GRAPE. The accuracy cost stays under one percent in relative terms. A second ingredient, the method of moving asymptotes, sharpens how the search converges. It beat a popular quasi Newton method and nearly matched Newton efficiency. Newton methods turn costly when time steps number in the hundreds, so the shortcut matters. Faster pulse design helps imaging and spectroscopy groups iterate on hardware limits.
arxiv-2510-04898:
Xiong and five coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on making robot brains fast enough to run on machines. Vision language action models read camera views and instructions and output motions. They generalize well, but running the model for every motion is costly. The authors propose HyperVLA, which splits the system in two. A hypernetwork reads the task once and generates a policy tuned to it.

Only that policy runs during control, so inference stays. Training a split system is tricky, and the paper adds three fixes. It reuses knowledge from pretrained vision models, normalizes the hypernetwork, and shapes how actions are produced. Against an open model, the activated parameter count fell ninety fold. Inference ran one hundred twenty times faster. Success rates matched or beat the model on tasks with no training. Few shot adaptation to tasks held up. Inference decides whether generalist robots leave the lab for warehouses and homes.
arxiv-2510-04998:
Daniel Majaess challenges a key anchor of the cosmic distance ladder in this 2025 arXiv paper. Astronomers measure distances with Cepheid stars, whose brightness pulses in a known pattern. The galaxy NGC4258 anchors many of those measurements. Majaess argues that its Cepheid data carry larger errors than the leading SH0ES program admits.

He compares the SH0ES team's 2016 and 2022 datasets for the same galaxy. Two versions of the Cepheid brightness relation disagree, one by about 0.3 magnitudes in his analysis. Dust extinction laws add further uncertainty, above all for reddened stars. He also reports wrong photometry for Small Magellanic Cloud Cepheids in the 2022 database. Together, he says, the Hubble constant from this anchor deserves fresh scrutiny.
arxiv-2510-05298:
Donovan Snyder builds a new random process out of pure algebra in this 2025 arXiv paper. Hopf algebras often hide Markov chains inside their squaring map. Famous examples include card shuffling and rock breaking. Snyder works with a quantum group that is neither commutative nor cocommutative, a case earlier work had not reached.

He constructs the resulting one-dimensional Markov chain explicitly. Standard tools fail here, so he turns to martingale theory instead. The analysis proves the chain has a genuine phase transition. It also bounds the chain's expected growth rates on each side of that transition. The work extends the Diaconis, Pang, and Ram program to wilder algebraic territory.
arxiv-2510-05498:
Kayan and Zhang present a light way to make language models reason better at test time. Most steering methods apply one fixed nudge to a model's inner states for every input. Such one-size methods cannot adapt to the needs of each new problem. Their 2025 method, called PDS, builds a custom nudge for each input instead.

The team first clusters the inner changes that step-by-step reasoning creates inside the model. Those clusters become prototypes, or model patterns of different reasoning styles. For a new input, the model's state is matched against the prototypes to form its steering signal. Tests on math and reasoning benchmarks showed steady accuracy gains. Gains held even when visible step-by-step text was switched off for cost savings. The method needs no fine-tuning and no prompt engineering from the user. It strengthens hidden reasoning rather than changing surface behavior.
arxiv-2510-05798:
Bufalino and colleagues audit whether software bills of materials actually agree across tools. Regulations now require vendors to share SBOMs listing every component inside software. Container images bundle operating system packages with far-reaching security impact. Their 2025 study compares generation and scanning tools, open-source and commercial.

The tools prove largely incompatible with each other in practice. Mixing one tool's SBOM with another's scanner produces inaccurate vulnerability reports. Many real vulnerabilities go undetected through this format mismatch. The authors name the failure mode the SBOM confusion vulnerability. A common package index let the team quantify the discrepancies precisely. Tools also inflate counts by flagging irrelevant packages as vulnerable. A converter they built, sbomvert, translates formats to restore interoperability. Alleged compliance, the paper argues, is not the same as security. Linux base images concentrate the risk because everything builds on them.
arxiv-2510-05898:
Sridharan and Vignesh extend the containment problem from groups to topological subgroupoids. Hulanicki's test links nearness of actions to amenability for groups. The subgroupoid setting allows far richer symmetries. Their 2025 paper introduces weak containment directly in that setting.

They prove a Hulanicki-style analogue linking weak containment to amenability. A continuous induction step carries group data into subgroupoid data. Weights along each orbit enter the proof, letting orbit structure shape the bound. The two notions split for transitive groupoids, unlike in the classical group case. Restricting to smaller subgroupoids preserves weak containment. Relative amenability and invariant means get matching mirror descriptions. The measured setting gets the same treatment. A clean framing for measured groupoids results. The work gives the containment toolkit a topological home.
arxiv-2510-06498:
Colin Vendromin, Samuel Fontaine, and John Sipe study a way to make unusual states of light inside tiny ring-shaped devices. Their 2025 paper models spontaneous parametric down-conversion in rings made of indium gallium phosphide. In that process, one photon splits into two photons with lower energy. The team asks when the light stops behaving in the usual smooth Gaussian way.

Their model adds a phantom channel to account for light lost through scattering inside the ring. With realistic settings, the model reaches a regime where the pump light becomes strongly depleted. The leftover state then shows Wigner negativity, a clear sign of non-Gaussian behavior, with a volume of about 0.18 recorded in the tests. Strong squeezing hides those features in the full state, though. The authors show that an inverse operation can strip away most squeezing and reveal the hidden features when losses stay low.
arxiv-2510-06998:
Martin Wilhelm, Franz Freitag, Max Tzschoppe, and Thilo Pionteck build a testbed for judging fast runtime forecasts on mixed hardware. Their 2025 paper serves mixed computing, where CPUs and GPUs share an application's tasks. Choosing which task runs where needs the total run time, the makespan. Full simulators are exact but need finished code, which is slow to write for custom logic chips.

Formula-based forecasts are fast but drift from reality. It scores such forecasts on real systems using apps built at random. Tests suggest rough forecasts often suffice to rank task mappings well. That ranking, not exact timing, is what mapping tools need. Streaming units make the call harder, since task links and run order affect each other. Changing the task graph's chunk size also shifted total times by a lot. The testbed gives builders solid feedback early. Better forecasts mean better mappings without months of test runs.
arxiv-2510-07298:
Buzet and Chailloux formalize measurements that sometimes answer with certainty and never lie. Their 2025 paper studies unambiguous measurements in quantum information. Such tools serve key distribution and state reconstruction. They also power recent quantum algorithms built on a famous reduction by Regev. The task there is to recover coordinates of a hidden code word from a noisy quantum state. The authors ask how many exact parity facts about the hidden word one measurement can deliver.

For symmetric state families, they turn that question into a linear program. Solving it gives the maximum number of parities any unambiguous measurement can return. The framework supplies the theory that earlier algorithmic work lacked. It tells algorithm designers exactly how much certain information is extractable per measurement. That bound guides how many state copies a decoding scheme must consume.
arxiv-2510-07698:
Cleveland, Nelson, and Jossou wrote this 2025 review on chromium-doped uranium dioxide, a candidate nuclear fuel. Power reactors mostly burn uranium dioxide pellets. Adding a trace of chromium oxide changes how the pellets form and behave. The fuel is a leading near-term accident tolerant design. The authors gather decades of industry and academic research and judge where the evidence is strong or weak.

Larger grains after firing are the fuel's signature trait, and they trap fission gas better. The review argues that chromium enters the lattice by substitution, which governs how much can dissolve. A liquid chromium oxide phase at grain boundaries explains the grain growth during sintering. Redox chemistry under set oxygen conditions explains the faster uranium diffusion instead. Uneven chromium spread across the microstructure remains a key gap. The authors point to new spectroscopy studies and modeling work that could close it.
arxiv-2510-08398:
Zeqing Wang and co-authors build VideoVerse in a 2025 arXiv paper, a benchmark that tests video generators as world models. Text-to-video tools now make sharp, smooth clips, so old benchmarks can no longer separate top models. Pretty frames and temporal consistency say little about real understanding. Event-level causality and world knowledge, the heart of world models, went largely untested.

VideoVerse collects videos across domains like nature, sports, indoor scenes, and science experiments. Annotators turned event descriptions with built-in temporal causality into text prompts for generators. Each prompt carries binary questions probing ten defined dimensions of dynamic and static traits. The final set holds three hundred carefully curated prompts, the authors report. The benchmark asks whether a generator grasps what causes what over time. It also checks broad world knowledge that plausible videos require.
arxiv-2510-08498:
Riadh Bouslimi and co-authors generate radiology reports for traumatic brain injuries with an AI model in a 2025 arXiv paper. Head trauma cases flood emergency rooms, and fast scan reading shapes patient outcomes. Their model reads CT and MRI scans and writes a diagnostic report automatically. A feature network called AC-BiFPN extracts details at several scales from each image.

Multi-scale extraction helps catch fine anomalies like intracranial hemorrhages, bleeding inside the skull. A Transformer then writes coherent reports, using attention to link findings across the scan. The team evaluated the model on the RSNA Intracranial Hemorrhage Detection dataset. It beat traditional convolutional models on both diagnostic accuracy and report quality, they report. Beyond speed for radiologists under pressure, the system gives trainee physicians real-time feedback. The authors frame it as support for clinical decisions, not a replacement.
arxiv-2510-08598:
Yingche Liu and Mengyang Li map a city's social divides from bike-sharing trips in a 2025 arXiv paper. Megacities like Shanghai generate massive mobility footprints through shared bikes. The authors ask whether daily travel patterns can quantitatively reveal underlying economic stratification. Fine-grained socio-economic data is notoriously hard to obtain, so they enriched the mobility data instead.

They annotated two thousand raw bike trips with local economic attributes using a language-model-based enrichment method. Built environment features were integrated into the same data set. A Random Forest model then ranked which factors govern the link between mobility and economic status. Housing prices, the proxy for neighborhood wealth, dominated all geographic and temporal factors. Three patterns followed: resources cluster in affluent areas, poorer zones ride from necessity while richer zones ride flexibly, and adoption follows an inverted U-shape.
arxiv-2510-08798:
Rafiuddin and Khan present a way for language models to forget most of a long document on purpose, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Standard attention makes a model compare every word with every other word, so cost and memory balloon as texts grow. Their method, Adaptive Retention, learns which words are worth keeping at each layer of the model. A strict global budget caps how many can stay.

Small probabilistic gates decide each word's fate during training, using a soft relaxation that keeps the choice trainable. At run time a simple rule keeps only the top scorers under the budget. Keeping just thirty to fifty percent of the words preserved nearly all of the full model's accuracy across classification, question answering, and long-document summary tests. Peak memory fell by roughly a third or more, and processing ran notably faster.
arxiv-2510-08898:
Das, Deepawansa, and Lahiri map poverty in fine geographic detail while counting its several faces at once, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Income alone misses much of what poverty means, from schooling to basic services. Estimating any poverty measure for small areas is already hard, because surveys sample few households there, or none. With several dimensions, a new question appears: how much does each dimension contribute to an area's overall poverty?

The team answers with a layered statistical model fitted by Bayesian methods, which borrow strength from census records to steady the small samples. Their method estimates a combined multidimensional poverty score for each area and the share owed to each dimension. They demonstrate it on a purpose-built survey from Sri Lanka's Uva province. The resulting maps give policymakers reliable local estimates and show which deprivations drive poverty in each region.
arxiv-2510-08998:
Birch and colleagues take the first X-ray pictures of magnetic domains inside an unconventional antiferromagnet, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Antiferromagnets hide their order because neighboring spins cancel out, leaving almost nothing for ordinary probes to see. The compound Mn3Sn breaks time-reversal symmetry, though, which lets a certain X-ray effect register its octupole order, a higher pattern of the spin arrangement. The team sliced a tiny device from the material with a focused ion beam.

Scanning X-ray microscopy resolved the domains through a faint signal, about a fifth of a percent in contrast, with sensitivity far finer still. Flipping the magnetic field switched the domains back and forth, and an electrical Hall measurement on the same device switched in step. That agreement confirms the contrast reflects the bulk material, not a surface artifact. They present the method as a general camera for this family of magnets.
arxiv-2510-09298:
Paliwal, Toscano, and Willitsch review how physicists use radiofrequency ion traps as miniature, fully controlled chemistry labs, in this 2025 arXiv paper. An ion trap holds charged atoms or molecules suspended in electric fields for minutes or longer. Inside, nearly every ingredient of a reaction can be dialed in: internal states, collision energy, even exact structure. The review surveys the toolbox, from trapping and cooling to the reactions they enable.

Cooling options include laser cooling in Doppler and resolved-sideband forms, sympathetic cooling by companion ions, and cryogenic buffer gas. States are prepared by internal cooling, optical pumping, selective photoionization, and quantum-logic spectroscopy. Collision energies are tuned through micromotion control, dynamic trapping, and molecular beams, while structure is chosen by isotopic substitution and isomer selection. Such control has exposed state-dependent kinetics, quantum resonances, and structure-sensitive reactivity. Challenges ahead include state-to-state reaction maps and complex chiral systems.
arxiv-2510-09798:
Jordan McCourt and six co-authors measure heat-driven voltage at a hybrid quantum interface in a 2025 arXiv paper. Interfaces between quantum Hall insulators and superconductors are a promising platform for topological quantum computing. They also host confounding effects that can masquerade as the sought-after excitations, so each side effect must be understood.

The team presents measurements of the thermoelectric effect at such an interface, where a temperature difference produces a voltage. They explain the heat transport through a hotspot that forms at the interface. The hotspot creates a non-equilibrium spread of electrons that can cross the superconductor through vortex cores, the tiny normal regions inside it. The resulting voltage changes sign on the quantum Hall plateaus and responds when the vortices rearrange. The authors stress that this interplay of thermal and charge effects must be kept in mind when interpreting transport measurements in similar systems.
arxiv-2510-09898:
Phan, Son Le Vu, and Ali Jannesari study code translation from PyTorch to JAX in this 2025 arXiv paper, which they call T2J. Both libraries build machine learning models in Python, but they differ in core design and in how code runs. JAX is newer, so public JAX code and matched PyTorch-JAX pairs are scarce.

The team focuses on bug context, the details of how translated code goes wrong. Large language models can translate between major languages, yet this pair stays hard for them. By learning from the bugs that appear in translation, T2J aims to make model output more faithful to JAX semantics, the rules that decide what code actually does. Better translation would ease moving projects between the two libraries.
arxiv-2510-10698:
Masoud Seddighin and Saeed Seddighin strengthen a fairness guarantee for dividing chores among people with different entitlements, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Chores are indivisible burdens, the mirror image of goods. The weighted maximin share asks what each agent could guarantee themselves if they partitioned the chores and took the worst bundle, weighted by entitlement. For chores, the best known existence guarantee was a factor growing like the logarithm of the number of agents.

The authors improve that upper bound to a constant. They prove that an assignment achieving a factor of 54/5 of the weighted maximin share always exists, using a layered moving knife algorithm. Variants run in polynomial time, or in almost linear time at a worse constant factor. They also give sharper guarantees for small cases, with factors near 2.06, 2.48, and 2.73 for three, four, and five agents respectively in their analysis.
arxiv-2510-10798:
Juan Antonio Barceló and three co-authors build Hardy spaces for elasticity, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Classical Hardy spaces collect harmonic functions in the unit ball whose sizes stay controlled on concentric spheres. The Lamé system governs elastic deformation, and the authors define its analogue: vector field solutions of the Lamé system satisfying the same integrability condition on spheres. Using the elastic Poisson kernel, they establish a Fatou type theorem about boundary behavior.

They show the elastic Hardy space matches the Lebesgue space of vector fields on the unit sphere for exponents above one, and matches vector valued measures for exponent one. For intermediate exponents, the space splits as a direct sum of three subspaces, each described with its boundary values. Two consist of solutions valid for all eligible Lamé constants: Riesz fields, which solve generalized Cauchy-Riemann equations, and fields built by crossing position with such Riesz fields.
arxiv-2510-10998:
Mahika Phutane and four co-authors audit how language models treat disabled job candidates, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Prior bias research is largely Western centric and rarely asks how disability intersects with gender or caste in the Global South. The team generated 2,820 hiring scenarios across six language models, varying disability, gender, nationality, and caste profiles. To catch subtle harms, they built ABLEIST, a metric set naming five ableism specific harms and three intersectional ones, including tokenism and superhumanization, grounded in disability studies.

The audit found significant increases in ABLEIST harms toward disabled candidates. Many of these harms escaped detection by state of the art safety tools. Intersectional harms rose sharply for candidates who were also gender or caste marginalized, with tokenism a standout. The authors conclude that current safety evaluations have structural blind spots exactly where stakes are high.
arxiv-2510-11198:
In shared wireless networks, freshness matters: a sensor reading is useful only if it arrives soon after it was generated, measured as Age of Information. Georgios Smpokos, Dionysis Xenakis, Marios Kountouris, and Nikolaos Pappas analyze freshness in a cognitive radio network in this 2025 arXiv networking paper. A primary user with bursty traffic shares the channel with secondary transmitters that harvest energy.

The model places the secondary transmitters randomly in space, gives the primary a fixed position. It draws two zones around the primary link: an energy harvesting zone near its transmitter and a guard zone near its receiver where secondary transmissions are banned. Secondary users access the channel probabilistically, depending on their battery state and their position relative to the guard zone. The authors' stated objective is to analyze the primary user's Age of Information performance under three packet management policies.
arxiv-2510-11798:
Shane O'Brien and a large team confirm two giant planets orbiting small red dwarf stars. Such giants, called GEMS, strain standard planet-formation ideas because their stars start with meager building material. Both planets were first spotted by the TESS telescope as they crossed their stars. The team's 2025 arXiv paper adds ground-based photometry and velocity data from the Habitable-zone Planet Finder to prove the planets are real.

TOI-5916 b measures about eleven point eight Earth radii and about two hundred nineteen Earth masses. Its sibling, TOI-6158 b, is a little smaller and lighter. Both have densities close to Saturn's, remarkably fluffy for their size. The authors note that Saturn-like density looks like a growing pattern among GEMS and warm Jupiters generally. They also spot early evidence that GEMS hug their stars closer than giants around Sun-like stars do.
arxiv-2510-11898:
Rayed Suhail Ahmad, Rehan Ahmad, and Quamar Niyaz build a lightweight watchdog for Wi-Fi networks. Home and office Wi-Fi carries sensitive traffic and invites intruders, so spotting hostile packets quickly matters. Their 2025 arXiv paper turns network traffic into two-dimensional pictures and feeds them to convolutional neural networks, the image-recognition workhorses of deep learning. Five different conversion techniques produce the pictures.

The team deliberately chose small, fast network designs so detection keeps a low latency, suiting live deployment. They trained and tested on AWID3, a public benchmark dataset for Wi-Fi intrusion research. The system handled both jobs asked of it: binary detection of attack versus normal traffic, and multi-class sorting of attack types. Results showed competitive detection performance at low inference time. The authors conclude the approach is practical for real-world Wi-Fi settings, where a slow detector is nearly as bad as none.
arxiv-2510-11998:
Luca Santosuosso and Sonja Wogrin speed up the minute-by-minute control of hybrid power plants. Their system chains hydropower dams along a river with wind and solar farms, selling power into the day-ahead market. Inflows, weather, and prices are all uncertain, so the controller plans against many scenarios. That stochastic planning is thorough but slow. Their 2025 arXiv paper redesigns it for real time.

The scheme pairs distributed stochastic model predictive control with time series aggregation. The near future, where accuracy matters most, keeps full detail.
