The far tail of the planning horizon is compressed into aggregated summaries, cutting computation hugely. Optimization is also split across assets and scenarios so pieces solve in parallel. The authors prove formal bounds on the approximation error. A real-world case study shows execution time down forty-two percent against centralized control.
arxiv-2510-12298:
Chalupa, Henzinger, and Oliveira da Costa study how different kinds of quantifiers change the power of logics that reason about many executions, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Hypertrace logic describes hyperproperties, which relate multiple execution traces of a system rather than judging one trace alone. Its formulas keep separate sorts for time points and for traces.

The authors add trace quantifiers that range over all possible traces, separating constrained variables, tied to a fixed set of traces, from free ones that may take any trace. They ask which patterns keep the satisfiability problem decidable. Without constrained trace quantifiers, the logic matches monadic second order logic of one successor and is decidable. The trace prefixed fragment matches the known logic HyperQPTL. Formulas whose only switch between constrained quantifiers goes from an existential to a universal one are also decidable. The framework also yields new decidability and undecidability results for time prefixed hyperlogics.
arxiv-2510-12398:
Fang and Li develop a structure theory for the limit spaces of Ricci flows that do not collapse, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Ricci flow deforms a metric so curvature evens out over time, and it was the engine behind the proof of the Poincaré conjecture. What spaces can arise as limits of such flows is central to geometry.

The authors first prove a weak compactness theorem for this moduli space of closed Ricci flows whose entropy is uniformly bounded. The proof uses pointed Gromov Hausdorff convergence and a natural spacetime distance on each flow. They then analyze the limit spaces themselves. The regular part, where convergence is smooth, has the structure of a Ricci flow spacetime, meaning the limit still behaves like a genuine flow. The singular set, where smoothness fails, has codimension at least four, so singularities are comparatively sparse. These results organize wild limiting geometries.
arxiv-2510-12798:
Jiang and colleagues reframe object detection as next point prediction in this 2025 arXiv paper. Classic detectors such as YOLO and DINO regress box coordinates directly, while recent attempts using multimodal language models suffered low recall, duplicate detections, and misaligned boxes. The team instead asks a language model to point at objects step by step.

Their model, Rex-Omni, has about three billion parameters and writes coordinates as special tokens spanning a quantized grid, which eases learning and saves tokens. They also built data engines, automated pipelines that produce training examples for grounding, referring expressions, and pointing. In zero-shot tests, meaning no task-specific training, Rex-Omni matched or beat strong regression detectors on the COCO and LVIS benchmarks, which the authors offer as a path toward more language-aware visual perception.
arxiv-2510-12998:
Cardenas-Gamboa and co-authors show how to select the handedness of a chiral crystal using light and electric fields in this 2025 arXiv paper. Chiral crystals come in left- and right-handed forms called enantiomers, and choosing between them on demand has been hard. Their materials are layered niobium oxyhalides, compounds whose structure twists in one direction or the other.

Computer simulations from first principles show that optical excitation strains the crystal, an effect called photostriction, and drives it from its low-symmetry ground state into a higher-symmetry structure. In that transient state, an applied electric field breaks the remaining symmetry tie and selectively stabilizes one enantiomer as the crystal settles back. The combined optical-electrical scheme allows reversible, non-contact enantiomer selection, which the authors connect to ultrafast switching, optoelectronics, and chiral information storage.
arxiv-2510-13198:
Xu and co-authors improve camera-based 3D occupancy prediction for self-driving in this 2025 arXiv paper. It infers the complete three-dimensional geometry and semantics of a scene from ordinary two-dimensional images. Most methods chase gains through structural tweaks such as lighter backbones or cascaded pipelines, leaving the diversity of features inside images little used.

Their framework, CIGOcc, works in two stages built on multi-level representation fusion. It extracts segmentation, graphics, and depth features from each image. It merges them with a deformable multi-level fusion mechanism. It then adds knowledge distilled from the large SAM segmentation model to sharpen accuracy. Without raising training costs, the system reached state-of-the-art performance on the SemanticKITTI benchmark. The authors frame representation fusion, rather than architecture surgery, as the untried direction for occupancy prediction.
arxiv-2510-13398:
Hayes and colleagues extend a recent notion called selflessness from single algebras to inclusions of algebras. Their 2025 arXiv paper works with C*-probability spaces, abstract structures that blend algebra with a probability-like averaging. An inclusion records a smaller algebra sitting inside a larger one. The authors define when such an inclusion itself counts as selfless. Selflessness was introduced by co-author Robert in earlier work.

A selfless inclusion forces every algebra between the two to be selfless as well. The team finds natural examples among Z-stable algebras and free product algebras. Those are two well-studied families where the new notion can be checked. As an application, they prove selflessness for reduced free unitary quantum groups. These spaces lie outside the free product and group algebra regimes covered before. The result widens the known map of selfless probability spaces.
arxiv-2510-13998:
Xun Wu and co-authors present BitDistill, a recipe for shrinking language models to very low precision while keeping them good at a task, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The target format stores each weight as one of three values, negative one, zero, or one, which slashes memory needs but costs accuracy compared with full-precision models.

The pipeline fine-tunes off-the-shelf models such as Qwen using three techniques. One is a normalization module borrowed from BitNet. Another is an attention distillation method based on MiniLM, which transfers knowledge from the original model. The third is a continual pre-training warm-up that closes the performance gap before task training. In tests, the distilled models matched their full-precision counterparts on tasks across model sizes. The payoff is up to ten times less memory. Inference on ordinary CPUs also runs more than two and a half times faster.
arxiv-2510-14098:
Juan Castillo and Emanuele Cozzo model the spiral of silence, the process by which minority opinions fade from discussion as holders fear isolation, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The setting is clustered, like-minded social networks. Discourse depends on wanting to speak and on network structure. Online platforms shape that structure.

The authors advance the field in three ways. They couple a network formation model with a mean-field model of opinion expression. In the network model, homophily, the tendency to connect with similar others, and triadic closure, the tendency of friends of friends to connect, co-evolve. They analyze the learning dynamics for tipping behavior, finding conditions for hysteresis and path dependence. They check predictions with Monte Carlo simulations that expose finite-size effects. Their result is a balance: moderate triadic closure can foster minority expression by reinforcing cohesion, whereas too much closure amplifies asymmetries and entrenches dominance.
arxiv-2510-14198:
Morium Akter Munny and co-authors present the first analysis of toll scam domains, the websites that impersonate road-toll agencies to harvest fraudulent payments, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The scams are rising fast and causing real harm, yet they had not been studied systematically.

The team assembled a data set of sixty-eight thousand confirmed scam domains, mostly registered in 2025, and mapped the criminals' infrastructure strategies. Registration is concentrated: most domains sit in five non-mainstream top-level domains, and nearly three-quarters were registered through a single provider. Over half the domains appeared in the first quarter of 2025, in coordinated bursts suggesting automated campaigns. A predictive model using registration data predicted which domains would later be suspended, a proxy for confirmed abuse, with accuracy above eighty percent and high sensitivity. The authors argue registrars and platforms can target these patterns, though metadata alone is not enough.
arxiv-2510-14698:
Prasetia, Saputra, and Putra propose, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a method for federated learning that respects how different each participant's data and hardware can be. Federated learning trains one model across many devices without moving their private data to a center. Personalized variants tune the model per client. But clients differ in computing power as well as data, and most methods handle only one of those gaps.

Their method, FedPPA, progressively aligns the weights of layers that clients share with the global model's weights, step by step during training. This reduces the drift between global and local models while keeping each client's local knowledge intact. An entropy-based weighted averaging then improves the global model without sacrificing personalization. On three image classification datasets, the handwritten digits of MNIST, the fashion items of FMNIST, and CIFAR-10, FedPPA consistently outperformed existing federated algorithms in personalized adaptation.
arxiv-2510-14798:
Berenbrink, Friedetzky, Kling, and Nagel analyze, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a load balancing process that never settles, because items keep arriving and being deleted at random. Balls are placed by the greedy two-choice rule: sample two bins, use the emptier one. At each step a coin toss decides whether a ball arrives or one is deleted from a random non-empty bin. The question is how uneven the loads can get as this runs forever.

The authors bound two measures of imbalance at any chosen moment. The discrepancy, the gap between the fullest bin and the average, stays on the order of the logarithm of the number of bins. A matching lower bound makes that estimate exact in shape. The overload, measured against the highest average ever seen, is smaller still, about the double logarithm. For well-behaved arrival patterns, even the discrepancy shrinks to that tiny scale.
arxiv-2510-15098:
Francesca Gladiali, Massimo Grossi, and Luigi Provenzano examine how the shape of a curved surface controls solutions of certain elliptic equations. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies positive, semi-stable solutions, meaning solutions that do not change wildly under small disturbances, on domains drawn on a sphere or on a hyperbolic plane. The central question is where such a solution reaches its critical point, its peak or turning location.

The authors prove that this critical point is unique and non-degenerate for a class of star-shaped domains meeting one geometric condition. On the sphere, their condition is weaker than requiring the domain to be convex, so more shapes qualify. On the hyperbolic plane it is likewise weaker than the stricter horoconvexity requirement. They finish by building examples that show the condition cannot be relaxed any further, so the boundary they found is exactly optimal.
arxiv-2510-15198:
Chao Tang, Arwa Dabbech, Adrian Jackson, and Yves Wiaux upgrade an imaging method for the next generation of radio telescopes. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds on AIRI, an algorithm that rebuilds sharp sky images from telescope data. It alternates between fitting the data and cleaning the image with a learned denoiser, a neural network trained to remove noise. The new version, HyperAIRI, handles many frequency channels at once.

Each channel's denoiser now sees its two neighboring channels and a map of how brightness changes with frequency, guided by a power-law model of the source spectrum. A shelf of pre-trained denoisers covers different brightness ranges, and channels update in parallel to keep huge images tractable. In tests on simulated and real observations, HyperAIRI beat its optimization-based sibling and the widely used CLEAN method. The code is released in a public MATLAB library.
arxiv-2510-15398:
Bingyu Li and five colleagues teach AI to find and outline sea creatures and objects underwater, including kinds it never saw in training. Their 2025 arXiv paper introduces MARIS, the first large benchmark for open-vocabulary instance segmentation at sea. Open-vocabulary means the model must handle category names given as text at test time, not just a fixed list.

Underwater images fight back with faded colors and murky contrast, and land-trained models also lack definitions for marine categories. The team's framework adds two modules to a standard system. One boosts geometric cues, the stable shapes and parts of objects, so identities survive visual degradation. The other injects domain knowledge into the language side, aligning category names with underwater meanings. On the MARIS benchmark the framework beat existing open-vocabulary baselines both within its home domain and across domains. The authors offer it as a foundation for underwater perception research.
arxiv-2510-15598:
Michael Sebek rebuilds a control tool inside quaternion arithmetic, where the order of multiplication matters. This solo 2025 paper concerns observers, systems that infer hidden states from measured outputs, designed over quaternions. Quaternions extend the complex numbers and suit rotation-heavy work, but classic observer formulas lean on tools that fail when multiplication does not commute.

Sebek derives a companion form for such systems and a matching polynomial that encodes how the observer's errors decay. The design flow mirrors the real case, adjusting coefficients in companion coordinates and transforming back. An Ackermann-type formula covers the key case where the target error polynomial has real coefficients. Worked examples beat flattening the problem into vectors or complex pairs. The paper also pins down when the classical one-shot formulas stay valid over quaternions.
arxiv-2510-16098:
Zhoujian Zhang and Yanxia Li built a machine learning tool to find ultracool dwarfs, the coldest, dimmest star-like bodies known. Their program, called USMILE, sorts these faint objects by type using only survey photos, a step called photometric classification. It draws on early data from the Rubin Observatory's LSST survey plus older sky surveys.

Two tree-based models do the work: one picks true dwarfs out from stars and distant galaxies, and one guesses each dwarf's type. They cope well when some photo bands are missing, a flaw that tripped up older tools. Checked against new Euclid space telescope spectra, the tool confirmed fifteen new dwarfs and flagged twenty-five more. Such tools will be vital as new surveys flood astronomers with more faint objects than people can sort by hand.
arxiv-2510-16298:
Zhiwei Zhao, Chixiang Chen, and Shuo Chen tackle a hard question in health research. How does an exposure that changes over time affect later outcomes? Sleep loss unfolding over years is one such exposure, and hundreds of shifting factors can muddy its true effect. Their method, nicknamed MASE, blends several machine learning tools into one sturdy estimator.

The blend models both the chance of exposure and the run of outcomes, so no single tool's quirks can sink the result. In fake-data tests it beats three standard methods, with less bias and sharper accuracy. Applied to a large study of young teens, it finds a clear pattern. Not getting enough sleep builds up harm to thinking skills over time. The method suits long studies where exposures and confounders both refuse to sit still.
arxiv-2510-16698:
Rafichha Yasmin and five co-authors design a chip interconnect based on an electromagnetic metastructure. Modern chiplet systems need links that carry signals fast while also moving heat away. Their design uses silicon for its good heat flow, plus a rippled metal pattern that guides signals as spoof surface plasmons, which are waves held close to the metal surface.

Tests reported by the team show low signal loss and much lower crosstalk than a standard line of the same size, with bandwidth about two and a half times as high. Short pulses passed with little distortion. The thin oxide layer under the metal barely hurt heat removal from the silicon.
arxiv-2510-16898:
Salih Salihoglu, Ibrahim Ahmed, and Afshin Asadi forecast power prices in a 2025 study. Day-ahead electricity prices guide choices for grid operators and producers. The team predicts California prices one day in advance. Their model reads past prices, weather, and the mix of energy sources.

The model uses an LSTM network, a design built for sequences over time. A custom scoring rule blends three error measures during training. One part punishes plain misses, one compares price patterns, one rewards smoothness. The model also keeps learning as fresh data arrives. That updating version beat a fixed model on every error measure. Adding the energy source mix improved the forecasts further.
arxiv-2510-16998:
Lucas J. Hyland, Simon P. Ellingsen, and Mark J. Reid sort maser sources for distance work in a 2025 paper. Masers are natural microwave amplifiers found near young massive stars. The methanol maser line studied here appears only around such stars. Watching masers shift can yield precise stellar distances.

Not every maser is compact or bright enough for that work. The team observed one hundred eighty-seven southern sources with a long-baseline telescope array. They found sixty-nine sources with spots compact and intense enough. Compactness depended strongly on position within the Galaxy. Nearby spiral arm sources looked more compact than distant ones. Scattering along long sight lines likely blurs the distant sources. The catalog tells observers which targets deserve precious telescope time.
arxiv-2510-17098:
Elias Hossain and three co-authors probe a weak spot in large language models in this 2025 paper. While a model writes, it stores past keys and values in a fast cache. That cache is rarely checked, even when prompts and weights are locked down. The authors test what harm small cache changes can do.

Their attack adds noise, zeros, or twists to stored keys at chosen spots. Math links the size of the harm to the size of the change. Tests on two model families show clear shifts in next-word picks. The harm also spreads to search-aided and agent tasks. The work marks cache safety as a key need for safe use.
arxiv-2510-17398:
A space based gravitational wave detector called LISA will soon catch thousands of long inspirals in which a small body circles a huge black hole. Shubham Kejriwal, Enrico Barausse, and Alvin J K Chua note that each signal is so long that tiny extra effects leave a mark. Those effects might come from gas or stars near the black hole, or from gravity itself differing from Einstein theory.

For one source alone, the two causes look much alike, so Kejriwal and his co-authors judge whole populations instead. Environmental effects should touch only some sources, while changed gravity would touch them all. In simulated populations, as few as about twenty detections let their method separate the cases, and even spot both acting together.
arxiv-2510-17498:
Long chains of thought have become the main route to hard reasoning in large language models, but checking each step is where smaller open models falter. Zihan Liu and five co-authors ask whether weak checking can still be enough, if the model is allowed to keep revising its answer many times. Their framework, called Deep Self-Evolving Reasoning, treats each revision as one random step in a walk through possible solutions.

The key claim is simple: if a step is even slightly more likely to improve the answer than to damage it, long runs drift toward the correct solution. Running several such processes side by side and voting sharpened the effect. Liu and his co-authors report that a compact model using their method solved several contest problems it had previously missed entirely.
arxiv-2510-17598:
Small language models write code cheaply and quickly, but they lack the step by step reasoning that very large models use to solve hard programming tasks. Amir Jalilifard, Anderson de Rezende Rocha, and Marcos Medeiros Raimundo transfer that reasoning into a smaller model through distillation. Their training teaches the student to follow correct solution paths and to match the structure of a problem with the structure of its solution, guided by a structure aware training loss.

The fine tuned model, built by a process the authors describe as cheap and simple, clearly beat its baseline on standard coding test sets. Gains showed up in how often the first generated program passed all tests, and in measures of data flow and syntax match. Jalilifard and his co-authors argue that grasping solution structure matters more than predicting likely tokens.
arxiv-2510-17798:
Samuel Talkington and seven co-authors bound the errors in power flow models when grid data is uncertain. Line failures and wrong parameters make real networks hard to predict. Their target is the admittance matrix, which encodes how current flows through lines. They also study the classic linear power flow models built on it.

The team imports concentration inequalities, tools that bound random matrix behavior. Those tools give careful probability bounds for spectra under uncertainty. The bounds grow with nodal criticality, a measure of how much uncertainty gathers at key nodes. Tests on standard IEEE networks matched the predicted scaling. The framework helps judge common shortcuts like DC power flow.
arxiv-2510-17998:
Nishant Subramani, Alfredo Gomez, and Mona Diab make big language model benchmarks easier to read by using score tables alone. Model selection is hard when a benchmark has dozens of data sets and long result grids. Their SimBA frame works in three phases: compare, pick a small stand-in subset, then predict the rest.

Applied to three popular benchmarks, the method shows data sets and models track each other strongly. Tiny subsets stood in for the full suites in their tests. For teams choosing a model, the paper offers a cheaper way to scan results without running or reading every single test.
arxiv-2510-18098:
Fernández-Rodríguez, with ten co-authors, reanalyzes the air of the sub-Neptune planet K2-18 b and urges care with earlier claims. Space telescope spectra of such worlds are hard won, and each reduction choice shapes the result. The team rebuilt the spectrum twelve ways, varying binning, edge darkening, and a new fix for a covered star spot.

Methane showed up robustly in every version. Carbon dioxide looked weaker and model-dependent. The hinted sulfur gas tied to life claims vanished in their fullest treatment. The paper is a firm lesson in how fragile bold atmosphere claims can be.
arxiv-2510-18198:
Haoran Chen, with nine co-authors, reports a way to measure light loss and gain inside a photonic chip without taking it apart. Loss and gain govern nearly every performance figure in integrated photonics, yet peering inside a sealed circuit has been very limited. Their method uses nonlinear devices inside the circuit as power discriminators to read the hidden values.

Precision beats a tenth of a decibel in their tests. The approach can even rate the coupling where fiber meets chip, plus unknown devices under test. Chip designers get a universal inspection tool for circuits that cannot be opened.
arxiv-2510-18498:
E. Caffau and twenty-nine co-authors take a fresh look at an old star called HE 0107-5240. It is one of the most iron-poor stars known. Most such old stars are oddly rich in carbon. That trait is a clue to their birth cloud. One or a few supernova blasts likely seeded that cloud. This star also belongs to a binary pair. The team tracked its motion for more than four years with a high-precision spectrograph.

The tracking set the orbital period at about twenty-nine years, confirming a long-period binary. All the data merged into one very clean spectrum. From it, the team updated the amounts of scandium, chromium, and cobalt. They set a tentative value for aluminum and fresh upper limits for other elements. Iron from neutral and ionized lines agreed well. That match casts doubt on some past corrections for this star.
arxiv-2510-18698:
Taishan Yi and Xiao-Qiang Zhao build an abstract theory of spreading. The systems are monotone evolution systems. In them, larger starting states stay larger. Such systems appear across biology and other sciences. The authors work in a general setting. They find when solutions spread through space. They find when steady states that vary with position exist. They find when such states cannot exist. They also find when those states attract nearby behavior.

Their assumptions contrast two limiting systems. One spreads leftward and rightward at set speeds. The other dies out uniformly. The theory is then applied to integro-difference equations. Their setting becomes uniform far away. The global dynamics follow from the theory. A counter-example adds a warning. Values of a nonlinear rule on a bounded stretch can create odd fixed points. Local details can overturn tidy global predictions.
arxiv-2510-18798:
Guanzhong He and his five co-authors train a web search agent. The agent reflects on its own work. Search agents gather data through repeated tool use. Errors pile up over long chains. Most systems keep their chains shallow for that reason. Their agent is called WebSeer. It trains with reinforcement learning. A self-reflection mechanism is added. A large data set supports the training. It is annotated with reflection patterns.

Training runs in two stages. A cold start is united with reinforcement learning. Both sit inside the self-reflection framework. The agent learns longer, more reflective tool-call chains. It works in real web environments. One model of moderate size reached leading results. It scored about seventy-two percent on a hard multi-hop benchmark. It scored ninety percent on a simpler one. It also generalized well to outside data sets.
arxiv-2510-19098:
Valia Efthymiou, Ekaterina Fedorova, and Chara Podimata study strategic learning when the changes people make in response to a decision rule are not all equally desirable. In strategic classification, people adapt their features to pass a learned rule, and most models only chase prediction accuracy.

Real systems also care about ethics, cost, and fairness, and may want to reward changes that are genuinely good while spreading the effort fairly across different groups. The authors unite causal structure, desirability, and information gaps in one constrained optimization framework. That gives decision makers a way to state trade-offs plainly instead of hiding them.
arxiv-2510-19398:
Yasser Hamidullah and four co-authors present SONAR-SLT. It is a multilingual sign language translation system. Sentence embeddings supervise it, and they are language-agnostic. Translation is usually trained on text in one spoken language. That limits scale and blocks transfer. Older embedding supervision stayed tied to one language and form.

New embeddings train on text and speech from many languages. They now supervise translation into several languages at once. A coupled scheme adds translated targets and perturbs the videos. That fights data scarcity. Tests show steady gains over text-only supervision. More signing communities could be served.
arxiv-2510-19598:
Alexander Ungar and seven co-authors develop tools to identify and control unknown spin defects in diamond without any applied magnetic field. Defects near nitrogen-vacancy centers can serve as extra qubits in quantum registers, but many remain uncharacterized. Working at the single-spin level, the team combines two resonance schemes to measure the defects self-consistently.

One scheme extracts the hyperfine couplings; a second, new triple-resonance protocol steers the nuclear spin through the stronger electron spin. Guided by these measurements, calculations identified a new hydrogen-related defect and confirmed a nitrogen-related one. The team then initialized and controlled the hydrogen nuclear spin as a qubit, keeping coherence for about a millisecond.
arxiv-2510-19798:
C. Murray, R. Kou, and J. G. Bartlett explore whether astronomers could detect gravitational lensing caused not by matter's density but by its motion. Moving matter adds a gravitomagnetic correction to the usual lensing effect. Their idea is to cross-correlate the weak-lensing map with a cosmic momentum field. That field is rebuilt from galaxy redshift surveys.

Simulations show the rebuilt momentum field does not correlate with the plain density lensing signal. So the motion-driven part can be isolated cleanly. Forecasts for upcoming wide-field surveys find a firm detection may be within reach under realistic conditions. Such a measurement would probe the universe's large-scale momentum field directly. It would also test general relativity and Lorentz invariance on cosmic scales.
arxiv-2510-19898:
Atharv Sonwane and ten co-authors manufacture realistic software bugs by asking AI agents to add features and letting them break things. High-quality bugs are the fuel for training software engineering agents, but deliberately planted bugs look artificial. In their BugPilot method, an agent implements a feature in a codebase and unintentionally breaks tests along the way, mimicking how human developers actually introduce defects.

Qualitative analysis shows the resulting bugs resemble human-authored mistakes more closely than perturbation-based datasets. Training on them was also more efficient: models fine-tuned on roughly half as many BugPilot bugs beat models trained on other bug collections. Combining the new bugs with existing data produced two models that set state-of-the-art scores on the SWE-bench Verified benchmark for their sizes.
arxiv-2510-20198:
Maggie Bai and three co-authors test how well large language models think about space from text alone. Five tasks probe this skill on grids. The tasks ask for the quadrant of a point, shape changes, gaps, word search, and tile slides. Each task grows in size, so the models must go past mere pattern match.

On small grids the models do fair work on all five tasks. As grids grow, scores drop fast. The mean loss is near 43 percent and the worst loss is far higher. Each task that starts above half right loses at least 48 percent in score terms. The team reads this as a lack of strong space maps in the models.
arxiv-2510-20398:
Nicolas Delporte and three co-authors compute the distributions of real eigenvalues and eigenvectors of random real antisymmetric tensors. A real eigenpair in their sense combines a real eigenvalue with a set of orthonormal real eigenvectors, one for each index of the tensor. Using a quantum field theoretical method on Gaussian random tensors, they obtain an analytic expression for the signed distribution at finite dimension.

Large-dimension asymptotic forms follow for both the signed and the genuine distributions, along with the edge of the distribution. One application gives an upper bound, believed tight, on the injective norm of the random tensor. The authors also find a universality across tensor families: the large-dimension forms for complex, symmetric, and antisymmetric cases share one shape, differing only in constants.
arxiv-2510-20498:
Ruochen Mao and three co-authors pick safe replies for a named taste with a method called Robust Preference Selection. Most train data show the mean taste of the crowd. So models serve plain asks well and odd tastes with poor skill. That gap is hard to close by fresh trains, which cost much and bend with ease. Their way needs no new train at all.

The method draws a pool of replies from a small zone of kin tastes, not just the one named taste. It then picks the reply that best fits the first aim of the user. A math frame shows the zone draw beats a strong base way. The team casts this as proof that near tastes guard the named one.
arxiv-2510-20798:
Jose J Orquin-Marques and seven co-authors pick useful input features with an analog quantum method run on neutral atom arrays. Feature choice matters because extra inputs add noise and cost, while a small clean set can predict just as well and read more clearly.

Relevance of each feature is coded as a local energy shift, and overlap between features is coded through atom interactions limited by a blockade radius. Slow evolution toward low energy states yields bit patterns that mark balanced feature subsets. On three public classification tasks the method matches or beats classic ranking and wrapper methods, and for tiny subsets it lifts accuracy while cutting feature counts by three quarters or more.
arxiv-2510-20998:
Martin Andersson leads two co-authors on whether repeater assisted massive MIMO networks can work with dynamic time division duplex, where links switch direction as traffic demands. Repeaters amplify and phase shift signals to strengthen users, a cheap boost for coverage.

The catch is that repeaters also amplify noise and interference, and dynamic switching creates cross link interference between access points and users sending in opposite directions. The team builds a framework to optimize repeater gain and phase jointly under that trade off. Findings guide whether repeaters remain a bargain once flexible duplexing enters real networks.
arxiv-2510-21098:
Jiashen Guo leads two co-authors on invariant circles in area preserving twist maps that lie beyond classical KAM theory, where perturbations are too large for the standard method. Invariant circles organize the dynamics of such maps, and their survival or breakdown decides whether motion stays orderly.

Constructive and non constructive techniques are combined to prove existence and breakdown results for these non KAM circles. The findings support affirmative answers to two open questions Mather posed in nineteen ninety eight. Progress here matters because twist maps model systems from particle accelerators to planetary dynamics.
arxiv-2510-21198:
Yang Zhong and four co-authors report how their team placed third in an image retrieval contest run through Kaggle as part of an ICCV workshop on food data. The task asked systems to find matching food images within a large, finely divided collection of pictures.

Four basic models were trained separately, each using a weighted mix of ArcFace and Circle losses, two tools that shape how image features are spaced. The team then combined model outputs and applied test-time augmentation to strengthen the features. A new reranking step, built on diffusion and a reciprocal neighbor method, reordered the first results. Final scores reached about 0.81 on both public and private leaderboards.
arxiv-2510-21298:
Aida Abiad, Harper Reijnders, and Michael Tait improve a classic lower bound for a family of error-correcting codes known as sum-rank-metric codes. The Gilbert-Varshamov bound says how large such codes can be, and beating it in some settings shows that bigger codes exist than the old bound promised.

Their route runs through graph theory rather than direct code construction. For certain parameter choices, they show that a whole space of matrices can be split into codes whose average size tops the old bound by a factor that grows like a logarithm. They also explain how these codes connect to a coloring problem for sets, tied to Ramsey numbers, which may interest readers in combinatorics as well as coding theory.
arxiv-2510-21398:
Ravindra Aribowo Tarunokusumo and Rafael Fernandes Cunha improve a test-time trick called budget forcing. The trick gives a language model extra room to think through math problems. It also prompts the model to correct itself. The trick usually relies on fine-tuning with long reasoning traces. Those traces can hurt smaller models by making their answers bloated.

Their recipe adds reinforcement learning after that fine-tuning. It uses only about fifteen hundred training samples. On the GSM8K grade-school math set, the combined model answers more problems correctly. It also spends far fewer tokens than the fine-tuned model alone. Token use drops by over forty percent across several thinking budgets. The learning stage appears to recover what long-trace training cost. It then adds accuracy on top.
arxiv-2510-21598:
Diana Cai and three co-authors build a flexible family for variational inference, the art of approximating a hard probability distribution with a tractable one. Their family multiplies several experts together, each expert a weighted multivariate t-distribution, a bell shape with heavy tails, and the products can bend into skewed, heavy-tailed, or multi-peaked forms.

Sampling from such products looks impossible until a trick from quantum field theory, a Feynman identity, rewrites the product as an average over a simplex with Dirichlet weights, giving a workable sampler. Fitting then adjusts the experts' weights by repeatedly matching the score, the gradient of the log density, between approximation and target. Each step is a tidy convex program, and updates converge exponentially fast under broad conditions. Tests on synthetic and real targets round out the case.
arxiv-2510-21698:
Daniel Bienstock and Matias Villagra sharpen bounds for the alternating current optimal power flow problem, the notoriously nonconvex puzzle of running a power grid at lowest cost without violating physics. High-quality bounds certify how good a grid schedule is, but the strongest known relaxations buckle on large, multi-period problems where operators need them most.

Their approach stays disciplined and linear: cutting planes added step by step to a semidefinite relaxation, keeping the numerics stable and the method scalable. The procedure can start warm from earlier work. Because each added cut is linear, it reaches tight, accurate bounds for multi-period relaxations far beyond the reach of nonlinear convex solvers. Early experiments on a standard library of grid instances look promising against the best published bounds.
arxiv-2510-21798:
Juan Gutiérrez, Victor Gutiérrez, Ángel Mora, Silvia Rodriguez, and José Luis Blanco test whether machine-made draft labels can speed up the slow hand-labeling of video. Careful manual annotation is still the trusted standard for dense video datasets, but it consumes large amounts of annotator time, especially when events in the footage are ambiguous.

In a single-round study, eighteen volunteers labeled difficult spatiotemporal footage with and without pre-annotations from a tuned vision-language encoder. Most participants finished about thirty-five percent faster with the machine drafts in place. Beyond the time savings, the authors offer a careful framework for judging assisted labeling workflows, weighing raw speed against whether human checking still catches machine mistakes.
arxiv-2510-22498:
Wearable heart signals might reveal feelings without cameras or interviews. Muhammad Irfan, with six co-authors, presents a light method in 2025 for telling negative emotions from positive ones using only electrocardiography, meaning heart activity traces. The work matters because negative emotions are linked to dementia risk yet hard to spot.

Their system pulls features from several signal views, selects the best mix, and combines classifiers by voting. Tests use recordings from the POPANE collection, covering many healthy participants, and compare one shared model against person specific models. The design avoids heavy extra sensors, aiming to save battery and data on small connected devices.
arxiv-2510-22898:
Tool calling agents often fail to transfer skills across domains. Vishvesh Bhat, Omkar Ghugarkar, and Julian McAuley study that gap in 2025. They evaluate leading models on several tool benchmarks. They also introduce MAVEN, a new out of distribution test. MAVEN stresses multi step reasoning with verification.

Most models scored below fifty percent on MAVEN. That exposes a large generalization gap. Their CoreThink Agentic Reasoner adds a symbolic layer. It supports structured decomposition and adaptive tool choice. No extra training is used. It reached leading results across benchmarks. Gains over baselines were large at lower cost. Adversarial task composition is central to MAVEN.
arxiv-2510-22998:
Gilber A Corrales and five co-authors introduce ProfileXAI, a system that tailors AI explanations to different kinds of users. A single explanation rarely fits both experts and lay readers. Their framework pairs standard explainers such as SHAP, LIME, and Anchor with retrieval-backed language models that write grounded stories.

For each case the system picks an explainer by measured criteria, then builds a chat-ready account. Tests on heart disease and thyroid cancer data checked fidelity, robustness, brevity, and user ratings. No single explainer won on all counts, with LIME giving the best fidelity-robustness balance on heart data.
arxiv-2510-23198:
Etienne Goffinet and six co-authors derive scaling laws for adapting language models to a new domain that account for the original training budget. Continual pre-training must gain skill in the target domain without losing ground on the base domain. Existing laws assume a fixed budget, usually counted in tokens per parameter, so they cannot forecast outcomes for differently trained models.

Their PTPP-aware laws make that budget an explicit variable. Trained on early stages of a multilingual setup shifting from English and Arabic toward French, the formulas predict adaptation loss at unseen budgets. Better forecasts help teams spend compute wisely.
arxiv-2510-23298:
Xavier Caruso, Florian Furnsinn, Daniel Vargas-Montoya, and Wadim Zudilin compute Galois groups for generating series of several famous number sequences reduced modulo primes. The sequences include Apery numbers, Domb numbers, and Almkvist-Zudilin numbers, each tied to deep arithmetic questions. Reducing their series modulo a prime p gives objects whose symmetry groups can be studied.

The authors find that the behavior of these Galois groups is governed by congruence conditions on p. Such patterns connect combinatorics, modular forms, and Galois theory. The results give number theorists concrete groups to test broader conjectures about Apery-like series.
arxiv-2510-23398:
Yakov Solomons and five co-authors present a practical way to interface free-space light with a two-dimensional array of single-atom tweezers. Typical paraxial light fields match poorly to the array multi-order diffraction pattern, which severely limits coupling efficiency. Their approach designs a field mode that naturally couples to the array instead.

The composite mode is a unique superposition of beams matching the diffraction orders, generated from one Gaussian beam with standard optics, spatial light modulators, and a single objective. Efficient light-atom interfaces are core hardware for quantum computing, simulation, and networking with neutral atoms.
arxiv-2510-23498:
Elena Celledoni, Brynjulf Owren, Lars Ruthotto, and Tianjiao Nicole Yang work on training neural ordinary differential equations, a kind of model that treats network depth as smooth time. Training such models is costly, and the cheap low-precision arithmetic used elsewhere in deep learning can cause rounding errors and unstable results here. Standard mixed precision tricks, safe for ordinary networks, do not carry over directly.

The team builds a training scheme that runs the network's velocity part in low precision while keeping key sums and gradients in higher precision. A custom scaling step for the adjoint equations keeps the math reliable, and explicit solvers handle the forward pass. Their open-source PyTorch package, called rampde, plugs into existing code. Tests on image classification and generative tasks cut memory use by roughly half and ran up to twice as fast.
arxiv-2510-23598:
Patrick R. Behr and six co-authors report the first far-ultraviolet look at KELT-20b, an ultra-hot Jupiter orbiting a bright, fast-spinning A-type star. The planet's steady temperature tops two thousand degrees, and earlier optical studies found hydrogen plus several metals in its air. Its upper atmosphere might behave oddly, since stars of this type produce little of the extreme ultraviolet light that usually drives escape.

Using the Hubble Space Telescope's Cosmic Origins Spectrograph, the team watched the planet cross its star and measured how much light it blocked across far-ultraviolet wavelengths. The transit grew deeper toward shorter wavelengths, rising from 1.88 percent to 2.28 percent across their bands. They found tentative signs of ionized iron and neutral nitrogen, no sign of several other atoms or molecules, and no evidence that the atmosphere is escaping into space.
arxiv-2510-23698:
Gonzalo F. Casas and a co-author argue that four-dimensional effective theories of gravity from string theory are incomplete without extra non-perturbative ingredients. In the small-volume regime, light states of non-perturbative origin must join the description, or the low-energy theory turns inconsistent. The cleanest windows are corners of the theory where supersymmetry locally grows stronger, predicting exactly such missing states.

The authors work in the Kähler moduli space of F-theory on Calabi-Yau fourfolds, where shrinking curves untouched by 7-planes create those enhanced corners. Guided by the extra supersymmetry, they identify the degrees of freedom the perturbative Type IIB picture lacks. Fitting the local sectors into one consistent four-dimensional theory requires complex structure moduli and spacetime-filling D3-branes. A heterotic dual view unifies the separate enhanced sectors, and the paper also treats cases with no local enhancement at all.
arxiv-2510-23798:
Gauthier Grimmer and five co-authors build a reproducible pipeline for watching floating trash in city rivers with fixed cameras. Plastic and other human-made debris drifting downstream harms wildlife, water quality, navigation, and recreation. Counting it continuously by hand is impractical, so the authors pair deep learning detection with a geometric model that estimates each object's real size from a flat image.

The study compares deep learning models for accuracy and speed under messy real conditions, and probes pitfalls like data leakage between training and test images. Two lessons stand out: including negative images — scenes without debris — matters greatly, and guarding against temporal leakage shapes honest scores. The geometric size estimates, corrected by regression, proved feasible. The authors frame the result as a blueprint for cheap, automated river monitoring that cities could actually deploy and maintain.
arxiv-2510-24398:
Youwan Mahé and four co-authors evaluate REFLECT, a generative model for finding brain abnormalities after stroke without labeled examples. Stroke MRI shows focal lesions plus secondary changes like atrophy and enlarged ventricles, which are emerging markers of recovery yet are poorly captured by supervised segmentation. Unsupervised detection could flag both kinds of change at once.

Using the ATLAS dataset with dual expert annotations, the team scores anomaly maps at the object level with free response ROC analysis. They train models on lesion free slices from stroke patients and on healthy controls to test how training data choice affects detection. The study gauges flow based models for broad post stroke screening.
arxiv-2510-24498:
Tejaswini Bollikonda writes alone on keeping cloud AI data private. Homomorphic encryption lets computers compute on locked data. The data stays scrambled, yet the result still comes out right. Cloud tools could thus give predictions without seeing private inputs. But locked computing is slow and hard to run at cloud scale.

Bollikonda builds a cloud-native workflow for this kind of computing. Locked modules ship in containers run by Kubernetes orchestration software. Kubernetes spreads work across many machines and scales it as needed. Tricks like packing values into one ciphertext cut delay and memory. Tests ran more than three times faster than standard pipelines. Memory use fell by forty percent in the same tests. The design points to safer AI services under zero-trust rules.
arxiv-2510-24798:
Evgeny Ukhanov, the sole author, proves core code for a token sale launch pad with math checks, not just tests. Such code sits in open finance systems, where a bug can drain funds at once. He wrote the code in Dafny, a tongue built for proof, and checked it step by step.

The proof work starts with base facts on whole number math, then builds up to sale rules. Those rules cover coin swaps, time based price cuts, and refunds when a sale cap is hit. Key proofs show refunds can never top what a user put in. Loss from round trips in the math is also shown to stay in a strict bound.
arxiv-2510-25198:
E Cappellazzo leads a team with nine co-authors who trace gas moves where young star zones push into cold clouds. A past guess says a set mark in hydroxyl lines, called the OH flip, flags gas that is hit by such a push. Their work tests that guess on three star zones in our galaxy.

A large radio array caught all four hydroxyl lines, plus hydrogen radio lines and the broad glow, for each zone. Split of the cloud lines showed rich in and out forms. The flip showed in two of the three zones, and its marks fit the guess on shape, moves, and light. That backs the flip as a probe of such hits.
arxiv-2510-25598:
Anton S Galaev, Thomas Leistner, and Felipe Leitner study holonomy in geometry. Their 2025 paper studies pseudo-Hermitian forms and contact forms. A sub-Riemannian form sits on a contact kernel. Its holonomy is associated to that form. Schouten and adapted connections are canonical choices.

Under a torsion setting, the two holonomies relate closely. They are either equal or differ by codimension one. The former is a normal subgroup in latter case. That yields complete holonomy classification when torsion vanishes. Main results focus on pseudo-Hermitian forms specifically. Symmetric sub-Riemannian forms are classified from that. Locally symmetric contact forms relate to homogeneous Riemannian ones. Geometry scholars gain a full holonomy picture here.
arxiv-2510-26298:
Jingran Zhang, Ning Li, and Justin Cui run an early evaluation of a web browsing AI agent on browser games. The agent, ChatGPT Atlas from OpenAI, can analyze pages, process user intent, and send cursor and keyboard inputs inside the browser. Its skill at information retrieval had been shown, but dynamic, interactive settings were less explored, so games serve as a controlled test bed.

The test games include a running dinosaur game, Sudoku, Flappy Bird, and a browser role playing game, scored by in game performance. Atlas performed strongly on logical reasoning, solving Sudoku puzzles far faster than human baselines in their tests. It struggled in real time games that need precise timing and motor control, often failing at the first obstacles.
arxiv-2510-26398:
Gabriele Centurelli, with four co-authors, studies the long trail of disturbed air behind offshore wind farms. Seen from above, these wakes are often lopsided: one side carries more turbulence, the churning motion of air, than the other. The team asks whether the Coriolis force, the sideways push from Earth's spin, is the cause.

Centurelli and his co-authors simulate a real wind farm in the German Bight under northern and southern hemisphere skies, plus made-up skies with parts of the effect switched off. The streak of strong turbulence flipped side with the hemisphere, and it traced back to veer, the slow turning of wind with height in the incoming flow. The streak also helped the wake recover a little, and field measures matched the pattern well.
arxiv-2510-26698:
Duarte Fontes and Robert Szafron compute quantum electrodynamics corrections to the decays of bound muons. A muon bound in an atom can decay or be captured, and those decays probe new physics, so precise spectra matter. Corrections from QED are large for the spectra's shape but very hard to compute below the nuclear scale.

Fontes and Szafron use the universality of effective field theory methods to build a framework that computes those corrections across a broad class of bound-muon decays. As the key application, they give the most accurate predictions yet for signal and background spectra in muon conversion. Radiative corrections shift the leading-order ratio of those spectra by five percent, with little energy dependence. That shift matters for the discovery reach of upcoming experiments.
arxiv-2510-26898:
Crystal Su, with four co-authors, unites structured engineering knowledge with language models for chemical plant control. Their framework aligns a large language model with the COPE ontology, a formal map of chemical engineering concepts, through data acquisition, semantic preprocessing, information extraction, and ontology mapping. The result is templated question-answer pairs that guide fine-tuning.

Su and the team add a control-focused decoding stage and a citation gate, which constrain outputs to ontology-linked terms and so enforce syntactic and factual grounding. Metrics measure both language quality and ontological accuracy. Feedback loops and planned extensions, such as semantic retrieval and iterative validation, aim to raise interpretability and reliability further. The authors present the approach as a transparent, auditable way to use such models in process control and safety analysis.
arxiv-2510-26998:
Thiago Puccinelli, Lucas Farigliano, and Gustavo Dalpian test a general machine learning model on tin-based materials that could replace lead in solar and light devices. The materials, CsSnBr3 and Cs2SnBr6, are halide perovskites, meaning crystals with a known flexible structure. Their stability and phase behavior at real temperatures are hard to predict.

The team runs molecular dynamics simulations, which track atoms over time, from cold to warm conditions using the MACE-MP-0 model without extra tuning. One material shifts from a tilted to a cubic form, though an in-between phase seen in experiments is missed. The other stays cubic and rigid throughout. The model captures the main thermal traits, making it a useful first step before finer tuning.
arxiv-2510-27298:
Rebeka Toth, Richard A. Dubniczky, and two other co-authors track a year of fake phishing drills in this 2025 study. Phishing emails trick staff into handing over passwords or cash. The team sent more than thirteen thousand fake lures to over thirteen hundred staff in twenty firms. The lures varied in mood, personal detail, and claimed sender.

Over six months, the share of staff who fell for lures dropped by about half. Steady drills plus focused training drove the fall, the team found. Staff turnover, though, made awareness wobble as new hires arrived untrained. Mood tricks and personal touches changed how often people bit. The group shared its lure templates and code openly. Their case: only nonstop training keeps the guard up.
arxiv-2510-27398:
Yu Wang, Rongguo Yang, and four other co-authors measure tiny tilts of a light beam in this 2025 paper. Knowing a beam's yaw and pitch, its left-right and up-down angles, matters for navigation, factory checks, and fine instruments. Weak value amplification is a quantum trick that magnifies small shifts by discarding most outcomes. Their setup doubles the trick.

Two shaped beams carry the yaw and pitch signals out of separate dark ports. Each port is read by a balanced detector tuned to a higher beam shape. The two angles can thus be read at once, apart from each other. The smallest tilts they could sense were under a hundred picoradians, with shifts under a picometer. The work stretches beam checks from one tilt to two at once.
arxiv-2510-27598:
Yunze Wu and fifteen co-authors present InnovatorBench in 2025, a test of whether AI agents can do real research on large language models. Past tests probe narrow skills in simple settings. Real research needs forming ideas, planning tests, writing code, running it, and reading results as one long chain.

Twenty tasks span data building, filtering, enriching, loss design, reward design, and scaffold building. Each task needs a runnable product scored on correctness, performance, quality, and doubt. A companion space, ResearchGym, supports long runs, remote jobs, and saved states. Frontier models show promise on code-led tasks but fail on fragile steps. The gap marks where agent research tools must grow.
arxiv-2511-00298:
Dániel Garamvölgyi, Bill Jackson, Tibor Jordán, and Soma Villányi study three matroids defined by Kalai in 1985, abstract structures that capture when partial data can be completed. The settings cover partly filled symmetric matrices, skew-symmetric matrices, and rectangular matrices, each tied to a graph problem. The team gives conditions under which a graph reaches the highest possible rank in each structure.

For two of the matroids, the conditions rest on the graph's minimum degree and cannot be improved. For the third, the condition rests on connectivity. The payoffs concern filling in missing matrix entries: almost all low-rank matrices of the kinds studied are pinned down uniquely by surprisingly partial data. This holds once each row or the entry pattern meets the stated conditions.
arxiv-2511-00998:
Ziye Wang and co-authors present GauDP, a representation designed to help teams of robots learn together from demonstrations. Each agent sees only its own camera view, yet the team needs a shared grasp of the whole scene. Balancing fine local control with global awareness has limited how well such systems scale.

GauDP builds one consistent three dimensional Gaussian field from the separate camera images, then hands each agent a local view drawn from that shared field. Agents can query the features their task needs while keeping their own perspective, with no extra sensors such as point cloud scanners. On the RoboFactory multi arm benchmark, GauDP beats image based methods, approaches point cloud methods, and scales well as agents are added.
arxiv-2511-01098:
Veronica Marsico, Antonio Quintero-Rincon, and Hadj Batatia test a statistics based method for spotting respiratory disease from chest X-rays. Their feature learner uses the Epanechnikov kernel density estimate, a nonparametric way to model the shape of data, with no fixed form assumed, which adapts well to varying pixel intensities.

The extracted features feed a bimodal logistic regression classifier. Tested on more than thirteen thousand chest X-rays drawn from the COVID-19 Radiography Dataset, the method reached about seventy percent accuracy, with sensitivity notably lower than specificity. The authors are candid that the results are moderate and sensitivity needs work, and that clinical expertise remains essential. The study's point is to show the promise of kernel density features in medical imaging.
arxiv-2511-01198:
Tariq Abdul-Quddoos, Tasnia Sharmin, Xiangfang Li, and Lijun Qian build a system that watches shared radio spectrum and names what it hears. As bands are shared more heavily, monitors must classify which protocol a transmission uses, such as LTE, 5G, or Wi-Fi, and identify which base station sent it, to enforce policy and security.

A convolutional neural network tackles the overlapping signal features and environmental variability, using a multi channel input strategy to extract useful structure. On radio data from the POWDER testbed platform, the system reached about ninety percent accuracy on protocol classification. It reached perfect accuracy on base station identification, and about ninety two percent on the joint task. The authors present it as a step toward stronger spectrum monitoring and management.
arxiv-2511-01798:
Dimitrios Tyrovolas and seven colleagues analyze pinching-antenna systems, a flexible antenna design for next-generation wireless networks in which radiating points are pinched onto a dielectric waveguide. Most earlier studies assumed the pinch positions could slide continuously. Real hardware fixes them at discrete points. It can only switch each one on or off.

The authors build a closed-form framework for the ergodic data rate of such a two-state system. In it, the antennas are fixed. Only activation states are controlled. They introduce pinching discretization efficiency, a measure of the performance lost relative to the ideal continuous design. Numerical results carry the practical message: near-continuous performance is achievable with only a limited number of pinching points, giving engineers a scalable design rule.
arxiv-2511-02098:
Salomon Guinchard, Yves Savoye-Peysson, and Joan Decker present an analytic model for bremsstrahlung, the radiation electrons emit when they are deflected by atomic nuclei. Reading electron behaviour in high-energy settings depends on describing this emission well. For thin targets containing heavy elements, the electric field of the nucleus is partly screened by its own electrons. That screening changes when atoms are partially ionised, as they often are in hot matter.

The model represents the atomic potential as a sum of Yukawa terms. That yields cross sections for any nuclear charge and ionisation state, for electron energies up to a few tens of MeV (million electron volts). Earlier analytic treatments covered neutral atoms; this framework extends them to partially ionised heavy species.
arxiv-2511-02498:
Antonella Perucca, a number theorist, writes down a complete formula for the linear relations among roots. Given a field and a group of elements in its algebraic closure. Adjoining those elements creates a field extension whose degree can be compared with a certain index built from the multiplicative group. When that index is finite, Perucca's formula gives the exact ratio between the two quantities.

The formula accounts for every linear relation over the base field among radicals. Beyond the relations that come from the multiplicative structure itself, all remaining ones are produced by relations among roots of unity and by single radicals. The work builds on results of Rybowicz, which themselves rest on classical contributions by Kneser and Schinzel. Kummer theory and its extensions govern how radical extensions behave, and this result gives that theory a clean, closed accounting identity.
arxiv-2511-02698:
Mateusz Duda and four colleagues review devices that can steer a single photon from one port to another. Their 2025 survey covers quantum emitters tied to tiny photonic structures, where a tunable light-matter link makes such switching possible. A good switch must be fast, efficient, and faithful, keeping the photon's state intact while it reroutes the photon.

The review gathers the main input-output theory, proposed routing designs, and lab demonstrations across four platforms: semiconductor quantum dots, neutral atoms, superconducting qubits, and color centers. The authors also press for shared reporting of speed, efficiency, and fidelity in future demos. Clear benchmarks, they argue, will help these switches grow into parts of reconfigurable quantum networks.
arxiv-2511-02798:
Chris Gilly and Steven Cranmer present a filter that makes solar images show both the bright disk and the faint outer corona. Standard views of extreme ultraviolet images hide faint off-limb detail, leaving a bright ball in a dark void. Their 2025 paper introduces the Radial Histogram Equalizing Filter, built for the Sun's huge range of brightness.

The filter blends radial graded filters, which respect distance from the Sun's center, with histogram equalization, which spreads contrast where the eye needs it. It runs frame by frame with no tuning and treats disk and off-limb features evenly. A companion function, Upsilon, offers gentle tonal compression when wanted. Benchmarks against older methods, plus examples from several instruments, guide users on when each tool fits.
arxiv-2511-03098:
Miftahur Rahman and six colleagues built ISC-Perception, a data set for teaching robots to spot parts of a new intermeshed steel connection system on building sites. Robotic assembly could speed steel framing and keep workers safer, but no image collection existed for these parts, and site photos are hard to gather safely. Their 2025 data set blends three sources to close the gap.

Procedural CAD renders and game-engine scenes supply most images, with automatic labels, plus a small set of real photos. Counting every hour of setup and checking, the team made ten thousand images in about thirty hours, against an estimated one hundred sixty-seven for hand labeling. Detectors trained on the blend far beat those trained on either synthetic source alone, reaching strong scores on a bench test.
arxiv-2511-03198:
Jiawei Zhou, Amy Chen, Darshi Shah, Laura Schwab-Reese, and Munmun De Choudhury ask what bad information from language models actually looks like. Low quality is often treated as simple falsehood, but the authors suspect the category is wider. Their 2025 study runs focus groups with public health professionals and people with lived experience in three sensitive areas: vaccines, opioid use disorder, and intimate partner violence.

The groups surfaced failure types beyond wrong facts, including misprioritization, stressing the trivial over the vital, and exaggeration. They also named traits that set model output apart from older information sources. The authors argue that quality debates must move past truth alone, since the new tools fail in new ways shaped by how they work and how people use them.
arxiv-2511-03298:
Oleg Senkevich and colleagues build KScaNN, a nearest neighbor search engine tuned for ARM-based Kunpeng servers. Finding near matches fast is core to search, ranking, and machine learning, yet most tuned engines grew up on a different chip family. A plain move to ARM leaves much speed on the table, the authors note.

KScaNN pairs data-aware algorithm changes with close use of the Kunpeng hardware traits. Its hybrid design reshapes how candidate points are gathered and checked. The goal is to close the gap that naive ports open up on this growing server base. Full detail in the study covers the added tricks and their payoff. The work matters as more data centers adopt ARM machines for daily search loads.
arxiv-2511-03498:
Kazi Reyazul Hasan and colleagues release BanglaSTEM, a paired corpus for translating technical Bangla into English without mangling specialist terms. Language models solve technical problems well in English but poorly in Bangla, and a translate-first workaround fails when terms shift meaning. Five thousand sentence pairs span computing, mathematics, physics, chemistry, and biology.

Over twelve thousand draft translations were generated, then human judges kept only pairs that preserved terminology faithfully. A T5 model trained on the kept pairs is tested against existing systems. Better technical translation could open strong model help to Bangla-speaking students and engineers on their own terms, rather than through lossy detours.
arxiv-2511-03598:
Hussam Al Daas and colleagues design randomized algorithms that squeeze tensors already stored in compressed train format even further. Tensor trains break huge multi-way arrays into chained small pieces, and rounding trims the ranks linking those pieces. Their sketches use Khatri-Rao products, structured random maps that respect the chain form.

When ranks are set ahead, costs match earlier sketch methods. The gain is adaptivity: error can be estimated from the same sketches, with proven guarantees, so ranks can settle at whatever a set tolerance demands. Tests run on synthetic tensors and on parametric kernel problems. Scientific computing leans on such compression to fit otherwise impossible data cubes into memory.
arxiv-2511-03698:
Pavel Kalugin shares a Julia toolkit that solves the phase problem in crystal studies. Diffraction tests record how strong each wave is. They lose the phase of each wave, though. Dual-space methods rebuild those lost phases step by step.

The toolkit is made for aperiodic crystals and quasicrystals. It backs space group symmetry in any number of dims. A smart sampling plan cuts waste that symmetry would force. That waste is a real cost when data stretch far in one way. A charge flipping method ships with the kit as a base case. Users can also script their own phasing runs with fine control.
arxiv-2511-03898:
Arup Datta, Ahmed Aljohani, and Hyunsook Do evaluate secure code generation with language models at scale, noting that code which runs is not always code which is safe. Five instruction-tuned code models were tested with plain zero-shot prompting and with a three-round reflexion method that feeds back security findings.

At baseline, about a quarter to a third of programs were insecure. Weak cryptography and configuration bugs were hardest to avoid, while templated flaws were handled better. Reflexion raised average security markedly by the third round, with most gains in round one. Python scored highest and C lowest, and one to two rounds captured most benefit.
arxiv-2511-04098:
Takako Endo, Yohei Matsumoto, Hiromichi Ohno, and Akito Suzuki determine the full eigenvalue picture for a non-unitary, one-dimensional, two-state quantum walk with a single defect and chiral symmetry. Eigenvalues in discrete-time walks connect deeply to localization, where a walker stays near its start instead of spreading.

Non-Hermitian walks with chiral symmetry also model open quantum systems and topological insulators, which makes a complete spectral account valuable. The abstract states the result compactly: the whole eigenvalue structure for this walk is given. For researchers, knowing exactly which eigenvalues exist, and hence which localized states can occur, anchors later work on topology and dynamics in this non-unitary setting.
arxiv-2511-04498:
Sheel Ganatra and his co-author construct the cyclic open-closed map for a large Fukaya category. The category encodes surfaces and curves in symplectic geometry, here with bulk deformations allowed. Their map links that category to variations of Hodge structures.

The authors show the map respects a polarized, semi-infinite form of those structures. They also give a natural test for when the map is an isomorphism. Batyrev mirror pairs pass that test. In such Calabi-Yau cases, rational Gromov-Witten counts can be read from the category, so enumerative mirror symmetry follows from homological mirror symmetry.
arxiv-2511-05098:
Wiesław Grygierzec and Wojciech Zajączkowski set bounds for swirling flow in a finite cylinder under the Navier-Stokes equations, with slip rules at the wall. Their goal is to control a key measure built from parts of the spin field.

Control hinges on how the angular flow part compares in two norms. They mark out a critical wedge in time, where that flow is both large and oddly spread. Their main bound is conditional, with any loss of control charged to time spent in that wedge. The work names a precise spot where blow-up could start.
arxiv-2511-05298:
Emiel Vanspranghels and co-authors design precoding methods for cell-free massive MIMO that use location data to curb interference. Future nets may spread antennas widely and serve each user from many of them, with no cell edges.

In dense set-ups, full channel data for all users at all antennas may not be at hand. Coexistence with radar and older mobile systems also matters. Location-informed precoding uses where users are to shape signals and cut clashes. The work suits a user-centric net where signal plans must do more with less channel data.
arxiv-2511-05498:
Ilya Tyagin and co-authors add an explainability layer to systems that propose biomedical hypotheses, so each claim comes with its evidence trail. A hypothesis tool that cannot show its grounds is hard to trust or to check, in a field where a wrong lead wastes lab years.

Their method, built on a context retriever, uses semantic graph search over published papers to pull the facts behind a hypothesis. Training with data limits mimics real discovery bounds. A feedback loop then finds and fixes weak parts of a model's account, which sharpens both the evidence path and the claim.
arxiv-2511-05698:
Hung-Yi Pu proposes a natural laboratory for settling what black hole jets are made of. Jets may be dominated by light particles or by heavier baryonic matter, and telling the two apart has stayed an open problem. His setting pairs a middle-weight black hole orbiting a supermassive one, in what is called an extreme mass ratio binary.

Each time the smaller black hole crosses the big one's disk, it feeds fast and launches a jet. As that jet plows into the disk, its light evolves. A baryonic jet should shine much brighter in gamma rays than a light-particle jet. Pu argues the ratio of gamma-ray to ultraviolet light could separate the two cases, above all when paired with other messengers.
arxiv-2511-06198:
Shoto Aoki, Yoshio Kikukawa, and Toshinari Takemoto examine the chiral anomaly for Kogut-Susskind fermions in a Hamiltonian picture with three space dimensions plus time. These fermions, also called staggered fermions, are a lattice tool for studying particle physics. A chiral transformation of them, built from shift operations, is the focus of the study.

From the transformation the authors define an axial charge that is spread out rather than sitting on single sites. They show it cannot be rewritten using quantized charges from a generalized Onsager algebra. Numerically, they verify that the charge's vacuum value follows the expected anomalous conservation law of the continuum two-flavor theory under slow changes of a background gauge field.
arxiv-2511-06298:
Xin Zuo and colleagues improve drone-based object detection that fuses visible and infrared imagery. Most fusion methods work only in the spatial domain and leave frequency information unused. Their method, SFFR, rebuilds features in both domains before fusion, using Kolmogorov-Arnold Network blocks designed for each side.

One module swaps selected frequency components between the visible and infrared streams to sharpen their agreement. A second module models spatial detail at several scales with Gaussian basis functions, helping the detector cope with changing flight altitude. Tests on three aerial datasets, covering sea rescue and vehicle scenes, showed clear advantages over competing multispectral detectors.
arxiv-2511-06398:
Leloko Lepolesa and co-authors set electric vehicle charging prices that shift with grid conditions. Mass charging can destabilize distribution networks never designed for that load. Their strategy pursues three goals at once: shaving peaks, filling valleys, and balancing load between nearby distribution networks.

The team first forecasts network demand from weather history, prices, and vehicle distributions across areas and times of day. Deep reinforcement learning then sets the dynamic price, and three algorithms were compared for that role, with the best one deployed for pricing. Simulations showed better use of the grid at the distribution level, pointing toward healthier operation at larger scale.
arxiv-2511-06598:
Mohammad Shirzadi, Ali Safarpoor Dehkordi, and Ahad Zehmakan keep deep graph neural networks from washing out into sameness. Message passing lets each node blend neighbor information, but stacking many layers smooths embeddings until nodes look alike. Residual connections that remix the original features help, and this work lets each node keep its own residual strength.

The authors prove the adaptive scheme keeps the embeddings' Dirichlet energy away from zero, blocking oversmoothing. The guarantee is the first of its kind, covering even fixed residual strengths together with activation functions. Experiments favor the method over leading message passing designs, especially where neighbors carry different labels, and a hand-set variant matches the learned one at lower cost.
arxiv-2511-06798:
B G Chae introduces a neural network layer built to let a model refer back to its own earlier internal states. The Fast-Weights Homeostatic Reentry Layer combines fast-weight associative memory, a stabilizing homeostatic rule, and learned feedback that re-enters past activity into current processing. Standard transformers, by contrast, run purely feedforward at inference time.

In controlled tests the author swept the strength of the feedback and tracked it with three new measures of internal dynamics. A stable band appeared at moderate feedback strength, where reentry was expressive yet orderly, with smooth growth in one measure and steady low-frequency cycles in another. The results are presented as evidence that balanced feedback and self-regulation can produce reflective, thought-like internal processing.
arxiv-2511-06898:
Boyan Tang and five co-authors forecast day-ahead electricity prices, a task that matters for grid operation and market decisions. Prices spike unpredictably during extreme weather and holidays, and those anomalies defeat many current methods. The team combines two models: a distilled attention transformer that weighs key stretches of past data, and an autoencoder-based model that detects unusual patterns.

The transformer captures both long-term trends and short-term fluctuations through its self-attention weights. The autoencoder part, trained without supervision, isolates anomalies caused by events such as heavy rain, heat waves, or festivals, so they distort the forecast less. Tests on market data from California and Shandong Province showed better accuracy, robustness, and efficiency than leading methods, suggesting value for grid resilience.
arxiv-2511-07098:
Yuanshao Zhu and four co-authors infer fine-grained city traffic flows with a model small enough to deploy. Estimating flows at high spatial resolution supports planning and intelligent transport, but leading models are heavily over-parameterized, and standard loss functions handle the strongly skewed distribution of urban flows poorly. Their answer pairs a lightweight design with a redesigned loss.

The design, PLGF, progressively fuses local detail with global context, capturing both street-level variation and citywide dependencies. DualFocal Loss supervises in two spaces and focuses adaptively on hard-to-predict regions. Across four real-world cases the method set state-of-the-art accuracy while shrinking model size by up to ninety-seven percent against high-performing rivals. Under equal parameter budgets it improved accuracy by over ten percent, and code is available.
arxiv-2511-07298:
Kagan Celik, Mehmet Ozan Unal, Metin Ertas, and Isa Yildirim assess the quality of low-dose CT images with a large language model. Lower radiation doses protect patients but add noise, blur, and contrast loss, so clinics need quality judgments that are consistent, robust, and explainable.
