Their system yields both a numerical quality score and a textual description of the degradations present in a scan.

The authors systematically compare inference plans, from plain zero-shot prompting to adding metadata and feeding back errors for correction, measuring what each step contributes. The resulting scores correlate highly with reference quality while the text output tells clinicians what is wrong, not just how bad it is. Code is publicly available, positioning the tool as an interpretable aid for clinical quality control.
arxiv-2511-07498:
Xin Liu and colleagues hunt for the attention heads that carry language skill inside multilingual models. Large models handle many languages, but which internal parts do that work stayed murky. Attention heads are a natural suspect because they steer what the model focuses on.

Their scoring method, LAHIS, rates each head with one forward and one backward pass. Applied to three open models, it finds heads tied to single languages and heads shared across many. Knowing which heads matter guides tuning and pruning without harming language coverage. The study turns a vague ability into located, testable parts that engineers can protect or improve.
arxiv-2511-07698:
Mohammadjavad Mehditabar, Saurabhsingh Rajput, and Antonio Mastropaolo weigh code models on correctness and energy together. A model that writes working code while burning excess power may lose to a thriftier rival in real deployment. Earlier work lacked a shared scale for that trade-off.

Their BRACE framework benchmarks twenty two leading models on code generation and summarization. Two rating schemes fold accuracy and energy into comparable grades. Results expose models that look smart but cost dearly per correct answer. As coding assistants spread through industry, energy-aware leaderboards can steer purchases and research toward efficiency without surrendering quality.
arxiv-2511-07898:
Chuanfu Xiao and Jiaxin Zeng fish the largest entries out of compressed tensors without unpacking them. High-dimensional data are stored in low-rank factorized form to save memory, yet applications often need only the top few values. Expanding the full tensor defeats the compression.

The retrieval task is recast as a continuous constrained optimization problem. A block-alternating iterative algorithm then attacks it piece by piece, converging on the extreme entries. Recommendation, signal processing, and data mining all ask for top elements of huge arrays. Methods that answer from the factorization alone keep big-data workflows affordable.
arxiv-2511-07998:
Yushan Zhu and colleagues propose self-correction distillation to help small language models answer questions over structured data. Table, knowledge graph, and temporal graph questions need exact structured queries. Small models often make query errors that larger unified frameworks handle better, limiting their use in systems like TrustUQA.

An error prompt mechanism spots mistakes during inference and returns tailored messages about them. A two stage teaching process then transfers query writing and error fixing skills from large models to an eight billion parameter model. Across five benchmarks, the method generalizes best among distillation rivals and nears GPT-4 on some data sets.
arxiv-2511-08298:
Luca Bindini, Simone Giovannini, Simone Marinai, and Valeria Nardoni test whether vision large language models can recover the hidden hierarchy inside complex scientific tables. Tables in papers often group columns and rows under layered headings, and reading values correctly depends on that structure. The team drew on the PubTables collection to build CHiTab, a benchmark of tables with hierarchical headings.

Prompt engineering in several formats and styles probes what off the shelf open weight models can infer without extra processing. Some models are then fine tuned for the task, and human performance on a small set gives a reference point. Generic models can do the job to a degree, revealing both potential and limits.
arxiv-2511-08598:
Yanhong Li and five co-authors build a benchmark machine for knowledge questions that never sits still. Static test sets drawn from textbooks go stale as the world changes, so their framework, OKBench, generates fresh benchmarks on demand, focusing on news where facts update daily.

Software agents handle the whole pipeline: sourcing material, writing questions, validating them, and distributing the finished test. Because the questions are new, they barely overlap with what models memorized in training, which also makes the tests fair for retrieval-augmented systems. Trying many open and commercial models, the team finds retrieval shrinks the gap between small and large models. Behavior on fresh facts differs sharply from behavior on memorized ones.
arxiv-2511-08898:
Simon Hempel-Costello and thirteen co-authors measure the low-frequency noise of a new kind of submillimeter detector being built for the NEW-MUSIC camera. The devices are lumped-element kinetic inductance detectors made of aluminum, coupled by microstrip, with parallel-plate capacitors formed from hydrogenated amorphous silicon.

Amorphous materials often bring two-level-system noise that ruins slow measurements, so the question was whether that capacitor choice would spoil the design. In darkness the devices stay limited by generation-recombination noise down to a tenth of a hertz. Under optical load they appear limited by that noise plus photon noise to similarly low rates. The readings cap the material's low-frequency noise at levels in line with kilohertz-regime results. The design should therefore be photon-noise limited in real observing, even for the slowest astronomy work.
arxiv-2511-09098:
Xiao-Song Yang and Zhi-Gang Wang test whether an exotic particle seen in experiments, the Y(4660), is really a tetraquark, a bound state of four quarks rather than the usual two or three. The Y(4660) is a vector charmonium-like state whose internal structure has stayed enigmatic since its discovery.

Four candidate tetraquark configurations are examined with three-point QCD sum rules, a method that ties quark-level calculations to hadronic observables through quark-hadron duality, keeping vacuum condensates up to dimension five. The calculation yields the hadronic coupling constants and from them the partial widths for the strong decays of each candidate. One configuration, a strange-charm tetraquark with the Y(4660)'s quantum numbers, predicts a total width of about sixty-one point five MeV, in excellent agreement with the measured value. The authors read that match as support for the tetraquark interpretation.
arxiv-2511-09198:
P. Vermot and co-authors use new JWST mid-infrared spectra to dissect the gas at the center of our own galaxy. The Mid-Infrared Instrument's spectrometer covered wavelengths from 5 to 27 micrometres across the circumnuclear disk and the central cavity. The team compared the spectra with synthetic ones from the CLOUDY photoionization code.

Four dominant gas phases emerge from the fitting. Warm ionized gas, at temperatures from ten thousand to roughly sixty thousand kelvin, produces most of the emission in both regions. Molecular gas is structured and significant in the disk but scarce in the cavity, while coronal gas sits between phases. Enhanced carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and alpha elements, with suppressed iron, point to recent massive star formation.
arxiv-2511-09498:
Martin Baránek and seven co-authors demonstrate a simple way to align an optical fiber precisely onto a superconducting single-photon detector. These nanowire detectors need light delivered to a tiny meander-shaped wire, and alignment usually relies on back-reflection or transmission tricks. Their method instead listens to the wire's own electrical resistance.

Light absorbed by the nanowire heats it slightly, changing its resistivity in a way a lock-in amplifier can track. Scanning the fiber maps the photothermal response, whose peak marks the optimal alignment spot. The technique centers the fiber on the meander with sub-micron precision. It stays robust when the fiber's angle and height vary, making it a practical complement to established alignment methods.
arxiv-2511-09598:
Tingyang Wei and five co-authors teach a generative model to answer whole families of multi-objective problems at once. Each working setup defines its own costly problem with competing aims. The space of setups is continuous, so solving problem by problem never ends. Their method instead learns an inverse model mapping setups and preferences to good solutions.

Training alternates between sampling candidate solutions from a conditional generative model and guided search that shares strength across tasks. Task-aware Gaussian processes back the faster convergence in theory by exploiting inter-task synergies. Tests on synthetic and real-world benchmarks verify the approach. Once trained, the model predicts solutions for unseen parameterized problems with no fresh costly runs.
arxiv-2511-09698:
Samuel J. Eschker and four co-authors quantify how natural disasters push homeowners toward mortgage default, using a state-space model. Mortgage default rates guide insurers' decisions and sit inside their asset-liability management, since mortgage assets fill insurer portfolios. Hazard losses that trigger insurance payouts may simultaneously raise defaults, compounding the strain.

The state-space approach separates the hazard effect from other economic drivers through latent variables. A sliced variant lets the relationship switch on only when hazard losses grow sufficiently large. The model confirms that this threshold relationship is statistically significant, the authors report. Their results clarify how disaster losses surface as mortgage defaults, information insurers can use when stress-testing portfolios against catastrophe scenarios.
arxiv-2511-10298:
Li-Yuan Zhang and eight co-authors use pion-nucleus femtoscopy to learn how light nuclei and antinuclei form in high-energy collisions. These bound states emerge at temperatures far above their binding energies, and whether they form by statistical hadronization, nucleon coalescence, or ongoing reactions has stayed unsettled. The team solves relativistic kinetic equations for pion-catalyzed reactions that create deuterons, adding final-state scatterings from an established interaction.

Their calculation reproduces the resonance peaks in pion-proton and pion-deuteron correlation data from proton runs at thirteen TeV. Interplay between them shifts both peaks down by about seventy MeV from naive expectations. Coalescence and that model, by contrast, underestimate the data and predict dips that are absent, making pion-driven production the favored mechanism.
arxiv-2511-10398:
Joscha Henheik, Vadim Kaloshin, Yunzhe Li, and Amir Vig study whether the spectrum of a surface determines its shape. They focus on a special family of metrics on a doughnut-shaped torus. Liouville metrics are the known examples whose geodesic flow is integrable, meaning moving paths stay orderly instead of chaotic. A long-standing belief says no other metrics on the torus have that property.

Working inside a fixed conformal class, the authors prove two rigidity results about deformations that keep the Laplace spectrum unchanged. Deformations that are affine in the small parameter must be trivial. Analytic deformations with well-behaved coefficients stay within the Liouville family and amount to rearranging the original metric piece by piece. The proofs recover path-length data from the spectrum using wave-trace methods.
arxiv-2511-10998:
M. Jabłońska, T. Różański, and their colleagues present SPICE, an open-source Python package that builds fake star spectra for stars whose surfaces are not uniform. Spots, chemical patches, pulses, and tidal pulls can all mark a star's face, and large sky surveys can now catch those marks. Most older tools assume a smooth, even surface, which limits what they can explain.

SPICE adds up light from each surface patch at the right viewing angle, so it can model changes in both brightness and spectra over time. Demo cases cover spotted stars, pulsing Cepheids, and eclipsing pairs. It can also import shapes from the PHOEBE package for complex pairs.
arxiv-2511-11098:
Georgi Angelov, Alberto Domínguez Corella, and Vladimir Veliov measure how accurate model predictive control is when its inputs are imperfect. That control method repeatedly solves a short-horizon problem and applies the first step, using fresh state readings each round. Forecasts, readings, and the short solves can all carry error, and users need to know how far the result drifts from ideal.

Their main result bounds that drift against the best open-loop answer for the perfect case. The proof stretches a regularity notion for set-valued maps and uses a new distance in the control space. They then tailor the bound to two broad problem classes.
arxiv-2511-11198:
Shambhavi Shanker, Manikandan Padmanaban, and Jagabondhu Hazra propose a satellite question-answering system that reasons step by step in geospatial terms. Such systems can scan vast remote sensing data, but complex spatial queries need structured thought, not a single leap to an answer. The stakes are high in climate work, from disaster watch to city resilience planning.

Their frame pairs chain-of-thought reasoning, where the model writes out middle steps, with preference tuning that rewards better reasoning paths. Step supervision raised accuracy by about a third over direct baselines, and the tuning added further gains. Tasks covered detection, classification, spatial relations, and comparisons.
arxiv-2511-11598:
Van-Vi Vo, Tien-Dung Nguyen, Duc-Tai Le, and Hyunseung Choo build shortest-path trees for internet-of-things sensor networks with distributed Q-learning instead of a central algorithm. Classic methods such as Dijkstra's need global knowledge and heavy computation, both scarce in networks of small battery-powered nodes.

Each node learns its best next hop from local information alone, using states based on position and routing history and rewards that favor progress toward the sink. Trained across varied layouts, the method transfers to unseen networks. Simulations with one hundred to five hundred nodes reach over ninety-nine percent routing accuracy, suggesting learning can replace central planning in dynamic sensor fields.
arxiv-2511-11698:
Chenghao Liu and nine co-authors present Moirai 2.0, a time series foundation model rebuilt around the idea that simpler can forecast better. Trained on a fresh corpus of thirty-six million series, it uses a decoder-only design with quantile forecasting, which predicts ranges rather than single points, and multi-token prediction for speed.

Compared with its predecessor, masked-encoder training, multi-patch inputs, and mixture outputs are all dropped. Ablations credit the decoder backbone and recursive multi-quantile decoding for most of the gains. On the Gift-Eval benchmark the smaller, simpler model ranks among the top pretrained systems, a useful data point in debates about scaling time series models.
arxiv-2511-11898:
Arnav Singhvi and four co-authors improve vision-language models on medical imaging benchmarks not by retraining them, but by optimizing their prompts in a structured, automatic way. Fine-tuning needs large domain datasets and heavy compute, while hand-written prompts rarely transfer between institutions or tasks.

Adapting the DSPy framework, which treats prompts as programs to be compiled and tuned, the team searches prompt space systematically while leaving model weights untouched. The method draws on knowledge already inside the model, making gains accessible to hospitals without machine learning teams. Weight-agnostic improvement is the draw: any institution using the same foundation model could apply the optimized prompts immediately.
arxiv-2511-11998:
Abinaya Swaruba Rajamuthukumar and four co-authors test whether a helium star donor explains D6-2, one of the hypervelocity stars flung out of the galaxy by a Type Ia supernova. These runaway survivors are precious because they were there: the companion star that fed the exploding white dwarf and lived to tell the tale.

Binary evolution calculations with MESA, plus population synthesis, follow hot subdwarf and white dwarf pairs through helium accretion. Donors can burn nearly all their helium and form compact carbon-oxygen cores before the explosion, and predicted ejection speeds reach roughly a thousand kilometers per second. D6-2 sits at the extreme fast tail of that distribution, consistent with the helium-star channel.
arxiv-2511-12598: Hongda Qiu constructs an example of a smooth closed surface in three-dimensional space. Topologically it is a sphere. All its normal curvatures are bounded by one in absolute value. Yet it encloses less volume than a unit ball. The example gives a negative answer to a question of Dmitri Burago and Anton Petrunin. Their question asked how curvature bounds constrain enclosed volume.
arxiv-2511-12698:
Kenichiro McAlinn and Kōsaku Takanashi question a habit every data analyst knows: splitting data for cross-validation by convention, such as eighty percent for training and twenty percent for testing. That split sets training size and test certainty, yet the usual choices are rules of thumb. The authors formalize the trade-off by scoring predictive performance while explicitly penalizing uncertainty in the evaluation itself, a quantity that needs stated assumptions.

They derive formulas for that uncertainty and turn them into a rule for choosing the hold-out size from an assumed noise level. Tests with linear regression and random forests across several domains, plus a high-dimensional genomics case, show the best split depends on the data, the model, and the noise assumption. The conclusions drawn from the same dataset can shift with the split, so the authors urge making the choice explicit rather than automatic.
arxiv-2511-12798:
Juan C. Rocha and twenty-six co-authors review two strands of sustainability science that grew apart: regime shifts and transformations. Regime shift research studies sudden, nonlinear changes in social-ecological systems, like a lake flipping to algae dominance. Transformation research studies deliberate, deep changes toward safer and fairer futures. Both fields share intellectual roots, yet they developed separately with little exchange, and the authors argue that split has cost both sides useful tools and ideas.

The review untangles the definitions and history of each stream, marking where they agree and where they truly differ. It then proposes research avenues that join them: preventing harmful shifts, promoting desirable ones, and anticipating both in time to act. Stronger integration, the authors argue, would give societies better ways to steer toward safe and just futures. The paper is a field-shaping synthesis aimed at researchers and practitioners who manage ecosystems under pressure.
arxiv-2511-13098:
Haiyang Li and Yijie Shen make a hidden property of light visible to the naked eye. The Pancharatnam-Berry phase is a geometric phase that light accumulates, normally measured with interferometers or by cutting beams with special apertures. In structured beams with an SU(2) pattern, wave packets travel along caustic paths, bright curves where light concentrates, as the beam propagates. The authors show that watching those caustic-linked packets evolve reveals the geometric phase directly, along with the Gouy phase, with no interferometer and no truncation.

The method turns an abstract phase into a picture that changes as the beam travels. It gives intuition for phase geometry and a simpler measurement route for labs lacking interferometers. The authors suggest optical systems designed around phase geometry can use the visualization both as a diagnostic and as a design aid.
arxiv-2511-13298:
Kazimierz Chomicz and 3 co-authors study a striking conic tied to a cyclic quadrilateral and its four orthocenters. The four vertices and the four orthocenters of the triangles formed by the other vertices all lie on one conic. They ask how far that neat fact can be pushed.

For points chosen on Euler lines so that a key ratio stays constant, they show the vertices and the isogonal conjugates of those points again share a single conic. Proofs are given in synthetic, projective, and algebraic styles. They also place the chosen points within the known catalog of triangle centers.
arxiv-2511-13398:
Gleb Berloff and 5 co-authors search for magnetic activity cycles in solar-like stars using sound-wave data from the K2 mission. Starspots and magnetic cycles shift the frequencies of a star's oscillations over time, much as they do on the Sun. The study draws on the KEYSTONE sample of stars that pulse like the Sun.

For twenty stars they could tell whether mode frequencies changed, using both cross-correlation and direct mode fitting. A few stars showed shifts beyond their errors by both methods, with more flagged by one method alone. Shift size grew with rotation rate and surface heat, and even one evolved subgiant showed a clear shift, hinting that older stars can stay magnetically active.
arxiv-2511-13598:
Jiaxiong Tang and 5 co-authors present RISE, a watermarking scheme that protects both sides of split federated learning. In that setup, clients run small models on private data and send middle outputs to a strong server, so no one party owns the whole model. Standard watermarks fail here because ownership is shared.

RISE embeds two kinds of marks at once: the server adds feature-based marks through a loss term, while clients add backdoor marks with preset trigger samples. Each side can then verify ownership on its own. Tests across datasets and network designs passed ninety-five percent detection in most settings, with no cross-interference and solid resistance to removal attacks.
arxiv-2511-14098:
Adit Jain, Vikram Krishnamurthy, and Yiming Zhang model teams of language models answering questions together. Each model in a network holds part of the documents needed, so they must share findings to estimate one ground truth. The risk is contagion: when evidence is thin, one model's hallucination can spread and flip previously correct partners.

The authors build a generative model that mixes mean-field dynamics from network science with a randomized utility model from economics. Each model carries a latent truthful-or-not state, and the team derives conditions for a unique stable outcome. They analyze how that outcome shifts with incentives such as extra test-time computing given to individual models.
arxiv-2511-14198:
Wendy Wong, Yuchao Jiang, and Yuekang Li use fake students to test course slides for a first programming class. Such classes often give all students the same slides. That load can swamp students with autism, ADHD, or dyslexia. Their pilot tool, DiverseClaire, uses language models to play students with mixed profiles, some of them neurodiverse. It has them try slides in plain form, and in a form rebuilt for access for all.

The fake neurodiverse students had a hard time with slides in forms they could not access. The point is plain: give slides in more than one format, so each student can pick what works. The team will share its pilot data to help future teachers of the class.
arxiv-2511-14698:
Sriram Srinivasan, Srinivasan Aruchamy, and Siva Ram Krishna Vadali propose HyMAD, a system that watches borders using buried seismic sensors. Ground sensors are small and hard for intruders to spot, avoid, or damage, unlike cameras or fences. The hard part is telling apart events that happen at once, such as people walking, animals moving, and vehicles passing.

HyMAD is built to detect several activities at the same time from noisy ground signals. Missing that overlap can cause wrong labels, missed events, and a poor picture of what is happening. The hybrid design aims to separate the mixed signals well enough for reliable alerts. Stronger separation would make quiet, low-cost border monitoring more trustworthy.
arxiv-2511-14998:
Yueru He, Xueqing Peng, and fourteen co-authors introduce FinCriticalED, a benchmark that tests whether document-reading systems preserve the facts that matter in finance. Modern multimodal models score well on ordinary text recognition, yet a single wrong digit or date in a financial page can flip its meaning. Surface similarity scores hide exactly those dangerous errors.

The benchmark holds hundreds of real financial pages with thousands of expert-marked facts across five types: numbers, dates, money units, reporting firms, and financial concepts. Systems are graded on whether critical evidence survives reading, not just on whether words look alike. The goal is a sterner test for tools that banks and auditors might trust.
arxiv-2511-15698:
Naveen Raman, Jingwu Tang, and five co-authors build RescueLens, a tool that helps a food rescue group act on volunteer feedback. Food rescue groups move surplus food from donors to people who need it, using volunteers. Feedback can flag problems early, but organizers at 412 Food Rescue in Pittsburgh had to sort it by hand, which made setting priorities slow and labor-intensive.

RescueLens uses a large language model to categorize feedback, suggest which donors and recipients to follow up with, and update volunteer directions. On labeled data it recovered most volunteer issues with solid precision. Ranking by issue rates showed a tiny share of donors caused a large share of problems, letting organizers focus effort where it matters.
arxiv-2511-15798:
Ali Rostami-Shirazi, Narges Rostami, Hosein Haghi, and Akram Hasani Zonoozi report a missing population of globular clusters near galaxy centers. Globular clusters are dense, ancient star balls orbiting galaxies, sorted by position and metallicity, the share of heavy elements in their stars. Across thirty-seven host galaxies, the authors mapped clusters by distance from the center and iron content.

A triangular region empty of metal-poor clusters appears in the inner parts of every galaxy, and it grows with host mass. They attribute the pattern to retained black holes inside metal-poor clusters. A compact, massive black hole subsystem stirs stars energetically, and strong central tides then dissolve those clusters faster. The region shape may even serve as a distance indicator.
arxiv-2511-16198:
Sebastian Haan introduces SemanticCite. SemanticCite is an AI system that verifies whether citations in scientific writing truly support the claims attached to them. Sound citations validate sources and guide readers to evidence. But semantic errors that misstate sources, hallucinated references from AI tools, and whole-paper pointers with no section guidance are growing problems. The system analyzes the full text of cited sources directly.

Several retrieval methods feed a four-class judgment: supported, partly supported, unsupported, or uncertain. That captures nuanced claim-source links and enables fitting remedies for each error type. Tests show fine-tuned lightweight models match large commercial systems at far lower cost. That makes large-scale checking feasible, with transparent, evidence-based reasons and text snippets for users.
arxiv-2511-16498:
Rui Wang and four co-authors segment breast tumors in dynamic contrast enhanced MRI by informing the model of each image's acquisition time. Contrast dynamics highlight tumors, but timing varies across protocols and patients. Images from the same nominal phase can therefore look quite different. Their method modulates network features with the actual acquisition time of each scan.

Lightweight feature wise linear modulation layers inject the timing information. The design handles a variable number of images per study, using the full sequence. Time aware features should separate tumor enhancement curves from normal tissue more reliably. Screening, assessment, and treatment monitoring all depend on accurate tumor outlines. Conditioning on time rather than phase labels alone addresses a real source of segmentation failure.
arxiv-2511-17298:
Artem Frenk and Roee Shraga introduce SAVeD, a system that recognizes when two structured datasets are versions of one another, without trusting metadata or labels. Data scientists waste effort redoing transformations because they cannot tell that a table on hand is a near-copy of earlier work. SAVeD learns the semantic fingerprint of a dataset by contrast: it creates altered views of a table through changes like deleting rows or perturbing encodings. It trains an encoder to pull views of the same table together and push unrelated tables apart.

Evaluated on five datasets from a semantic versioning benchmark, the trained model classified version pairs on completely unseen tables far more accurately than before training. Its separation between versioned and unrelated pairs also grew substantially. Against an untrained baseline and the prior leading discovery method, the custom encoder was competitive or better.
arxiv-2511-17398:
Abhijeet Nayak and 12 co-authors grow and characterize a new family of kagome lattice magnets, compounds where iron atoms sit on a corner-sharing triangle pattern prized for exotic magnetism. Most kagome compounds are hexagonal. These, with formula built from a rare earth, iron, and germanium, crystallize in a rarer orthorhombic form, derived from a hexagonal prototype by replacing every other rare-earth atom with a germanium pair. That substitution slightly distorts the kagome net and makes the three iron sites inequivalent.

The iron and rare-earth sublattices order independently: iron moments align above 400 kelvin in ferromagnetic planes stacked antiferromagnetically, while rare-earth moments order only below 9 kelvin. The terbium and dysprosium members behave differently from each other, the latter showing two transitions shaped by crystal electric fields. Density functional calculations explain the iron ordering and reveal a hierarchy of structural energy scales.
arxiv-2511-17498:
Ana Sofía M. Uzsoy and 53 co-authors examine whether a galaxy's surroundings change the shape and brightness of its Lyman-alpha emission line. Lyman-alpha emitters are young, star-forming galaxies used to trace large-scale structure at high redshift. The team combined spectroscopy from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument with narrow-band imaging from the ODIN survey, mapping local environmental density for emitters in two redshift slices. They then stack spectra by density and by whether galaxies sat inside protoclusters.

In the higher-redshift slice, protocluster galaxies showed about 15 percent higher line luminosity, suggesting boosted star formation there; the lower slice showed no such gain, hinting the effect evolves with time. The line's shape, however, did not vary with environment at all, implying shape changes come from local processes inside each galaxy. The results connect environment, ionized gas, and emission strength.
arxiv-2511-17598:
Zhizuo Chen and Theodore T. Allen generalize the decision framework beneath reinforcement learning. The classic Markov decision process assumes a stationary world and usually an infinite horizon with a fixed discount rate, assumptions that strain in changing environments and finite tasks. Their NVMDP framework lets the environment be non-stationary and the discount rate vary with time and transitions, while containing the stationary, infinite-horizon, and finite-horizon formulations as special cases. It also gives designers a new lever for shaping optimal policies without touching states, actions, or rewards.

The authors build the theory from value functions and optimality conditions through policy improvement, then adapt dynamic programming and generalized Q-learning with convergence proofs. They extend the policy gradient theorem and trust region bounds for function approximation. In a non-stationary gridworld, their algorithms recovered optimal behavior under several reward and discounting schemes where ordinary Q-learning failed.
arxiv-2511-18198:
Wentao Yang, Bao Yan, Muxi Zheng, Quanfeng Lu, Shijie Wei, and Gui-Lu Long revisit Regev's quantum factoring algorithm. A newer variant of the quantum method that threatens RSA encryption by factoring large numbers. Regev's version shrinks the circuit but demands far more qubits, and working builds have been lacking. The team attacks the space problem with qubit reuse, undoing intermediate steps so qubits can serve again, a trick borrowed from reversible computing.

Their basic plan cuts the space cost sharply, and refined plans reach a level they identify as the floor within this model. Simulations chart the trade between time and space, and compiled circuits factor the number thirty-five under noisy simulation. A simplified experimental circuit is also reported, moving the algorithm closer to practice.
arxiv-2511-18298:
Svitlana Volkova and eight co-authors build BioSage, a compound system meant to help scientists find and join facts across fields. Papers now grow so fast that no reader can track work outside a narrow lane. A find in one field may solve a block in another, yet the link stays hidden by distinct terms and habits.

BioSage pairs large language models with search over source texts. One agent plans queries and drafts answers backed by cited sources. Other agents translate terms across fields and weigh claims with a clear trail. Tests on science question sets, plus a new cross field biology test, gauge the design. The aim is faster, checkable synthesis for joint work.
arxiv-2511-18398:
Xiangzhou Zhu, Patrick Rinke, and David Egger predict how defects change a semiconductor's electronic behavior at real temperatures. That task is costly with standard quantum calculations because many atoms and many thermal configurations are involved. Their framework pairs two equivariant neural networks, one for atomic energies and forces and one for the electronic Hamiltonian.

An active learning loop trains the networks efficiently. For point defects in gallium arsenide, the method matches density functional accuracy at a fraction of the cost. It also predicts the temperature dependent band gap from large simulations within a few tens of milli electron volts. The approach suits complex, evolving materials.
arxiv-2511-18498:
Yue Li, Ifteher Alom, Wenhai Sun, and Yang Xiao design DEXO, a fair market for data from linked devices. Sensor and phone data hold real value, but buyers cannot check if data are true, and sellers fear no pay for true data. With no trust on either side, trade stalls.

DEXO grows the oracle network model used in blockchain systems. Trusted hardware enclaves, secret sharing, and smart contracts are woven so the buyer can verify how data were made, and the seller is paid for true data by rule. The platform pledges correctness of the swap itself. The design scales to many spread providers. It aims to unlock device data value with trust built into the trade.
arxiv-2511-18698:
Aman Verma, Keshav Samdani, and Mohd. Samiuddin Shafi build a room monitoring system that watches video and audio in sync to recognize actions and detect anomalies in real time. They describe two generations of the system, from a lightweight first version to a much richer second one.

The advanced version ensembles three audio models, pairs two object detectors, and fuses the streams with attention that works in both directions, plus several anomaly detection methods. Evaluation shows it works well in general monitoring and in factory safety uses, with real time speed on standard hardware. The evolution illustrates how multi-type fusion lifts robustness for useful deployment.
arxiv-2511-18798:
Dinesh Kumar gives a plain test for when a networked reaction diffusion system stays stable near a uniform state. Patches at the nodes may run unlike local rules, a case classic tools exclude: both the bookkeeping method of Jansen and Lloyd and the master stability method need like nodes. Real patchworks, from tissue to coupled reactors, break that sameness.

His condition splits in two clean parts. One part is a diagonal dominance check on the space averaged Jacobian of the local dynamics, read straight from model parameters with no full eigen solve. The other part is a low cost check on the network's spread. Two quick checks replace one huge one. Mixed patch networks gain a usable stability screen.
arxiv-2511-19198:
Ann-Sophia Müller, Moonkwang Jeong, Meng Zhang, Jiyuan Tian, Arkadiusz Miernik, Stefanie Speidel, and Tian Qiu generate three-dimensional anatomical data without patients. Machine learning for surgery needs many 3D organ models rebuilt from scans, but gathering them from real patients hits legal. Ethical, and technical walls, especially for soft organs with poor imaging contrast like the prostate. Their workflow starts instead from physical organ models made of biomimetic gels that image like real tissue across several zones.

Those physical models are scanned and used to simulate endoscopic surgery, producing labelled training data. A generative network then expands the set into a manifold of varied 3D models for downstream learning tasks. The pipeline offers surgical AI teams a way to train and test without waiting on scarce, sensitive patient data.
arxiv-2511-19698:
George E. Andrews and Brian Hopkins extend a counting theorem about integer partitions, the ways of writing a number as a sum of parts. The crank-mex theorem links partitions whose crank is non-negative with those whose smallest missing part, the mex, is odd. Andrews and Newman had refined that link using the count of parts larger than one.

The new work adds a companion result tying together partitions with even mex, partitions with fixed points, and those with negative or positive crank, again refined by parts larger than one. Both analytic and combinatorial proofs are given, so the identities are seen from two distinct angles.
arxiv-2511-19998:
Nikit Phadke presents REWA, a proposed general theory of likeness-preserving encodings. Many known tools, from Bloom filters and locality sensitive hashing to random Fourier features and transformer attention, measure or keep likeness in their own ways. Phadke claims they are all cases of one mechanism, which he calls functional witness projection over monoids.

Working in that frame, he states encoding bounds with ranking preserved for all algebraic structures, with full proofs under four-wise independent hashing. Heavy-tailed witnesses are handled by normalization and clipping, and explicit constructions are given for Boolean, natural, real, tropical, and product monoids. He also proves tight concentration bounds and composition rules for building multi-part systems. The claims are sweeping and are presented as the author's results.
arxiv-2511-20098:
Chug, Bass, Beyene, and the J-PET Collaboration test a bedrock symmetry of physics with positronium. Their 2025 paper measures CPT symmetry in ortho-positronium decays. CPT combines charge, parity, and time reversal operations. Quantum field theory demands it hold exactly. Positronium is an atom of electron plus positron.

The J-PET detector uses 192 plastic scintillator strips. A sodium-22 source at its center emits positrons. Positronium forms inside a porous-lined spherical chamber. Reconstructed annihilation points reveal each atom's flight direction. That direction sets the polarization axis without magnets. Data taking ran for 356 days in total. About 47.8 million three-photon decays were identified. The CPT-sensitive angular correlation was measured precisely. Its asymmetry amplitude came out near minus three ten-thousandths. The uncertainty shrank fourfold versus the previous best. Results agree with CPT holding exactly. Fundamental physics keeps passing ever sharper tests.
arxiv-2511-20198:
López, Karlsson, and Bientinesi compile matrix chains whose sizes are unknown until runtime. Their 2025 paper handles generalized matrix chains with symbolic sizes. Such chains multiply matrices with features like symmetry or triangularity. Software must map them onto fast BLAS and LAPACK kernels. The cheapest kernel order depends heavily on sizes.

With sizes symbolic, no single order wins everywhere. Their code generator uses multi-versioning instead. At compile time it emits a few chosen variants. At runtime it picks the best variant for actual sizes. New theory guarantees near-optimal cost for all sizes. The cost stays within a constant factor of optimal. Empirical tuning then tightens the gap further. Across tested chains, ninety-five percent stayed within fifteen percent of optimal. Naive left-to-right evaluation sometimes cost five hundred times more.
arxiv-2511-20298:
Tenkorang and Yacoub work out fading stats for a new radio channel model. Their 2025 paper studies second-order behavior over Log-mu channels. Wireless signals fade as obstacles and reflections interfere. Merging several received copies boosts reliability. Designers need crossing rates and fade lengths.

Three merging schemes are analyzed in depth. Pure selection picks the strongest branch. Equal gain adds branches with matched phases. Maximal ratio weights them by quality. Closed forms emerge for selection. Level crossing rate and average fade duration are exact there. The other two schemes yield exact integral formulas. Channels are unbalanced and not identically distributed. That breadth matches messy real use better. Monte Carlo simulations validated every formula. Agreement between theory and simulation was excellent. The Log-mu model captures nonlinear spread effects. Designers gain ready performance forecasts.
arxiv-2511-20598:
Khan and Leuenberger predict frictionless flow of light-like particles in a single atomic layer. Their 2025 paper theorizes exciton superfluidity in a breathing-kagome material. The compound mixes niobium, tellurium, and chlorine in one layer. Dark excitons there behave as hard-core bosons on a lattice. Whether they can flow without resistance was unknown.

Tellurium swaps create vacancies that free the excitons to move. A Bose-Hubbard model with strong repulsion maps to a spin model. Between empty and full fillings a superfluid phase emerges. Its mean-field form comes from a canted-spin solution. A Landau-Ginzburg continuum theory then describes phase fluctuations. Vortex unbinding drives the transition, BKT style, in two dimensions. The stiffness setting the transition temperature comes from microscopic numbers. An exciton insulator state sits at about minus 0.14 electron volts. Charge-neutral flow could suppress heating in future devices.
arxiv-2511-20698:
Tsubasa Masumura and Masato Taki, of Rikkyo University, sharpen in 2025 a known link between two memory ideas. One is the modern Hopfield network, a model of associative memory borrowed from neuroscience. The other is self-attention, the core mechanism inside Transformer models. Earlier work showed the two coincide only under a simplifying approximation.

Masumura and Taki drop that approximation and find the match survives in fuller form. The price is one extra element: a hidden state taken from the Hopfield network itself, carried inside attention. Their mechanism, modern Hopfield attention, passes attention scores from the first layer through to the last. This attacks rank collapse, a failure where representations in deep Transformers blur into near-copies. In a plain GPT-2, token similarities pile up at maximum by layers 12 and 24, while the Hopfield version keeps them low. Accuracy improved on Vision Transformer and GPT tasks, with no new training parameters added.
arxiv-2511-21098:
Gayoung Lee and colleagues solve in 2025 a shiny problem in 3D reconstruction: mirrors and polished metal break the assumption that a surface looks the same from every angle. Their framework, named for the Pygmalion myth, first translates each photo of a reflective object into a clay version. The clay rendering is matte and neutral: it keeps the shape and drops the glare. A dual-branch network then reconstructs geometry. A BRDF-based reflective branch works on the original views, steadied by a clay-guided branch that refines surface normals.

The clay images act as reflection-free supervision, teaching the system what the geometry should be. On synthetic and real datasets, the method improved surface-normal accuracy substantially. Mesh completeness also beat existing reflection-handling approaches. The authors frame the lesson poetically: seeing by unshining, turning radiance into neutrality, is a powerful bias for learning the geometry of reflective things.
arxiv-2511-21798:
Boisseau tackles conjectures by Gan, Gross, and Prasad about when certain integrals over automorphic forms, highly symmetric functions in number theory, are nonzero. The setting is the split, non-tempered case for general linear groups, where the integral in question, the Rankin-Selberg period, may not even converge as written. Earlier versions of these conjectures covered only nicer, tempered representations.

Boisseau's approach builds a regularization, a way to assign a finite value to the divergent integral, using residues of zeta integrals, which extract the part of a function near a pole. He proves this regularized period satisfies the global non-tempered conjecture and its sharper Ichino-Ikeda refinement. He constructs a matching local version that is nonzero where it should be. Combined with earlier work by Chan, Chen, and Chen, the results settle these conjectures over local fields of characteristic zero.
arxiv-2511-22098:
Song, Song, Peng, Gao, and Shou, computer vision researchers, teach video generation models to translate between first-person and third-person views of the same scene. A hiker's own camera view and a bystander's shot of the hiker show the same events from radically different angles. Converting between egocentric and exocentric footage matters for filmmaking, embodied AI, world models, yet video diffusion models have barely attempted it. Their framework, WorldWander, treats the translation as in-context learning.

Two mechanisms, In-Context Perspective Alignment and Collaborative Position Encoding, synchronize the views inside a video diffusion transformer without auxiliary networks. To train and test it, the team curated EgoExo-8K, a dataset of synchronized egocentric-exocentric triplets from synthetic and real-world sources. In experiments WorldWander beats prior approaches on perspective synchronization, character consistency, and generalization, setting a new benchmark for the task. The code is publicly released.
arxiv-2511-22398:
Xie and Harting simulate what happens when two liquid lenses merge. A liquid lens is a droplet resting on another liquid surface, and merging lenses matter for inkjet printing and fog harvesting. When two lenses touch, a liquid bridge forms and grows until they become one. The team uses the pseudopotential lattice Boltzmann method, which tracks fluid motion on a grid. They study low-viscosity lenses across a wide range of contact angles. The contact angle measures how flat or domed a lens sits.

In two dimensions, simulated bridge-height growth matched experiments closely for small contact angles, and a simpler thin-sheet theory described the growth well up to contact angles of about 40 degrees. In three dimensions, early growth of the bridge radius did not depend on the contact angle at all. The link between bridge height and radius changed from curved to straight as merging progressed.
arxiv-2511-22998:
Kuang and colleagues build a better checker for multimodal AI reasoning, the step-by-step solutions that models produce when they solve math or science problems involving images. Ordinary process reward models grade each step with a single score or a written critique. But they tend toward sycophancy, agreeing with whatever the solution claims, even when it invents a visual fact that is not in the picture.

Their verifier, TIM-PRM, instead plans an investigation. It asks fresh, independent questions through external tools, checking the image evidence separately from the reasoning text so it cannot simply echo it. Their 8-billion-parameter model reached an F1 score of 61.7 on VisualProcessBench, ahead of much larger rivals scoring 60.5 and 52.6 on the same benchmark. Even the 2-billion version beat a dedicated 8-billion scoring model, suggesting that active checking beats simply building a bigger judge.
arxiv-2511-23198:
Mocko and colleagues run the first malware-clustering study on complete public benchmark datasets rather than hand-picked subsets, asking which unsupervised algorithms best group malicious programs by family. They also extend the task in a way earlier work avoided, mixing benign programs into the pool instead of assuming a detector has already filtered them out. So the clustering must handle clean and malicious samples together.

On the Bodmas and Ember benchmarks, plain K-Means took the top spot with 92 percent homogeneity on Bodmas and 82 percent on Ember. BIRCH also beat the fashionable density-based DBSCAN and hierarchical clustering, contrary to popular opinion in the field. Adding benign samples did not significantly degrade cluster quality. And quality varied considerably between datasets sharing the same features, which the authors read as a warning that dataset composition drives results as much as algorithm choice.
arxiv-2511-23298:
Marti-Shahandeh and colleagues present algorithms built into the Oscar computer algebra system for computing zero-dimensional tropical varieties. A tropical variety is a pattern-based shadow of the solution set of polynomial equations. Zero-dimensional means this shadow is just a finite set of points. Such computations help prove results elsewhere, from results in celestial mechanics to better ways of solving polynomial systems.

The method uses triangular decomposition and root approximation, but fixes a practical flaw in how Oscar handles inexact numbers. Oscar stores polynomials sparsely, so terms that look like zero get deleted and precision is lost. The team adds extra variables that track those error terms instead. Unlike earlier versions, the code no longer sends root approximation out to magma, so the needed precision is controlled directly. It also leans on Oscar's built-in algebraic closure tools rather than tracking field extensions by hand.
arxiv-2511-23398:
Trezzini and colleagues build an exact renormalisation scheme for fermionic cellular automata, the discrete, reversible. Local dynamics of fermionic modes on a lattice used in digital quantum field theory and simulation. Grouping neighboring cells into tiles and selecting subspaces inside them, several microscopic evolution steps become a single step of a coarser effective automaton. And the authors derive a necessary and sufficient condition for when this coarse-graining is possible.

For the concrete case of two-cell tiles and two time steps of nearest-neighbor automata on a chain of spinless modes. They fully characterize the renormalisation flow and identify all of its fixed points. The fermionic setting admits more renormalisable evolutions than the earlier qubit version, yet a striking limitation persists. Since no renormalisable automaton in this class propagates information in a nontrivial way, motivating studies of larger local algebras.
arxiv-2512-00098:
Most cyber defenses assume attackers act rationally, weighing costs and gains like careful accountants. Brandon Beltz and a large team of co-authors challenge that assumption in a 2025 study of GAMBiT. Their framework treats human biases and cognitive limits as a defensive surface that security systems can use.

GAMBiT, short for Guarding Against Malicious Biased Threats, uses cognitive sensors and triggers designed around how real attackers actually behave. The study also includes behavioral impact analysis of the design. If defenders can predict biased choices, they may steer attackers toward traps and away from the systems that matter most. Cyber teams can use behavior-based traps alongside the firewalls and scanners they already run.
arxiv-2512-00198:
Breast cancer is one of the leading causes of death among women worldwide. Shantanu Ghosh and a large team introduce Mammo-FM in 2025, a foundation model built specifically for mammography. Foundation models are large AI systems pre-trained on broad data, then adapted to many tasks.

Mammo-FM was pre-trained on what the authors describe as the largest and most diverse mammography dataset to date, drawn from four United States institutions. The model targets diagnosis, prognosis, and report writing in one system. A breast-specific foundation model could make screening support tools more accurate and more consistent across hospitals. A shared foundation could also cut the cost of building tools for smaller clinics.
arxiv-2512-00598:
Predicting complications after spinal fusion surgery for scoliosis is hard, and models can quietly inherit demographic bias. Yining Yuan and co-authors present FAIR-MTL in 2025, a fairness-aware multitask learning framework for fair prediction of complication severity after surgery. Spinal fusion is a high-risk procedure with varied outcomes.

Many fairness methods flatten outcomes and spread bias by accident. Decomposing the prediction task in a fairness-aware way gives finer-grained, more equitable estimates. Families and surgeons deserve risk predictions that are accurate for every demographic group, not just on average across a hospital's population. Severity prediction is finer than a yes-or-no complication flag, and harder to bias quietly. Multitask learning shares strength across related outcomes instead of isolating them. For families, the gain is fair odds. The risk call should be as true for their child as for any child in the ward.
arxiv-2512-00698:
Five researchers, led by Bahrul Ilmi Nasution, compare ways to make synthetic data tables in a 2025 paper. Synthetic data can stand in for real records when sharing the real thing would risk privacy. Diffusion models have set recent benchmarks for building such tables, row by row.

Flow matching is a newer alternative for generating data. The team studies several ways to apply it to tabular data, where columns mix numbers and categories. They compare plain and variational flow matching against leading diffusion methods. Their broad empirical study helps practitioners choose a generator that keeps data useful while protecting the people behind it.
arxiv-2512-01498:
Ali Nafisi and co-authors report winning entries for the Rayan AI Contest. Three tasks were set. One was image search from mixed text and image cues. One was spotting odd items with no prior cases. One was finding models that had been secretly tampered with.

Their image search tool blends visual and text cues to fetch the right image. It scored well above the next team. The report walks through all three tools step by step. Shared winning methods help other teams lift their own work on search, anomaly spotting, and model safety checks.
arxiv-2512-01898:
Extremal black holes sit at the edge of what physics allows, carrying the largest charge or spin possible for their mass. Chiara Coviello and Ruth Gregory take a fresh look in 2025 at whether such objects could really exist within ordinary, non-supersymmetric low-energy physics.

A charged black hole can shed its charge by creating particle pairs, a process called Schwinger discharge. By including prefactors and volume effects that earlier estimates skipped, the authors show this discharge in charge-neutral surroundings is far more efficient than commonly assumed. That efficiency tightens the case about which extremal black holes nature could actually sustain.
arxiv-2512-01998:
Dark matter may carry its own sound waves in the early universe, leaving ripples called dark acoustic oscillations in how matter clumps. Jared Barron and co-authors use 2025 measurements of distant galaxies to hunt for those ripples and limit how strong they can be.

They rely on the ultraviolet luminosity function, a census of galaxy brightness at high redshift, which is sensitive to clumping on small scales. The search is kept model-agnostic, so the limits apply across many possible dark sector theories rather than one. Any ripple found or excluded sharpens the picture of what dark matter can be.
arxiv-2512-02698:
Natascha Gray and three co-authors build gels that stiffen themselves over time and place. Smart materials that answer outside signals are prized for future devices. Living systems go further, using chemical energy from out of balance reactions to act on their own.

Enzymes inside the hydrogel change local acidity, which in turn modulates how the network crosslinks. Earlier work steered the assembly of building blocks; this work steers the network itself. Self stiffening gels could serve soft robotics and medicine, where a material that firms up on cue is valuable. A gel that firms on its own cue could wrap a wound or grip a soft part with no wires at all.
arxiv-2512-02798:
Luca Vannucci and Niels Gregersen work out the theory of a quantum light source built from a single quantum dot. Excitons, bound electron hole pairs inside the dot, can emit one photon at a time. Neutral and charged excitons offer two versions of this source for photonic quantum computers and simulators.

To make photons truly identical, the source is pumped on resonance with polarized laser pulses. Output is collected in the crossed polarization, filtering the pump light away. Their theory of emission in a polarization selective cavity guides builders chasing clean, indistinguishable single photons. Dots that fire one by one, on cue, are the bricks from which large light based rigs will be built in time.
arxiv-2512-02898:
Pedro Orvalho and three co-authors improve automated debugging for software and circuits at once. Debugging eats huge time and money in both fields. Formula based fault localization proposes sets of components whose repair would fix failing tests.

Existing methods may miss diagnoses spanning all failing tests, or list redundant sets that are not minimal. Multiple faults make both flaws worse. A unified approach for C software and Boolean circuits promises complete, subset minimal diagnoses. Tighter fault lists send engineers straight to real causes instead of chasing duplicates. One list that is both full and lean cuts the hunt for a fault. Days of guess work shrink to a short walk down the true leads.
arxiv-2512-03198:
Thin semiconductor layers react to light in ultrafast bursts. Henry Mittenzwey, Oliver Voigt, and Andreas Knorr present a theory of that response in this 2025 work. They study two-dimensional confined semiconductors at high particle densities, below a key transition.

Their approach centers on excitons, bound pairs that carry the light response. It covers both a coherent regime, where pairs and double pairs rule, and a later regime ruled by populations. A sound theory helps design fast optical switches and lasers. It also guides how lab results are read. The theory spans fast coherent bursts and slower regimes, a range lab data often cover.
arxiv-2512-03298:
Forecasts break when the pattern of a series suddenly shifts. Echo Diyun Lu and co-authors tackle regime-switching forecasts in this 2025 work. When regimes change, honest uncertainty matters as much as the point forecast itself.

The team couples deep switching state-space models with adaptive conformal inference. Conformal methods give error bands without assuming a data distribution. An aggregated variant is also studied. Calibrated bands help planners in finance, energy, and health act on forecasts with known risk, even when conditions flip. Bands that stay honest through regime shifts help users trust forecasts in volatile times.
arxiv-2512-03598:
Teeth scans often miss regions hidden from the scanner. Jianan Sun, Yukang Huang, Dongzhihan Wang, and Mingyu Fan present Mem4Teeth in this 2025 work. Partial dental point clouds suffer large gaps from occlusion and limited views.

Encoder-only features can be biased by those gaps, forcing decoders to hallucinate structure. Mem4Teeth adds a prototype memory to standard encoder-decoder pipelines in a retrieval-augmented design. Remembered tooth shapes guide completion toward realistic anatomy. Better reconstructions help dentists plan crowns, implants, and orthodontics. Prototype memory grounds completion in real tooth shapes, curbing invented anatomy.
arxiv-2512-03798:
Ground-based telescopes that catch gamma rays, the most energetic light in the universe, are entering a period of rapid growth. Jim Hinton offers a personal tour of that future in a 2025 instrumentation preprint, written after the 2024 Gamma conference in Milan. He sets out why new instruments are worth building and which projects will lead the field.

Two approaches dominate, and Hinton stresses how well they complement each other. Particle detector arrays watch a wide patch of sky at once, while Cherenkov telescope arrays measure gamma rays more precisely. The CTAO and SWGO projects should define the coming decade, pushing performance and coverage of the whole sky. Beyond them, he surveys ideas for the far future. They range from a plenoscope concept at low energies to lake-based detectors and swarms of small Cherenkov telescopes.
arxiv-2512-04198:
Machine learning folklore says the design you train is the design you ship. Vighnesh Subramaniam and co-authors challenge that assumption in a 2025 preprint, named for the ship of Theseus, whose planks were replaced one by one. If a network's parts can be swapped gradually, training and deployment could choose different designs.

Their method, Network of Theseus, converts a guide network into an entirely different target design piece by piece. At each stage, one component is replaced by a target module and aligned using representational similarity measures. Functionality largely survives even dramatic changes: a convolutional network becomes a multilayer perceptron, and GPT-2 becomes a recurrent network. The point is freedom. Architectures that optimise awkwardly but infer efficiently, or vice versa, become usable. The authors frame the technique as a way to widen accuracy-efficiency trade-offs and explore the design space.
arxiv-2512-04298:
Atoms in Rydberg states, with electrons boosted to giant orbits, make sensitive radio-frequency receivers. Anton Tishchenko and co-authors push that sensitivity further in a 2025 quantum sensing preprint by adding a metamaterial lens. The lens is a gradient-index, Luneburg-type design that concentrates the field where the atoms sit.

The team reads the receiver through electromagnetically induced transparency in caesium vapour, comparing performance with and without the lens under far-field excitation at two microwave frequencies. The window grows a lot when the lens is introduced. That matches the theory: local field enhancement at the vapour cell lowers the smallest electric field it can detect. The authors present the result as experimental validation of lens-enhanced quantum sensing, with uses from compatibility testing to quantum radar and wireless links.
arxiv-2512-04798:
L. E. Golub proposes a new effect in altermagnets: a current that runs along a sample's edge, driven by the spin of its charge carriers. Altermagnets are a fresh class of magnetic materials whose spins split by direction without net magnetization. In the edge spin galvanic effect, that splitting plus scattering at the boundary turns a sideways spin imbalance into an edge current. His 2025 arXiv paper works out the effect for d-wave altermagnets.

The current's strength and sign depend on how the edge is cut against the crystal's main axes. Flip the incoming spin direction or the Néel vector, and the current reverses. Golub also proposes a pure spin photocurrent at the edges under polarized light, and shows how a magnetic field converts it into a plain electric current. Such edge effects could give spintronics a new readout for these quiet magnets.
arxiv-2512-05198:
Rowan Bradbury and Dazhi Zhong argue that the standard way of blending images inside diffusion models is quietly wrong. Inpainting tools work in the model's compressed latent space and usually average the latents under a shrunken mask. The authors state a simple principle: blending latents should give exactly the result of blending the decoded pixels. Modern compression networks see global context, so averaging cannot meet that standard — it leaves seam artifacts, washed-out colour, and degraded detail.

Their fix, DecFormer, is a small transformer that predicts per-channel blend weights plus a correction term, trained so that decoding the fused latents reproduces true pixel-space compositing. It plugs into existing pipelines without retraining the main model and adds negligible cost. On a leading model family it restores colour consistency, sharp edges, and soft masks, cutting edge errors by about half, and it enables colour-correction edits too.
arxiv-2512-05298:
Grant Johnson, Ammar Hakim, and James Juno present a numerical algorithm for tracking particle motion on curved surfaces and spaces. Kinetic theory follows a gas through the positions and velocities of its particles. Doing that on a smooth manifold — a curved arena — is needed for flows on spheres and more exotic geometries. Their discontinuous Galerkin scheme is built to conserve what physics conserves.

The method handles both canonical and non-canonical Hamiltonian accounts of the motion. The canonical route proves notably efficient and conserves particle density and energy exactly. A simplified collision operator relaxes the gas toward local equilibrium. An iterative fix keeps density, momentum, and energy preserved numerically. Even a rotating manifold is handled by adjusting the Hamiltonian. Tests include a kinetic shock problem and swirling instabilities on a sphere and a paraboloid. The authors also sketch a path toward kinetic theory in general relativity.
arxiv-2512-05798:
Kanha Behera, Junming Liu, and P Muthukumar revisit a claimed theorem from a 1969 thesis and find the story more subtle. The setting is spaces of analytic functions: Hardy spaces, the Bloch space, Besov spaces, and weighted Bergman spaces. The question concerns operators that are almost multiplicative, respecting products of functions. Schwartz had claimed that, on Hardy spaces, the only such operators are composition operators.

The authors show the claim fails on the largest Hardy space, where counterexamples exist. For the remaining Hardy spaces they repair Schwartz's proof, which had a gap, and the result stands. They then extend the characterization widely: on Bloch, little Bloch, Besov, and weighted Bergman spaces, almost multiplicative again means composition operator. A final result sorts out which composition operators are multiplicative for the Duhamel product, a twisted way of multiplying functions. The paper fixes a fifty year old proof and draws its true borders.
arxiv-2512-05898:
Lorenzo Cipriani and four co-authors extend a classic simulation code to ask what dark matter does inside a spinning neutron star. Dark matter is expected to sink and gather in these dense stellar corpses. A dark core would change a star's structure. It matters most when two neutron stars merge, where differential rotation, layers spinning at different rates, delays the remnant's collapse.

The team extends the RNS code to describe two gravitationally coupled fluids in differential rotation. Ordinary matter follows a realistic nuclear equation of state. Dark matter is modeled as a self-interacting bosonic condensate, a condensate. With the upgraded code they build equilibrium sequences for a representative rotation law, stars settled into balance at each spin profile. From these sequences, later studies can read off how a dark core shifts a remnant's mass, size, and spin.
arxiv-2512-06098:
Seyoung Jeon and fourteen co-authors trace the origin of the ghostly glow between galaxies in a cluster. Intracluster light is starlight belonging to no galaxy, and it records the cluster's assembly history. Its faintness has kept its origins contested. Using the NewCluster simulation, the team tracks billions of particles to their birthplaces.

Most, they find, come from satellite galaxies, both survivors and ones already torn apart. Preprocessed stars follow the dark matter profile best, and are old and metal poor. Stripping is set by infall time and closest approach. The glow becomes an archive of the cluster's past.
arxiv-2512-06198:
Oussama Sifour, Soulaimane Berkane, and Abdelhamid Tayebi design a way for a moving body to find its full position and pose from very few sensors. Their setup uses an inertial unit, one body fixed vector reading such as a compass, and a single distance reading from a fixed point on the ground. With so little input, most past designs could not track the whole state.

Their method works in two linked stages. The first stage builds a time varying linear model that recovers position, speed, and the direction of gravity. The second stage joins that gravity direction with the vector reading to rebuild the body's full tilt and turn. The authors prove the scheme settles to the true state from almost any start, and tests on three dimensional paths show close tracking. It offers a light, cheap aid for self guided machines.
arxiv-2512-06498:
D Panigrahi, S Chatterjee, and B Paul revisit a cosmic model that tries to cover the whole history of the universe with one exotic fluid. The fluid, a modified Chaplygin gas, is built to act one way in the young universe and another way late, when cosmic expansion speeds up. Its governing equations resist exact solution, so the team works with a first order approximation for the universe's size over time and the moment it flips from slowing to speeding.

In one regime the model gives an emergent universe: it never shrinks to a point, starts from a finite smallest size, and settles into a steady late expansion like the standard picture. Checks on the geometry show no singularities hide in it. Microwave background data, alone and with expansion measures, fit the model within usual margins. A Raychaudhuri check confirms the solutions hold together.
arxiv-2512-06598:
Muhammad Adil and ten co authors build a satellite only forecast for toxic algae blooms in Lake Champlain. Cyanobacterial blooms threaten water, wildlife, and health, and this lake's northern bays suffer them often, fed by nutrient runoff and shifting climate. Ground sampling is sparse, so the team leans on satellite indices of the blooms and satellite water temperature, which cover the whole lake on a steady rhythm.

Their model joins a transformer, good at long range patterns, with a bidirectional memory network that reads sequences both ways. It predicts bloom intensity up to two weeks ahead across the lake's northern segment. The data were full of holes, with large shares of both feeds missing, so a two stage cleaning filled gaps pixel by pixel and smoothed the result. Features were then binned to sharpen the signal. The framework shows remote sensing alone can carry a working early warning for blooms.
arxiv-2512-06798:
Imed Basdouri, Mariem Jendoubi, and Ahmed Zahari Abdou Damdji work in pure algebra, on structures where a twisting map changes how the usual rules apply. Their subject is a family of objects called Hom-rhizaform algebras. The team links these objects to a second tool, Rota-Baxter operators, which split algebraic products in a controlled way. They also define a broader family version of the algebra, with room for many twists at once.

The central finding is constructive: starting from a suitable operator, one can build brand new algebras of the kind they study. That gives algebraists a machine for producing examples instead of hunting for them one by one. The authors also sort the new structures into classes and describe the cones of maps that keep their defining rules intact. The work widens the known map of Hom-algebra theory.
arxiv-2512-07098:
Samuel Goodman studies how many well-behaved functions live on a class of arithmetic surfaces that mix formal and analytic geometry. These surfaces sit over the integers, and their rings of regular functions are expected, under a claim of Bost and Charles, to be huge: as large as the continuum. Goodman shows that, for surfaces admitting one nonconstant specimen of a special kind, that claim follows from a purely complex one.

Under the assumption, a closeness argument in the style of Fekete and Szegő produces a function that is large relative to the given function. That largeness is then parlayed into a vast range of distinct regular functions. Goodman also derives a formula describing how Green functions, which measure capacity on a bordered Riemann surface, move under a holomorphic map.
arxiv-2512-07398:
Ilya Popov and co-authors test two ways of computing the inner electronic states of chromium atoms sprinkled into wide band gap crystals. Such doping tailors materials for lasers, and lately for spin qubits, the atoms serving as tiny quantum memories. Chromium in its three-plus state carries three electrons in its d shell, whose many interacting arrangements produce strongly correlated excited states that single-reference methods handle badly.

The usual workhorse, density functional theory, is exactly such a method. The challenger is a crystal-field Hamiltonian approach built for periodic solids, which had already shown it could dodge some of those failures. The authors benchmark both on the electronic structure and the d-to-d excitations of the dopants in their hosts. Their verdict is meant as guidance for computational materials design: which tool to trust for which question when inventing new doped materials.
arxiv-2512-07498:
Chih-Chung Hsu, Shao-Ning Chen, Chia-Ming Lee, Yi-Fang Wang, and Yi-Shiuan Chou wrote this 2025 paper on spotting fake videos. DeepFake clips grow more realistic each year and harder to catch. Most detectors quietly assume the faces they see form a clean, steady sequence.

Real video rarely cooperates with that assumption. Compression, blocked views, and attacks scramble face detection, leaving missing or wrong faces. The authors build a detector that expects such mess from the start. It is trained only on clean face data, yet works on noisy or shuffled input. Their method links frame features into a sparse graph by meaning, not by time order. Extra sparsity trims the pull of invalid faces at two levels. A spectral prior then highlights odd structures that betray a forgery. Tests on three major benchmarks show top results and better robustness.
arxiv-2512-07698:
Arslan Artykov, Tom Ravaud, Corentin Sautier, and Vincent Lepetit wrote this 2025 computer vision paper. Robots and digital twins need models of hinged objects, from laptops to cabinets. Learning those models from one casual phone video is the challenge here.

Older methods want many camera views, exact object scans, or long point tracks. Those tracks often break in real, messy recordings. The authors answer with sim2art, a framework trained only on synthetic data. Its core picture samples surface points in each frame of the video. Short-term scene flow and semantic features enrich that picture. Because nothing depends on fragile long-term matching, simulation and reality nearly coincide. The system reads the video and returns a part segmentation with joint parameters. Two new datasets widen the tested range. On real sequences, sim2art handles big camera moves and complex joints. It beats optimization and tracking rivals in trials.
arxiv-2512-07998:
Mostafa Kamali Tabrizi, Mingshi Chi, Bir Bikram Dey, and five co-authors wrote this 2025 robotics paper. Robots that merely stare cannot match animals that move their eyes. DIJIT is a binocular robotic head built for active observation.

The head serves mobile agents meant to behave as active observers. Its design supports research on human-like eye and head-neck motion. How those motions interrelate, and what each adds to vision, is the quarry. Nine mechanical degrees of freedom drive the head and eyes. The cameras and lenses add four optical degrees more. Ranges and speeds were matched to human performance targets. Peak saccade speed reaches most of the human maximum. Convergent stereo needs vergence, version, and cyclotorsion, all included here. A novel method maps camera orientation directly to motor values. Its saccades land close to human accuracy for both cameras.
arxiv-2512-08098:
Erin Coleman and Eliot Finch, gravitational wave physicists, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about black hole ringdown. After two black holes merge, the remnant rings like a bell, and fitting that ringdown with extra tones called overtones can sharpen the measurement. General relativity predicts the overtone frequencies exactly, which makes the ringdown a possible test of the no hair idea.

The authors ask a practical question: how much does each added overtone actually help? They study how the best start time for a fit shifts with the number of overtones, and whether deviations from relativity could be detected. No single maximum overtone emerges; each new one simply helps less than the last. Using Bayesian estimation, they also map how overtone amplitudes and phases correlate. The highest overtones blur together individually, but their joint pattern still senses the frequencies and decay times, offering a route to consistency tests.
arxiv-2512-08498:
Yijia Guo, Tong Hu, Zhiwei Li, and a large team of computer vision researchers in China posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. They reconstruct three dimensional scenes on the fly from multi camera rigs, using the Gaussian splatting technique that renders realistic views quickly. Single camera versions rebuild in real time but see only a narrow slice at once, leaving coverage holes.

Their framework fuses the overlapping video streams of a rig into one growing Gaussian model as the rig moves. A staged camera initialization aligns the cameras coarsely with no calibration, and a light bundle adjustment then steadies the trajectories without breaking real time speed. A sampling strategy avoids duplicate Gaussians, and a frequency aware schedule trims the optimization work. The system rebuilt hundreds of meters of scene within about two minutes from raw video alone, a speed and fidelity combination that mobile mapping and robotics both need.
arxiv-2512-08698:
Ilya Kokorin, Evgeny Chernatskiy, and Vitaly Aksenov address the gap between a distributed system design and its actual code. Designs are often checked with formal methods, but code can still contain bugs that the design check cannot see. Model based testing is offered as a bridge, by generating tests from the formal model and running them on the real system.

When the model can be seen as a finite state automaton, tests can in principle cover all states and transitions. The authors show how to generate such suites efficiently for systems written in the actor model. Their method needs no changes to the code or to the running environment. As a test case, they check an implementation of Viewstamped Replication used in a real world system, showing the approach works in practice.
arxiv-2512-09198:
Phevos Paschalidis leads a large medical and data-science team studying valve choice in TAVR, a catheter procedure replacing a narrowed aortic valve without open-heart surgery.
