Several approved replacement valves exist, but doctors still debate which patient should get which type. One major risk after the procedure is that the patient will need a permanent pacemaker.

The team built a decision-support tool whose goal is to pick the valve type that lowers that pacemaker risk for each patient. They combined records from United States and Greek patients, merging demographics, CT scans, and ultrasound heart images though the two countries code their data differently. Their analysis works leaf by leaf on patient subgroups instead of trusting uncertain estimates of what would have happened otherwise. The final model cut pacemaker rates in both test groups, and the authors call it the first unified personal prescription strategy for this choice.
arxiv-2512-09298:
Arturo de Pablo, Fernando Quirós, and Julio D. Rossi study a fully nonlinear heat equation that models fluid moving through an elasto-plastic porous material, like rock or soil that deforms as fluid passes. The equation's coefficient jumps between two positive values depending on whether the solution is rising or falling in time. The problem is set in a bounded region with fixed boundary values.

The authors ask whether viscosity solutions of this equation exist, whether they are unique, and how they behave over long times. They also examine two limiting regimes, when one coefficient shrinks toward zero or grows without bound. Finally, they characterize the solutions as limits of a dynamic game based on minimization, giving the equation a second interpretation. The work connects a concrete filtration model with the modern theory of nonlinear partial differential equations.
arxiv-2512-09398:
Hongjun Wang and colleagues present ConFormer, a traffic forecasting model that accounts for accidents and road regulations. Predicting traffic is a core problem in traffic data mining, but crashes and rules strongly shape real flows and are often missing from the data models learn from. Without them, forecasts miss exactly the disruptions managers care about.

The team first built two enriched datasets, from Tokyo and California, that add accident and regulation records to traffic data. ConFormer itself is a transformer with a conditional design: graph propagation spreads information between road sensors, and a guided normalization layer adjusts relationships between places and times based on historical patterns. In extensive tests it beat mainstream baselines across multiple metrics. It also surpassed a leading transformer model in both accuracy and efficiency, with lower computing cost and fewer parameters, which the authors offer as a step toward more resilient transport systems.
arxiv-2512-09498:
M. Bhuyan and colleagues ask whether neutron stars can reveal the nature of dark matter. Such a particle could be Dirac type, distinct from its antiparticle, or Majorana type, its own antiparticle. The answer would reshape search strategies, and neutron stars, with their extreme densities, offer a laboratory.

The team mixes fermionic dark matter into nuclear matter inside a relativistic mean-field model, with a Higgs-like portal coupling between dark matter and nucleons. They build the equation of state for both cases and solve the equations of stellar structure. Because a Dirac particle carries more internal degrees of freedom, it softens the equation of state more, giving smaller radii and lower maximum masses than the Majorana case. Comparing with NICER telescope measurements and gravitational-wave constraints, they map the parameter space each case allows and argue that compact-star observations could discriminate between the two.
arxiv-2512-09598:
Ryan Alweiss, Matthew Bowen, and Marcin Sabok prove a Ramsey theory result: no matter how the natural numbers are colored with two colors, large structured sets in a single color are unavoidable. Ramsey theory studies exactly this tension between arbitrary coloring and forced order. The sets they guarantee combine addition, multiplication, and exponentiation at once, operations that usually resist being controlled together.

Specifically, for any two-coloring of the natural numbers and any length k, there is a monochromatic set with two base numbers and their product. It also holds a family of sums built by adding multiples of one to the other. A second guaranteed configuration swaps in an exponential term and powers multiplied against one of the bases. Results mixing sums, products, and powers in one color are rare because each operation behaves so differently. The paper strengthens the known picture of unavoidable patterns in the natural numbers.
arxiv-2512-09798:
Misael Mamani and colleagues built a solar powered robot boat that collects water samples on its own. Judging water quality well needs samples from many places, yet most unmanned surface vehicles carry few samples or depend on a single sensor. Their vehicle uses a syringe based system that can gather dozens of separate samples in one mission while keeping contamination low. It steers itself with satellite navigation, laser and camera obstacle detection, and long range radio supervision.

Field trials took place in Achocalla Lagoon near La Paz, Bolivia. The boat hit most of its waypoints, navigated steadily on its own, and measured temperature, acidity, conductivity, and dissolved solids in line with samples gathered by hand. Its sampling system is modular, so parts can be swapped quickly and faults stay isolated. The authors present the platform as a scalable way to monitor remote waters at high spatial resolution.
arxiv-2512-10098:
A team led by Midhat Urooj presents MedXAI, a medical imaging system that mixes deep vision models with clinician knowledge. Image based diagnosis struggles in the real world: data patterns shift between hospitals, rare diseases get biased against, and black box outputs lack the transparency clinics require. MedXAI adds retrieval augmentation and self verification on top of deep models, guided by expert knowledge. Instead of post hoc heat maps, it explains by pointing to the diagnostic features themselves, in terms a clinician can inspect and contest.

The authors test two hard tasks: locating seizure onset zones from resting state brain scans, and grading diabetic retinopathy. Across ten multicenter datasets, the system improved cross domain generalization and rare class accuracy over strong deep learning baselines. Ablation studies show the symbolic knowledge parts act as effective clinical priors and regularizers, adding robustness when the data shifts.
arxiv-2512-10398:
Sherman Wong and a large team present the Confucius Code Agent, a software engineering agent built to work on huge real-world codebases over long sessions. Their paper observes a split in the field: research agents are open and easy to inspect but falter on heavy production work. While commercial systems perform well yet offer little control or room to extend.

The agent runs on the Confucius SDK, which is organised around the experience of the agent, the user, and the developer. It adds strong context handling, a note-taking system that persists across sessions so the agent keeps learning, and modular tools. A meta-agent builds and refines agents through a build-test-improve loop. On the SWE-Bench-Pro benchmark, the agent resolved well over half the tasks at first attempt, ahead of earlier research and commercial results.
arxiv-2512-10898:
Elena Braverman and Jenny Lawson ask how to harvest two competing species without driving either extinct. Culling can erase a species, but a harvesting rule that guarantees coexistence is harder to design, especially when the species differ in how they disperse across the landscape. The authors propose a harvesting policy that varies across space in step with each population's dispersal strategy.

Under their policy, the two managed populations form an ideal free pair, a state in which neither can do better by moving, and coexistence is guaranteed. The guarantee is sturdy: perturb the harvesting of one population somewhat and coexistence survives. And if the pair disperses ideally freely, a slight change in one species' dispersal strategy does not break coexistence. They also show an invader with a carrying-capacity advantage that mimics the resident's distribution is certain to invade, though simulations hint invasion can succeed without that advantage.
arxiv-2512-11098:
Nazanin Mahjourian and Vinh Nguyen adapt vision language models to understand infrared images inside factories and enclosed machines. Conventional cameras struggle in low light, while thermal cameras reveal heat differences clearly. The problem is that large vision language models were trained on ordinary colour images, so they cannot read thermal data directly, and labelled infrared training sets are rare.

Their framework, VLM-IRIS, converts infrared frames from a thermal sensor into a colour mapped form that standard image encoders accept. It then combines several text prompts around image locations to judge whether a workpiece sits on a three dimensional printer bed. Heat differences between plate and parts make that task well suited to thermal sensing. The system reached high accuracy with no retraining, showing a label free route to thermal monitoring.
arxiv-2512-11498:
A. Shrestha, E. Kirkinis, and M. Olvera de la Cruz study how salty water flows in a narrow channel whose walls carry patterned charge under an alternating field. With a steady field, such electroosmotic flows form fixed vortices whose swirl direction follows the field. Alternating the field changes the picture qualitatively.

The authors find a variety of layered flow forms, including vortices that reverse their circulation in step with the field's oscillation. Adding a time period removes degeneracies present in the steady problem. Net mass flow vanishes, but electric charge still flows, carried by an oscillating longitudinal current. That current shows hysteresis and an unusual conductance behaviour tied to an applied voltage. They explain the effects through a memory time set by frequency, viscosity, and the charged layer's thickness near the wall. It suggests ways to control signal carriers in tiny fluidic devices.
arxiv-2512-11598:
Klaas Willems and co-authors present a new way to simulate thin gases that flow past moving walls and solid bodies. The gas obeys the BGK equation, a simpler stand in for full gas physics. Their grid points drift with the local gas flow, so the grid can follow moving shapes.

Since the drifting points sit in no neat pattern, the team uses a mesh free method based on moving least squares. A guard called MOOD keeps sharp jumps clean, with no fake wiggles. New wall rules need no repeated fix up loops. The method hits fourth order accuracy in one dimension and second order in two, and it handles test flows like a driven cavity and a shock tube.
arxiv-2512-11698:
Tanuj Gupta and Emil J Straube prove a regularity result in several complex variables. They study smooth bounded pseudoconvex domains, regions whose shape curves the right way for complex analysis. On such a region sits the complex Green operator, a tool that solves key equations.

The question is when this operator keeps functions smooth all the way to the edge. The team assumes the region Levi form has comparable eigenvalues, a balance rule coded as D(q0). They show that if the Diederich-Fornaess index of the region equals one, the operator is globally regular for a middle band of form degrees. The band runs between q0 and n minus 1 minus q0, in either order.
arxiv-2512-11998:
Glenn Zhang and co-authors tackle a trust problem in large language models: the confidence a model states often clashes with the confidence its token odds imply. A model may sound sure while its inner numbers hedge, or the reverse. That mismatch misleads users and breaks calibration tools.

Their method, Direct Confidence Alignment, trains the model with preference optimization to match stated confidence to internal confidence, not to ground truth. Three new error metrics grade the match. Across several open models the method tightened alignment on some architectures. On others it barely helped, a split the authors flag honestly. Confidence honesty, they argue, needs methods tuned to each model family.
arxiv-2512-12198:
Jirui Jin and seven co-authors present MolGuidance in a 2025 paper on making new molecules with AI. A good generator must make valid molecules, hit target traits, stay varied, and sample fast. Vision research had built many guidance tricks, but drug and materials work had not yet used them well.

The team adds three guidance methods to a flow matching generator that respects 3D symmetry. Their hybrid plan guides steady values and discrete parts apart, and tunes both scales by search. On the QM9 and QMe14S data sets, it set new best marks for matching target traits. The molecules also stayed highly valid in structure.
arxiv-2512-12298:
Andreas Konstantinou studies rotating compact stars made of strange quark matter in a 2025 paper. Such stars are self bound: their surface density stays high instead of fading to zero. That trait may break the universal relations that link how mass and radius change as a star spins.

Konstantinou shows the breaks grow as the ratio of surface to center energy density rises. A toy model captures how that ratio drives shifts in mass and radius. Drawing on equilibrium rules for both Newtonian and relativistic stars, he proposes improved relations. The new formulas aim to model fast spinning, self bound stars more accurately than the standard ones.
arxiv-2512-13298:
Anna Aksenova and co-authors introduce MiniLingua, a small open-source language model for European languages. Big models are costly to run and often English centric, and they raise privacy concerns. A one billion parameter model built for 13 European languages aims at on-device and private use.

MiniLingua was trained from scratch with a balance of language coverage and instruction following. Its instruction-tuned version beat EuroLLM, a similar but larger budget model, on summarization, classification, and question answering tests. It stayed competitive with stronger state-of-the-art models on open-ended writing. The team released the weights, tokenizer, and full training code.
arxiv-2512-13398:
Akanksha Tripathi, Suraj Kumar Rai, and Vivek Kumar Tiwari map the critical regions around the critical end point of the quark matter phase diagram. That point, where a first-order transition line ends, is a major target in the study of hot, dense nuclear matter. Models disagree on its location.

Working with renormalized quark-meson models, with and without a Polyakov loop extension, they compute contours of quark number susceptibility to chart the critical region. They test how a stronger coupling, back-reaction of quarks on the glue sector, and a vector interaction shift the picture. The critical point and first-order line survived up to a strong vector coupling, a result relevant to compact star models.
arxiv-2512-13698:
Jung-Ah Lee introduces the Adaptive Merit Framework for university admissions that aims to be both fair and merit-based. Many systems juggle those goals with quotas, split tracks, or opaque tweaks that lack clear rules. Lee offers a mechanism with transparent steps instead.

The framework corrects each applicant's score for socioeconomic status, but regular admits are still set by raw merit alone. Only corrected scores above the same threshold earn conditional admission, so no one is displaced. A five-stage pipeline removes discretion at each step. Applied to PISA 2022 Korea data with N of 6,377, it found 4 to 9 extra candidates, all from the bottom SES half and above the merit threshold. Admissions grew by under 0.15%.
arxiv-2512-13798:
Arturo de Giorgi, Ivan Martinez Soler, and Sergio Sevillano Muñoz derive new limits on scalar-tensor gravity from neutrino physics. In such theories, a background scalar field varies across space and shifts Standard Model masses by place and density. Neutrinos are a special probe: they travel galactic distances and pass through dense media like Earth.

Those traits let neutrinos reveal the scalar field through changes in flavor oscillation and supernova time delays. The authors derive formulas for the relevant observables and set new bounds on a broad class of scalar-tensor models. They map those bounds onto known screening models, such as the Symmetron and Chameleon. The work arrives as precision neutrino physics begins in earnest.
arxiv-2512-13898:
Rachit Bansal and co-authors argue that long-context language models should train on their context at test time, not just read it. Models can now hold millions of tokens, yet they use far less than they can hold. Inference-time tricks like extra thinking tokens show fast diminishing returns on long-context tasks, in their controlled tests.

They blame score dilution, a flaw inherent to static self-attention, which can block retrieval of relevant long-context signals. Their method makes targeted gradient updates on the given context, which provably overcomes that limit. It gave large gains across models and benchmarks, including 12.6 and 14.1 point average improvements for Qwen3-4B on LongBench-v2 and ZeroScrolls subsets. A little context-specific training beat more thinking tokens.
arxiv-2512-13998:
Qilin Li, C. L. Philip Chen, and Tong Zhang release Memo2496, an expert-annotated data set for music emotion recognition, plus a recognition framework called DAMER. Emotion recognition from music is limited by scarce expert labels and weak robustness across different corpora. Memo2496 aims to fix the data side of that problem.

The data set holds 2,496 instrumental tracks with continuous valence-arousal labels from 30 certified music specialists, with calibration steps to keep labels consistent. DAMER fuses Mel spectrogram and cochleagram views with dual-stream attention, builds pseudo-labels by a progressive confidence scheme, and anchors same-emotion embeddings with a memory queue. Across Memo2496, 1000songs, and PMEmo, it took top arousal accuracy on two sets and top valence accuracy on PMEmo.
arxiv-2512-14198:
P Fauverge and a large team report gamma ray detections of two classical novae in a 2025 paper using the Fermi LAT telescope. Novae are stellar eruptions that can emit gamma rays above 100 MeV, likely from particles sped up in shocks inside the ejected gas.

V1723 Sco in 2024 shone as a very bright gamma ray source for 15 days, which let the team pin down its spectrum and proton energy. V6598 Sgr in 2023 was seen for just two days, among the shortest durations recorded. No matching non thermal X rays appeared, yet late emission more than 40 days after one outburst hints that acceleration can restart. Both cases fit a hadronic origin better than a leptonic one.
arxiv-2512-14298:
Arnab Das and Soumik Mukhopadhyay study the topological Hall effect in a layered magnet, Mn3Si2Te6, in a 2025 paper. The Hall effect is a voltage that appears across a material in a magnetic field, and a topological version is often blamed on chiral spin textures.

The authors argue the signal here comes instead from chiral orbital current, which creates an emergent magnetic field for conduction electrons through real space orbital textures. The signal grows stronger from bulk samples down to nanoflakes, but fades as current rises, along with the orbital current state. It also tracks the colossal magnetoresistance of the material. The work suggests large topological transport can arise from orbital degrees of freedom alone.
arxiv-2512-14498:
Artem Semidetnov works in algebraic topology, on crossed simplicial groups, structures that blend symmetry groups with the simplex shapes used to build spaces. He adds extra structure to them, defining what he calls an operadic crossed simplicial group. From each such object he then constructs an operad in groupoids, an algebraic device that encodes how operations compose.

The two classic examples behave as hoped. Feeding in the symmetric and braid versions returns two famous operads, matching known answers. Semidetnov also builds a general bar construction that covers Fiedorowicz's symmetric and braided versions, and links the resulting monads to Barratt-Priddy-Quillen type spaces.
arxiv-2512-14698:
Video temporal grounding asks a system to find the exact moments in a video that match a text description, a core skill in video understanding. Multimodal large language models do well at many video tasks, yet the recipes for training them for grounding remain under-explored.

Rather than a novel method, TimeLens establishes a straightforward, incremental, yet essential baseline for the task, as its authors state plainly. A solid baseline matters because later claims of progress need something honest to be measured against. The work gives the field a reference point and a clearer picture of what current models can and cannot ground in video.
arxiv-2512-14798:
Maggie Barker and three coauthors build a model to predict final medal counts at the Olympic Games. Their program strength model rates how strong each country is in each event. It also weighs how that country did at past Games, since strong programs tend to stay strong.

They test the model against the real final counts from the Paris 2024 Games. Monte Carlo runs, which repeat the Games many times with random draws, help them tune the constants in the model. With the tuned model, they then forecast the final medal counts for the 2028 Games. The study gives sports analysts a clear and testable way to turn past form into medal forecasts.
arxiv-2512-15198:
Mohsen Nafar and two coauthors speed up a bounding technique for hard discrete optimization. Relaxed decision diagrams over approximate a problem's solution space by merging nodes, which yields dual bounds on the best answer. How tight those bounds are depends heavily on the order in which variables are fixed during compilation.

Dynamic ordering heuristics tighten bounds but cost too much when run over all variables at once. The authors cluster the variables first, then order within that structure, shrinking the heuristic's search space. Two strategies are studied: processing cluster by cluster with aggregate criteria, and a pick and sort method that draws representatives from each cluster. Theory on diagram growth for the Maximum Weighted Independent Set Problem guides how many clusters to use. In a branch and bound solver, the method cut costs against the standard baseline.
arxiv-2512-15698:
Davide Bonomi and co authors probe stringy flux tubes with large R-charge in a 2025 paper. The generalized cusp anomalous dimension is studied at strong coupling. It can also be read as a quark antiquark potential on the three sphere. A local operator of large charge sits on a cusped Wilson loop. The dual string picture gives the computational handle.

The authors solve the dual string configuration for general cusp angles, covering near BPS, antiparallel line, and large charge regimes in one description. At small line separation, behavior changes non analytically at a critical charge, from a Coulomb like form to deconfined Luscher corrections. Small fluctuation spectra near the transition are also derived.
arxiv-2512-15898:
Francesco Benini, Eduardo Garcia-Valdecasas, and Stathis Vitouladitis extend entanglement asymmetry to higher form symmetries in a 2025 paper. Entanglement asymmetry is a relative entropy that diagnoses symmetry breaking inside a quantum state, possibly within one spatial region. Higher form symmetries act on extended objects rather than points, and needed the same test.

A central result is an entropic Coleman Mermin Wagner theorem for zero form and p-form symmetries, valid even on sub areas. It forbids spontaneous breaking of continuous p-form symmetries in spacetime dimensions up to p plus 2. When breaking does occur, the asymmetry grows toward the infrared and counts Goldstone fields. Closed form Renyi measures are derived for a compact scalar and for gauge fields.
arxiv-2512-16098:
Jiliang Jing, Weike Deng, and Sheng Long extend a key gravity framework in an arXiv paper posted in 2025. The effective one-body approach maps two orbiting black holes or neutron stars onto one body moving in a deformed spacetime. That picture needs an effective metric, a stand-in geometry from which motion, radiation reaction, and waveforms all follow.

The authors build that metric up to fifth order in the post-Minkowskian expansion, which counts powers of Newton's constant. Third-generation gravitational wave detectors demand at least that accuracy. Their metric is of algebraic type D, a special form that lets wave equations split into separate, solvable pieces. The result lays the groundwork for a fully self-consistent effective one-body theory at fifth order, ready for future detector data.
arxiv-2512-16698:
Mahbub E Sobhani and coauthors test whether teams of AI agents solve diagram-based geometry problems better than a single agent. Geometry with figures is a hard test for multimodal language models, and the value of splitting work across agents was unclear.

The team compared single and multi-agent setups on four sets: Geometry3K, MathVerse, OlympiadBench, and We-Math. Open models gained clearly from teams, with Qwen-2.5-VL at 7 billion parameters up 6.8 points on Geometry3K. The closed Gemini-2.0-Flash model did better alone on classic sets, gaining only slightly from teams on the newer We-Math. The verdict is that agent teams help open models most, and are not always the best design.
arxiv-2512-17498:
Georg Schwefer and Jim Hinton ask what the next great gamma-ray observatory will see inside pulsar wind nebulae, the glowing wreckage blown off spinning neutron stars. These nebulae dominate the Galaxy's highest-energy sky and show fine structure in X-rays. The coming CTAO southern array should sharpen gamma-ray vision to under one arcminute, fine enough to read that structure.

The pair model two known nebulae from X-ray and gamma data, then fake CTAO observations of each model. The fakes show the real array should tell rival models apart and map the nebulae's magnetic fields and fastest electrons. Sharper reconstruction helps a great deal. One brake remains: at the highest energies, so few photons arrive that counting limits what sharpness alone can win.
arxiv-2512-17698:
Vanessa Yanza and five co-authors hunt for stars flung away from two stellar explosions caught in the act. DR 21 and G5.89 are nurseries where a burst, perhaps a stellar merger, blasted gas outward in streamers. If stars were ejected, sharp radio eyes should spot them as compact sources fleeing the blast center.

The Very Large Array found 13 compact sources in DR 21, nine near the core. Three shine with the nonthermal glow of magnetically active stars, and all 13 are prime targets for motion checks. Curved arcs of ionized gas point back to one source, number 11, as the likely engine of it all. In G5.89, bright shell glow hid most sources. The arcs, the team notes, trace explosion origins well.
arxiv-2512-17798: Valeria Banica and Nicolas Burq give a very short proof of an endpoint case of the div-curl lemma, a workhorse result about when products of vector fields behave well in the limit. The classical lemma pairs fields in matching Lebesgue spaces; the borderline case, one side only a measure and the other merely bounded, resisted standard treatment. Their route defines the product through a microlocal Hodge decomposition. The same argument recovers the classical cases and covers mismatched regularity, so one brief proof serves the whole family.
arxiv-2512-17898:
Robin Schimmelpfennig, Mark Díaz, Vinodkumar Prabhakaran, and Aida Davani test what happens when a chatbot is made to feel more human. Over a billion people now talk with such systems, and fears about misplaced trust are common. The team ran two experiments with 3,500 people in ten countries, using live open chats.

People judged human likeness by chat flow, reply speed, and whether the bot took their view, not by deep claims about minds. Making the bot more human raised that feeling in every country, yet trust and engagement rose in some places and fell in others. Rules for such design, the authors argue, must respect local culture.
arxiv-2512-17998:
Maria Ramos, Timothy Cohen, and Mariangela Lisanti question a quiet shortcut in dark matter simulations. When dark matter particles are imagined to bump into each other often, galaxy shapes should record the effect. Simulations stand in for single particles with heavy tracer clumps, and codes assume the clumps obey the same flow rule as the true particles.

For frequent bumps, the team shows that shortcut fails in general. They build a direct bridge from the particle level rules to the clump level, and an extra force between clumps pops out of the math. The clump cross section follows from the true one, which should make galaxy forecasts from such codes more honest.
arxiv-2512-18198:
Wei-Ren Syong and colleagues at the University of Colorado Boulder and the National Institute of Standards and Technology present a new package for measuring superconducting quantum devices at cryogenic temperatures. Conventional packages need wirebonds and printed circuit boards, which slow down testing. Their 2025 design is a drop in alternative with neither. It consists of a superconducting aluminum cavity and a suspended tungsten transmission pin.

The cavity's fundamental mode sits far from the 4 to 8 gigahertz band of interest. The pin transmits with less than 3 decibels of ripple across that range. Using the package, the team measured the loss tangent of superconducting ring resonators. The value, about 1.10 times ten to the minus six, agrees with wirebond based measurements of quarter wave resonators. Because chips swap in quickly, the system can generate large datasets fast. That throughput supports qubit improvement work and time sensitive studies of surface treatments and oxide regrowth.
arxiv-2512-18298:
Sudip Chakrabarty, Pappu Bishwas, and Rajdeep Chatterjee build a speech emotion reader that holds up in noise and can show its reasons. Call centers and care tools need such readers, yet street and room noise often wreck their accuracy, and their choices are hard to audit.

Their design runs two streams at once: a transformer that reads raw sound over long spans, and a compact network that reads steady sound traits. Tested on four standard sets with real world noise mixed in, the pair beat single stream rivals by a clear margin. Built in explainers draw maps of what the model heeded, which shifts between word flow and sound traits as noise grows.
arxiv-2512-18498:
Mustafa Bakr, Tongyu Zhang, and Smain Amari ask why the angular indices of waves inside a spherical cavity must be whole numbers. Textbooks treat integer values of l and m as a law. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, shows the integers come from domain rules, regularity at the poles and single-valuedness around the sphere, not from Maxwell's equations themselves.

For sectoral modes they prove that sin to the power m of theta solves the angular equation for any real m above zero, giving a continuous dispersion curve. Other mode types stay pinned to isolated integer points on a full sphere, but cones and wedges free them into continuous families. At the limiting point the field vanishes while the Debye potential does not, a subtlety for mode counting. Full-wave simulations confirm the theory to sub-percent accuracy.
arxiv-2512-18998:
Takafumi Akahori and three co-authors study a wave equation used for internal waves in layered fluid of finite depth. The equation allows dark soliton waves, which keep a nonzero height far away. That trait put its solutions outside older proofs that equations behave well over time.

The team proves local and global well-posedness for a generalized form of the equation, in spaces built for nonzero values at infinity. They also prove the deep-water limit, where solutions approach those of a related derivative equation. Their proof uses a modified energy method with frequency envelopes, a first use of these tools in such spaces.
arxiv-2512-19098: Anatolii Puhalskii proves a large deviation principle for long queues in a generalized Jackson network, a standard model of linked service stations. The result describes the stationary distribution of queue lengths when the network runs below capacity. It assumes a Cramér condition on the gaps between arrivals and on service times. The rate function in the principle is the quasipotential, which prices how unlikely each large queue pattern is.
arxiv-2512-19498:
Giacomo Brunello, Manoj Mandal, Pierpaolo Mastrolia, and Raj Patil compute a missing piece of the gravity of two merging compact objects. Waveform models for observatories need the conservative two-body dynamics pushed to the sixth post-Newtonian order, a demanding corner of general relativity. Their arena is the static limit of that expansion.

Working inside effective field theory, they evaluate six-loop Feynman diagrams recast as two-point integrals with a gauge-theory flavor, a first for this problem. The seventh-order term in Newton's constant comes out finite in three spatial dimensions. The authors call the result the most technically demanding missing ingredient at that order.
arxiv-2512-19598:
Jyotiranjan Beuria and Venkatesh Chembrolu ask where one-way influence in a group of moving agents can come from. In living and active matter, agent A often pushes B more than B pushes A. Most models just put that one-way push in by hand. This work lets it grow out of the agents' own inner structure instead. Each agent moves on an inner space tied to a Chern-Simons gauge field.

That field reacts very fast, so it can be removed from the math. What is left is a sideways force that acts one way only. Computer runs then show clear signs of the one-way effect. Vortex cores live a long time, flow keeps a steady swirl, and news flows one way. Sweeps of the settings also show a memory effect. Such memory cannot occur in systems where the push runs both ways.
arxiv-2512-19898:
Hanna Noyce and four co-authors study what access means for wheelchair users in their towns. Taking part in town life aids body and mind. Yet people who cannot walk well often cannot get around with ease. Access is not one thing. It shifts with the person and with the world around them. Past work logged the hurdles, but a model that sorts the key factors was missing.

The team proposes a model with three axes. They are the user, the wheelchair, and the environment. They then test the model with the users themselves. The tools are semi-structured interviews and participatory action research. The work backed many of their guesses about access. It also surfaced a clear unmet need. Users want better tools to plan routes they can actually take.
arxiv-2512-20098:
R. D'Amicis leads a forty-author Solar Orbiter study sorting the solar wind by character, not speed. Fast and slow wind are most often told apart by velocity. But Alfvénic slow wind blurs that scheme. It carries wave-like magnetic behavior more typical of fast streams. In September 2022, the craft sampled five streams: one fast, three Alfvénic slow, and one moderate fast. The Solar Wind Analyzer suite dissected all five.

The team joined plasma traits with magnetic field data. They added spectral checks of the fluctuations, and maps of each stream back to its solar source. The fast wind traced to a large coronal hole. The slow Alfvénic streams linked to a pseudostreamer and a coronal hole edge. Their charge-state ratios matched slow-wind origins, despite their Alfvénic manners. Speed alone, the authors conclude, cannot sort wind or tie it to its source.
arxiv-2512-20398:
Boris Y Rubinstein revisits a classic device in number theory: Sylvester's decomposition of the partition function. The partition function counts how many ways an integer splits into summands. Sylvester wrote it as a polynomial term plus wavy terms, one per denominator.

A recent formula expressed each Sylvester wave as a finite sum over higher-order Bernoulli terms with periodic coefficients. The same wave can instead be written as a weighted sum of such terms evaluated at shifted arguments. Rubinstein's manuscript supplies a formal proof that this second form is valid. The result tidies a corner of the theory where explicit formulas matter in practice.
arxiv-2512-20498:
Luigi De Masi studies how a measure looks when magnified around a point. For signed Radon measures on Euclidean space, the blow-up procedure zooms in repeatedly; at some points the limit is unique and flat along a subspace of some dimension. De Masi stratifies points by that dimension.

He proves the set of points with unique blow-up and invariant subspace of dimension k is itself k-rectifiable, meaning it can be covered by nice k-dimensional surfaces up to a negligible remainder. Two applications follow quickly. One is a rectifiability criterion for signed Radon measures. The other extends a result of Mattila about measures with unique blow-ups almost everywhere. The theorem sharpens the geometric measure theory toolkit.
arxiv-2512-20698:
Jose Luis Blázquez-Salcedo and co-authors study black holes that spin, carry both electric and magnetic charge, and sit at the extremal limit where temperature vanishes. The arena is four-dimensional Einstein-Maxwell-dilaton theory, where a scalar dilaton couples to the electromagnetic field. They specialize to the stringy value of the dilaton coupling.

A general approach for asymptotically flat, spinning, dyonic extremal black holes is set up first. Within it, a one-parameter family of pathology-free solutions exists, provided the electric and magnetic charges are equal. The near-horizon geometry explains why that condition is required. Both perturbative closed-form solutions and fully numerical ones are presented. Extremal black holes are prized as theoretical laboratories, and dyonic spinning examples have been scarce.
arxiv-2512-20998:
Koushiki, Rituparno Goswami, and Pankaj Joshi study gravitational collapse in its cleanest theoretical setting: a massless scalar field falling in on itself. Two tendencies compete inside the field, a collapsing mode that pulls matter inward and a dispersing mode that spreads it out. Their covariant analysis shows the balance between those modes decides the ending, either a black hole or complete dispersal.

Exactly at the boundary sits a locally naked null singularity, visible in principle to outside observers. A single dimensionless parameter selects which side of the boundary a given collapse lands on, and the result needs no special ansatz, so it holds for every family of massless scalar fields. The geometrical mass of the critical singularities shrinks to zero, tying the work to long-standing questions about critical collapse and cosmic censorship.
arxiv-2512-21098:
Alexander Guterman and Andrey Yurkov ask how large a family of matrices can be if every member is invisible to the Cullis determinant. That determinant is a rectangular generalization of the classical one. For square matrices and the ordinary determinant, Dieudonne bounded such annihilating spaces long ago. The authors extend the bound to rectangular matrices: the dimension cannot exceed the columns times one less than the rows.

At the maximal end they identify the extremal spaces completely for a range of sizes. When the column count is odd and rows are plentiful, the only maximal example is the space of matrices whose alternating row sum vanishes. The proofs import matroid theory in a new form. A matroid is attached to a linear variety. The proofs track how projections and restrictions become matroid contractions and restrictions. That dictionary, capped by a lemma about coindependent sets, may serve problems well beyond determinants.
arxiv-2512-21598:
Jian Lang, Fan Zhou, and their co-authors present ALARM, a system for detecting harmful memes without any labeled training data. Harmful memes spread quickly online, and detection methods usually need large hand-labeled datasets. That labeling burden slows adaptation as harmful content keeps changing form.

ALARM instead improves itself, starting from easy cases. A confidence-based mechanism picks out explicit memes, the shallow ones whose harm is plain, and assigns them pseudo-labels. Those memes are then reorganized into contrastive pairs, harmful against harmless, from which a large multimodal model agent derives high-level detection cues. The refined agent applies those cues to subtler memes built on metaphor and implication. On three datasets, ALARM beat label-free baselines and adapted well to newly evolved memes. It even outperformed methods trained with labels, suggesting self-improvement can substitute for annotation in fast-moving content areas.
arxiv-2512-21798:
Christophe D. Hounwanou and Yae Ulrich Gaba study deep generative models as suppliers of synthetic financial data for building portfolios and modeling risk. Real financial data are private, expensive, or hard to share, which hampers research. Synthetic series that behave like real returns could stand in for them.

The authors generate synthetic daily return series modeled on the S and P 500 with two methods: TimeGAN, an adversarial network built for time series, and an autoencoder. They judge the output by statistical similarity, temporal structure, and performance in downstream tasks. TimeGAN's series closely matched real returns in distribution shape, volatility patterns, and autocorrelation. Portfolios optimized on its data had weights, Sharpe ratios, and risk levels close to those from real data. The autoencoder trained more stably but smoothed away extreme moves, distorting risk estimates. Synthetic data can stand in for real data, provided the generator captures the dynamics over time.
arxiv-2512-21898:
Chaoqi Liu, Yilun Du, Kris Hauser, and their co-authors teach robots tasks with a policy built from specialized pieces rather than one monolithic network. Robot action distributions have many modes across tasks, so a single diffusion policy often underfits, smearing strategies together, and adapts clumsily to new tasks.

Their method factorizes the action distribution into specialized diffusion models. Each component captures a sub-mode of the behavior space, a cluster of related strategies, and together they represent the full policy faithfully. The modularity pays off during adaptation: a new task can be handled by adding or fine-tuning pieces instead of retraining everything, which limits catastrophic forgetting of older skills. In simulated and real-world manipulation tests, the factorized policy outperformed strong monolithic and modular baselines. The design treats a robot's skill library as something that can grow piece by piece.
arxiv-2512-22198:
Alexandra Friesen, Yu. Kalinovsky, and four co-authors compare two versions of the extended Linear-Sigma Model, a theory of mesons, the particles made of a quark and an antiquark. One version, SU(3), includes three quark flavors; the other, SU(4), adds the charm quark. Using a mean-field approximation, they compute masses for pseudoscalar, scalar, vector, and axial-vector mesons in both versions.

The SU(4) version's mass estimates land closer to experimental values, so the authors conclude that more quark degrees of freedom improve the simulations. They then track how each meson's mass shifts with temperature. States dissolve over a similar temperature range, though each follows its own pattern, while quarkonium states barely respond to temperature changes at all.
arxiv-2512-22298:
Vesal Ahsani, Babak Hossein Khalaj, and Hamed Shah-Mansouri build a driver monitoring system that watches for distraction and drowsiness from a single camera, running entirely on cheap hardware. In-cabin systems must answer fast under tight limits on computing power, energy, and cost. Their pipeline pairs a compact per-frame vision model with a label scheme designed to separate easily confused behaviors, plus a temporal decision stage.

Alerts fire only when predictions are both confident and sustained, which steadies the output. The system recognizes seventeen behavior classes and was trained on over 800,000 labeled frames with drivers kept separate between training and testing. Live in-vehicle tests reached roughly sixteen frames per second on a Raspberry Pi 5 and twenty-five on a Google Coral board.
arxiv-2512-22398:
Ozan Oguztuzun and Cerag Oguztuzun personalize knowledge graph predictions without retraining the underlying model. Base models for knowledge graphs predict links well for whole populations yet miss single tastes, a gap between general relational reasoning and personal ranking. Their system, GatedBias, bolts personalization on at use time while the embeddings stay frozen.

Profile features pass through binary gates derived from the graph itself, producing interpretable per-entity biases from only about three hundred trainable settings. On Amazon-Book and Last-FM data, alignment with single users rose greatly while population-level results held. Counterfactual tests showed the personalization is causally responsive: boosting a preference signal lifted exactly the entities tied to that signal, several times more than others.
arxiv-2512-23498:
Henrique De Medeiros and four co-authors study whether self-adaptive cloud software can watch its own energy use, and what that watching costs. Data centers consume a growing share of electricity, and applications that adapt at runtime could in principle include energy among their goals. Until now, few tools have measured energy across a distributed adaptive system while it runs.

The team built EnCoMSAS, a monitoring tool that gathers energy consumption from distributed applications and feeds live adaptation decisions. They tested it on the Adaptable TeaStore benchmark running on the Grid'5000 testbed, varying the workload on its recommender service. Energy use tracked processor use closely, depended on the deployment environment as well as the algorithm, and the monitor's own energy cost stayed modest.
arxiv-2512-24098:
Liling Tan writes for researchers new to cloud platforms. Many know language models well. Few know how to train them on Amazon SageMaker. The service offers computing power that many labs lack. But its learning curve is steep. Official documents leave gaps. Users end up hunting scattered answers across the web.

Tan's demo paper gathers the essentials in one place. It walks through a first training run from scratch. The model is a Hugging Face model. The platform is SageMaker. The goal is stated plainly. Smaller teams should be able to train in the cloud without tears. The guidance reflects what newcomers actually struggle with. It turns a trial-and-error process into a guided path.
arxiv-2512-24198:
Krzysztof Sienicki writes a short technical comment on a philosophy-of-physics essay. Jeffrey Bub's essay argues there is no quantum world. Sienicki stresses that his note is friendly. He is not attacking Bub's interpretive goals. He checks the mathematics instead.

One unambiguous slip is flagged. A cardinality identity in the essay quietly assumes the Continuum Hypothesis. A few other passages need sharper wording. They concern infinite tensor products and a notion called sectorization. Measurement updates also get a comment. The aim is to separate what math forces from what depends on choices. Algebra, representation, and philosophical stance all involve such choices. The note ends with a brief remark on Philippe Grangier's reply to Bub.
arxiv-2512-24498:
Iman Poernomo introduces Open Horn Type Theory, a new foundation for mathematics. It extends dependent type theory with two primitive judgments. Coherence and gap stand side by side, under a mutual exclusion law. Gap is not defined through negation. It is a positive witness that something fails to cohere. Judgments can also stay open, neither coherent nor gapped.

The central construction is the transport horn. A term and a path both cohere. Yet transport along the path is witnessed as gapped. Homotopy type theory cannot express that situation. Its Kan condition forces all transport to succeed. Semantics come from ruptured simplicial sets and ruptured Kan complexes. Homotopy type theory embeds as the fully coherent fragment. Topological, semantic, and logical obstructions are developed in detail.
arxiv-2512-24698:
Dongyun Kang, Min-Gyu Kim, Tae-Gyu Song, Hajun Kim, and colleagues tackle dynamic motion for legged robots, where reinforcement learning often needs heavy reward tuning or good demonstrations. Their plan starts simple and grows harder. First a policy learns core motion patterns on a single rigid body model, a reduced picture of the robot.

Then a continuation strategy, inspired by model homotopy, gradually transfers that policy to the full-body robot. Step by step the gap between the simple and real models closes. Readers get a way to produce complex, lively gaits while reducing the tuning burden that usually blocks such transfer.
arxiv-2512-24798:
Dai, Molochkov, and Niemi construct quantum gates from geometric phases in a deformable three-body system shaped like a triangle. Qubits live in a near-degenerate vibrational doublet of that system. Using Kendall's shape theory, they derive the connection that governs slow transport within that doublet and show its holonomy covers all single-qubit rotations.

Explicit loops in shape space give a quarter-turn phase gate and a Hadamard-type gate. Linked cycles in arrays could add an entangling two-qubit gate through a Chern-Simons phase. Readers in quantum control get universal control driven by shape changes alone, a holonomic route that may resist certain errors.
arxiv-2512-24898:
Zihao Chen, Alexandre Andre, and Wenrui Ma present PRISM, a forecasting method that splits a time series into a learnable tree of scales. Real series mix global trends, fine local structure, and patterns in between, which single-scale models miss. At the tree root, a global representation captures coarse trends, while recursive splits reveal finer detail level by level.

Iterative sequence modeling over that partitioned representation is the core of the method, whose full name spells out partitioned representation for iterative sequence modeling. Finance, biology, and healthcare forecasting are named targets. Readers get a multiscale design that lets a model attend to slow drift and quick wiggles together.
arxiv-2601-00098:
Paraschos Koutris, Stijn Vansummeren, Qichen Wang, Yisu Remy Wang, and Xiangyao Yu survey a classic database algorithm. The algorithm is named for Yannakakis. It answers queries that join several tables. For joins whose structure has no cycles, it is known to be optimal. Yet it has seen little use in practice. Its real-world speed has been poor.

The paper reviews recent work on this gap. Some of that work makes the algorithm faster. Some makes it easier to build. The authors also point to open paths for future research. Their aim is to bring a sound old method into real use.
arxiv-2601-00398:
Tao Wu, Qing Xu, Xiangjian He, Oakleigh Weekes, James Brown, and Wenting Duan introduce a dataset for spotting roadside litter in dashcam footage. Litter harms the environment, safety, and public budgets, yet checks still rely on slow manual surveys and public reports. Their 2026 paper notes that existing litter datasets use still street photos, aerial views, or water scenes, none of which match dashcam video.

Their collection, RoLID-11K, holds more than eleven thousand labeled images from varied driving conditions in the United Kingdom. Litter in them is tiny, sparse, and set against cluttered road edges. The team benchmarks many modern detectors, from accurate transformer models to fast YOLO models. The results set a hard new test for finding very small objects in moving scenes.
arxiv-2601-00998:
Yue Zhou and a thirteen-author team benchmark whether vision-language models can find objects in drone imagery when the request is phrased indirectly. Remote sensing grounding datasets mostly use explicit descriptions, positions, sizes, and colors, but real users describe targets through scenario knowledge instead. Their benchmark, DVGBench, supplies both explicit and implicit queries for each object.

The scenarios span six domains: traffic, disaster, security, sport, social activity, and productive activity. On top of the benchmark the team builds DroneVG-R1, a model trained with reinforcement learning around a reasoning method that converts implicit references into explicit ones step by step. The setup measures, and then trains, the domain knowledge that implicit grounding demands.
arxiv-2601-01198:
Madhavan Varadarajan asks whether two deep ideas about space can live together. Loop quantum gravity suggests that area comes in discrete steps, like rungs on a ladder. Special relativity, meanwhile, demands that boosts between moving observers act cleanly on the quantum states. Using a reformulation of a free scalar field on flat two-dimensional spacetime, he shows that they can.

The consistency rests on a quirk of the loop approach: its space of states is non-separable, meaning it holds more independent directions than usual quantum theory allows. Rather than a defect, that largeness is what lets boosts act as proper unitary maps while area stays discrete. Varadarajan suggests the extra room may reflect the different perspectives of different observers. The result eases a long-standing tension between quantum gravity and relativity, and it hints that odd features of the math may carry physical meaning.
arxiv-2601-01298:
Jorge Ruiz Williams proposes Warp-Cortex, a design for running huge numbers of AI agents on ordinary home hardware. Today's multi-agent frameworks store a full copy of model context for each agent, so memory grows in direct proportion to the agent count. That makes deep, parallel reasoning impractical on a consumer graphics card.

The design shares one copy of the model weights among all agents, so weight memory stops growing with agent count. A sparsification step, borrowed from topological data analysis, trims each agent's stored context while keeping its key structure. A further mechanism lets helper agents feed results into the main agent's context without breaking its output stream. On one high-end consumer card, the author reports one hundred agents running at once in about two gigabytes of video memory. The paper frames far larger counts as a theoretical capacity, not a measured one.
arxiv-2601-01498:
Hao and 13 co-authors introduce HardGen, a pipeline that makes hard training examples for agents that use outside tools. Current training sets are often too easy and too alike, missing the hidden links between steps in a real task. HardGen starts instead from cases where agents already failed.

It builds a graph of program interfaces based on those failures, samples hard action traces, and creates advanced abstract tools from them. Hard questions and checked step-by-step answers follow, with test feedback guiding more rounds. A small model trained on the resulting data beat several leading larger models on tool-use tests. Code and data are promised as open releases.
arxiv-2601-01698:
Engineers often judge a neural network's computing cost by counting multiply-accumulate operations, but Chankyu Lee, Woohyun Choi, and Sangwook Park show that this number can badly mislead on small embedded devices. Their study runs image classification on an embedded system and compares measured inference times against the standard cost figures.

Ten deep learning models were timed on the CIFAR-100 dataset, and the rankings by theoretical operations did not match the rankings by real speed. Extra work moving and combining tensors between operations, largely invisible in the usual metric, slowed models in ways the count never predicted. For designers of real-time systems on modest hardware, the paper is a warning to measure, not just count.
arxiv-2601-01798:
Face verification software decides whether two photos show the same person, but it usually cannot say why, which limits trust in security and forensic settings. Syed Abdul Hannan and six co-authors introduce VerLM, a vision-language model that both verifies faces and explains its decision in natural language.

VerLM is trained with two explanation styles: short summaries naming the key factors, and detailed accounts of the specific differences between the images. The team adapted a modeling approach first built for telling apart audio, transferring it to visual inputs, and reports accuracy and interpretability above baseline and existing models. Verbal explanations of biometric decisions could make verification systems more transparent and easier to audit.
arxiv-2601-02198:
Pathologists zoom: tissue architecture at low magnification, cell detail at high. Alexander Möllers and five co-authors show a quiet flaw. Pathology foundation models are uneven across that zoom range. Training samples magnifications only at a few standard scales. That is the cause.

Magnification choice is framed as multi-source domain adaptation. The theory then predicts gaps. Standard discrete sampling leaves performance gaps at intermediate magnifications. New benchmarks confirm it. Continuous magnification sampling closes the gaps. It gains up to four percentage points of balanced accuracy between the standard scales. The standard scales are not hurt. Optimized sampling distributions help further. Magnification emerges as a primary driver of differences among current foundation models.
arxiv-2601-02498:
Roel R. Lefever and six co authors re analyze six bright nitrogen rich Wolf Rayet stars in our galaxy, of the WN4b type with strong emission lines. These stars blow thick winds that hide the star's true surface, so standard spectral analysis cannot pin down radius or the deeper wind structure, because many parameter combinations fit the same spectrum. Evolutionary conclusions then rest on shaky ground.

Their fix is hydrodynamically consistent modeling with the PoWR-HD code, where star and wind parameters are coupled by physics instead of chosen freely. That coupling breaks the degeneracies, constrains the wind, and yields a mass estimate for each star. With updated Gaia distances, the new stellar and wind values let the team test current mass loss recipes for Wolf Rayet stars and draw firmer evolutionary implications.
arxiv-2601-02998:
Yuqi Yang and Ying Jin study conformal prediction, a method that wraps a model's output in a set guaranteed to contain the true answer with a chosen probability. Their setting is harder: labeled data come from several different source distributions, and the test point may come from any of them, or a mixture. The prediction set must stay valid no matter which source the test point came from.

They propose a max-p aggregation scheme that delivers finite-sample coverage across all the sources at once, for any per-source conformity scores. Studying how to make the sets as small as possible under that guarantee, they prove their scheme is optimal and tight. Experiments on synthetic and real data show valid worst-case coverage with much smaller sets than baselines.
arxiv-2601-03098:
Meghna Roy Chowdhury, Shreyas Sen, and Yi Ding present MyoText, a system that turns muscle signals into typed text without a keyboard. Sensors on the skin read surface electromyography, the electrical activity of muscles, which could one day drive text input for wearables and mixed-reality headsets. Earlier work tried to recognize letters directly from the signals, a hard jump from muscle to language.

MyoText instead follows the natural hierarchy of typing. It first classifies which fingers are active. Then it uses ergonomic typing priors to infer letters. Finally, it rebuilds full sentences with a fine-tuned T5 transformer. Tested on thirty users from a public dataset, it reached strong finger-classification accuracy with low character and word error rates. The staged design narrows the decoding problem at every step.
arxiv-2601-03198:
Weilei He and five co-authors test how well multimodal language models follow instructions that hide inside the picture, not just the text. Existing benchmarks mostly judge verbal commands, missing the implicit constraints carried by semantically rich images. Their new benchmark, VC-IFEval, builds vision-dependent constraints directly into its instruction design, giving a finer-grained measure of how faithfully a model honors both the image and the words.

A systematically constructed dataset accompanies the benchmark. Fine-tuning models on that dataset produced substantial gains in visual instruction-following accuracy and adherence. The authors also evaluate a range of representative models on the benchmark. Their results give a clearer picture of where current multimodal models still fail to do what the combined instruction actually asks.
arxiv-2601-03398:
Liam Merz Hoffmeister, Brian Scassellati, and Daniel Rakita formalize a hard version of robot planning: zero-knowledge task planning. In this problem, the system must build a sequence of actions for a goal, without any task-specific knowledge or setup. Their approach leans on a large language model. The model turns natural language instructions into subtasks, and then into behavior trees that a robot can execute.

When execution errors arise, the same model adjusts the behavior trees on the fly, in a refinement loop, rather than failing outright. Experiments in the AI2-THOR household simulator show the approach improves overall task performance. It beats alternatives that do use task-specific knowledge. The authors present the work as a first investigation. It shows language models can cover several parts of the zero-knowledge problem, from decomposition to repair.
arxiv-2601-03498:
Brett J. Kagan and five co-authors propose a measurable test for agency, meant to work across brains, cell cultures, and machines. Debates about agency often rely on top-down descriptions that are hard to quantify. Their framework instead grades how a system processes information over time, asking whether its response rules stay fixed or rewrite themselves with experience.

Three classes emerge. Class I systems react without memory. Class II systems hold internal states but follow fixed rules. Class III systems are adaptive, changing their own transformation rules based on past activity. The authors stress these traits are necessary, not sufficient, for true agency. Still, a shared scale could help labs compare claims about minds in very different materials.
arxiv-2601-03698:
Pharath Sathya, Yin Jou Huang, and Fei Cheng propose a structured way to judge creativity in AI-generated stories. Standard metrics compare text against references, which misses the subjective heart of creativity. Their scheme scores four parts, Novelty, Value, Adherence, and Resonance, broken into eleven sub-parts, and tests them through controlled story generation.

Using a prompting method they call Spike Prompting, they got judgments from one hundred fifteen readers in a crowdsourced study. Creativity turned out to be judged in stages rather than as a simple sum, with varied dimensions mattering at first read and on reflection. Reflective judging also changed ratings and agreement among readers. The scheme exposes creative traits that reference scores flatten, helping writers and tool builders judge made-up fiction more honestly.
arxiv-2601-03798:
Taisiia Tikhomirova and Dirk U. Wulff map where psychologically meaningful aspects of word meaning sit inside transformer language models. They probed fifty-eight psycholinguistic features, from word frequency to emotional tone, across ten encoder and decoder models, layer by layer, comparing three ways of pulling out embeddings. The picture that emerged depends strongly on the extraction method chosen.

In-context embeddings showed sharper feature selectivity and varied layer profiles than lone ones. Final layers were rarely the best place to recover meaning features with simple probes. Still, models shared a depth ordering: word-level traits peaked earlier, while experiential and feeling dimensions peaked later. Anyone reading model internals, or borrowing embeddings for psychology research, should know the answer depends on how and where they look.
arxiv-2601-03898:
Kyle Burns and three co-authors introduce the maximum common bigraph problem, asking for the largest structure two bigraphs share. Bigraphs are a mathematical framework for modeling spatial and non-spatial relationships between agents, used in smart technologies, networks, sensor systems, and biology. Finding shared structure is a prerequisite for determining what transitions an agent state allows, yet no algorithm existed for it.

The team defines the problem formally and adapts McSplit, a leading algorithm for maximum common induced subgraphs, to compute the maximum common bigraph between two states. That opens a path toward bisimulation checking inside bigraph tools, a simplification technique proven in other modeling paradigms. Tool support matters here: without algorithms for basic comparisons, a rich modeling language stays hard to use in practice.
arxiv-2601-03998:
Koustav Banerjee, with Kathrin Bringmann and Atul Dixit, studies two restricted counting families: overpartitions with limits and concave compositions. Counting problems like these often hide deep links to special functions. Here those links turn out to be mixed rather than pure.

The three authors show that the generating functions involve modular forms alongside mock theta functions, mock Maass forms, and false theta functions at the same time. They also work out the main growth terms as the counted objects grow large. A further part treats related rank statistics, which split counts into finer groups. The result shows how one restricted problem can blend several kinds of modular behaviour.
arxiv-2601-04098:
Maryam Rahimi, Mahdi Nouri, and Yadollah Yaghoobzadeh measure where in a text a transformer model actually looks, layer by layer. Models are known to favour certain input positions no matter what the words mean. Past work saw this bias in task scores or in attention maps, not in how positions drive each prediction.

Using a layer conductance method inside a sliding window, the three authors study short-context next-word prediction. The position profiles stay stable across varied texts and even scrambled words, which points to a built-in trait. Favour for recent words grows steadily with depth, while favour for early words is faint and fades. The bias also splits by word type: function words lean recent, content words lean early.
arxiv-2601-04798:
Long-duration drone tracking is the problem Tamara R. Lenhard and 3 co-authors take up in a 2026 paper. Surveillance systems need to follow drones steadily, yet detector-based methods lose them in frequent dropouts, breaking tracks over time. Foundation models such as SAMURAI track objects well in other domains, but drone footage poses its own difficulties, and research using ordinary colour video remains limited.

The authors build a detector-augmented version of SAMURAI, pairing fresh detections with the tracker's memory of its target. The design aims to keep frame-level accuracy while fixing the gaps that end long tracks. Reliable long tracks matter for airspace security, where a briefly lost drone can mean a missed warning.
arxiv-2601-04998:
Yiting Mao and 4 co-authors build a quantum circuit stage that pins down how a quantum system warms to a set heat in a 2026 paper. The mark is a calm state where flows in and out weigh the same on each path. When the world around a system keeps a trace of the past, the rules for that calm state tend to break. That loss of grip hurts work on rigs meant to cook up states at a chosen heat.

The stage uses extra qubits, built as small plug-in units, tied to the main system. It forces a strict form of warm-up, one with no trace of the past. A twist in the states of the spare qubits drives the lopsided warm-up by a reshaped rule. Firm grip on heat is a core need for quantum rigs that aim to mimic real stuff at a real warmth.
arxiv-2601-05198:
Rémi Goerlich and 3 co-authors test, in the lab, how a key law of the small world bends when a system is out of rest in a 2026 paper. At rest, how much a system shakes tells how it will react to a push. Out of rest, that law is known to crack. Their test bed is a small bead of glass, held in a soft trap by a beam of light. Noise with a tune to it drives it out of rest.

They tweak how stiff the trap is and read the bead's reply. Read one way, the bead's acts crack the law. But when the hidden parts are brought to light, the law is met in full. Those parts are the ones that make its acts free of a past. The find shows what extra facts lab work must track to call how a driven bead will react.
arxiv-2601-05898:
Darren W Moore and 7 co-authors provide in 2026 a real-world way to measure sub-Planck structures, tiny aspects inside the probability distributions that describe bosonic quantum systems. Such structures appear almost whenever these systems are driven or measured in ways that bend their response. Until now they could be spotted but only compared qualitatively.

Their method identifies, quantifies, and compares these aspects using probability densities of a single phase-space variable, quantities that tests can measure or estimate. Tests on high-order Fock states of a single-atom mechanical oscillator showed provably finer sub-Planck structure as occupation increased. That held despite growing uncertainty in the phonon, position, and momentum descriptions, confirming the method captures structure that ordinary uncertainty measures overlook. The test bed was one atom in a trap, set up to vibrate like a tiny spring.
arxiv-2601-06198:
Biryani varies enormously across India, and Shubham Goel and 4 co-authors study that diversity through cooking videos in a 2026 paper. The celebrated rice dish differs by region in ingredients, steps, and presentation. Online videos offer a rich record, but existing video tools miss fine-grained, culturally grounded procedural differences.

The team curated 120 high-quality YouTube recordings covering 12 regional styles. Their framework uses vision-language models to split videos into small procedural steps and align them with spoken transcripts and standard recipe text. A comparison pipeline then identifies and explains how regional variants differ. A question-answer benchmark tests procedural understanding at several reasoning levels, with human checks for precision.
arxiv-2601-06498:
Rare celestial objects still need a human expert's eyes before entering catalogs, and surveys now produce far too many candidates. Minghui Jia and 7 co-authors present Spec-o3 in a 2026 paper, a tool-augmented vision-language agent that inspects spectra the way astronomers do, using specialized tools and stepwise reasoning.

Training came in two stages: supervised fine-tuning on recorded expert inspection trajectories, then outcome-based reinforcement learning on rare-type verification tasks. On five rare-object tasks from the LAMOST survey, the agent raised the macro-F1 score dramatically, beating proprietary vision-language models and specialized deep classifiers with a modest base model. It generalized to unseen tasks and to other surveys. Experts rated its reasoning traces coherent and physically consistent, supporting trustworthy decisions.
arxiv-2601-06698: Z. Brzeźniak and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers stochastic Cahn-Hilliard-Brinkman model. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. The authors consider a stochastic version of the Cahn-Hilliard-Brinkman model in a smooth two- or three-dimensional domain with dynamical boundary conditions. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-06898:
Sonia Yeh wrote a 2026 arXiv paper with Rishabh Ghotge, Yujia Shi, and Luka de Koe. The paper sets out a score for how well a truck charge site holds up under stress. The sites serve heavy-duty trucks and charge at megawatt scale. The score is called a Resilience Key Performance Indicator, or Resilience KPI.

The score does not rest on one kind of threat. It tracks how a site holds up when parts fail or load spikes. It uses signs that staff can see on site each day. These signs cover how long the site can ride through a fault. They cover how fast it can get back to full work. They cover work kept up with one part out of use. They also cover charge not served and lines of trucks that wait.
arxiv-2601-07198: Yan Xie and Junjie Liu wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on how to read the heat of a tiny quantum system. The field is quantum thermometry. It does for tiny systems what a home thermometer does at our scale. Heat is not a trait quantum rules let us read at once. Most past work set bounds on how sharp such a read can be, via the quantum Fisher information and the Cramer-Rao bound. Xie and Liu work on a system out of balance, with a direct readout as the aim.
arxiv-2601-07598:
Christopher Couzens uses a symmetry trick to compute quantities in a supergravity theory, in this 2026 preprint. The setting is a class of AdS3 solutions in type IIB supergravity that preserve a certain amount of supersymmetry. Equivariant localization is the method: symmetry can pin a hard integral down to a few special points. Couzens applies it to several observables of these solutions.

His route to localize the odd-dimensional internal space is unusual. He reduces along a shrinking circle, which creates a boundary in the remaining even-dimensional spacetime. That boundary makes the localization workable. Results like these feed the holographic dictionary linking gravity solutions to field theories. The paper is written for string theorists who compute exact quantities in supersymmetric backgrounds.
arxiv-2601-07998:
Hongwei Lin and colleagues predict where people will look in a visual search, using texture and oriented filter features. Understanding human visual search matters for vision science and computer vision. It also models how observers allocate attention when a target's location is unknown. Their 2026 preprint studies the link between Gabor features and texture features from gray-level co-occurrence matrices. The focus is early-stage search behavior.

Early attention decides which regions get examined at all. Statistical texture may tell the visual system where a target is plausible. Comparing two feature families shows which better tracks human gaze. Such models feed image quality assessment and interface design. The paper serves vision scientists and medical imaging scholars. It continues a line of work on predicting regions of interest in search tasks.
arxiv-2601-08098: Philip Korman wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a broad form of Pohozhaev's identity for radial solutions of p-Laplace equations. An identity of this kind gives a sum that each solution must match, which can rule out solutions in some settings. Korman's route builds on work by Brezis and Nirenberg, where the identity sat hid in the proof for the plain Laplace equation. The new form widens that tool to the p-Laplace case, for readers in the study of partial differential equations.
arxiv-2601-08198: Yibo Wang and six co-authors improve self-play fine-tuning for large language models. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that self-play methods adapt models where expert labels are scarce. They do so by training on responses the model itself generates across iterations. A flaw is that reward advantages of labeled over synthetic responses can vanish during training. That vanishing leads to unstable optimization in the SPIN method. The authors argue triplets beat pairs for stable, effective training. Their change targets steadier gains when human annotation is limited.
arxiv-2601-08698:
Lorenzo Casalino and co-authors present Double Strike, an attack on side-channel defenses for neural networks. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that deep networks support driving assistants and medical diagnoses. Training them is lengthy and expensive, so the trained weights are valuable intellectual property.

Side-channel analysis has emerged as an effective way to recover those weights from implementations. Defenses based on approximation aim to block such recovery. Double Strike shows how to break approximation-based countermeasures, per the title. For chip and model vendors, the result is a warning: defenses must be tested against adaptive attacks before deployed networks can be called protected.
arxiv-2601-08898:
A. Capolupo, G. Pisacane, and A. Quaranta study how to set a rest frame for bits that are a mix of masses. Some bits, such as neutrinos, act as a blend of mass states at once. A rest frame needs one mass, so a blend breaks the plain idea. The team says a new frame view from quantum work is a must here.

In that view, frames are set by a quantum bit, not a fixed grid. Shifts to the rest frame then make links grow between parts of the blend. The team checks what this means for neutrinos and for plain mesons that mix. A reader in core physics gets a warn. Links between bits can rest on the frame you pick, in a deep way.
arxiv-2601-08998:
Alexander Berndt and four co-authors study flaky tests made by chat models for large database tools. A flaky test passes at one run and fails at the next, with no code change. Such tests waste staff time, since a fail may mean no bug at all. Labs now use chat models to write tests fast, but the flake rate of those tests was not known.

The team runs model made tests on both firm tools and open tools. They track how oft flakes show, and what makes them show. Causes span time waits, test order, and shared state. A reader who uses AI test help gets hard rates, not fears. The work shows where a human must check model tests with most care.
arxiv-2601-09498:
Leonhard Grosse, Sara Saeidian, Tobias J. Oechtering, and Mikael Skoglund measure how privacy tools contract information. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies Dobrushin coefficients of Markov kernels that satisfy pointwise maximal leakage bounds. Pointwise maximal leakage is a privacy notion that limits what any single output can reveal.

The bounds are taken over distributions whose smallest probability stays above a fixed constant. In the limit where that constant goes to zero, the notion recovers local differential privacy. The Dobrushin coefficient tracks how much a kernel shrinks differences between inputs. Linking the two gives a clean way to certify how private mechanisms mix data.
arxiv-2601-09698:
Tony Danjun Wang, Tolga Birdal, Nassir Navab, and Lennart Bastian rebuild 3D human poses from a few camera views. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents COMPOSE, a hypergraph optimization method for multi-view pose estimation. The task feeds action recognition, sports analysis, and human-robot interaction.

Standard pipelines first find 2D keypoints in each view, then match them across views and triangulate. Matching is the fragile step, since points hide and swap identities. A hypergraph can encode richer matches than pairwise links. Better matching should give steadier skeletons from sparse camera setups in gyms, clinics, and studios.
arxiv-2601-09798:
