Noam Nissan and Yakov Varshavsky extend affine Springer theory to rings of mixed characteristic. Their 2026 arXiv paper builds on work by Bouthier, Kazhdan, and Varshavsky. The new setting involves Witt vectors, which mix prime characteristic with characteristic zero.

The authors introduce perfectly placid perfect infinity-stacks and set up their dimension theory. Affine Springer fibers encode deep data about reductive groups and orbital integrals. Extending the theory to mixed characteristic widens its reach in the Langlands program. The stack language gives these singular spaces a clean, workable form for use in proofs.
arxiv-2601-09898:
David Elsweiler, Christine Elsweiler, and Anna Ziegner study how politeness shapes chats with AI helpers. Their 2026 arXiv paper investigates user politeness in human-AI information seeking, set in a cooking-assistance scenario. Politeness is a core dimension of human communication, yet its role with AI is little explored.

The authors annotated thirty dialogues and found four user clusters. They range from the hyperpolite to the hyperefficient. How users phrase requests may steer what the system returns and how satisfied users feel. Knowing the styles helps designers tune assistants for real human manners, not ideal ones.
arxiv-2601-10498:
Nilin Abrahamsen gives a new train rule for agents that learn from rewards. The rule is named PROMA. Past top rules grade each act next to a fixed ref model. That ref can bind the agent and cost a full model in memory. PROMA drops the ref.

It works at the level of small batches. As slopes add up across batches, it trims the sum. The trim cuts the part that lines up with the batch at hand. The trim is done layer by layer in the back pass. That keeps it cheap to run. The aim is firm updates with no ref model.
arxiv-2601-10598:
John H. Livingston and a large team of co-authors study how the Galaxy's most common planet systems are born. These systems hold several planets of Earth-to-Neptune size in tight orbits. At small distances from their stars, big planets are far rarer than small ones. The team presents a young system that may be an early form of this common type.

A young progenitor lets astronomers watch the class while it is still forming. Its traits can show how compact systems of small planets take shape. The case bears on why mid-size planets end up so common and so close to their suns. Planet formation models gain a rare snapshot of youth to test against.
arxiv-2601-10798:
Carolina Casadio and a large team of co-authors present the POLAMI study of AGN jets across wavelengths. Active galactic nuclei fire jets of plasma across space. Millimeter-band polarimetry probes these jets where opacity and Faraday rotation blur longer radio waves less. The study compares millimeter results with optical ones for the same jets.

Polarization reveals the magnetic fields that shape a jet's flow. Reading it at two bands shows how the jet changes from its base outward. POLAMI is a monitoring program, so it tracks change over time as well. The work serves astronomers who trace how black holes launch and steer the most powerful outflows in the universe.
arxiv-2601-11098:
Yuhua Liu and co-authors map magnetic fields in two massive clumps of the 20 km/s cloud. The cloud sits in the Central Molecular Zone, the dense heart of our Galaxy. Using ALMA, the team observed linearly polarized continuum emission at 870 microns. The resolution is about 0.2 arcseconds, near two thousand astronomical units at that distance.

Polarized dust light traces the field's shape in the clumps named Clump 1 and Clump 4. The derived field strengths span a stated range for both clumps. Fields help decide whether a clump collapses into stars or holds. In the Galaxy's turbulent center, that contest is fierce, and these maps give rare, fine-grained evidence.
arxiv-2601-11398:
Kurt Thomas and four coauthors study how people seek help for digital safety. Their 2026 preprint maps that help seeking in the wild. Privacy, safety, and security threats online are complex to face. The burden of that complexity falls on users themselves.

Users turn to many sources when threats hit them. Family and peers are a first port of call for many. Platforms, advice guides, and niche communities also serve. Even large language models now field such pleas for help. To fix any part of that ecosystem, its shape must be known. The study gives a ground view of who helps whom. It sets the base for better tools and guides.
arxiv-2601-12198:
Ilya Archakov builds an estimator of how two random variables move as one, based on how alike they are in direction and size. Under set conditions, the measure acts as a robust, consistent gauge of linear correlation. For that case, an exact sampling spread is known.

A robust correlation gauge resists outliers that can fool the classic Pearson gauge. An exact spread lets users make firm tests and intervals. The work gives both the new gauge and its theory. It should suit finance and other fields with wild data.  The exact spread is a rare gain for such a gauge.
arxiv-2601-12298:
A hardware team design a processing-in-memory chip for low-batch language models at the edge. Edge runs face a memory bandwidth wall on matrix-vector work, the core of such models. Digital PIM puts compute in memory to ease that wall.

Past PIM edge chips still had three flaws: small bandwidth gains, poor use of parts in mixed work, and low compute in each unit. Their design, CD-PIM, rests on LPDDR5 memory. It aims to lift all three at once. Faster edge models would cut cloud use and delay.  Low batch work is the norm for edge chat tools.
arxiv-2601-12898:
Jiahao Yang, Hao Tian, Si-Yu Pan, and Gang V. Chen revisit triangular lattice spin liquids under magnetic fields. Spin liquids are exotic phases where spins stay fluid down to low temperatures. Recent progress in moire superlattices and triangular antiferromagnets motivates a fresh look. Magnetic responses of ordered phases can be mundane by contrast.

The team study how orbital magnetic flux and Zeeman coupling act together. Their synergy generates internal gauge flux inside spin liquid phases. Emergent gauge flux and spin ordering are the outcomes named in the title. Applications target the Hofstadter Hubbard model, a hub for correlated electron physics. The work links spin liquid theory with moire materials now in labs.
arxiv-2601-13098:
Wenge Xu, Foroogh Hajiseyedjavadi, Debargha Dey, Tram Thi Minh Tran, and Mark Colley test how noise hurts sound cues from self driving cars. Such cars may use outer screens and sounds to talk to people on foot. The mix is called an audio visual outer interface.

Just as dim light can blur a visual cue, loud noise can mask a sound cue. The team asks how that plays out for three groups. They cover people who hear well, deaf people, and people with weak hearing. The study shows that sound cues cannot be judged in a quiet lab alone. Car teams must test them in real street noise if all walkers are to stay safe.
arxiv-2601-13298:
Joachim Dahl Thomsen and co-authors work toward sound electric marks of superconductor tools inside an electron scope. To tie plan to acts is core to build quantum stuff well. Such stuff bends with small flaws. An electron scope can see plan, charge, and magnet traits at fine scale.

Yet live electric tests in a scope stay rare. They are rarest at the cold of liquid helium, where many tools must run. The team shows a route to such tests that holds up. For quantum tool teams, a live check in the scope can tie a flaw to a fail in one run, not two.
arxiv-2601-13598:
Stephan Wong and co-authors study how to sort new materials by their deep structure in 2026. For crystals, math based on wave-like patterns in momentum space does much of this work. Materials with no fixed repeating pattern break that method, since they lack the needed symmetry. Their class then stays hard to pin down.

The team builds a local test based on parity, a simple sign-like trait. A local test can probe one spot at a time, not the whole bulk at once. That suits materials with no neat grid of atoms. The work seeks a clear class label for such odd materials, which may host new effects.
arxiv-2601-13698:
Arjun Nichani and co-authors ask if privacy must always cost fairness in machine learning in 2026. Fairness and privacy are two pillars of systems people can trust. Each has been studied much on its own. How the two interact, with accuracy in the mix, has drawn far less work.

The team uses Chernoff information, a measure from information theory, to probe the link. They build a neural way to estimate it from data. Their point is that the trade-off shifts with the data at hand. Blanket claims that privacy harms fairness may just be wrong.
arxiv-2601-14098:
Cristian Sestito and co-authors let language models help design electronic circuits across many domains in 2026. Large language models are transforming electronic design automation. They enhance schematic design, simulation, netlist synthesis, and place-and-route steps. Existing methods focus these gains within isolated open-source tools.

They often lack flexibility for analogue, digital, and radio-frequency design at once. The team's flexible framework is assisted by language models across that range. One flexible assistant could speed chip design for mixed products. Hardware teams face long cycles, so any sound speedup counts. One tool that spans all three design kinds can cut hand-offs in a build. Fewer hand-offs mean fewer slips as a chip moves from plan to tape-out.
arxiv-2601-14198:
A. Jääskeläinen and co-authors make electrical scans of a region ignore changes outside it in 2026. Electrical impedance tomography infers conductivity inside a body from surface voltages. Changes outside the region of interest can pollute the image. Their method approximately eliminates that outside effect.

The method forms a local reconstruction in the region of interest only. It considers the Jacobian matrix of the forward map, which links conductivity to voltages. Local imaging suits cases where only one area can be modeled well. Medical and industrial scans could both use cleaner local views.
arxiv-2601-14398:
Zhi-Qiang Gao, Hui Yang, and Yan-Qi Wang extend a theory of phase changes in this 2026 paper. A deconfined quantum critical point is a direct quantum phase transition between two ordered phases. The two phases break distinct, seemingly unrelated symmetries. Such points give a route to continuous transitions beyond the conventional Ginzburg-Landau paradigm, and they need no fine tuning.

The team adds internal supersymmetry to that picture. In their setup, the on-site Hilbert space carries a representation of a Lie superalgebra. The Hamiltonian stays invariant under the matching Lie supergroup. Readers get a new model class where two major ideas, deconfined criticality and supersymmetry, meet in one system.
arxiv-2601-14498:
Marlena Bannick and a working group team present software for clinical trials in this 2026 paper. Covariate adjustment is a statistical technique that can increase efficiency in randomized trials. It uses patient traits measured at the start to sharpen the treatment comparison. The United States FDA has issued guidance with recommendations and best practices for the method.

A gap stood between that guidance and usable software. The statistical literature is extensive, but tools that follow best practices were missing. The RobinCar family fills the gap with R tools for robust covariate adjustment. Readers get software built to match the FDA's stated rules.
arxiv-2601-14598:
Yonatan Gizachew Achamyeleh, Harsh Thomare, and Mohammad Abdullah Al Faruque improve AI decompilation in this 2026 paper. Large language models have recently been applied to binary decompilation, turning machine code back into readable source. They still treat code as plain text, though. They ignore the graphs that govern program control flow. That limitation often yields syntactically fragile and logically inconsistent output, especially for optimized binaries.

Their framework, HELIOS, reframes LLM based decompilation as a structured reasoning task. Its full name is Hierarchical Graph Abstraction for Structure-Aware LLM Decompilation. The gain shows most on hard files. Those are the ones that used to come back with the most flaws. Readers get a method that feeds the model the program's true structure, not just its text.
arxiv-2601-14698:
Michael Theologitis, Preetam Prabhu Srikar Dammu, Chirag Shah, and Dan Suciu build a fact-checking benchmark in this 2026 paper. Fact-verification benchmarks have made substantial progress. Claims grounded in large-scale structured data remain underexplored, though. Most benchmarks check claims against text passages. Real data claims rest on tables.

Their benchmark, ClaimDB, is the first fact-verification benchmark where evidence derives from compositions of millions of records and multiple tables. A claim may need sums, joins, and filters across a whole database to settle. Readers get a test that grades systems on database-grounded truth, a much harder bar than passage matching.
arxiv-2601-15198:
Shashwat Singh, Christian E. A. Chapman-Bird, Christopher P. L. Berry, and John Veitch look ahead to what space-based wave detectors will teach us. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with extreme mass-ratio inspirals. In these events, a small object spirals into a massive black hole.

The waves from such events can pin black hole traits to sub-percent precision. The LISA mission should detect many of them. The authors use hierarchical inference, a method that pools many events at once. Pooled, the events reveal the demographics of massive black holes and how they formed.
arxiv-2601-15498:
Jingwei Song and eight co-authors work on speeding up large language models in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their method is called MARS, and it targets speculative decoding. That technique speeds up text generation by splitting the work. A draft model proposes tokens, and the target model checks them. Recent work has tightened the link between drafter and target. Verification itself, though, has changed little.

Most systems still check drafts by strict token-level rejection sampling. MARS replaces that step with margin-aware verification. The name suggests checks that weigh how close a draft token is, not just right or wrong. Looser but sound checks could accept more draft text per pass. That would cut the time and cost of running large models.
arxiv-2601-15698:
Mingyu Yu and four co-authors probe the safety limits of multimodal models in a 2026 arXiv paper. These models handle both text and images. Their rise has brought complex security challenges. Text safety has been studied heavily. Visual safety boundaries remain underexplored, the authors say. Their work examines jailbreaks aimed at harmful image generation. The attacks use inputs that are semantic-agnostic, per the title.

A semantic-agnostic input carries little clear meaning of its own. Such inputs may slip past filters tuned to meaning. If they can still trigger harmful images, the filter logic has a hole. Mapping that hole is the paper's service to defenders. Red-team work like this is how safety teams learn where the fence is low.
arxiv-2601-15798:
Zhikai Xue and six co-authors present a health platform driven by language models in a 2026 arXiv paper. Chronic diseases are now the leading cause of death worldwide. Strained medical resources and aging populations intensify the challenge. Patients often cannot read early signs of decline on their own. Adherence to care plans also slips without support. Their system is called VitalDiagnosis.

It aims at round-the-clock vital monitoring and chronic disease management. The design shifts care from passive monitoring to proactive, interactive engagement. A system that checks in can catch problems earlier than one that only records. It can also nudge patients to stay on plan. For overstretched clinics, such an ecosystem promises reach that staff alone cannot provide.
arxiv-2601-16098:
Zack Dewis and six coauthors build a new net for sorting hyper views of land. Their 2026 preprint deals with views that hold many bands of light. Such views help map crops, rock and water from the air. Mamba nets sort these views well, but their token order can be weak. A weak order wastes the rich bands in each view.

The team guides the token order with clumps found in the data. Clumps group like spots by both place and light band. That guide shapes a space and light Mamba net. A better order should lift sort scores on test views. The work targets fast, sharp maps from air and space views.
arxiv-2601-16398:
Hannah Cyberey and Yangfeng Ji audit models from in with steer paths. Their 2026 preprint deals with checks of large language models. Most checks now test just inputs and outputs of a model. Such black box tests can miss flaws hid in the build. White box checks read the deep acts of the model as it works.

Steer paths shift deep acts in set ways for the check. Shifts show how touchy a pick is to deep traits. Touch maps help rule teams set fair test terms. They also show where a flaw lives in the build. The work gives a new audit tool with deep reach.
arxiv-2601-16498:
Chen Long and five coauthors use expert facts to tune calls on tree types. Their 2026 preprint deals with fine sorts of tree kinds. True sorts back wood counts and life watch work. Past tools chase scores by more complex builds. They oft miss long tail kinds and kin kinds that look much like.

Expert facts guide the last call step of the sort. Facts span traits that split kin kinds in the field. Guided calls should lift scores on rare and kin kinds. That lift counts most for life watch in rich woods. The work adds field craft to deep sort tools.
arxiv-2601-16698:
Jannik Ströhle and Nikolija Momčilović study a way to reap quantum links from empty space. Pairs of probes can pull shared links from a field's base state. Past work set those probes in free space. Their 2026 preprint moves the probes in a closed tube. Walls of the tube shape the field in new ways.

The pair sits on the tube's core line. Both probes share the same form and soft link to the field. The team works out the math and runs screen tests. Walls can boost or curb the shared link yield. Such yields could feed small quantum nets and sensors.
arxiv-2601-16798:
A dwarf nova named ER Ursae Majoris flares up far more oft than its kin. Such stars are tight pairs where one star feeds the next. Gas piles up, then bursts in bright flares. Bumps in the light, called superhumps, mark each big flare. A 2026 preprint reports fresh light checks on this star.

The team used ground scopes and a space scope named TESS. They traced flare length, gaps, and bump beats over time. Charts of drift show how the bump beat shifts. Those shifts tell how the gas disk warps and shrinks. Wild stars like this test our tales of disk flow.
arxiv-2601-16998:
Mario Zitelli tracks how light modes share power in a flawed glass fiber. Wide fibers bear many light paths, called modes. Modes trade power as light runs down the fiber. Their 2026 preprint tests that trade with four unlike ways. Lab tests and screen sims both join the check. All four ways point the same way in the end.

Fiber flaws alone can settle modes in a lopsided spread. Low modes gain power at the cost of high modes. A weighted Bose-Einstein law fits that spread well. Such spreads shape how wide fibers carry fast data. Phone and lab nets lean on those fibers daily.
arxiv-2601-17198:
Sehyeok Park, Jay P. Lim, and Santosh Nagarakatte study a small but key step in computer math. The step is called FastTwoSum. It splits a sum into an exact head and tail with no loss. Such lossless steps guard long sums from slow drift. The authors ask when the step stays lossless under broad rounding rules.

They give new, wider conditions that still keep the step exact. The rules cover all faithful rounding modes. They add firm claims for round-to-odd mode as well. They also give a split method made for round-to-odd, with bit spread that can be set. Chip and software teams can use these rules to prove numeric code is safe.
arxiv-2601-17498:
Zijian Yu and Sijia Cai report a galaxy with almost no heavy elements. They found it with infrared spectroscopy from the James Webb Space Telescope. The galaxy, CAPERS-39810, sits at redshift 3.654. Its oxygen abundance is far below that of the Sun. That makes it extremely metal-poor by any scale.

Such a galaxy shows the cosmos in a near-pristine state. Early galaxies held little of the heavy elements that stars forge over time. Each one found this poor in metals tests how the first stars lived and died. The 2026 paper adds one sharp case to that small set.
arxiv-2601-17698:
Paramesh Mahapatra probes sine dilaton gravity with a flow central charge. He builds a holographic c-function for that gravity in domain wall gauge. The work shows equivalence between sine dilaton gravity and two copies of Liouville conformal field theory. He computes the central charge from that link. The holographic c-function reproduces the Liouville charge in the UV limit.

Central charge counts degrees of freedom in a field theory. A matching count is a strong check on a duality. Sine dilaton gravity is a test bed for quantum gravity ideas. Firm duals help sort which gravity models hold up. Mahapatra's result ties two frames with a number both must share. That kind of check is the field's gold standard.
arxiv-2601-17898:
Qi Zhan, Yile Wang, and Hui Huang take stock of how well language models find names in text. Their 2026 preprint assesses named entity recognition, the task of spotting people, places, firms, and other named things. With large language models, the task is shifting. It used to be done by tagging each word in turn. Now models can write out the entities as text, a generative style.

The authors test open-source models in a systematic way. They cover both flat lists of entities and nested ones, where names sit inside names. They also probe the gap between the new generative style and the older tagging style. The findings help users pick tools for search, records, and text mining.
arxiv-2601-17998:
Benjamin Mako Hill and Aaron Shaw argue that Wikipedia is a research treasure hiding in plain sight. Their 2026 preprint marks twenty years of the free encyclopedia. Its founders, they note, never dreamed it would become a lab. Yet Wikipedia and its sister projects now support a thriving body of scholarship. The authors ask just how thriving that body is, and they set out to measure it.

A shared, open, and logged community makes a rare test bed. Scholars can study how people write, argue, govern, and build tools together. The paper surveys the scale of that work. It makes the case that this lab is the most important one in social and computing research history.
arxiv-2601-18398:
Elia Buono and three colleagues built a lab rig to watch how a burst dam wave spreads and to read its depth from shots. When a dam wall breaks, a sheet of water rushes out and thins as it runs. How deep that sheet is at each spot shapes the force it can hit with.

Their rig holds a known mass of dyed water in a tank with a wall that lifts out. The sheet runs over a wide flat bed that can tilt from flat to a steep slope. Bright light from below and a camera read the dye shade, and shade gives depth at each point. A tool like this lets teams test flood math with hard facts from the bench, not just from code.
arxiv-2601-18598:
A study takes on a gap in the checks for joint models, a tool that tracks two kinds of health facts at once. Joint models pair a stream of tests over time with the time to a key event, such as death or cure. They are used in health, in life maths, and in fields far from both. Yet the usual scores that rank two models do not say if one model fits the facts well at all.

A model can win a rank yet still fit the facts in a poor way. The study sets out checks that can flag a bad fit and point to the part that is off. The checks are named for Dimitris Rizopoulos, whose work frames the field. Such checks would help staff trust a joint model or know to build a new one.
arxiv-2601-18698:
Xiao Liu and Jiawei Zhang ask if video tools that build clips from text know the world in a fair way. Such tools can now make strikingly real clips from a line of text. But their training sets lean to rich, well-shot lands. A prompt for a famed sight in a poor land may give a clip that looks wrong or stock. The team test that slant with sights as their probe.

They ask tools to build clips of known sights across the globe. Judges then grade how true each clip is to the real place. Gaps in the grades map where the tools' world lore is thin. A fair map of those gaps could push firms to train on a wider world. It could also warn users where a clip is apt to mislead.
arxiv-2601-18798:
William Han and eight colleagues drop a whole part from tools that read heart wave charts with the help of text. Such tools pair a chart of the heart's beats with a text model that can talk about it. Past tools first run the chart through a trained coder that turns it into a code. That coder adds bulk and cost to the build and to each train run.

Their tool, named ELF, swaps the coder for a lone thin sheet that maps the chart straight to the text model's space. The sheet trains with the model as one. A lean build could make heart chart tools cheap to train and swift to run. It could also bring them to small clinics with small kit. The team test if the lean form can match the grades of the full form.
arxiv-2601-18998:
Zahra Hashemi and three co-authors warn that open science goods can be turned to harm by language models. Big models are now praised for dreaming up and judging fresh research ideas on their own. The flip side gets less study: the same models could reuse open papers, data, and code to build harmful work.

This risk grows as models grow more able and open goods grow more rich. The paper maps how such misuse could work and why current guards may miss it. Naming the path early gives funders, journals, and labs a chance to set rules before misuse scales up.
arxiv-2601-19698:
Marco Manetti and Gabriele Rossetti work in homological algebra on a transfer principle. Their objects are DG-Lie algebras, algebraic structures that mix a grading, a differential, and a bracket. Such algebras control deformation problems across mathematics. A key fact is formality: some of these algebras are equivalent to much simpler ones.

A formality transfer theorem says formality passes along maps between algebras. The authors give a convenient reformulation of that theorem. They also slightly generalise it and show applications. The examples demonstrate where the cleaner statement does work the old one could not. Tools like this quietly support large parts of modern algebra and geometry.
arxiv-2601-19898:
Shubham Patle and colleagues build a benchmark for Arabic calligraphy understanding. Arabic calligraphy blends language with art; letters stretch and curve into decoration. Multimodal models have advanced across many languages and scripts. Their grasp of Arabic script, especially in stylised calligraphic forms, remains largely untested.

Their benchmark, DuwatBench, bridges language and visual heritage. It tests whether models can read and interpret calligraphic works. Such art carries religious and cultural weight across the Arab world. A model that fails on calligraphy fails on real cultural material. The benchmark gives researchers a way to measure and close that gap. The gap is plain to see.
arxiv-2601-19998:
P. Díaz and E. Mainar study when families of functions form a totally positive system. Total positivity is a strong regularity property: certain matrices built from the functions have all minors of the right sign. Such systems are prized in approximation and design because they behave predictably. The authors examine analytic bases, families built from analytic functions.

Their route goes through bidiagonal factorisation of collocation matrices. They derive explicit formulas for the initial minors using Schur functions, classical objects from algebra. The structure of those formulas yields sufficient conditions for total positivity of generic analytic systems. Knowing a basis is totally positive guarantees stable interpolation. The work links symmetric function theory to practical approximation. The tests are strict by design. One bad sign and the whole set fails. That is why the checks mean so much here.
arxiv-2601-20198:
Ratnavibusena Don Shahain Manujith and three colleagues present DeRaDiff, a method for aligning diffusion image models with human preferences. Alignment aims to raise aesthetic appeal and reduce artifacts and bias in generated images. At the same time, the model must not drift too far from its pretrained behavior, a balance usually enforced by a penalty term.

DeRaDiff works by realigning the denoising time steps of the model. The authors frame alignment as a trade-off between reward and closeness to the prior. Better alignment methods give users prettier, safer images while keeping the range of what the model can produce.
arxiv-2601-20598:
Lakshman Balasubramanian surveys person re-identification in 2025, the task of matching images of the same person across cameras. He reviews training paradigms and evaluates how robust leading models are in cross-domain use, where the test cameras differ from training. He also examines how foundation models help, through richer and more transferable visual features.

Three paradigms are compared: supervised, self-supervised, and language-aligned models. The question in the title is what actually works. A clear-eyed survey matters for surveillance and retail analytics teams choosing a system that must survive a change of venue.
arxiv-2601-20698:
S. Simón-Díaz leads a team of sixteen authors on a study of the most massive stars. Their 2026 paper, part of the IACOB project, deals with O-type stars. These are hot, bright, short-lived stars. Since the early 1980s, some O stars have shown surfaces rich in products of the CNO cycle. That cycle is the fusion chain that powers such stars.

For years, the standard view blamed slow mixing inside the rotating star. Rotation was thought to churn the star and bring fusion products to the surface. The paper takes a fresh look at that claim within the IACOB project. It adds to a long effort to map the chemistry of these stars. The work helps show how massive stars stir their insides as they age.
arxiv-2601-20798:
Petro Maksymovych and four co-authors present a new way to fingerprint superconductors. Their 2026 paper uses tunneling Andreev reflection spectroscopy, or TAR. The method reads how electrons reflect at the edge of a superconductor. From that signal it can tell apart pairing symmetries, such as s-wave and d-wave. It works at the atomic scale.

Traditional conductance methods struggle to make these distinctions cleanly. TAR instead exploits the sharp sensitivity of the excess tunneling decay rate to Andreev reflection. That sensitivity makes the fingerprint robust, the authors argue. It can separate simple pairing states from more complex ones. For physicists hunting new superconductors, the technique offers a sharper tool for a basic question: how do the electrons pair up?
arxiv-2601-20898:
Sergio Burdisso and a large team of co-authors make speech recognition less touchy about its prompt. Their 2026 paper concerns LLM-based automatic speech recognition. In this design, a speech foundation model feeds a large language model. A projector links the two parts. The approach yields promising results. Yet most systems use one fixed, hand-written prompt at training and test time.

That fixed prompt is a weak point. Small wording changes can sway the model's output. The authors add a learnable projection to cut this prompt sensitivity. Learning the prompt's role, rather than freezing text, steadies the system. The work helps voice tools that must work for many speakers and phrasings. It is a small change with a wide effect on reliability.
arxiv-2601-21398:
Meng-Long Song, Zan Cao, Xue-Ke Song, Liu Ye, and Dong Wang use quantum steering to track energy in quantum batteries. A quantum battery stores energy in quantum states and may charge faster than classic cells. In their setup, the charger and battery share a common environment.

The team tunes the setup for high stored energy, then watches the steering at work. Steering is first stored while the system settles toward balance. After that, it is spent to keep boosting the stored energy. Seeing steering act as a resource helps designers plan charging schemes that waste less of it.
arxiv-2601-21498:
Thanh-Nhan Vo, Trong-Thuan Nguyen, Tam V. Nguyen, and Minh-Triet Tran unify image creation and image editing under one frame. A scene graph describes the objects in a picture and how they relate. Most tools handle making an image and changing it as separate jobs, which breeds inconsistency.

Edits can drift away from the layout of the original scene. A graph gives both jobs the same structured plan to follow. It also gives users control over where objects sit and how they connect. The unified design aims for images that stay coherent from first draft through every edit.
arxiv-2601-21698:
Mohamed Elgaar and Hadi Amiri ask whether the order of training data changes how a language model learns, or only what it sees when. Curriculum learning borrows from schooling: easy first, hard later. Whether that reorders real learning or just exposure was unclear.

The team trains models of several sizes on a huge token budget under three curricula based on language development. Each is compared against random ordering, with a larger check at the top size. The answer guides data teams: if order only shuffles exposure, effort is better spent on data quality than on lesson plans.
arxiv-2601-21998:
Lin Li and co-authors argue that watching video can teach robots cause and effect. Alongside vision-language training, they say, video world modeling offers a fresh and independent foundation for robot learning. A world model lets a robot imagine the near future by understanding how actions change what the camera sees.

Their 2026 preprint introduces LingBot-VA, an autoregressive diffusion model built on that causal idea. It generates future views step by step, conditioned on the robot's actions. A robot that can picture the results of its choices before moving could practice in imagination, recover from surprises. And need fewer costly real-world trials to learn new skills.
arxiv-2601-22198:
Judith Vilella-Cantos and co-authors map how farm bots can know where they are. A bot that drives itself must track its place at all times. Farm work stands to gain as much from this as road cars do. One strong way to fix place is to match a fresh laser scan to scans saved from known spots.

Most work on this match was done on town streets. Farms look far from towns: rows of crops, glass houses, and few hard marks. Crops shift with the year, too. The team sums up the best new tricks for this task and how they fare on farms. Their map can help teams build bots that do not get lost in the field.
arxiv-2601-22298:
Qidong Yang and five co-authors bring honest error bars to models that dream up new samples. Such models map inputs to rich, high-end outputs, from images to forecasts. Their 2026 preprint notes a gap: users get no firm sense of how much to trust one output.

The team adapt a method that groups model outputs into clusters. Density reads on those clusters then set the trust bounds. The bounds aim to hold at the stated rate, case by case. Trust marks like these matter most where stakes are high. They help users know when to check a dream twice.
arxiv-2601-22398:
Aarush Noheria and co-authors jailbreak vision-language models by way of their own step-by-step reasoning. Such models answer questions about images and write captions. Their 2026 preprint notes that outputs swing with small prompt changes, which can expose weak safety training.

Their frame turns the model's chain of thought into the attack path. Each step nudges the model past its own guards. The work shows a risk that plain text attacks miss. Builders can use the frame to test and harden their models. It presses for safety checks that match how models think.
arxiv-2601-22498:
Wei Yang and six co-authors sharpen product suggestions by reading items in the frequency domain. Modern recommenders blend item images and text to guess what a user wants. Their 2026 preprint, FITMM, notes that most blends work in plain space, which can blur signal shape and add clash and waste.

Their method learns shared codes with information theory as its guide, tuned to each frequency band. A cleaner blend should guess taste more truly. It may also explain its picks in a clearer way. The work fits shops, media, and feeds. It is a fresh angle on a daily tool.
arxiv-2601-22898:
In Woo Park and five co-authors use a short-lived particle to probe spinning matter in heavy-ion collisions. When heavy nuclei crash, the matter formed can swirl with huge vorticity. The spin of the particles produced carries a trace of that swirl.

They focus on one particle, named in the title, and its decay into two pions. Its spin comes from both quark spins and orbital motion, in the quark-model picture. Reading these signals could reveal how the hottest, densest matter in the lab behaves. Polarization measurements of produced hadrons are the observational handle, tying the particle's decay pattern back to the swirling medium.
arxiv-2601-22998:
S. Ramakrishna and S. Fritzsche measure magnetic fields with structured light and atomic vapor. When shaped light passes through the vapor, its absorption carries marks of the field's full direction, not just its strength. One flaw remains: fields pointing in opposite directions with equal strength leave look-alike marks.

Their method removes that ambiguity, giving an unambiguous reading of the field vector. Precise field direction matters in navigation, medicine, and tests of fundamental physics. A vapor-cell sensor is small, sensitive, and needs no cryogenic cooling. Structured light in atomic vapor offers a compact sensing route, avoiding bulky coils or cryogenic detectors for field measurement.
arxiv-2601-23198:
Jin-Yi Cai, Ashwin Maran, and Ben Young classify the difficulty of counting planar graph homomorphisms. The problem is parameterized by a symmetric matrix of weights with non-negative entries. For matrices whose diagonal values are all distinct, they prove a complete dichotomy.

Every such problem is either solvable in polynomial time or as hard as the canonical counting class, with a simple criterion deciding which. They also expose a barrier coming from quantum groups. Dichotomy theorems give counting complexity a clean, finished map. A simple criterion decides each case in the dichotomy, which is what makes the classification usable in practice.
arxiv-2602-00098: Oliver Preuß and coauthors add new landscape traits for auto choice of algorithms in multi goal tuning. Such choice works well for single goal problems with survey traits, but few traits exist for multi goal problems. Their MO-ELA set adds traits drawn from a random sample across choice and goal space. The traits fall into five groups: non dominated sorting, descriptive statistics, principal component analysis, graph structures, and gradient data. A study on set benchmarks shows the added traits help pick algorithms.
arxiv-2602-00298: Abhishek Mishra and colleagues assess domain level susceptibility to emergent misalignment from narrow fine tuning. They fine tune a population of models on insecure data sets spanning 11 diverse domains, testing with and without backdoor triggers on unrelated user prompts. On Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct and GPT-4o-mini, triggers raise misalignment across most domains, with risky financial advice and toxic legal advice showing the largest effects. Domain vulnerability varies widely, from zero misalignment for incorrect math answers to very high misalignment for gore movie trivia.
arxiv-2602-00598: Ruiqi Shu and colleagues balance speed and accuracy in ocean modelling, where solvers are accurate but costly and pure deep learning lacks physics and long-term staying power. Their HybridOM system uses a light, differentiable solver as a frame enforcing laws, with a neural net as flesh fixing subgrid dynamics. A flux-gated downscaling step enables efficient high-resolution work. Tests on GLORYS12V1 and OceanBench show top accuracy with physics kept intact across seasonal simulation and forecasts with FuXi-2.0.
arxiv-2602-00698: Chen Lu and colleagues show Van Hove singularities in multi-orbital systems can support several orders with zero wave vector. One is intrinsic altermagnetism from orbital antiferromagnetism, with antiparallel spins on orbitals, found across all four 2D Bravais lattices. Spin fluctuations resolved by orbital and hopping between orbitals drive it, needing suppressed Hund coupling, strong mixing, and filling near a Van Hove point. Hubbard-U-JH phase diagrams map changes. These run from ferrimagnet to d-wave extrinsic altermagnet and from d-wave intrinsic altermagnet to ferromagnet.
arxiv-2602-00898: Behrooz Zarebavami and colleagues cut permutation time and improve solve speed by up to 6.27x across graphics applications with a fast sparse matrix order. Their order targets linear systems from triangle meshes, producing nested-dissection-style orders while cutting runtime overhead. They relax strict balance and separator quality for fast partitioning. The method splits order into patch-level local orders plus a compact quotient-graph order of separators, keeping Cholesky factorization while skipping its costliest parts. It runs in vendor sparse Cholesky solvers on CPUs and GPUs.
arxiv-2602-01498: Mingyu Han and co-authors study geometric generalization in neural operators via kernel integrals. They mimic PDE solution maps for many queries. Variable shapes make transfer to unseen shapes central in engineering design. Their kernel-integral view shows how linear models extend geometrically, linking model learning to fast kernel sums. They propose a multiscale point-cloud model from Ewald sums, joining Fourier terms with local geometry corrections. Guarantees follow for singular-kernel models, and tests show robust transfer on varied shapes, Laplace-type maps, and a nonlinear vehicle flow case.
arxiv-2602-01698: Wenhui Tan and colleagues restore exploration in reasoning models after training, where temperature sampling stops helping accuracy. Post training collapses exploration: final layer entropy falls, while middle layer entropy stays high. Their Latent Exploration Decoding adds middle outputs by cumulative sum and picks depth settings with entropy as exploration options. With no extra training, it lifts accuracy by under one point at pass one and just over one point at pass sixteen across reasoning benchmarks and models.
arxiv-2602-01798: Leonardo Pelonero and colleagues build a Science Gateway framework for portable post event pipelines that run on their own. They assess extreme natural events and their impact on risk exposed assets. Climate change worsens floods, droughts, storm surges and landslides, while earthquakes add constant risk, making better assessment and mitigation urgent in susceptible areas such as Italy. Their pipelines integrate photogrammetry, data visualization and artificial intelligence applied to aerial images.
arxiv-2602-01898: Sanna Jarl and colleagues improve active learning sample efficiency, where Gaussian processes with variance based scores pick measurement points. Two flaws: posterior variance ignores measured values and follows locations only, and variance inflates near boundaries, causing excess edge sampling. The authors derive a reconstruction density and build a warp from the posterior mean, placing more measurements where the target varies rapidly. A geometric equalizer corrects boundary bias. In tests on sixteen synthetic and two real benchmarks it improves reconstruction, with the warp adding gains where the posterior mean varies rapidly.
arxiv-2602-02098: Yannik Schnitzer and colleagues present an approach for high-trust multi-task policy performance guarantees on tasks not seen during training. Multi-task reinforcement learning trains generalist policies, yet existing approaches rarely provide formal guarantees, indispensable in safety-critical settings. They introduce a new generalisation bound composing task-level generalisation from finitely many tasks with lower trust bounds per task from finitely many rollouts, giving new tasks a high-trust guarantee. Across state-of-the-art multi-task methods, the guarantees are sound and informative at sample sizes.
arxiv-2602-02398:
Hyemin Lee and 3 co-authors examine insurance claim count models that must handle far more zeros than standard models expect, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Most policyholders file no claims, so zero-inflated and hurdle models add parameters for the excess zeros. Random effects extend these models to repeated observations over time.

Lee's team asks whether such models respect stochastic monotonicity, a fairness principle saying worse claim history should not lower assessed risk in a disordered way. They show standard random-effect versions can violate the principle, which distorts posterior credibility, the updated trust placed in a policyholder's record. The authors then build new model classes that keep the excess zeros while guaranteeing monotonicity. Their credibility adjustments stay fair and coherent as histories evolve.
arxiv-2602-02498:
Baturay Saglam and 1 co-author detoxify language model output at test time without training or learning anything new, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Models can emit toxic text even for harmless prompts, and most fixes need retraining, gradients, or extra learned components that may not transfer to black-box systems.

Their procedure approximates how completion toxicity changes with the input embeddings, the numeric vectors representing the prompt. A few descent steps on those embeddings, computed with zeroth-order optimization that needs only forward evaluations, steer generation toward safer continuations. The method needs just embedding access and a toxicity scoring function. Across models and prompts it delivered robust toxicity reductions. In most settings it achieved the best overall balance between safety and generation quality. The authors frame embeddings as practical control knobs for black-box optimization.
arxiv-2602-02698:
Armando Bellante and 6 co-authors build a compiler that prepares quantum states specified as regular languages, posted to arXiv in 2026. State preparation usually sits at two extremes: generic routines treating the target as an opaque vector, or handcrafted circuits for a few famous states. Their compiler accepts structure-aware descriptions instead.

Users specify a uniform superposition over accepted bitstrings by listing strings, writing a regular expression, or giving a finite automaton, with an optional complement flag. The compiler minimizes the automaton and maps it to an optimal matrix product state, exposing hidden structure cheaply. Two hardware-aware backends follow: one yields linear-depth, ancilla-free circuits for nearest-neighbor hardware, the other logarithmic depth for all-to-all connectivity. Preparation of a state or its complement costs the same asymptotically. Proven bounds tie depth and gate counts to system size and entanglement rank.
arxiv-2602-02998:
Bochao Chen and 2 co-authors advance the theory of surface plasmon resonances in a 2026 paper. Plasmon resonances are non-radiative electromagnetic waves at interfaces between materials with opposing permittivities. They support tech such as biosensing and cloaking. Scalar versions of the basic Neumann-Poincaré operator are well understood, but the vectorial Maxwell version was not.

The authors introduce a symmetrization principle for the matrix-valued Maxwell version of the operator. That yields a spectral decomposition for traces in a space of vector fields with well-defined curl. Building on it, they carefully characterize how weak plasmon sequences localize at material boundaries. The result settles a long-standing quantitative question for the full Maxwell system, strengthening the theory.
arxiv-2602-03298:
Extremal graph-like forms behave pseudorandomly, and Noé de Rancourt, with 2 co-authors, documents fresh cases of that phenomenon during 2026. Graph-codes, a notion put forth by Alon, are discrete forms with code-like distance properties built on graphs. Extremal examples, the largest forms avoiding certain setups, tend to exhibit strong pseudorandom actions, a fact with consequences across extremal combinatorics and theory-based computer science research.

The paper presents cases of uniformity for extremal graph-codes. Related problems connected to the density polynomial Hales-Jewett conjecture are also treated. That conjecture concerns unavoidable regular patterns in high-part combinatorial cubes. By establishing uniformity in these settings, the authors extend the general principle that maximal avoiders cannot help looking random in key statistical respects.
arxiv-2602-03398:
Shunxi Xu and 2 co-authors record sound fields with a hybrid device that mixes a spherical microphone array with linear arrays. Their 2026 paper proposes a data-driven method to reconstruct sparse sound fields from such mixed hardware. Earlier approaches handled each array type separately and then stapled the results together.

The method takes the singular value decomposition of the transfer operator, which splits the measurement into orthogonal microphone and field modes. The linear arrays add modes that spherical harmonics alone cannot express, improving spatial selectivity. Tests in reverberant rooms show smaller errors than spherical-only processing at many frequencies, distances, and source counts. The result is one unified treatment for hybrid arrays.
arxiv-2602-03498:
A young giant planet with an unusually puffy atmosphere gets a close look from the ground. A. Lavail and 11 co-authors observed the exoplanet HIP 67522 b during a transit with the CRIRES+ instrument on the Very Large Telescope. The planet is only about 17 million years old, so its atmosphere still records its early evolution.

The spectra clearly detect water vapor and, more weakly, carbon monoxide, confirming an extremely extended atmosphere. A small velocity shift points to winds blowing from the day side to the night side, and the slow rotation fits tidal locking. The analysis suggests a heavier planet than space-based estimates found, and it tentatively detects a deuterium-bearing molecule at an extreme enrichment level.
arxiv-2602-03698:
Filtering signals on graphs, from sensor networks to molecules, works best when the filter matches the graph's own spectrum. Dylan Sandfelder and 2 co-authors introduce Adaptive Spectral Shaping in a 2026 paper, a data-driven way to learn such filters. A reusable baseline spectral kernel is modulated by a few Gaussian factors, creating multi-peak responses across the Laplacian spectrum.

The Gaussian centers and bandwidths stay explicit, so the learned filter remains interpretable. Chebyshev polynomial expansions make the filters scalable without costly eigendecompositions. A transfer variant learns the baseline on source graphs and adapts only the shaping parameters on a target, enabling few-shot transfer. Across synthetic benchmarks the method cuts reconstruction error versus fixed wavelets and learned linear banks.
arxiv-2602-03798:
Code agents demos build pretty web pages and quietly skip the database behind them. Zimu Lu and 6 co-authors tackle genuine full-stack generation in a 2026 paper with FullStack-Agent, a unified system for building working websites. Real applications demand controlled data flow, current package knowledge, and bug hunting across a whole repository.

Three parts make up the system. FullStack-Dev is a multi-agent framework for planning, editing, navigation, and bug localization. FullStack-Learn improves the underlying model by back-translating crawled and synthesized website repositories into training material. FullStack-Bench tests frontend, backend, and database behavior separately. The development system beats the previous state of the art on all three test sets, and self-improvement lifts even a mid-size model.
arxiv-2602-04398:
Bias in a language model can be traced to a few neurons and muted there. Yujie Lin and 4 co-authors present a bi-directional bias attribution method in a 2026 paper. Fine-tuning and prompt engineering, the usual debiasing routes, scale poorly or degrade multi-turn user experience.

The method first finds stereotype-inducing words by comparing outputs across demographic groups. Integrated-gradient attribution then assigns the biased behavior to specific neurons, using two strategies. Acting on those activations at the projection layer reduces bias while preserving overall performance on three widely used models. Debiasing without touching prompts or weights' training keeps the fix deployable anywhere.
arxiv-2602-04498:
Man Jia and 4 co-authors present a new kind of wave result in a 2026 math paper on the AKNS system, a set of equations used across nonlinear physics. Their objects are called Painlevé solitons, waves that move over a background set by a Painlevé transcendent, a special function from a classic equation family.

A new symmetry method makes these waves by mixing scaling, Galilean, and square eigenfunction symmetries. Picking special cases then gives explicit forms for the linked nonlinear Schrödinger equation. The new classes include waves built from irrational and rational algebra. These results widen the known range for models used in optics, ultracold gases, and fluid flow.
arxiv-2602-04598:
Lucile Favero and 3 co-authors warn that AI in classrooms affects far more than test scores, in a 2026 paper built around cognition, agency, emotion, and ethics. Schools are adopting AI for personal support and speed, but the authors see mutually reinforcing harms in careless use.

Drawing on work from education, cognitive science, psychology, and ethics, they describe several risks. Offloading thought can weaken critical thought. Tools can shrink learner agency and emotional engagement. Practices built on watching pupils can erode trust. Yet design and rules matter. Well-aligned tools can prompt effortful thought, support autonomy, and keep social contact. The paper gives practical advice for teachers, designers, and schools.
arxiv-2602-04698:
Celia Merino and 5 co-authors test a proposed shortcut for measuring primordial non-Gaussianity, small departures from pure randomness in the early universe, in a 2026 cosmology paper. Some had suggested that unclustered galaxy tracers, objects with zero clustering bias, would be ideal probes.

Using state-of-the-art simulations with two strengths of the effect, the team picked tracers by local density from halos and galaxy models. Most density bins showed no response of the kind the proposal needed. For bias-zero tracers, the response was near zero in all cases. The picking method itself distorted clustering away from simple assumptions. That distortion hinders using such tracers to pin down early-universe physics. The null result closes off an appealing but flawed strategy.
arxiv-2602-04798:
Wenbin Zhou, Liyan Xie, and Shixiang Zhu detect not just when something changes but also where, in a 2026 study of spatio-temporal point processes. Such processes record events spread over space and time, from crimes to disease cases. Classic quickest detection methods focus mainly on timing.

Their likelihood-free scheme uses a local score that gauges how far each event strays from normal behavior. A cumulative-sum style statistic adds those scores across candidate spatial regions. Running step by step, the method outputs both a stopping time and an estimated change region. Theory backs control of false alarms, detection delay, and location accuracy. Tests on simulated and real event data showed the method works.
arxiv-2602-05198:
A monitoring robot should measure just enough: enough to know a field of temperature or salinity within a promised error, and no more. Kalvik Jakkala and 3 co-authors plan such routes in this 2026 robotics paper, presented at RSS 2026. Lawnmower surveys guarantee coverage but waste effort on predictable regions, while most informative planners save effort without promising any accuracy.

Their three-stage method learns a Gaussian process model of the field, converts the model's kernel into coverage maps showing where measurements can push uncertainty below a user-set threshold. It then plans a near-shortest route that meets the bound everywhere. Non-stationary kernels handle patchy phenomena, and obstacles and non-convex regions are allowed. Approximation guarantees cover both site selection and routing under a travel budget. Trials on real topographic data and with surface and underwater vehicles beat baselines on sites visited and distance traveled.
arxiv-2602-05598:
Vision transformers read images through self-attention over patches, but the way they mix feature channels stays fixed, no matter what the image shows. Aon Safdar and Mohamed Saadeldin introduce CAViT, a design that makes channel mixing dynamic. Each block runs spatial self-attention first, then channel-wise self-attention, so features recalibrate themselves based on the whole image's context.

Across five benchmark data sets from natural and medical domains, CAViT beat the standard vision transformer baseline, with accuracy gains at the top end of several points. It did so while cutting parameter count and computing cost by over thirty percent. Attention maps from the model looked sharper and more meaningful than the baseline's, which supports the design claim. The authors present the unified, content-aware mixing as a way to gain expressiveness without deeper or heavier models. The work was presented at a CVPR 2025 workshop on transformers for vision.
arxiv-2602-05698:
Solving the Poisson equation on a complex shape usually means building a mesh that fits the boundary, a costly step. Raphaël Bulle, Michel Duprez, Vanessa Lleras, and Killian Vuillemot analyze a penalized variant of the phi FEM scheme. That scheme is an unfitted finite element method that describes geometry with a level set function instead. Boundary conditions are enforced through a penalty term rather than built into the space.

That choice has a practical edge: the level set function is needed only on cells next to the boundary in the variational form. A ghost penalty technique stabilizes the scheme. The authors derive error estimates showing optimal convergence in one norm and near optimal convergence in another, under stated regularity assumptions. Numerical experiments validate the theory against the original phi FEM and the standard fitted method.
arxiv-2602-05798:
Picking factors in high dimensional data while keeping false finds in check is a balancing act: provable methods tend to be cautious and miss real signals. Arnau Vilella, Jasin Machkour, Michael Muma, and Daniel Palomar improve the T Rex Selector frame, which caps the false find rate. Their change swaps a math guess of the false find share for a neural network.

The network is trained only on varied fake data sets, yet it nears the false find share more tightly and truly. That lets the method run much closer to the target rate, gaining find power while keeping rough control. Wide tests and a hard fake genome wide link study show the method finding more true factors than current rivals. The work appeared at a major signal processing meeting. It targets analysts in gene study and other high dimensional fields.
arxiv-2602-05998:
Turning a screenshot into working front-end code means matching both layout and style. Current multimodal models map the image straight to code, but they never see what their code actually looks like when rendered. Jie Deng and two co-authors copy the human habit instead: render, compare with the design, and learn how each visual gap traces back to a code change.

Their system, VisRefiner, builds supervision that ties each visual difference to the edit that fixes it. A reinforcement learning stage then lets the model refine its own code by watching its rendered output against the target. Tests show much better first-try code and layout fidelity, plus a stronger knack for self-repair. The lesson is simple: models code better when they learn from seeing their own mistakes.
arxiv-2602-06098:
Coding assistants increasingly write software inside a test-driven loop, where tests guide each new draft. Nicolas Menet and 3 co-authors build a probability framework for two common strategies. One picks the best draft after running tests. The other feeds test results back and asks for a fresh draft.

Their proofs show that judging drafts by fuzzy similarity beats judging by exact match, because it gives a cleaner signal. They also frame the feedback loop as a sampling method and bound how much it can improve. Tests with seven open models backed the theory. The work also produced a harder benchmark for quantum programming tasks.
arxiv-2602-06298:
Electrons in a two-dimensional material can enter a strange pseudogap state, where some energy levels vanish without full superconductivity. Y M Vilk and A M S Tremblay use a refined theory method to explain recent cold-atom tests on a Hubbard model simulator. That model captures electrons hopping on a grid with repulsion.

The experiments found that compressibility, how easily the electron density squeezes, peaks at a certain doping level. The theory ties that peak to the moment a shadow band from spin order crosses zero energy. A magnetic response measure, the Knight shift, should peak the same way, both with doping and with temperature. The authors trace these peaks to critical spin fluctuations.
arxiv-2602-06498:
Federated learning splits training across user devices, but devices differ wildly in speed and memory. Arno Geimer proposes a realistic test framework that emulates that spread on one machine. Small real-device trials are hard to scale and repeat, while trace or probability simulations carry compounding uncertainties.

The framework reproduces each client's compute capacity and memory limits at run time, capturing how those limits interact. Unlike fixed traces, it is workload-aware: the same device group can run and fail differently depending on the task. Across several workloads, it preserved relative device performance and matched hardware behavior, giving researchers a repeatable way to judge hardware-aware methods.
arxiv-2602-06598:
Yang Li, Alexander Skopalik, and Marc Uetz study road-like networks where each user picks their own route and can pay extra for priority lanes. Priority users go first on each road segment, so they may face less delay than those who pay nothing. The paper asks when this kind of voluntary pricing leads to good outcomes for the whole network.

The authors show that stable outcomes exist when delay grows in a simple linear way, and that the delay on each segment is the same in every stable outcome. Their main result is that setting the priority fee equal to the cost each user imposes on others makes the selfish outcome match the best possible flow. They also note the limits of charging one flat fee for priority everywhere.
arxiv-2602-06898:
Gautam Chinta and Ajith Nair give explicit composition identities for Bhargava's higher composition laws. In 2001 Bhargava proved a composition law for two-by-two-by-two integer cubes, generalizing Gauss's composition of binary quadratic forms, and derived four more laws on other spaces of forms. Each law equips a set of equivalence classes of forms with a group structure, through a correspondence with ideal classes of quadratic rings.

The aim of this paper is to write those laws out explicitly, in the style of Gauss's original formulas for binary quadratic forms. An explicit identity lets a reader compose two forms directly, rather than passing through the abstract correspondence with ideals. The paper covers all five cases, giving concrete formulas for the group laws that Bhargava's theory guarantees exist.
arxiv-2602-07098:
Lars Kühmichel and thirteen co-authors offer BayesFlow 2.0, a Python library for amortized Bayesian inference. Modern Bayesian work mixes many computational methods. Those methods figure out, validate, and draw conclusions from probabilistic models, yet they run slowly. Slow fitting often blocks complex models on large data sets. Amortized inference trains neural networks on model simulations, then rewards users with fast answers for any quantity the model implies, from point figures and likelihoods to full posterior distributions.

Version 2.0 covers direct posterior, likelihood, and ratio figuring. It supports multiple popular deep learning backends, with a rich set of networks that make samples and gauge densities, full customization, and high-level interfaces. New features add tuning of settings, design tuning, and layered modeling. A test case that fits parameters of a dynamical system, plus comparisons with similar software, shows a streamlined, user-friendly workflow with strong potential for broad adoption.
arxiv-2602-07198:
Generating full 3D heads is unstable without a conditioning signal, but the usual choice, the viewing angle, biases the result toward that view and breaks coherence across regions.  Heyuan Li and twelve co-authors argue the conditioning should instead be a view-invariant meaning feature.

They build a synthesized head-image dataset to derive such a feature for each training image, decoupling generation quality from viewing direction.  The change targets a visible flaw: heads that look good from the conditioning angle and worse from others.  Graphics teams get a principled fix for coherence in full-head 3D generation.
arxiv-2602-07298:
Recommender systems lack the predictable scaling laws that guide language model development, and noisy, biased, incomplete interaction data may be why.  Benyu Zhang and twelve co-authors build a layered method for generating principled synthetic data as a clean curriculum for continual pre-training.

Sequential models trained on that synthetic data beat models trained on real data by a wide margin on downstream ranking, including a large recall gain for a standard baseline. The result shows the curriculum teaches generalizable preference patterns rather than noise.  The paper then uses the clean setup to state the first scaling laws for language models in recommendation.  Recommender teams get both a data recipe and a planning tool.
arxiv-2602-07998:
The bilayer nickelate La3Ni2O7 becomes a high-temperature superconductor under pressure, but first it passes through a density-wave shift near 150 kelvin whose origin remains contested. A large team led by Ge He probed that state with polarization-resolved Raman scattering on high-quality single crystals.

Below the shift, spectral weight redistributes in a balance-dependent way consistent with spin-density-wave gaps. The gaps are momentum-selective, with intermediate-to-strong coupling near the Brillouin zone's X and Y points and weaker coupling along the diagonal, pointing to an unconventional density wave driven by anisotropic charge correlations. The results ground future theories of nickelate superconductivity in measured charge structure.
arxiv-2602-08098:
Assigning labels across a network where each node's reward depends on its neighbors arises in bandits with interference and beyond. Mohammad Shahverdikondori and three co-authors study neighborhood-aware graph labeling, where the objective sums local rewards over closed neighborhoods and the dependency structure is the graph's square.

They prove the problem is NP-hard even on stars with binary labels, and that no algorithm can beat a treewidth-based running time under the strong exponential-time hypothesis. A matching exact dynamic program on a tree decomposition of the squared graph achieves that bound, and approximation results round out the picture. Algorithm designers gain tight complexity limits and an optimal exact method for a natural networked optimization problem.
arxiv-2602-08698:
India's NPTEL platform brings tech lectures to millions, but translating them into Bangla, Malayalam, and Telugu is far from mechanical. Basudha Raje and seven co-authors examine machine translation for these tongues in new workflows and against existing test frames. Their arXiv paper draws on speech corpora of live tech delivery.

Tongue choice reflects linguistic diversity and the goals of national education policy, with NPTEL as the corpus. Findings highlight metric-specific sensitivity and the difficulty of rich word forms and compact meaning under surface-overlap metrics. Curating corpora that preserve register and word choice for lucid tech delivery emerges as crucial. Readers get a grounded view of translation hurdles for Indian tech education.
arxiv-2602-09198:
Mauro Bonafini and two co-authors analyze the steadiness of Arbitrary-Lagrangian-Eulerian ADER broken Galerkin methods, high-order schemes for curve equations on moving meshes. They strictly study Courant steadiness limits for the open method, backing widely used results while marking their limits. They pin down the allowed grid speeds once a target Courant number is fixed.

The study extends to flat spacetime pieces, which start and end the time step with zero size yet nonzero spacetime volume. Such pieces, brought in to relink Voronoi tilings after shape changes, are modeled in a one-dimensional stand-in by inserting fake flat pieces between cells. Both open and hidden schemes yield the same Courant limits as on old shapes, backing their use in moving-mesh methods.
arxiv-2602-09498:
The Hubble tension, a persistent gap between early- and late-time measures of cosmic expansion, motivates changes to pre-recombination physics. Y Bisabr's single-author 2026 paper studies an early dark energy field coupled to radiation before recombination. The coupling exchanges energy between the two components and alters the standard relation between cosmic microwave background temperature and redshift, read as effective photon non-conservation.

Linear perturbations in the tight-coupling regime show the interaction shifting background evolution without adding new dynamical degrees of freedom at perturbation level. The main observable effect runs through the sound horizon at recombination, which sets the angular acoustic scale. Applying the Planck constraint on that scale yields a consistency bound on coupling strength, tightly limiting deviations from the standard temperature-redshift relation.
arxiv-2602-09998:
Regenerating tissue balls form patterns through a dialogue between chemistry and mechanics. A 2026 paper led by Szymon Cygan, with three co-authors, analyzes steady states in a mechanochemical model of that process. Stretching boosts morphogen production, morphogen levels tune tissue elasticity, and global strain conservation supplies long-range inhibition.

For exponential coupling between elasticity and morphogen, the system admits a variational form. The authors prove nonconstant steady states exist at small diffusion and only the uniform state survives at large diffusion. Stability analysis finds only single-peaked patterns stable, with pitchfork and fold bifurcations creating bistable regimes. Mechanochemical feedback alone, they show, can build a single peak without a second inhibitor.
arxiv-2602-10098:
Pretraining robot policies on internet video is attractive, yet current latent-action objectives often learn pixel variation instead of action-relevant change. A 2026 paper led by Jingwen Sun, with eight co-authors, introduces VLA-JEPA, a pretraining framework built around leakage-free state prediction. A target encoder reads future frames while the student sees only the present observation, so future information supervises but never leaks into inputs.

Forecasting in latent space instead of pixel space yields dynamics abstractions robust to camera motion and irrelevant background change. The recipe is simple: JEPA pretraining, then action-head fine-tuning, without multi-stage pipeline complexity. Tests on simulated benchmarks and real-world manipulation show consistent gains in generalization and robustness.
arxiv-2602-10198:
Adaptive optics surveys of young stars occasionally catch faint companions that test planet formation theories. A 2026 paper led by Samuel Walker, with six co-authors, reports the second discoveries from the KOINTREAU survey of Taurus and Ophiuchus star-forming regions with Keck. Two faint comoving companions orbit young stars, one around ISO-Oph 96 and one around a second Ophiuchus-area star.

The ISO-Oph 96 companion sits three hundred and forty astronomical units out and weighs about three and a half Jupiter masses, assuming shared extinction with its host. The second companion sits one hundred and eighty astronomical units out. It weighs about eleven and a half or about fifteen Jupiter masses depending on whether its host belongs to Ophiuchus or Upper Scorpius.
arxiv-2602-10498:
Qianli Wang and three co-authors expose a quiet attack surface in AI agent tooling in a 2026 paper. Language-model agents rely on Skills, documents that describe ready tools and steps. When a Markdown Skill is rendered to HTML, comment blocks can vanish from human view while the raw text still reaches the model verbatim.

Tests show that malicious instructions hidden in such a comment can sway two frontier models into outputs revealing sensitive tool intentions. The attack hides in plain sight: reviewers see a legitimate Skill, while the model reads the hidden payload. A short defensive prompt that treats Skills as untrusted and forbids sensitive actions blocks the malicious calls and shows the suspicious instructions instead.
arxiv-2602-10798:
Philippe Bergault and two co-authors model trading across centralized and decentralized exchanges in a 2026 paper. The system mixes steady controls with impulse interventions subject to random execution delays. It extends standard impulse control in two ways: the controller chooses the mean delay of impulses, and multiple orders can pend and execute asynchronously.

The motivation is optimal trading between centralized and decentralized venues. In decentralized exchanges, traders shape the delay spread through priority fees, trading delay, doubt, and cost against each other. The authors derive the associated dynamic programming principle for an agent exploiting trading signals across both venues. That gives quantitative finance a control system matched to how decentralized execution works.
arxiv-2602-11198:
Declarative design does not guarantee that AI can use a frame well. Shafiuddin Rehan Ahmed and Sourabh Deshpande offer AI-assistability, a metric joining structural matching with functional correctness. They test it with DDL2PropBank, a task mapping relational schemas to PropBank rolesets, built same way across ten multi-agent frames.

Results overturn intuition: Agno, with one canonical pattern and convention-aligned API, scores highest, while DSPy, the most declarative by design, scores lowest. Convention matching, not declarative style alone, drives assistability, with a moderate link to correctness. All artifacts are released, giving frame builders a principled way to measure how easily AI assistants can generate correct code for their tools.
arxiv-2602-11298:
Live transcription must be both fast and accurate, a pair offline models rarely offer jointly. The Mistral AI team offers Voxtral Realtime, a natively streaming speech recognition model trained end to end for streaming, not adapted by chunking. A causal audio encoder and adaptive scaling improve delay conditioning.

Pretraining spans thirteen languages at large scale. At a sub-second delay, Voxtral Realtime matches Whisper, the most widely deployed offline transcription system, in quality. Model weights are released under an open Apache licence. The work targets live captioning, voice agents, and other settings where waiting for a full utterance is not an option.
arxiv-2602-11498:
Flow networks also struggle to converge in large state spaces. Xuan Yu and four co-authors propose Partial GFlowNet, which partitions the full state space into overlapping partial spaces via a planner. Actors explore those smaller spaces, efficiently finding higher-reward subregions.

A heuristic switching strategy prevents wasting time on fully explored or low-reward partial regions. Iterating across partial spaces, the actor converges toward high-reward subregions of the whole space. Tests on widely used data sets show faster convergence than current methods on large spaces, with candidates that score higher and vary more. Partitioning thus tames a scaling problem that free exploration cannot.
arxiv-2602-11598:
Embodied navigation has long been split into separate systems for separate jobs, from reaching a point to following a person. Zedong Chu and a large team unify five such tasks in ABot-N0, a vision-language-action foundation model built on a hierarchical brain-action design. A language-model brain handles semantic reasoning while a flow-matching action expert generates smooth, continuous trajectories.

Scale is central to the work: the team curated nearly 17 million expert trajectories and 5 million reasoning samples across more than 7800 high-fidelity 3D scenes. The model sets new best results across seven benchmarks, beating specialized rivals, and its agentic navigation system pairs a planner with hierarchical topological memory for long missions in changing real environments.
arxiv-2602-11798:
Next-generation networks promise ultra-high reliability, ultra-low latency, massive connectivity, and wide coverage, but they face liquidity and security challenges. Upfront costs for network resources strain limited capital, which also limits deployment of expensive defense tools, while a spread-out design invites threats from Byzantine nodes. Tingxuan Su and five co-authors propose tokenizing real-world assets to address both problems at once.

Tokenization uses blockchain to convert ownership rights in real assets into digital tokens that can be programmed, divided, and traded. The paper analyzes criteria for identifying suitable assets, then tests the framework in a case study on dynamic spectrum allocation. Under resource scarcity the approach shows strong resilience against collusion and default attacks, outperforming alternatives. The authors close by mapping fruitful research avenues in this nascent field.
arxiv-2602-11898:
Benchmarks underpin trust in large language model progress, yet apparent convergence in accuracy can hide deep divergence. Eddie Yang and one co-author show that models with comparable scores still disagree on 16 to 66 percent of items across two major reasoning benchmarks. Among top frontier models the gap is 16 to 38 percent. Those discrepancies point to distinct error profiles for different models, not shared understanding.

When such models annotate scientific data, hidden disagreements propagate into results. In re-analyses of published education and political science studies, switching the annotation model can change estimated treatment effects by more than 80 percent, and in some cases reverses their sign.
