Geometry-guided appearance modeling fuses the exposures, and a meta-network supplies scene-specific tone mapping that generalizes across scenes. A new pretraining set of 168 rendered scenes supports training, and the initialization runs about 700 times faster than optimization-based methods.
arxiv-2603-11498: Guo and co-authors present ActiveFreq, an interactive segmentation framework that asks users for fewer, better clicks. Interactive tools label medical images pixel by pixel, with users fixing wrong regions round after round. Most tools treat every wrong region alike and pick fixes at random. ActiveFreq's AcSelect module ranks wrong regions by how much each fix should help. Its FreqFormer backbone also reads frequency-domain features, not just spatial ones, through a Fourier module. On ISIC-2017 and OAI-ZIB, it tops prior best scores while needing fewer clicks.
arxiv-2603-11598: Khan, Shahid, and Farooq turn survival analysis into a classification tool for early chronic disease risk. Their models cover five common diseases: diabetes, hypertension, CKD, COPD, and chronic ischemic heart disease. Older models usually pick one camp, survival or classification, and stay there. The team re-engineers survival methods so they can classify as well, on big electronic record data. Scores for accuracy, F1, and AUROC match or beat strong baselines like LightGBM and XGBoost. A new explanation method, checked by three physicians, rounds out the models.
arxiv-2603-11898: Glazenburg and Staals study color frequency reporting: store colored points so a query box lists which colors appear, and how often. The goal is strictly output sensitive time, growing mainly with the colors reported. They give a simple plane data structure with fast query times. For the weighted case they prove a lower bound in the arithmetic model that nearly matches it. Higher dimensions, a space-saving transform, and a batch algorithm for dominance queries complete the work.
arxiv-2603-12098: Dong, Sheng, Mao, and Chen build maximum-entropy random walks on directed hypergraphs. Plain walks miss flows that run one way, along with uncertainty and spread, in complex systems. Their frame covers two moves: broadcasting, where one node wakes many receivers, and merging, where many nodes sway one receiver. A KL projection onto stochastic and stationary limits yields the transition kernel. Sinkhorn-style iterations compute it, and ergodicity checks follow. Synthetic and real examples show the frame works.
arxiv-2603-12998: Tangzheng Lian and co-authors give a closed-form method to debias vision-language models with utility guarantees. Such models can inherit social bias from training data and pass it into new tasks. Most fixes chase fairness with no bound on lost utility. Their solution works in the cross-modal space and is Pareto-optimal in fairness. It needs no training and no labeled data. Tests across classification, retrieval, and generation beat prior methods on fairness while holding task scores.
arxiv-2603-13198: Arthur Forey, with Javier Fresán, Emmanuel Kowalski, and Yuval Wigderson, introduces a new family called jacobian graphs. These regular graphs look like random graphs when judged by their spectra. Their local structure, though, is very unlike that of random graphs. The construction rests on generalized jacobians of curves over finite fields. It also uses equidistribution theorems for character sums. The result gives explicit graphs that fool spectral tests while keeping a distinct local shape.
arxiv-2603-13398: Daxiang Dong and co-authors present Qianfan-OCR, an end-to-end model for document intelligence. The 4B-parameter vision-language model unifies document parsing, layout analysis, and document understanding in one design. It converts images to Markdown and handles table extraction, chart questions, and key information extraction by prompt. A Layout-as-Thought phase first writes bounding boxes, element types, and reading order before final output. That step restores layout grounding and lifts accuracy on complex layouts. It ranked first among end-to-end models on two benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-13498: Jinghao Deng and co-authors report magnetic-field-induced superconductivity in hexalayer rhombohedral graphene. In conventional superconductors, magnetic fields suppress superconductivity due to spin-singlet pairing. Here a small in-plane field makes a superconducting state emerge along a narrow phase boundary. Its region shifts toward higher electric field as the in-plane field grows, and its transition temperature rises too. The state stays robust up to 14 T, far past the conventional Pauli limit. Quantum oscillation data link its birth to nematic Fermi surface reconstruction.
arxiv-2603-13798: Neroli studies random walks on fractals built by edge iterated graph systems, a wide class that includes hierarchical lattices. The work proves that scaled-up simple random walks converge to a limiting diffusion. That limit matches Brownian motion when the resistance dimension is positive. The proof gives sharp heat-kernel bounds and names the degree dimension as the key correction term. It also settles an open problem on the diamond hierarchical lattice percolation cluster. Early sections have been formalized in Lean.
arxiv-2603-13998: Heidrich and co-authors set out a strict protocol for judging graph-derived signals in tabular machine learning. Past studies use small setups and report only average gains, so real value stays unclear. Their protocol sorts signals by type and tests each under one shared, reproducible setup. It adds tuned hyperparameters, multi-seed statistics, formal significance tests, and checks under graph damage. A large case study on crypto fraud data shows which signal types give gains that hold up.
arxiv-2603-14098: Weinstein and Garratt study how well nearly critical toric codes protect stored quantum information. The codes come from pushing topological stabilizer codes toward a phase transition, where fluctuations run strong. Under local Pauli noise, they show a finite noise strength is still needed to wipe the stored data for good. A replica mapping turns the noise into a defect inside a three-dimensional model. Field theory shows that defect cannot shift the bulk critical point, so a real error threshold survives.
arxiv-2603-14898: Chen and co-authors distill knowledge with photonic quantum processors in PQKD. Photonic chips yield random outcomes by nature, a built-in noise source. A programmable circuit turns that noise into a compact guiding signal. The signal steers a lean student network learning from a big teacher. Dictionary convolutions swap full kernels for shared basis filters. Channel mixing weights come from shot-limited photonic features. Training alternates gradient steps for the student with sampling updates for the photonics. MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 trace the compression trade-off.
arxiv-2603-15098: Ntalampekos surveys uniformization problems in the complex plane, where domains get mapped to simple model shapes. The central case is Koebe's conjecture, open for almost 120 years. It predicts that every planar domain can be mapped conformally onto a circle domain. The survey traces the history of the conjecture and recent progress. It also covers the related uniqueness question. A second thread asks whether compact sets can be sent to Schottky sets by quasiconformal self-maps of the plane.
arxiv-2603-15298: Jost and co-authors study how AI help and developer experience affect the security of written code. A total of 159 developers took a security-focused programming task. Groups used no AI, the free tier of Google's Gemini, or the paid tier. Using Gemini made no significant difference to code security in either tier. Programming experience did improve security in a clear way. The authors conclude that experience cannot be fully replaced by the AI tool.
arxiv-2603-15498: Camacho Ibarra and co-authors give a systematic design route for photonic nanobeam cavities that host quantum dots. Their workflow tunes lattice period, hole shape, and cavity length at the same time. That joint control sharpens light confinement while holding radiative loss and linewidth growth in check. The method extends to crossed nanobeams, with matched or mismatched resonance frequencies. It cuts the need for broad parameter sweeps. The resulting structures suit direct integration of single-photon emitters.
arxiv-2603-15698: Rabinowitz orders triangle centers against each other in global ways. Centers are usually studied one by one or in small clusters. He defines several partial orders, among them isosceles, vertex, side, and trace orders. The orders compare centers across families of triangles. Barycentric coordinates and symbolic computation map the first 100 Kimberling centers. Surprising patterns emerge from the maps. In one case, the Gergonne point always sits closer to the shortest side than the nine-point center.
arxiv-2603-15798: Lacoste and co-authors propose CUBE, a shared standard for agent benchmarks. Each new benchmark now demands bespoke wiring into test platforms. That integration tax slows full evaluation across the field. CUBE wraps a benchmark once so any platform can run it. The protocol builds on MCP and Gym ideas. Task, benchmark, package, and registry layers stay apart in the design. Compliant tools can serve evaluation, training, or data generation. The team invites community help before platform forks harden.
arxiv-2603-15898: Dindoš and Liu extend a solvability result to bounded cylinder domains. Parabolic Neumann problems on endless graph domains gained an extrapolation theorem recently. Solvability at one exponent spreads there to all lower exponents. Twin Dirichlet solvability for the adjoint equation joins the assumptions. Bounded Lipschitz cylinders escape that earlier proof entirely. The pair builds a markedly unlike approach for this case. Their theorem mirrors the unbounded claim on cylinders. Spatial parts now sit in a bounded Lipschitz region.
arxiv-2603-16098: Hirsch and co-authors release a layered dataset for graphic design research. Flat pixels hide the structure that designers actually edit. LICA holds 1,550,244 multi-layer design compositions in total. Each design carries typed parts: text, image, vector, and group layers. Per-part metadata covers geometry, type traits, opacity, and visibility. The set spans 20 categories and 971,850 unique templates. Animated layouts add 27,261 video cases with motion data. Layer-aware inpainting and controlled editing become trainable tasks. Models can learn design structure, not just design pixels.
arxiv-2603-16198: Zhao and Chen design leader-following consensus protocols for mixed multiagent systems. The network is fixed and shaped around a directed spanning tree. Link weights are asymmetric matrices, which makes design harder. Their protocol uses only the tree neighbor of each agent, so links stay minimal. A change of variables turns consensus into a partial stability task. They then extend the method to use all neighbors. Simulations back the theory.
arxiv-2603-16298: Dobbins and Lee build polytopes whose transversal ratio nears one. The ratio is the smallest share of vertices that meets every facet. Their new family exists in each dimension from five upward. As the vertex count grows, the ratio approaches 1. This beats the best earlier bounds of 2/5 and 1/2. A side result follows: the weak chromatic number of such polytopes is unbounded.
arxiv-2603-16698: Azenhas settles the quantum Littlewood-Richardson map with a direct proof from combinatorics. Watanabe's map pairs symplectic tableaux with recording tableaux of skew shape. The map was known to hit every target pair, but only through deep theory. Her proof builds the missing direction step by step. It iterates reverse Schensted insertion, steered by slack data. Each step undoes one bump with an inverse step on the bumped column. The map also narrows to a known symmetry on Sundaram tableaux. Certain highest-weight tableaux then gain a concrete description.
arxiv-2603-17198: Rahmati and co-authors test whether training language models on structural abstractions helps them learn under change. Cognitive science says humans learn schemas, not single instances. Their method, Abstraction-Augmented Training, adds a loss term over concrete cases and their abstractions. They build two benchmarks: one on relational cycles, using entity masking, and one on narrative abstraction through proverbs. In non stationary training, the method reduced forgetting and raised generalization.
arxiv-2603-17698: Guo and He bring the Long quantum search algorithm to gravitational-wave detection. Wave observatories pour out data faster than classic matched filtering can comfortably scan. Their quantum matched filtering frame keeps the quadratic speedup of quantum search. Simulations show much stronger robustness than Grover-based designs, they report. Weak spots of the older approach fall away in their tests. The work marks the first use of this algorithm on wave data.
arxiv-2603-17898: Growiec, Prettner, and Szkróbka work out when a tax system should start taxing AI. Their economy mixes manual labor, cognitive labor, capital, and artificial intelligence. The model extends a known dynamic taxation setup to that four-input world. Taxing AI turns optimal once cognitive workers eye a switch to manual jobs, they find. That point arrives when AI grows able enough to swap in across cognitive tasks. The rule ties tax timing to worker incentives.
arxiv-2603-17998: Ekin and Gandelsman show that simple shifts in text embeddings can steer image edits with fine control. An LLM builds debiased contrast pairs for a target trait, such as photorealism or facial expression. The mean gap gives a steering vector added to the prompt embedding. An elastic range search finds safe strengths that avoid weak or messy edits. The training-free method matches trained tools on image and video tasks.
arxiv-2603-18098: Groote, Chatterjee, and Naeem overview heavy flavour work from their Tartu group in hadron physics. They cover production and nonleptonic decays of charmed baryons with a current algebra approach. Tensor invariants frame the method, which also targets CP violation through rescattering effects. Other topics include neutron beta decay, radiative corrections to polarized W decay, and Higgs decay to four leptons. A second part treats intrinsic charm and a nonlocal Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model from QCD.
arxiv-2603-18398: Xu and co-authors deconstruct open-world game mission design with an action-block framework. About 2,200 missions from 20 AAA titles are parsed into structured action sequences. Their Mission Action Quality Vector scores combat, exploration, narrative, emotion, problem-solving, and uniqueness. An interactive dashboard lets designers expose the formulas behind large mission portfolios. Studies with players and designers validate the pipeline and surface pacing trade-offs by quest type.
arxiv-2603-18898: Bhanusree and co-authors compare three chatbots on maternal health questions in Telugu and other languages. Low-resource languages remain little studied for pregnancy advice. A bilingual dataset feeds ChatGPT-4o, Gemini, and Perplexity. BERTScore gives one view of answer quality. Gynecologists also rate accuracy, fluency, relevance, coherence, and completeness by hand. Gemini leads for accurate, coherent Telugu pregnancy answers in their tests. Perplexity does well when prompts are written in Telugu. The authors stress that model choice and prompt language both shape answer quality.
arxiv-2603-18998: Song and co-authors give a fast way to compute heat entropy in a doped electron model. Their frame works in the grand setting, where energy and particle count can shift. Four schemes write entropy as path sums over heat, interaction, and chemical terms. Each sum needs only basic values like energy and site filling. They test the schemes with an unbiased Monte Carlo method in two and three dimensions. The schemes agree well and check out against known relations. Results also match a second Monte Carlo method closely.
arxiv-2603-19098: Lin and co-authors build a vision-language system that spots and explains odd traffic events at roundabouts. Their data set comes from real roundabout video shot with the city of Carmel, Indiana. It holds 342 clips and over 2,000 question-answer pairs. The system works in two layers. A light classifier sorts events into coarse types. A larger reasoner then writes a full event summary. Training pairs a split-question tuning stage with a reward stage tuned to the task. Scores stay strong while the system stays lean to deploy.
arxiv-2603-19198: Bloch and co-authors extend state-space models with a new tool called the exponentially weighted signature. It adds up steps along a path, with each step weighted by a learned time factor. They prove it solves a linear control equation and keeps key traits of the classic signature. At depth one it matches known models like Mamba. On six long time-series data sets, it posts the best average scores. Learned clocks prove key for tracking state in formal language tasks.
arxiv-2603-19598: Yang and co-authors present FlowScene, a model that generates indoor scenes with consistent style. Language-driven tools fetch objects from a database but lack fine control and style unity. FlowScene works from multimodal graphs that encode object relations. Three branches generate layouts, object shapes, and object textures together. A rectified flow core lets objects exchange information during generation. That coupling gives fine control over shapes, textures, and relations. Tests beat language- and graph-based baselines on realism, style consistency, and human preference.
arxiv-2603-20198: Zhang and co-authors probe a fresh attack class where harmful content hides in plain visual reasoning. Older multimodal attacks wrap payloads in typed text or noise, and defenses strip them once seen. Visual Exclusivity attacks instead make harm emerge from reasoning over images like technical schematics. Their MM-Plan framework trains a planner to design whole multi turn strategies at once. Group based policy optimization lets it discover tactics without human guidance. On their VE-Safety benchmark, success reached 46 percent against one frontier model.
arxiv-2603-20398: Kupferman and Shenwald introduce coverage games, a new framework for multi-agent planning. A coverer runs several agents toward a set of objectives. A disruptor acts against them inside the same setting. The coverer wins when each objective is met by at least one agent. The setup extends classic two-player games by letting objectives split among agents. Uses include multi-robot surveillance and guarding shared resources from exhaustion. The authors study determinacy and the cost of deciding who wins.
arxiv-2603-20498: Bhattacharya and co-authors recast Lagrangian mean curvature flow on Kim-McCann spaces in a generalized flow frame. Kim-McCann metrics come from optimal transport theory. Their view shows that para-Kähler methods fit this setting in a natural way. They prove the Lagrangian condition stays true along the flow. Ma-Trudinger-Wang regularity theory then applies to these flows. With positive cross curvature, flows converge smoothly and fast. The limit is locally the graph of an optimal transport map. The work links special Lagrangian geometry with transport.
arxiv-2603-20698: Zheng and co-authors present CogAlign, a framework that aligns multimodal models with clinical thinking for gut diagnosis. General models often reason off the path doctors use in endoscopy. They may also key on background cues, not the lesion itself. CogAlign first fine tunes on a tiered dataset of expert diagnostic steps. It then uses counterfactual training with masked lesion samples. Rewards push the model to ground calls in true lesion traits. Tests reached state of the art scores on several benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-20898: Khawand and Colliaux bring natural gradient descent to online continual learning for image classification. In this setting, models learn from a stream of images and can forget old tasks. Fast learning is hard without that forgetting. Their method uses a Kronecker factored approximation of the Fisher information matrix. It boosts results across several existing continual learning methods. Gains are largest when it is paired with known training tricks. Tests cover Split CIFAR-100, CORE50, and Split miniImageNet.
arxiv-2603-20998: Wang and co-authors study a biased form of Tit-for-Tat in a donation game. Tit-for-Tat cooperates first, then copies the partner's last act. Their biased version treats unconditional cooperators and fellow Tit-for-Tat players differently, through two bias settings. Even under strong dilemmas, the three strategy system shows rich phase diagrams. When one bias is small and the other large, a hidden phase appears where the weakened Tit-for-Tat dominates. It wins by wiping out cyclic dominance clusters fast, then spreading slowly.
arxiv-2603-21098: Koushiki and co-authors examine whether an apparent horizon forms when an isolated dust cloud collapses. They use expansion functions to track the horizon's existence. Far from the gravitational singularity, they find the system does have a horizon. In that case, the singularity stays covered. They note the method may apply only in a limited way near the singularity. Quantum effects are expected to matter in that inner region.
arxiv-2603-21198: Ghirlanda gives a canonicity test for toric varieties and classifies canonical 4-simplices. Using the Reid-Shepherd-Barron-Tai criterion, he characterizes when a toric variety is canonical or terminal through its local class group actions. For Picard number one, this yields an algorithm that classifies such fake weighted projective spaces in any dimension. In dimension four, it yields over seven hundred thousand such spaces. He also looks at the Calabi-Yau hypersurfaces they carry.
arxiv-2603-21398: Sun and Zhang build persona vectors for traits like altruism, forgiveness, and expectations of others in strategic games. They make the vectors with contrastive activation addition in large language models. Steering with them shifts both the choices models make in classic games and the reasons models give. Yet words and actions can pull apart under steering. Vectors for own behavior and for beliefs about others also partly differ, the authors report.
arxiv-2603-21498: Tao and co-authors survey Rydberg atomic receivers, a quantum technology proposed for greener 6G wireless systems. These receivers use electron transitions in Rydberg atoms to sense radio signals. The authors claim benefits in antenna size, sensitivity, interference resistance, and compact form. They review the basic principle, recent progress, and fresh experiments. Their team verified Rydberg-based OFDM transmission and tested deep learning designs for tuning such systems. They close with routes for merging these receivers into future wireless applications.
arxiv-2603-21898: Schnizer argues that chart literacy tests should read eye movements, not just right and wrong answers. Scores alone say little about how a reader worked through a chart. Gaze data, from visualization research, reveal mental load that timing and accuracy miss. They also expose strategy gaps between fluent and struggling readers. The proposal merges test scores with gaze markers like attention per chart part, cross-part linking, and path spread. That mix could split fluent success from labored success. A roadmap lists open needs in evidence and design.
arxiv-2603-22398: Smulders and Noller find stable black hole solutions that carry cosmological hair. Dynamic dark energy adds a time-based field to the universe. A black hole inside that setting feels the field, not just its own mass and spin. Known hairy solutions of this kind were unstable. The authors work through the cubic Galileon as a test case. They derive solutions that behave well at both long and short range. The hair near the hole encodes data about the wider cosmos.
arxiv-2603-22498: Ilnytskyi and Patsahan model the spread of COVID-19 with an SEIRS model. Their version lets immunity fade over time and allows for shots that prevent spread. It also counts the many cases that are never spotted. For the simpler grouped form, they find steady states with no disease and with disease settled in. They weigh how limits on contact trade off against shot uptake. A grid version of the model then tests how shrinking each person's contacts slows spread.
arxiv-2603-23198: Cetin and five co-authors work on making large language models cheaper to run. They use unstructured sparsity in the feedforward layers, where most weights and compute sit. They build a new sparse packing format and CUDA kernels that fit modern GPU pipelines. They show that plain L1 regularization can push sparsity past 99% with little loss in task scores. With their kernels, that sparsity turns into real gains in speed, energy use, and memory. They plan to release the code as open source.
arxiv-2603-23298: Bruned and Clarisse revisit the molecule reduction algorithm of Deng and Hani. That algorithm backs a rigidity theorem used to derive wave kinetic equations from the cubic Schrödinger equation. The pair show the algorithm is really a graph walk of Kruskal type. They prove it builds a Kruskal spanning tree of the input molecule. This exposes where the main tool behind such derivations comes from. The same style of argument served the long-time derivation of the Boltzmann equation.
arxiv-2603-23598: de la Hamette asks how far quantum observers can disagree about a system's entropy. Quantum reference frames describe systems only relative to an observer. She finds a family of diagonal Rényi entropies that no frame choice can change. Those invariants yield a trade-off between coherence and entanglement across parts. For ideal frames, entropy gaps split exactly into frame coherences plus cross-frame links. For rougher frames, a bound from the shared space's size takes over. The limits may matter where gravity meets observer-based entropy.
arxiv-2603-23798: Boras and co-authors introduce a quantum photonic neural network that works in time bins. Most such networks encode data in space and need more parts as they grow. A time-based design needs the same number of parts at any size or depth. Their model includes losses, routing errors, and photon mismatch. Trained as a Bell-state analyzer, the network reaches fidelity of 0.96 with a realistic quantum dot source. Time gating lifts that fidelity above 0.99 in their results.
arxiv-2603-23898: Karam and co-authors survey how robot teams work together. In multi-robot research, three terms are often mixed up: cooperation, coordination, and collaboration. The authors define each term and show how they relate. They stress that the third can give a team skills no single robot has. With those definitions set, they review frameworks that support such teamwork. They close with open technical problems and promising paths for future work on robot teams.
arxiv-2603-24298: Holden and co-authors present SpinGQE, a generative method that designs quantum circuits for spin Hamiltonians. The variational quantum eigensolver struggles with flat training landscapes and narrow circuit forms. SpinGQE treats circuit design as a generative task. A transformer decoder learns which circuit patterns yield low-energy states. Training compares model scores with circuit energies at each gate step. On the four-qubit Heisenberg model, it converges near the ground state. Smaller models, longer gate sequences, and tuned operator pools work best in their search.
arxiv-2603-24498: Echiburu and co-authors test educational comics as a teaching tool in physics workshops for chemistry and biochemistry students. Concept learning was measured with the Force Concept Inventory, and motivation with a Likert survey, both before and after. The average normalised gain was 0.21, in the low-to-medium range. Items tied to the taught content gained slightly more than other items. Students also showed more interest, stronger self-efficacy, and fewer negative feelings toward physics. The authors conclude comics can scaffold learning for non-physics students.
arxiv-2603-24998: Tang and co-authors compute how single-charm molecular pentaquarks with strangeness might decay. These five-quark states are key tests of quantum chromodynamics where it is hard to solve. The team uses an effective Lagrangian method with molecule wave functions from a one-boson-exchange model. Widths vary a lot by state. One narrow state decays at under 1 MeV, while wider mixed states reach tens of MeV. Branching ratios stay steady as binding energy changes. The patterns give clear targets for searches at LHCb and Belle II.
arxiv-2603-25298: Jeon and co-authors teach a robot planner to pick start and goal poses that can actually connect. Some pose pairs sit in split regions that no valid path joins. Constraints shrink the free space further, and one hand pose allows endless arm shapes. Their system embeds joint poses at many scales, from local to global. Clusters from that map label a contrastive learner. The learned score favors pose pairs in one linked region. On manipulation tasks, success rose about twofold and planning time fell by more than half.
arxiv-2603-25698: Fu and Liu study the coaction of wavefunction coefficients for a simple cosmology model. Their example has conformally coupled scalars in an FRW background, on a two-site graph. They show the coaction has a neat diagrammatic reading. It splits twisted integrals into parts tied to subtopologies and cuts. Those parts can be read as time-ordered integrals. The authors say this clarifies the analytic structure of the coefficients. They suggest the picture extends to more general cosmological diagrams.
arxiv-2603-26098: Kawano and Sasaki present HEAR, a compact model for learning from audio inspired by human hearing. Standard transformers are too big and costly for small devices. HEAR splits the work into two parts. An acoustic model pulls out local sound features. A task model then weaves in global meaning. A distilled tokenizer supports masked audio modeling during training. HEAR needs only 15 million parameters and 9.47 GFLOPs per run. That is a small share of the usual 85 to 94 million parameters. Scores stay competitive across audio classification tests.
arxiv-2603-26698: Brisson introduces partial partial aggregates, a query optimisation trick for distributed engines. Aggregating after a join normally forces two network shuffles, and pushing the full aggregate below the join adds a third. His method pushes only the local compute phase of the aggregate through the join. Data shrinks before the join with no extra shuffle to pay. The trick rests on the distributive property of aggregates. It needs sound estimates of distinct value counts so the optimiser can judge when the push pays off.
arxiv-2603-26798: Schwalbe and co-authors present a post-hoc framework to explain and fix the semantic hierarchies inside vision-language embeddings. Models like CLIP sort classes into trees that users rarely inspect. Their method clusters class centres into a binary tree and names inner nodes from a concept bank. Plausibility is scored against human ontologies, and a light transform can bend the space toward a wanted tree. Across 13 models, image encoders split classes more sharply, while text encoders build trees closer to human ones.
arxiv-2603-27098: Wei and co-authors estimate the correctness of generated code by pooling samples across several models. Single-model consistency checks fail when one model settles on the same wrong answer repeatedly. Their Ensemble Semantic Entropy measures agreement across an ensemble instead. On LiveCodeBench, it tracked true correctness more strongly than single-model entropy. Under strict false-positive limits, prediction accuracy rose by 53.4 percent. A cascading framework built on the signal kept performance while cutting compute by 64.9 percent. The work reframes test-time scaling across models, not just samples.
arxiv-2603-27798: Rayón and co-authors propose wireless sensing for private emotion reading. Camera-based tools raise sharp privacy concerns. Their high-frequency sensing builds 3D face pointclouds from wearables. No raw face images need to be stored. Labeled 3D emotion data are scarce, though. A FLAME-based pipeline converts 2D sets into 3D form. That yields AffectNet3D from the AffectNet base. Tests probe the quality of the synthetic set.
arxiv-2603-28098: Zantedeschi argues that the QCD axion's dark matter abundance is less fixed than often claimed. The standard story gives a one-parameter prediction after inflation. He shows that small explicit Peccei-Quinn breaking, if it matters early, adds a new mass scale that steers the axion's early motion. The string-wall network then dies sooner, and the final abundance depends on that scale too. The effect can cover much of the favored axion parameter space.
arxiv-2603-28198: Hu studies online prediction when the best expert keeps changing over time. Chasing one fixed expert is then the wrong goal. His framework, Policy-Controlled Generalized Share, fixes the classic share recursion but lets the post-loss update controls adapt each round. A causal Transformer acts as that controller, seeing each loss only after the round ends. Hu proves regret bounds against switching expert paths. On synthetic tests and a household power benchmark, the method posted the lowest dynamic regret.
arxiv-2603-28798: Acharya and co-authors design a resistor-capacitor PUF that resists machine learning attacks for IoT security. Physically Unclonable Functions use hardware randomness for device authentication. Attackers can try to learn challenge-response patterns with ML models. Their dynamically reconfigurable PUF uses 32-bit challenge-response pairs. They trained neural networks, gradient boosted networks, decision trees, random forests, and XGBoost on a generated dataset. All models hit 100 percent training accuracy, yet test accuracy stayed near random guessing, around 50 to 53 percent. The simple design offers low-cost authentication with minimal overhead.
arxiv-2603-28998: Cai and co-authors set out design principles for a benchmark of security operation skills in multi-agent AI systems. Most existing benchmarks test red team skills, yet security centers are dominated by blue team work. No systematic benchmark for coordinated blue team AI existed, they note. Their principles guide the construction of SOC-bench. A conceptual design follows from the principles. It holds a family of five blue team tasks. All five sit in the context of large scale ransomware attack incident response.
arxiv-2603-29298: Hazra and co-authors map how uneven strain changes the electronic structure of monolayer MoS2. Wrinkles and nanobubbles are common in real devices. The team combines density functional theory with a recurrent neural network. Strain maps come from microscopy topography and Raman data. Biaxial bending strain proved far stronger than uniaxial or in-plane strain. A 0.35 percent strain cut the band gap by about 22 percent. Predicted gap maps matched light-emission measurements. The framework extends to other 2D materials.
arxiv-2603-29498: Sun and co-authors hunt for the loss that limits hybrid gatemon qubits. Gatemons use semiconductor Josephson junctions and offer gate tuning. Their relaxation times still lag far behind standard transmons. The team built gatemons and transmons side by side with matching layouts. Only the Josephson element differed on purpose. Transmons reached tens of microseconds, while gatemons stalled at a few. A loss budget ruled out the usual decay paths. Extra loss inside the junction itself explains the gap.
arxiv-2603-29698: Arshid and co-authors survey how open-source projects use machine learning models in the wild. Foundation models now power many downstream apps, some safety-critical. Such use may break model terms or government rules. They examine 173 GitHub projects across 16 application domains. For each, they ask if models make decisions and how wide those decisions reach. They also check for risk-reducing post-processing steps. Terms-of-use compliance is assessed as well. The study lays groundwork for developer guidelines and checking tools.
arxiv-2604-00298: Santos and two colleagues propose SANA-I2I, a high-resolution image-to-image framework extending the SANA family without any text input. Unlike SanaControlNet, which mixes text and image control, SANA-I2I learns a conditional flow model in latent space from paired images alone. They test it on fetal MRI motion artifact reduction, using synthetic paired data simulating realistic motion artifacts, since real pairs are hard to acquire. It suppresses motion artifacts while preserving anatomy, with competitive performance in few steps.
arxiv-2604-00998: Liao and team tackle ground roll, a coherent seismic noise that overlaps reflections and resists removal. Their large vision model-guided masked low-rank method uses a promptable vision model to map ground-roll regions and build fine masks. A global low-rank rule keeps reflections continuous, while a mask-guided local rule confines ground-roll separation to masked regions. Tests on synthetic and field data show stronger attenuation with less signal leakage than baselines.
arxiv-2604-01098: Li, Jiang and Xue propose XOR-SMOO for multi-objective optimization, trading off clashing goals under uncertainty to find the Pareto frontier of non-dominated decisions. With probability 1 minus delta, it obtains gamma-approximate frontiers, only a factor gamma below the frontier, by querying a SAT oracle poly-log times in both. Experiments on road network strengthening and supply chain design show it beating baselines with higher values, better coverage and more spread. The work thus makes intractable SMOO problems solvable with only SAT oracle queries and approximation guarantees.
arxiv-2604-01198:
Neelay Junnarkar and two co-authors find a new way to check hard systems in a 2026 paper. Some parts of a system do not fit the math tools used for checks. The team wraps those parts in bounds stated as sums of products of the inputs.

With those bounds in place, strong check tools can be used at last. One such tool works with sums of squares to prove a system safe. The paper also gives a step-by-step way to build the bounds from data. This widens the class of systems that can pass a formal check. It is not just what can be run in a test on a screen. The work helps where safety must be proved, not just hoped for.
arxiv-2604-01498: Liu and colleagues propose NESA, a method replacing template matching with a shifting match path, for ECG-text pretraining. ECG-text pretraining gives usable models for zero-shot diagnosis, but training signals are uneven. NESA scores each ECG token's share in the cross-modal match and slowly drops leading tokens in latent space to reveal the rest. To keep meaning lined up when tokens drop, it builds flexible match states. Tests with MIMIC-IV-ECG and three later benchmarks show gains in zero-shot tests and label-light transfer.
arxiv-2604-01598: Shang and Li propose SympLoc, a coarse-to-fine method with multi-level coarse-stage matching, for text-to-point-cloud search. Instance matching links objects in point clouds to textual hints through Riemannian self-attention in hyperbolic space. Relation matching models pairwise spatial links using the Information-Symplectic Relation Encoder, which reframes relation features through Fisher-Rao metric and Hamiltonian dynamics. Global matching synthesizes global tags via the Spectral Manifold Transform. On KITTI360Pose, SympLoc improves Top-1 recall at 10 meters by 19 percent over state-of-the-art approaches.
arxiv-2604-01898: Khalin and colleagues make medical AI safer by teaching it to judge its own doubt. Doctors already use AI as a second opinion, yet its mistakes are hard to foresee, and current doubt estimates miss the fuzziness that comes from unclear data. The team trains models on where human experts disagree, splitting total doubt into two parts with a paired-ensemble design and a lighter version. Tests on image sorting, image outlining and multiple-choice questions lifted doubt-estimate quality by 9 percent to 50 percent, depending on the task.
arxiv-2604-01998: Gruie, Jebelean and Serban ask when a discrete singular phi Laplacian system has solutions under a broad two point boundary rule. When the added term has no potential form, they prove that solutions exist by a priori estimates. When the term has gradient form, they use an energy method for convex, lower semicontinuous perturbations, finding solutions as low points or saddle points of the energy. The work thus covers both the non potential case and the gradient case in one frame.
arxiv-2604-02298: Gonçalves, Yang and Lin show chiral superconductivity can arise from doping a Chern ferromagnet with holes. Exact calculations on a Kane Mele Hubbard model find a Cooper pair of a magnon bound to two holes, stable at strong interactions and large Ising spin orbit coupling. The pair carries finite spin chirality and chiral wave symmetry, set by the parent Chern number. Pair interactions flip from repulsive to attractive with coupling, opening a window where chiral superconductivity condenses.
arxiv-2604-02398: Piersall and colleagues improve MPI error detection and repair by giving language models bug references. Direct use of large language models yields suboptimal results, since the models lack knowledge of correct and incorrect MPI usage and its bugs. Combining bug detection and repair with few shot learning, chain of thought reasoning and retrieval augmented generation lifts error detection accuracy from 44 percent to 77 percent over a direct ChatGPT baseline. The bug referencing technique also generalizes well to other large language models.
arxiv-2604-02598: Kambhamettu and four colleagues make written mathematical proofs explorable by grounding them in Lean, a language for machine-checked proofs. Their system translates a theorem and its proof into Lean code linked to the written text, so readers can step through proofs, test custom examples and counterexamples, and trace logical dependencies. In a study with 16 readers, those with the explorable features produced better, more correct and more detailed answers.
arxiv-2604-02698: Kobakhidze rebuts recent claims that theta-vacuum theories, including quantum chromodynamics, lack CP violation. He argues that an open boundary in finite volume needs edge modes to preserve large gauge invariance and capture topology faithfully. In the infinite-volume limit those edge states turn non-dynamical, leaving the standard theta-vacuum structure intact and yielding observable CP violation after consistent quantization of the theory.
arxiv-2604-02898: Saramgi and seven colleagues use phosphorus and copper NMR to trace successive electric and magnetic ordering in the layered van der Waals magnet CuCrP2S6. The compound passes from a high-temperature paraelectric state through a quasi-antiferroelectric state near 185 kelvin and long-range antiferroelectric order below 150 kelvin to antiferromagnetic order below 30 kelvin. The NMR spectra, shifts, and relaxation rates give direct microscopic fingerprints of these transitions. NMR line splitting below that transition reveals two distinct phosphorus sites.
arxiv-2604-03098: Wang and colleagues attack the thin, delayed rewards that stall training of language agents over long tasks. Their Self-Guide method lets an agent write its own guidance for its next move, then turns that signal into step-level rewards during training, so policy and guidance improve together. On three agent benchmarks, guidance alone helped, and joint training beat baselines using only environment rewards by 8 percent.
arxiv-2604-03298: Yang and colleagues present ENEC, a lossless compression method for AI model weights tuned for Huawei Ascend processors, where moving weights bottlenecks inference. Using block fixed-length coding plus chip-specific tricks, it beats leading Ascend compressors on ratio and speed, and tops GPU rivals on throughput and ratio. It speeds end-to-end inference about sixfold, the first open Ascend weight compressor to match top GPU tools.
arxiv-2604-03598: Wang's 2026 AttackEval is a careful hands-on study of prompt injection attack power against large language models. He builds a map of ten attack kinds in three parent groups, with 25 prompts per kind. He tests them against a mock production victim system under four rising shields. OBF posts the highest single-attack success rate at 76 percent against intent-aware defenses, while the OBF plus EM pair reaches 97.6 percent.
arxiv-2604-03698: Yasutaka Nakanishi, Tetsuo Shibuya, and Tatsuya Tsukamoto studied self delta-equivalence of pretzel links, a way of judging when links can be turned into each other by a local move. For two-component links, they worked out the full classification in terms of Conway polynomials, computing the values outright. For links with three or more components, they gave a necessary and sufficient condition for self delta-equivalence.
arxiv-2604-03798: Nishant Kashyap and colleagues rebuilt band theory for periodic media from time-domain wave motion, aiming at students who find the usual reciprocal-space eigenvalue version abstract. A broadband pulse travels through a layered medium in a finite-difference simulation, and its transmission spectrum reveals the Bloch dispersion relation plus attenuation inside band gaps. The approach exposes multiple scattering and phase coherence at work, and handles finite size, disorder, and defect modes in one frame.
arxiv-2604-04098: Riasad Alvi and team built a physics-based digital twin that forecasts core body temperature in dairy cattle two hours ahead. The twin joins a heat-balance equation for metabolic heat, a Gaussian process for cow-specific quirks, a Kalman filter for live sensor data, and a behavior chain for activity shifts. Its outputs feed a three-stage stacked ensemble of LightGBM expert models tuned with Optuna. Cross-checked results gave an R2 of 0.783 with strong F1 and interval coverage scores, backing early heat-stress warning.
arxiv-2604-04498: Cionca and colleagues test three open-source satellite constellation emulators — StarryNet, OpenSN and Celestial — side by side with real WetLinks measurements. Satellite emulation tools matter since teams lack real testbeds. Good emulators must yield observations that match the real world well, with fair resource costs for set-up and runs. The side-by-side test finds flaws in current satellite emulation methods and points to good paths for research and growth.
arxiv-2604-04698: Bunea and four colleagues develop explainable machine learning models for sepsis outcome prediction from a Romanian digital health record dataset of 12,286 hospital stays. The dataset includes patient details, ICD-10 codes and 600 lab test types. The study seeks strong signs across three tasks: deceased versus discharged, deceased versus recovered, and recovered versus ameliorated. The best performance came for deceased versus recovered, with area under the curve 0.983 and accuracy 0.93. SHAP analysis named top signs such as heart conditions and urea levels. Eosinopenia emerged as a top predictor absent from current checklists.
arxiv-2604-04898: Qu and colleagues, in the LM-Provers collaboration, ask whether a small open model can rival large closed systems on Olympiad-level proofs. Proprietary systems reach gold-level results, but their pipelines stay secret and their size makes them costly and hard to reproduce. The team builds QED-Nano, a 4B model, starting with supervised fine-tuning distilled from DeepSeek-Math-V2, then reinforcement learning with rubric-based rewards. The question is whether small open models can reach competitive reasoning on hard proofs, and QED-Nano is their test case.
arxiv-2604-05298: Park, Touri, and Vasconcelos study a two-stage game where people weighing a joint action get noisy clues about a shared payoff factor, then choose whether to act now or wait. Waiting reveals who already acted. That clue is valuable, but the payoff shrinks if the joint effort succeeds. The authors show this trade between fresh information and a discounted reward can actually sharpen coordination and raise the efficiency of group decisions, rather than merely delaying them.
arxiv-2604-05398: Guo, Hu, Yang, and Zhu build a mesh-free actor-critic solver for continuous-time control with jumps, where time-varying drift, volatility, and shocks defeat standard policy methods. Their method rests on a time-inhomogeneous action-value function and an occupation measure, while conditional normalizing flows express flexible non-Gaussian policies with exact likelihoods. Tests on linear-quadratic control, Merton portfolio choice, and a multi-agent portfolio game show stable learning and accurate policies.
arxiv-2604-05698: Flaschel and three colleagues make material fingerprinting flexible, so it can find blends of material models, not just one fixed model. A flexible model library plus stepwise pattern matching refines the model bit by bit, covering multi-term Ogden and anisotropic Holzapfel-Gasser-Ogden models. Tests on rubber and animal skin data show it finds rich models while keeping polyconvexity on tap.
arxiv-2604-05998: Piccina, Bertoni, Cenedese, and Michieletto tune cant-angle choice for tilting hexarotor drones doing contact tasks, using a force-polytope lookup table. Offline tables of zero-moment force shapes flag workable angles for each wanted push, and the best angle balances efficiency with smoothness. Monte Carlo runs plus a wall-inspection simulation show faster compute, tighter pose tracking, and matching drive economy.
arxiv-2604-06298: Yadav, Yadav, and Goyal test preference optimization in small models. They apply GRPO with LoRA to models up to 3 billion parameters. As difficulty rises, accuracy hits a capacity boundary: GRPO reshapes preferences without reliably improving the hardest tier. Training only on easier problems matches full accuracy using about 45 percent of steps, showing diminishing returns from harder samples. GSM8K-trained beat MATH-trained on MATH's numeric subset by about 5 percent at 1.5 billion and 3 percent at 3 billion. Best gains depend on base-model reasoning skill and dataset difficulty.
arxiv-2604-06398: Perezhogin, Adcroft, and Zanna tackle biases in coarse global ocean models, where raw eddies leave values tuned ad hoc. It frames tuning as calibration using Ensemble Kalman Inversion. The method tunes a neural network eddy parameterization in two toy coarse ocean models. The tuned version cuts errors about 2 to 3 times in fluid interfaces and variability, versus the unparameterized model. Ensemble Kalman Inversion stays robust to chaotic noise. A fast plan skips the run to equilibrium. Systematic calibration lifts coarse ocean simulations and reduces global model biases.
arxiv-2604-06598: Singh and three colleagues train a diffusion-based planner on few robots that still copes when many more appear at deployment. Most learned planners handle fewer robots than trained on but fail when the count rises, and training for large teams costs heavily. Pairing one shared diffusion planner with attention between agents and temporal convolution, their method generalizes upward in team size. It compares well against multi-agent reinforcement learning and heuristic controllers across several scenarios.
arxiv-2604-07398: Miller proposes seven output-side rules to curb the false sense of agency that language-model text creates in research and development toolchains. The rules aim at known linguistic triggers and ship as a config-file system prompt with no model change. In 780 two-turn chats, anthropomorphic markers fell from 1233 to 33, a drop above 97 percent. Outputs also shrank by 49 percent in word count, and an adapted AnthroScore verified the shift toward machine register. Output quality under the tight register was not tested, and only one model was used.
arxiv-2604-07498: Pesciotta and five colleagues study hydrolyzed hazes on water-rich exoplanets, measuring how water changes haze optics. Temperate sub-Neptunes show both water vapor and light-made hazes, whose haze cover hides gas features sought as clues about life. Hydrolysis tests on haze analogs, measured from 0.4 to 28.5 microns, reveal changed chemical groups and higher overall darkening. The authors report derived optical constants for modeling and show, via model spectra, that hydrolyzed hazes nearly flatten spectral features, with serious harm for studying water-rich sub-Neptunes.
arxiv-2604-07598: Radica and three colleagues reassess Ariel spectra by mission tier for a hot Saturn, a warm Neptune, and a temperate sub-Neptune. Simulating Ariel spectra at different tiers, they assess which species are well constrained. Tier 1 suffices for giant planets to constrain water and carbon dioxide within about 1.5 dex, even with grey clouds. Tiers 2 and 3 improve precision and make other molecules constrainable, such as hydrogen sulfide and carbon monoxide. Tier 1 also identifies methane in a temperate sub-Neptune, while carbon dioxide needs at least Tier 2 precision.
arxiv-2604-07698: Elliott and Ruzicka build a noncommutative Villadsen algebra and describe its trace space. Traces extending a given extreme trace on the canonical AF subalgebra form the Poulsen simplex. So when that subalgebra has a unique trace, the whole trace space is Poulsen. They also show that in some cases the tracial cone of a classical AF-Villadsen algebra matches the cone left after deleting point evaluations.
arxiv-2604-07898: Nakatsuyama, Takahashi, and Yamamoto introduce curvature equivalence for Legendre curves in the unit tangent bundle over the Euclidean plane. A Legendre curve is a planar curve with a moving frame, and its curvature obeys existence and uniqueness theorems. The new relation groups curves that share bend structure. The paper studies the traits of this relation and gives Legendre curve classifications, local and global, under it. The classes organize a geometric object by a single bend measure.
arxiv-2604-07998: Nguyen and Hirose tackle model selection by the Bayesian information criterion in fixed-dimensional factor analysis. The candidate family is a finite set of compact covariance classes. Their main result shows it is consistent for the pseudo-true order under misspecification. Consistency requires three conditions. All best models share a common pseudo-true set. The population Gaussian rule shows a local quadratic gap away from that set, and complexity counts separate orders there. Candidate models may carry unknown means, exact-zero restrictions, and diagonal or spherical error terms.
arxiv-2604-08598: Zhang and three colleagues adapt text based person search at test time without labeled target data, replacing the usual pretrain then fine tune path. Their UATTA framework estimates uncertainty from bidirectional retrieval disagreement: pairs ranking high in both directions count as certain, others as uncertain. That signal recalibrates the model offline with no labels, beating existing offline adaptation methods across four benchmarks and two model frameworks.
arxiv-2604-08698: Huang and six colleagues design EvoLen, a tokenizer for DNA language models guided by evolved patterns rather than language habit. DNA lacks natural token edges, and byte pair encoding captures human language patterns, not life science patterns. EvoLen groups sequences by cross species evolved signals, trains separate token makers per group, merges vocabularies favoring kept patterns, and decodes with length awareness. It keeps functional motifs better and matches or beats standard byte pair encoding on benchmarks.
arxiv-2604-08798: Kurbucz studies how to find a latent group effect when the marker is unseen but the analyst sees a tuned chance score. Under a constant value frame mean model, the latent group value is pinned by a closed form ratio of seen moments. It fails exactly when the score is a fixed function. The overall latent mean gap is the value plus a pinned mix term. The oracle gauge is root n steady and normal in the limit, with tuning error bias sharply bounded, backed by Monte Carlo tests.
arxiv-2604-08898: Siangliulue and four colleagues build Omakase, a research assistant offering timely, actionable suggestions as a scientific project evolves. Researchers now query deep research systems by hand, squeezing rich project context into short questions, then face exhaustive reports that hide concrete next steps. Omakase watches project documents, infers timely queries for a deep research system, and distills long reports into suggestions fitted to the evolving project. In evaluations, participants found its queries useful and timely, and rated its suggestions far more actionable than the original reports.
arxiv-2604-08998: Rather studies domination polynomials of friendship and book graphs, taking up questions left open by earlier work. For friendship graphs with even size, the polynomial has exactly three real zeros. They are zero and two simple zeros in the intervals minus two to minus one and minus one to zero. The paper also bounds root size explicitly. For book graphs it determines the full limit set of roots and parity-dependent facts about real roots. Neither family has a nonzero integer root, while corona families admit only minus two.
arxiv-2604-09098: Abbott and colleagues report a radio monitoring campaign of the highly active repeating fast radio burst FRB 20220912A with CHIME. The campaign collected about 200 hours of data with CHIME/Pulsar over 1.5 years after discovery, analyzing 828 bursts in the 400 to 800 megahertz band. The team estimates the total energy released across the campaign at 2 × 10^43 ergs. They find a tentative linear rise in dispersion measure and no significant trend in rotation measure. Compared with other active repeaters, which evolve differently, the source may sit in a unique local environment.
arxiv-2604-09298: Gunara, Mulyanto, Fadhilla, and Akbar study massless Maxwell fields in the outside region of slowly spinning, charged Kerr-Newman spacetime. They build a finite-energy scattering theory after setting aside the static Coulomb part. Kept electric and magnetic fluxes match exactly the static non-fading part. That splits Maxwell Cauchy space into static parts and charge-free wave parts. For the wave field, a finite-order transfer method moves from spin-one curve measures back to the Maxwell tensor field, yielding bounds, energy decay, wave operators, and asymptotic completeness.
arxiv-2604-09598: Nguyen and Gehlenborg argue that visualization retrieval should become core infrastructure for data literacy teaching. Galleries and datasets give examples but no way to search, compare, and explore chart designs. Search across the data lifecycle helps learners explore designs, grow their word stock, judge charts side by side, and gather resources. The authors sketch next steps: tools that join search with authoring, models of what fits a lesson, and shared teaching collections. The goal is learners who state their intent and reason with data on their own.
arxiv-2604-09698: Liang and five co-authors define Immersive Conversational Recommendation, where picked items appear marked with in-situ labels. While picking items is well studied, choosing which details belong in scene labels remains open. The authors sort needs into stated-intent match and unasked needs, and define metrics for picking labels. They benchmark retrieval, language-model, and vision-language-model across fashion, movie, and retail tests. Three limits emerge: methods ignore setting-tied modes, show repeats clear from sight, and poorly foresee unasked needs from chat alone.
arxiv-2604-10098: Su and 26 colleagues survey attention sink in transformers, where a large share of focus lands on a small set of empty tokens. The effect muddies clarity, disturbs training and use, and spawns false outputs. Until now no survey had pulled the spread-out research into one place. Their survey, the first on the topic, sorts work into use, explanation, and mitigation. It maps key concepts and trends to help readers manage attention sink in current transformers and spark next designs.
arxiv-2604-10298: Allu and Kumar find sharp second and third Hankel determinants for a starlike subclass of analytic functions. They consider functions in the class S-star of phi, defined by a subordination condition with phi of z equal to one plus z over two, squared. The functions are normalized with value zero at zero and derivative one at zero in the unit disk. Beyond the determinants, they determine the extremal functions for the coefficient bounds of functions in this class.
arxiv-2604-10598: Zhang and four colleagues give survey drones a way to look around without new hardware. Their AWARE system turns the drone body, pointing its narrow-view laser scanner where the information is richest. A predictive controller picks the best viewing direction, while a learning agent retunes its priorities as the scene changes. A safe-flight corridor keeps the operator's route separate from the automatic turning. Tests in simulated and real settings show steadier position estimates in feature-poor scenes where narrow sensors usually drift.
arxiv-2604-10698: Hasanzadeh and three colleagues trace quasi-biennial oscillations, signals riding alongside the Sun's 11-year cycle, using helioseismic shifts from GONG across Cycles 23 and 24 and into Cycle 25. Wavelet analysis shows periods depend weakly on latitude: shorter, less persistent signals near the equator, nearly constant near 3 years at higher latitudes. Cycle 24 runs slightly longer than Cycle 23, within uncertainties. Amplitudes grow with mode frequency and run higher at low latitudes, tracking surface magnetic activity. The link between oscillation amplitude and cycle amplitude differs in slope between cycles, suggesting decoupling from cycle strength.
arxiv-2604-10798: Ni and Akan study a control-referenced tri-channel organic electrochemical transistor receiver for brain organoid links. Dopamine- and serotonin-tuned pixels sit beside a gel-matched control pixel for drift correction, with a silver-silver chloride gate. The study couples timed release, limited diffusion with clearance, aptamer binding, transistor readout, and linked noise. At 45 microns, control use mainly helps the hybrid branch, cutting its symbol error rate from about 0.037 to about 0.011 at 14,000 molecules per symbol. MoSK, CSK-4, and a 2-bit hybrid decoder are tested with Monte Carlo runs.
arxiv-2604-10998: Brenner and three colleagues study price-anticipatory spatial load shifting by large flexible users. Such consumers can move demand across sites, shifting dispatch and prices in wholesale markets. Flexible load is often assumed to raise efficiency, but that view rests on price-taking. Using one large flexible consumer as a Stackelberg leader, they show local shifting need not minimize system cost. Misalignment arises at regime boundaries, where small load changes flip marginal generators or congestion.
arxiv-2604-11698: Sridhar and five colleagues study strong waves in pair plasmas. A single parameter governs the interaction: wave strength over wave frequency in plasma units, both in the plasma rest frame before interaction. Below one, wavelengths crossing without attenuation from induced Compton scattering run roughly as the inverse parameter to the two-thirds power, imprinting narrow sub-structures on the pulse. Above one, the pulse acts as a relativistic piston driving a shock into the plasma. The framework bears on intense neutron-star radio pulses and multi-petawatt pair plasma experiments.
arxiv-2604-11798: Brioso and six colleagues build a budget-aware quality check for auto-segmentation in radiotherapy, using nnU-Net. Their maps show, voxel by voxel, where the model is unsure, so reviewers can focus manual checks where they matter most. They test four ways to gauge and tune that doubt on total marrow and lymph node cases. Tuning with temperature scaling sharpens calibration most, and tuned checkpoint-based runs best match doubt to real errors.
arxiv-2604-11898: Liang and Oh argue that one diffusion coefficient misses much of cosmic-ray transport, since different mechanisms can share it yet yield different particle distributions. Their propagator framework centres on the position distribution P(x,t), which exposes memory: flux can depend on earlier gradients when trapping or phase changes are averaged away. With Montroll-Weiss methods they measure the propagator from trajectories and recover its memory kernel, represented by a Prony expansion. Slow regions, they find, can regulate escape without dominating total stay.
arxiv-2604-12198: Huang tests whether autonomous agents can scrutinize published computational physics by reproducing papers from scratch and raising concerns from execution rather than reading alone. Across 111 open-access Quantum ESPRESSO papers, an agent raised substantive concerns on about 42 percent, and 96.6 percent of its critiques surfaced only after running a calculation. In depth, a fresh agent built a 14-concern inventory and a full Comment revising one paper's 5 nanometer headline.
arxiv-2604-12598: T. Boismard and M. Rieutord ask whether equatorial Kelvin waves can destabilize Be stars. Be stars are B-type stars ringed by self-fed discs. The team derives gravito-inertial modes in a shallow-water model. Numerical work tracks Kelvin modes as settings vary. Waves persist in a finite shell, though less confined at the equator. Under shellular differential rotation plus viscosity, the waves can destabilize. Growth rate behavior traces to a critical layer where flow speed matches wave speed. Kelvin waves may thus trigger the Be phenomenon.
arxiv-2604-12798: Yupeng Sun and seven colleagues speed up FlashAttention by easing vector work. Online softmax streams score tiles and tracks a running maximum. Near peak throughput, rowmax and rowsum reductions dominate latency. Vector Relieved Flash Attention seeds the maximum from key-block summaries. It visits sink and local blocks first, then freezes the maximum. A sparse variant adds block-sparse skipping. Both avoid the conditional rescale step of FlashAttention 4.0. Tests show no performance loss. One setting nearly doubles speed over the baseline.
arxiv-2604-12998: Jonan Richards studies how developer needs shape programming assistants. Conversational assistants now support many software tasks at once. Varied minds and work settings complicate meeting those needs. Open-ended talk adds further difficulty. The paper maps diversity effects and tests personalization for wider inclusion. Current and future work explores these questions.
arxiv-2604-13098: Chen and five colleagues tackle a limit of traffic control systems that coordinate lights and connected autonomous vehicles. Hand-crafted rewards miss safety, flow stability, and comfort. Their C2T framework distills common-sense knowledge from a language model into a learned intrinsic reward, then guides a cooperative multi-intersection controller on CityFlow benchmarks. It beats strong multi-agent baselines on efficiency, safety, and an energy proxy, and prompt changes can shift policy between efficiency and safety focus.
arxiv-2604-13298: Ghimire and eight colleagues test whether agent-based language models can automatically hide hardware designs against reverse engineering and piracy. Their staged system plans locks from retrieved knowledge, compiles locked netlists deterministically, checks functional equivalence, and scores security with SAT attacks. On standard ISCAS-85 benchmarks it produces correct locked circuits with clear output corruption under wrong keys, though SAT attacks still succeed, showing both promise and present limits.
arxiv-2604-13398: Shihao Zhang and eight colleagues build ABSA-R1, a tool that makes sentiment analysis reason before it predicts, like people who give reasons for a feeling. A reward model that lines up reasoning with the final label keeps the two in step. Rejection sampling picks hard cases where the model's own reasoning wobbles. On four benchmarks, explicit reasoning improves both clarity and scores in sentiment classification and triplet extraction over baselines that do not reason.
arxiv-2604-14098: Gorecki and Koch protect Heisenberg scaling in quantum metrology with dressed states from a constant Hamiltonian. For low-temperature noise, Heisenberg scaling holds exactly when the signal generator sits beyond the range spanned by the system-environment coupling operators. Dressed states can thus enable the scaling even where the undressed Hamiltonian-not-in-Lindblad-span test forbids it, illustrated by NV-center thermometry under magnetic-field fluctuations.
arxiv-2604-14298: Brady, Wang, García-Pintos, and Gorshkov set precision limits for measuring random signals carried by Markovian Lindblad dynamics, allowing any control and helper systems. Markovian noise still forces standard-quantum-limit scaling in sensing time, yet entangled probes can gain Heisenberg-type scaling in channel count when signal correlations rank high across channels. For collective many-body dissipation this becomes super-Heisenberg scaling with system size. A rapid prepare-and-measure scheme tracking many quantum jumps at once reaches the bounds when parameters sit in dissipative rates.
arxiv-2604-14598: Li and five colleagues build CPGRec, a video-game recommender balancing accuracy against diversity. Current game recommenders chase accuracy and suggest similar games, while diversity methods often ignore item category and popularity in neighbor modeling and message passing. CPGRec's accuracy module links games more strictly, and its diversity module links neighbors across categories and uses popular nodes to lift long-tail games. A comprehensive module reweights negative-sample scores to balance the two. On Steam data, the method improves game recommendations on both fronts.
arxiv-2604-14698: Dong, Zhang, and Cheng replace the many-step diffusion models often used as robot policies with MeanFlow models, which generate actions in far fewer steps. They train these policies by soft policy iteration under maximum-entropy reinforcement learning, solving the action-likelihood and policy-improvement problems specific to MeanFlow. On MuJoCo, DeepMind Control Suite, and HumanoidBench, the resulting MFPO method matched or beat diffusion-based rivals while cutting training and inference time considerably.
arxiv-2604-14798: Amaro-Alcalá and Pineda show that one all-to-all Ising spin model can host integrable, mixed, and chaotic motion at a single fixed parameter set. Earlier studies varied parameters; here the variety lives across symmetry blocks of the same system. Each symmetry sector maps to a kicked top whose parameters hinge on the sector dimension. The system also resists noise when the noise Hamiltonian norm sits near 1. Like the Bunimovich billiard for classical chaos, it offers a fresh platform for quantum chaos set by symmetry sector.
arxiv-2604-14998: Shahbazi and four others study a shielded quantum emitter in hexagonal boron nitride on a waveguide. The emitter glows brightly above 10 million counts per second, with two zero-phonon lines from one complex. Spectra show the lines differ in drift, via distinct donor-acceptor-pair-like paths sensitive to electric shifts. Off-resonance blue light redistributes emission between lines and raises duty without changing low-temperature drift rates, pointing to repumping from shelving states. Magnetic tests reveal millisecond relaxation and field-dependent contrast, showing spin-dependent shelving dynamics.
arxiv-2604-15098: Sarkar breaks down the tangent bundle of a special geometric object, the punctual Hilbert scheme built from a smooth projective surface, into pieces that cannot be split further. That breakdown settles a recent conjecture on how products of such schemes classify. It also answers when two products of symmetric powers of one smooth variety count as isomorphic. Along the way he characterizes abelian varieties anew: from dimension two up, a variety whose tangent bundle is trivial up to a line-bundle twist is abelian.
arxiv-2604-15198: Stolarski and Waldron prove Ricci-flow stability near a Ricci-flat ALE metric that is linearly stable and has integrable deformations, by a shorter route than before. The core link joins integrability with a near-orthogonality feature of the Ricci-DeTurck tensor, which they then study head-on. In weighted Hölder spaces this yields the L^p stability results of Deruelle-Kroncke and Kroncke-Petersen.
arxiv-2604-15298: Gretta, Gupta, and Joshi show that Dicke states of polylogarithmic weight can be prepared in QAC0. Such states are uniform superpositions over bit strings of a given Hamming weight, and QAC0 is the quantum analogue of AC0 with wide Toffoli gates. This gives the first QAC0 construction of any super-constant-weight Dicke state. More broadly, any weight-k Dicke state needs only FANOUT gates up to the smaller of k and n minus k, yielding a tight characterization.
arxiv-2604-15398: Służalec and three colleagues present a Python library for solving partial differential equations with discrete variational formulations. Users define discrete domains, functions, inner products, and weak forms with Kronecker delta test functions, then train a discrete neural network with finite-difference derivatives. A Stokes-flow example plus a rigorous well-posedness and robustness proof show the loss tracks true error during training.
arxiv-2604-15498: Khiste, Tarte, and Joshi characterize when the zero-divisor graph of a poset with zero is complemented, in terms of quasi-complemented posets. They prove complemented and uniquely complemented zero-divisor graphs coincide for any such poset, and give both algebraic and topological characterizations. Applications cover zero-divisor graphs of reduced semigroups, comaximal ideal graphs of Artinian rings, and nonzero component union graphs of finite vector spaces.
arxiv-2604-15598: Simpson and Plank ask when trajectory data actually matter for pinning down random transport models of dispersal. Mixing agent runs, mean-field PDE estimates, likelihood fits, identifiability checks, and forecasts on a lattice random walk, they show count data alone can hit structural non-identifiability. Adding path data eases the snag, and gathering rules shift real-world identifiability and estimate sharpness.
arxiv-2604-15698: Xu studies squashed sends from a claim source in a proof world, where faithfulness means keeping proof closure, not matching signs. Fixed proof rules and a set scan order split signs into a lean core plus spare stored fallouts. With split cores, the zero-loss rate is core weight times core-given entropy. With tangled cores, a hypergraph-entropy sum rules. Rebuild signs inside source closure leave the full rate-loss curve hanging on the core alone.
arxiv-2604-15798: Iwamoto and Ioka revisit induced scattering of strong, linearly polarized waves in pair plasmas. This process shapes how fast radio bursts escape magnetar winds. They show the nonlinearity hinges on a combined parameter involving wave amplitude and plasma frequency, not amplitude alone. Standard linear analysis still holds even for strong waves once the plasma's motion is boosted correctly. Saturation follows the ratio of wave energy to plasma energy, so very energetic waves barely scatter at all.
arxiv-2604-15898: Létoffé, Huang, and Marques-Silva survey the push for rigorous explainability in machine learning through feature attribution, assigning each input feature its share of a decision. Non-symbolic explanation methods have ruled for a decade, yet they lack rigor and can mislead human decision-makers, a grave flaw in high-stakes uses. Shapley values and the SHAP tool exemplify the problem, with a provable lack of rigor. The paper overviews symbolic methods as a rigorous alternative for ranking feature importance.
arxiv-2604-15998: Xiong and four colleagues introduce SCHK-HTC, a method for few-shot hierarchical text classification, assigning texts to labels in a tree under scarce data. Current methods enforce parent-child consistency but struggle to separate similar-meaning sibling classes for lack of domain knowledge. The new framework pairs hierarchical knowledge extraction with sibling contrastive learning, teaching the model sharp features at each level. It beats existing leaders on three benchmark datasets in most cases, telling confusable classes apart.
arxiv-2604-16098: Liu and three colleagues compare three methods for gauging Poynting flux and helicity flux on NOAA active region 12673. The methods, PDFI, DAVE4VM, and DAVE4VMwDV, give total energy and helicity values that differ widely, even in sign. Using the Helmholtz-Hodge split, the authors show Doppler speed adds much through the non-inductive, curl-free electric field. Their treatments of Doppler and sideways speeds plainly cause the gaps. The paper notes future data that could better constrain the methods.
arxiv-2604-16998: Athanassoulis proves global well-posedness for the Alber equation, the mixed-state nonlinear Schrödinger equation with a singular delta kernel, used to model stochastic ocean waves. Working in a Schatten-Sobolev space, he covers both focusing and defocusing cases for self-adjoint, non-negative data, with energy conserved. In the focusing case, estimates give a global bound with no smallness condition, and small perturbations around Penrose-stable backgrounds grow at most polynomially.
arxiv-2604-17298: Li, Duan, and Tao propose FReMuRe, a rate-guided model for video scene graph building that lifts long-tail links. Split branches handle gradient conflicts, yielding more even, tail-aware learning. A rate-aware network models high- and low-rate links apart, lifting tail-class recall through gated fusion. Two swap-in sorting heads — Bayesian for doubt scores and a new Gaussian Mixture Model Head for intra-class variety — further strengthen the model. On Action Genome, FReMuRe clearly lifts long-tail recall and overall strength.
arxiv-2604-17398: Desimone and Alonso offer a method for finding subtle bias in language-model output without a fixed list of suspect words. Controlled synthetic texts form minimal pairs that differ only in the social group named, keeping story conditions comparable. Word forms are then generalized, and a mutual-information variant flags forms that appear far more often for one group. A ranking step surfaces the most concentrated passages for expert review, linking stats to qualitative judgment.
arxiv-2604-17598: McLean and eight colleagues present CCSVI, a web-based map platform that joins climate hazard data with social, economic, and infrastructure data for Hawai'i. Hazards there are growing more frequent and severe, striking vulnerable communities unevenly, yet hazard and vulnerability data are usually collected separately and prove hard to combine. CCSVI lets users explore how environmental risk lines up with social vulnerability through interactive maps and layered views. The tool aims to help decision-makers, researchers, and residents spot at-risk populations, improve disaster readiness, and shape climate adaptation plans.
