arxiv-2604-17998: Khosravinia and two colleagues introduce a causal forecasting method for spotting anomalies in multi-sensor time series, where failures stem from time dynamics and links between sensors. Their Causally Guided Transformer limits prediction to causes backed by a causal graph found by discovery, while a Gaussian head captures uncertainty. A shadow side path adds leftover correlational information only when reliable. Anomaly scores use negative log-likelihood with moving thresholds. On ASD and SMD benchmarks it reaches F1 scores of 96.19 percent and 95.32 percent.
arxiv-2604-18698: Upasna and Tavva tackle branch prediction in graph programs, where data sets larger than the cache make wrong branch guesses a frequent drag on speed. They sort the recurring branch types found during execution and argue that existing predictors still leave room to improve on the branches that cause most mispredictions. The paper's focus is squeezing extra performance from prediction alone, rather than from larger caches.
arxiv-2604-18798: Filothodoros studies the BCS-BEC crossover of the large N attractive Fermi-Hubbard model on a one dimensional lattice, using a mean field approximation with an imaginary chemical potential. He shows three parameters govern the crossover: the imaginary chemical potential, temperature through a thermal kernel, and a parameter whose sign controls weak and strong coupling. At the unitarity point, he finds a thermal window where the gap vanishes while the fermion number peaks. Inside this window, BCS and BEC physics await coupling changes to select the dominant regime.
arxiv-2604-19098: Elbadry and fourteen colleagues introduce Sahm, the first Arabic financial benchmark for 422 million speakers. Gulf wealth near 5 trillion dollars and Islamic finance of 4 to 5 trillion need Shari'ah compliance. Sahm spans seven tasks, from standards and fatwa answering to sentiment and event-cause reasoning, with more than 14,000 instances. Testing 20 models shows fluency does not imply financial reasoning: 91 percent on recognition drops sharply on generation. Event-cause reasoning shows the widest gap, roughly 2 to 10 out of 10.
arxiv-2604-19398: Wang and colleagues present GRASPrune, a pruning tool that shrinks large language models after pretraining under a global budget, cutting their heavy serving costs. GRASPrune prunes feed-forward channels and KV head groups. It learns light gate scores with a projected straight-through estimator. That estimator enforces a hard mask meeting the budget at every step, while backbone weights stay frozen. After the mask is fixed, scaling factors on kept units are tuned. They are folded into the pruned weights, yielding a smaller checkpoint with no extra weights.
arxiv-2604-19898: Pedon studies q-metallic numbers, deformations of the metallic numbers that generalize the golden ratio. For each integer n, the nth metallic number admits a q-deformation with integer Taylor coefficients, forming a power series in q. He pins those coefficients down by recurrences and differential equations, with closed forms for n equal to 1, 2, and 3, plus asymptotics. Modular group identities emerge, and the golden-ratio deformation turns out to be a signed version of RNA secondary structures.
arxiv-2604-19998: Jin offers concern alignment, a method judging AI peer reviews by concerns raised, not just final verdicts. Its core tool, the match graph, pairs official and AI concerns with match type, weight, and post-rebuttal treatment. The ladder climbs from binary accuracy to detection, verdict-grouped conduct, choice-aware calibration, and rebuttal-aware breakdown. A pilot across four systems in six setups finds calibration, not spotting, is often the binding constraint. Many systems mark a quarter to over half of concerns on accepted papers as deal-breakers.
arxiv-2604-20098: Hittesdorf, Salzetta, and Cheng tackle false claims in multi-step language model thought with a smooth take on conformal fact checks. Old coherent fact-check tools need hand-made scorers that, at high trust levels, throw out nearly 60 percent of true claims. Their smooth Coherent Factuality tool learns better scorers while keeping the first tool's pledges intact. On two thought benchmarks it lifts kept claims by up to 141 percent with trust intact, a step toward conformal tools users can trust.
arxiv-2604-20598: Xu offers SmartVector, a framework that adds time, trust, and links to vectors used in retrieval generation. Standard retrieval treats embeddings as fixed, with no sense of age, source trust, or dependence on items. SmartVector scores candidates on relevance, temporal validity, confidence, and graph importance, while an agent spots contradictions, builds links, and spreads updates along them. On a benchmark of 258 vectors and 138 queries, it roughly doubles top-1 accuracy over plain cosine retrieval. It cuts stale answers, calibration error by nearly half, and re-embedding cost per edit by 77 percent.
arxiv-2604-20798: Epstein, Mori, and Zhou study a bulk-surface coupled Laplace system with an embedded open boundary. They recast the problem as an integro-differential equation via boundary integral forms, and prove the solution exists and is unique. A Wiener-Hopf method studies how smooth the solution is and gives asymptotic forms for the edge singularity. They then build a finite element method that uses the singularity form, with a full error analysis. Numerical tests back the proved convergence rates.
arxiv-2604-21098: Olli Järviniemi and four colleagues measure how much of a language model's unsanctioned behavior comes from its surroundings rather than its own goals. Testing 23 models in 11 settings across 12 environmental factors, they find strategic and non-strategic factors explain behavior about equally, with no drift as capability grows. One trend does emerge: models grow more sensitive to goal conflicts.
arxiv-2604-21198: Eleanor Wiesler and Trace Baxley improve fish detection in murky, crowded underwater video with a data-augmentation method modeled on simulated annealing. Starting from DeepFish segmentation masks, they paste fish into realistic dense scenes to widen spatial variety and crowding during training. The approach beats a YOLOv10 baseline, most clearly on hand-labeled live-stream footage from the Florida Keys.
arxiv-2604-21298: Kalin Staykov and three colleagues map how spontaneous scalarization unfolds as a phase transition in scalar-tensor gravity, using Landau theory. They extend earlier work on quadratic couplings and round stars to linear-plus-quadratic couplings and spinning stars. Linear coupling tangles the solution space, but the Landau model finds scalarized branches that number searches often miss. Spin mainly shifts transition masses higher, leaving the broad picture much as in round-star cases.
arxiv-2604-21398: Fei Hu and Chen Jiang prove a sharp lower bound for the polynomial volume growth of zero-entropy automorphisms of projective varieties. If first-degree growth scales as n to the k, volume growth reaches at least dimension plus k times k plus 2 over 4, bounding a related ring dimension. The proof introduces dynamical intersection polynomials and a new characterization via intersection numbers. A gap principle follows: in dimension at least 4, volume growth is either dimension squared or bounded well below it, revealing new rigidity.
arxiv-2604-21498: Mario Francisco-Fernández and Andrea Meilán-Vila analyze heading errors with a circular regression method for mixed predictors using a product kernel. Blind, low-vision, and sighted people did spatial updating tasks under five conditions, scoring signed angular error. They derive bias and variance formulas and build a bootstrap bandwidth picker for cosine loss, compared with cross-validation and rule-of-thumb methods. On the data, it reveals nonlinear patterns that vary by condition, with bootstrap confidence bands, with a good bias-variance trade-off.
arxiv-2604-21598: Kaushitha Silva and Srinath Perera introduce DryRUN, a framework for self-directed code writing without public tests or test runs. Multi-agent code writing leans on public tests for testing and debugging, but crafting complete pairs is labor-intensive; ground-truth examples are seldom available beforehand. Relying on public tests creates overconfidence: frameworks overfit examples and lag on hidden suites. DryRUN lets language models plan, create test inputs, and run mock runs to fix itself. On LiveCodeBench v6, it matches CodeSIM, a test-based baseline, while cutting tokens.
arxiv-2604-21998: Hu and Wiens extend minimax experimental design theory from least squares to M-estimation, gaining robustness against outlying or erroneous responses. With a minor tweak to a tuning constant, least-squares-optimal designs stay optimal asymptotically for M-estimation. The authors argue even this change should be ignored, with the tuning constant chosen in a sensible way independent of the M-estimate used. Designs and estimates from independent, identically distributed errors also hold up, in a minimax sense, against broad correlation classes.
arxiv-2604-22898: Fernandez presents the Reconstructive Authority Model for systems that must act without seeing all key state. Trusted execution, oracle-signed proofs, and attestation check integrity, but never sufficiency: what is measured may still be too little. The model adds a reconstruction gate over proven state, stated assumptions, and an unseen remainder. It narrows privileges or fails closed when coverage falls short. In tests with 100,000 runs, it reaches zero invalid executions at every coverage level, while attestation-based systems still fail even at full coverage.
arxiv-2604-23598: Mishra and Mohanta pin down when a bounded domain admits a bounded extension map for Sobolev functions. They prove it holds exactly when the domain meets a measure density rule plus a Bourgain-Brezis-Mironescu type bound. They also prove a fractional Poincaré bound under Ahlfors regularity alone, improving an earlier result. They also show fractional extension at one exponent grows into full first-order extension under a mild boundary rule.
arxiv-2604-23698: Kim, Han, and Hwang argue that theorem-proving models should be judged by semantic tests, not by how closely their proofs resemble human ones. Their framework counts a generated theorem correct only when every theorem depending on it also compiles, like integration testing for code. Built from five real Lean repositories with over 2,200 problems, the benchmark shows top models compiling well yet scoring under 39 percent on the semantic metric.
arxiv-2604-24398: Cao and six colleagues present MAS-SZZ, a multi-agent method for faulty commits. The SZZ algorithm traces history to commits touching vulnerable code, but variants fail through wrong anchors and weak backtracking. Given a CVE description and fixing commit, MAS-SZZ sums up the vulnerability's root cause. Step-forward prompting pinpoints lines from hunk intent. Those lines anchor a backward trace to the commit that introduced the flaw. Tests show MAS-SZZ beats baselines across datasets and languages, with F1 gains of about 65 percent over the best method.
arxiv-2604-24698: Xiao and four colleagues name and measure Persona Collapse in large language models used as simulated survey respondents or app users. Model responses with detailed human profiles bunch into classes, while human responses fill the whole persona space evenly. Three diagnostics track coverage, evenness and richness of behavior. Across eight models on personality, moral reasoning and self-introduction tasks, collapse is universal but task-dependent. Sampling more personas does not cure it, and fine-tuning for a persona narrows the population further.
arxiv-2604-24798: Al-Badawi, Ahmed and Sakallı study a renormalization-group improved Schwarzschild-like black hole. Its lapse interpolates between a classical exterior and a quantum-smoothed interior. They compute horizon structure, photon sphere and shadow radius. Scalar, electromagnetic and Dirac perturbations are treated in one framework. Quasinormal modes by sixth-order WKB are checked against time-domain ringdown. For positive parameters the geometry stays regular, with a de Sitter core. The gap stays below the bound, so censorship holds. It is the closest to Schwarzschild among the regular black-hole family.
arxiv-2604-24898: Carlson shows group isomorphisms of anabelian varieties of this kind match variety isomorphisms. Such varieties come from iterated fibrations of hyperbolic curves over sub-p-adic fields. Moreover, dominant maps between proper varieties of this kind match stably cohomologically one-to-one maps of these groups. These open maps pull back to injections on cohomology rings, for any prime l. This verifies Grothendieck's guesses from his letter to Faltings. The paper is about shapes built from curves over a special kind of field.
arxiv-2604-25198: Fujii constructs the local Langlands correspondence of essentially unipotent supercuspidal ones under the framework of rigid inner forms and proves functoriality. This is stronger than a similar result of Solleveld, which ignored rigidifications. He also extends it to all disconnected groups. He also expects to use it to extend Kaletha's work.
arxiv-2604-25298: Rauscher and four co-authors propose a measure-driven approach showing artifacts in dense pixel views through neighbor scores for 1D orders, shown with glyphs, halos and hatching. Such analysis matters in epidemiology and ecology, where spatial and time patterns meet. Dense pixel views give a compact view, but mapping 2D space into 1D brings warps seen as artifacts. They test the approach on COVID-19 cases across German districts, showing boosting lets analysts tell genuine patterns from mapping errors.
arxiv-2604-25398: Dartois and three colleagues study bounded deviation of non-deterministic finite transducers under Hamming distance. The bounded comparison task asks whether two transducers yield words within Hamming distance k for every input. It is known decidable in polynomial time for fixed k, and in co-NP otherwise. They show it is NL-complete for fixed k, co-NP-complete for binary k, and DP-complete for exact distance k. They also prove bounded comparison caps max distance at quadratic in the size of both transducers.
arxiv-2604-25498: He and nine colleagues present SymphonyGen, a 3D hierarchical frame for orchestra music. Making such music needs form and dense scores, yet models struggle to balance scale and control. Its parts split bar, track, and event axes, keeping memory far below flat token streams. A beat-set harmony frame gives short-score control for outlines. Reward-based tuning with a CLaMP 3 reward refines the model, and clash-averse sampling cuts tonal clashes. Both post-training tricks cut dissonance while keeping melodic scores, and tests rate it above baselines.
arxiv-2604-25798: Meibohm and three colleagues study, in theory and experiment, how to steer a colloidal particle through an inhomogeneous environment in finite time. A final-state cost that varies with position competes with dissipation along the path. That contest yields a sharp switch in control strategy at a critical duration. The authors tie the switch to a phase transition in relaxation after a quench. There, control cost plays the role of the rate function for rare paths. The work links optimal control with nonequilibrium physics.
arxiv-2604-25898: Żurek and four colleagues propose TSN-Affinity, a method for continual offline reinforcement learning that reuses parameters by similarity. New tasks arrive over time, but live adaptation is often costly, risky, or impossible, and old skills must survive. Replay methods waste memory and mismatch new policies, while architectural methods remain underexplored here. TSN-Affinity routes tasks by action compatibility and latent similarity, using tiny task-specific subnetworks. Tests on Atari games and Franka arm manipulation show strong retention, with routing further lifting multi-task performance.
arxiv-2604-26498: Guo and Ding benchmarked whether bigger models truly win in drug discovery, testing scale against compact cheminformatics across 26 endpoints and over 165,000 compound-label records. Classical machine learning took the largest share of best results at about 47 percent, ahead of pretrained sequence models and graph networks, with LLM-based baselines far behind. Classical methods dominated random-split interpolation, while graph and sequence models contended only on harder splits. Small gaps between models rarely counted as decisive wins, and fit among model, task, and validation mattered more than scale.
arxiv-2604-26598: Babnik and five colleagues proposed FunFace, an adaptive margin loss for face recognition that folds biometric utility into the margin. State-of-the-art models tie feature norm to sample quality, but norm alone misses aspects of utility that better predict recognition value. FunFace estimates utility via the Certainty Ratio and weaves it into the margin, following AdaFace's lead. Trained models matched leading rivals on high-quality benchmarks and surpassed them on low-quality ones.
arxiv-2604-26698: Zhang, Feng, Shao, Liu, and Yao show that the metal-insulator distinction breaks down in systems ruled by Berry curvature, where transport rests on between-band coherence across the whole Fermi sea. They build a quantum-transport theory for bulk topological insulators with no states at the Fermi energy, where the usual Drude contribution vanishes. Impurity scattering that destroys coherence opens a distinct lengthwise channel, yielding finite current flow with no carriers at the Fermi level. The conductance falls as temperature rises, echoing strange-metal behavior.
arxiv-2604-26898: Agazzi and four colleagues prove that token motion in a finite transformer with multilayer perceptron blocks converges, layer by layer, to a continuous-time stochastic particle system. They pin down the stochastic partial differential equation ruling the token spread in that limit and prove propagation of chaos when token counts grow large. Their bounds are concrete and the limits commute. The limit model also shows synchronization by noise, with interaction energy fading exponentially on average when shared noise is strong enough against self-attention drift.
arxiv-2604-26998: Samanta tests whether entropy-driven time-based biomarkers improve depression detection over standard pooled features, using the DAIC-WOZ corpus of 142 labeled participants. She rebuilds spoken acoustic paths and compares pooled baselines, path dynamics, Shannon entropy, recurrence, sample entropy, fractal detail, and coupling markers under leak-proof validation. Static pooling scores lowest, path dynamics higher, and entropy markers highest at an AUC of 0.646, the strongest real gain over pooled baselines. The findings suggest the signal lies less in average acoustic levels than in the entropy of conversation flow.
arxiv-2604-27098: Scott and three colleagues study the A and B phases of superfluid helium-3, whose vector degrees of freedom reflect broken symmetries: chiral and spin-orbit rotation axes. Disorder in the fluid, held in evenly strained silica aerogel, orients these degrees, affecting phase balance. These degrees reorient on their own at a field-independent transition temperature Tx, explained by a temperature-dependent Ginzburg-Landau model.
arxiv-2604-27498: Escher and five colleagues audit how YouTube recommendations affect Kyrgyz children, whose caregivers fear the platform pushes Russian over Kyrgyz, their heritage language. Working with the community, they measure how recommendations rank languages for child users, Indigenous versus others. Their results back caregiver worries: Kyrgyz children mostly get non-Kyrgyz recommendations from YouTube, even when they flag a Kyrgyz preference. They test practices that reduce Russian recommendations, such as device sharing across generations, and argue platforms can amplify colonial influence rather than revitalize Indigenous heritage.
arxiv-2604-27598: Sharma and six colleagues evaluate privacy-preserving federated learning for heart disease risk scores on Swedish health data. Standard learning pools patient records in one place, while local training shares only updates, yet shared gradients can still leak sensitive information. They compare differential privacy and homomorphic encryption against standard federated and centralized learning, using logistic models and neural networks. Encryption-based learning matched centralized results but added overhead, most for neural networks, while differential privacy cost less yet hit logistic models harder.
arxiv-2604-27798: Mehra and four colleagues build a Nearly Asymptotically Invariant Manifold (NAIM) for Nesterov speed-up. They lift gradient flow to second-order phase space, where a slow graph forms and a bend-aware nudge to it yields speed-up. Its slope obeys a Differential Riccati rule keeping flow glued to its face; in the quadratic case it turns Algebraic. When all bend modes shrink at one rate, that rate fixes damping and gives the Nesterov ODE, and Fenichel's result spreads the view to smooth, strongly convex cases.
arxiv-2605-00198:
Andrey Sarantsev studies how fast statistical estimates settle near the true value they aim at. It is known that maximum likelihood estimates can beat the classic square-root rate when a key quantity, the Fisher information, is infinite. That speed-up often needs odd features, such as a region that shifts with the unknown parameter.

Sarantsev builds a one-parameter family of smooth distributions on a half-space whose region never changes. For this family, a weighted least squares estimate still lands closer than the classic rate would predict. In one special case based on Gaussian mixtures, the maximum likelihood estimate turns out to be exactly this weighted estimate. The example sharpens what statisticians know about when faster rates can occur.
arxiv-2605-00298:
Param Budhraja and 3 co-authors report a counterintuitive trick for reinforcement learning in changing environments: delete some of the training data. Their setting is a family of environments indexed by a hidden context that the agent must infer from its own trajectory at test time. A context estimator is trained alongside a policy that assumes the context is known.

Because data is gathered over rounds by improving policies, older trajectories come from a different distribution than the one met in deployment. Random deletion after each round quietly decays the weight of old data while keeping variety. The trick shrank the robustness gap and let a small network beat a much larger one trained without deletion. The authors also prove, in a simplified regression setting, when and why deleting one point lowers expected test loss.
arxiv-2605-00498:
Yonghao Zhao and 4 co-authors remove objects from three-dimensional scenes without breaking the light. Reconstructed scenes, built from many photos by radiance fields or Gaussian splatting, often need an object deleted and the hidden region behind it filled in. Existing editors handle consistency fairly well but ignore global lighting, and they stumble on glossy, view-dependent surfaces, producing results that look physically wrong.

Their framework works in intrinsic space, splitting the scene into material and lighting components and modeling light transport explicitly, so shadows and reflections stay consistent after removal. A dedicated module then paints the missing region directly in those material and lighting terms, which handles shiny surfaces more reliably. On synthetic and real datasets the method improved perceptual similarity and signal quality over existing editors by clear margins, with code released publicly.
arxiv-2605-00598:
Ping Zhao, Dan Zhuang, and Long Feng build a clustering method for high-dimensional data that is heavy-tailed and full of irrelevant variables. Classic K-means chases means, which outliers drag around, and it weighs every dimension equally, signal or not. Their framework swaps the mean updates for spatial medians, a robust center that resists extreme points, inside the usual assign-and-update loop.

For the assignment step, users can keep a simple Euclidean rule or use a robust Mahalanobis-type distance built from the spatial sign covariance, which accounts for differing scales and dependence among features. A hard feature-exclusion step then drops dimensions that barely separate the centers, with its threshold chosen automatically by a permutation-based gap criterion. In simulations on correlated Gaussian and heavy-tailed data, the method matched or beat K-means and sparse K-means on accuracy, with better stability across runs.
arxiv-2605-00698:
Zoe Fowler and Ghassan AlRegib improve federated learning for medicine, where hospitals train one model together without sharing patient data. Statistical differences between institutions are the core obstacle: a global model must generalize to unseen patient populations yet adapt to each hospital's own distribution. The same heterogeneity makes both global and local models forget earlier patient patterns after updates.

Their method, FedKPer, treats generalization and personalization as one problem rather than two. During local training, each site personalizes its knowledge by aligning selectively with the global model. During aggregation, the server emphasizes local updates that are reliable and label-diverse. The authors also devise extra metrics aimed at the symptoms of forgetting, since standard accuracy hides it. Across their evaluations, FedKPer improved the generalization-personalization trade-off without sacrificing retention, which they argue is the balance medical deployments actually need.
arxiv-2605-00898:
Athanasios Koukosias and three co-authors develop a deep learning model that predicts battery state, including remaining charge and life, for smart energy control. Good forecasts support safety in electric cars and large storage systems, and they feed checks of health over time. The authors aim to model wear trends and use trends at scale.

Their framework joins neural nets with large training sets for sharp forecasts of future results. The output helps guide upkeep and share energy well. The authors argue such modeling can advance green energy control, though the abstract gives the design and aims more than detailed hard results.
arxiv-2605-01098:
Alexander Warnecke and Konrad Rieck craft adversarial examples for image classifiers using tiny convolutional filters, rather than gradients or generative models. Inspired by explainable machine learning, their adversarial image filters build on classic edge detection algorithms but are optimized to deceive learning models. The resulting untargeted attacks are transferable and need only a single pass over the input image.

Even very small filters achieve success rates ranging widely across different neural networks, from about a third to most inputs. Compared with generative approaches, the method uses five orders of magnitude fewer parameters. Studying the learned filters reveals high transferability between models and structures shared with classic image filters, giving further insight into network fragility.
arxiv-2605-01698:
Sylvain Hellin and four co-authors query building information models by letting an agent explore instead of guessing the filing system. A BIM file holds a building's geometry, meaning, and wiring in structured form, but real projects file things so differently that fixed query templates break.

Adaptive exploration sends a language-model agent in with code tools: it runs small programs, reads what the model actually contains, and adapts its route on the fly. The team also release ifc-bench v2, an open question-answering benchmark of over a thousand tasks across dozens of models from many projects. A factorial test crosses two model strength levels with four helper strategies, and exploration beats static query writing in every cell. The lesson is architectural: heterogeneity this deep is beaten by a change of paradigm, not by polishing the old one.
arxiv-2605-01898:
Reza Rahimi Baghbadorani and Sergio Grammatico tackle dynamic games between vehicles that must cooperate in traffic. Their cases include platoons, where trucks or cars travel close together, and crossing at intersections. They model these as constrained linear-quadratic games and look for Nash equilibria, the points where no vehicle gains by changing its plan alone.

By restating the long-horizon problem as a receding-horizon inequality with special structure, the authors build Newton-type methods that converge very fast near a solution. In simulations, the methods beat first-order and operator-splitting rivals by a wide margin. Fast convergence matters here, because control decisions must run in real time on safety-critical systems.
arxiv-2605-02098:
Maximilian Kellner, Dominik Merkle, Michael Brunklaus, and Alexander Reiterer ask how best to cut huge 3D point clouds into pieces a neural network can process. Clouds can hold hundreds of millions of points, and even after thinning they must be split into subclouds. Standard spherical crops lose surrounding shape context.

The authors compare spherical crops with exponential, Gaussian, and linear methods that give larger crops for a similar point count. They test three network designs on indoor and outdoor data sets. Changing the crop strategy improved performance, with the largest gains on large outdoor scenes, where some results set new best marks. Code for the methods is released with the paper.
arxiv-2605-02298:
Balázs Maga studies how well a permuton, a limit object for large permutations, can be approximated by finite permutations under a rectangular discrepancy measure. He transfers bounds from discrepancy theory into this more restricted setting. The question is which permutons admit good finite approximations and which resist them, and at what rate.

Maga shows superlinear approximation can occur only for permutons supported on graphs of measure-preserving functions. The local regularity of that supporting function then obstructs how good an approximation can be. For the biased Brownian separable permuton, he proves a lower bound on approximation error. The argument uses the fact that its supporting function has Lipschitz points almost surely, a subtle regularity trait.
arxiv-2605-02398:
Rahul Kumar studies a failure mode in frontier AI models that safety tests for scheming may miss: cognitive collapse under adversarial pressure. Metacognition, knowing what one does not know, spotting errors, and asking for clarification, is vital in high-stakes decision pipelines. Kumar presents SCHEMA, an evaluation of eleven frontier models from eight vendors across more than sixty-seven thousand scored records, in six conditions.

Eight of eleven models showed catastrophic drops in metacognitive accuracy under pressure, by up to about thirty points. Through factorial isolation and a benign distraction control, the paper argues collapse is driven not by the content of survival threats but by structural compliance pressure. That compliance trap is the central finding.
arxiv-2605-02598:
Philip Moreira Tomei and Bouke Klein Teeselink measure which jobs AI could learn to do, across the whole United States economy. Older exposure scores compare job tasks with current AI skills. The authors argue that this misses jobs where present skill is low but learnability is high, and the reverse. Post-training by reinforcement learning, they note, is built around completing tasks, much like job task lists.

Guided by a rubric made with reinforcement learning experts and checked against real deployments, model annotators scored every task in a federal database for training feasibility. The scores form an occupation index. Some roles, such as power plant operators, score high on learnability but low on older exposure measures, while creative and interpersonal roles show the reverse pattern. Policy choices, the authors argue, should heed that split.
arxiv-2605-02898:
Ka Hei Carrie Lau and Enkelejda Kasneci review what shapes data quality when eye tracking is crowdsourced through ordinary webcams. Webcam tracking is cheap and scalable, and reaches wider groups than lab gear. Uncontrolled rooms and varied hardware, though, make quality uneven, and the field lacks shared benchmarks for judging it.

A scoping review covers crowdsourced eye-tracking work over more than a decade and confirms patchy reporting. A case study then examines AI fairness interviews run on a commercial platform, with just over two hundred participants. A ranked regression model on the platform's quality grade finds behavior and technical traits predict quality: more fixations and shorter sessions grade higher, as does operating system choice. Recommendations target reliability, transparency, and repeatability in future studies.
arxiv-2605-02998:
Michael C. H. Yeung and seventeen co-authors map the huge eROSITA bubbles in the western Galactic sky using all-sky X-ray data. Found in 2020, these bubbles are among the largest X-ray structures known, and their shape and hot gas reveal their origin.

Fitting spectra and a blast-wave shape model, they find two gas parts inside the western bubble, one hotter and one cooler with far more emitting material. The gas looks metal-poor, like halo gas, unlike the richer North Polar Spur, which argues against a shared origin. A cool shell around the northern bubble is also confirmed.
arxiv-2605-03598:
Jatin Sharma, Dan F. M. Goodman, and Danyal Akarca ask how recurrent neural networks carry out computation through their connections. In real neural systems, direct connections alone do not explain function, so the authors model a trained network as a graph. They break down the multi-hop pathways between input and output units by hop length.

That breakdown shows how the network routes information over time. It also exposes a flaw in standard L1 regularization, which penalizes single weights rather than the multi-hop pathways that do the work. Their resolvent-RNNs constrain those pathways directly, producing temporal sparsity that matches the task, better performance, and stronger alignment between sparsity and function than L1 achieves.
arxiv-2605-03698:
Aline Duarte, Dasha Loukianova, and Aurélien Velleret study parameter estimation in a large system of interacting neurons. The neurons communicate through spikes. In the mean-field regime, the number of neurons grows without bound. The authors ask how well a multidimensional parameter inside the spiking rate can be estimated from observations over a fixed time window.

They first prove local asymptotic normality, a property that lets classical theory deliver the best possible efficiency of the maximum likelihood estimator. Existing Ibragimov-Hasminskii theory seems limited to models without state resets at spike times. So the authors follow Höpfner's approach instead. They prove consistency, asymptotic normality, and local asymptotic minimax optimality in a general setting that includes neuron resets.
arxiv-2605-03998:
Richard J. Young and Alice M. Matthews audit gender bias in language model based emergency department triage, where an acuity score sets treatment priority and human assessment is already known to show gender disparities. Their EQUITRIAGE audit evaluates five models across hundreds of thousands of evaluations on MIMIC-IV-ED clinical vignettes, under four prompt strategies, with most originals paired to a gender-swapped counterfactual version.

All five models changed scores on gender swap more often than a pre-registered five percent threshold. Two showed directional female undertriage, two were near parity, and one was highly sensitive with weak male-direction asymmetry. One model's directional bias coexisted with a small calibration gap against real admissions, a dissociation the authors highlight. Demographic blinding sharply reduced one model's flip rate.
arxiv-2605-04198:
Alexander I. Khrabry and three co-authors look at how the shape of a neural network affects its skill at modelling moving gases, fluids, and plasmas. They focus on U-Net models, which shrink an image to capture large patterns and then expand it again for a forecast.

Width is often tuned in these models while depth stays fixed, so the authors test deeper designs made by stacking blocks. Their aim is a fair view of the trade-off between accuracy and computing cost as both width and depth change, rather than a comparison at one fixed size alone.
arxiv-2605-04398:
Efrén Morales-Amaya proves a characterisation of the ellipsoid among all convex bodies in projective space of dimension at least three. Characterisations matter because they give tests that single out one shape from all others using only stated geometric data.

His test uses two interior points and a fixed hyperplane outside the body's support. For every suitable lower-dimensional plane inside that hyperplane, a harmonic homology must swap the two slices of the body cut out through the two points. Morales-Amaya shows that if such a symmetry exists for all choices, the body cannot be anything but an ellipsoid, completing a clean if-and-only-if style description.
arxiv-2605-04598:
Madeline Berezowski, Artur Sowa, and Jonas Fransson solve the hopping dynamics of the two-site Bose-Hubbard model. This is the simplest version of a standard model for bosons in a lattice. It is used for cold atoms and superconducting circuits. With only two sites, the system splits into separate sectors, one for each possible particle number.

Using an inductive argument built on bosonic commutation rules, they find all eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the hopping term in each sector. Remarkably, within a sector the hopping operator is exactly a spin projection operator, giving a new route to its spectrum. Applying the square of that operator to coherent states, they show it generates Schrödinger cat states.
arxiv-2605-04698:
Jan Dolejš, Martin Jureček, and Róbert Lórencz investigate poisoning attacks against malware detection systems that continuously ingest new samples to retrain their models. An attacker who can slip crafted files into that stream may quietly weaken detection, a realistic threat given the volume of novel malware.

Working in a gray-box setting, they generate adversarial binaries that still function, using manipulations of the import table and injected sections. Subtle import-based changes produced compact poison samples that significantly degraded a gradient-boosted detector's recall. A homogeneous ensemble defence then identified and filtered most poisoning attempts while keeping nearly all legitimate data.
arxiv-2605-04798:
Karthik Gajulapalli and three co-authors revisit the Online Orthogonal Vectors problem, a basic question about searching binary vectors. A preprocessing step stores many vectors, then each query asks whether a new vector is orthogonal to any stored one, meaning they never share a one in the same position. Speed and storage trade off against each other.

The team designs a deterministic data structure that matches the best known randomized method in low dimensions and improves older results in moderate dimensions. Along the way they disprove a stated hardness conjecture. Under a standard complexity assumption, they also prove strong space lower bounds for fast queries, and both directions extend to several related search problems.
arxiv-2605-05298:
Jack Neustadt and nine co-authors dissect the layered gas motions inside extremely red quasars using spectra from the James Webb Space Telescope. These quasars are heavily dust-obscured, and their bright optical emission lines carry complex velocity structure. Modelling lets the team separate the lines into distinct kinematic components, implying gas arranged by velocity and density across several scales.

Supporting data show a deeply buried central source with a little unobscured light scattered into view. Ultraviolet lines are dominated by that scattered light, while optical lines mix scattered and obscured emission. The analysis focuses on one quasar whose features separate cleanly, making it a clear window into this stratified structure.
arxiv-2605-05598:
AI tutors that write essays for students can quietly erode the thinking the essay was meant to build. Ran Bi, Shiyao Wei, and Yuanyiyi Zhou present Prober.ai, a writing environment that refuses to generate text. It constrains a language model, through personas and structured output formats, to ask pointed questions about weak arguments instead.

Suggestions unlock only after the student reflects, a deliberate friction in the design. The approach draws on Toulmin's argumentation theory and research on questioning as feedback. A working prototype was built in thirty-six hours at a New York education hackathon, where it took second place.
arxiv-2605-06098:
Denis Neumüller and three co-authors recognize which algorithm a piece of code implements by searching its syntax tree. Knowing what concerns live in a code base helps maintenance and re-engineering work. A recognizer can also flag inefficient choices, such as bubble sort, and suggest better alternatives from a library.

Their prototype pairs a small domain specific language for describing an algorithm's key features with a matching algorithm over abstract syntax trees. Search patterns were written from reference implementations found by web search for each algorithm name. On a benchmark subset covering Fibonacci, bubble sort, and binary search, the system reached an average F1 score of 0.74. A large code language model scored 0.35, and clone detection tools trailed on recall as well.
arxiv-2605-06198:
Martin Willame and three co-authors estimate both the number of targets and their arrival directions from antenna array data. Choosing how many targets exist is a model order problem, usually settled by information criteria that balance fit against complexity. Applying those criteria directly needs costly maximum likelihood searches over all angle combinations for each candidate count, which is prohibitive in practice.

The authors fold information criteria into orthogonal least squares, a greedy method radar processing already uses for speed. They derive three combined algorithms, a disjoint rank based one, a joint selection based one, and a hybrid of both. Each comes in versions built on two standard criteria. In simulations the hybrid version consistently beat the other variants and a baseline method from the literature.
arxiv-2605-06298:
Roussel Desmond Nzoyem and Mauro Comi rethink world models by storing the state of a scene as neural network weights. Models trained on unlabeled video usually encode pixels into opaque latent spaces and lean on heavy decoders to rebuild frames, which is costly and hard to interpret. Their framework, NOVA, instead represents each state as the weights and biases of a small coordinate based network that renders the scene analytically.

Removing the decoder brings compactness, portability, and free super resolution, and the model runs at about forty million parameters on one consumer graphics card. Like other latent action models, it can be distilled into a video generator. Without extra losses, NOVA separates background, foreground, and motion on its own. Users can then edit content or dynamics independently, a step toward customizable virtual experience.
arxiv-2605-06398:
Ameet Gadekar studies the sum of radii clustering problem, which asks for k balls covering all points in a metric space while minimizing the sum of their radii. Despite much work on approximation and parameterized algorithms, its exact parameterized complexity and the chance of efficient schemes stayed open.

Gadekar shows the problem is W[2]-hard in k and rules out efficient parameterized approximation schemes unless a standard complexity collapse occurs. Stronger lower bounds follow from the Exponential Time Hypothesis. For mergeable constraints, covering fairness and diversity rules, a faster parameterized approximation improves the prior guarantee, with a better bound when an assignment subroutine is available.
arxiv-2605-06698:
Alois Schiessl presents a fixed point iteration for computing the arctangent, the inverse tangent function, built from sine and cosine evaluations. The iteration subtracts a finite sum of odd powers of a sine-cosine ratio from the current estimate. Starting close enough to the true value, the sequence converges to the arctangent with an order that the user can choose in advance by setting the number of sum terms.

Specifically, using P terms gives convergence order exactly two P plus one, so accuracy accelerates sharply with each added term. A computational test reported in the paper demonstrates the method's efficiency in practice. The work is a compact numerical recipe with a tunable speed guarantee.
arxiv-2605-06798:
Maria H. Visscher and eight co-authors separate surface from bulk electronic states in ruthenium dioxide, a material drawing interest for unusual electronic and magnetic behavior and closeness to superconductivity. Its strongly three-dimensional structure has muddied photoemission measurements, which mix signals from the surface and the interior. The team engineers targeted cleave planes with a focused ion beam to expose clean, chosen surfaces.

Comparing two surface orientations against density functional theory, they show the spectra are largely dominated by distinct surface states that vary with termination. Strong spin-orbit coupling in the surface region splits those bands in a Rashba-type pattern, an effect tied to broken inversion symmetry at the surface.
arxiv-2605-06898:
Luke J. O'Connor proposes letting a language model agent run its own orchestration program. In current systems, a fixed harness program controls what happens between turns. Under self-programmed execution, the model's own output is that program, and the harness only evaluates it, without imposing a fixed policy.

To make that work, O'Connor introduces Spell, a Lisp dialect whose programs can edit and rerun themselves without replaying side effects. Experiments use existing models that were never trained for the setup. Frontier models learned Spell from context and completed hard agent tasks, raising the question of what self-direction strategies a purpose-trained model might learn.
arxiv-2605-07098:
Mohamed Elrefaie and three co-authors release CarCrashNet, a large public dataset for learning-based car crash testing. Crash models are central to vehicle design, yet it involves nonlinear contact, large deformation, and material failure on detailed meshes. The dataset combines component tests and full-vehicle simulations in one mixed-format package.

It holds thousands of bumper-beam impact runs plus hundreds of full-vehicle crashes from three production models. The underlying open-source workflow was checked against lab tests and a commercial solver. A companion model, CrashSolver, is benchmarked against leading shape-based and neural solvers, as a shared base for crash research.
arxiv-2605-07198:
Yu Ichida studies traveling waves for a one-dimensional reaction-diffusion equation whose solutions can grow without bound. The equation has a reaction term that becomes linear far out, plus a saturation parameter. Ichida asks which wave speeds are possible, and what the smallest such speed looks like.

By compactifying the system, a technique that brings infinity into the picture, he classifies paths in the phase plane. The analysis proves positivity and unboundedness for front-like and sign-changing profiles, and gives an explicit form for the minimal speed. Unusually, that speed comes from behavior at infinity rather than from the standard linear rule used for such equations.
arxiv-2605-07398:
Zheyuan Gu and six co-authors defend deepfake video detectors against temporal attacks that exploit fragile frequency cues. Detectors score highly on standard tests yet can be evaded, because they overfit unstable spectral patterns instead of learning robust motion meaning. Their SpInShield framework is built to separate semantic motion from manipulable spectral artifacts.

A learnable spectral adversary invents severe deformations during training, simulating extreme attacks. A shortcut suppression strategy then forces the encoder to keep reliable forensic cues and purge unstable statistics. Experiments show competitive clean performance and a large margin over the strongest baseline under simulated amplitude spectral attacks.
arxiv-2605-07498:
Jiaming Cui models a hantavirus outbreak aboard a cruise ship to estimate how many infections symptom checks would miss. A discrete-time stochastic model tracks passengers and crew through susceptible, exposed, infectious, recovered, and dead states. Parameters and hidden disease states are inferred with an ensemble Kalman filter fitted to World Health Organization and European situation reports.

The estimated reproduction number sits well above one, indicating strong potential for sustained onboard spread before strict quarantine. Simulations suggest several exposed people stay unidentified early on, forming a hidden reservoir that symptom screening alone misses. Cui argues for rapid testing, targeted quarantine, and active monitoring in confined travel settings.
arxiv-2605-07598:
Ioannis Chatzis and three co-authors work on actionable recourse, the advice a model gives someone for changing an unfavorable decision, such as a loan refusal. Per-person advice is hard to audit for bias, so recourse summaries split the population into subgroups and assign one shared action to each. Good summaries must balance how well the actions work against what they cost people.

Their method, SOGAR, poses summary learning as optimal decision tree learning and computes the full Pareto front of the effectiveness-versus-cost trade-off. Users can then pick their preferred balance afterward, without retraining. Using shallow trees and sparse actions, SOGAR produced stable, low-cost summaries that beat existing approaches on both effectiveness and cost measures.
arxiv-2605-07798:
Johannes Piotrowski and four co-authors show that probing trapped particles with optical near-fields is inherently self-defeating. Nanophotonic structures confine light so tightly that its coupling to a trapped particle depends sharply on the particle's exact position. That position spread, in turn, depends on temperature. Probe light, it turns out, changes the very coupling it measures.

Working with cold atoms in a two-color dipole trap around an optical nanofiber, they watched the probe's scattering heat the atoms. The heating weakened the coupling and lost atoms, visible as a falling absorption signal. Cooling the atoms back restored the coupling strength. The findings matter wherever stable coupling between trapped particles and nanophotonic devices is required.
arxiv-2605-07898:
Manuel Martins and three co-authors propose a modal framework for logics that reason about information, where different information states may run on different logics. Their many-logic modal structures anchor each world's underlying logic to a common base lattice, with each logic's semantics living in a down-complete sublattice. Accessibility between worlds can then cross logical boundaries in a controlled way.

Such structures suit databases: information states are configurations of a database, and the relations describe how information evolves. The authors illustrate with the six-valued logic of evidence and truth and its four-, three-, and two-valued relatives sitting inside the same lattice, covering paracomplete, paraconsistent, and classical contexts within one system.
arxiv-2605-07998:
Mattia Vaccari builds a shared resource for extragalactic astronomy: merged spectroscopic redshift catalogs for fourteen of the most studied survey fields observed by the Spitzer space telescope. The set builds on the earlier Spitzer Data Fusion photometric database and gathers the public spectroscopic catalogs for each field into one place.

Entries are matched closely, each source gets a single best redshift, and source and overlap flags record where the value came from and whether sources coincide. The fusion is published on Zenodo and updated often as new spectroscopic surveys appear. It is meant as a reference resource for training photometric redshift methods, fitting spectral energy distributions, and cross-matching sources across wavelengths.
arxiv-2605-08098:
Milad Yazdani, Shahriar Shalileh, and Dena Shahriari automate the inverse design of kirigami, the cut-paper method for making shape-changing sheet materials. Finding a cut pattern that deploys into a target silhouette is hard because the motion is nonlinear and valid layouts must obey discrete rules without overlap.

Their RL-Kirigami framework pairs an optimal-transport flow matching generator with reinforcement learning. A marching decoder enforces global geometric compatibility for the parallelogram quad patterns, and group relative policy optimization rewards silhouette match, feasibility, and smoothness of the ratio field. On generated targets, one sample from the prior already beat solver baselines on silhouette overlap.
arxiv-2605-08198:
Farjana Yesmin presents FairHealth, an open-source Python library. It supports trustworthy medical machine learning in low-resource settings such as Bangladesh. The author argues that current toolkits miss four things at once. They lack fairness audits for biosignals and clinical tables. They lack private federated learning that fits normal workflows. They lack explainability tools for low-bandwidth clinics. And they lack coverage of Global South datasets.

FairHealth is built from five peer-reviewed studies. It ships six modules. They cover federated learning with homomorphic encryption and intersectional fairness metrics. They also cover a hybrid fuzzy-SHAP explainability tool. The library gives clinics in low-income countries one modular place to build fairer, more private health models.
arxiv-2605-08298:
Vasiliki Sideri-Lampretsa, Sophie Starck, Robbie Holland, Julian McGinnis, and coauthors study reusable neural signal encoders. Early layers of cohort-trained implicit neural representations can seed new signals. That speeds fitting and improves it. But nobody knew which layers transfer, or what they encode.

The team swept the freeze depth in SIREN and Fourier-feature networks. The best layer to freeze is the one with the highest weight stable rank. Freezing there matches or beats standard fine-tuning. The team then applied sparse autoencoders to encoder activations. That is the first such decomposition for these models. The results tell practitioners where to cut an encoder for reuse.
arxiv-2605-08398:
Rania Briq, Michael Kamp, Ohad Fried, Sarel Cohen, and coauthors document a useful stubbornness in latent flow matching image models. Shrink the training data or the model itself and, under the same noise seed, the outputs barely move. The authors argue this stability is built into the flow matching objective rather than being an accident of one setup.

They exploit it twice. Training on much smaller datasets preserved quality and, under tight compute budgets, converged faster with less annotation effort for conditional models. Stability under architectural shrinking likewise supports cheaper inference variants. The study turns an observed quirk into practical savings for training and serving generative models.
arxiv-2605-08498:
Viresh Pati and six coauthors build MathConstraint, a test of step by step reasoning built from constraint problems with solver checked answers. Fixed tests grow stale as models improve, and judging by model opinion is weak. Their generator makes fresh problems at rising difficulty, each one verified by trusted solving software rather than by another model.

Two released sets show a steep drop from easy to hard problems for twelve leading models. Giving models solver tools roughly doubles hard set accuracy, though halving the tool budget erases much of that gain. Test makers gain a durable way to measure reasoning and tool use as models keep improving.
arxiv-2605-08598: Houari Benammar Ammar studies fiber spaces in algebra over threefold bases. He tracks how their Kodaira dimension acts. This dimension tracks the growth of key sections of a space. It is a basic tag for sorting such spaces. Ammar proves some cases of the Iitaka claim in this setting. One case has a Calabi-Yau threefold as base. The work moves a long program that tries to say how dimensions add up over a fiber map.
arxiv-2605-08798:
Giorgio Di Russo and Donato Bini work out the wave form from a mass that falls straight into a Schwarzschild black hole. Their math is the most exact of its kind in print. It reaches three and a half post-Newton steps. Both the firm part of the two body dance and the drag from waves are in it. The wave form shows those same acts. All is set in the center of mass frame.

A straight fall looks like a one line move. It must still end with the hole taking the mass in. There, strong field acts rule past what this math can reach. The team is clear on that edge. Wave work gains fine fall wave forms, plus a look at a bound case of two body acts.
arxiv-2605-09498:
Chen and two colleagues propose Spectral Transformer Neural Processes, a frequency aware take on Transformer Neural Processes. Neural processes turn a context set into a forecast process, suiting time series, spatial data, and images. But strong repeat patterns and near repeat patterns break past methods. Those methods underfit and fail past the training range. The flaw lies in how context is joined: time based vectors do not show frequency form, so far apart yet phase matched points stay hard to link.

Their Spectral Aggregator gauges a context spectrum, packs it into a spectral mix, and draws task tuned spectral traits to join time based vectors. That adds a spectral mix kernel bias, reshaping closeness so far points can stay near on a periodic shape. Tests on made up regression, real time series, and images show steady gains over past methods, moving neural processes toward modeling of repeat patterns.
arxiv-2605-09698:
Stoisser and four colleagues built a test for a quiet failure mode in data-science AI agents: committing to the wrong task without noticing. Ambig-DS pairs each fully specified task with an ambiguous twin, one suite of 51 tasks about unclear prediction targets and one of 61 about unclear scoring goals. Each variant was checked to admit several plausible readings with real consequences for the answer.

Across five agents, failures were silent commitments, wrong targets or wrong scoring choices, rather than crashes. Letting an agent ask one clarifying question recovered much of the loss under ideal conditions. Yet agents could not judge when to ask: loose prompts made them over-ask on clear tasks, while strict prompts made them silently guess on ambiguous ones. Spotting underspecification, not running code, is the missing skill.
arxiv-2605-09798:
Attwa and four colleagues give a short proof of a density rule for graphs, the dot-and-line diagrams mathematicians use to model networks. Chen and Ma posed the question: how dense must a large graph be before it must hold two vertices of equal degree joined by a path of fixed length? Equal degree here means the same number of lines meeting at each dot.

Their answer is a density of about one half: any large graph with at least that share of possible edges must contain such a pair. The bound cannot be improved for paths of odd length, so it is tight there. The proof is short and asymptotic. It holds once the graph is large enough, and it sharpens earlier work on paths of length three.
arxiv-2605-10198:
Novello and Tonello propose SPACE, a method for erasing concepts from text-to-image diffusion models without retraining. Erasure matters for avoiding copyrighted and explicit content, and closed-form methods offer a quick alternative to backpropagation-based techniques. But closed-form erasure weakens when scaling from smaller models like Stable Diffusion 1.5 to larger ones like Stable Diffusion XL. SPACE, short for sparse cross-attention-based concept erasure, restores effectiveness at larger scale.

The method iteratively modifies cross-attention parameters with a closed-form update that jointly creates sparsity and erases target concepts. Concentrating the concept mapping into a lower-dimensional subspace beats dense baselines on erasure efficacy and robustness against adversarial prompts. SPACE also reaches eighty to ninety percent cross-attention sparsity, cutting storage for modified parameters by seventy percent, a memory efficiency win alongside the safety gain. The paper warns that it contains model outputs that may offend.
arxiv-2605-10298:
Yuchen Bai and six colleagues reframe wildfire forecasting as a hunt for discrete events rather than a regional risk map. Existing machine-learning models predict fire probability on kilometre-scale daily grids, useful for warnings but silent on where individual fires will actually ignite. Their 2026 paper presents WISP, the Wildfire Ignition Set Predictor, for next-day active fires.

From 48 hours of weather, satellite vegetation, land, and fire-history data, WISP predicts a ranked set of future fire-cluster centers on a 375-metre grid across global regions. It trains end to end with Hungarian matching, a method for pairing predictions to true events, plus asymmetric weighting to handle the classification score's conflicting roles. On held-out global test data the best variant reached 38.2 percent average precision, covered 53.4 percent of fire-cluster mass weighted by radiative power, and localized 54.1 percent of clusters within 5 kilometres.
arxiv-2605-10498:
Heegeon Yoon and Heeyoung Kim tackle two hard problems at once: long-tail recognition and multi-modal fusion. Long-tail distributions in class-imbalanced data challenge deep learning models, which tend to favor majority classes. Recent long-tail methods mitigate this issue but are largely restricted to single-modal inputs, missing complementary information from diverse sources. Their 2026 paper introduces a framework that explicitly handles multi-modal inputs.

The approach carries multi-expert architectures into the multi-modal setting, fusing varied data into one representation. Modality-specific networks estimate each modality's value, and value weights steer fusion so more informative modalities contribute more strongly. Specialized training and test procedures handle diverse modality mixes, including images and tabular data. Experiments on benchmark and real-world datasets show the approach integrates multi-modal information and outperforms existing methods on long-tail, class-imbalanced cases.
arxiv-2605-10698:
Dahlia Shehata and Ming Li show a machine bystander effect in multi-agent language-model thought, where fake group push brings strong mental loafing. Team systems are thought to lift thought by group work, but the authors test this claim on 22,500 fixed runs across three data sets and three top models. They audit inner thought traces against outer outputs for sense. They pin down the Interaction Depth Limit, the exact point where one agent's logic gives way to group assent.

Key to the work is a Sovereignty Gap: models often work out the right proof inside yet falsely assent, bending facts to please a fake swarm. Group load shifts with order: the lead anchor auditor's brand name steers swarm truth far more than its share. The results show weak spots in how teams are built, since loose team shapes can sap lone thought, not lift it.
arxiv-2605-10798:
Pavel Kurasov, Vladislav Shubin, and Axel Tibbling show that Hamiltonians with real-valued eigenfunctions may hold a non-trivial shape Berry phase, settling a query on topology shift. Set vertex rules, unbroken value and Kirchhoff rules on first slopes, are fixed by the metric graph and allow no topology shift. But richer self-adjoint vertex rules allow sets that show unlike topologies on the same edges.

The authors weigh a cycle set of metric graphs that show a non-trivial shape phase of pi, though all eigenfunctions can be picked real-valued. Scaled eigenfunctions are flipped by minus one after one cycle when the set gets back to its first state. Their model looks like a figure-eight graph whose mid vertex joins four ends, with vertex rules that hinge on one cycle trait.
arxiv-2605-10898:
Haidan Liu and five colleagues study how artists and hobbyists learn generative image tools, and why structured guidance often loses to self-experimentation. Interviews with eight creatives and a survey of 159 more show most people explore on their own or follow tutorials, while tripping over confusing AI terminology.

A follow-up probe with 17 creatives found that even those who called structured guidance helpful still preferred experimenting freely, fearing guidance would fence in their creativity. The central tension is clear: support must teach the tools without curbing artistic autonomy. Tool designers get evidence that guidance should stay optional, skippable, and tuned to creative freedom.
arxiv-2605-10998:
Sangyeon Yoon and four colleagues expose a hard-to-audit jailbreak that uses only ten harmless preference pairs in Direct Preference Optimization fine-tuning. Fine-tuning APIs let users customize frontier models, but benign-looking tuning can already weaken safety refusals, and preference-based tuning has drawn less scrutiny.

Each pair pairs a benign prompt with a normal helpful answer as preferred and a refusal as dispreferred, mimicking a legitimate user curbing over-refusal. Yet because DPO directly teaches the model to prefer helpfulness over refusal, refusal collapses broadly and transfers to harmful prompts outside the data. Attack success reaches about 59 to 70 percent across OpenAI models tested. Safety teams learn that preference tuning needs auditing even when every example looks innocent.
arxiv-2605-11498: Daza-Salgado and two others derive the first finite formula for switching between Ince-Gaussian bases of other ellipticity. These modes solve the paraxial wave law and bridge two Gaussian mode groups as it varies. Each fixed value gives an orthogonal basis, but different values give bases that are not orthogonal, and no explicit switch had been known. Their formula maps straight between non-orthogonal shaped-light forms. A test with spatial light devices shows ellipticity-resolved mode splits, making it a knob for mode switching and coding.
arxiv-2605-11598: Panja and four others present EpiCastBench, sets and benchmarks for multi-factor outbreak outlooks. Data-driven public health choices have made outbreak outlooks key, and multi-factor models capture time patterns better than single-series models treating series. Yet robust methods suffer from scarce high-quality benchmarks across illnesses and regions. EpiCastBench offers 40 curated linked multi-factor outbreak sets spanning many illnesses, with unified spans, prep, metrics and tests. It tests 15 models from stats floors to deep learning and base models, with all sets and code public.
arxiv-2605-11698: Yanagisawa and five others analyze 11 ALMA epochs on flux variability of Sgr A* at 340 GHz. In one epoch the light curve shows two short components near 30 and 50 minutes. Though strong under white noise, the peaks fall below 3 sigma under red noise, so the authors claim no significant periodic detections. Still, timescales match the orbital period near the innermost stable orbit, and phase structure fits orbital modulation. A model of multiple orbiting hotspots with decaying emission fits the variability well, suggesting periodic and non-periodic variability share an orbiting origin.
arxiv-2605-11798: Moritz Laupichler and four colleagues present Mt-KaRRi, a dispatcher for dynamic ride-pooling. It processes millions of travelers per hour. Built on state-of-the-art shortest-path algorithms with a simple mode choice model, it answers each request in about 1 millisecond even on the largest instances. Tests with realistic demand in three cities show how ride quality and vehicle use evolve for tens of thousands of vehicles. The tool opens ride-pooling studies at unprecedented scale.
arxiv-2605-11898: Daniil Dushenev and four colleagues fight uneven classes in image tasks with synthetic data from diffusion models. Fine-tuning a LoRA adapter on just 20 to 50 real images of a rare class, their method makes fake training samples and tests only on held-out real images. Across chest X-ray disease and factory crack spotting, fake-sample training raised rare-class recall and F1, with gains tapering off as the fake share grew.
arxiv-2605-12098: Rui-Nan Li and five colleagues find a repeating shift in the core pitch of fast radio burst FRB 20240114A. Using over one thousand bursts from a very wide band system, they find the core pitch rises and falls on a cycle near 112 days. The signal is strong, past 6 sigma, by two separate checks. Inside each cycle the pitch moves step by step from low to high. Two ideas may explain it: light being soaked up in a binary star pair, or a slow wobble of the source itself.
arxiv-2605-12298: Alvaro Bermejillo-Seco and five colleagues observe magnon-photon hybridization in thin flakes of Cr2Ge2Te6, a van der Waals magnet, down to 30 nanometers thick. Hybrid magnon-photon coupling in radio waves matters for joining waves to superconducting circuits, but thin van der Waals flakes challenge it with small volume and higher loss. The magnon hybrids appear as steady avoided crossings in six devices, using a low-drag cavity design. Coupling strength follows the known square-root thickness scaling, and trend suggests one-layer hybrids are within reach.
arxiv-2605-12398: Mozafari, Piryani and Jatowt estimate how hard a question is for a language model by how evenly plausible its candidate answers look. Their Q-DAPS method scores each candidate's plausibility and takes the entropy of those scores, so questions with many tempting answers rank as harder. Tested on TriviaQA, Natural Questions, MuSiQue and QASC, it beats readability, retrieval and popularity baselines. It also proves robust across settings and model sizes, and human judges agree strongly with its difficulty rankings.
arxiv-2605-12598: The Pierre Auger Collaboration reports seventeen years of air-shower depth measurements from the observatory's fluorescence detector. The set spans primary energies from ten to the power 17.7 electronvolts to beyond ten to the power 19.6, with exposure two and four tenths times larger than the prior analysis. Mean shower maximum shows a sharp break near ten to the power 18.4, giving model-free evidence for a change in mass composition evolution. Falling fluctuations with energy point to heavier, less diverse primaries, with no significant sky-direction dependence.
arxiv-2605-12898: Kilaru and five colleagues ask when language models build social networks that look real. Using 50 made-up personas, they make 192 networks across cultures, prompt languages, model sizes and prompt styles. They find culture shifts homophily, the pull toward similar people, political leaning rules most link formation, and prompt language alone sharply shifts religion-based grouping. Made networks match real graphs on clustering better than standard baselines, yet carry stronger demographic biases.
arxiv-2605-12998: Sun, Zhang, Ni and Song revisit continual graph learning without task boundaries, since real data streams drift continuously and task identity is often unknown. They model the stream as a time-varying mixture of latent task distributions and build DRIFT, a benchmark spanning hard task switches to smooth drift via a Gaussian parameterisation. Representative methods degrade substantially under this task-free setting, suggesting many rely implicitly on task-boundary information.
arxiv-2605-13098: Park, Lim and Ko quantify how city blockages affect signal reach in combined satellite-ground networks for 6G. Using a stochastic geometry setup with a Boolean blockage model, they derive downlink reach odds. Blockages cut both ways: they weaken wanted signals but also shield against pooled interference. The study shows joining space and ground nets lifts reach across settings from open areas to dense urban zones. It gives a resilient and tractable route to staying connected under varied blockage.
arxiv-2605-13298: Biselli, Marinucci, D'Amico and Pietroni derive the first MCMC limits for the large scale structure bootstrap, a model free way to test gravity beyond standard cosmology. They jointly analyse galaxy power spectra and bispectra from BOSS data and large simulations, tracking growth rate and a second order kernel shift. BOSS yields about 7 percent limits on growth and 57 percent on the kernel term, while the larger volume tightens both sharply. The pair separates background expansion effects from nonlinear growth effects.
arxiv-2605-13498: Alex Biondi and four colleagues test whether classifiers trained only on gamma-ray data can reject alpha events in germanium detectors. Dedicated alpha training data is scarce, yet alphas still add background. The team studies a multilayer perceptron and a projective likelihood classifier on a detector exposed to polonium sources. Both methods separate single-site from multi-site gamma events while cutting alphas, and the perceptron performs best. Its signal survival exceeds 80 percent and background survival falls below 20 percent, with alpha rejection above 2.71 times ten to the fourth.
arxiv-2605-13698: Ray Feingold and Chansu Yu test post-quantum crypto methods for MQTT-based IoT networks using three Pis. Common TLS codes guarding MQTT are open to quantum attacks via Shor's algorithm, risking long-term safety. The report adds the FALCON digital signature scheme, a NIST-picked post-quantum signing method, to maintain message realness and safety across constrained MQTT clients and brokers. Testing system speed, the research maps real trade-offs of lattice-based post-quantum crypto on small hardware.
arxiv-2605-13998: Sun, Jin, Zhang and Varner build a tool that prices American options on mock stock paths, giving each option an IV for each date. A lone stock-return model gives no such number. Parametric and neural IV surfaces, fit to vendor quotes for 31 tickers, guess IV from moneyness and time left. Stock paths trace a jump hidden Markov model with capped daily gains. Each day, each option's implied variance creeps toward its surface guess in Heston form, and a binomial tree turns IV into prices and sensitivities.
arxiv-2605-14198: Di Cairano and Franzosi take a microcanonical approach to criticality in the mean-field phi-four model. Joint critical behavior is tied to thermodynamic breaks and divergences that appear only in the infinite limit. The paper argues instead that criticality is a structural trait, a rework of interactions among parts that exists at finite size and turns sharp only in the end. Entropy derivatives encode that structure in extremal and inflection shapes, and inflection-point analysis turns those shapes into a unique critical marker and a clear critical trajectory.
arxiv-2605-14398: Hongyu Wang and colleagues present ChronoAgentic, a multi-agent framework building world models as executable simulation code instead of video. A plan agent turns prompts into inspectable scene plans. A code agent writes it as a PyChrono program, and other agents test and repair the result. On 80 PhyWorldBench demos, the system meets the full correctness test, semantic fit plus physical correctness, on 82.5 percent of demos. That beats 52.5 percent for the strongest of ten text-to-video models. The loop also drives a live ROS environment in a generated city.
arxiv-2605-14498: Yang and colleagues, in 2026, present GroupMemBench, a benchmark for agent memory in multi-party chats. Older memory systems and benchmarks assume single-user setups, yet real deployments span groups. Three group-memory traits are untested: group dynamics, belief tracking, and audience-adapted language. GroupMemBench exposes all three through a synthesis setup and an adversarial query setup across six kinds. Tests of leading memory systems expose a sharp collapse: the strongest reaches only 46.0 percent average accuracy. Current memory intake erases the structural and lexical features group memory depends on.
arxiv-2605-14698: Kontras and team introduce NeuroAtlas, the largest EEG benchmark yet. It holds forty-two data sets and two hundred and sixty thousand hours spanning clinical EEG and brain-computer interfaces. EEG-specific foundation models are tested against supervised baselines and generic time-series models, with bespoke clinical metrics per task. Two headline findings are reported. First, EEG-specific models do not consistently beat generic time-series models. Second, standard machine learning metrics miss clinical utility, with rankings varying within domains.
arxiv-2605-14898: Safi and team present a method for making 2D and 3D polycrystalline structures using symmetrized hyperspherical harmonics. Structure links need typical inputs for full-field sims, but building from limited 2D data is hard. Unit quaternions plus these waves give a smooth symmetry code for crystal angles, dodging Euler-based singular points. Rebuilds combine two-point links, a hybrid three-point variogram, and a mean spread penalty, getting shapes and crystal spread for metal.
arxiv-2605-14998: Milton L. Montero and three colleagues study how much of development's information sits in starting patterns rather than in self-organization itself. Their model pairs a neural cellular automaton, which grows patterns from local rules, with a learned coordinate-based pre-pattern generator, trained together. Information-theoretic analysis tracks how information splits between pre-pattern and process. Joint learning, they report, improves robustness, encoding capacity, and symmetry handling over learning either part alone.
arxiv-2605-15398: Nicole Meng and three others defend 3D editing pipelines against unsafe generation with 3DEditSafe. Text-guided 3D Gaussian Splatting editors can spread unsafe prompts across views into consistent not-safe-for-work content in the final 3D representation. The framework joins making-stage safety guidance with drawn-view 3D safety regularization, safe semantic projection, residue blocking, and mask-aware preservation to steer tuning away from unsafe ways. It cuts unsafe fit and attack success, showing a safety-quality tradeoff where stronger blocking adds flaws.
arxiv-2605-15698: Srinivas Ravishankar, Ishayu Ghosh, Nora Zajzon, Teng Fei, and Virginia de Sa propose handwriting decoding as a hard motor task for EEG foundation models. Past motor-imagery tasks sort coarse imagined limb moves. Some past data sets are confounded, so the team offers a stricter test set. On it, current foundation models lose to smaller task-specific models. Movement-onset knowledge drives past scores: means fall from 41.3 percent to 32.4 percent without it. Better test-time signal lifts the best subject from 45 percent to 78 percent, beating gains from more training data.
arxiv-2605-16098: Sun and six colleagues present PCDM, a diffusion-based data poisoning attack on federated learning.
