Poison data made by GANs can give itself away through outputs that look too alike. Their model uses a tunable poison vector for fine control and a jumping diffusion trick for light, fast generation. Across four open data sets plus a wireless set, it hid odd patterns better than rivals while harming the shared model more.
arxiv-2605-16198: Alamdari, Klassen, and McIlraith examine how formal methods can audit and monitor new AI systems for compliance across the build cycle. They combine formal methods with machine learning to check time-spanning rules, such as safety rules and laws, against black-box systems. Their tools cover offline audits, online runtime watching, and intervening watchers that preempt predicted breaches. Even small-model judges matched or beat frontier language-model judges at spotting breaches, while predictive watchers cut breach rates with task results largely intact.
arxiv-2605-16398: Papamichalis and Ruane build their filter around a failure: a filter giving a workable contact change zero chance can drop the path the robot is on for good. Their VHYDRO guards that loss by blending its learned guess with a workable transition rule per step. That blend precedes sampling and weighting, so every transition its model carrier keeps stays covered. From that cover, the filter tracks a continuous hidden state and a discrete contact mode. It fits a sparse port-Hamiltonian rule to each regime it finds.
arxiv-2605-16498: Nagarajan, El-Badry, and Sanghi search for tertiaries to compact binaries with near-infrared imaging of five binaries, Gaia BH1, and twelve Gaia stars. They detect several faint stars unseen in survey imaging, but none rule out matches. Reference star differential imaging models each target's point-spread function. Tertiary candidates appear, but injection-recovery tests suggest most are likely artifacts. Contrast curves limit main sequence and white dwarf temperature. They rule out main sequence and young white dwarf tertiaries above 500 au for Gaia binaries and 2000 au for distant LMXBs.
arxiv-2605-16598: Jenkins, Vinayak and Hu present GRASP, an agent system for questions that need several linked facts. It breaks a hard question into planned steps, scales up sub-agents with difficulty, and searches a three-layer graph of entities, claims, and passages. On three multi-hop benchmarks it tops accuracy in open retrieval while using far fewer tokens than rival systems, and it also leads in an extended-context setting.
arxiv-2605-16698: Ng and colleagues build a model for how cosmic rays move through magnetized molecular clouds and their dense parts. They compare straight-line motion, diffusion, and a mix with a diffusive outer layer and a near-straight core, predicting gamma-ray, ionization, and hard X-ray signals. Applied to the Taurus cloud complex, the model finds scattering much stronger on clump scales, with diffusion below standard interstellar values. The result ties cosmic rays more closely to dense gas and predicts hard X-ray emission that near-future telescopes may detect.
arxiv-2605-17098: Eldadi and Loeb test whether old Pluto brightness records can tell reflected sunlight from self-powered glow. Of twenty-two Pluto data bins, none recovers the expected reflected-light slope when each instrument and color band is kept apart. They then screen over eight thousand bins for distant icy bodies. Twenty-four look self-lit, yet all come from one survey, which points to a calibration quirk rather than a true glow.
arxiv-2605-17298: Kim links holomorphic disks bounded by a group-invariant Lagrangian submanifold with those bounded by its quotient in the GIT quotient space. Under positivity and topological assumptions he derives a workable formula for the quotient's disk potential from the original's, via the semistable disk potential tied to a moment-map level set. The correspondence bridges disk counts before and after quotienting.
arxiv-2605-17398: Joseph presents MiniGPT, a compact from-scratch rebuild of GPT-style autoregressive language modeling using PyTorch, written independently in a single notebook after studying nanoGPT. It implements embeddings, causal multi-head attention, pre-LayerNorm blocks, residual links, feed-forward layers and teacher-forced training. On Tiny Shakespeare, a small baseline with under a million parameters reaches validation loss near 1.72 after 3000 training rounds. A stronger version with nearly eleven million parameters reaches about 1.48 and writes text with clear Shakespeare-style dialogue structure.
arxiv-2605-17698: Seth Karten, Cameron Crow, and Chi Jin ask what happens when language-model agents trade on their own. Their Agent Bazaar is a simulation that tests whether such agents keep markets stable and honest. Two staged breakdowns anchor the work. Firms drive prices until a market collapses, while one cheat runs many fake seller accounts that flood buyers with fraud. Tested models mostly fail to police themselves, though a trained 9-billion-parameter model and two proposed safeguards improve matters.
arxiv-2605-17898: Yu-Hsueh Fang presents LightGP, a standalone C++17 library for Gaussian process regression with Python bindings. Python GP libraries built on deep learning frameworks carry heavy dependencies. LightGP supports Apple Metal and NVIDIA CUDA backends plus tuned CPU paths, with four routes: exact Cholesky, matrix-free conjugate gradients, sparse variational free energy, and structured kernel interpolation with FFT. It covers problems from 100 to 500,000 points. On an Apple M4, LightGP CPU runs 2.6 to 8.7 times faster than GPyTorch CPU for exact GP, and its CUDA build is faster to 2,048.
arxiv-2605-18098: P. V. Sreenivasa Reddy and Guang-Yu Guo study six-sided HfRuAs by solving varied Migdal-Eliashberg rules from electron structure, phonon, and coupling inputs alone. The Eliashberg function shows strong electron-lattice coupling near 1.56, led by low-pitch modes from Hf and Ru shakes. The state has a single varied gap of s-wave shape, set near 2.9 meV with a spread near 0.8 meV. The gap ratio near 4.2 beats the BCS weak-coupling limit, marking HfRuAs as strongly coupled, with Tc matching tests in order of size.
arxiv-2605-18698: Zhicheng Liu, Jason Li, and Greg Briskin outline, in a 2026 paper, a vision for Contextualized Dynamic Explanations, or CODEX, an agentic way to present data. Asynchronous accounts often fail when content and format ignore the audience, with little room for active engagement. CODEX builds custom multi-modal interfaces on the fly, guided by a changing audience model and a set communication intent. The premise: speakers cannot foresee every interactive scenario with their audience. Open tasks include agents that track talk progress, decide with context, and craft good representations.
arxiv-2605-18798: Taiki Miyagawa and Akinori F. Ebihara give flexible estimators for quickest changepoint detection under short, uneven sequences. Average run length and detection delay guide theory and tests, yet real data rarely offer the long regular runs those criteria assume. Their KM-ARL and KM-ADD borrow survival analysis to model alarm chances under truncation. They prove bias bounds and stay unbiased unless extrapolation is needed, and tests on simulated and real data show sturdier estimates.
arxiv-2605-18898: Tiexin Ding uses the two-parameter Weibull distribution as a measuring stick for transformer weights. At initialization, Gaussian weights give a shape value near 1.20, an anchor for reading later shifts. Across twelve models from seven families, feed-forward modules and attention output projections stay near that anchor. Attention input projections drift away instead, with drift shaped by how query and key weights are stored. The scale parameter grows through training with the learning-rate schedule, so shape marks class and scale marks progress.
arxiv-2605-18998: Sokolovskii, Humphries, Blumberger and Groenhof study how strong light-matter coupling changes exciton-exciton annihilation in disordered molecular systems. With poor exciton mobility, coupling to a shared cavity mode spreads excitons and raises links, lifting the annihilation rate. In high-mobility systems, where excitons already interact strongly, the rate can fall below bare molecules because photon leakage opens a competing decay channel. In the weak-coupling regime the same leakage suppresses this loss regardless of transport traits. Their simulations resolve mixed experiments and guide efforts toward polariton Bose-Einstein condensation.
arxiv-2605-19298: Cassandra Hopkin, Victor Albert, and Dominic Williamson unify a large family of translation-symmetric quantum error-correcting codes. Fracton codes in three or more dimensions lacked one shared picture, while newer long-range codes in two dimensions performed strikingly at small sizes. Their balanced-product construction starts from a higher-dimensional fracton parent, and different ways of compactifying it yield many descendant codes, including all bivariate bicycle codes. The same parent also extends known code-parameter bounds, and the authors conjecture that parent limits cap descendant gates and energy barriers.
arxiv-2605-19398: Jeon and colleagues diagnose why image-to-video models often produce near-still clips. Non-reference frames pay too much self-attention to reference-frame keys, flooding later frames with the still image and choking motion. Their DyMoS method rebalances that attention path during early denoising steps, with one scalar dialing motion strength up or down. It needs no extra training, leaves image and weights untouched, and across several leading backbones it boosts motion while preserving look and likeness.
arxiv-2605-19998: Nicolas Vidal-Silva and Alejandro Leon study how elliptical magnon orbits affect spin and heat flow in easy-plane ferromagnets. Starting from the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation with perpendicular anisotropy, they derive magnon dispersion and spin, then apply Boltzmann transport theory to obtain spin and thermal conductivities. Ellipticity raises or lowers spin transport depending on the axis type, while heat transport is enhanced for both easy- and hard-axis systems.
arxiv-2605-20098: Gabriel Freedman and six co-workers build a neurosymbolic system for claim checking that allows uncertain verdicts. When evidence is incomplete or conflicting, a ternary true, false or uncertain answer may beat a binary one, and faithful explanations matter. Their argument system used at run time trains language models to make arguments and score their own strength, then computes verdicts from those scored arguments by formal rules. Because verdicts derive by rule from explicit argument structures, they stay faithful by construction rather than resting on post-hoc reasoning traces.
arxiv-2605-20398: Maduro and seven co-workers use optical activity in rubidium vapor to make spatio-spectral vector light. Pumping with circularly polarized light magnetizes the vapor, giving dichroism and birefringence that vary with frequency. A vortex probe beam whose polarization varies in space maps that effect onto the light's shape. Reading brightness in one polarization slice then turns frequency shifts into image rotations, with a rotation slope near 98 milliradians per MHz on resonance.
arxiv-2605-20698: Fuxiang Xu and fifteen colleagues survey carbon monoxide and atomic carbon lines in quasars beyond redshift six. Such quasars track the first supermassive black holes and intense star formation at cosmic dawn. Using ALMA Band 3, they detect CO(7-6) in 15 of 18 sources, atomic carbon in 6 of 18, and dust continuum in 13 of 18. Line and continuum data feed molecular gas mass estimates, cross-checked across four tracers with a hierarchical Bayesian method.
arxiv-2605-20898: Hyunwoo Lee, Jeongyeol Kwon, and Dohyun Kwon study continuous-time analysis for minimax and bilevel problems via single-loop gradient-flow dynamics. In nested optimization, the outer variable shifts while auxiliary variables follow the inner solution map. While existing analyses usually rely on problem-specific Lyapunov constructions, the authors propose the first single Lyapunov template for continuous-time analysis. That template covers minimax, single via a raised penalty formulation, and min-min-max, with a modular proof from reusable lemmas.
arxiv-2605-21198: Chen Su and colleagues present SURGE, a benchmark for social media sentiment time series built around public events. Existing sets cover few events in one category and drop the interaction structure between posts. SURGE pairs event-level time series with aligned text and interaction links, built by an automated pipeline at three time granularities. It covers sixty-seven events and over eight hundred thousand posts across five categories, enabling controlled study of how interactions shape collective dynamics.
arxiv-2605-21498: Yash Madhwal and co-authors uncover how nonce collisions in ECDSA compromise Polygon MEV searchers. ECDSA signatures underpin blockchain transaction authentication, yet security critically depends on proper nonce generation. Analyzing on-chain data, they find searchers, driven by sub-second response needs in sealed-bid auctions, use predictable nonce patterns. These patterns create linear links between signatures, letting passive attackers derive private keys with elementary algebra. They provide a compact linear-system account of such attacks, including cross-wallet nonce collisions, with concrete evidence of exploitable patterns on Polygon.
arxiv-2605-21898: Adam Wills and co-authors study code concatenation over high-rate quantum low-density parity-check codes, a way to ease the trade-offs between overhead, error suppression, and hardware connectivity. An outer code borrows non-local connectivity from an inner code's logical operations instead of from hardware directly. Prior work cut memory overhead mainly for local low-rate inner codes like the surface code. Here the concatenated gross code enters the teraquop regime, which it could not reach before, with lower space overhead than the 288-qubit two-gross code.
arxiv-2605-21998: Yu Wang, Dan Li, and Huiqiu Lin characterize graphs that maximize spectral radius among minimally (k,k)-edge-connected graphs. For l above 1, l-edge-connectivity is the smallest number of edges whose removal leaves at least l components. Minimal (k,l)-edge-connectivity means that count is at least k but drops below k after any single edge removal. Building on Hennayake, Lai, Li, and Mao, the authors combine edge-switching with a double eigenvector method. Their results generalize the k equals 2 cases of Lou, Min, Huang, Chen, Guo.
arxiv-2605-22298: He and colleagues build a mid-infrared ghost imaging system that uses two-photon absorption. A coded near-infrared pump stamps a pattern onto a mid-infrared signal at a silicon detector. No extra nonlinear crystals are needed, so coding and sensing happen in one step. The rebuilt wave forms beat the detector speed limit by over forty times. Sensitivity reaches 0.05 picojoules per pulse. Compressed sensing cuts the needed measurements by 80 percent. The system works from 2.5 to 3.8 micrometres at room temperature.
arxiv-2605-22398: Nayak, Vemparala and Chaudhuri study soft ring assemblies squeezed cold past the jamming point. Further squeezing buckles the rings, softening the material on large scales. Under repeated squeezing, uniform rings anneal toward a reversible path through an ordered state. Mixed-size rings instead settle into stable, hysteretic limit cycles. Those cycles store a robust memory of training history, kept even under later overdriving. Large-scale hysteresis traces to lopsided microscale deformations with the contact network mostly intact. Particle softness thus governs organisation and memory in jammed soft matter.
arxiv-2605-22498: Sheneman presents the Neural Compiler, translating Scheme-like programs into frozen, differentiable PyTorch modules. Compiled modules match the source program to floating-point precision and provide gradients. In hybrid models, compiled modules encode known physics exactly. Across six domains, compiled modules match hand-coded implementations numerically. With only 1 to 4 trainable parameters, compiled models recover physical constants to under 1 percent error in most cases. PINN baselines with over 8500 parameters show 7 to 93 percent error. Compiled modules also compose with zero error. The main value is composability.
arxiv-2605-22698: Brunken and others present mlip version 2, an open source library for machine learning interatomic potentials that aim for near ab initio accuracy at lower cost. A reworked API improves control over training, data handling and simulation. An e3j backend speeds equivariant operations. The release adds the eSEN mixture of experts architecture for diverse data sets and more charge modelling with long range interactions. Advanced tools for NPT ensembles and nudged elastic band searches round out the release. They widen the library toward reactive systems out of equilibrium.
arxiv-2605-22798: Gil-García and Shahbazi develop the theory of complex spinorial forms tied to irreducible complex spinors in every dimension. They recast constrained parallelicity rules as systems for forms. Applied to the spin-c Killing equation in low dimensions, this refines prior results. They then prove every quasi-supersymmetric solution of Freedman gauged supergravity lies in a clear four-parameter family of gyratonic Brinkmann waves. A case in six dimensions yields a foliation result.
arxiv-2605-22898: Hedjam proposes FIRMA, a family of three federated learning protocols that aggregate models around a ring with no central server. Fibonacci-weighted blending mixes each client with its neighbors while keeping classification heads permanently private. Later variants add accuracy-gated suppression of weak peers and a ring permutation that maximizes class diversity among neighbors. Across 28 configurations the full system beat the FedAvg baseline in all label-skew cases, peaking at 20.7 points on CIFAR-10.
arxiv-2605-23198: Cho and three coauthors propose SemiPrune, a dataset pruning framework needing only a small labeled subset. It uses semi-supervised learning to make pseudo-labels for unlabeled data, so existing supervised methods can run on the pool. Difficulty is then estimated from pseudo-label training dynamics, and a coreset is selected. Learning from the target dataset captures its distribution better than pretrained features. Tests on domain-specific, image-corrupted, plus long-tailed datasets give top results among label-free baselines, with competitive standard scores.
arxiv-2605-23798: A. S. Detinko, D. L. Flannery and A. Hulpke turn a deep theorem about dense matrix groups into working code. For finitely generated Zariski dense groups inside special linear groups over number fields, with prime matrix size, their algorithms list all congruence quotients modulo maximal ideals of a suitable ring. The code runs in GAP, and degree two trials, centered on Bianchi groups, show what the experiments can reveal about these groups.
arxiv-2605-24098: Richard and four co-authors tackle sensor occlusion in driving vision-language models with D2-V2X, a question-rationale-answer benchmark from vehicle and infrastructure sensors. A baseline aligns 3D LiDAR features with the model's latent space and forces natural-language reasoning before structured JSON outputs, making spatial relations explicit. Cooperative LiDAR grounding lifts occluded-hazard recall to 24.4 percent, against near zero for zero-shot models, and cuts spatial error for visible objects by 77 percent. Decision-making F1 reaches 53.5, while 3D-to-2D projection remains the fundamental bottleneck.
arxiv-2605-24598: Yuxin Zhang and others tackle the device-cloud dilemma for language-model agents. On-device models are inexpensive but brittle, while cloud models are powerful but costly. Their coordinator, Hera, routes each step rather than each whole task. It first learns from cloud trajectories, then refines with cost-aware reinforcement learning that weighs success against future cloud calls. On ALFWorld, WebShop, and AppWorld it keeps 92.5 percent of cloud-only success while using the cloud in under half the steps.
arxiv-2605-24998: Qihuang Zhong and colleagues harness self-training for large reasoning models, which learn from self-made paths without outside help. They diagnose two flaws: data imbalance, with simple samples common and hard samples scarce, and overthinking, with extra steps harming training. Their HSIR method counters that gap with verify-then-exit sampling that gathers right answers for hard queries. It counters that bloat with an Intrinsic Diversity score that filters bloated ones. Results show up to 10.9 percent average score gains and up to 42.4 percent lower run-time cost.
arxiv-2605-25098: Yevgen Grynko and Jens Förstner present proof for resolved 3D Anderson localization of light in dense dielectric disorder. Full-wave Maxwell runs of dense high-index slabs are read at late times after the diffuse part leaves. Transmission grows a long tail, and effective diffusion nears trapped-state scaling. Late-time spectra show narrow peaks with Thouless flow below one. Near fields reveal compact still modal domains split by lasting dim channels, weakly linked.
arxiv-2605-25498: Nobutaka Ito and Yoshiaki Bando track multiple moving sound sources passively, without knowing the emitted signals. Existing track-before-detect methods assume each target's contribution depends only on motion, which fails when unknown and shifting source signals shape the sensor mixtures. Their subspace method represents each hypothesis with the span of source steering vectors. It scores raw mixtures with a source-insensitive likelihood from a complex spherical Student's t distribution. Acoustic tests with two moving speakers in noisy, echoing rooms beat a steered-response baseline in every condition.
arxiv-2605-25598: Daiyun Shen and colleagues tackle pose estimation for textureless surgical tools, where occlusions, missing depth, and scarce labels defeat generic object methods. They first build SynSurg6D, a synthetic set that widens pose coverage. They then propose SurfSurg6D, a dense-correspondence framework for RGB-only estimation. Tests on three surgical sets show the synthetic data lifts existing methods, and SurfSurg6D itself outperforms them, giving a robust route to precise tool poses from ordinary color video alone.
arxiv-2605-25998: Frauen and twelve colleagues argue that many questions in language-model development are causal at heart. Examples include what adding a data domain does in pretraining, and whether a prompt should go to a large or small model given cost limits. Logged development data suffer confounding and distribution shift, yet causal tools remain underused in the field. The paper explains how causal methods fit model building and evaluation, and how they can yield reliable, scientifically grounded design choices. It offers a map for bringing causality into everyday model work.
arxiv-2605-26098: Wang and five colleagues measure three-dimensional microwave fields with Rydberg atoms, needing no outside reference. Full local field mapping has stayed hard, though Rydberg atoms promise sharp sensing. They use Zeeman-resolved tests of electromagnetically induced transparency in a laser-cooled cloud. Three polarisation strengths come from one spectrum, and relative phases emerge from closed loops in the atoms' inner state space. The method calibrates itself, with field traits largely separable from each other and from other effects.
arxiv-2605-26298: Cong Wang and Yusheng Zheng's 2026 sandbox, Sandlock, cages untrusted agent code with no root rights, containers, or images. Fixed policy that ignores inputs turns into kernel rules, while a narrow supervisor handles run-time choices and virtual effects. That split guards files, networks, inter-process links, and system calls, plus live network choices, HTTP-level control, safe execve checks, and effects that can be undone. Startup costs about five milliseconds, Redis runs at bare-metal speed, and a pipeline tool holds each stage apart.
arxiv-2605-26698: Correnson, Kuhn, and Finkbeiner build almost fair simulation links, a lighter way to prove that one system can mimic another while honoring liveness rules. Plain simulations cannot prove liveness claims, and current fair simulations stack inductive and coinductive steps in ways that block hands-on proof. Their links come with plain reasoning rules, are built and proved sound in the Rocq proof tool, and are shown at work on examples.
arxiv-2605-26798: Li and five colleagues analyze how quantum nonlocality can be shared in sequence when each observer passes the qubit through a noisy local channel. Arbitrarily many observers can share Bell, GHZ, and W nonlocality through noise-immune channels, but that unbounded sharing vanishes under other noisy channels. New measurement strategies can switch which channel is noise-immune, and the authors give concrete two-observer schemes for Bell and Mermin nonlocality.
arxiv-2605-26898: Kjellberg, Fotrousi, and Staron test four prompting strategies for guiding 13 language models to use the Singleton design pattern in Java code. The best strategy depends on the model, but iterative binary feedback gives the best overall alignment while preserving or improving functionality. With plain instructions, Llama 3.3 produced Singleton classes in every case and raised tests passed by 34.1 percentage points. Even simple guidance strategies, they conclude, can steer models toward design patterns.
arxiv-2605-26998: Sheng, Zhu, and Boedecker present PRISM, a probabilistic recurrent intention switching model for inverse reinforcement learning. Older multi-intention methods segment paths but treat goal shifts as memoryless chains or fixed-history add-ons. PRISM maps past observations to per-step goal odds with a lightweight recurrent network. Its EM objective splits exactly into per-goal reward subproblems with closed-form answers, and tests on gridworld, mouse labyrinth, and robot tasks show the highest held-out scores.
arxiv-2605-27298: Thomas Berkane, Qianyi Wang, and Maimuna Majumder extract tables from chart images by sampling one vision-language model many times. They align the candidate tables and take per-cell medians, stopping once the consensus steadies and reporting spread as uncertainty. On a new World Bank benchmark with far denser charts, the method improves accuracy by up to 23 percent over single-pass output.
arxiv-2605-27498: Hamid Shafieasl and Jeff Phillips build a vector code for flat shapes that stays the same under rotation. For star-shaped objects in standard form they sketch a short vector that tracks shape distance, letting search and grouping run directly in shape space. The code maps distinct shapes to distinct vectors up to rotation and a mirror-flip step called reverse of complement.
arxiv-2605-27598: Arianna Meinking, Julie Campos, and Kenneth Brown test correlated decoding for bias-tailored compass codes under biased noise. Circuit-level simulations of Clifford-deformed elongated compass codes show correlated minimum weight perfect matching lifts thresholds for all noise biases over standard matching. The relative gain grows largest for codes with asymmetric stabilizers under biased noise.
arxiv-2605-27698: Yusufcan Masatlioglu and Tri Phu Vu build an economic model of choice on the psychological idea that two mental systems compete: a fast automatic one and a slower deliberate one. A single weight sets how much each system matters, and even the simplest version produces behavior patterns distinct from standard models. The model also fits several known findings and beats familiar rivals in choice analysis.
arxiv-2605-27898: Zhu and colleagues unify agent benchmarking so scores reflect the model rather than the quirks of each test harness. UniACE recasts benchmarks as instruction-tool-environment triples run under one shared harness with fixed success rules. Migrating seven benchmarks and testing fifteen models exposed ranking reversals and large score swings hidden by single-package results.
arxiv-2605-28198: Junfeng Nie, Alvin Jin, and Xiaohui Chen build synthetic tabular data with both rules and statistics. Their hybrid framework draws logical structure top-down while learning local patterns bottom-up, merging both in one synthesis engine with feedback. On financial benchmarks mixing tables and sentiment text, it beat neural baselines on train-synthetic-test-real scores while preserving meaning.
arxiv-2605-28398: Yansong Ning and four colleagues introduce HRBench, a common testbed for thinking-mode switching in hybrid-reasoning language models. It crosses three switching families with four training regimes, giving twelve controlled settings. Six models and five reasoning benchmarks are tested in one pipeline. Prompt methods often gave the best accuracy per token, routing cut cost most steadily, and speculative methods raised accuracy at higher cost.
arxiv-2605-28498: Mert Yazan, Frederik Bungaran Ishak Situmeang, and Suzan Verberne study whether pairing chatbots with web search curbs overreliance on AI answers. In a mixed-subjects question-answering experiment, participants used either a warm or a neutral chatbot alongside search. Reliance persisted despite fact-checking access, and the choice to verify tracked prior trust in chatbots more than answer features. Warmth acted indirectly, raising agreement with the chatbot even when it was wrong, while consulting extra AI sources predicted higher accuracy and plain web search did not.
arxiv-2605-28998: Alessio D'Errico and colleagues sharpen images of objects in weakly scattering media with entangled photon pairs. Coincidence checks plus post-selection on correlated events singles out ballistic photons from scattered ones and drops background light. Tests in two setups confirm the simulations. Contrast beats single-photon detection at the cost of higher shot noise from fewer events. Pooling events across post-selection windows partly offsets that noise, extending quantum imaging where adaptive optics or gating fail.
arxiv-2605-29098: Jiachen Lu, Hailan Shanbhag, and Haitham Al Hassanieh present GeRaF 2, a joint neural geometry framework for radar reconstruction from visible and hidden scenes. Radio signals pass cover but give low detail and high noise, and prior hidden-scene methods find coarse surfaces with shaky tuning and unclear shapes. Using outside visible geometry to guide radio travel into hidden regions, GeRaF 2 gives stable training and steady rebuild of seen and hidden geometry. Visual priors built into the neural field set a new best in radio-based geometry reconstruction.
arxiv-2605-29198: Shufan Li and colleagues offer Guidance Contrastive Policy Optimization, giving discrete policy learning per-token credit instead of uniform sample rewards. Group methods such as GRPO and DAPO broadcast one advantage across all tokens, missing individual contributions. GCPO contrasts predictions under good and bad prompts, giving token gains proportional to the difference between those predictions. The method highlights relevant regions, such as visual areas matching textual prompts in picture generation and keywords in reasoning traces. Across picture and reasoning benchmarks, GCPO outperforms its GRPO and DAPO norms.
arxiv-2605-29398: Xiaohang Tang proposes Guided Denoiser Self-Distillation for diffusion language models. Reinforcement learning can improve the denoiser, but its likelihood cannot be computed directly. Standard methods swap in an evidence lower bound, but this adds bias. It distills the denoiser from an optimal self-teacher, matching logits with a normalization-free objective. On planning, math, and coding benchmarks, it beats prior evidence lower bound methods with more stable rewards.
arxiv-2605-29598: Letizia Bottani and four colleagues present an implicit-explicit discontinuous Galerkin solver for Euler equations with spin. Time stepping uses a Runge-Kutta scheme, treating stiff sound modes in the hidden step and flow terms in the open step. The solver runs on the deal.II library with matrix-free math, tuned non-fitting meshes, and spread-out memory. Two treatments of spin and gravity source terms are tested for closeness, toughness, and speed. Checks cover spinning wave benchmarks and 3D layered flow over hills, showing closeness and steady runs.
arxiv-2605-29698: Roel J. Leenhouts and four colleagues argue that raw hit rates hide what mixture models get wrong. Their test frame splits mixture error into a pure-compound share and a share from non-ideal mixing, using leak-aware splits and excess-property scores. They also gather seven matched sets of pure and mixture properties so models face the same ground on both sides. Across tasks and model types, strong raw scores often masked weak grasp of non-ideal mixing, and scores fell sharply on strict splits by molecule.
arxiv-2605-29998: Constantia Alexandrou and eight colleagues compute moments of the internal momentum maps of the pion and kaon. These particles are made of quarks, and the team models quark forces with lattice quantum chromodynamics. From one set of simulated quark masses near their real values, they rebuild the valence maps from the connected parts of the first moments up to fourth order. Their numbers line up with earlier lattice estimates, giving a firmer picture of how momentum is shared inside these particles.
arxiv-2605-30098: Harsh Anand couples force-free electrodynamics to gravity via higher-form structures, from the Reissner-Nordström black hole. Swapping the Maxwell field strength for a gauge-invariant mix of two-form and gauge fields preserves a higher-form symmetry. Its conserved charge counts field lines piercing a surface, not particles. Fixing a gauge yields the geometry dual to the boundary theory. Whether the two-form field is exact or twisted like a monopole, the result is known: the Reissner-Nordström geometry first, and its dyonic cousin second.
arxiv-2605-30298: Luca Dal Molin and Frank Neumann determine the mod 2 cohomology algebra for real vector bundle moduli stacks of fixed rank and degree on a type I real algebraic curve. The algebra is expressed through characteristic classes induced from the complex Atiyah-Bott classes. The work thus describes the cohomology ring structure for real bundles on such curves via classes pulled from the complex setting.
arxiv-2605-30398: Muhamad Ashraf Azman studies how the cosmological constant shapes dark energy stars in Finch-Skea spacetime under Einstein gravity. He builds a static, anisotropic star of ordinary matter and dark energy, via the complexity factor method. The inner solution joins smoothly to a Schwarzschild-(anti-)de Sitter outer spacetime at the boundary. He tests the compact star candidate Vela X-1 in detail: positive constants give larger, less compact stars, while negative constants give denser, more compact stars with stronger gravity.
arxiv-2605-30698: Wang and colleagues argue mere answer agreement cannot make multi-agent visual QA trustworthy: shared image-region backing is what consensus needs. Their EAGLE framework shows every agent's grounded regions as shared proof, lets agents check each other against it, and steers the final call by proof agreement. EAGLE needs no extra training, stays centered on evidence, and coordinates several vision-language agents. On six visual QA benchmarks it posts the best average scores, staying light, easy to follow, and fit for real use.
arxiv-2605-30898: Huang and colleagues unify two ways of scaling language-model inference that are tuned apart. Model routing swaps among varied models to fit request difficulty, but gives coarse jumps; test-time scaling tunes compute inside one model, but hits capacity ceilings and diminishing returns. Their UniScale framework joins routing and test-time scaling in one optimization space and learns policies with a contextual bandit method. Efficiency-aware learning and cost modeling keep search stable over action spaces. Tests show a finer quality-versus-cost trade-off across shifting settings.
arxiv-2605-30998: Ling and colleagues give a systematic security analysis of x402 payments for the agentic web. Bridging web requests with blockchain finality creates state-sync problems. Around five invariants, they trace violations to their layer, finding four flaw classes with leakage reaching full loss in live tests. For pay-per-token pricing, they prove no output-only pricing can be both fair and bounded against hidden token inflation. They propose mitigations and a defense triple, cutting reasoning cost at low overhead.
arxiv-2605-31198: Bezerra, Dexheimer and Negreiros apply physics-informed neural networks to the neutron-star equation-of-state puzzle. One network represents the equation of state while another solves the stellar-structure equations, trained jointly on X-ray timing and pulsar mass data. The inferred physics respects causality, nuclear saturation and high-density theory bounds, and the speed of sound softens at two to four times saturation density, consistent with a quark-hadron crossover.
arxiv-2605-31498: Peñaherrera, Aggarwal, and Koes present SITA, a scalable method for sampling the Boltzmann distribution of molecules at low temperatures. Diffusion models fine-tuned along a temperature ladder promise to replace costly simulation. But they need a divergence over the score field to weight samples, which grows intractable for larger systems. SITA trains flow models anew to draw samples at ever lower temperatures. It uses an energy-based model for fast surrogate likelihoods, and reaches state-of-the-art results on two alanine peptides.
arxiv-2605-31598: Eyzaguirre and team present StateKV, a method that adapts pretrained long-video vision-language models to linear-time video prefill. Most video encoders rely on spatiotemporal self-attention, so compute grows with frame count. StateKV carries cross-frame context in a fixed-capacity recurrent state, paired with a second per-frame cache for decoding. Across three benchmarks and seven models, StateKV stays close to full self-attention and beats sliding-window and recency-based streaming approximations. It needs no fine-tuning or architectural changes, and cuts prefill cost.
arxiv-2606-00098:
Izaldein Al-Zyoud and El Saddik make deepfake detection both stronger and self-explaining by classifying only selected face regions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Whole-face detectors often learn dataset shortcuts like compression traces instead of manipulation evidence, so they fail on new datasets. Their design reverses the usual order: a face parser labels each image patch with its semantic region. Tokens from irrelevant regions are discarded, and a linear classifier judges only the kept region, such as the mouth. Explanations become built-in, because a fake verdict used only that region's evidence.

On the Celeb-DF v2 benchmark, the mouth-focused probe reached an AUC score, a quality measure, near 0.91 without any fine-tuning of its pretrained components. That beat two detectors by 8 and 17 percentage points in tests. Removing region selection dropped performance by about 26 points, and swapping the underlying image representation cost about 21 points, showing parts are necessary.
arxiv-2606-00198:
Lin and co-authors ask if AI agents keep track of their own spend. Agents now burn more time, calls, and cash on each task. Cost is most often tallied once the run is done. Their bench, BAGEN, treats budget as a live guide, not a late count.

They split spend into inner costs from thought and outer costs from acts. A sound agent should guess a range for what is left at each step. It should warn when a task looks doomed. Tests span four worlds and five top agents. Strong task scores do not mean strong budget sense. Top models stay too rosy and burn cash on lost tasks. Early stops save a large share of tokens. Training sharpens warns, but range guesses stay rough.
arxiv-2606-00798:
Shafi and co-authors fix a hidden flaw in shrinking diffusion models in this 2026 paper. These models make images from noise, guided by a class label. Guidance blends two score branches: one sees the label, and one does not. When a big model is distilled into a small one, training often watches only the blended output.

That leaves the two branches unpinned. Both can collapse to the same output while the loss stays low. Guidance then loses its force when the model runs. Their method, DASH, trains each branch on its own. An anchor term pulls the labeled branch toward true noise. The teacher's learned per-step plan passes to the student as a fixed prior. On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-64, a student shrunk over five-fold stays within four FID points of its teacher. It also keeps at least 89 percent of the teacher's guidance gap.
arxiv-2606-00898:
Ovcharov shows that a popular check for fake legal citations mostly measures its own database in this 2026 paper. The check, citation grounding, looks up model-made citations in a graph drawn from real court rulings. No human graders are needed. He scores 400 replies: 100 Ukrainian legal queries run through four commercial models.

Two snapshots of the same national graph give wild gaps. Against a sparse graph of 470,000 records, scores run from 79.1 percent to 85.5 percent in the sparse graph test, which looks like 15 to 21 percent fake cites. Against a dense re-draw of 330 million records, the same replies score from 98.9 percent to 99.9 percent on the dense graph. A simple sampling model, fed only the record count, replays the sparse scores to within two hundredths. Worse, no pair of models can be told apart at 95 percent trust at any graph size. Sparse graphs rank harvest coverage, and dense ones rank nothing, he concludes.
arxiv-2606-01098:
Yang and co-authors give robot policies a one step generator that keeps the wisdom of slow ones in this 2026 paper. Diffusion and flow policies clone behavior well. Their iterative sampling is too slow for high frequency control. One step versions cut the wait but lose the mid course corrections that keep actions valid. Rebuilding that correction as an explicit field is ill posed: expert demos near any state are too sparse.

Their policy, IDP, recovers the correction in implicit form. It reads a conditional expert geometry from how near twin expert actions vary. A global reference geometry then isolates what the condition truly demands. That structure weights a scalar potential objective. An expert proximal final check enforces manifold limits on the one step output during training. Across 2D, 3D, and real manipulation tasks, IDP holds to valid action manifolds, they report. It beats explicit drifting methods.
arxiv-2606-01298:
Tekanlou, Bakhtiyarzadeh, and Razmara sort hate speech from reclaimed speech. Reclaimed words are slurs reused by the groups they target. Context decides which class a post falls into. That makes labels hard and nuanced to assign. Their system was built for the MultiPride shared task. It uses dense semantic embeddings of the text. A Cleanlab step filters label noise with logistic regression.

A multilayer perceptron then makes the final call. The setup runs on limited compute by design. Scores use precision, recall, and F1, with macro averages. Results stay robust despite extreme class imbalance. The team stays interpretable through the pipeline. Bigger embedding models may lift scores further, they note.
arxiv-2606-01398:
Chen and co-authors release a sonar-visual dataset from a Norwegian fjord. Underwater robots pair cameras with sonar for perception. Vision gives rich semantic detail about a scene. Sonar gives robust range data where cameras struggle. Cross-modal prediction between them lacks paired training data. SOVIS holds over 76,000 paired frames for that gap. Seventeen dives at six Trondheimfjord sites produced the frames.

A pipeline cleans and synchronizes the sensor streams. An interactive tool speeds labeling of paired data. A proof-of-concept task tests cross-modal fish detection. It uses just a small labeled subset of the data. Detection beats a monocular camera baseline by seven times. The dataset opens paths like dense sonar prediction from images.
arxiv-2606-01498:
Kong and co-authors benchmark agents on multi-turn time series reasoning. Time series inform key decisions in many real domains. Agents can analyze data through language and tools. But reliable analysis across a long conversation is unproven. Past benchmarks test single-step tasks like forecasting. Real workflows evolve as user goals shift over turns. Conclusions emerge from accumulated evidence in those workflows. TimeSage-MT holds 240 tasks and 2,680 dialogue turns.

Eight real-world domains span basic exploration to decisions. A reproducible pipeline builds the tasks from real data. Answers stay verifiable by construction in the pipeline. Frontier models show sharp drops on decision-oriented tasks. Memory failures drive much of that drop. Uncertainty handling and domain decisions also fail often.
arxiv-2606-01598:
Guo and co-authors make particle-mesh Ewald differentiable for learned potentials. Machine learning potentials can near quantum accuracy for short-range chemistry. Most designs stay local in their receptive field. They miss long-range electrostatics and polarization effects. Those effects are essential for ionic, polar, and interfacial systems. Ewald-based designs recover some long-range physics from local variables. But many compute reciprocal terms by direct summation. That leaves a gap with production molecular dynamics practice. Their framework embeds PME inside a tensor message passing network.

Charges come from scalar local features. Dipoles come from equivariant vector features. Both enter the same particle-mesh solver as charge density. Forces train end to end through FFT-space electrostatics. On molten NaCl, their channel gives the lowest force error.
arxiv-2606-01698:
Yang and co-authors make medical image diagnosis easier to label and to read. Deep nets score well on medical images today. Their black-box choices block clinical use, though. Placenta Accreta Spectrum is a sharp case: cues in ultrasound are subtle. Concept Bottleneck Models route choices through clinical concepts. Clinicians can then check and refine the outputs. Plain versions miss links between concepts. They also need costly expert concept labels.

Their semi-supervised frame uses hypergraph learning at two levels. A concept-level hypergraph sharpens reasoning over concepts. An image-level one makes pseudo-labels that adapt to the domain. Tests use a new PAS ultrasound set, a breast ultrasound set, and SkinCon skin images.
arxiv-2606-01898:
Coquand reports an auto-formalization of Gödel's second incompleteness theorem. The proof is built in Agda for Basic Recursive Arithmetic. The outline follows Guard's 1963 lecture notes. The full development runs near 50,000 lines of code. It contains no postulates at all.

All Agda code was produced through talks with Claude. The author wrote no Agda code by hand. An early attempt based on Rose's paper failed. A false lemma led that attempt astray. It proved a claim that merely resembled Gödel's theorem. The flaw was a weak spec of the provability predicate. The case study shows strengths and limits of current models. Careful specification emerges as the key lesson.
arxiv-2606-01998:
Luu and co-authors set second-order conditions for sparse optimization problems. Both objective and constraint functions are differentiable here. Their gradients are locally Lipschitz continuous maps. Sparsity shapes which solutions matter in this class. First-order conditions alone cannot certify local optima fully.

The team use a limiting second-order subdifferential tool. It is the Mordukhovich form applied to the Lagrangian. New necessary and sufficient conditions follow from it. Local optimal solutions are the target of the results. Mild assumptions keep the results broadly usable. The theory extends several known results in the field. Sparse multiobjective problems get an application as well. Sufficient conditions for efficient solutions are derived there. Examples show the results at work in practice.
arxiv-2606-02198:
Singh and Castillo study how equally good models can judge the same person differently in recidivism risk tools. Prediction over individual futures is inherently noisy, so many models can reach similar accuracy while disagreeing on single cases. When those models give different predictions for the same individual, concerns about arbitrariness in decision making arise. The team ask how severe that arbitrariness can be, in theory and in practice, and how it can be resolved.

Their test bed is a machine learning decision support system for recidivism risk that has been in use for over fifteen years. They translate complex legal rules into an algorithm that labels post release outcomes, building a data set of thousands of inmate releases. Interpretable models learned on that data improve predictive performance. The models also reduce error rate disparities between groups, the authors report.
arxiv-2606-02398:
Yang and co-authors study a known pain in training large language models. Training on one domain can erode skills learned in others. The domains here are math, code, question answering, and creative writing. Full-model gradients across domains look nearly orthogonal. Yet selective losses still appear.

Their analysis finds sparse, weakly shared edits on shared computation routes. A local perturbation model splits loss shifts into two terms. One is a first-order term. The other tracks curvature along the path. Tests back this local account. After chained training across all four domains, a short math refresh lifts math scores from 57.66 to 66.04. A rollback with no training recovers much of a QA-caused math drop. The authors back sparse fixes and targeted refreshes as the cure.
arxiv-2606-02498:
Yuan and co-authors build a light deep learning tool to predict brain injury in preterm infants. The data are T2-weighted MRI scans from the dHCP dataset. Their network, GloResNet, rests on a ResNet-10 base. It is pretrained on MedicalNet to fight data scarcity. A global manifold mapping step comes first. Each volume is resampled to a standard cube. Subject-wise z-score normalization then standardizes intensity.

That mapping preserves global topology while it evens out appearance. Training adds mixup, class weighting, and test-time augmentation. Five-fold cross-validation gives 75.18 percent average accuracy. The peak fold reaches 81.82 percent. The authors present the tool as a non-invasive screen. A topology-aware light network, they show, can predict neonatal injury well. Source code is public on GitHub.
arxiv-2606-02698:
Cutler and co-authors measure color gradients inside ancient, massive, quiet galaxies. Such galaxies, found within the first 2 billion years, strain formation models. Past claims rest on slit spectroscopy. Slits capture only the galaxy center. The core is then assumed to represent the whole. Four galaxies at redshift above 3 are studied. All exceed a hundred billion solar masses in stars. Medium-band photometry from the MINERVA JWST program gives resolved light profiles.

Elliptical annuli trace the light out to about four effective radii. Three galaxies show negative color gradients. In the most extreme case, stellar mass falls by 0.1 dex versus slit-based measures. If age drives the gradients, tensions with extreme value models lessen out to redshift 9.5. Modeling choices also contribute significantly. The team calls for integral field spectroscopy. Spatially resolved spectra can break the age-dust-metallicity degeneracy at last.
arxiv-2606-02898:
Kania works in set theory, on when a mathematical structure keeps its standard form across models. The structures at issue are algebraic or topological-algebraic ones. Each has a standard form F(X) indexed by a set X. The question is whether being of that form is absolute between transitive models.

Kania isolates a simple preservation principle. If the index X can be recovered from F(X) by one uniform definable construction, the class is downward absolute from forcing extensions. This answers a question raised by Noah Schweber. In particular, no group that is not a full symmetric group can become one after forcing. The result holds in ZF alone. The same mechanism covers many other classes, from transformation monoids to operator algebras. Kania also gives clean obstructions that separate ZF failure from ZFC descent. These use finite covers and a finite-support normed space as key examples.
arxiv-2606-03098:
de Lacy, Noakes, and Pfefferlé use shape change methods to study plasma balance in a split region. The region is cut into parts, each part closed and smooth at its edge. On each part sits a field that is smooth, has no divergence, and runs tangent to the boundary. The work links this setup to multi-region relaxed magnetohydrodynamics, or MRxMHD.

The team shows that the MRxMHD balance laws are just the conditions for a still point of the magnetic energy. The limits fix pressure, flux, and a quantity called relative helicity. The authors spot a gauge condition that past work missed. They define relative helicity, prove it does not depend on gauge choice, and show a gauge where it matches the standard form. For a single region, an added condition makes a still point a true minimum of the energy.
arxiv-2606-03198:
Baek, Hur, and Kim show that how an AI rater is told to score changes what it finds. Clinics now use language models to grade the outputs of clinical support systems. The team tests this in adult type 2 diabetes drug care, at a 12-month follow-up visit. Four open models act as both the support systems and the raters.

Each output was graded two ways. One way used a gold rubric tied to the patient's own case. The other used no rubric. Scores with no rubric were higher and squeezed into a narrow band. Rubric scores ran far lower and spread much wider. The rubric also sharpened the split between two prompt styles by up to fivefold. It revealed wide gaps between rater models that the free method hid. The authors back rubric-anchored scoring for such work. The authors say free scoring cannot stand in for such work.
arxiv-2606-03398:
Singh asks whether transformers truly use the stack-like structures they seem to learn. The test bed is a family of formal counter languages. Past work showed that trained models hold states that match a stack. But matching states alone does not prove the model needs them. Singh probes the causal role of those states in next-token prediction.

Linear probes learn to read stack depth from the model's hidden states at each token. From the probe, one main direction in the hidden space is pulled out. Removing that direction from the model makes its sequence accuracy fall to near zero. The drop shows the stack signal is not a side pattern. The model depends on it to perform the task. Readers get rare causal proof, not just correlation, for an inner mechanism. The approach can guide similar checks in other models.
arxiv-2606-03698:
Park and Kwon split long-horizon agent decisions between two levels in Multi squared. Language model agents can plan and act in dynamic settings. Their long runs often drift from the original goal. Objective drift grows over extended interaction. Multi squared attacks that fragility with a hierarchy of agents.

A high-level agent creates context-aware sub-goals, trained by supervised fine-tuning. A low-level agent executes atomic actions, trained by offline-to-online reinforcement learning. The split gives stable control over long horizons. It also allows efficient adaptation as settings change. Tests across varied interactive environments beat strong agentic baselines. Robustness and coordination improve in multi-turn runs. Three hierarchical benchmark datasets are released with the method. They fill a long-standing gap in training hierarchical agent systems. Teams building long-lived agents get both a design and test data.
arxiv-2606-03898:
Tebyanian derives the certified rate for semi-device-independent quantum randomness from squeezed states. The setup trusts a binary pure-state source. The binary detector is untrusted, and its side information is classical. A closed-form Shannon rate follows from two inputs alone. Those are the trusted Gram overlap of the source states and the observed symmetric error rate.

Full optimization over binary qubit POVMs must include two deterministic extreme points. Projective-only treatments omit them and overstate the rate. Including them gives a substantially lower, correct bound. The formula is an unconditional upper bound on the certified rate. It turns tight on a numerically verified region covering all working points used. Squeezed-coherent BPSK sources then show how squeezing trades distinguishability against certified randomness. Lossless and lossy regimes are both covered. An adversary model with a purification register is also clarified.
arxiv-2606-04198:
Achraf Ben Ahmed finds in 2026 the physical quantity that decides when patch-based methods beat global ones for remote heart-rate sensing. The method reads pulse from face video. It is squeezed hard by video compression in telehealth calls.

The key quantity is coherence: how much of the pulse signal survives the compression. When coherence stays high, patch methods win by pooling clean local signals. When it drops, global methods do better. Tests across video datasets and compression levels matched this rule. The rule also explains why results in the field have seemed inconsistent. Ahmed offers the coherence check as a quick way to pick a method for a given call setup.
arxiv-2606-04398:
Wang, Zhang, and Zhu work on a formula from operator theory that links curvature to a counting invariant for Hilbert modules, in a 2026 arXiv mathematics paper. Hilbert modules are function spaces that also carry an algebra of multipliers. Arveson's Gauss-Bonnet-Chern formula relates the curvature of such a module to its Euler characteristic, a single number summarizing its shape. The authors prove the formula holds without extra conditions over the full multiplier algebra, for a broad class of such spaces on the unit ball.

They also settle Arveson's finite defect problem in the same setting, classifying submodules whose defect is finite. The defect structure governs both curvature and the Euler characteristic. Using commutative algebra, they apply the classification to show when two finite-codimensional submodules of vector-valued function spaces must be unitarily equivalent, meaning different-looking modules are really the same.
arxiv-2606-04898:
Di Via and colleagues pretrain a diffusion model so that locating anatomical landmarks needs only a handful of medical images, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Landmark detection supports workflows, but clinical deployment demands reliability and robustness. The role of representation learning here is underexplored. Their CDPM-Align performs multi-scale, conditional diffusion pretraining for landmark detection.

Downstream, they test low-annotation regimes with ten and twenty-five annotated images. The results confirm that pretraining lets the model learn a robust representation, improving both accuracy and uncertainty estimates. A model that knows what anatomy looks like before being taught landmarks, and that knows when it is unsure, is safer to deploy than one trained on a tiny labeled set. The authors present the work as a step toward safe, clinical deployment of landmark detection.
arxiv-2606-04998:
Nils Vu and co-authors present a new way to compute gravitational self-force using numerical relativity methods in this 2026 arXiv paper. Self-force calculations describe how a small body perturbs its own motion through curved spacetime, and second-order results are needed to model extreme mass-ratio inspirals for the future LISA space mission. So far such calculations exist only for circular orbits around a non-spinning black hole.

The method separates variables mode by mode, uses horizon-penetrating coordinates with null slicing, and solves the resulting equations with high-order discontinuous Galerkin discretization, adaptive mesh refinement, and a parallel iterative solver. For a scalar point charge orbiting a spinning Kerr black hole, it converges exponentially even at spin 0.998 near the Thorne limit, on orbits as tight as the innermost stable circular orbit. Twenty modes solve in parallel within a few seconds, inside the open-source SpECTRE code.
arxiv-2606-05298:
N. Bianchetti and colleagues build dynamical models of galaxies inside two strong-lensing clusters in this 2026 arXiv paper. Strong lensing models and simulations disagree about the mass properties of cluster subhalos, and stellar dynamics offers an independent check. The team targeted early-type galaxies in Abell 2744 and MACS J0416.1-2403, at redshifts 0.309 and 0.397.

Using spectroscopy from MUSE on the Very Large Telescope plus Hubble Frontier Fields photometry, they measured velocity dispersions for 109 cluster members. These extend out to 15 kiloparsecs in some cases. Fitting a dual pseudo-isothermal mass distribution with a Jaffe profile recovered the velocity dispersion for every galaxy, with values from 40 to 370 kilometers per second. The models fit them better than strong lensing models did. The Faber-Jackson scaling relations they calibrated came out higher in normalization than kinematic estimates, which the authors show were biased by point-spread and aperture effects.
arxiv-2606-05398:
Christian Kuehn and Jan-Eric Sulzbach propose a unified framework for reducing partial differential equations on thin domains in this 2026 arXiv paper. Thin domains, where one direction is confined, appear in films, coatings, channels, tubes, and biological tissues, and the geometry forces a lower-dimensional description.

The framework combines three parts: a boundary-condition analysis, a splitting for general thin domains, and a slow-manifold viewpoint for the resulting fast-slow system. Homogeneous Neumann conditions on the thin faces emerge as the most relevant and physical regime. They preserve the transverse zero mode and so yield a lower-dimensional reduced equation. They give a splitting-based Lyapunov-Perron slow manifold when a spectral split exists, plus slow manifolds and corrected reduced dynamics from the invariance equation. The Schnakenberg reaction-diffusion system serves as the test problem, and it extends to curved thin domains.
arxiv-2606-05498:
Gu studies the energy cost of noisy rhythms in a 2026 arXiv paper on statistical physics. Many living and chemical systems pulse on their own without any outside clock. Such self-driven rhythms need a steady push of energy, and that push is lost as heat. A bold earlier claim set a floor on the heat produced per cycle. Gu asks whether that floor can be proved in full.

Gu proves a weaker version of the claim that still holds with full rigor. The new bound adds a factor that measures how evenly the main rhythm spreads across the states of the system. The proof shows the older form can fail when the rhythm clings to a few states. For systems arranged in a ring, the new bound matches the older claim exactly. A simple drift and spread model on a circle reaches the bound with no slack.
arxiv-2606-05598:
Kun Huang and colleagues report a surprising fragility in ring-shaped laser cavities in a 2026 arXiv paper. The work targets mid-infrared light, prized for sensing and medicine. A crystal inside the cavity converts light to the wanted color while the ring boosts the pump. Even a faint bounce off the crystal, just three parts in ten thousand, split the cavity's tones apart. The split broke the one-way flow of light in the ring.

With light running both ways, the boost for the stored field fell sharply. A straight linear cavity, which always runs both ways, shrugged off the same small bounce. Tests of mid-infrared output confirmed the linear layout gives steadier and stronger gains. Computer models matched the measured behavior closely. The team offers the finding as a design guide for conversion cavities that use such crystals.
arxiv-2606-05698:
Zuo and colleagues ask when knowledge baked into a model beats knowledge kept in context in a 2026 arXiv paper. One memory channel stores a document as a small LoRA adapter, a plug-in tweak to the model's weights. The other keeps the document's key-value cache, its live context memory. The team shrank the cache step by step during document questions. They measured when the adapter starts adding value beyond the surviving context.

With the cache mostly intact, the adapter added little. Under heavy compression its value grew fast. When no document context remained, it recovered thirteen to twenty-one points on a standard answer score. Gains peaked when the base model encoded the document and the adapter fired only while answering. Training adapters with question-answer supervision beat plain next-word training by a wide margin. Document memory, the authors argue, works best as decoding-time support.
arxiv-2606-05798:
Hannah Menke, Scanziani, and Rücker argue that rock imaging should count as supply-chain infrastructure in a 2026 arXiv paper. Britain and Europe have set bold targets for home-grown critical minerals. Many local resources are complex, old, or marginal, though. Targets alone cannot say which ores and waste streams can be processed cleanly at a profit. Digital Rock Physics scans rocks in three dimensions and models flow and reactions pore by pore.

Linked with chemical mapping and AI image analysis, the scans connect mineral texture to processing choices. Uses span ore grading, leaching, lithium extraction from brines, mine waste reuse, and battery recycling. The authors propose a shared agenda: pilot demonstrators, cross-field training, and a Digital Ore Passport standard. One federated Digital Ore Database and joint imaging endstations complete the plan. Treated as common infrastructure, they argue, rock data turns mineral strategy into working supply routes.
arxiv-2606-06098:
Fanì and Ersoy route each prompt to a specialist language model with nothing fancier than ridge regression in a 2026 arXiv paper. Expert models beat generalists in their niches, but choosing among them usually needs an expensive trained router. IR3DE fits a linear model on prompt features and predicts which domain expert fits. Cheap and fast are the design brief.

Two language-modeling settings tested next-token prediction across domains. A third setting gave each domain its own distinct reasoning task. The linear router matched heavier baselines in both modeling settings. In the reasoning setting it surpassed them, reaching a normalized performance near ninety-eight percent. Experts can join or leave the pool without retraining the router from scratch. That modularity suits serving stacks where models churn weekly. Sophistication, the authors suggest, is not always where routing quality lives; a well-fit line can beat a network.
arxiv-2606-06198:
Simone Vilardi and colleagues speed up a cosmic web mapping technique in this 2026 arXiv paper on astronomy data analysis. The cosmic web is the vast network of galaxy filaments, walls, and clusters that structures the universe. The Locally Aligned Ant Technique sends virtual ants through point clouds to trace faint filaments, guided by pheromone like signals. Dense hubs, such as galaxy clusters, trap the ants' attention and waste enormous computing effort.

Their fix works in two stages. A fast preprocessing step finds the hubs first and replaces each with a fitted likelihood model, a statistical stand in for its dense core. The ants then cross those regions using a mix of likelihood and pheromone guidance instead of exploring every point. On synthetic data and a large N body simulation, the hybrid search recovered filaments faster and more robustly, with lower memory overhead than the original technique.
arxiv-2606-06298:
Licheng Zhang and Yuanqiu Huang bound how dense a restricted kind of graph can be in this 2026 arXiv paper. A k cactus is a graph where each edge lies on at most k cycles. Forests are the case k equals zero, and ordinary cacti are k equals one. The maximum possible edge count was classical for those small cases and known up to k equals four, but open for general k.

The key observation is that limiting cycles per edge forces the graph to exclude a large complete graph as a minor, making the class minor closed. From that fact, they bound the edges of any n vertex k cactus by a term growing like n times log k over a root of log log k. A matching construction shows the bound is near optimal. The result settles the density question for all k.
arxiv-2606-06498:
Zhida Sun and co-authors teach AI to draw charts that stay honest in this 2026 arXiv paper on visualization. Pictorial charts dress data in pictures: bars become trees, slices become objects. They are memorable and engaging, but generative models usually wreck the numbers while decorating. The team's framework treats generation as a dual task, steered by a text prompt carrying the intended meaning and a plain chart image carrying the exact structure.

Inside a multimodal diffusion transformer, two mechanisms keep the two signals apart. Structural alignment anchors the layout to the input chart, while semantic alignment borrows expressive textures from reference images. The method generalizes across the main visual channels, length, area, angle, and position, and across many subject domains. In quantitative tests and user studies it beat controllable generation and image editing baselines, producing charts judged both artistically compelling and structurally faithful to the data.
arxiv-2606-06598:
Yanzhe Wang and co-authors perform surgery on logical qubits in this 2026 arXiv paper on quantum computing. The surface code protects quantum information across many physical qubits, and lattice surgery is the standard way to operate between two logical qubits: merge their patches, measure jointly, split again. On a planar superconducting processor, the team ran lattice surgery between two distance three logical qubits, the smallest useful size, through repeated error correction cycles.

The logical qubits held per cycle error rates of about three point seven and two point eight percent after rejecting leakage events. With joint initialization and splitting, they prepared an entangled logical Bell state and verified genuine entanglement. They then executed a two qubit Deutsch Jozsa algorithm entirely at the logical level. Finally, magic state injection with gate teleportation produced a non Clifford rotation gate with logical fidelity of zero point nine four three.
arxiv-2606-07098:
Shrinking a large language model usually means cutting its weight matrices down to lower rank. Lavrinovics and co-authors improve that surgery in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their method, SigmaScale, prepares each matrix with learned scaling before the cut. Singular value decomposition then keeps the most valuable directions.

Earlier methods derived the scaling from formulas. SigmaScale instead learns two sets of scaling vectors directly. The training loss is activation aware, respecting which inputs the model actually sees. Learned scaling lowered the effective rank of the matrices. That drop tracked compression loss closely across experiments. Tests used two eight billion parameter models from different families. Performance matched leading decomposition based compressors on perplexity and zero shot tasks. The authors note a caveat: quality degrades sharply at aggressive compression ratios. Choosing the operating point matters as much as the method.
arxiv-2606-07498:
Kage, Hedges, Siddharth, and Andreadis create training data for contrastive learning without touching the data, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Contrastive learning works by comparing altered copies of each sample, but for scientific observations, perturbing the data can destroy the phenomenon. Radar echoes from meteors, their test case, are delicate that way. Their method instead perturbs the network's weights to generate the contrastive views, leaving the observation's structure intact while producing representations.

A SimCLR-based pipeline, a framework, applied to meteor radar data showed performance gains under protocols against data-augmentation baselines. The weight-space trick generalizes the idea that augmentation need not live in the input. For datasets where labels are scarce and expert labeling is slow, preserving the measurement while varying the learner helps. The authors position implicit data synthesis as a safer strategy for domains where the data are the ground truth, not an approximation of it.
arxiv-2606-07698:
Dietrich tests whether gene-based drug knowledge can improve predictions of drug-drug interactions, harmful clashes between medicines taken together, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Graph neural networks usually judge such interactions from molecular structure alone, and earlier work in this series argued that structure imposes an information ceiling no architecture can beat. The question is whether outside knowledge can lift that ceiling.

Dietrich adds twelve features drawn from the PharmGKB database, covering how four liver enzyme families handle each drug as substrate, blocker, or activator. Under pair-level test splits, interaction-type classification jumped sharply, with the macro F1 score rising from about twenty-four hundredths to about fifty-three hundredths. One enzyme family, CYP2C9, showed the clearest gain on held-out compounds, with predicted probabilities rising from a few hundredths to well over half. Gains vanished, though, when the test required generalising to entirely unseen drugs.
arxiv-2606-07998:
Ian Seet, Jonas Bozenhard, and Simon Osterman argue that the road to interpretable AI may run through smaller, local machines rather than bigger clusters, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Deep neural networks are powerful but diffuse: computation spreads across millions of weights on parallel hardware, making them hard to interpret and expensive to run. Localised models, where each node handles a small neighbourhood, tend to be more interpretable and efficient on small datasets.

By analogy, the authors propose localised hardware architectures: lower bandwidth between nodes, but higher expressivity per node. Such designs, they argue, could be far more interpretable than networks on graphics clusters while staying competitive where datasets are modest. The paper surveys candidate hardware paradigms, rating each on per-node expressivity, energy efficiency, and technological maturity. It is a position and survey piece, not an experiment: a map of which physical substrates could host localised learning.
arxiv-2606-08198:
Shimon and colleagues study hand gestures for controlling ear-worn devices in this 2026 arXiv paper. Earables, meaning earbuds and similar hearable gadgets, have almost no room for buttons or touch surfaces. The authors explore an off-device alternative: swiping one hand in the air or on the skin above the neck, near the ear. Earlier work mostly covered straight horizontal and vertical swipes, leaving diagonal and angular shapes such as L, U, and V paths largely untested.

In a motion-capture study, twenty-four participants produced more than five thousand swipes of varied shape, direction, and complexity. The results revealed preferred starting and ending regions for different swipe types, and which shapes people found natural to perform. The authors also discuss whether current sensing technology could recognize these swipes reliably, giving designers a concrete map of the gesture space around the ear.
arxiv-2606-08398:
Anlong Qin and Qu show that averaging data across groups can hide the very patterns economists want to detect, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Regime-switching models describe time series that alternate between distinct states, such as expansion and recession. The authors demonstrate that cross-sectional aggregation substantially attenuates regime-switching signals, making switches harder to detect in pooled data. Building on that insight, they develop models and an estimation algorithm that work directly on disaggregated data.

They apply the approach to a United States macroeconomic dataset of ninety-four series. The resulting estimates give sharper business cycle classifications than those typically found in the literature, because downturn signals in individual series are no longer diluted by averaging. Monte Carlo simulations show the computation stays practical for datasets with a few hundred time series.
arxiv-2606-08498:
Yunyi Zhang tests whether two high-dimensional time series are independent when neither is stationary, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Testing independence between two such series is hard when autocovariances change over time, violating the weak stationarity most methods assume. The usual remedy, whitening the series first, is itself challenging here. Zhang proposes a bimodal weighted-average test statistic. It removes the bias induced by temporal dependence under the null hypothesis directly, avoiding whitening.

For inference, a dependent wild bootstrap generates the reference distribution while respecting the dependence. Zhang also derives a bound for quadratic forms of time-series data. That yields the null distribution of the statistic and the bootstrap's validity. Experiments show the test holds its size and keeps good power even when dimension exceeds sample size. The test is meant for data where the old rules of thumb break down in daily use at scale.
arxiv-2606-08598:
Jayasurya, Upadhyay, and Rana report a possible fingerprint of a neutron star's magnetic field in a bright X-ray source, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The source is a transient hyperluminous X-ray source in the galaxy NGC 3583. It episodically exceeds luminosities suggesting accretion onto a compact object at extreme rates, then drops by a factor of more than forty-five into a deep low state. The authors present a broadband study using data from three X-ray observatories plus monitoring with a fourth.

The spectra show a clear cutoff at a few kiloelectronvolts. It is well modeled by a soft thermal component combined with thermal Comptonization or an inner advection-dominated disk. In the highest-quality spectra they detect a statistically significant absorption line near two kiloelectronvolts . They interpret the line as a candidate proton cyclotron feature, an imprint of charged particles spiraling in a magnetic field.
arxiv-2606-08698:
Yushan Li formalizes a decision problem about admitting evidence into certified classes, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The quotient admission problem takes as input a finite row set, an evidence map, semantic labels, and witness-support graphs. The output is a decision on each evidence atom: certificate, residual, low-confidence, or blocked. The problem asks for the maximal guard-respecting decision map using no refinement beyond the admissible evidence partition.

Li proves an atom-union characterization of the classes. He gives a witness-support guard for certificate admission, and shows projected-label conflicts are exactly the blocked atoms. Quotient admission algorithms follow, with correctness guarantees. With explicit evidence vectors and hyperedges, they run in near-linear expected time by hashing.
arxiv-2606-08798:
