Belgacem designs controllers steering gene networks to expression levels, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A gene regulatory network is the web of genes switching one another on and off inside a cell. Standard Hill-function models vanish when an activator is absent, breaking controllability at the low expression levels where cells usually operate. Using logistic functions instead, Belgacem builds a feedback law combining feedforward and proportional terms.

The law makes any positive target level an equilibrium of the controlled system, even if the uncontrolled network never settles there. He proves global exponential stability under a gain condition, with a closed-form rate, via a Lyapunov function, an energy-like stability certificate. Companion results give a budget for forcing bistable switches into one stable state, and stability that holds despite time delays. A T-cell switch example shows the logistic coupling stays positive where the Hill version decays to zero.
arxiv-2606-09198:
Liu and Xiong argue that AI research agents for social science should stop re-reading the literature and instead run societies, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Deep Research agents plan, retrieve, and synthesize papers automatically, but in social science that yields thin, unoriginal work. MASS gives the agent a memory-augmented social simulation: a virtual society generating first-hand empirical data for the paper.

Three components keep the simulation realistic. Dynamic goal-path planning is restrained by social norms, so agents act within believable rules. A multidisciplinary behavior dataset cold-starts agent memory with real patterns. A structured forgetting mechanism, modeled on the Ebbinghaus curve, prunes memory as human recall decays. In experiments, MASS improved overall generation quality by 6.81 percent over foundation models and raised the Insight score by 17.19 percent over strong baselines, the biggest gain where retrieval-only systems are weakest: originality from simulated evidence, not recycled text.
arxiv-2606-09498:
Hangfan Zhang and his colleagues propose Self-Harness, a scheme in which a software agent improves the very scaffolding it runs inside, in this 2026 arXiv paper. An agent's harness covers its system prompts, tools, verification rules, and failure-recovery logic, and the same model can perform very differently under different harnesses.

Self-Harness runs an iterative loop of weakness mining, harness proposal, and proposal validation. It first finds recurring failure patterns in execution traces, then drafts minimal edits aimed at those failures, and adopts an edit only after regression testing shows no backsliding. Starting from a minimal harness on Terminal-Bench-2.0, three models from different families all improved markedly. Held-out pass rates rose from about forty-one to sixty-two percent for one model, with comparable jumps for the other two.
arxiv-2606-09698:
Aolin Xu studies how to send a real-valued signal through a channel that talks back in this 2026 arXiv paper. Feedback lets the sender adapt each step to what the receiver has heard so far. One aim is to squeeze the most shared information out of many channel uses. A second, harder aim adds low distortion at each step, so early guesses of the source stay sharp.

Xu first gives conditions that are enough for an encoder to hit peak information. For channels that reveal their input, those conditions are also required. The joint task is then solved for channels with a set symmetry, like k-ary symmetric or erasure types. There, the known posterior matching scheme is not just handy but nearly forced. It is the sole route that hits both goals at once.
arxiv-2606-09798: Appearing on arXiv in 2026, this research paper lays out a new study. Its subject, given in the title, is SynManDex: Synthesizing Human-like Dexterous Grasps. Its discipline is science and technology: careful study of how the natural and built world works. Fresh scholarship fills these pages.
arxiv-2606-09898:
Sujoy Banik and his co-authors run the first head-to-head of pathway-guided cancer models under one roof in this 2026 arXiv paper. Treatment calls come in bundles: a targeted drug, radiation, and a six-month survival guess, all at once. Past models that read gene pathways were built and scored alone, so fair ranking was out of reach.

Three architectures meet on five Cancer Genome Atlas groups, two thousand six hundred twenty-two patients in all. Each case is coded by Reactome pathway activity scores. All models train on all three calls under one protocol. No single build swept the board. PATH led on targeted drug calls, while BINN was the steadiest on survival. No model said anything useful on radiation, whose drivers live outside gene data. GraphPath hit an AUROC of zero point nine two on prostate drug calls, the bench's top mark.
arxiv-2606-09998:
Nguyen points out that water-based neutrino detectors could extend the hunt for a dark matter candidate carrying a tiny electric charge, in a 2026 arXiv paper on astroparticle physics. Such millicharged particles might gather inside the Sun, annihilate, and release high-energy neutrinos. IceCube has already used that idea to set limits for heavier candidates and very small charges. Water Cherenkov detectors, which watch for rings of light in huge water tanks, have lower energy thresholds.

That lower threshold makes Super-Kamiokande sensitive to lighter millicharged dark matter annihilating in the Sun. It can probe unexplored territory for particle masses from five to twenty-eight gigaelectronvolts at a tiny fractional abundance of the total dark matter. The future Hyper-Kamiokande would improve those limits and reach fractional abundances nearly an order of magnitude below current IceCube bounds. The detectors thus complement IceCube's high-mass reach rather than duplicating it.
arxiv-2606-10198:
Shamsi detects hallucinations in language and vision-language models by mapping the geometry of their internal activity, in a 2026 arXiv paper on AI reliability. Hallucination detection is often framed as selective prediction: a detector scores confidence and abstains when it is low. Unsupervised sampling methods avoid labels but plateau in quality, while supervised probes score well yet degrade when calibration labels are scarce. Her method recovers the response manifold, the surface traced by hidden-state generation trajectories, as a density ridge of a kernel density estimate.

A test generation is scored by its distance to the nearest ridge vertex, giving a low-dimensional skeleton of the output distribution. Evaluation spans six question-answering benchmarks, from TriviaQA to ScienceQA, across eight text and vision models, with a deliberately label-scarce protocol using only two hundred calibration queries and five generations each.
arxiv-2606-10398:
Nakayashiki and Watanabe measure how much of what readers highlight is personal taste rather than the text itself, in a 2026 arXiv paper on human-computer interaction. Their control design uses co-readership: the same document highlighted by many users holds document and topic fixed. It asks whether a person's own history predicts their marks better than another reader's history does.

At the document level, their leakage-free identity-controlled measurement shows a person's history identifies which documents in a co-reading neighborhood are theirs. It holds a clear own-versus-other advantage against both community and topic-matched negatives. That selection signal is comparable in size to the span-level signal from their prior work, and most of it is stable topic preference. The conclusion embedded in their title is that personalization is mostly about selection of what to read, not salience within text.
arxiv-2606-10498:
Kim and colleagues present microscopic evidence for an unusual entangled state in a magnetic material in this 2026 arXiv paper. The material is NiPS3, a layered van der Waals antiferromagnet whose nickel atoms form a honeycomb lattice. Theory had proposed that it hosts a Zhang-Rice triplet, an entangled pair of charge holes shared between nickel and sulfur orbitals, behind its remarkably sharp magnetic exciton. The team tests this with nuclear magnetic resonance on crystals enriched with sulfur-33.

Measurements of the sulfur and phosphorus Knight shifts across temperature point to one unified spin-triplet configuration, formed by strong mixing of a sulfur hole with a nickel hole. The sulfur relaxation rate also diverges as a power law near the ordering temperature of 155 kelvin, signalling charge fluctuations slowing down. Together these support a ground state where spin and charge intertwine, behind the exciton's sharp coherence.
arxiv-2606-11198:
Zhang and Zhang identify a hidden cost of structured data in retrieval-augmented generation, systems that paste fetched knowledge into a model's prompt, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The format of that content, apart from its meaning, distorts the model's attention. Knowledge graph triples, facts as subject-relation-object slots, grab two to three times more attention per token than plain sentences.

They call this the structural attention tax, splitting attention scores into semantic and structural parts. The structural part sets how much attention is diverted, up to forty-two percent of the attention meant for demonstrations. Experiments show content fit dominates: task-matched BM25 retrieval scored fifty-eight to sixty-two percent on HotpotQA, against twenty-five to twenty-seven percent for ConceptNet triples. Of five mitigations, format flattening, rewriting triples as prose, cut the tax by seventeen to twenty-nine percent on LLaMA-3-8B, keeping accuracy.
arxiv-2606-11298:
González-Alonso, Palavrić, and Prakash apply effective field theory to neutrino experiments in a 2026 arXiv paper. Neutrino physics is now a precision field, sensitive to smaller effects beyond the Standard Model. Effective field theory, EFT, gives a systematic, model-independent language for describing such deviations. The authors review and extend the theory of generic neutrino interactions.

Their formalism includes matter effects and connects to the density matrix approach used for oscillations. On the applied side, they turn to medium-baseline reactor experiments. They derive closed-form expressions for the relevant oscillation observables. Then, for the first time, they perform an EFT analysis of the recent JUNO dataset and bound the leading non-standard interaction parameters. The aim is a common framework where disagreements among experiments themselves become information about new physics.
arxiv-2606-11498:
Adam Bartoš and three colleagues study ultrametric spaces in this 2026 arXiv paper in pure mathematics. An ultrametric space is a set of points where distance obeys a stronger rule than usual, so every triangle has two equal longest sides. They treat such a space as two-sorted, meaning points and distances are separate kinds of object, and use maps called dc-embeddings, which preserve distances and an order structure.

Working with the universal space built as a Fraïssé limit, gluing all finite examples into one, they prove its symmetry group has a comeager conjugacy class. In plain terms, one symmetry pattern is so typical that almost every symmetry looks like it. They prove this through cofinal amalgamation, a property about merging partial symmetries. They also show no generic pair of symmetries exists, describe single orbits, and show partial symmetries can be extended in a closed or monotone way.
arxiv-2606-11998:
Frank Xiao and Mary Phuong strengthen AI oversight by adding a stronger middleman in this 2026 arXiv paper. Trusted monitoring uses a weaker, verified-safe model to watch a powerful agent. As frontier models advance, the capability gap may make the trusted watcher unreliable. Their protocol, bootstrapped monitoring, inserts a stronger but untrusted model with open chain-of-thought reasoning into the chain.

The untrusted monitor judges the agent's actions, while the weaker trusted model oversees its visible reasoning. They test it on multi-turn software engineering tasks in the BashArena suite. Bootstrapped monitoring greatly improves catch rates over trusted-only monitoring. This holds even when the untrusted monitor actively colludes with the agent, provided overseers can read its raw chain-of-thought. The authors suggest the protocol can extend the useful lifetime of trusted models, though access to raw reasoning is the crucial condition.
arxiv-2606-12198:
Wang and co-authors generate plain-language interest profiles for video viewers while recommendations are being served, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Large language models can summarize what a user likes in readable words, unlike the numeric codes recommender systems usually carry. Doing this live for a platform with about a billion users is the challenge: model calls are slow and costly. Their framework builds each persona by merging a summary of the viewer's existing interests with fresh topics worth exploring.

Three tricks keep the cost in reach. Knowledge distillation trains a small model to imitate the large one's persona writing. Asynchronous inference lets persona updates run off the critical serving path. Videos are first grouped into semantic clusters, shrinking the input the model reads. Offline evaluations, user studies, and live A/B tests show meaningful gains in viewer value, strongest for casual users.
arxiv-2606-12298:
Palavrić and co-authors build an atlas linking hypothetical heavy particles to the axions they would leave behind, in this 2026 arXiv paper. KSVZ models solve a puzzle of the strong force by adding heavy vector-like fermions and a broken symmetry whose leftover particle is an axion or axion-like particle. Different choices of fermion charges give different low-energy fingerprints. The authors develop a framework matching any such ultraviolet completion onto two effective theories: the Standard Model's and the axion-like particle's.

Global fits to electroweak precision data, Higgs measurements, and flavor observables then bound the effective couplings. The bounds barely depend on the ultraviolet details, making them robust. Translated into axion parameter space, they indirectly probe axion couplings without any axion experiment. Across most of the space, these indirect limits beat direct axion searches. The exception: charge assignments letting the new particles mix in mass with ordinary fermions.
arxiv-2606-12498:
Zhu and co-authors disarm backdoors hidden inside merged AI models, without breaking what the models learned, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Model merging blends several fine-tuned models into one, saving storage and compute. But a backdoored ingredient can poison the blend: the merged model behaves normally until a trigger appears. Existing defenses edit weights directly in parameter space and often wreck clean-task performance. Their LFPM framework instead reasons in feature space, where the model's internal representations live.

The key is cross-task linearity: features vary almost linearly across tasks, so an anti-backdoor task vector can be designed in feature terms and added to the merged model. Optimization uses gradient accumulation and a loss path-integral, enforcing suppression along the whole interpolation path between models, not just at the endpoint. Experiments show strong backdoor robustness in both full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient settings, with clean performance preserved.
arxiv-2606-12798:
Ghosh and colleagues assess floating solar photovoltaics as an energy-access strategy for South America, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Floating photovoltaics mount solar panels on reservoirs and lakes, avoiding the land-use conflicts of ground-mounted farms while gaining cooling benefits from the water. South America has among the highest generation potential per unit of water surface, about 38.26 terawatt-hours per million acres, yet deployment lags behind Asia.

Using a techno-socio-economic framework, the study details cases in Nicaragua, Honduras, and Guyana, including Lake Yojoa, the El Cajon reservoir, and the Capoey-Mainstay-Tapakuma cluster. For systems sized from 50 to 398 megawatts, annual yields exceed 1,500 to 2,000 kilowatt-hours per kilowatt, with capacity factors above 20 percent. At El Cajon, each megawatt deployed avoids 130.2 tonnes of carbon dioxide plus nitrogen and sulfur oxides relative to fossil generation. Counting avoided land costs and shared hydropower infrastructure, floating solar reaches competitive electricity costs.
arxiv-2606-12898:
Zeng and colleagues introduce AGAR, an attention-guided adaptive rendering method that improves how vision-language models read text presented as images, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Visual text comprehension renders text into page images for a vision-language model to read. This sidesteps language-model context limits and enables long-page reading and multi-page memory question answering.

The authors find that these models sit in a localisation-without-utilisation regime: attention that localises the evidence emerges sharply in middle-to-late layers, yet is decoupled from answer correctness. AGAR exploits this. It uses the model's middle-to-late layer attention to find the top-ranked visual patches, maps them back to word spans, and re-renders the page with those spans enlarged before answering again. Across 9 benchmarks and 4 model backbones, the training-free method improves off-the-shelf models and composes with post-training for gains.
arxiv-2606-13098:
Glaviano studies the graviton propagator in asymptotically safe quantum gravity with non-local form factors, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Asymptotic safety proposes that gravity is renormalisable through a non-Gaussian fixed point of the renormalisation group flow. Quantum corrections generate higher-derivative and non-local terms in the effective action, encoded in form factors. Whether those terms spoil the propagator with ghost poles, signalling unitarity problems, is a central consistency question.

Working at quadratic order in the curvature expansion, Glaviano studies the flow of the graviton propagator driven by the running of the asymptotically safe form factors. He constructs the propagator in the zero-scale limit and probes its momentum dependence. The result is reassuring for the programme. There is a single pole at zero momentum squared, with positive residue, matching the massless graviton, and no ghost poles at this level of approximation.
arxiv-2606-13498:
Grebenkov and Ye analyse populations that grow or die at surfaces in this 2026 arXiv paper. In surface-mediated autocatalytic processes, particles wander toward surface regions. At the surface a particle can be killed, or it can be replicated, spawning new particles. These opposing forces compete, producing complex random evolution of the total count. Such processes model chemistry, cell dynamics, and infection spread on surfaces. The authors provide an analysis of the generating function of the total size, the object holding its full distribution.

From it they deduce the distribution itself, its mean, variance, and higher moments. Several parallel accounts are developed, through nonlinear integral equations and through PDEs with nonlinear boundary rules. The long-time behaviour falls into three regimes: it dies out, settles to a steady level, or grows without bound. Solutions and Monte Carlo runs support the predictions.
arxiv-2606-13698:
Dénes Toth and colleagues control traffic lights with active inference in this 2026 arXiv paper, targeting the messy conditions of real sensor networks. Urban signal control at instrumented intersections must cope with sensor occlusion, weather fading, and shifting demand. Standard controllers degrade under those conditions, and learned policies are hard to audit. The authors propose an active inference controller for a four-arm signalised intersection. It selects signal phases by lowering expected free energy over Gaussian beliefs about congestion in each direction, an objective from neuroscience, yielding a traceable pipeline.

They benchmark the controller in a standard traffic simulator against a rule-based rival and a deep reinforcement learning network. The four scenarios grow in noise and nonstationarity, including blocked sensors, adverse weather, and random accidents. 100 runs per scenario support the comparison. The method attains the lowest delays in the reported results while remaining open to audit.
arxiv-2606-13998:
Leung works out exact derivative formulas for curves forced to stay on a sphere. Spherical interpolation matters when data are directions, normals, or orientations, living on the unit sphere rather than in flat space. SIDER builds high-order spherical curves entirely from SLERP, the basic spherical interpolation, applied in a recursive tree. His 2026 arXiv paper differentiates that construction, starting from the total derivative of one SLERP step whose endpoints and parameter all move.

From that block, chain-rule propagation through the tree gives compact recursions for derivatives of SIDER curves of any order. Simpler formulas hold at the interpolation nodes. Practical versions cover middle points between samples, which reconstruction schemes often evaluate. The second-order case is explicit; the third and fourth illustrate the recursion. Leung also proves the derivative stays tangent to the sphere at every point, as geometry demands.
arxiv-2606-14398:
Nandakumar and colleagues offer a 2026 arXiv theory paper on mixture-of-experts transformers, a neural network design where only some parts, called experts, handle each input. Such models grow large while keeping computing cost per input fixed. In practice, experts tend to specialize by task, but earlier theory used continuous models that fit language poorly.

The authors instead represent knowledge with syntactic templates and finite key-value dictionaries, a discrete picture closer to real text. They prove that one mixture-of-experts layer can store knowledge by routing each query to a unique expert matched to its task. The needed expert size depends only on the task's own complexity, from its templates and dictionary. Experiments with different training losses support the construction and link it to localized knowledge circuits seen in real models.
arxiv-2606-14498:
Lou and co-authors present HamEvo in a 2026 arXiv paper on machine learning for quantum chemistry. Predicting the Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian, the central matrix in density functional theory, can speed up electronic structure calculations while keeping orbitals and energy levels accessible. HamEvo learns the single self-consistent update step and returns the converged Hamiltonian as its fixed point.

Pretrained on intermediate self-consistent trajectories and calibrated with density-matrix supervision, HamEvo cut Hamiltonian errors by roughly thirty-five to forty-nine percent against direct-regression and deep-equilibrium baselines across standard benchmarks. Its orbital energy errors on drug-like molecules sat near chemical accuracy. Fine-tuning with only twenty reference shapes extended it to molecules of up to one hundred twenty-two atoms, and inference ran up to two hundred forty-two times faster than conventional calculations.
arxiv-2606-14698:
Arulandu settles a quantum measurement puzzle in a 2026 arXiv paper. The quantum pyramids problem asks for the best possible measurement on a set of states. The states are equal-angled and equally likely pure states, set out like a pyramid. Englert and Řeháček had guessed the answer. Recent work cut the proof down to a few entropy bounds by Holevo and Utkin.

Arulandu proves the missing bounds. That certifies the best measurement for obtuse and flat pyramids. For obtuse pyramids, the key step shows local minima cannot take three distinct values. Removing that family leaves an algebra bound. It concerns branches of the Lambert W function. For flat pyramids, he proves a tight norm bound for zero-sum vectors. It holds in every dimension of two or more. The proof uses the equal variables method from symmetric bounds.
arxiv-2606-14798:
Cotton shows that weather modeling and portfolio building secretly use the same math in a 2026 arXiv paper. Spatial statisticians fitting huge weather fields and fund managers splitting portfolios arrived at the same object on their own. It is a damped Schur complement, a conditional spread adjusted by one clear parameter. In spatial models it makes Gaussian pseudo-likelihoods workable when stations outnumber readings.

In allocation, the same object is the leftover risk of a bet net of its hedge. The parameter slides between hierarchical risk parity and the minimum-variance portfolio. Cotton proves both are one operation: reliability shrinkage of a conditional Gaussian. Its closed-form optimum matches classic shrinkage formulas. Each field has supplied what the other lacks. A small test suggests the spatial side's fitted intensity sets the damping better.
arxiv-2606-14898:
Zhang and coauthors propose a pricing framework that treats insurance fairness as a continuum in a 2026 study. Actuarial fairness charges each policyholder their own expected loss, while solidarity fairness pools costs so higher-risk people stay covered. Granular modern data sharpen the tension between those two goals. Regulators also face pressure to protect vulnerable groups from steep premiums.

The alpha-FISP framework adjusts actuarially fair premiums under a budget that limits cross-subsidization inside each risk class. A single parameter, alpha, traces the full spectrum between purely actuarial and purely solidarity pricing. Solvency, the requirement that premiums cover total claims, is guaranteed by construction. The authors prove theoretical guarantees and run numerical experiments showing the method stays computationally tractable. It also aligns with the differing state-level fairness rules found across United States regulation, letting decision-makers pick an explicit operating point.
arxiv-2606-14998:
Condie and coauthors present Rumoca, a Rust-based compiler for the Modelica modeling language, in a 2026 study. Modelica describes cyber-physical systems as equations, but optimization and machine learning workflows live in other tools. Models are usually rewritten by hand for each environment, risking mismatches. Rumoca aims to make one Modelica source feed every backend.

The compiler runs through explicit phases, from parsing to differential-algebraic equation construction and template-driven code generation. Backends emit code for CasADi, SymPy, JAX, Julia, and other targets, agreeing to machine precision. A native Rust runtime also supports real-time, software-in-the-loop simulation. The team reports coverage of the Modelica Standard Library plus compile and simulation benchmarks against an open-source reference. End-to-end cases include real-time control of a quadrotor model. The compiler ships as a VS Code extension and runs in the browser through WebAssembly.
arxiv-2606-15298:
Wang and Yang review theories of superconductivity in bilayer nickelates in a 2026 condensed matter paper. These layered materials superconduct at high temperature under pressure, echoing the cuprates. Their electrons live mainly in two nickel orbitals with different shapes. Strong coupling between the layers is the ingredient most theories build on. The review distills observations and model frameworks. It centers on interlayer pairing, where pairs form between the two layers.

One picture starts from local singlet pairs in the half-filled orbital. Hybridization with the itinerant orbital then spreads those pairs into a coherent superconducting state. The scenario predicts an anisotropic pairing symmetry with gap minima along the zone diagonal. It predicts how the transition temperature should vary with doping and pressure. Several predictions match photoemission and thin-film experiments. Weak-coupling spin-fluctuation theories get a shorter treatment at the end. The review gives the field a shared map.
arxiv-2606-15498:
Safari, Shaveisi, and Nikandish define a new graph for commutative ring theory in 2026, the inclusion graph of annihilators. Its vertices are the nonzero zero-divisors of a ring, the elements that multiply some nonzero element to zero. Two vertices are joined when the annihilator of one, the set of elements that kill it, contains the annihilator of the other.

The team proves the graph is disconnected exactly when the ring is reduced with precisely two minimal prime ideals. When the graph is connected, its diameter is at most four, and its girth is at most six whenever a cycle exists. They also relate it to the complement of the known annihilator graph, which shares the vertices under a different rule. Finally, they characterize all rings whose inclusion graph is complete. The results tie the algebraic shape of a ring to the geometry of a graph built from it.
arxiv-2606-15698:
Sofos studies the Bateman-Horn conjecture on average in 2026, for generalised von Mangoldt functions, asking how polynomial values factor into primes. The conjecture predicts how often an irreducible polynomial takes prime values, tangled with the parity problem, which blocks sieve methods from telling products of two primes from products of three.

Averaging over families softens that barrier. As an application, Sofos proves that for k equal to two or three, almost all Bouniakowsky polynomials represent integers that are a product of exactly k primes. Bouniakowsky polynomials are the irreducible ones not ruled out from taking prime values by local obstructions. The result sidesteps the either-or ambiguity of classics like Chen's theorem on x(x+2), which guarantees infinitely many values with two or three prime factors but cannot say which. Such average-case theorems map the typical factoring behaviour of polynomial values where pointwise answers stay out of reach.
arxiv-2606-15798:
Glozman argues in 2026 that QCD matter above the chiral crossover is still confining, even though one signal makes it look like a free quark gas. Fluctuations of conserved charges behave as if quarks were free, which many read as deconfinement. Meson correlators at the same temperatures tell another story: massless quarks bound into colour singlets by a chromoelectric string.

The resolution is directional. Conserved quark number densities do not propagate in time, only in space. Their propagator in QCD, above about 220 MeV, sits close to the free quark loop. The charges do not see the confining contributions dominating the meson correlators. Glozman pictures the medium as a stringy fluid of overlapping colour-singlet clusters, where quark interchange between clusters, forced by the Pauli principle, makes them quasifree. The same quark-hadron duality is familiar at zero temperature. Apparent freedom can be an artefact of which observable you ask.
arxiv-2606-15998:
Ghosh and Chatterjee argue in 2026 that entity labels are not entity signals, splitting two notions of relevance that retrieval research has conflated. One notion is conceptual: is the entity on-topic for the query? The other is observable: does its presence separate relevant documents from non-relevant ones? The distinction matters because entity links are guesses from an imperfect linker, not ground-truth observations like terms: an entity fired on everywhere carries no signal.

Across four collections, including human judgments, the two notions agree at near-chance levels. Measures of the observable notion, by contrast, agree well with each other. Training on the conceptual notion selects plausible but weak entities, pruning under four percent of non-relevant documents on some collections. Aligning training with the observable notion improves pruning tenfold and lifts open-world retrieval over baselines. The bottleneck, they conclude, is the training target, not the model.
arxiv-2606-16098:
Jangra and colleagues optimize waveguide bends in 2026 for photonic chips built on low-index-contrast materials. Waveguides route light around a chip, and tight bends raise integration density. Bend loss grows severe in platforms such as indium phosphide, where core and cladding indices differ only slightly.

Their answer is an elliptical bend whose width varies along the curve. At a 6 micrometer radius, its loss is 0.22 decibels per 90 degree bend in simulations and analysis. That figure is a 40 percent reduction versus conventional circular bends and 27 percent versus circular width-modulated bends, at only 15 percent more footprint. The team also extends the analytical bend-loss model, based on effective index ideas, to include width modulation effects. The new formulas agree closely with full three-dimensional simulations. Designers gain a quick, trustworthy way to plan compact, low-loss photonic circuits.
arxiv-2606-16598:
Wang and co-authors review in 2026 how ultracold atoms arranged in grids have become programmable machines for topological phases. Topological phases host robust edge states that are hard to study in ordinary materials. Cold-atom systems now sit at a pivotal stage, moving from textbook setups into versatile quantum simulators. The review surveys work across four classes.

The first covers optical lattices, with laser-assisted tunneling and optical Raman lattices. The second builds synthetic ones in momentum space or internal-state space. The third uses Floquet engineering, driving that reshapes the effective lattice. The fourth uses optical tweezer arrays. For each class the authors highlight key breakthroughs, the topological models realized, and the detection and readout techniques used. The field's arc runs from single-particle physics toward hybrid platforms, reaching strongly correlated and nonequilibrium phases; the review maps who can build what, and which probes read it out.
arxiv-2606-16998:
Lesniewski, DeLyser and Noid release a major software upgrade for building coarse-grained models in a 2026 computational chemistry paper. Coarse-graining replaces clusters of atoms with single beads so simulations can reach realistic lengths and times. The BOCS package derives the bead interactions from detailed atomic simulations by force matching, a variational fitting principle.

Version 5.0 adds potentials that depend on the local density around each particle, and on the square gradient of that density, which captures how sharply the density varies. A companion package, PKG-BOCS, runs these potentials inside the LAMMPS simulator, handles complex molecular topologies and lets users define local density flexibly. Test calculations verify the implementation and probe the physics of the new terms. The headline result is practical: local-density potentials markedly improve coarse-grained water models in structure, thermodynamics and transferability at once. That combination is what bottom-up modelers have struggled to achieve.
arxiv-2606-17098:
Akbari benchmarks fast neural X-ray fitting against the slow gold standard in a 2026 astrostatistics paper. Neural posterior estimation fits in milliseconds where nested sampling takes minutes, but drops the older method's calibration guarantees. Trust diagnostics exist in the inference literature, yet nobody had tested them on X-ray spectra.

The benchmark uses one real telescope response, a five-parameter continuum, three brightness regimes and four misspecification families. A posterior-predictive check does catch an unmodeled emission line once counts are high enough. But a small detector gain shift defeats every per-spectrum score, at chance level while distorting the continuum. Only nested sampling's evidence flags it. One neural flow passed all recovery checks while badly calibrated; the cause was undertraining, repaired by conformal methods. The verdict is pointed: recovery metrics never certify calibration, and fast fits still need an evidence check.
arxiv-2606-17298:
Shen, Ding, and Unberath present a 2026 arXiv paper on searching operating room video by text. The hardest queries are implicit and need reasoning, such as asking for the step right before clipping. Standard retrieval matches global embeddings of text and video, which cannot follow such temporal hints. Their method first converts each clip into an action-driven digital twin, a structured record of who did what to which object over time.

Retrieval then works by imagination: a language model drafts a hypothetical digital twin from the query. Matching happens inside one modality with a single encoder instead. An evidence-based refinement step revises the imagined twin against top candidate clips to catch procedure-specific patterns. On a benchmark of implicit queries over robotic knee surgery clips, the method beat the strongest baseline at both rank-one and rank-five recall.
arxiv-2606-17398:
Kwon and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper systematising what is known about using AI to reverse engineer compiled software, a field that has grown fast and fragmented just as quickly. Binary reversing underpins vulnerability hunting, malware analysis, and firmware auditing, yet compilation strips the semantic clues analysts need. The authors analyse well over a hundred papers published since the middle of the last decade. They sort them into dozens of reversing domains by the inference task each one tackles in its pipeline.

A unified taxonomy links classic analysis techniques, the artefacts drawn from binaries, representation choices, learning methods, and downstream tasks. Special attention goes to the emerging roles of large language models and agentic systems in that pipeline. The study finds shared structures beneath approaches that look unrelated on the surface. Persistent technical challenges and evaluation gaps are flagged, with opportunities mapped for the next generation of tools.
arxiv-2606-17598:
Liu and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on MuseVLA, a robot control model that can call extra senses the way a person picks up a tool. Most vision-language-action models see only camera images, so traits like temperature, sound, or radar returns stay invisible to them. MuseVLA first writes a sensor token naming which modality to invoke and what to attend to. It then turns that reading into a grounded sensor image, one shared format for fusing with vision and acting.

Keeping sensor handling outside the main backbone lets new modalities join without retraining the whole model. A synthesis pipeline also dresses existing camera-only video data sets with grounded sensor images, cutting the need for costly multisensory robot data. On a real robot doing dexterous hand tasks, from heat-guided picking to radar-assisted retrieval, success averaged well above the rival baselines.
arxiv-2606-17798:
Yang and colleagues introduce LiveStarPro, a 2026 system for understanding live video streams as they unfold. Video language models usually struggle to watch a continuous stream, decide on their own when to speak, and remember events from long ago in the stream. The design tackles all three problems together for long-horizon viewing.

Three parts carry the design. Streaming Verification Decoding picks the right response moment through single-pass perplexity checks, without special silence tokens. Streaming Causal Attention Masks train the model to align video and language incrementally over streams of varying length. A tree-structured hierarchical memory stores pushed-out history as event chains that can be retrieved later. Together the parts aim at a proactive assistant that answers promptly and forgets far less during prolonged sessions.
arxiv-2606-17898:
Huang and Yao close a long-open gap about wave operators for one-dimensional Schrödinger equations, in a 2026 analysis paper. Wave operators compare a particle moving under a potential with one moving freely, and they were known to behave well on most function spaces. At the two endpoint spaces, however, boundedness was only suspected to fail, largely because of a Hilbert transform lurking in the low-energy part, and no rigorous proof existed.

The authors supply counterexamples. Even for a bounded potential that vanishes outside a bounded interval, the wave operators are unbounded on both endpoint spaces in the generic case. They fail in the remaining exceptional case too, and there the map does not even land in the larger BMO space when starting from bounded inputs. The results complete the endpoint picture for one-dimensional scattering theory.
arxiv-2606-18298:
Checa and colleagues study trivariate splines, piecewise polynomial functions in three variables glued together with set smoothness, in a 2026 mathematics paper. Their setting is the fan formed by a central hyperplane arrangement in three-dimensional space, a first step toward understanding splines on three-dimensional cross-cut partitions, which generalize a well-studied planar case.

The authors bound the counting function for these spline spaces using dimensions of specific Koszul homology modules built from the equations defining the arrangement and the chosen smoothness pattern. That algebraic link lets them compute the spline space dimension in high degrees, settle all values for generic arrangements of five or fewer planes. It also gives the full counting function for larger generic arrangements with constant smoothness. They also apply the method to two concrete smoothness levels for every degree, turning an abstract dimension problem into explicit answers in important cases.
arxiv-2606-18598:
Edmonds and colleagues at Stanford frame lithium mine planning as a decision problem under deep uncertainty and solve it with a partially observable Markov decision process, in a 2026 operations research paper. Deciding which mines to open, when, and with which extraction technology, direct lithium extraction or hard-rock mining, must contend with unknown geology, shifting demand, and volatile prices. Earlier models ignored several of these uncertainties at once.

Their framework plans over belief states using the POMCPOW solver. Across static, linear, exponential, stochastic, and historical price regimes it generally outperformed a suite of human-inspired heuristics, delivering the highest or near-highest discounted reward with competitive emissions and strong demand fulfillment. A tunable parameter traces a smooth trade-off frontier between profit and emissions. The practical lesson is to sequence exploration before committing: belief updates help planners avoid opening early and big into demand ceilings.
arxiv-2606-18798:
Oya and a large team describe the software that will run the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory, the largest gamma-ray observatory, in a 2026 astronomy software paper. The observatory will span northern and southern hemisphere sites. Its telescopes come in three sizes, covering different energy ranges. Someone must plan observations, control the hardware, and absorb data streaming in at multiple gigabits per second per telescope.

That central system is ACADA, the Array Control and Data Acquisition software, built on the ALMA Common Software scheme. Beyond control and oversight, ACADA runs a real-time pipeline that generates science alert candidates as data arrive. Its Transients Handler feeds alerts to the Short-Term Scheduler, so observations can be redirected on sub-minute timescales. That pairs with the telescopes' fast slewing for transient astronomy. The first major release was completed in July 2023, and integrated in tests with the prototype large telescope.
arxiv-2606-18898:
Uray and the team detect anomalies in multivariate time series that arrive sparse, with irregular sampling and gaps, in a 2026 machine learning paper. Industrial monitoring, cybersecurity, and healthcare all depend on spotting patterns across many sensors. Yet detection methods assume evenly sampled data. Real use violates that assumption by design, since protocols transmit only on change.

Their approach models the data with a latent stochastic differential equation. It projects readings onto a continuous-time stochastic system, which handles missing values and irregular sampling, while capturing the cyclic behavior many exhibit. A model is trained on benign data alone. Anomalies are flagged as out-of-distribution samples under it. On six anomaly benchmark datasets, the method ranked first among leading baselines. It remained robust when data were made sparse, a regime where the baselines' performance fell. That supports latent dynamics as an inductive bias for irregular series.
arxiv-2606-18998:
Sinha and colleagues search in 2026 for a superdisk in the radio galaxy J0116-473, a vast flat structure thought to surround the galaxy. Their main goal was to find hydrogen absorption linked to that disk. Data came from the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope in three bands, plus archive X-ray data. A compact bright source near the core also let them probe along the disk plane.

No hydrogen absorption was found, which points to little or no neutral hydrogen in the disk. Maps in the three bands show the galaxy shape in detail, and spectra steepen in a steady way from core to lobes. That pattern fits aging plasma that shines by synchrotron light. The north inner lobe is much steeper than the south one, which may reflect the disk's effect on its surroundings. X-ray data show diffuse glow tied to the lobes.
arxiv-2606-19398:
Ioannides and colleagues introduce S-JEPA in 2026, a self-supervised speech encoder trained with soft clustering anchors. Standard speech encoders predict discrete hard cluster labels at masked positions. That recipe collapses acoustic ambiguity at category boundaries. It also requires pausing training to re-cluster the whole corpus between iterations. Both flaws blur borderline sounds a good representation should keep distinct.

S-JEPA instead trains an encoder-predictor pair to match the soft posteriors of a Gaussian mixture model at masked positions. Training runs as one continuous trajectory in two phases. A fixed mixture model over acoustic features comes first, then an online mixture model over encoder features follows. On a standard speech benchmark suite, S-JEPA reaches the lowest word error rate among evaluated methods under ninety million parameters. It matches a leading baseline on emotion recognition at about half the size, a new efficiency frontier.
arxiv-2606-19498:
Francisca Guzmán-Lastra and Néstor Sepúlveda simulate tiny magnetic swimmers that push themselves through fluid, in a 2026 study. The swimmers are spherocylinders, rod-like grains with rounded ends, each carrying a magnetic dipole. The motion is overdamped, meaning friction rules and inertia barely counts, as at very small scales.

Magnetism enters as two opposite charges set a short distance apart along the rod, a dumbbell that stays well defined at close range. That gap works as a lever arm for magnetic torque, which fights the alignment caused by rods bumping each other. By tuning charge gap and dipole strength apart, the pair map five shared states. The states are gas, polar flock, chain, vortex-aligned, and locked-dimer phases. Rod length plus spread-out charge thus give simple knobs for steering magnetic active matter and microswimmer design.
arxiv-2606-19598:
Ameya Salvi and Jie Hu present Fail-RAG in 2026, a framework that spots robot failures in warehouses. Warehouse robots handling goods must react when operations go wrong, from dropped loads to blocked paths. Rule-based detectors crack when failure forms shift with changing tasks and settings.

Fail-RAG embeds failure images and context, then searches a failure database by similarity. That retrieval step follows the retrieval-augmented generation pattern used in language systems. Vision-language models then analyse matched failures and describe details under a fixed instruction template. Tests run in simulation and on real hardware, with fixed arms and a mobile manipulator. Tasks mirror common warehouse automation work. Failure detection accuracy beats off-the-shelf vision-language models by 25 percentage points on average. The margin holds across five types of robot operations, pointing to real-world readiness.
arxiv-2606-20098:
Sina Beyraghi and five colleagues test whether generative models can fabricate realistic wireless channel data for a specific place, sparing engineers the cost of measuring every site by hand. Their 2026 paper compares two location-aware generators for MIMO channels, the matrices describing how signals travel between many antennas: a conditional diffusion model and a conditional flow matching model. Both take user coordinates as input, so synthetic channels keep the spatial layout of the real site.

Judged on fidelity, speed, and usefulness for tasks such as channel compression and beam alignment, both models captured site character well at 28 and 3.5 gigahertz, in clear and blocked settings alike, even from scarce real data. The flow matching model matched diffusion quality at roughly a tenth of the sampling time. Padding small real datasets with synthetic channels gave hefty downstream gains, a practical route toward AI-native network design.
arxiv-2606-20298:
John Palastro and twelve colleagues remove the main speed limit on laser wakefield accelerators by structuring the laser pulse inside a plasma waveguide. Their 2026 paper addresses dephasing: electrons trapped in a plasma wave eventually outrun its accelerating phase, capping their energy. Flying-focus pulses can drive a wake at light speed, but at the cost of varying spot size, long pulses, or huge plasma volumes. The team's alternative superposes waveguide modes with chosen frequencies, forming a pulse whose wake travels at light speed.

The spot size stays constant and the pulse ultrashort, while the waveguide shrinks the required plasma volume sharply. Scaling laws and quasi-3D simulations show the single-stage energy gain growing linearly with the number of modes in the pulse. Compact accelerators built this way could serve as photon sources beyond the few national laboratories hosting today's machines.
arxiv-2606-20698:
Kai Tang and many colleagues propose SafeDojo in 2026, a safe reinforcement learning framework for vision-language-action robot policies. Safe control is required before such robots can work in open settings. Older safe methods need costly real-world trials or hand-built safety functions. Neither scales well. SafeDojo instead lets a policy learn safe actions inside an interactive video world model, imagining outcomes before acting.

The world model predicts future frames for a proposed action chunk. A ResNet classifier estimates task progress from imagined frames. A small safety head predicts safety cost per step from latent context and the action. Task reward and safety cost stay separate, then are balanced during learning. Learning in imagination could cut dangerous real trials. It also gives a clearer signal about which actions advance a task and which ones create risk, a split that single-score training often hides.
arxiv-2606-21098:
Younghan and three colleagues, named by given names in the hosted text, propose an LLM-based evaluation method in 2026 for phrase break annotations in speech. Phrase breaks mark where a speaker pauses. Subtle differences shape clarity and naturalness. Single-reference scoring assumes one correct phrasing per utterance. Many utterances, however, allow several valid phrasings. Human judgment is flexible but costly and unscalable.

Their method generates multiple valid phrasings from minimal demonstrations. It models the one-to-many nature of prosodic phrasing directly. A Korean testbed holds over a thousand annotations across five strategies. The method aligns with human judgment better than single-reference scoring. Both acceptance behavior and score correlation improve. Scalable multi-reference scoring could improve text-to-speech training, where punishing a valid phrasing teaches systems to sound stilted and less human.
arxiv-2606-21398:
Rithvik Jonna and four colleagues present BIT-Nav in 2026, a brain-inspired memory that helps vision-language models navigate over long routes. Such models usually pick a fixed set of past camera frames as context, which thins out badly as journeys lengthen; more frames bring no gain. BIT-Nav instead compresses the whole motion history, turn patterns, total displacement, and path shape, into one learned memory token.

A recurrent encoder trained with a contrastive objective on augmented route pairs produces the token, modeled on how the hippocampus compresses experience. Appended at each decision step, it adds negligible cost whatever the route length. BIT-Nav reaches 0.83 accuracy on cumulative heading estimation and matches frame-heavy baselines on action-frequency inference at twenty-two times lower token cost, where single frames collapse on long routes.
arxiv-2606-21698:
Erik Voogd, Einar Broch Johnsen, Åsmund Aqissiaq Arild Kløvstad, Jurriaan Rot, and Alexandra Silva give symbolic execution a free correctness guarantee in 2026. Symbolic execution, running programs with symbolic rather than concrete values, powers bug finding and verification. But its semantics is usually hand-built apart from the language's real semantics, and proving the two agree is tedious.

Their symbolic SOS is a rule format that states both the concrete and the symbolic semantics at once. From any specification in the format, the generated symbolic semantics is provably both correct and complete relative to the concrete one. It needs only the language's algebraic signature, so it works for any language. Building on the GSOS tradition of compositional rule formats, the work turns a per-language proof burden into a by-design property.
arxiv-2606-21798:
Jo and colleagues, writing in 2026, use leftover pump light as a diagnostic for high-power Yb:YAG thin-disk lasers. In these lasers a thin crystal disk is pumped through thirty-two passes, and the pump power that survives the final pass reflects how much energy the disk absorbed. Absorption shifts while the laser runs, because stimulated emission lowers the population inversion that drives it.

The team coupled a rate-equation model to accumulated pump flux, signal flux inside the cavity, and a term for amplified spontaneous emission draining the inversion. Two disks were tested both idle and lasing in many modes. The model reproduced residual pump fractions within 2.4 percent when idle and 1.8 percent while lasing, and output power within 1.3 percent of measurements. Lasing raised effective absorption above the idle level, though it stayed below the room-temperature small-signal value, and the fitted state also guided heat-load estimates.
arxiv-2606-22098:
Celebre and colleagues simulate, in 2026, how plasma turbulence can be driven by waves colliding with density holes, treating the holes as obstacles in the flow. In weakly collisional plasmas, turbulent energy cascades from large scales toward small ones, eventually heating particles. Density gaps at the Debye scale and below distort passing electrostatic waves and reshape that cascade in ways that remain poorly understood.

Using high-resolution Vlasov-Poisson simulations, which evolve the full particle distribution in phase space, the team built an idealized kinetic regime for the interaction. The interplay between electrostatic waves and density gaps redistributed a strongly anisotropic energy cascade throughout the full phase space, not just along the wave direction. The results reveal how inhomogeneities steer structure formation and the small-scale-directed turbulent flow. The authors present the regime as a clean model of a transition to nonlinearity, now shown inside a kinetic plasma.
arxiv-2606-22698:
Isadora White, Yasaman Jafari, and Taylor Berg-Kirkpatrick investigate forensic identification of chatbots in this 2026 paper. Scams powered by language models run through anonymous endpoints, hiding which provider's model does the talking. Attribution means naming that base model without access to parameters or the hidden system prompt. Fingerprinting means detecting when two endpoints share the same prompt.

Their classifiers identified the base model with ninety-eight percent accuracy from a few turns of ordinary conversation. Attributing the system prompt itself proved possible but costly, since each new prompt demands retraining on large data. For the open-ended case, their cross-encoder fingerprinting reached an AUC around 0.77 on entirely unseen system prompts, with an F1 score of about zero point seven. Aggregating fifty conversations from each target agent boosted the AUC to 0.943, near-perfect separation. Unseen prompts, they conclude, can be fingerprinted robustly from a few ordinary turns.
arxiv-2606-22798:
Kang Chen and five colleagues ask whether the same token means the same internal state in this 2026 paper. In sparse mixture-of-experts models, a router assigns each token to a few expert subnetworks. Even with the emitted token held fixed at repeated anchor points, the experts producing it still separate task context, history, and reasoning-effort mode.

That leftover structure supports control at test time. Near anchor tokens that open or close a final answer, routing patterns already align with the eventual answer's basin. Their method, RAD, represents each rollout by its routing states near an anchor and returns the densest cluster center, without parsing answer strings. Across ten model configurations and six datasets spanning math, science questions, and code, RAD matched majority voting where string voting works. It also selected code answers directly, where exact-string voting is ill-defined, and improved patch choice on a software benchmark.
arxiv-2606-22998:
Jianuo Cao and colleagues make humanoid robot motion obey the robot's own controller in a 2026 robotics paper. Text-to-motion generators turn a written instruction into movement. Most train on human motion retargeted onto robot bodies. Such data teaches what motion means, but not what a specific controller can balance, actuate, or survive. Generated moves can therefore look right yet prove impossible to perform. The team calls its framework Texedo.

Cao and colleagues keep the original generator and scale up effort at test time instead. For each prompt, Texedo samples several candidate motions. A feasibility judge, trained on real controller rollouts, rejects moves the robot cannot execute. Among the survivors, a second judge picks the motion matching the text best. In large simulations and on a real Unitree G1 robot, the selection raised both tracking accuracy and text agreement.
arxiv-2606-23198:
Raphaël Berthier and Loucas Pillaud-Vivien explain incremental learning inside mirror flows in a 2026 machine learning theory paper. Mirror flows are continuous training dynamics built from a loss and a mirror potential, a convex function shaping the geometry of updates. Neural training often learns in stages, capturing simple structure first and detail later. The authors study mirror flows from a convex quadratic loss with a general convex potential. Starting near the boundary of the potential's domain turns out to be the key regime.

Berthier and Pillaud-Vivien show that rescaled trajectories converge to a limiting flow whose potential is the indicator of the domain. In that limit, the variable at each time minimizes the loss over a hypothesis set that grows with the dual variable. This picture explains incremental learning in mirror flows through one general mechanism.
arxiv-2606-23698:
Matsuoka shows how a flagship AI chip with crippled double precision arithmetic could still run high precision Fourier transforms at full speed, in a 2026 paper on high performance computing. NVIDIA's newest Blackwell Ultra processor slashes FP64 throughput, the double precision arithmetic scientific codes rely on, to a fraction of its predecessor. Emulation schemes route arithmetic through fast FP8 tensor cores instead. A companion study covered matrix operations but not the three dimensional fast Fourier transform.

The proposed Ozaki Bailey FFT splits the transform so its heavy steps become FP8 matrix products. The reconstruction step becomes the bottleneck, and a fixed point accumulator design answers it with exact summation on the integer pipeline. Closed form analysis gives bandwidth floors the chip can meet, projecting a transform time close to the memory bound. The author stresses these figures are model upper bounds, not measurements.
arxiv-2606-24398:
Ortiz and colleagues report a nebula around a kind of star that should not be able to produce one. Subdwarf B stars emit too few ionising photons to light a circumstellar shell. A handful wear nebulae anyway. The new case, described in 2026, surrounds TYC 3315-1807-1, a star moving unusually fast across the sky. Its parabolic hydrogen-alpha nebula points its apex half an arcminute ahead of the star, 

A wider parabolic nebula appears in infrared images from WISE. Far-ultraviolet emission from GALEX wraps around the star inside both. Like most nebula-bearing subdwarfs, this one races across the Galactic plane at high speed. Its low luminosity cannot give its wind the momentum a bow shock needs. The authors argue instead for a Mach wave: a shock cone from supersonic motion, partly excited by shocks and photoionisation. Ortiz's discovery adds a data point to a small, puzzling class.
arxiv-2606-24498:
Li and colleagues teach object detectors to follow a pointing finger. Grounding deictic gestures, understanding what someone points at, supports augmented reality and human robot teamwork. Transformer detectors excel at general object detection. Their global attention neglects micro geometric links, though. The pointing ray implied by a finger's pose is captured poorly. The failure shows as pointing drift and ambiguity, when targets are distant or crowded.

VistaRef, their 2026 framework, enhances spatial direction awareness inside the detection pipeline. It begins with local geometric analysis of the pointing hand and ray. The design goal is to anchor the search for the referent along the direction the gesture actually indicates. Li's team frames pointing not as ordinary detection with an extra cue, but as a geometry problem first. Recover the ray faithfully, and the target object follows from where that ray lands in the scene.
arxiv-2606-24798:
Ismaele Masiello and four colleagues find a simpler way to measure weak values in an interferometer. Weak values describe quantum systems between a chosen start and end state. Standard extraction uses weak interactions with a meter state, which adds complexity and slows measurement. The new method needs neither meter states nor weak interactions. It works in a generalised Mach Zehnder interferometer, a device splitting a wave along two paths. Only output intensities and controlled phase shifts between paths are used.

The team demonstrates the technique with matter wave interferometry. They recover path weak values fully from the intensity data. Anomalous weak values show up, as expected for genuinely quantum behaviour. Equivalently, the data imply negative quasiprobability distributions. Accuracy matches or beats the conventional approach. Measurement times shrink because the setup is simpler. Masiello and colleagues note the scheme transfers directly to a broad class of two level quantum experiments.
arxiv-2606-24898:
Rituraj Sharma and Tu Vu expose a blind spot in how looped language models are trained. Looped models reuse one block many times, turning hidden states into a running state. Each loop's state is decoded into a prediction and fed onward. The authors ask which state variables the per loop loss actually controls. Their answer: only the variables the readout can see.

Common readouts like RMSNorm are blind to radial scale, so the loss cannot feel it. The recurrent loop, though, keeps carrying and updating exactly that scale. In looped transformers of 44 and 129 million parameters, hidden state norms balloon into the thousands despite per loop training. Scale visible readouts and explicit norm penalties hold norms in the tens instead. Removing scale from the recurrence is the complementary fix. Scale controlled variants then reach lower perplexity at matched depth. The design rule: dense supervision trains exits, not loop scale.
arxiv-2606-24998:
Jessica Chudnovsky and eight colleagues measure how repeated training data damages language models. Models are running out of quality text, and deduplicated corpora keep some repetition. Older studies predated Chinchilla style scaling, so the cost was only measured indirectly. The team fits a no repetition scaling law and reports damage as compute equivalent gain or loss.

With compute on repeated data held fixed, loss peaks at an intermediate repeat count. Repeating a moderate subset a moderate number of times hurts most. The peak's location follows a power law in model size, and the most damaging repeat count grows faster than compute itself. When repeated documents eat ten percent of the training budget, the loss can equal a clean run on far less compute. A misspecified regression model with duplicates reproduces it, so the effect is not specific to language models.
arxiv-2606-25598:
Data re-uploading circuits feed classical data into a quantum processor again and again. Making the uploads fixed rather than tunable strips the design down. Remarkably, the stripped circuits keep full expressive power. Anthony Yuezhang Liu and Lirandë Pira price that stripping in 2026. How much deeper must a fixed circuit grow to match a tunable one at a given accuracy? Their answer: the depth grows only polylogarithmically in the inverse error. That improves the polynomial growth known before, at the same overhead.

The proof uses tools for smooth functions plus a generalised quantum signal processing theorem. A catch also emerges. Some target circuits carry a periodic mismatch that fixed uploads cannot dodge. A classical inequality turns that block into a matching lower bound, also logarithmic. Expressive power, the authors show, moves from tunable frequencies into depth at a precisely measured exchange rate.
arxiv-2606-25998:
Eyasu Getahun Chekole and colleagues build a login system around an unusual signal: the sound of a user blowing. Fingerprints and faces are hard to revoke when stolen. They can also be faked, and their stored templates can leak private traits. BlowLive pairs blow acoustics with facial scans as two login factors. One factor is behaviour, and the other is body-based.

Raw templates never get stored. A fuzzy extractor turns the noisy signals into stable cryptographic keys instead. Those keys then carry out the authentication. A Doppler shift check adds liveness proof, which guards against recordings and deepfakes. Tests with fifty participants reach very high accuracy. Blow acoustics alone score above ninety-nine percent. Face and fused modes reach full accuracy, and liveness detection scores nearly as high. Templates stay protected, and credentials can be revoked and reissued.
arxiv-2606-26098:
Quinn Casey and colleagues hunt local lookalikes of the Little Red Dots, compact red sources JWST found far away. Those distant dots show broad hydrogen lines, faint X-rays, and spectra that fit neither stars nor normal active nuclei. Nearby analogues would allow far richer study. Filter arithmetic opens the door. Sloan survey filters at two modest redshifts sample the same light JWST used at high redshift.

About thirteen hundred Sloan quasars share the dots' photometric colours. The team names this sample Local Red Dots. A subset with V-shaped continua shows strong higher-order Balmer absorption and high-ionization neon emission. JWST would likely miss both features. Composite spectra of the local sample match stacked distant dots well. A reddened active nucleus plus host galaxy, with or without a cool blackbody, fits the shape. Surprisingly, the local dots show X-rays at normal quasar rates.
arxiv-2606-26198:
Kenan Qu, Daniel Bhatti, and Nathaniel Fisch propose a lensless way to photograph fusion plasmas at finer scales. X-ray radiography reads the shape and dynamics of inertial confinement implosions. Apertures cap its resolution near several microns: smaller holes starve the detector and worsen diffraction blur. Submicron views would link large implosion asymmetries to the fine turbulence where mixing happens. Their method uses intensity correlations instead of a lens.

Chaotic far-field speckles carry the image. Fourier-transforming their spatial correlations rebuilds the plasma's shape, a Hanbury Brown-Twiss style trick. Third-order correlations supply closure phases that restore the missing Fourier phase. A numerical test probes a spiral plasma structure with fifty-kilovolt X-rays. Submicron reconstruction succeeds in the simulation. The single-shot design suits implosions, which cannot be repeated for a second exposure. Low self-emission conditions are the stated operating regime.
arxiv-2606-26298:
Jakob Salfeld-Nebgen proposes governing AI agents by their actions, not their inner reasoning. Agents are nearing jobs with irreversible stakes, like prescribing medicine and deploying production software. Human institutions faced powerful autonomous actors before, and their answer was attestation: demand independently checked evidence at the moment of action. His model formalizes that pattern for software agents. The agent plans and reasons freely, but holds no power to execute high-risk acts alone.

Execution needs preconditions. Each one must be attested by its own authoritative source, bound cryptographically to a declared intent, and passed by a deterministic policy. Every decision lands in a tamper-evident log that outsiders can re-verify. A proof-of-concept implementation shows the machinery working. Software deployment and clinical prescribing serve as the worked examples. Governance moves from watching the agent think to checking the evidence before it acts.
arxiv-2606-26498:
Erhan Bayraktar, Martin Hernandez, Qinxin Yan, and Yuhua Zhu bridge two views of mean-field control. Mean-field problems steer a whole population, described by its overall distribution, rather than one agent. The population evolves continuously by an unknown equation. Only snapshots at discrete times are observed. Standard evaluation equations need the unknown drift and diffusion, which snapshots cannot identify.

The authors' Mean-Field PhiBE folds discrete-time transition data into a continuous-time equation on the space of distributions. It replaces the unknown dynamics terms with observable quantities built from the data. The structure of the classical evaluation equation is preserved. Model-free learning from discrete data thus becomes possible without pretending the dynamics are known. The work extends an earlier single-agent method to the population setting.
arxiv-2606-26698:
Eleni Papadopulos, Firoj Alam, and Giovanni Da San Martino improve automatic detection of logical fallacies. A fallacy is a defective pattern of reasoning that misleads. Fallacies appear in subtle, varied forms that resist fixed templates. The authors ask whether combining abstract logical structure with everyday language cues classifies them better. Their framework extracts such patterns directly from examples.

A large language model reads flawed texts with their explanations. It draws out pattern descriptions that merge logical form with everyday wording. Those patterns then guide classification in zero-shot and one-shot settings, meaning with no example or one example given. Results improved significantly over zero-shot baselines and beat competing approaches. Tests on a second data set confirmed the method generalises. The authors present pattern mining from data as a good way to build logical descriptions.
arxiv-2606-27198:
Omland studies when twisted group algebras enjoy a strong tidiness property called selflessness. Such algebras, built from a discrete group with a twisting rule, arise in operator algebra theory. Selfless algebras are simple, have a single trace, and compare pieces cleanly. Amenable groups, whose algebras are nuclear and tame, are the hard side of the question. For infinite finitely generated virtually nilpotent groups, In 2026, Omland shows selflessness holds exactly when Kleppner's condition holds.

For the wider FC-hypercentral class, the same answer holds up to a stability proviso tied to finite nuclear dimension. Inclusions built from normal subgroups get a parallel treatment. A relative Kleppner test governs those cases. An inclusion is selfless exactly when the smaller algebra is selfless and the relative condition holds. For the nilpotent family, inclusion selflessness reduces to that relative test alone. Classical simplicity questions thereby merge with modern tidiness theory.
arxiv-2606-27598:
Ultra-fine entity typing assigns very specific labels to names in text. A label might call someone a minor-league coach, not just an athlete. Rare labels in the long tail are hard to learn. Mreedul Gupta and four colleagues point to one cause. Most systems read only the sentence around a mention. The clues often sit several sentences away.

Gupta's team created Narrative-UFET to test this idea. Each mention is paired with a short generated story built around it. Two versions were tested. In one, the entity's type stays constant through the story. In the other, the type shifts midway. Narrative context improved typing on long-tail types. It beat sentence-level baselines in both versions. The shifting version gave the stronger signal. Synthetic narratives even beat naturally occurring context. Controlled stories can expose signals that real text leaves buried, though large room for improvement remains.
arxiv-2606-27898:
Geometric statistics summarise spatial point patterns by adding up local scores. Central limit theorems say such sums turn Gaussian for large samples. Tianshu Cong strengthens those results in 2026 for marked point processes with dependent marks. Earlier work needed fast decay of correlations. Cong and Xia had derived convergence rates for unmarked processes in 2023. The new paper pushes further, to weak mixing conditions.

The mixing conditions are stated through checkable geometric criteria. They yield rates of normal approximation in the Wasserstein distance. A large class of such processes is covered. Examples include determinantal point processes and continuum percolation. Unevenly spaced time series and interacting diffusions on spatial random graphs also qualify. Local U-statistics are included. Stein's method underlies the rate calculations. The result widens the reach of quantitative limit theorems for spatial data.
arxiv-2606-27998:
Marcus Chijoff, Michal Ferov, and Stephan Tornier study groups acting on trees in 2026. The groups are (P)-closed, a class parametrised by Reid and Smith. Their parameters are local action diagrams, graph-based combinatorial structures. Group properties like being locally compact, discrete, or simple can be read off the diagram. The authors describe translations of these groups and their axes in diagram terms.

Two applications follow. The scale function of (P)-closed groups is determined. Unimodular and uniscalar such groups are characterised. The uniscalar characterisation answers a question posed by Thomas Weigel. The scale function measures how a group element stretches certain subgroups under conjugation. Computing it for a whole class at once is the advance. Local action diagrams turn topological questions into combinatorial ones. The paper exploits that translation systematically.
arxiv-2606-28498:
Manuel Szewc, writing alone, protects collider searches from their own machine learning. Modern analyses often let a learned model estimate the background likelihood directly. But systematic effects inside that estimate are hard to quantify and can bias the signal strength a search reports, the very number the experiment exists to measure.

Szewc's Minimum Resolution Likelihood method defines a fiducial signal region chosen so that the troublesome systematic effects are converted into ordinary statistical uncertainties. On toy examples and on a realistic application, a di-Higgs search using the HI-SIGMA technique, the resulting signal strength estimates come out either unbiased or consistent with zero. Rather than trusting a black box harder, the method redraws the analysis boundary so its errors become countable.
arxiv-2606-28698:
Straeter, Tsesmelis and Kwek tackle a detection problem in quantum optics: proving that two light-based systems are entangled when their states are not of the simple Gaussian kind. Entanglement, a link where measuring one partner affects the other, is easy to certify for Gaussian states from basic statistics. Some non-Gaussian states slip past every such test, and catching them has needed complex detectors and several copies of the state.

Their protocol needs only one copy and ordinary homodyne measurement, which reads one property of light at random settings. From those readings they build unbiased estimators, meaning averages that aim at the true value, for the moments behind a known entanglement test. On six families of states, the method reached a 95 percent one-sided detection chance. It used roughly a thousand to ten thousand readings for states of modest energy. That puts such tests within reach of current laboratories.
arxiv-2606-28998:
Sivapiran and Uddin study whether aligning language models, tuning them on preference data, helps or hurts code generation. Alignment is well studied for chat, but little is known for coding, where output must be both correct and well crafted: readable, secure and maintainable. They also ask whether alignment should start from a base pretrained model or from its instruction-tuned version.

Five leading models were tuned with two reward-free alignment methods, starting from both versions of each. Preference pairs came from a pipeline that labels one solution accepted and another rejected. Correctness was tested on four code benchmarks. Quality was scored on a separate benchmark across five dimensions of software practice. Starting from pretrained models gave larger relative gains, but those models still trailed their finetuned counterparts in accuracy. Alignment narrowed that gap. Quality gains came more reliably than correctness gains. Starting from finetuned models sometimes made results worse.
arxiv-2606-29498:
Karim, Nguyen, Bekit, and Yilmaz extend weakly supervised video anomaly detection, which learns from videos labelled only as normal or abnormal overall. Most work finds when an anomaly happens but ignores where it sits inside the frame. That spatial gap hurts real deployment, where operators need to see the exact region involved.

Their patch-based framework scores small grid regions of each frame under multiple instance learning, which trains from bag-level labels alone. A strategy called Proximity-Aware Top-k selection picks the most suspicious regions while respecting their closeness in space and time. The model thus produces fine-grained spatial anomaly maps without any bounding-box supervision during training. The authors report that it surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods across several benchmarks, with large gains. They also release test-set box annotations, code, and pretrained models.
arxiv-2606-29598:
