Amir, Chriki, and Omer argue that liability insurance could unlock artificial intelligence legal services while protecting users. Automated advice could widen access to justice, yet two barriers loom: catastrophic risk to a user from bad advice, and weak accountability when failures occur.

Current regulation leans on human oversight requirements, which raise costs and limit scale. Insurance, the authors propose, spreads risk across many users instead. Performance-based premiums would reward providers that improve quality. Their model sets clear risk thresholds, simpler compensation mechanisms, and ongoing performance monitoring. Rather than trying to eliminate every risk in advance, the framework manages risk directly. That, they argue, lets automated legal services scale while keeping robust user protections in place.
arxiv-2606-29698:
Laukkonen proposes that many findings from meditation science fit one measurable construct: the brain's functional signal-to-noise ratio. Signal means neural activity that tracks goal-relevant causes of input. Noise means leftover activity. A clear mind, on this account, is a high-ratio mind.

Meditation, he argues, boosts the ratio two ways: boosting signal, and clearing noise. Deepening practice further reduces self-focused filtering and shifts brain activity toward a critical regime, an efficient state for passing information. The framework can be tested, and could be proven wrong, with standard neural measures. It also helps explain why meditation aids many conditions linked to low signal-to-noise states, and it suggests meditating brains may be easier for brain-computer tools to read.
arxiv-2606-29898:
Huang and four colleagues tackle a bottleneck in robot learning. Checking a manipulation policy in the real world is costly and sparse. Yet the usual offline proxy, validation loss on demonstrations, tracks real performance poorly.

Their metric, Critical Interval MSE, computes prediction error only on the task-critical segments of a demonstration, the moments that decide success. It pairs this with simple action-alignment steps that mimic rollout conditions. Across simulation and real robots, the metric's correlation with real rollout performance reaches a Spearman rank value of minus 0.87. That is much closer to the ideal minus one than raw error's minus 0.61. Sensitivity checks show the metric is robust to its settings, and the authors map where it can mislead under distribution shift.
arxiv-2606-29998:
Adrienne Tuynman and Timothée Mathieu build sequential tests for election polls that can stop early. Pollsters want to quit collecting data as soon as results are safe. E-values, a modern tool for sequential testing, make that possible. The authors develop their theory of posterior optimal e-values. Voting systems provide their running example throughout.

They design tests for Condorcet, Borda, and Schulze voting rules. The Schulze test is, they note, the first statistical treatment of that system. The core construction handles multivariate Bernoulli data with composite hypotheses. The null and alternative parameter sets may even be non-convex. A Frank-Wolfe algorithm computes the optimal e-values efficiently. That algorithm also computes reverse information projections quite generally. Simulations and real French 2022 presidential election data show the gains. Both statistical power and sample size improve over leading methods.
arxiv-2606-30498:
Laines Schmalwasser and four colleagues check whether interpretable AI models' concepts mean what they claim to mean. Concept bottleneck models route predictions through human concepts first. Post-hoc versions learn those concepts without task-specific labels. They borrow outside datasets or vision-language model labels. High accuracy can hide meaningless concepts. Random projections sometimes score well, a warning sign. The authors analyze the learned projections directly.

Two failure modes are identified and formalized. Concepts learned from outside data can shift off-target harmfully. An upper bound sizes the error that shift introduces. Labels generated by vision-language models carry steady noise instead. That noise also produces unfaithful projections. New metrics separate faithfulness from raw accuracy cleanly. Experiments span real-world and synthetic benchmarks. The metrics catch unfaithful behavior that accuracy checks miss. The work argues evaluation must test meaning, not just scores.
arxiv-2606-30598:
Estimating the 3D pose of hands and held objects from head-worn camera video is the goal for Siddhant Bansal and five colleagues, who introduce two linked contributions in 2026. Real-world, or in-the-wild, egocentric footage is hard to learn from because hands hide objects and contact points stay ambiguous. Lab datasets are scarce and scripted, so the team built training data from everyday kitchen activity instead.

Their EPIC-Contact dataset holds about twenty-three hundred clips and sixty-two thousand frames, with dense two-way contact maps and posed 3D meshes. Their model, HOPformer, predicts both hands and the object together in one pass, using hand cues to guide object features. On the lab benchmark ARCTIC it reached a success rate above eighty-two percent, beating the prior best by six points. On EPIC-Contact it nearly doubled success and cut contact error by three quarters.
arxiv-2606-30698:
Wentong Tian and six colleagues give a surgical robot a sense of where it is in a procedure. Their setting is endovascular intervention, steering a thin guidewire through a patient's blood vessels. Vessel shapes differ per patient, and fixed reward functions, the scores that guide a learning controller, cannot adapt as the task moves from one vessel segment to the next.

Their framework puts a multimodal language model in charge of procedural reasoning. It reads live images, infers the current navigation context, and reweights the reward components for that phase. The model never issues low-level motor commands; it only reshapes what the controller values, so one policy can balance competing goals across tricky transitions. Experiments on a physical robotic platform, across varied vessel scenarios, showed better task reliability and smoother navigation than static-reward methods.
arxiv-2606-31098:
Liu and six colleagues present PiLoT v2, a system that tells a drone where it is when satellite navigation is blocked or lost. The earlier PiLoT matched drone video against a single rendered view from a 3D mesh. That worked well but needed heavy meshes. Storage, map capture, and rendering costs all blocked use on small onboard computers.

PiLoT v2 matches pixels directly against flat map products instead: true digital orthophoto maps and digital surface models. Cropping a map is far cheaper than rendering a 3D scene. A cross-view network bridges the gap between flat map crops and slanted drone views. Gravity direction and a single-point laser range feed into the pose calculation as extra anchors. Tests show accuracy matching or beating the older system, at far lower storage and compute cost.
arxiv-2606-31298:
Fragkos and eleven colleagues probe the normal state of TiSe2, a layered crystal known for charge density waves, patterns where electrons settle into a regular ripple. Using time- and angle-resolved photoemission with extreme ultraviolet light, they map excited electron bands in three related materials at room temperature. First-principles electron-phonon calculations sit beside the measurements.

In HfTe2 and ZrTe2, heat-driven lattice vibration only broadens bands a little. In TiSe2, strong electron-phonon coupling wipes out spectral weight in a momentum-dependent way, opening pseudogaps that reach about 1 electron volt above the Fermi level. The normal phase of TiSe2 is thus a phonon-induced pseudogap phase ruled by charge density wave fluctuations, a missing piece of its phase diagram with lessons for similar layered crystals.
arxiv-2606-31598:
Shafir and Kosloff tackle a memory wall in quantum simulation: the main step applies a Hamiltonian, the operator encoding a system's energy, to a state vector. Yet storing that operator can exceed any single accelerator's memory. Their answer is a matrix-free framework in which the operator is never built in full. Blocks are generated, loaded or cached only when their action is needed.

An adaptive planner chooses block size, cache strategy, GPU grouping and row distribution from memory and workload estimates. It uses analytic, measured or learned rules to pick among procedural generation and several caching schemes. Dropping the requirement that the whole dense matrix fit in memory turns a hard barrier into a tunable trade-off among generation cost, data movement, parallel scheduling and accuracy.
arxiv-2608-00098:
Fan, Li, and Zhu argue that the active ingredient is the right unit for safe medication recommendation. Drug codes treat each medicine as one indivisible token. Molecular substructures sit finer than interaction knowledge is organized. The ingredient level fills the gap between those two. Their GRAIN framework is built around it.

A selective state space backbone reads patient trajectories in linear time. Diagnoses, procedures, and past medicines form those trajectories. Three knowledge sources join on a shared vocabulary: drug-level DDI graphs, ingredient-level DDI graphs, and co-prescription graphs. A proportional controller tunes the accuracy-safety trade-off from validation data. On MIMIC-IV, GRAIN beat a MambaHealth baseline on all standard metrics. Its drug-level DDI rate fell from 0.1875 to 0.0948.
arxiv-2608-00198:
Ruiz and co-authors present AutoCause, a Python framework for causal discovery in environmental time series. Such work demands expert choices at many points. Method choice, independence tests, lag horizons, and sample size all matter. Multiple-testing control and evidence reading add more. Applied unevenly, these choices yield graphs that cannot be compared or audited.

AutoCause records each decision and derives defaults from a causal-audit module. Domain-informed overrides are still admitted. It wraps four causal discovery methods from three families. Non-causal reference models join the toolkit. Links are graded by method-count support. On 145 data sets, methods recovered complementary parts of reference graphs. Majority-supported links were more precise on synthetic tests, they report.
arxiv-2608-00298:
Cui and co-authors set a test standard for interactive driving simulators. World models can react to the planner under test in real time. They can produce rare and safety-critical rollouts on demand. A scenario thus becomes a family, not a fixed replay. The question shifts to what closed-loop evidence is enough for a test intent.

Their WM-Cov layer turns raw provider outputs into requested, realized, and valid evidence. It reports coverage growth, valid-failure discovery, and failure-mode diversity. Realism, artifact suppression, and duplicate accounting join the score set. Studies span TeraSim events, mixed trace pools, and a DriveArena matrix. Dangerous-looking events included valid failures, duplicates, and artifacts. Valid evidence under budget, not raw failures, should judge such testing, they argue.
assemblies-al-hariri-steingass-1898:
F. Steingass completed the first English Assemblies of Al-Hariri with Volume II, published in 1898 for the Oriental Translation Fund. Thomas Chenery had begun the work a generation earlier and died with it unfinished. Steingass carried the Maqamat to their fiftieth assembly, where Abu Zayd's long career of disguise and eloquence closes.

The rogue's tricks grow bolder and his speeches finer as the end nears. Rhymed prose in Arabic is nearly untranslatable, yet the translators' effort opened the book's design to English readers. With Volume II the West gained the whole of a work Arabic letters rank among their highest ornaments.
balzac-courtesans-life-waring-1898:
Esther, a courtesan who found brief peace in love, is dragged back into Paris's hidden world in Scenes from a Courtesan's Life. James Waring's 1898 translation carries Balzac's vast sequel to Lost Illusions, full of crime and disguise. Lucien de Rubempré returns, now kept by the banker Nucingen and watched by the convict Vautrin.

Vautrin, posing as a priest, runs a web of blackmail, theft, and police spies across the city. Esther's fate shows the price of trying to leave that world alive and free. The novel opens the criminal depths beneath the Human Comedy's bright salons, where money and crime trade places nightly.
bargarran-sadducismus-debellatus-1698:
Strange fits seized Christian Shaw of Bargarran in 1696, and the tale grew into Scotland's last great witch case. Sadducismus Debellatus, printed in 1698, gives the full narrative of the Bargarran witchcrafts. Its account supplied much of the proof behind the Paisley trials of 1697.

The book tells of pins and wool cast up, of names cried out, and of neighbors charged one by one. It builds the case that seven people were witches who tormented a child of eleven. Readers get the raw claims on which a court sent people to die. No source sits closer to the heart of the Paisley affair.
barruel-memoires-jacobinisme-t1-1798:
Augustin Barruel was a French priest who fled the French Revolution and wrote in exile. His Mémoires pour servir à l'histoire du Jacobinisme, first printed at Hamburg in 1798, runs to four volumes. The first volume lays out his central charge against the thinkers of his age.

Barruel claims a Jacobin sect rose at the start of the revolt, bent on crushing altars and thrones in the name of freedom. He blames anti-church writers, whom he calls sophists of impiety, for plotting the fall of altar and throne alike. His tale of a vast secret plot shaped much later writing on secret societies. Few books did more to fix the modern fear of hidden rule.
barruel-memoires-jacobinisme-t2-1798:
The second volume of Barruel's Mémoires, printed at Hamburg in 1798, widens his charge from the church to the crown. Barruel was a French priest writing in exile while the Revolution remade his country. Here he argues that the same writers who attacked faith soon attacked kings as well.

He names them sophists of rebellion and traces their plot against all thrones. The volume then turns to a sect he says hid in the back lodges of Freemasonry with the same oath. Barruel splits his case in two halves, one on the thinkers and one on the lodges. The two halves meet, in his telling, in the fall of church and king in France.
barruel-memoires-jacobinisme-t3-1798:
Volume three of Barruel's Mémoires turns from writers to Freemasons themselves. The French priest, writing in exile, printed the volume at Hamburg in 1798. His claim grows bolder here: the lodges, he says, gave shelter to a far more dangerous inner sect.

Barruel argues that Illuminati men worked inside Masonry and bent its secrets toward revolt. In his account, that hidden link helps explain how the French Revolution took the course it did. The volume fused Masons, Illuminati, and revolution into one single tale. That fused tale has echoed through two centuries of writing on secret plots.
barruel-memoires-jacobinisme-t4-1798:
The fourth and last volume of Barruel's Mémoires was printed in London in 1798. By this point his story has moved past the writers and lodges of the first volumes. His subject now is the Illuminati order itself, its rise, and its reach into France.

Chapters trace the first age of the order, the chief aides of its founder Adam Weishaupt, and the work of Knigge in the lodges. The congress of Masons at Wilhelmsbad gets its own long treatment. Barruel closes by warning that Jacobin groups still spread the same creed. The volume ends the work that set the mold for modern plot theories.
bhartrihari-more-1898:
Paul Elmer More selected A Century of Indian Epigrams from Bhartrihari in 1898, a small book with a long reach. Bhartrihari, the Sanskrit poet of perhaps the fifth century, wrote satakas, centuries of verses, on love, worldly wisdom, and renunciation. More chose epigrams that show the poet's cool eye on courts, lovers, and his own restless heart.

Bhartrihari swung between palace and hermitage, and the verses bear both addresses. Their polish and bite made them proverbial across India for a thousand years. More's selection introduced American readers to a poet of worldly wisdom matched by few in any tongue.
blau-altjudische-zauberwesen-1898:
Ludwig Blau published the first systematic survey of ancient Jewish magic in 1898, in German. His study drew on rabbinic literature, inscriptions, and archaeological finds. Amulets, angel names, and exorcisms all fall within his map.

Blau showed that magic ran alongside official religion, not apart from it. Rabbis condemned some practices while quietly accepting others in daily life. Folk cures, demon beliefs, and protective charms receive orderly treatment. The book was written for scholars and remains the subject's starting point. Later work on the Talmud and magic bowls builds on Blau's frame. His German title translates as the ancient Jewish magic system.
bohm-bawerk-karl-marx-close-of-system-18:
Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk published Karl Marx and the Close of His System in German in 1896, and Alice Macdonald's English version followed in 1898. Bohm-Bawerk led the Austrian school of economics, and Marx's third volume of Capital had just appeared after its author's death. The Austrian set out to test whether Marx's system held together.

His charge was precise: the third volume, where prices rule, contradicts the first, where labor alone gives value. If goods sell at prices set by costs and profit rates, the labor theory cannot stand as Marx stated it. Defenders of Marx answered for decades, and the book is still the classic statement of the case against him. It is widely read as the sharpest attack the Austrian school ever made on Marxian economics.
book-of-dead-hieroglyphic-budge-1898:
Wallis Budge published the hieroglyphic text of the Book of the Dead in 1898. He used the Theban recension, the version tied to Thebes. This volume gives the spells in their original script.

Students can read the glyphs line by line as scribes wrote them. Charms for breath, memory, and safe passage crowd the pages. Budge's standing made the set a standard scholar's tool. The work is not a light read but a working text. It serves Egyptologists and keen amateurs who want the afterlife spells unfiltered, in the signs themselves.
brown-wieland-1798:
Charles Brockden Brown called Wieland an American tale in 1798, and its preface sets out a moral aim. The incidents, he warns, come close to wonders yet stay within human nature. At the center stands Theodore Wieland, a devout man in rural Pennsylvania who begins to hear strange voices.

The voices urge him toward dreadful crimes against his own family. Behind some of them stands Carwin, a man who can throw his voice to any place, a gift Brown calls biloquism. The horror cuts deeper than one trick, though, since the novel asks whether reason itself can be trusted at all.
budge-book-of-dead-english-1898:
E. A. Wallis Budge put the great tomb text of Egypt in English in The Book of the Dead, out in 1898. The Book of the Dead is a set of spells laid with the dead to guide them past tests to a blessed life. Budge used the Theban form, the most full form kept on rolls of reed paper.

Spells for gates, foes, and the weigh of the heart fill the text. His English is grave and clear. For years this was the take most fans read. It still stands as a chief door to the text.
bullen-cruise-of-the-cachalot-1898:
Frank Bullen shipped on a whaler as a boy and wrote its classic in 1898. The Cruise of the Cachalot sails the world in chase of the sperm whale. Bullen rose from the fo'c'sle to tell the sea's life as few landsmen could.

Storms, whale fights, and strange ports fill the book, told in a sailor's plain voice. Its famed set piece tells of a vast fight between a whale and a giant squid by moonlight. Whalers backed his tale as true to their hard trade. The book brought the deep sea's wonders home to dry land.
chinese-poetry-english-verse-giles-1898:
Herbert A. Giles gathered Chinese Poetry in English Verse in 1898, a pioneering anthology in rhymed English form. The poems run from the ancient Book of Odes through the Tang masters: Li Bai, Du Fu, and Bai Juyi among them. Giles, a sinologist and translator of wit, fitted Chinese lyrics into the verse shapes his age expected.

Exile, wine, war, and old friendship sing in his pages with Victorian polish. Later translators chose freer methods, but Giles reached the wide public of his day. His anthology stands as the first English-verse bridge to China's poetic treasury, still charming to browse.
cia-0000008698:
August 1970 brought results for photo comparison case number 12,221, part of the CIA's POW identification work. Analysts matched pictures of possible prisoners against records of missing Americans. The method demanded patience with poor film, changed faces, and thin clues.

Each comparison tried to answer a narrow question: could these two images show the same man? A careful yes or no shaped what officials told families and where searchers looked next. The case number keeps the file impersonal, but the work was anything but. It represents the technical core of the missing-persons effort during the war years.
cia-0000010398:
Names of United States prisoners of war in North Vietnam, seventy-three of them, are listed in a January 1967 CIA paper. The heading states the count plainly: lists 73 names. In early 1967, a confirmed name was gold; lists were guarded, compared, and updated by hand.

A name on the list meant a man was known held, not merely missing. Families could be told something solid at last. The list also fixed the known prisoner population at that date, a baseline later lists grew from. This file is the roster itself, the most human kind of document in the series.
cia-0000011498:
Austria sat between the blocs in 1952, still occupied by four powers seven years after the war in Europe ended. In November the CIA examined what security forces Austria could field once the occupation troops withdrew. The small republic had no real army of its own, and Soviet forces stood on its eastern border.

The paper weighs the men, arms, and time Austria would need to guard itself. It also considers the shadow of neutrality, the course Austria in fact took in 1955. The study shows the exposed position of a buffer state whose safety rested on geography and goodwill.
cia-0000012298:
Helms carried the Penkovsky matter to the very top in December 1961, writing to the Director of Central Intelligence himself. The subject line points to the Soviet journal Military Thought, the colonel's hunting ground for military secrets. When material mattered enough, it rose past every desk to the director's own, and this memo made that climb at the year's end.

The letter shows the case's summit traffic in the crisis-building months. Its presence in the file marks how prized the source had become. For readers, it is the spy's reporting arriving where it counted most, briefed at the peak.
cia-0000012398:
London again, April 30, 1961: meeting number ten brings the debriefings back to the capital. Ten sessions in eleven days was a pace without precedent. It had never been done with a source of this rank. By now the handlers knew their man well. They knew his memory, his moods, his courage, and the fears he carried home to Moscow.

The record marks the rhythm as established. Questions now ran ahead to tasking, to what he should seek next. For readers, the page shows first contact settling into an enterprise, with a capital city as its office.
cia-0000012498:
Communist insurgency in Thailand is the subject of a CIA paper from June 1966, at the war's height. The kingdom's northeast simmered with guerrilla activity backed from abroad. Thailand was America's firmest ally in mainland Southeast Asia. It hosted bases for the war in Vietnam. Its internal security therefore mattered far beyond its borders in Washington's domino thinking that year.

The paper surveys the insurgency's strength, ground, and outside support. It measures the wobble in a domino Washington could not afford to lose. For readers, it shows the secret war's logic spreading: every neighbor of Vietnam graded for the same disease.
cia-0000013298:
A communist hospital in Cambodia, designated C-3B, is located and described in a CIA item from February 1969. The item maps part of the enemy's medical network across the border. Jungle hospitals were as vital to the other side as any base area. They treated the wounded of the southern war, hidden under canopy, supplied by trail, and moved when the bombers found their range.

The item sets out the hospital's wards, staff, and place as sources reported them. Medical geography was targeting geography too, which gives the page its edge. For readers, it shows the hidden infrastructure that kept an army in the field.
cia-0000013598:
Stability in the Dominican Republic over the next year or so is forecast in a CIA paper from March 1967. The island's fragile peace was two years old. The American intervention of 1965 had ended the civil war, and an elected government now ruled. Yet the old divisions had not healed, and the analysts' doubts had not eased with time or elections.

The paper revisits the calm's durability a year on. It weighs the parties, the military, and the habits of the old regime. For readers, it shows the Dominican watch continued: a peace recorded, and doubted, in the same pages.
cia-0000013898: American prisoners of war were observed in Binh Dinh Province, in a CIA note dated November 2, 1967. Binh Dinh, in South Vietnam, was a province of hard fighting and strong Viet Cong roots. Prisoners seen there were held in the south, not yet moved north. The note helps show how wide the southern camp network reached.
cia-0000015398: Photographs and background notes on an unidentified object make up a redacted CIA case file dated October 4, 1957. The case name was cut before release, so who took the pictures and where stays unclear. What survives is the shape of a working file: images plus the checking done around them. Such files show how the agency stored claims it could neither prove nor dismiss.
cia-0000028298: Current developments in Iran fill a CIA paper dated in 1951. That spring Iran nationalized its oil industry under Prime Minister Mossadegh, setting off a crisis with Britain. Current developments was the right title for a country moving week by week. The paper dates from the opening of a struggle that ended in the 1953 coup. Oil, pride, and foreign pressure all drove the story that year.
cia-0000038498:
American crewmen and a jet aircraft were downed in South Vietnam, according to a CIA record dated January 1, 1973. The title notes that the deceased crewmen were part of the report's subject. The record came in the war's final month for American combat forces.

Inside, the downing is recorded with its human cost stated plainly. Late-war losses carried a special sting, falling so close to the war's end. The file adds one incident to the closing chapter of the air war. Aircraft were still flying missions in the first days of 1973. Crews were still being lost so near the end.
cia-0000042798:
A list was provided of soldiers near the UCA killings, in a CIA record dated January 4, 1990. UCA was the university where the Jesuit priests lived and taught. Knowing which soldiers stood near the scene was the case's first need.

Inside, the roster of names is the record's whole point. A list turns rumor into named men who can be questioned. The file shows the investigation taking its most concrete shape yet. Before there could be charges, there had to be names. This record preserves the moment names began to attach to the crime in an official form.
cia-0000044998:
The CIA headquarters handbook on files management, dated January 28, 1983, is preserved in a record filed January 5, 1983. Files management rules how papers are named, stored, and found again. An agency of secrets runs, in part, on the strength of its filing.

Inside, the manual sets out the craft of keeping the agency's records. Numbered rules governed everything from folders to burning bags. The system worked only when thousands of clerks followed them alike. The file shows the bureaucracy describing itself with care, in the plain conviction that good records were a form of power in their own right.
cia-0000045198:
Ungo reacted to Ines Duarte's release, in a CIA record dated September 5, 1985 in the catalog. Her freedom ended the crisis that had gripped the country. The opposition's response to good news is its own kind of record.

Inside, the FDR leader's reaction to her release is preserved. Relief crossed the lines of the war in that moment. Even opponents could welcome a young woman's safe return home. For one day, the kidnapping ended in the way every family in the country had hoped it would. The file holds that brief easing of the country's tension, before the war's ordinary hatreds closed over the story again in the days that followed.
cia-0000049098: El Salvador's president asked the military high command in 1984 to remove a lieutenant named Lopez, and a CIA item preserves the request. A president petitioning his own generals showed where power sat in wartime San Salvador. The item survives in the Truth Commission files, one page of the long struggle over officers' fates.
cia-0000049198: El Salvador's army high command commented in 1990 on coming changes among senior officers, and a CIA item preserves the remarks. Promotions and postings were the institution's real politics, deciding which faction held which command. The item survives among the Truth Commission records, a window on the brass in the war's late phase.
cia-0000049398: An HPSCI request for information on background on the Jesuit killings is preserved as declassified CIA document 0000049398, dated February 4, 1992. The heading names the House committee by its initials and states what it asked for. The short file records congressional interest in the Jesuit case background, kept in the Truth Commission materials.
cia-0000096498: Progress report on the implementation of Recommendation number four is declassified CIA document 0000096498, dated March 2, 1957. The heading is cut short in the catalog after the report wording. The short file adds a fourth numbered entry to the March progress run, each one tracking a separate recommendation from the same presidential board report.
cia-0000107298: News That Missing U.s. Pilots StillL Alive Is Goundless' is the heading, with groundless misspelled and stray marks, on declassified CIA document 0000107298, dated June 6, 1991. The title dismisses reports that missing American pilots were still alive. That dismissal is stated flatly, in the heading's own rough spelling. The brief record is a rebuttal item in the June 1991 MIA cluster as released.
cia-0000107498: Dated June 4, 1964, declassified CIA document 0000107498 reports a march on Washington planned by Cuban exiles for 21 July 1964. Its heading times the march to the start of an OAS session, then breaks off at Se. The planned date and city are given in full in the title itself. The brief record is a protest planning item from the summer of 1964.
cia-0000113198: Dated January 1, 1945, with that date marked as an estimate, declassified CIA document 0000113198 holds a list of names and descriptions. Its untitled heading notes pages as received, in a word that breaks off at Receiv. No person is named in the surviving heading text itself at all. The brief record preserves the estimate note and the broken ending as released.
cia-0000117898: OPEC Tri-ministerial Conference: Focus on Strategy is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000117898, dated August 4, 1980. The heading names a three-minister meeting of OPEC, with strategy as its focus. Strategy is the stated topic after the colon in the title itself. The brief record is a conference item on oil politics from the summer of 1980.
cia-0000119698:
A January 1953 CIA paper weighs the probable results of prosecuting an antitrust suit against certain defendants. The heading breaks off before naming them, so the targets stay unknown from the file's face. The paper still shows the agency being asked to judge a domestic legal case.

Antitrust actions against large firms could ripple into defense work, prices, and foreign opinion, which is why analysts took an interest. The paper sets out what officials expected to follow from pressing the suit. It preserves an unusual corner of the agency's work: intelligence judgment applied at home, to courts and companies rather than to foreign armies.
cia-0000124298: A December 1957 CIA scientific report deals with electronics. Soviet progress in circuits sat beneath the rockets and satellites drawing the headlines, since better electronics meant better missiles as well. The report surveys what Washington could identify of that hidden layer. Electronics decided how well missiles could be guided and how clearly satellites could speak, so this quiet subject sat near the center of the whole competition.
cia-0000132298:
Smoke from Kuwait reaching Iran leads Situation Report 607 in the CIA's series. The report is dated January 1, 1991. It then turns to political developments cut short in the title. Kuwait's burning oil fields sent smoke across the Gulf in huge amounts, darkening skies well beyond the war zone.

The report tracks that fallout as an early sign of the war's environmental damage. Oil fires and spills became one of the most visible harms of the whole conflict. Readers get a period account of the smoke problem as analysts first measured it. The entry shows concern for the damage beginning while the fighting that caused it still had weeks to run.
cia-0000132398: Latin America as a whole fills a CIA briefing for the National Security Council dated October 4, 1960. Cuba dominated the agenda that year, but the briefing ranges across the hemisphere. The region had become the hottest front of the Cold War in American eyes. The short briefing gives the council the full regional picture in one sitting, from Mexico to Argentina.
cia-0000132498:
A break in relations frames this CIA briefing on Cuba, dated January 4, 1961. The United States had cut diplomatic ties with Castro's government only days before, on January 3. The paper assesses the island at the start of a decisive year.

Its timing gives it weight: written between the diplomatic break and the Bay of Pigs landing that April, it records the agency's view as confrontation replaced diplomacy. Readers get the post-break picture in the CIA's own reporting, one of several Cuba papers filed that same day. The document was declassified and released years later.
cia-0000132598: Khrushchev possibly visiting Cuba and Mexico fills item 1 of a CIA general series dated August 5, 1960. A Soviet premier traveling in the Western Hemisphere would have been a sensation. No such visit had ever taken place during the Cold War. The short item tracks the reports of a possible trip and how analysts judged them at the time.
cia-0000133198: A pro-communist student group in Colombia planning protests fills a CIA paper dated July 5, 1960. The target was a meeting of the Organization of American States. The headline breaks off at the word meetin, short for meeting. Students were the shock troops of the Latin American left in those years. The short paper tracks the protest plans and their backers.
cia-0000135698: Spanish records of Brigade 2506 include this document, dated 4 January 1961. The exile brigade, trained by the CIA for a landing in Cuba, kept much of its internal paperwork in Spanish. January 1961 was a month of hard training with the plan still secret. The catalog gives this item no subject of its own. It is preserved as released, a dated page in the brigade's archive, and its meaning rests in the text.
cia-0000135798: A typed copy of a cable fills a CIA record dated May 3, 1952. The cable's own title was deleted before release. cia-03019098: CURRENT INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1955/12/01, a CIA publication. The December briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. The paper lived through the years. It waits for future eyes. It retains its place in time. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
cia-03169398: CURRENT INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1957/07/27, a CIA publication. The July briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
cia-06627998: A technical intelligence officer lied about his schooling, and this CIA file tells the story. The false diplomas came to light internally. The agency documented its own embarrassment. The paper lived through the years. This paper preserves that declassified record.
cia-06754998: AR 3-19 MILITARY RESERVE PROGRAM, a CIA regulation. The reserve program. This file preserves that declassified paper. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers. The historical record keeps it. Readers can find it here.
cia-06933698: MEMO TO ADSO RE OGC MEETING WITH EMERSON BIGELOW, a CIA document. The meeting memo. This file preserves that declassified paper. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
clarke-outline-christian-theology-1898:
William Newton Clarke taught theology at Colgate and wrote An Outline of Christian Theology in 1898 for students and pastors. Clarke's book is a liberal Baptist system, built from the Christian consciousness rather than from proof texts alone. It charmed readers with its clarity and warmth.

He argues that doctrine should state what Christians have actually found true in experience with Christ at the center. His treatments of God, sin, and salvation soften older Calvinist edges without dropping their seriousness. The Outline trained a generation of northern Baptist ministers in a gentler, modern key. His gentle tone won readers who found older systems harsh.
conrad-tales-of-unrest-1898:
Tales of Unrest, published in 1898, was Conrad's first story collection. It gathers five tales from the years when he was turning from sailor to writer. The settings run from Brittany to the Malay Archipelago.

Among them are 'Karain', a Malay chief haunted by a ghost, and 'An Outpost of Progress', two traders rotting at a Congo station. 'The Lagoon' is a tale of love and loss told at dusk. 'The Idiots' and 'The Return' turn to Europe and to marriage. The collection shows Conrad testing his powers, and in places already reaching the level of his great work.
crane-open-boat-1898:
Stephen Crane survived a real shipwreck in 1897, spending thirty hours in an open boat off Florida after his ship sank. Within weeks he turned the ordeal into The Open Boat, published in book form in 1898 with other stories. It is his most perfect piece of writing, by wide agreement.

Four men, a correspondent, a captain, an oiler, and a cook, row a tiny dinghy through heavy seas toward a shore that keeps receding. Crane shows nature's flat indifference to human effort with icy clarity. The strongest swimmer dies almost within reach of land. The Bride Comes to Yellow Sky, a companion masterpiece, brings a Texas marshal's bride home to a town whose gunfighter finds the old West ending. The volume holds Crane's essential short fiction.
dannunzio-child-of-pleasure-1898:
Georgina Harding translated D'Annunzio's Child of Pleasure into English in 1898. Andrea Sperelli, a handsome young Roman noble, stands at its center. He worships art, women, and strong feeling above all other goods.

Salons and love affairs carry him through a round of intense pleasures. Each delight spoils in his hands, and emptiness waits at the end. Lush and feverish prose made the novel a sensation across Europe. Its author became the most famous Italian writer of his age on its strength. Readers still meet in Sperelli the pure type of the decadent hero, charming and hollow at once.
dannunzio-intruder-1898:
Arthur Hornblow translated The Intruder, D'Annunzio's tense novel of 1898. Tullio Hermil loves his wife yet cannot stay faithful to her. That split in his nature poisons their marriage from the start.

When his wife bears a child by another man, jealousy takes full hold. His wounded pride curdles by degrees into a monstrous plan. D'Annunzio dissects a husband's mind with cool and cruel precision. Lovely and disturbing at once, the tale asks a hard question. How far can wounded pride drive a man who thinks himself above the morals that bind plain and honest people in daily life?
dannunzio-triumph-of-death-1898:
Hornblow also translated The Triumph of Death, printed in English in 1898. Giorgio Aurispa, a weak and over-fine noble, stands at its center. He drags his lover with him to a bleak cliff above the Adriatic Sea.

Thoughts of a joint lovers' death grip his mind and will not loosen. Music, deep thought, and erotic longing fuse in the long brooding pages. The result reads as much like a prose poem as a novel. Of all D'Annunzio's romances, this one stares darkest at self-destruction. It shows the decadent mood at its most extreme: beauty and ruin locked in one long, fatal embrace.
doe-osti-3344454-system-study-emergency-: Emergency power got system-studied 1998-2024, and this DOE text covers the power system. The pages detail the findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The study was system. The data were nuclear. The 1998-2024 were system. The power were emergency. The nuclear were folks.
doe-osti-3376014-system-study-residual-h: RHR got 1998-2024-studied, and this DOE system study covers residual heat. The pages detail the removal findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The study was system. The data were nuclear. The RHR were heat. The 1998-2024 were study. The removal were residual.
edict-of-nantes-1598:
King Henri IV of France issued the Edict of Nantes in April 1598, and the French text is preserved here. The edict closed decades of civil strife known as the Wars of Religion, fought between Catholics and the Protestant Huguenots. Henri had changed his own faith to take the throne, then chose toleration as the price of peace.

Huguenots won the right to worship in set places, hold public jobs, and keep troops in named safe towns for a time. Catholics kept the top place in the kingdom, and limits on Protestant worship stayed strict. Louis XIV revoked the edict in 1685, which drove many Huguenots to flee France for good.
europmc-pmc10247998:
Yin and co-authors review immune-related side effects of immune checkpoint inhibitors in a 2023 paper. These drugs release the brakes on T cells so they can attack cancer, and they have improved survival in many cancers. The same unleashed immunity can also strike healthy organs, causing a distinct set of side effects.

The review catalogs these harms by organ, from skin and gut to lung and hormone glands. It explains how doctors spot and treat them, often with immune-calming drugs. The paper is a practical guide to the price of a powerful therapy.
europmc-pmc10334598:
Inoue, Shue, Bu, and Kanekiyo reviewed in 2023 how small blood vessels in the brain can fail. When these tiny vessels clog or leak, blood flow drops and memory can fade. This damage is a main cause of vascular dementia. It is the second most common form of dementia, at about 20% of cases.

Signs on brain scans include white spots, tiny strokes, and small bleeds. Inoue links the damage to four paths: low blood flow, a leaky brain barrier, poor fluid drainage, and vessel swelling. Care today rests on control of blood pressure, blood fats, and blood sugar. No drug yet treats the root cause, so the review maps targets for future work.
europmc-pmc10349198:
Xuan and co-authors reviewed in 2023 how tiny particles may harm human health. These particles, called nanoparticles, are far smaller than a cell. They serve in scans, drug delivery, and other medical tasks. Yet a gap remains in what is known about their risks and how to test them.

Xuan maps harm across the lungs, nerves, hormones, immune defences, and the reproductive system. The review also covers cancer risk from long exposure. Harm paths include stress from reactive oxygen, damage to cell power parts, and breaks in DNA. Test models range from cells and mice to lab-grown mini-organs, called organoids. The authors call for stronger models to close the gaps.
europmc-pmc10667098:
Harrison led a phase 3 trial in 2023 on resmetirom for fatty liver disease. The severe form, called NASH, scars the liver and had no approved drug at the time. The trial ran 52 weeks in adults with fatty liver and presumed NASH. Arms got 80 mg or 100 mg of the drug, or a dummy pill.

About 972 patients joined the blinded arms, plus 171 in an open arm. Side effects hit 86 to 88% on the drug, versus 81.8% on the dummy pill. Harrison reports more diarrhoea and nausea at the start on the drug. Liver fat fell sharply by week 16, by 34.9% and 38.6% past the dummy arm. Blood fats and liver stiffness also improved.
europmc-pmc10725898:
Bahar, Kim, and Kim reviewed the RAS/RAF/MAPK pathway in 2023, a signal chain often faulty in cancer. The chain passes growth orders from RAS through RAF and MEK to ERK, step by step. It steers cell growth, division, and survival. Faults in the chain help tumours grow and spread.

Drug pairs that block RAF and MEK are approved for melanoma and some lung and thyroid cancers. Resistance still caps their worth, Bahar notes. One escape route is autophagy, the cell's recycling system, which can shield cancer cells. New RAF blockers aim for a stronger profile with fewer flaws. The review weighs pairs that hit RAF and the recycling path at once.
europmc-pmc10869798:
Loh and colleagues review the two-way talk between gut microbes and the brain in this 2024 paper. The gut holds a vast community of microbes with huge gene and chemistry power. Signals from that community reach the brain and shape support cells there, called glial cells. Those cells guard and feed nerve cells, so gut signals can sway brain health.

The review traces how gut microbes talk to three glial cell types in health and in brain disease. It then looks at chemical products of microbes, brain signal chemicals, and gut hormones as key couriers. Faults in this axis are tied to diseases where nerve cells die off slowly. The authors argue that tuning gut microbes could become a therapy route. They survey early attempts to do just that.
europmc-pmc10970998:
Wang and hundreds of co-authors present the full genome of a scallop in this 2017 paper. The scallop Patinopecten yessoensis is a bivalve mollusc, a soft sea animal with a hinged shell. Its genome changes slowly and keeps many ancient traits. Such slow lines are key to rebuilding the genomes of animal ancestors, the authors note.

The genome is anchored to its 19 chromosomes, they report. Those chromosomes match the 17 linkage groups thought to mark the ancestor of all bilaterians, animals with left and right sides. The match is tighter than any seen before. The team also found a new timing pattern in Hox genes, the genes that lay out body plans. Eye tissue in the shell edge showed a surprising range of light-sensing paths. The genome is offered as a window on early animal evolution.
europmc-pmc11223798:
Pang and a large team introduce version 6.0 of a metabolomics platform in this 2024 paper. Metabolomics reads the small molecules in a sample to reveal cell activity. The platform, MetaboAnalyst, processes and interprets such data from mass spectrometry, a method that weighs molecules to identify them. Version 6.0 pursues two goals: fuller use of tandem mass data and support for exposomics, the study of environmental exposures.

New modules headline the release. One processes spectra with support for second-stage mass data and a named algorithm called asari. Another annotates peaks against fragment-level reference databases. A causal analysis module estimates cause links using a genetic method called Mendelian randomization. A dose-response module computes benchmark doses. Pathway analysis now spans about 130 species, and visuals and databases were updated.
europmc-pmc1314898:
Olsvik and co-authors ranked reference genes for salmon gene studies in 2005. Quantitative PCR needs stable reference genes to normalize results. Salmon are major model fish, yet no systematic ranking existed. Six candidate genes were tested across eight tissues.

Tissues ran from gills and liver to brain and muscle. Six untreated adult fish plus a smoltification group were sampled. Stability software ranked two elongation factor genes at the top. GAPDH, a common default choice, ranked last of the six. Olsvik gives salmon researchers a validated pecking order for controls. Six adult fish were sampled for the tissue ranking.
europmc-pmc1413498:
How much of height comes from genes? Visscher and co-authors gave a fresh answer in 2006, free of the usual twin study guesses. They used full siblings, who share a random share of DNA from each parent. By scanning the whole genome, they measured the exact share each pair held in common.

The team studied more than 4,400 sibling pairs and had height for most of them. Height heritability, the share of spread due to genes, came out near 0.80. Visscher found no sign that shared home life drove the match. The result backs older twin work, but rests on direct gene counts.
europmc-pmc1450098:
The Abl kinase, a cell switch, drives a blood cancer when stuck on. Levinson and co-authors captured a new off state of that switch in 2006. The cancer drug imatinib works by locking a flipped off shape. Akin switches in the Src family rest in a unlike off shape, and the drug fails on them.

The team caught Abl in a Src-like off shape, bound to a fuel-like compound. Computer runs hint this shape frees room for the flip the drug needs. Some drug-proof mutants may act by wrecking this rest shape. Levinson suggests Abl hops between two off states, a trait that shapes drug design.
europmc-pmc1557398:
A single cell that swims in ponds holds two genomes in two nuclei. Eisen and co-authors sequenced one of them in 2006 for Tetrahymena thermophila, a model organism. The micronucleus stores DNA for sex. The macronucleus, sequenced here, runs daily gene activity.

Its genome runs about 104 million letters across roughly 225 chromosomes. It holds over 27,000 predicted genes. Many gene families grew large, covering sensing, eating, and movement parts. Uniquely, its stop signal can also code an amino acid, so it may read all 64 DNA codons. Eisen presents the genome as a base for studying cell complexity.
europmc-pmc1564298:
Diseases of immune attack fall into two broad kinds. McGonagle and McDermott proposed a classification in 2006, drawing on new genetic findings. Autoimmune diseases stem from faults in the adaptive arm, the B and T cells that learn targets. Autoinflammatory diseases stem from the innate arm, which reacts without learning.

Gene studies of rare and common diseases exposed this split. Some conditions mix both patterns. The pair argue sorting diseases by mechanism, not just symptoms, sharpens treatment choices. A century ago, self-attack was deemed impossible. McGonagle shows it now anchors a map of immune disease.
europmc-pmc2125098: A medical paper on the purines and purine metabolism of some tumors in domestic animals. The tumor purines. This article preserves that oncology. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
europmc-pmc2125498: A medical paper on proteose intoxications and the metabolism of fasting dogs. The starved protein. This article preserves that biochemistry. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers.
europmc-pmc2131198: A medical paper on the occurrence and trend of spontaneous variations in organ weights of normal animals. The varying organs. This article preserves that anatomy. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2131398: In the Andes two fevers sometimes hit the same sick folk, and this paper looked at how they mixed. The team watched one change the path of the other. The paired fevers, studied. The article keeps that fever study.
europmc-pmc2131498: A medical paper on experimental pneumonia in guinea pigs, the effect of toxic autolysates. The guinea pig lungs. This article preserves that research. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2140498: A biology paper on the temperature coefficient of phagocytosis. The heated eating. This article preserves that cell biology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2140798: A biology paper on some general properties of proteins. The proteins' nature. This article preserves that biochemistry. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2235898:
Lindesmith and colleagues analysed in 2008 how the epidemic norovirus type GII.4 persists in human populations. Noroviruses are the leading cause of viral gut outbreaks in communities, hospitals and cruise ships. GII.4 has caused most outbreaks since the mid-1990s. The team compared capsid gene sequences across twenty years and built virus-like particles for the five major evolutionary clusters they found.

Evolution proceeded in epochs: long still periods, then rapid emergence of new epidemic strains replacing older ones in sequence. Binding tests showed each era's particles attach to different gut carbohydrates. Those sugars are controlled by the human FUT2 and FUT3 genes, so strain sensitivity to inherited susceptibility varies over time. Changes clustered on surface residues near the binding site, supporting antigenic drift, gradual immune evasion, as a persistence mechanism.
europmc-pmc2265698:
Aziz and a large team described the RAST Server in 2008, a service for annotating bacterial and archaeal genomes that runs fully automatically. Genome sequences were arriving faster than experts could annotate them by hand. RAST identifies protein-coding, rRNA and tRNA genes, assigns gene functions, and predicts which subsystems, sets of related cellular processes, a genome contains. From those assignments it reconstructs the organism's metabolic network.

Annotated genomes are normally delivered within twelve to twenty-four hours of submission. Output can be downloaded easily or browsed in the SEED environment, which supports comparison with hundreds of maintained genomes. Throughput reaches fifty to one hundred genomes per day. By the time of writing, over 120 external users had annotated more than 350 distinct genomes with the free service. The authors discuss accuracy, consistency and completeness as the true quality tests.
europmc-pmc2447598:
Bagshaw, George, and Bellomo, with the ANZICS Database Management Committee, evaluated early kidney injury in sepsis across Australia and New Zealand in 2008. Sepsis is a body-wide infection response that can crash organs. Acute kidney injury, a sudden loss of kidney filtering, is one of its deadliest complications.

They mined records for 120,123 intensive care patients admitted over 24 hours between 2000 and 2005 at 57 units. Of these, 33,375 had sepsis, and 42.1% of the septic group had kidney injury within the first day. Those patients were sicker on nearly every measure than patients whose kidney injury had other causes. Their intensive care death rate was 19.8% versus 13.4% in the comparison group, and the gap held after statistical adjustment, with an odds ratio of 1.60 in the adjusted model. Hospital stays were also longer at every injury grade.
europmc-pmc2553198:
Loerch and colleagues compared brain ageing across species in 2008, measuring how gene activity in the cortex changes with age in humans, rhesus monkeys, and mice. Ageing disorders like Alzheimer's are oddly specific to humans. The team asked which ageing changes are shared. They also asked which are new in primates.

Only a small set of changes appeared in all three species, including a rise in the protective gene APOD and a fall in CAMK4, a gene for synaptic signalling. Humans and monkeys had diverged sharply from mice through a broad switching-off of neuronal genes with age. Genes for GABA signalling, the brain's main braking system, fell steeply in humans at both message and protein level. The shutdown was not explained by neuron loss.
europmc-pmc2580798:
Carpenter, Beis, Cameron, and Iwata reviewed membrane protein crystallography in 2008. Solving these structures lags far behind other proteins. New methods are closing the gap. About 25 percent of all proteins sit in cell membranes, yet fewer than 150 unique structures were known. Their greasy surfaces, flexibility, and instability make them hard to produce and crystallise.

The authors survey the high-throughput revolution reaching the field. It brings better ways to express these proteins in host cells. It brings detergents that dissolve them out of membranes while keeping them intact. It also brings purification pipelines and crystallisation tricks adapted to their nature. They predict these advances will soon multiply the number of solved structures. That would open drug targets that have resisted study.
europmc-pmc2600198:
Coque and colleagues traced in 2008 how a potent antibiotic-resistance enzyme, CTX-M-15, spread around the world inside Escherichia coli. The enzyme destroys most penicillin-like drugs and rides on plasmids, mobile DNA circles that hop between bacteria. The team analysed 43 CTX-M-15-producing clinical isolates from seven countries plus plasmids from India, typing both the bacteria and their plasmids.

Half the isolates belonged to phylogenetic group B2 and a quarter to group D, the lineages tied to hospital infections. Within B2, most fell into one globally disseminated clone, ST131, found across France, Canada, Spain, Portugal, Kuwait, and Switzerland. A second clone, ST405, appeared in group D. The resistance gene travelled mainly on multidrug-resistant plasmids of the IncFII family. The authors conclude clones and plasmids together drove the spread.
europmc-pmc2602598:
Osipova, Hermes, and Jensen recorded brain activity in 2008 and found that fast gamma rhythms in the visual brain are timed by slower alpha waves. Brain oscillations at different speeds are known to matter for cognition, but how bands interact was unclear. The team used magnetoencephalography in healthy volunteers resting with eyes closed. They tested whether gamma power rises and falls in step with the alpha cycle.

Gamma power between 30 and 70 hertz proved phase-locked to alpha oscillations of 8 to 13 hertz, strongest over the back of the head where alpha dominates. Gamma activity alone was invisible in the spectra and appeared only when analysed against alpha phase. Recordings from inside the skull of an epilepsy patient confirmed the coupling. The authors suggest the visual system is inhibited through most of the alpha cycle, with gamma bursts marking windows of excitability.
europmc-pmc2672098:
Kell argued in 2009 that loose, poorly bound iron is a hidden common cause behind many long-term diseases. Breathing cells constantly make peroxide and superoxide, reactive oxygen forms that are fairly tame on their own. When they meet free iron, though, the pairing brews the hydroxyl radical, one of the most destructive molecules in biology.

The review gathers wide evidence tying this iron-driven chemistry to heart and vessel disease, diabetes-like metabolic failure, and brain degeneration. Iron shows up at the scene in plaques and damaged tissue again and again, and it tracks with aging itself. Kell's remedy follows from the cause: bind the iron tightly with chelators, natural or man-made, so it cannot brew radicals. He also warns that single-cause thinking misleads here, since the damage needs the unlucky combination of factors at once.
europmc-pmc2694998:
Ripoll and colleagues read in 2009 the complete genome of Mycobacterium abscessus, a fast-growing relative of the tuberculosis germ that is emerging as a lung pathogen. It causes a tuberculosis-like lung disease, and people with cystic fibrosis are especially vulnerable. Its genome runs to about 5.07 million letters, holding some 4,920 predicted genes, plus a full virus fossil and a small mercury-resistance plasmid.

Comparison with a harmless cousin showed a genome stocked with weapons the cousin lacks. Many belong to classic mycobacterial families of surface and transport proteins. Many others, though, were plainly stolen from unrelated soil and water bacteria, including iron grabbers and a toxin enzyme. Several stolen items also appear in the two germs most often found in cystic fibrosis lungs. Borrowed genes, the authors argue, explain this species' unusual menace among its kin.
europmc-pmc2701598:
Mathieu and colleagues reported in 2009 that two seemingly unrelated flowering repressors in Arabidopsis team up to delay blooming. One, SMZ, belongs to the AP-2 family of gene switches and is itself targeted by a small RNA, miR172. The other, FLM, is a MADS family switch. Plants time flowering carefully, since blooming too early or late costs seeds.

Against expectation, the two repressors work through the same target: FT, the gene whose product is the mobile flowering signal made in leaves. Both repressors damp FT's expression, holding the plant in leafy growth until conditions and age align. The finding ties the small-RNA pathway that reads a plant's maturity to the classic repressor machinery. It also shows flowering control is not a set of parallel routes but a web, where unlike parts converge on one switch.
europmc-pmc2713398:
Quan and Tian introduced in 2009 circular polymerase extension cloning, a one-step way to join and copy DNA parts without the usual cutting and pasting enzymes. Synthetic biology, building new gene systems by design, needs fast ways to assemble many parts and whole pathways. Older flexible methods needed extra steps to make sticky ends and often joined parts in the wrong order.

Their method uses a single polymerase, an enzyme that copies DNA, to assemble several inserts into any vector in one reaction in a tube. No restriction cutting, ligation, or single-strand joining is needed. They prove it on hard tasks such as mixed gene libraries and multi-part pathways in a single step.
europmc-pmc2718498:
Mestdagh and co-authors proposed in 2009 a universal way to normalize microRNA data from RT-qPCR, a precise method that counts gene activity in a sample. Normalization corrects for uneven sample amounts so true biology stands out. For messenger genes, teams test several reference genes first, but few stable reference microRNAs were known.

Their method uses the mean expression value, the average of all microRNAs measured in that sample, as the yardstick. Tested on profiling data, it proved stable and cut unwanted variation better than common small-RNA controls. Since it needs no prior hunt for reference genes, it can serve any microRNA profiling study, including cancer signature work.
europmc-pmc2780998:
Lakhan, Kirchgessner, and Hofer reviewed in 2009 inflammatory mechanisms in ischemic stroke and the treatments that might target them. Stroke ranks third among causes of death in industrialized nations. It is also the top cause of lasting disability in adults. The only approved drug, a clot dissolver, must be given within three hours and risks bleeding. Two processes drive much of the damage: oxidative stress and inflammation.

Brain tissue holds weak antioxidant defenses, so free radicals from inflammatory cells threaten tissue around the blocked vessel. The review covers the molecular side of both processes and candidate therapies aimed at neuroinflammation and the innate immune system. Recent work casts regulatory T cells as major protectors of the brain after stroke. Boosting that built-in immune brake, they suggest, may yield new protective treatments.
europmc-pmc2781298:
Ramage, Connolly, and Cox carried out in 2009 a comprehensive analysis of toxin-antitoxin systems in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the bacterium behind tuberculosis. These two-gene stress elements, each pairing a toxin with its blocker, are unusually plentiful in this pathogen, and their purpose was unknown. The team identified every candidate system in the genome and tested what each one does.

They found eighty-eight candidate systems, far more than previously thought. Most are conserved across the tuberculosis complex but absent from other mycobacteria, and many sit in genomic islands, suggesting recent arrival by gene transfer. Thirty systems proved to encode a working toxin and its antidote. The largest family blocks protein production by cutting messenger RNA. Four systems switched on under stresses the bacterium meets in the body, such as low oxygen and life inside macrophages, pointing to a role in disease.
europmc-pmc2790698:
Macleod and colleagues reviewed why people with cancer symptoms wait before seeing a doctor, and why doctors sometimes wait before sending them on for tests. Their 2009 work drew on two worldwide reviews of published studies, prompted by concern that late diagnosis helps explain weaker cancer survival in the United Kingdom.

Across cancer types, the main reason patients waited was failing to see that a symptom could be serious. Older age, lower income, and less schooling each tracked with longer waits for certain cancers, and fear of cancer also held people back. On the doctor side, the biggest problem was misreading symptoms and treating them as something else.
europmc-pmc2842698:
Bell argued in 2010 that Darwin's picture of evolution inching along under weak, steady selection needs a major supplement: strong selection whose direction keeps flipping. Field studies now routinely measure fierce selection in wild populations, and gene studies pin adaptation to a few genes of large effect. Yet traits stay highly heritable, and fossil lineages show amounts of change unrelated to elapsed time, which clashes with the fast-selection picture.

Changing environments resolve the clash, Bell contends. Conditions vary on every timescale, so the fitness target keeps moving and variation never drains away. Long-term studies confirm selection reversing direction again and again. Adaptation, he concludes, often rests on a handful of genes exposed to commonplace, strong, fluctuating selection.
europmc-pmc2843598:
Mozaffarian, Micha, and Wallace pooled randomized trials in 2010 to test whether swapping saturated fat for polyunsaturated fat in the diet actually prevents coronary heart disease. Guidelines have long urged cutting saturated fat, but they rarely name what should replace it, and trial results on heart events were mixed and poorly summarized.

Across the qualifying trials, people who ate more polyunsaturated fat in place of saturated fat suffered fewer heart attacks and heart deaths. Risk fell by roughly a fifth in the pooled estimate. Each added chunk of energy from polyunsaturated fat lowered risk further. The authors argue the replacement nutrient matters as much as the cut, and name polyunsaturated fat the proven stand-in.
europmc-pmc2880998:
Wilms and colleagues tested in 2010 whether dimethylfumarate, a drug ingredient already used for psoriasis, can quiet the brain's own immune cells. Brain inflammation driven by microglia and astrocytes, the brain's resident support and defense cells, sits at the center of multiple sclerosis. Early clinical results suggested the drug also eases that relapsing disease.

In rat cell cultures, the team provoked inflammation with a bacterial toxin and added the drug at several doses. Treated glial cells, meaning microglia and astrocytes together, made far less nitric oxide, a toxic gas-like messenger, and released much lower amounts of three inflammatory signals. The drug also lowered the enzyme that makes the oxide. Direct calming of glial cells may explain part of the drug's benefit in the brain.
europmc-pmc2881098:
Hercberg and colleagues described in 2010 the design of NutriNet-Santé, a French web-based cohort study linking diet and health. Untangling food's true role among genetic, behavioral, and social causes needs very large groups with precisely measured diets. The internet offered a way to recruit and follow volunteers cheaply, with data checked and processed automatically.

The study planned five years of recruitment and ten years of follow-up, entirely through a dedicated website. Volunteers report foods, nutrients, activity, and health outcomes, plus the social and cultural forces that shape eating. The design paper lays out the tools for measuring diet online and the safeguards for data quality. Its scale aims to let single nutrients, whole foods, and eating patterns each be tested against mortality and disease.
europmc-pmc2882898:
Paterson and Warburton reviewed in 2010 the proof that being active helps older adults stay able and free. They looked at studies that followed healthy adults over age sixty-five in their own homes. The outcomes were limits on function, disability, and loss of the ability to live on one's own. They also checked exercise trials that reported function, and studies of memory and thought.

Moderate and high levels of activity cut the risk of new functional limits by about half. The proof for thought and memory was positive but thin. The graded results back clear minimum targets for older adults.
europmc-pmc3002198:
Marks and colleagues linked prenatal pesticide exposure to attention problems in young Mexican-American children in California's farm country in a 2010 report from the CHAMACOS study. Organophosphate sprays are known nerve poisons, and early exposure was suspected to shape behaviour.

Exposure was gauged from breakdown products in urine during pregnancy and childhood, with attention tested at ages three and a half and five. Pregnancy exposure showed little link at the younger age but clear links at five: more parent-reported attention trouble and higher odds of crossing a test threshold for attention deficit patterns. Child's own later exposure mattered less in their analysis.
europmc-pmc3031198:
Huang, Takebayashi, Qi, and Hickerson presented in 2011 a software package for testing whether related species split apart at the same time. The tool, called MTML-msBayes in short, works with DNA from many species pairs and many gene regions at once. It uses simulations rather than exact formulas, an approach known as approximate Bayesian computation.

Simulations showed the method gains power as more gene regions are added, and stays reliable when mutation rates differ across regions. Allowing for migration between populations made timing estimates harder, but naming the right migration model helped. Applied to three Australian bird pairs, the tool pointed to a shared split followed by some later gene flow. The package was released as free, open source software for other biologists.
europmc-pmc3091298:
Fisher and a large sequencing team described in 2011 a fully automated factory process for fishing out just the protein coding parts of the human genome for sequencing. Reading only the exome, the coding fraction, costs far less than reading a whole genome and still finds most disease causing mutations. Their method automates an established capture technique, in which DNA is hybridized to baits for the wanted regions.

Robots and checkpoints carry each sample from raw DNA to a sequence ready library, at a scale of thousands of samples that manual work cannot reach. Quality control gates catch failures early instead of after expensive sequencing. The improvements also work in a hand run version of the protocol for smaller labs. The authors argue targeted sequencing will stay economical for large disease studies for years. Their pipeline was built to meet that demand at production scale.
europmc-pmc3116198:
Benjamin Pariente and a large international group set out methods in 2011 for a new score tracking lasting bowel damage in Crohn disease. Existing scores capture how active the illness feels at one visit, yet the gut can scar, narrow, and need surgery over years even between flares. Their project, run across many centres, aimed to measure that built-up harm.

The planned score weighs where damage sits, how severe and wide it is, whether it grows, and whether it can heal. It draws on scans, scope exams, and surgery history suited to each gut section. Patients would be followed on a chart plotting damage against time, so the slope shows speed of worsening. Such a tool could test whether treatments truly slow long-term damage.
europmc-pmc3126798:
Carol Tenopir and colleagues surveyed more than thirteen hundred scientists about sharing research data for a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Modern science produces floods of data, and sharing allows checks and new work, yet habits vary widely. The survey asked about access, storage, preservation, and willingness to share.

Most scientists were content with collecting and short-term handling of their data, but not with keeping it safe long-term, and many workplaces offered little support. Lack of time and money were the top reasons data stayed private. Willingness rose when conditions such as formal credit were promised. Practices differed by funder, field, age, and region. The authors see new funder rules and shared data networks as levers for change.
europmc-pmc3177898:
Johann Steiner and colleagues found a stress-linked brain chemical raised in the brains of severely depressed patients in a 2011 paper in the Journal of Neuroinflammation. Blood immune signals rise during depressive episodes, and brain immune cells may mirror them in a region where signalling by the transmitter glutamate is disturbed in depression. The team stained post-mortem tissue from acutely depressed patients who had died by suicide and from healthy controls.

Cells carrying the chemical, a glutamate-receptor activator made by brain immune cells, were significantly denser in two of three subregions of the cingulate area. The rise traced to major depression specifically, not bipolar disorder. Since blocking that receptor relieves depression fast in trials, an immune-driven excess of its activator offers a fresh disease mechanism and treatment angle.
europmc-pmc3180398:
Gary Collins and colleagues audited how diabetes risk calculators are built and reported in a 2011 paper in BMC Medicine. With hundreds of millions of cases expected by 2030, spotting undiagnosed or future diabetes early matters, and dozens of scoring models promise to help. The team reviewed thirty-nine studies presenting forty-three models.

Weak methods were widespread. Many models rested on too few outcome events per variable, screened candidate predictors by a discouraged significance filter, chopped continuous measures into crude bands, and ignored or hid missing data. Reporting often omitted the details needed to judge a model at all. The authors warn such shortcuts quietly corrupt the risk estimates doctors would act on, and they press for stricter building and reporting standards.
europmc-pmc3184498:
Hang Cui, Yahui Kong, and Hong Zhang reviewed the vicious circle linking oxidative stress, failing cell power stations, and aging in a 2012 paper in the Journal of Signal Transduction. Aging brings steady functional decline and rising disease, conserved across nearly all organisms, yet its molecular drivers remain debated. Two classic theories both blame cumulative damage from reactive oxygen chemicals, especially inside mitochondria, the cell's power stations.

The chemicals damage mitochondrial DNA, which degrades power output, which in turn leaks more chemicals, deepening the damage in a self-feeding loop. The review gathers current evidence on this interplay and its reach into age-related diseases. The authors present the loop not as settled fact but as the leading framework guiding experiments on slowing aging itself.
europmc-pmc3188798:
Li Yang and colleagues mapped RNAs lacking the usual tail in human cells in a 2011 paper in Genome Biology. Nearly all gene messages carry a long tail of one letter that standard sequencing uses as a handle, so tail-less RNAs stayed largely invisible. Sequencing both fractions in a cancer cell line and in human stem cells exposed the hidden set.

Most transcripts were tailed as expected. But a significant share were tail-less or appeared in both forms, and many ordinary messages carried only short tails, clustering in particular job categories. Some chopped-out gene segments accumulated as a new class of long tail-less RNAs. A subset of histone messages without tails marked undifferentiated stem cells and vanished on maturation, returning when adult cells were reprogrammed. The dataset opens the tail-less landscape to study.
europmc-pmc3194798:
James Shorter established that animal cells possess their own protein-unclumping machinery in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Bacteria, fungi, and plants use a powerful enzyme to dissolve protein aggregates and revive the proteins, but animals were thought to lack any equivalent, leaving their aggregate handling mysterious. Shorter tested extracts from mammalian cells for exactly that activity.

The extracts slowly dissolved large disordered aggregates and refolded the recovered protein, powered by chemical energy. Three helper proteins together proved necessary and sufficient for the trick, each with defined jobs in gripping the aggregate and feeding the central enzyme. The trio could not quickly crack the tough amyloid fibres of disease proteins, though it boosted the bacterial enzyme against them. Animals, it turns out, kept a quieter version of the machinery.
europmc-pmc3277298:
Karin Kiontke and colleagues rebuilt the family tree of the Caenorhabditis roundworms and added many new species, in this 2011 paper in BMC Evolutionary Biology. The group includes a premier laboratory model, yet only ten species were in culture, mostly from compost heaps, and their natural home was unknown. Fieldwork targeted what turned out to be their real habitat: rotting fruit, flowers, and stems.

The team barcoded every species with a standard DNA stretch and built a phylogeny from eleven genes across twenty-six cultured species, resolving two sister super-groups.
