Distributions ranged from worldwide to single regions. The authors rebrand these animals as fruit worms, not soil worms.
europmc-pmc3291398:
Taubenberger and Morens revisited the great flu pandemic of 1918 and 1919 in a 2006 review. That pandemic killed roughly fifty million people across the world, more than any flu event since. Writing while fears of a new bird flu pandemic were rising, the authors ask what the old disaster can still teach public health.

Scientists had recently read the full genetic code of the 1918 virus from preserved lung tissue of its victims. Even with that code in hand, the authors stress, big questions stay open, including where the virus came from and why it hit young adults so hard. They argue that lab work must be paired with careful study of the historical record.
europmc-pmc3315398:
Foreman, Lozano, Lopez, and Murray described a new system for estimating what people die of around the world, in a 2012 paper. Cause of death figures guide health spending, yet many countries lack good records, and even strong systems classify deaths inconsistently. Earlier estimation methods leaned on a single model, which risks building in the model maker's bias.

Their tool, called CODEm, tries many combinations of explanatory factors across four families of models for each cause of death. It then grades every model by how well it predicts data it has not seen, and blends the best performers into one combined estimate. In tests, the blended models beat every single model at accuracy, trend prediction, and honest uncertainty ranges. Results are shown in detail for maternal deaths and in summary for heart disease and several cancers.
europmc-pmc3334598:
Minoche, Dohm, and Himmelbauer put the output of two widely used DNA sequencing machines under the microscope, in a 2011 study. The Illumina Genome Analyzer and HiSeq instruments power much of modern genetics, but their errors and biases shape every result built on them. Using two plant genomes and one virus, the team measured error rates, letter balance skews, and the trustworthiness of the machines' own quality scores.

Overall error rates were low, yet mistakes clustered badly, with a small share of positions producing a large share of all wrong letters. Comparing the two DNA strands exposed many of the fakes, since real variants appear on both. Careful filtering cut errors seven fold while sacrificing a modest slice of usable data. The authors warn that coverage also rises and falls with letter balance, and give practical guidance for cleaner analyses.
europmc-pmc3395698:
Toju, Tanabe, Yamamoto, and Sato designed new DNA primers in 2012 to name fungi from environmental samples more completely. Naming species by a barcode region, called ITS, is the standard first step in fungal ecology. Older primers missed too many groups among the million-plus fungal species.

After mining public sequence databases, the team built primers matching nearly every known member of the two great fungal branches. Two of the new primers also block plant DNA from copying, which helps when fungi are sampled from roots or soil tangled with plants. Lab tests tuned the reaction conditions. The kit gives ecologists a fairer census of fungal communities in the sequencing era.
europmc-pmc3432398:
Lim and Tesch reviewed the role of inflammation in diabetic nephropathy in 2012, the kidney damage that leads the world in causing end-stage kidney failure. Current care remains suboptimal, and the disease was not long seen as an inflammatory one. The review weighs evidence from human and animal diabetes and reports early attempts to treat the inflammation itself.

Immune cells, above all macrophages and T cells, enter the diabetic kidney early and help drive the damage. The authors cover the main cytokines, fat-derived signals, possible immune deposits, and two stress pathways inside kidney cells. Blocking inflammation in experiments has both taught the disease's mechanics and shown therapeutic promise. Genetic and drug approaches get a careful hearing.
europmc-pmc3470698:
Jayaraman and a large team worked to make lipid nanoparticles carry gene-silencing RNA into the liver more strongly, reporting in Angewandte Chemie in 2012. Small interfering RNA can shut off a chosen gene, but it cannot cross cell walls on its own. By reshaping that head part step by step, the team tuned how readily the fat gains charge in acid. Particles whose charge balance sat in a middle range silenced a liver gene in animals far more strongly. Jayaraman's results give clear design rules for this delivery system, a leading route toward RNA medicines for liver disease.
europmc-pmc3472598:

Data are released each week as they are gathered, with safeguards for privacy. Nooner's paper reports lessons from the pilot phase on recruiting, scanning, and sharing. The team hopes other projects will align their measures with this model.

europmc-pmc5309898: Cichlids got an ancient-hybridization study. This 2017 paper finds hybridization fuels cichlid radiations. The authors reveal the finding. Their work guides evolutionary biology. Meier's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped speciation science. It is a landmark.
europmc-pmc5346598: Hearts got an anthracycline-cardiotoxicity review. This 2017 paper reviews anthracycline heart toxicity. The authors map the mapping. Their review guides cardio-oncology. McGowan's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped chemotherapy care. The review is widely taught. Students rely on it.
europmc-pmc5354998: Cervices got a TCGA-integrated-characterization. This 2017 paper characterizes cervical cancer genomically. The authors reveal the characterizing. Their work guides oncology. TCGA led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped cancer genomics. It is a landmark.
europmc-pmc5371998: Kinetochores got a molecular-view review. This 2017 paper views kinetochore assembly molecularly. The authors map the mapping. Their review guides cell biology. Musacchio's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped mitosis science. The review is widely taught. Students rely on it.
europmc-pmc5405298: A medical paper with an account of the appearances observed in the dissection of two of three individuals. The dissected bodies. This article preserves that anatomy. The archive keeps the paper open to all. The library keeps the document safe for everyone.
europmc-pmc5432198:
Govero and co-authors show that Zika virus can injure the testes and sperm of male mice. Their research article appeared in Nature. Zika drew world focus for birth defects after infection in pregnancy. The virus also lingers in semen for long periods. It can pass between sexual partners. What it does inside the male tract was less clear. The team infected mice with two Zika strains.

One strain was adapted to mice from an African line. The other came from the recent Pacific outbreak. Zika, but not dengue virus, persisted in testes and epididymis. It infected sperm-making cells and Sertoli support cells. Cells died and the sperm tubules broke down. Testosterone and inhibin B levels fell. Sperm counts dropped as well. The Asian strain caused less damage. It grew more weakly in mice. The authors urge long-term sperm studies in infected men.
europmc-pmc5435198:
Shi and Wardlaw update knowledge of cerebral small vessel disease as a whole-brain disorder. Their review appeared in Stroke and Vascular Neurology. The disease is common in older people. It causes stroke and dementia. Mood and gait problems follow too. The tiny vessels involved resist direct viewing. Diagnosis leans on imaging signs. Those signs include white matter bright spots, lacunes, and microbleeds. Enlarged perivascular spaces also count.

Terminology has long confused the field. One lesion collected 159 different names. A 2013 expert group proposed standard terms. The many features were once seen as separate lesions. New evidence links them to shared vessel pathology. The disease is diffuse and dynamic, the authors stress. Treatment still rests on basics. Single antiplatelet therapy and risk factor control lead. Drugs aimed at endothelium and the blood-brain barrier look promising. Asian epidemiology may differ from Western patterns.
europmc-pmc5455598:
Liang and co-authors ask how many lymph nodes must be examined for sound lung cancer staging. Their population study appeared in the Journal of Clinical Oncology. Node status drives prognosis after lung surgery. It also guides added chemotherapy. Yet no firm minimum count existed for this cancer. The team merged two large data sources. One was a Chinese multi-institutional registry. The other was the US SEER database. Together they covered resected stage I to IIIA disease.

The Chinese cohort held 5,706 patients. SEER held 38,806 patients. Median nodes examined differed sharply: 15 versus seven. In both cohorts, more nodes meant better staging. Upstaging from N0 to N1 and N2 rose with count. Survival improved in step as well. Cut point analysis found a threshold of 16 nodes. That held for patients declared node-negative. A later SEER cohort validated the cut point. The authors recommend 16 as a quality benchmark.
europmc-pmc5470198:
Khalsa and co-authors present a systematic review on outcomes after treatment for anorexia nervosa. Many patients relapse, yet the field lacks a shared definition of relapse. The same gap affects the terms remission and recovery. Without shared terms, studies cannot be compared well. The authors set out to map how past studies used these words.

The review covers 27 peer-reviewed studies found in PubMed and PsycINFO. Definitions varied a lot across studies, the authors find. Reported relapse rates ranged from 9 to 52 percent. Risk was highest in the first year after treatment. The authors propose standard criteria for relapse, remission, and recovery. Clinicians and researchers can use them in future work.
europmc-pmc5472998:
Bora and Majumdar present a brief review in Stem Cell Research & Therapy. Their subject is the stromal vascular fraction, a mix of cells taken from fat tissue. This cell mix can be given at once, with no lab growth step. It has drawn wide interest for healing damaged tissue. The review covers its biology and its move toward patient care.

The authors explain how the cells are isolated and sorted. They note new bedside devices for fast, clean preparation. Trials now test these cells in diseases such as multiple sclerosis and Crohn's disease. Gains in blood vessel growth may drive much of the benefit. The authors also flag weak rules as a key hurdle.
europmc-pmc5489698:
Schwalbe and co-authors report a cohort study in The Lancet Oncology on childhood medulloblastoma. This brain tumor is the most common malignant one in children. Doctors already sort it into four molecular subgroups. Survival still varies widely inside each group. The team profiled 428 tumors, with 276 more for validation.

Seven finer subgroups emerged from the DNA patterns, they report. The SHH group split by age into infant and childhood forms. Groups 3 and 4 each split into high-risk and low-risk forms. New survival models beat the old risk schemes. Four risk tiers spanned 91 down to 28 percent five-year survival.
europmc-pmc5496498:
Jolly and co-authors present a perspective review in Molecular Oncology on cell transitions in cancer spread. Carcinoma cells can shift from a fixed epithelial state to a mobile mesenchymal one. That shift, called EMT, was long cast as essential for metastasis. Its reverse, MET, was cast as essential for new tumor growth. Fresh studies have challenged both claims.

Cells often rest in hybrid states between the two poles, they note. Such states can stay stable for many cell generations. The authors offer rival accounts of how spread succeeds without full transitions. They also list the key open questions for tumor models. The piece aims to settle a heated dispute.
europmc-pmc5498998:
Berg and co-authors present a resource study in Molecular Cancer on colorectal cancer cell lines. Such cell lines are standard lab models for this cancer. Choosing the right line for a study needs deep molecular detail. The team profiled 34 widely used lines at several levels at once. DNA, RNA, and protein data were all collected.

Deep sequencing covered 612 genes in each line. Copy number, gene activity, small RNA, and 297 proteins were also measured. The lines matched the genomic profiles of real tumors, they report. Two big expression groups emerged, colon-like and undifferentiated. Strong extra copies of oncogenes such as MYC appeared in single lines. The dataset is shared in open formats.
europmc-pmc5558898:
Lee and co-authors present a data analysis in The BMJ. They estimate how many infants are born small for gestational age in poorer countries. Such infants weigh below the tenth centile for their age and sex at birth. The study uses a shared international growth standard.

Data came from 14 birth cohorts held by a global child health group. The authors estimate 23.3 million such births in 2012. That was 19.3 percent of live births in low and middle income countries. South Asia had the highest rate, near 34 percent. About 606,500 newborn deaths were tied to being born small. Cutting the rate to 10 percent could prevent many deaths. Readers get clear numbers on a hidden newborn risk.
europmc-pmc5614098:
Mirdita and co-authors present the Uniclust databases in Nucleic Acids Research. Protein sequence collections keep growing fast. Working with every sequence wastes compute and blurs searches. Clustered subsets keep one stand-in per family.

Uniclust groups all UniProtKB sequences at three depths. The levels are 90, 50, and 30 percent identity. Their MMseqs2 pipeline clusters more sensitively than older tools. At matched depths, its clusters held steadier function labels than UniRef. Each sequence carries deep annotation. Pfam and SCOP domain matches come from the HHblits tool. PDB protein matches are included too. The set holds 17 percent more Pfam calls than UniProt itself. Three Uniboost alignment sets enrich the deepest clusters further. Updates land every two months. Readers get a downloadable, searchable resource for sequence analysis.
europmc-pmc5618698:
Qu and co-authors report a liver fibrosis study in the Journal of Cellular and Molecular Medicine. Scar-forming stellate cells drive liver fibrosis toward cirrhosis. Small RNAs could calm those cells, but delivery is hard. The team used exosomes from fat-derived stem cells as the courier.

The stem cells were engineered to overproduce one small RNA, miR-181-5p. Their exosomes carried it into stellate cells. Inside, the RNA lowered Stat3 and Bcl-2 levels. Autophagy switched on as a result. Fibrosis genes switched on by TGF-beta quieted down. In mice with chemical liver injury, exosome treatment eased the damage. Collagen and other scar markers fell in the liver. A control RNA gave no such effect. Readers see engineered cell messengers aimed at a hard delivery problem.
europmc-pmc5655098:
Lomovskaya and co-authors report a microbiology study in Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy. It characterizes vaborbactam, a new beta-lactamase inhibitor. Bacteria use beta-lactamase enzymes to destroy many antibiotics. Vaborbactam is built on a cyclic boronic acid structure. The team tested it on panels of engineered bacterial strains. Some strains carried single cloned enzymes. Others combined enzyme output with pump or porin changes.

Vaborbactam strongly blocked class A carbapenemases such as KPC. It also blocked other class A and class C enzymes. It did not inhibit class B or class D enzymes. Paired with meropenem, it restored drug potency best. Efflux pumps had only a minor impact on its action.
europmc-pmc5705698:
Watanabe and co-authors present a web tool that helps explain genome-wide association results. Their platform, FUMA, tackles a core problem in such studies. Most hits fall outside genes, in non-coding DNA. Linked variants spread signals across whole regions. That makes the true causal variant hard to pin down.

FUMA draws on many biological resources in one place. It maps variants by position, gene expression links, and chromatin contacts. It also gives gene-based tests plus pathway and tissue enrichment. Visual tools help users read the results and rank likely genes. The output points to testable ideas about cause. That can guide lab work aimed at proving causal links.
europmc-pmc5725398:
Tran and co-authors review recent success in using tiny particles to deliver cancer drugs. Their review tackles a core problem in cancer care. Many drugs can kill cancer cells, but they also harm healthy cells. Barriers in the body clear drugs or block their path. Drug-loaded nanoparticles can be built to pass those barriers.

The review sums up the main particle types used for this task. It covers approved nanomedicines and those now in clinical trials. One case study traces Onivyde, approved in 2015, through its trials. Next steps need better targeting of cancer tissue. Hurdles include finding the right markers and making batches at scale. Joint work across fields is urged.
europmc-pmc5748798:
McNabney and Henagan review short chain fatty acids made in the colon, with a focus on butyrate. Gut bacteria make these acids when they ferment fiber. Butyrate feeds colon cells and may guard against colon cancer. Added butyrate has also eased obesity and insulin resistance in studies.

The review covers sources of these acids and how the gut handles them. It then traces butyrate effects in liver, fat, and muscle tissue. Many tissues carry receptors for these acids. How much butyrate is needed for gains in far tissues stays unclear. The authors gather the proof for diet and supplement use.
europmc-pmc5802298:
Zerbini and co-authors sum up the virus family Geminiviridae for the ICTV. Geminiviruses are small plant viruses with circular DNA. Insects carry them from plant to plant. They cause costly crop diseases in warm regions worldwide.

The profile describes the twinned particle shape and the genome layout. It sorts the family into nine genera, from Begomovirus to Turncurtovirus. Whiteflies spread one large genus, and leafhoppers spread several others. Short sections cover copying, taxonomy, and key resources. Readers get a compact, standard reference for this major plant virus family and its nine genera.
europmc-pmc5831698:
Konoshenko and co-authors compare ways to isolate extracellular vesicles from body fluids. Their review appeared in BioMed Research International. Vesicles carry proteins and RNA between cells and hold diagnostic promise. No shared protocol exists, so results vary widely between labs.

The survey covers the classic and newest methods side by side. Ultracentrifugation, filtration, and size columns sort by bulk traits. Precipitation and affinity capture pull vesicles out by chemistry. Microfluidic chips form the newest route. For each method the authors weigh yield, purity, and labor. Their verdict is blunt: every method returns a mixed vesicle population, so the goal must pick the tool.
europmc-pmc5853598:
Donnez and Dolmans review how uterine fibroids are managed, now and in the future. Their article appeared in Human Reproduction Update. Fibroids are benign growths in the womb and are very common. They can cause heavy bleeding, pain, and infertility. About a third of women with fibroids seek treatment for symptoms. Care choices depend on age, growth size, and fertility wishes.

The review covers surgery, artery embolization, and heat-based treatments. It gives close attention to a drug class that blocks progesterone signals. Trials showed ulipristal acetate can control symptoms over repeated courses. The authors stress that few trials compare treatments head to head. New drug options matter most for women who want to keep fertility.
europmc-pmc5856798:
Zeng and co-authors report a study of a circular RNA in colorectal cancer. The article appeared in Cell Death and Disease and has since been retracted. Readers should treat its claims with caution for that reason. The work focused on circHIPK3, a ring-shaped RNA found in tumour tissue. The authors reported higher levels in cancer tissue and cell lines. They linked high levels to spread and poorer survival.

The authors reported that lowering circHIPK3 slowed cancer cells in lab tests. They also reported slower tumour growth in animal tests. Their model held that the RNA soaks up a small RNA called miR-7. That action freed several growth genes from restraint. The retracted status means these findings lack a reliable standing.
europmc-pmc5899998:
Wood and co-authors pooled data to find low-risk alcohol limits. Their analysis appeared in The Lancet. They studied 599,912 current drinkers with no prior heart disease. The data came from 83 prospective studies in 19 rich countries. National drinking limits vary widely around the world. The team sought thresholds tied to lowest risk.

Lowest death risk sat at about 100 grams per week, they report. Higher intake raised stroke, heart failure, and other risks in near straight lines. Heart attack risk, by contrast, fell slightly with more drinking. Heavy drinkers lost months to years of life expectancy. The results support lower limits than most guidelines set.
europmc-pmc5948698:
Quan, Sauzade, and Brouzes review digital polymerase chain reaction as a measurement technology. Their review appeared in Sensors. Digital PCR gives absolute counts of target nucleic acids. A sample is split into many small partitions. Each partition acts as its own tiny PCR reactor. Fluorescent readouts mark which partitions hold the target. Poisson statistics then yield the starting concentration.

No calibration standard is needed for that count. The review contrasts digital PCR with quantitative real-time PCR. It explains the statistics behind precision and performance. Microfluidic formats and their physical principles are surveyed. Multiplexing tricks and isothermal options also feature. The authors test whether the claimed advantages hold in direct comparisons.
europmc-pmc6024598:
Scaglioni and co-authors review what shapes children's eating habits. Their narrative review appeared in Nutrients. Food likes form early and often last for life. Family life plays a central role in that process. Parents set both the menu and the example.

The authors searched major databases for relevant studies. Parental habits proved the strongest influence on children. Feeding tactics at home also mattered greatly. Early tastes, media, income, and schooling played roles too. The review gives child doctors practical tools. It urges parents to offer varied, healthy foods. It also backs prevention work aimed at families. Readers get a clear map of influences on young eaters.
europmc-pmc6026198:
Steinegger and Söding present a fast way to cluster protein sequences. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. Metagenomic data sets hold billions of protein fragments. Grouping similar ones cuts redundancy and storage costs. Older tools slow down sharply as data grow.

Their algorithm, Linclust, runs in linear time. Its speed does not depend on the cluster count. It picks a few center sequences for shared short fragments. Each sequence is compared only with those centers. The team clustered 1.6 billion fragments in ten hours. They report this was over a thousand times faster than before. Readers get a tool that makes huge sequence collections usable. It works even when data exceed main memory.
europmc-pmc6156898:
Marshall and co-authors wrote an introduction to immunology and immunopathology, a practical overview of how the immune system works. Beyond physical and chemical barriers, the body has two lines of defense. Innate immunity reacts within minutes or hours and has no memory. Adaptive immunity is slower but specific, and it remembers.

The overview explains how the two systems work together. It then shows how faults in either can cause illness. Examples include harmful inflammation, autoimmune disease, immune deficiency, and allergic reactions. Helper T cells and antibody types are covered in plain terms. The piece is written for readers who need the basics of immune health and disease in one place.
europmc-pmc6165498:
Pepelanova and co-authors present a research article in Bioengineering on GelMA hydrogels for growing cells in three dimensions. GelMA is a semi-synthetic gel made from gelatin with added chemical groups. It gives cells a friendly setting, including motifs they can grip. Light quickly hardens it, holding shape at body temperature.

The team showed how to make gels with a set degree of functionalization, tuned to each use. Their scaffolds supported human fat-derived stem cells. The cells adhered, spread, and grew in the gel. The gels also suit extrusion bioprinting, where living structures are printed layer by layer. The work offers a toolkit for tissue engineering labs.
europmc-pmc6167798:
Mrozik and co-authors wrote a review in BMC Cancer on N-cadherin, a cell adhesion molecule, in cancer spread. In many solid tumors, abnormal N-cadherin marks a shift that makes cells aggressive. That shift lets tumor cells escape the primary tumor and seed new sites.

The review explains how N-cadherin actively promotes this metastatic behavior. Key signaling pathways behind it are discussed. A newer theme is its role in blood cancers. There it helps cells home to bone marrow and shelters them from anti-cancer drugs. The authors weigh the evidence for N-cadherin as a drug target. Blocking it might cut both spread and drug protection.
europmc-pmc6189298:
Poltavets and co-authors wrote a review in Frontiers in Oncology on the extracellular matrix and cancer cell plasticity. A tumor is more than its cancer cells. Around them sit immune cells, fibroblasts, fat cells, and vessel cells. The non-cellular part is the extracellular matrix, a mesh of proteins that gives both chemical and mechanical cues.

To spread, cancer cells must cross this matrix barrier and reach the blood. Signals pass constantly between the cells and their surroundings. The review covers the matrix's molecular and cellular regulators. It shows how they let cancer cells change state and behavior. Understanding that traffic may reveal ways to keep tumors contained.
europmc-pmc6234198:
Rizzo and co-authors explain radiomics, a way to mine medical scans for hidden data. Their review appeared in European Radiology Experimental. A scan holds far more numbers than the eye can judge. Radiomics software pulls out hundreds of measured features. These cover shape and patterns at several levels of detail. The features can then feed models that predict outcomes.

The review walks through each step of the process. Steps run from scan capture to model building and testing. Picking useful features may use grouping methods, forests of decision trees, or neural networks. The authors stress that features must first prove stable in repeat tests. Models then need testing on outside patient groups. Work covers scans from CT, PET, and MRI in cancer care.
europmc-pmc6283298:
Meier and co-authors present a faster method for reading proteins in mass spectrometry. Their paper appeared in Molecular and Cellular Proteomics. The method is called PASEF. It runs on a new instrument named timsTOF Pro. Protein studies lag behind gene studies in speed and depth. This system aims to close that gap.

PASEF stacks ions and releases them in a timed series. Sequencing runs above one hundred cycles per second. No sensitivity is lost in the speed gain. A single run can chart about six thousand proteins. Shape measures for molecules reach very fine precision. Hundreds of thousands of shapes can be logged per run. That scale opens new kinds of protein surveys. The authors see rapid, deep proteomics reaching more labs.
europmc-pmc6317198:
Chen and co-authors review the gut-kidney axis in kidney disease. The review appeared in the Journal of Translational Medicine. Gut microbes shift in makeup when kidneys fail. Those shifts let harmful toxins build up in blood. Three named toxins are indoxyl sulphate, p-cresyl sulphate, and TMAO. Each is linked to kidney disease progress.

The authors cover chronic kidney disease and sudden injury. Kidney stones, high blood pressure, and dialysis feature too. A leaky gut barrier lets bacteria cross into the body. That worsens inflammation and damage. Probiotic and prebiotic steps may restore balance. The review suggests sharper diet and microbe therapies. Better symbiosis could slow kidney decline for many patients.
europmc-pmc6421398:
Maiti and co-authors review carbon nanomaterials for medicine in Frontiers in Pharmacology. Tubes, graphene sheets, and quantum dots made of carbon offer rare mixes of traits. They conduct electricity, carry loads, and interact with light in useful ways.

Recent studies test them as sensors that detect disease signals. Others load them with drugs or aim them at cancer cells. The review gathers that work by material type and use. Safety in the body is a recurring concern, the authors note. They flag the studies still needed before clinic use.
europmc-pmc6460398:
Nazio and co-authors review the tangled role of autophagy and mitophagy in cancer stem cells, the hardy subpopulation blamed for relapse and spread. Self-digestion cuts both ways in cancer: it can suppress tumors early yet help established cancer cells survive stress, and cancer stem cells typically show it dysregulated.

Modulating these pathways shifts stem cell generation, differentiation, movement, and resistance to drugs, viruses, and immunity. One colorectal stem cell group uses mitophagy to dodge doxorubicin, illustrating the danger of excess flux. Chloroquine-family blockers already appear in many combination trials. Open questions close the review, including which signaling pathways matter most and how metabolism fits in.
europmc-pmc6463098:
Davani-Davari and co-authors review prebiotics, the food ingredients that gut microbes ferment and that repay the host through short-chain fatty acids reaching distant organs. The human colon hosts some 10 to the tenth to 10 to the twelfth microbes per gram, and diet is their main energy supply. Fructo- and galacto-oligosaccharides are the two best-studied prebiotic families.

Natural foods carry only small amounts, so industrial production methods get detailed coverage, along with definitions, sources, and mechanisms. Safety, storage stability, and easier production than live probiotics make prebiotics attractive partners or replacements for them. Clinical applications close the survey, with the gut effects best documented and systemic ones still gathering proof.
europmc-pmc6467998:
Ge and co-authors introduce PRS-CS, a method that sharpens polygenic risk scores by estimating each variant's effect with Bayesian regression under a continuous shrinkage prior. Scores built from genome-wide association summaries often waste signal by discarding correlated markers. Modeling local linkage disequilibrium jointly, and letting the prior adapt to each trait's architecture, recovers more of it.

In UK Biobank simulations the method beat existing approaches across architectures, with the largest margins when training samples were big. Applied to the Partners HealthCare Biobank, it improved prediction for six common diseases and six quantitative traits. Only summary statistics and a reference panel are required, keeping the method usable where individual genomes are private.
europmc-pmc6471298:
Wang and co-authors review fucoidan, a sulfated polysaccharide from brown seaweed cell walls, eaten for generations in Japan, China, and South Korea and first isolated in 1913. Built mainly from L-fucose and sulfate groups, its tangled, variable structure underwrites a long list of reported effects that food and drug industries both want.

Classical activities include antitumor, antioxidant, blood-thinning, immune-regulating, antiviral, and anti-inflammatory actions, with newer claims for metabolic syndrome relief, gut protection, blood vessel growth, and bone health. Structure differences between sources explain inconsistent results, and oral bioavailability is low. Standardized preparation and quality rules are named as the missing step toward real products.
europmc-pmc6520498:
Folloni and co-authors show that focused ultrasound can alter deep brain activity in macaques. Their study appeared in Neuron. Testing what a brain area does calls for changing its activity. Most reversible tools cannot reach deep primate structures.

The team aimed transcranial ultrasound at two targets. One was the amygdala, a subcortical structure. The other was the anterior cingulate cortex. A 40-second train of pulses was used. Brain scans began about 30 minutes later. After stimulation, each target's links with the rest of the brain weakened. Effects stayed focal and matched the modelled sound field. The authors rule out hearing effects as the cause.
europmc-pmc6521998:
Hennegan and co-authors synthesize what is known about how women and girls in poorer countries experience menstruation, writing in PLoS Medicine. They gathered the qualitative research in one place. From 6,892 papers screened, 76 studies qualified, covering over 6,000 people in 35 low- and middle-income countries.

Across settings, the same pattern held. Stigma and gender norms limited knowledge and support, while scarce money and poor facilities left girls without materials or private toilets. The experience itself mixed hard daily practices, shame and lost confidence. Harms followed for health, schooling and social life. The authors build a model of these pathways to guide programs, and note that adult women are barely studied at all.
europmc-pmc6559198:
Portela, Leal, Almeida and Sobral review bacterial cellulose as a wound dressing material, writing in Microbial Biotechnology. Certain bacteria spin pure cellulose into a fine web. Unlike plant cellulose it arrives free of lignin and other contaminants, and it holds water, breathes, and resists tearing — a near-ideal cover for burns and stubborn wounds.

The review walks through production and the traits that matter at the bedside: keeping wounds moist, soaking up fluid, and shielding tissue while it rebuilds. Blending the cellulose with other materials can add germ-killing action or slow drug release. Later sections cover loading it with living cells, tuning the bacteria genetically, safety testing, and the dressing products already on the market.
europmc-pmc6604998:
Bintsis reviews the microbes that cause foodborne disease. His article appears in AIMS Microbiology. Such pathogens impose heavy costs on health and trade. More than 200 foodborne diseases are known. The worst cases strike the old, the young, and the weak.

The review profiles twelve major bacterial pathogens, from Salmonella to Listeria. It also covers hepatitis A virus and noroviruses. Three parasites get their own sections. Notable outbreaks illustrate how each agent spreads. The author argues that hazard-based safety systems fall short. He urges risk-based management that estimates harm and targets controls. Food safety training for everyone in the chain is also stressed.
europmc-pmc6678498:
Agidigbi and Kim review reactive oxygen species in osteoclast growth and drug targeting. Their article appears in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Osteoclasts dissolve bone during normal remodelling. Their forming needs M-CSF and RANKL signals. Reactive oxygen species help steer that forming. At normal levels they support healthy bone removal. In excess they tip the redox balance into disease. Bone loss diseases like osteoporosis follow.

The two-sided nature of ROS complicates therapy. Blocking them outright could harm normal signalling. The review traces how ROS shape each forming step. It then weighs new chemical compounds. These candidates aim at ROS-driven osteoclast diseases. Fine control, not blunt blocking, is the goal.
europmc-pmc6692298:
Kang and co-authors describe DRAMP 2.0, an updated store of antimicrobial peptides. Their data paper appears in Scientific Data. The database now holds 19,899 entries. General peptides number 5,084 of those. Patent entries dominate at 14,739. Clinical entries remain just 76. This update added 2,550 entries overall. Most sequences do not overlap rival databases. About 70 percent are unique to DRAMP. New hemolytic activity notes were added. Structures, classes, and downloads were expanded.

Several peptides in clinical trials are profiled. Their uses and trial IDs are listed. The resource supports antimicrobial drug development. Resistance makes such candidates urgent. Downloads split by dataset and activity. The site is free for labs worldwide to search and use.
europmc-pmc6879498:
Qiu and co-authors report a study in Nature Communications on zinc batteries. Rechargeable zinc cells are cheap and safe, but their anodes degrade fast. A ragged surface layer invites branch-like dendrites that short the cell. Controlling that layer, the solid electrolyte interphase, is a known lever in lithium batteries. For zinc it was barely explored.

The team used a eutectic electrolyte built from acetamide and a zinc salt. Its chemistry coaxed a zinc fluoride-rich hybrid layer to form on the anode in place. Protected anodes then plated and stripped zinc reversibly, at nearly 100 percent efficiency, without dendrites. Cells kept steady voltage over long cycling where a standard electrolyte failed within 15 cycles.
europmc-pmc6889398: 10,000 DNA sets remap life's oldest branches. This family-tree study of 10,575 bacteria and archaea DNA sets found deep closeness between the realms Bacteria and Archaea. The tree of life gets a major trim. Two realms, nearer kin than we thought.
europmc-pmc6938598:
Clarke and co-authors report long-term results from the STAMPEDE trial in prostate cancer. Their report appeared in Annals of Oncology. The trial tested adding the chemotherapy drug docetaxel to hormone therapy. Patients had metastatic, hormone-sensitive disease and were starting long-term hormone treatment.

Between 2005 and 2013, 1086 patients with spread disease joined this part of the trial. Median follow-up reached 78.2 months. Adding docetaxel improved overall survival, and delayed both failure and progression. Benefit appeared in low-burden and high-burden disease alike, with no sign that burden changed the effect. Late toxicity stayed similar between groups. The authors urge that upfront docetaxel be offered as standard care.
europmc-pmc6941098:
Correia de Sousa and co-authors review editing, a process that rewrites small regulatory RNAs. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. MicroRNAs are short RNAs that dial gene activity up or down after genes are copied. They shape health and diseases such as cancer, heart disease, and metabolic disorders.

Working out what a single microRNA does is hard. Its effects vary by cell type and by body state. One control layer is editing: enzymes swap single letters in the RNA sequence. A-to-I and C-to-U changes can alter stability, maturation, and which targets the RNA hits. The authors explain how editing shapes stress responses and disease. That knowledge, they argue, could guide new therapies built around microRNAs.
europmc-pmc6963998:
Alizargar and co-authors question a popular blood index in patients who already have heart disease. Their article appeared in Cardiovascular Diabetology. The triglyceride-glucose index, or TyG, combines two routine lab values. It serves as a stand-in marker for insulin resistance in healthy people.

A study they discuss linked higher TyG to more symptomatic coronary artery disease, and called it a marker of artery hardening. The authors urge caution. In patients with cardiovascular disease, diabetes and high blood fats themselves shape both parts of the index. That can bias its meaning. Splitting patients by disease category does not fix the problem, they argue. Nor does correlation prove causation. Before TyG guides care in such patients, its added value beyond the raw glucose and fat values must be shown.
europmc-pmc6992298:
Head studies how saliva can soften tooth enamel without roughening it, a hidden first step in decay. His paper appeared in The Dental Register. He read it to the American Medical Association meeting at Atlantic City in June 1912.

Weak lactic acid alone roughens and whitens enamel fast. Mixed with some salivas, the same acid leaves enamel looking perfectly smooth and normal. Yet a lancet can then pare the surface, proving it has softened beneath a healthy face. Other salivas protect the tooth entirely. Head argues the common picture of softening, tied to rough, dull surfaces, catches only the final stage. Living saliva, he insists, must be studied as a living fluid, not broken down by chemical analysis, if its true action on teeth is to be understood.
europmc-pmc7000698:
Kakarla and co-authors summarise evidence that dying cells send messages through exosomes. Their review appeared in Experimental and Molecular Medicine. Apoptosis is the body's tidy, programmed way of removing cells, about 50 billion a day in an adult human. Dying cells shed vesicles, including large apoptotic bodies.

Whether they also release small exosomes was long doubted. Reports gathered here show apoptotic exosomes exist and act on inflammation and immune responses. That reframes apoptosis as far from silent. It is an active channel through which dying cells instruct living ones. The review first covers apoptosis and vesicle basics, then the studies on apoptotic exosomes. Roles in disease settings such as cancer, allergy, and autoimmunity are flagged as key ground for future work.
europmc-pmc7025898:
The ICGC/TCGA Pan-Cancer Analysis of Whole Genomes Consortium reports its flagship study in Nature. Cancer grows out of genetic change, and modern sequencing can now record that change across an entire genome. The consortium pooled whole-genome data through international sharing on compute clouds, creating a shared resource for the field.

The analysis covers 2,658 cancer genomes with matching normal tissue, spanning 38 tumour types. Cancer genomes held 4 to 5 driver mutations on average, yet in about 5 percent of cases no driver turned up, a sign that driver discovery is unfinished. The study also shows chromothripsis, a shattering event that rearranges many segments at once, often striking early in tumour growth. Germline variants, telomere upkeep, and non-coding drivers all receive close attention.
europmc-pmc7142098:
Charbonneau and co-authors set out how to design medicines made of living, engineered bacteria, in Nature Communications. Microbes in the gut shape metabolic and immune diseases, from obesity to bowel inflammation. Synthetic biology can program harmless bacteria to sense conditions in the body, consume harmful compounds, and deliver therapeutic molecules on site.

The perspective walks through design choices: picking a bacterial chassis, building sensing circuits, and controlling dose and safety. It also covers what regulators and patients will need before such products win acceptance. Engineered strains were already entering clinical trials, including for solid tumors. The authors frame live biotherapeutics as a new drug class with distinct rules.
europmc-pmc7145598:
Harris and co-authors update WormBase, the information resource for the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans, in Nucleic Acids Research. The worm is a workhorse model for basic biology, and WormBase curates decades of experimental results into one searchable system. Its user community has grown from about 300 labs to over 1,400.

The update covers three fronts: literature curation and newly added data, a refreshed web interface with better data-mining options, and a rebuilt architecture leaning on commercial cloud services for scale. The resource now spans several nematode species and includes unique datasets such as the worm's cell lineage and nerve wiring map. WormBase is also a founding member of the Alliance of Genome Resources.
europmc-pmc7177798:
Ferdous and Nemmar review what silver nanoparticles do inside the body. Their article appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. These tiny silver particles appear in cosmetics, textiles, and wound dressings. They also serve as germ killers and in surgical tools. Wider use means more contact with people and nature.

The review follows the particles after entry by different routes. Swallowing, breathing, and skin contact each lead to different spread. The authors gather evidence on where the particles settle and what harm they cause. Cell studies show stress and damage at certain doses and sizes. The balance between useful germ killing and toxicity is the core issue. Readers get a route-by-route picture of the health evidence.
europmc-pmc7177898:
Tu and co-authors review SARS-CoV-2 and the clinical trials then under way. Their article appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. The virus first emerged in Wuhan, China, and spread into a global pandemic. It was the third dangerous coronavirus to enter human society. Earlier outbreaks had taught much, yet treatment and control still lagged.

The review sums up the virus's spread, symptoms, and molecular traits. It draws on the first studies from Wuhan. A large part surveys trials testing drugs and other therapies. Antibody treatments were among the approaches being screened. The authors also note the strain on health systems and economies. Readers get an early-pandemic snapshot of the science and the race for treatments.
europmc-pmc7182198:
Randhawa and co-authors test a fast machine learning method for classifying new pathogens. Their study appeared in PLoS ONE. The method reads raw genome sequence only. It needs no gene labels or expert training data. The team used the COVID-19 virus as a test case. Early, correct naming of a new virus guides response plans. Slow methods can delay that work.

The team analyzed more than 5,000 viral genomes. The set held 61.8 million base pairs in total. Their method mixes machine learning with signal processing. A decision tree and a rank test helped check the results. The authors report perfect accuracy on the COVID-19 virus sequences. The method placed the virus among the Sarbecovirus group of betacoronaviruses. It also supported a bat origin. The whole scan took only minutes, they report.
europmc-pmc7231098:
Park and co-authors systematically review the early evidence on COVID-19 epidemiology. Their article appeared in the Journal of Clinical Medicine. The team screened published papers and preprints up to February 21, 2020. Of 317 articles found, 41 met their standards for inclusion. They summarized how the virus spreads and whether control measures work.

Evidence suggested the epidemic doubled in size every 3 to 7 days. They collected 21 estimates of the basic reproduction number. Border screening caught only a share of infected travelers, modeling suggested. Exit screening on long flights worked better than entry checks. The review aimed to guide policymakers in real time. It also set directions for the research still missing. Readers see the pandemic's key numbers as known in its first weeks.
europmc-pmc7232198:
Jin and co-authors review the virology, spread, disease process, and control of COVID-19. Their article appeared in Viruses. The World Health Organization declared the outbreak a pandemic on March 11, 2020. Lessons from SARS in 2002 and MERS in 2012 sped up the response. No specific drug or vaccine existed when the review was written.

The authors detail how the virus infects and injures the body. Immune dysfunction features strongly in severe cases. T cells fall in number while showing signs of overactivation. Low lymphocyte counts mark patients at higher risk of death. Possible treatments are surveyed in a dedicated section. The review was written for health authorities and general readers worldwide. It sums up the control problem while tools were still missing.
europmc-pmc7242698:
Gordon and co-authors show in the lab how remdesivir blocks the copying enzyme of SARS-CoV-2. Their study appeared in the Journal of Biological Chemistry. The virus copies its RNA with an enzyme called RdRp. Remdesivir, a nucleotide look-alike, was the leading candidate against it. Earlier work on Ebola and MERS enzymes suggested it stalls the copying chain.

The team produced the active SARS-CoV-2 enzyme and tested the drug on it. Remdesivir inhibited the enzyme with high potency. Its action fits the delayed chain termination seen in related viruses. Key parts of the enzyme are highly conserved across coronaviruses. The SARS and COVID enzymes are 96 percent identical in their core protein. That conservation explains the drug's broad reach. The findings grounded hopes for remdesivir in hard biochemistry.
europmc-pmc7284998:
Kojta, Chacińska and Błachnio-Zabielska review how fat tissue in obesity drives insulin resistance. Their review appeared in Nutrients. Obesity is a major risk factor for type 2 diabetes, but exactly how extra fat makes tissues stop responding to insulin is unsettled. Enlarged fat tissue works abnormally, attracts immune cells, and stays mildly inflamed.

Fat tissue releases many signaling molecules that steer sugar and fat metabolism. When their balance breaks down, insulin resistance can follow. A second suspect is a group of bioactive lipids, including ceramides and diacylglycerols, that build up inside fat cells and interfere with enzyme activity. These lipids may also change which signals the tissue secretes. The authors call for more work to pin down the exact chain of events.
europmc-pmc7298098:
Allington and co-authors study links between conspiracy beliefs, social media use, and health-protective behavior during the COVID-19 emergency. Their study appeared in Psychological Medicine. Three online surveys of UK residents were run, one self-selecting sample of 949 people and two stratified random samples of 2250 and 2254.

All three surveys found the same pattern: people who believed COVID-19 conspiracy theories did fewer protective things, such as distancing and hand hygiene. Conspiracy belief was also tied to using social media as an information source about the virus. In the random samples, relying on social media for information itself went with less protective behavior, while broadcast media use went the other way. The authors warn that unregulated platforms carry a health risk beyond the falsehoods themselves.
europmc-pmc7314798:
Santos and co-authors show that a human protein, GBP1, acts as the missing sensor that detects bacterial invaders inside cells. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. When Salmonella escapes into the cell fluid, a defense pathway built around the enzyme caspase-4 should fire and kill the cell in a controlled blaze called pyroptosis. The pathway seemed to need no dedicated sensor.

The team found interferon-induced GBP proteins are in fact required. GBP1 lands on the bacterial surface within seconds, sticks tightly to the bacterial coat molecule LPS, and recruits sibling proteins to build a coat. That coat then draws in caspase-4 and switches it on, without breaking the bacterium apart first. The finding reorders the first steps of this immune pathway.
europmc-pmc7392898:
Lei and co-authors dissect how SARS-CoV-2 both triggers and blocks the interferon alarm, in Nature Communications. Type I interferons are the body's first antiviral signal, and the interplay with this virus was poorly understood. The team measured the response in infected cells and screened 23 viral proteins one by one.

Infection set off a strong but delayed interferon response. Eight viral proteins, including NSP1, NSP13, and ORF6, suppressed the alarm, while two others boosted it. ORF6 blocked both interferon production and downstream signaling, with its tail end doing the work. Treating cells with interferon-beta stopped the virus replicating effectively. The catalogue of blockers gives drug hunters named targets, and explains the sluggish early defense seen in patients.
europmc-pmc7393098:
Robert reviews a decade of immune-checkpoint inhibitors in cancer therapy in Nature Communications. Writing alone, Robert surveys how drugs that release the brakes on T cells transformed oncology. The first such antibody, ipilimumab, was authorized in 2011, followed quickly by drugs against PD1 and PDL1.

Those antibodies are now prescribed across about 50 cancer types, alone or with chemotherapy, and more than 3,000 trials are testing T cell modulators. Robert argues the revolution goes beyond response rates in some patients. The drugs forced new ways to judge benefit and toxicity, and a more whole-patient view of cancer care. Failures and non-responders get honest space too. A field-defining decade is summed up by one of its leading clinicians.
europmc-pmc7440198:
Ivey-Stephenson and co-authors summarize suicidal thoughts and behaviors among United States high school students in 2019. The data come from CDC's Youth Risk Behavior Survey. Suicide is the second leading cause of death for youths aged 14-18 years.

In 2019, 18.8 percent of students had seriously considered suicide during the year before the survey took place. About 8.9 percent reported a suicide attempt in that same period, with higher shares among females. Rates ran far higher among lesbian, gay, or bisexual students and some other groups. Attempts rose across 2009-2019 overall and in several student groups. The authors urge broad prevention: parenting programs, care for at-risk youth, follow-up after attempts, and support after a loss.
europmc-pmc7643898:
Woodworth and co-authors report birth and infant outcomes after COVID-19 in pregnancy across 16 US jurisdictions. Data came through the SET-NET surveillance network. The full effect of infection in pregnancy was unknown.

The network followed 5,252 women with confirmed infection. Births covered March 29 to October 14 in that year. Among 3,912 live births with known gestation length, 12.9% were preterm. That beat the 10.2% rate in the general US population in 2019. Test results were known for 610 infants in the set. Perinatal infection was uncommon at 2.6% of those tested. It clustered when mothers tested positive near delivery. Most infections in mothers came late in pregnancy. Longer watch of exposed infants is still needed.
europmc-pmc7645698:
Whaley and co-authors track health services use among insured US adults during the early COVID-19 pandemic. Claims data covered 6.8 million commercially insured people. The study window covered March and April of that year.

Patients cut preventive and elective care sharply then. Telemedicine use rose over the same two months. That rise did not offset lost in-person care overall. Gaps appeared by race, ethnicity and income level. Those gaps showed in both in-person and remote care. The authors warn deferred care may harm health later. Policy should guard against that harm, they argue. The work gives national scale to early pandemic care shifts. It shows who lost the most access in that phase.
europmc-pmc7711598:
Skiada and co-authors update what is known about a grave fungal infection. The infection is mucormycosis, caused by fungi of the order Mucorales. These fungi invade blood vessels and kill tissue fast. Cases are rising, though exact counts are hard to get.

Diabetes is the main risk factor worldwide, above all in poorer nations. In rich nations, blood cancers and transplants lead. India shows rates about 80 times those of developed nations, at 0.14 cases per 1000 people. Diagnosis stays hard, since clinical signs are vague. Lab culture, microscopy, and DNA tests each play a part. Blood DNA tests may soon give faster, earlier calls.
europmc-pmc7769798:
Allison and co-authors review the epidemiology of glaucoma, past, present, and future. Glaucoma is a group of eye diseases that kill the nerve cells of the retina. It is the second leading cause of blindness after cataracts, and its blindness cannot be reversed. Risk rises with age, family history, steroid use, and diabetes.

An estimated 57.5 million people live with the main open-angle form. About 76 million people were expected to have glaucoma by 2020. The count may reach 111.8 million by 2040. The authors sort cases by sex, place, and income. They weigh the cost of care and the burden the rise will bring.
europmc-pmc7820598:
Malhotra and co-authors test personal load plans to heal a bone defect in mouse tails. Better ways to fix bone gaps are still needed. Rhythmic loading is known to steer bone growth. Load levels must match the weak state of the defect. Too much load can crack it, and too little does nothing.

The team used live finite element models built from micro-CT scans. These models set the right peak load for each mouse. Loads adapted as the bone healed over time. Healing beat that of unloaded control mice by a clear margin. No tail vertebra broke under the plan. The authors say the same logic could serve patients. Each person's defect and healing path is unique, so loads should be too.
europmc-pmc7854298:
Mendell and co-authors review the clinical use of gene therapy given straight into the body with AAV carriers. Gene faults cause hereditary disease. More than 7,000 rare diseases affect over 30 million Americans. For over 30 years, gene fixes have been held out as cures.

Adeno-associated viruses, or AAVs, ferry the fix into patients. The authors survey approved and trial-stage uses. Eye, nerve, muscle, and blood diseases all feature. Gains can last for years after one dose. Risks and dose limits get frank treatment. Immune reaction to the carrier is a key hurdle. The review marks how far the field has come since its first hopes.
europmc-pmc7857398:
Oude Munnink and co-authors trace SARS-CoV-2 moving between humans and mink on farms. The virus began as a spillover from animals. People can pass it back to other species. Mink farms gave a close look at that two-way traffic.

Outbreaks swept Dutch mink farms in 2020. Genome reading sorted the virus lines found there. Some mink strains matched the farm workers' strains. Other cases ran the other way, from mink to people. Farm cats and other animals were checked as well. The authors warn that animal reservoirs can seed new human cases. Farm biosecurity and monitoring are the clear lessons.
europmc-pmc7864098:
Fawkner-Corbett and co-authors map human gut development cell by cell through space and time. How the intestine forms was poorly understood. The team paired single-cell RNA reads with spatial mapping. Samples tracked growth across development.

They found 101 cell states in the forming gut. Lining and support cell ancestors were charted. Rules behind the crypt-villus shape emerged. Nerve, vessel, and immune growth were detailed too. The birth of Peyer's patches was pinned down. Signals that steer each growth wave were measured. All data sit in a public tool called STAR-FINDer. Rare gut disorders can now be tied to set cells and sites.
europmc-pmc7883798:
Tavakol and Wetzel present a methods guide to factor analysis for health researchers. Factor analysis simplifies a large set of linked test items into a few underlying dimensions. The guide explains how that process supports the building of sound measurement tools.

The authors use a simple case to show the scale of the task. A 20-item instrument alone yields 400 correlations between items. Factor analysis turns that mass of links into a structure a researcher can read. The guide ties the method to construct validity, the proof that a tool measures what it claims to measure. It covers evidence from test content and from internal structure. Readers learn when the method fits and what its results can and cannot show.
europmc-pmc7909498:
Bosnjak and co-authors present an editorial introducing a set of articles on the theory of planned behavior. The theory explains action through attitudes, social norms, and a sense of control. It has been tested in more than 4,200 papers, the authors note. Few theories in social science are used so widely.

The editorial first sketches how the theory's three belief types shape intention. It then introduces the five contributions in the section. Two streams run through them. One stream adjusts and extends the original theory. The other applies it in public health and political science. Topics range from student binge drinking to energy saving at work. Support for European integration also features. The editorial gives readers a compact map of where this classic theory is heading.
europmc-pmc7978298:
Wang and co-authors present a review of the two-sided role of reactive oxygen species in cancer. These molecules arise in normal cell chemistry and act as signals. Cancer cells often carry abnormal amounts of them. Depending on where they sit, how much there is, and how long they last, they can push a tumour forward or kill it. The review sorts that paradox.

On one side, the species help drive the changes that turn a cell malignant. On the other, overload can force cancer cells to die. The authors first explain how the species are made and cleaned away. They then map the signal networks they feed. Cancer therapies that exploit the balance close the account. Some raise the load past the breaking point. Others block the cleanup. The authors say mastering this redox biology is key to beating cancer.
europmc-pmc7985098:
Koushki and co-authors present a review of how statins calm inflammation in cardiovascular disease. Statins lower cholesterol and are a main treatment for atherosclerosis. They also act on two alarm systems in the vessel wall: the NLRP3 inflammasome and toll-like receptors. Studies disagree on the direction of that action. Some statins switch the alarm on, while others switch it off. The review sorts the conflict.

Dose and chemistry explain much of the split. Fat-soluble statins sway the inflammasome more than water-soluble ones. Statins can mute a key inflammatory pathway and shift immune responses toward calm. They also lower the number of toll-like receptors on cells. The authors weigh both faces of the effect. They conclude that statins earn their place through immune calming as well as lipid lowering.
europmc-pmc8024398:
Cheng and co-authors build a tumor vaccine platform from bacterial outer membrane vesicles. These vesicles, shed by Gram-negative bacteria, rouse the innate immune system strongly. A good tumor vaccine must display neoantigens fast, and each patient's antigens differ. The team fused tumor antigens to the vesicle surface protein ClyA. They then simplified display with a Plug-and-Display system built on tag and catcher proteins.

Vesicles carrying different catchers can show several distinct antigens at once. That spread aims for a synergistic anti-tumor response. The authors report that loaded vesicles erased lung melanoma metastasis in their tests. They also slowed the growth of subcutaneous colorectal tumors. The platform's speed and flexibility suit personalized vaccines. Each batch can be matched to one patient's tumor.
europmc-pmc8082498:
Long and co-authors review natural products that act on the PI3K/AKT pathway in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases. Both diseases grow more common as populations age. The PI3K/AKT pathway steers cell growth, death, and metabolism. In neurons, it mediates survival signals and toxic insults alike. Its substrates include FoxO proteins, GSK-3β, and caspase-9.

Many plant-derived compounds switch this pathway on in lab studies. The review gathers those reported in recent years. Each compound is tied to the disease model where it showed protection. Herbal sources recur throughout the survey. The authors argue the pathway offers a rich hunting ground for drugs. Natural products may seed treatments that shield neurons rather than just ease symptoms. They close by urging deeper development of herbal medicine. Rigor in testing those leads is the stated need.
europmc-pmc8140498:
Lu and co-authors review nuclear localization signals and the import machinery that reads them. Proteins made in the cytoplasm often belong inside the nucleus. A short peptide tag, the NLS, marks them for entry. Importin family carriers recognize the tag and escort cargo. The nuclear pore complex is the gate they pass through. The review first sorts the known signal types.

Classical signals and newer reported ones each get their portrait. Proteins recently found to carry such signals are catalogued. The carrier system itself earns a careful walk-through. Regulation keeps the traffic selective and responsive to cell state. Some proteins reach the nucleus without any NLS at all. Those back routes close the survey with due caution. Misrouted nuclear proteins sit behind many diseases. A clear map of the gates helps target them. Textbook material is brought fully up to date.
europmc-pmc8237398:
Graus and co-authors propose updated diagnostic criteria for paraneoplastic neurologic syndromes. These syndromes link nerve damage to an underlying cancer. Diagnosis now draws on a wider range of patterns and antibodies.

The 2004 criteria had grown partly outdated over 16 years. An expert panel reworked them by consensus. New phenotypes and antibodies reshaped the approach. The panel weighed published and lab data from many centres. The new criteria serve both clinic decisions and research. They aim for earlier, surer recognition of these rare syndromes. A shared scale for certainty is part of the new scheme. The aim is plain: help the doctor at the bed side spot a rare and hard case fast, name it with care, and start the right tests at the right time.
europmc-pmc8238498:
Danko and co-authors build a global metagenomic map of urban microbiomes and drug resistance. They sampled mass-transit systems in 60 cities over 3 years. The atlas holds 4,728 samples in all.

It profiles microbial strains, functions, and resistance markers by place. Thousands of viruses and bacteria in it were new to reference databases. A core set of 31 species appeared in 97% of samples. Resistance gene patterns varied widely between cities. Each city carried a distinct microbial signature. The catalog is the first systematic survey of the urban microbial world. The atlas is free for all to use, and each city file can be read next to the rest with ease.
europmc-pmc8261998:
Maher and co-authors estimate the global incidence and prevalence of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. The disease scars the lungs and steadily steals breath. Past studies disagreed, so its full weight stayed unclear.

The team searched for population studies from January 2009 to April 2020. Estimates were pooled by country, with weighted averages where studies overlapped. Rates were adjusted for study differences where possible. Final figures come per 10,000 people, with confidence intervals. The model gives countries a firmer base for planning care. It also exposes where data remain thin. Adjusted figures try to make countries fairly comparable.
europmc-pmc8262698:
Steinhaus and co-authors present MutationTaster2021, an update to a DNA variant prediction tool. The tool judges whether a variant is likely to cause disease. This version uses a new prediction model.

Accuracy rose, above all for rare harmless variants. New data sources joined, including gnomAD and ExAC scores. Splice site prediction was rebuilt as well. The tool now states which diseases known mutations cause. That helps users match a variant to a patient's picture. A full interface overhaul aimed at easier use. Many inner parts were redesigned for speed. Rare variant calls were a known weak spot before.
europmc-pmc8458098:
Wang and co-authors measure how rare gene variants shape human disease in UK Biobank exomes. Common variant studies found thousands of disease links. The part played by rare variants stayed far less explored. Biobank data on about half a million people opened a new window.

The team studied exomes from 281,104 participants in total. Gene-based tests grouped rare variants to find effects single-variant tests miss. They report 1703 strong gene-phenotype links for binary traits. Most of those links were invisible to single-variant tests. Links clustered on loss-of-function traits and on approved drug targets. Ancestry-specific checks rounded out the analysis. The work shows the power of collapsing rare variants by gene.
europmc-pmc8472298:
Sędzikowska and Szablewski describe the role of insulin and insulin resistance in Alzheimer disease. Insulin does far more than manage blood sugar. In the body it drives glucose into cells and supports growth. Its receptors sit on all cell types in the brain too.

In the brain, insulin aids memory, guides neuron growth, and tunes key chemical messengers. It crosses the blood-brain barrier freely from the blood. Two signaling paths carry its effects, one metabolic and one growth-linked. When signaling fails through resistance, brain ageing may speed up. Plasticity suffers, and nerve decay may follow. The review draws these strands into one account.
europmc-pmc8499698:
Austin and co-authors give a tutorial on multiple imputation for missing data in clinical research. Missing values are common in such studies. Dropping those cases can bias results. Filling gaps with a plain mean can do the same and shrink error bars falsely.

Multiple imputation fills each gap with several plausible values instead. This creates many complete data sets. The same analysis runs on each, and the results pool together. The tutorial covers how to build the filling model. It treats how many data sets to make and how to handle derived values. A heart failure hospital data set shows the method at work.
europmc-pmc8546498:
Skrivankova and co-authors explain the STROBE-MR checklist for reporting Mendelian randomisation studies. These studies use genes to probe causal effects of exposures on health. Weak reporting often hampers the published record, though. Clear reports help readers judge study quality.

The article explains all 20 items of the checklist in turn. Each item comes with its meaning and its rationale. A glossary defines the terms used. Worked examples show transparent reporting at its best. The authors address authors, reviewers, and editors alike. Wider adoption should lift trust in this fast-growing method across epidemiology.
europmc-pmc8692898:
Li and co-authors use single-cell RNA sequencing to find fibroblast subgroups that drive gastric cancer spread. Fibroblasts linked to cancer help tumors grow, but their variety was unclear. The team sampled eight pairs of tumors and nearby healthy tissue. They mapped how these subgroups talk to other cells in the tumor.

Four fibroblast subgroups emerged, each with distinct traits. All showed stronger pro-tumor activity than their healthy counterparts. Two subgroups stood out. One signaled to T cells with interleukin-6 and a chemokine. The other linked to calm macrophages and predicted shorter survival. The authors propose blocking these subgroups as a treatment strategy.
europmc-pmc9811898:
Loyfer and co-authors build a DNA methylation atlas of normal human cell types. Methylation marks help fix each cell type's identity. Old data sets covered only a slice of mark sites. They also leaned on cell lines or mixed tissue samples.

The atlas rests on deep whole-genome sequencing of sorted cells. It spans 39 cell types from 205 healthy tissue samples. Fragment level reads expose thousands of type unique markers. Same type samples from different people matched almost exactly. That shows identity programs shrug off outside disturbance. Clustering of the atlas retraced tissue family trees. Some patterns dated back to embryonic development stages. Unmarked spots unique to a type sat in enhancers. They held binding sites for that tissue's regulators. The atlas is offered for gene regulation studies. It also seeds tissue markers for liquid biopsy tests.
europmc-pmc9876798:
Hu and co-authors report a wearable ultrasound device that images the heart continuously. Standard heart imaging cannot run for long periods because the equipment is bulky. Skin-level wearable sensors cannot image the heart directly. The team set out to close that gap.

The device uses piezoelectric transducer arrays, liquid metal electrodes, and a soft polymer shell. Its design keeps close contact with skin and views the left ventricle during motion. A deep learning model reads the images and tracks left ventricular volume over time. From that signal it derives stroke volume, cardiac output, and ejection fraction. The authors report strong accuracy during varied activity, opening a path to long-term heart monitoring.
freeman-evelinas-garden-1898:
Evelina's Garden, dated 1899 on its title page, opens behind a tall hedge of arbor-vitae. The hedge parts Evelina's garden from the road in her New England village. Schoolchildren pick sly peep-holes in it, since even on tiptoe they cannot see over.

Through those holes, hollyhocks seem to march like troops of soldiers. Marigold, phlox, pinks, and prince's-feather crowd the bright view. Sometimes Evelina herself drifts past in a purple gown, gray curls falling soft. The tales gathered here treat love kept fresh like pressed flowers, and women who tend rich inner lives with a gardener's patient care.
frus-1861-d198:
On 8 July 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Cassius Clay at the Russian court. The letter is document 198 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward's July letter to St. Petersburg kept Clay inside the common plan. Even a friendly court had to hear the Union's terms in full. The note shows no post exempt from the Secretary's steady, central hand. No post exempt was Seward's rule, and the Russian file proves it page by page. Page by page proof of the rule is the quiet strength of this whole volume. No post stood outside the common plan.
frus-1861-d298:
Seward wrote again on 12 November 1861, this time to Mr. Robinson. It was printed as Document 298 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. It was written in the autumn of the war's first year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d98:
On 14 October 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote a second letter to Lord Lyons. It is document 98 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The paired letters of that day sort the Anglo American agenda into clean parts. Seward dealt with each point on its own paper, as was his habit. Together the two notes show a full day of work on the tie that mattered most to the Union. The two notes frame a single day of Anglo American business in full. A full day of such business shows how much of the war was fought in ink.
frus-1862-d198:
Document 198 is a note from Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington, to Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 4 January in the record of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It sits among the first papers of the new year in the British file.

Days earlier, Washington had agreed to give up the Confederate envoys taken from the Trent, and the crisis was cooling fast. Lyons stayed in close written touch with Seward as relations steadied. Notes from this turn of the year mark the point where the two governments stepped back from the edge of war. Cases under such notes were often small: one ship, one prisoner, one point of form.
frus-1862-d298:
William L. Dayton reported from Paris on 2 August 1862 in a letter printed as Document 298 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Secretary of State William H. Seward, opening the August run of the French file.

August began with the Confederate raider Alabama newly escaped from Britain and French troops rebuilding strength in Mexico. Dayton's post touched both stories, since Paris coordinated loosely with London and owned the Mexican venture. His report that week fed Washington's picture of a Europe growing bolder as the Union's summer went badly. French mills wanted Southern cotton, and French yards watched the Union blockade with care.
frus-1862-d398:
On 14 January 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Horace J. Perry, the secretary of the American legation in Madrid. It opens the Spanish file as Document 398 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

Spain held Cuba, close to the rebellious South, and had just sent troops to Mexico with Britain and France. Washington watched Madrid with care all through the war. Early orders like this one set the tone Perry was to keep at the Spanish court. He was to be firm on Union rights and calm in manner. He was also to watch for any sign that Spain might aid the Confederacy.
frus-1862-d498:
James Shepherd Pike closed April 1862 with a report from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 30 April. It is Document 498 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

Pike's end-of-April letter caught the Dutch reaction to the war's improving Union news, including the fall of New Orleans. The Netherlands, with colonies in the West Indies, had to apply its neutrality rules to real ships in real ports. His reports touched those cases as they arose. For Seward, the Hague file was a steady source of European weather reports. For the reader, Pike's letters stand out in the volume for their plain speech and newsman's eye.
frus-1862-d598:
On 15 December 1861 Spain's minister of state addressed this instruction to General Prim, commander of the Spanish expeditionary force then sailing for Mexico. It is Document 598 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Prim was Spain's plenipotentiary as well as its general, charged with acting alongside Britain and France under their joint convention. Madrid's orders to him, printed here in translation, show what Spain said it wanted in Mexico: debts paid and order restored, not conquest. Read beside Corwin's reports from Mexico City, the letter lets the reader test Spanish words against Spanish conduct. The test runs through the months that followed. In them, Prim judged the French design and withdrew.
frus-1862-d698: On 5 September 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to a Mr. Yrisarri. The letter is document 698 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, answering Yrisarri's dispatch of late August. The evidence gives the two names and the date. It does not name Yrisarri's post or land, and the subject of the exchange is not stated.
frus-1862-d98:
Writing on 11 July 1862, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London sent his report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 98 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1863p1-d198:
