One of the Secretary's regular instructions to London, this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, is dated 9 May 1863. It appears as document 198 of the 1863 papers. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

For readers today, these instructions reveal the thinking inside the State Department as clearly as any memoir. They show choices being made in real time, with poor information and high stakes. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d298:
On 22 September 1863, orders left Washington for London: Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The paper is document 298 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

The CSS Alabama, built near Liverpool, had slipped away in 1862 and was raiding Union trade. Washington pressed London to stop such ships and answer for the losses. It belongs to the tense autumn when the fate of two Confederate ironclad rams in British yards hung in the balance. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d398:
One of Lord Lyons's regular notes to the State Department, this paper to Secretary of State William H. Seward is dated 19 February 1863. It appears as document 398 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

Once emancipation became Union policy in January 1863, British protests grew harder to frame. Lyons had to press neutral rights for a government whose public mostly hated slavery. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d498:
8 May 1863 is the date on a letter from William H. Seward, Secretary of State to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d598:
A 1 August 1863 dispatch from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons reached Secretary of State William H. Seward. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the late summer of 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d98:
On 2 March 1863, William H. Seward sent this letter to Charles Francis Adams, the second of twelve he sent him that day in this file. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 98 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Batch days like 2 March let Washington speak on many heads at once. Each head sat in its own sheet, so Adams could act on them one by one. The London brief held much to sort: claims, ships, talks, and tone. This letter holds one slice of that day's work. Its sense comes from the set it sits in, a full brief laid out in a row.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d198:
Robert Kelley, the American chargé in Ankara, sent an urgent, most-secret telegram to Washington on 8 November 1943. The report is addressed to the President, the Secretary of State, and the Under Secretary. It tells what Kelley had learned about the recent Cairo talks between Britain's Anthony Eden and Turkey's foreign minister, Numan Menemencioğlu.

Eden had asked Turkey to open its air bases to the Allies. Numan refused, saying Turkey was not armed well enough to face the German attack that would surely follow. Kelley adds two shrewd points: the demand came under strong Soviet pressure from the Moscow conference, and the Cairo meeting itself had been arranged at Numan's own request, not Eden's.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d298: President Roosevelt sent Ambassador Laurence Steinhardt in Ankara a short personal and secret telegram from Cairo on 24 November 1943. Our next plans have been advanced, he writes, and he hopes to see Steinhardt in Cairo in about a week. On the subject of Steinhardt's number one, he will advise him in a day or two. The editors explain that the number one in question was President Inönü of Turkey. Roosevelt hoped to bring him to Cairo after Tehran. Steinhardt in fact reached Cairo that same afternoon.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d398:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent President Roosevelt a telegram from Washington on 30 November 1943 on Latin American affairs. Its lead item is naval: a German submarine has sunk a second small Colombian vessel in the Caribbean.

Colombia's government, with Senate approval, has proclaimed a state of belligerency with Germany, which will bring her adherence to the United Nations declaration. President López, in the United States for his wife's medical care, is expected home within weeks, his position improved but not fully recovered from a recent crisis. The message then turns to Senator Butler's Reader's Digest article and Senate reports attacking American aid programs in Latin America. Hull calls the charges sweeping and unfounded, notes the vigorous answers by the Vice President and Nelson Rockefeller, and warns the effect abroad cannot be minimized.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d498:
The secretaries of the Combined Chiefs of Staff issued this note on December 6, 1943, as the Second Cairo Conference ended. The secretaries were the officers who kept the joint command's records, circulated its papers, and drafted its formal acts. The State Department printed the note in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

A secretaries' note is the alliance's paperwork speaking for itself: it records, transmits, or confirms what the chiefs had settled. Such notes rarely make headlines, yet historians depend on them to date decisions and fix the order of business. For the reader, this small record helps lock the conference's crowded final day into a clear sequence.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d98: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on November 6, 1943, and a second Churchill note follows with the same date. This one is Document 98 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The prime minister was preparing his own journey east, by sea and air, as was the president. The record for the note gives the date and the names. Its contents are a matter for the printed text in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1944-quebec-d198: An editors' note marks another gap in the Quebec record. No record of the discussion during this luncheon meeting has been found. The meeting itself is mentioned only in the Morgenthau Presidential Diary, volume six. The note is printed so readers know the luncheon took place, even though nothing of what was said at it can be recovered from the files.
frus-1944-quebec-d298: John Winant, the American ambassador in London, wrote to President Roosevelt on 18 September 1944. His message is document 298 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume covering the second Quebec Conference, issued by the Department of State. It forms part of the reporting reaching the president from London while the decisions taken at Quebec were still fresh and unsettled.
frus-1944-quebec-d98:
Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on August 23, 1944. The State Department printed the message in the Quebec 1944 volume. It belongs to the leaders' exchanges before the September conference. Their written dialogue had run since 1939.

Late August 1944 brought triumph and new problems together. Paris was about to be liberated by Allied troops. Planners already argued over Germany's treatment after defeat. Churchill's letter forms part of that written preparation for Quebec. For readers, it shows the Prime Minister pressing his views early. He rarely waited for a conference room to make his case. The conference opened at Quebec City the next month.
frus-1945-50-intel-d198:
Minutes record the Fourth Meeting of the National Intelligence Authority on 17 July 1946. It stands as document 198 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. Central intelligence then sat with the National Intelligence Authority, a board of top officials served by the Central Intelligence Group.

Minutes are the formal record of a meeting: who sat in, what was put on the table, and what the group agreed to do. Read with the papers before and after it, the record shows a policy taking shape one meeting at a time. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d298: Dated 6 August 1948, "Memorandum of Conversation and Understanding" comes from the top level of the government. Readers meet it as document 298 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The Council had sent in an outside team to grade the CIA, and the whole town knew a blunt report was coming. A memorandum of conversation is the note a participant or aide wrote after a talk, setting down who was there and what was said.
frus-1945-50-intel-d398:
Fisher Howe, deputy to the State Department's intelligence chief, sent a memo to his boss, W. Park Armstrong, on 8 September 1949. The paper is document 398 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Howe and Armstrong led the Bureau of Intelligence and Research, the State Department's team of analysts. A deputy writing to his own chief is staff work at its most basic. Yet such notes set the line the bureau took when it faced the CIA and the military services across the table. The bureau's small staff punched far above its weight through notes of exactly this kind.
frus-1945-50-intel-d98:
Lyon, acting director of the State Department's Office of Controls, wrote to McCormack on 15 November 1945. The Office of Controls handled sensitive department business such as passports and visas. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

An approach from the controls office to the intelligence chief shows the seams where secret work touched the department's public duties. Names, travel, and papers crossed both desks, and the two offices had to agree on how to handle them. Readers gain a finer-grained picture of the State Department here than the top-level fight provides. The intelligence system was not only chiefs and plans; it was also clerks' questions about files, answered in memos like this one.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d198:
Captured German guns could arm the French occupation force, Roosevelt replied on 26 November 1944. These excerpts from his telegram number 658 to Churchill are printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. They answer the alarm in Churchill's message about holding western Germany.

There should be no difficulty, Roosevelt writes, in equipping as much of a French occupation force as a disarmed Germany requires. The arms would come from the German army itself, taken when it surrenders or is destroyed. On the wider request he does not move. He has no authority now to equip any postwar foreign army. The prospect of getting such authority from Congress, he adds, is more than doubtful.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d298:
A formal dinner is the meeting behind this editorial note in the Malta and Yalta volume. The editors state that the only record of the meeting's substance they have found is a summary of a conversation between Stettinius and Churchill. That summary stands in Stettinius's own published account, at pages 60 to 62.

The occasion was a large formal dinner at Government House in Malta. The Governor and Commander in Chief of Malta, Lieutenant General Schreiber, gave it in honor of the American and British delegations. All the information the note gives about the meeting and its participants is drawn from Stettinius's book. The entry shows the editors at work, marking exactly how thin the record runs for one evening of the Malta Conference.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d398:
Wording decided who would be invited to found the United Nations. This delegation memorandum of February 8, 1945, preserves the fix. The foreign secretaries' report was accepted with one change. Paragraph 2(b) would now limit invitations to the United Nations as they stood on February 8. Associated Nations that declared war on the common enemy by March 1 would also qualify.

At that stage, the memorandum adds, British and American delegates would back original membership for two Soviet republics: Ukraine and White Russia. Matthews later recalled that he thought Hiss drafted the paper. A single amended paragraph set the guest list for San Francisco.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d498:
Churchill answered Roosevelt's votes letter on February 11, 1945, the conference's last day. He had given consideration, he wrote, to the political difficulties that might arise in the Senate. America stood alone among the three great powers with one Assembly vote. Britain's position, he explained, rested on the long-standing representation of the Empire and Commonwealth.

The Soviet side was represented by its chief member plus Ukraine and White Russia. The United States, Churchill held, should propose the form in which its undisputed equality with every other member state would be expressed. He assured Roosevelt he would do everything possible to assist. The exchange kept a delicate promise inside the alliance.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d98:
John Hickerson urged a bold step in a secret note to the Secretary of State on 8 January 1945. Hickerson was deputy director of the Office of European Affairs. His proposal, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, asks the President to put a new body to Churchill and Stalin.

Hickerson wants a Provisional Security Council for Europe, set up at once. Its members would be the United States, Britain, the Soviet Union, and France. Sitting in continuous session, it would supervise the return of popular rule and keep order in the freed states and in Germany's former satellites. It would last until the world body of the United Nations was ready to take over.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d198:
Ambassador Harriman reported a talk with China's T. V. Soong in an extract dated July 7, 1945. The extract is document 198 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Soong was in Moscow negotiating with Stalin over the price of Soviet entry into the war against Japan, set by the Yalta agreement.

At an informal lunch, Harriman told Soong that the President and the Secretary wished to be consulted before any arrangements were concluded on the basis of the Yalta agreement. Soong readily agreed. Harriman then passed the same word to Molotov that afternoon. Molotov asked whether consultation at Berlin or before was meant, and said he would consult Stalin. The exchange shows Washington guarding a bargain, struck at Yalta over China's head, that gave Russia ports and railroads in Manchuria.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d298:
Ambassador Winant cabled from London on June 26, 1945, with the British Foreign Office's first answer on the Control Commissions. Britain, he reported, would act in parallel with Washington in Hungary, Bulgaria, and Rumania. The stand still needed Prime Minister Churchill's approval before it became final.

The Foreign Office doubted that Moscow would ever grant real equality to British and American representatives. At best it expected small concessions, like fewer travel limits and more planes admitted. Even so, London agreed to join one more joint request to the Soviet government, a sign of allied unity before Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d398: One position on Germany's west stands in an extract from a briefing book paper of June 29, 1945. The paper covers European territorial settlements. The extract states the American line in one point. The United States government is opposed to the separation from Germany of the Ruhr. It is opposed, too, to separating the left bank of the Rhine. Neither change should come by internationalization, nor by any other means. The short extract is one piece of a wider paper on the border questions.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d498:
Surprise and a plea for delay fill Churchill's personal, top secret reply to Truman of July 3, 1945. He was surprised, he writes, by the President's message giving him only a few hours' notice of the decision to recognize the new Polish government. Britain's position, he explains, is different from America's. The old Polish government is seated in London.

That government has officials and very large staffs, and it administers a Polish army of 170,000 men, whose attitude has to be carefully considered. London intends to recognize the new government, but hoped to give the London Poles at least twenty-four hours' notice. Churchill therefore proposes recognition on July 4 rather than July 3, or else no synchronization at all.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d598:
Minutes by Brigadier General McFarland record a White House meeting on the war against Japan, June 18, 1945. They form document 598 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. President Truman sat with his top military and civilian chiefs to learn the campaign plan in detail.

General Marshall compared the moment to the run-up to Normandy. He read a Joint Chiefs digest picking November 1 for the landing on Kyushu. By then, he said, air attack would have smashed Japan's key factories and its navy would be powerless. A landing in Korea, at Pusan or Seoul, would cost more and gain less ground. Marshall argued that Kyushu was vital to tighten the blockade and to force a yield. He also named Soviet entry into the war as a blow that might help bring Japan to yield short of total defeat.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d698:
Ambassador Wilson reminded Under Secretary Grew of a promise made at the White House, in a wire of July 5, 1945. The secret priority message is document 698 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Wilson writes as Soviet pressure on Turkey mounts.

Wilson recalls being presented to President Truman on April 25, among envoys bound for the field. Truman asked him about Turkey, and Wilson gave his forecast in plain terms. If Moscow sought only changes to the Straits rules, Turkey would likely prove cooperative and reasonable. If Moscow made demands touching Turkish independence, Turkey would resist. Wilson urged that U.S. interests in the Middle East and in world security should then lead Washington to back Turkey. The President, Wilson records, replied that he agreed and thought that course right. Wilson's closing hope ties that April pledge to the present menace.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d98:
Vyshinsky answered Harriman's requests in a letter from Moscow dated June 25, 1945. The reply, printed in translation, is document 98 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Harriman had asked to scout Zehlendorf, to use the Halle-Berlin highway without asking each time, and to enlarge General Parks's party in Berlin.

Vyshinsky puts off most of it. Zehlendorf, he says, falls under the agreed plan for taking over the occupation zones. Free use of the highway and a bigger party for Parks can be considered only after Marshal Zhukov reaches Berlin. The cool, brief reply kept the Americans waiting on the one man whose return the Soviets had cited all along, and it fed American doubts about Soviet good faith.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1098:
Charles Kindleberger cabled Edwin Pauley from Washington on July 21, 1945. He sums up draft proposals on Italian reparations and restitution prepared by a colleague, Reinstein. The proposals lack department approval so far. Their thrust is that forcing Italy to pay reparations would be highly undesirable.

Italy will need large outside aid for some time, most of it American. Any reparations now would thus be paid largely by the United States. Politics may still demand token payments to Greece, Yugoslavia, and perhaps Ethiopia, which suffered Italian attack. Such payments should take forms with no direct cost in foreign exchange, like labor services. Kindleberger also urges pressing Italy's prewar debts, after a grace period of some years.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1198:
The Joint Chiefs of Staff wrote to President Truman on 21 July 1945, one week into the summit. Their direct channel to the commander in chief stayed open at Potsdam, as it had through the war. The chiefs kept the president supplied with the armed forces' latest thinking.

A message of this kind could carry word on the Pacific war or the forces in Germany. It could touch any point where the talks met the sword. Truman read his chiefs' notes beside his envoys' reports. This one is the top brass advising mid-bargaining, in the plain channel the war had built between them.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1298:
The Combined Chiefs of Staff wrote jointly to the State Department and the British Foreign Office on 18 July 1945. The combined body spoke for both Western high commands at once. Addressing both foreign ministries in one letter matched that joint voice.

A letter of this kind carried the soldiers' shared view to the envoys of both nations. It bound the military and foreign arms of the alliance in a single text. This one dates from the summit's second day. It shows the joint staff speaking over the heads of the talks, straight to the two offices that would live with the peace.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1398:
A second Caffery letter to Foreign Minister Bidault dated 1 August 1945 follows in the volume. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Paired letters on one day often split a subject in two: one for the record, one for the harder point. Whatever the split here, the pace tells its own story. Paris and Washington were settling France's role in the postwar order at speed, while the ink dried at Potsdam. Readers following the Caffery and Bidault run get diplomacy at working level, where alliances are kept alive by prompt, exact paper rather than by speeches.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-98: The editors of the second Potsdam volume inserted this note among the unnumbered pieces that follow document 710. In the Foreign Relations series, such notes carry the editors' own voice, not a wartime official's. They exist to keep the record honest and easy to follow. A reader can use this one to place the papers around it in the conference's crowded summer of 1945.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d798:
The Acting Secretary of State wrote to Schoenfeld in Hungary on July 17, 1945, in document 798. Washington answered its Budapest representative as Potsdam opened. Guidance flowed outward while the leaders met. The letter was printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

Instructions to a field post show policy becoming action. Schoenfeld needed lines he could hold in Budapest. Readers see Washington steering a distant mission in real time. The document pairs with the representative's own reports. Together they form a circuit: facts up, orders down. That circuit is how a far-flung department acts as one mind.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d898: Edwin Pauley sent this brief secret telegram from Babelsberg on July 17, 1945. He addresses Alan Sprout, acting head of the American reparations delegation. Pauley asks that Abramovitz cable three figures at once. First, what share of German prewar capital assets sat in the zone assigned to the Soviet Union. Second, the 1938 value of movable capital assets east of the Oder-Neisse line. Third, the value of industrial and mining output from that same area in 1938.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d998:
American staff drafted this memorandum for General Clay at Babelsberg on July 28, 1945. A note on the paper says it was not sent. It asks Clay to press the Control Council to issue an attached decree vesting German external assets, as soon as possible. Taking power of disposal over those assets is called most urgent.

The draft also coaches Clay for debate on one article of the decree. He may point out that American and British officials have handled such asset problems for years. Their people, it argues, are best fit to seize the assets in practice. Signature spaces were left for Pauley, Clayton, and McCloy.
frus-1952-54v10-d398: A 1952-1954 FRUS editorial note mentioning a Nixon report on Iran. The Vice President toured the region. This note preserves that context. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
gao-gaoreports-b-295698: OMNIPLEX World Services filed a March 2005 double protest — two dockets — and GAO's ruling settles the pair. The services firm's twin claims got one careful answer. Both dockets faced the same gavel. The gavel fell twice as one. The pair was settled.
gao-gaoreports-b-297398: Crane & Company took its January 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298698: General Electrodynamics Corporation doubled its November 2006 protest — two case numbers, one tech fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-299798: Savantage Financial Services fought a 2007 award at GAO — two case numbers, one verdict. The firm said the agency's pick was unfair; the combined ruling weighs each protest point. Money-management contracts get the same fair-play scrutiny as any federal buy.
gao-gaoreports-b-400198: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Sea Box, Inc. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-198: The Visas Mantis program eased science students' burden in 2005, and GAO's report says the streamlined checks helped, though further work remained. The review balances the win with the backlog. The foreign scholars deserved the speed. The burden was lowered. The foreign scholars deserved the speed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-298: The war memorials' 2004 and 2003 books got a GAO audit in 2005, and the report checks the money. The review grades the ledgers. The fallen's memorials deserved the honest books. The books were honest. The ledgers were graded. The money was checked.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-798: Troop pay fairness got a GAO probe in 2005, and the report says the Pentagon's bonus math had to be opened up. The findings demand the daylight. The report warns that the troops' price tag deserved honest reckoning. The troops' price tag deserved honest reckoning.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-898: Swamp swap deals lacked real watchdogs in 2005, and GAO's report says the Corps had no good way to check the trades. The findings demand the oversight. The report warns that the marshes deserved real replacement. The marshes deserved real replacement.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-298: State Department travel billing lost taxpayer money in 2006, and GAO's report says control breakdowns and weak oversight were to blame. The findings follow the waste. The report warns that the diplomats' travel tabs needed watching. The controls had to be fixed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-498: The National Guard's civil support teams needed a clearer mission in 2006, and GAO's report says the bureau had to clarify their role and address management challenges. The findings demand the definition. The report warns that the homeland helpers needed a sharp mission. The mission had to be clear.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-798: Consumer-directed health plans got an early review in 2006, and GAO's report shares enrollees' experiences with the savings accounts and plans. The findings take the measure. The report warns that the do-it-yourself health funds needed watching. The plans had to work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-98: The Valles Caldera trust was making some progress in 2005, and GAO's report says more was needed to meet statutory goals. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the New Mexico preserve deserved its promised care. The goals had to be met.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1198: This 2007 GAO report wades into the drug-patent fight: a world trade pact lets poor nations break patents in a health crisis, but U.S. guidance on the deal read murky. GAO says Washington's line may need sharpening. The report sits at the crossroads of pill profits and sick patients half a world away.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-498: The polar weather satellites were being rebuilt mid-flight in 2007 — GAO's report says the restructuring moved ahead despite technical storms. The findings track the high-wire act. The report's tension: fix the plane while flying it, or lose the forecast.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-98: Veterans' disability claims needed faster records in 2007, and GAO's report says the VA could improve how it got military service files. The findings target the delays. The report warns that the wounded should not wait on paperwork. The files had to follow the veteran.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-198: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at federal-Aid Highways: Increased Reliance on Contractors Can Pose Oversight Challenges for Federal and State Officials. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-298: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at defense Acquisitions: DOD's Practices and Processes for Multiyear Procurement Should Be Improved. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-398: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at traffic Safety: Grants Generally Address Key Safety Issues, Despite State Eligibility and Management Difficulties. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-598: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at nuclear Security: NRC and DHS Need to Take Additional Steps to Better Track and Detect Radioactive Materials. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gawain-green-knight-weston-1898:
Sir Gawain and the Green Knight is a Middle English poem by an unknown fourteenth-century author. Jessie Weston retold it in plain English prose in 1898. Her version opened the poem to readers who could not face the old language.

A giant green knight rides into Camelot at Christmas and offers a game. Any man may strike him once with an axe, if Gawain will take the same blow in a year. Gawain accepts, cuts off the stranger's head, and watches him pick it up and ride away. What follows tests Gawain's courage, honesty, and honor at the Green Chapel.
geminus-elementa-manitius-1898:
Geminus wrote a clear first book on the heavens for Greek readers of the age of Rome. Elementa Astronomiae, in Karl Manitius's 1898 Greek text, gives that handbook whole. Geminus taught in the first century before Christ, when star lore was a prized art.

He explains the zodiac, the calendar, the risings and settings of stars, and the paths of sun and moon. His aim is order and clarity, not new finds of his own. The book shows what a well taught student of that age learned about the sky. Manitius's edition prints the Greek in its classic school form.
gilman-women-and-economics-1898:
Charlotte Perkins Gilman published Women and Economics in 1898. Gilman, a lecturer and writer from a famed reform family, gave the book a long subtitle on women, work, and the home. It became the classic statement of feminist economics in its generation.

Gilman argued that women's dependence on men for food and shelter warped both sexes and stunted human growth. The housewife, she said, does full work yet is paid in keep, like a servant or a child. She proposed kitchenless homes and trained, paid housework to free women for wider labor. Her analysis of how economics shapes women's lives still frames debate in the field she helped found.
guyau-sketch-morality-1898:
Jean-Marie Guyau asked whether moral life needs commands from above or threats of punishment. His French answer, issued in 1884, claimed it needs neither. Gertrude Kapteyn translated the work into English in 1898. Its full title promises morality independent of obligation or sanction.

Guyau grounds duty in life itself, in the urge to grow, give, and act with full strength. A rich life, he argues, spills over into care for others without any rule forcing it. He died young, yet the book kept a wide reach. Thinkers on ethics still cite its bold central move. It reads as fresh as it sounds.
guyon-short-easie-method-prayer-1698:
Madame Guyon was a French widow whose teaching on prayer drew crowds, suspicion, and finally prison under Louis the Fourteenth. Her Short and Easie Method of Prayer, in this 1698 English edition, is the Quietist classic that spread her method abroad. Fenelon, the great archbishop, defended her, and the quarrel divided the French church.

Guyon teaches interior prayer: sit still before God, let words fade, and rest the soul in quiet trust. She claims this simple way suits ploughmen and children as much as scholars and priests. Church authorities feared her method slighted sacraments and effort, but ordinary readers kept the small book alive.
haddon-the-study-of-man-1898:
Haddon wrote this 1898 introduction to anthropology just as the Torres Straits expedition made his reputation. It presents the young science of man to students and general readers: its questions, its tools, and its evidence.

Chapters cover race and the body, language, tools, custom, and belief, drawing on the ethnology of the Torres Straits and other regions Haddon knew. He urges fieldwork over armchair guessing, a plea his own expedition soon answered. The book also preserves period views of human difference that later science discarded. As a record of anthropology finding its feet, it holds real historical interest.
haeckel-last-link-descent-of-man-1898:
Ernst Haeckel delivered The Last Link at Cambridge in 1898, a lecture on the descent of man near the end of his long career. Haeckel, once Darwinism's loudest German voice, was now its elder statesman. The lecture reviews what fossil evidence existed for human origins at the century's turn.

He presents the Neanderthal skulls and Dubois's new Pithecanthropus from Java as links in the chain. Against Rudolf Virchow's skepticism, he defends the ape-man as fact, not fancy. The talk is shorter and calmer than his big books, but the conviction is undimmed. It is a useful snapshot of the missing-link debate just before the great African finds.
hardy-wessex-poems-1898:
Thomas Hardy turned back to poetry late in life, after harsh reviews pushed him away from novels. Wessex Poems and Other Verses, published in 1898, was his first collection. It holds fifty-one poems, many written years earlier and kept in drawers.

Hardy also drew the illustrations himself, sketching the Dorset churches, roads, and houses of his youth. The poems look backward with regret: lost loves, old wars, and the indifference of fate. His plain, rugged style puzzled some early readers. Today the collection marks the start of a second career that made Hardy one of England's most loved poets.
harpers-classical-1898:
Harper's Dictionary of Classical Literature and Antiquities appeared in 1898 under the editorship of Harry Thurston Peck. Peck, a Columbia professor, aimed to give America its own version of William Smith's famous British dictionaries. The one thick volume covered the Greek and Roman world for American students and general readers.

Entries explain authors and their works, gods and heroes, places, customs, and the objects of daily life. Peck wrote in a livelier style than his British model, and the articles often quote the ancient writers themselves. The dictionary became the companion of a generation of American classicists, found in every college library. It made the ancient world orderly and approachable for a country whose classical schools were then at their height. Peck's own later fall from grace never dimmed the book's usefulness.
hastings-dictionary-bible-vol1-1898:
James Hastings, a Scottish minister and editor, published Volume One of his Dictionary of the Bible in 1898. It covers entries from A to Feasts. Hastings enlisted the leading biblical scholars of Britain, Germany, and America.

Articles treat the language, lands, peoples, and ideas of the Bible with the best learning of the day. Maps, plans, and a synopsis of feasts and fasts support the text. Hastings aimed at a dictionary both scholarly and usable by ministers and teachers. The set became the great turn-of-the-century Bible dictionary in English, found in studies and vestries everywhere.
high-history-holy-graal-evans-1898:
The High History of the Holy Graal is Sebastian Evans's 1898 English version of the French romance called Perlesvaus. Its author is unknown. The French original is among the strangest of all Grail books, and Evans kept its wildness intact.

Gawain and Perceval ride out on quests that fill thirty-five branches, or chapters, of the tale. They meet violence, visions, and marvels that test faith as much as courage. Castles, hermits, and strange beasts crowd the road. Readers who know only Malory's Grail will find this one fiercer and more fevered, closer to a dream than to a chronicle.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-1597-9:
John Lothrop Motley's chapter thirty-three recounts the march to Turnhout in his History of the United Netherlands. Marcellus Bax, the boldest of Holland's cavalry officers, urges Maurice to strike first. The Spanish force at Turnhout threatens Zeeland across the frozen morasses. Maurice ponders privately, then confers with the state council in mid-January.

The attack that follows became the republic's model cavalry victory. Speed, frost, and surprise did what sieges could not. Motley uses the episode to show Maurice grown from pupil to master. The cautious prince of the earlier chapters now risks a winter march on a subordinate's advice. Turnhout's fame outlasted its scale because it proved Dutch horse could beat Spanish veterans in open field. This chapter is among the most purely military in the later history.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-1598:
John Lothrop Motley's chapters thirty-four and thirty-five close the year 1598 in his History of the United Netherlands. The States send a mission to Henry IV to prevent his separate peace with Spain. The mission fails, and the treaty of Vervins is concluded. France buys its nobles' allegiance and leaves the Dutch to fight on.

Spain transfers the Netherlands to Albert and Isabella, whose marriage seals the gift. Then Philip II dies, and Motley pauses for a famous review of the reign. He reckons Spain's dominions, revenues, church wealth, and wars. A whole chapter judges the Spanish character, self-esteem included. Few Victorian historians wrote a bolder obituary of a king. These chapters end an era: the republic has outlived its great enemy, and the war changes masters.
hume-essays-moral-political-literary-gre:
David Hume's Essays, Moral, Political, and Literary, appear here in the Green and Grose edition of 1898, the complete collection. Hume issued his essays across his career and kept revising them for new editions. They made him famous in drawing rooms and coffee houses long before his history did, and they show his mind at play on every topic.

Commerce, money, and interest stand beside parties, eloquence, tragedy, and taste in these pages. Two famous pieces ask how populous the ancient nations were, and sketch the idea of a perfect commonwealth. The style is urbane, dry, and endlessly quotable. Together, the essays form the best short road into Hume's world.
huxley-darwiniana-essays-1898: Darwiniana, essays by Huxley, 1898. The Darwin essays. This book preserves that collection. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
huygens-celestial-worlds-1698:
Christiaan Huygens was a great Dutch star man who found Saturn's moon Titan. His book on the worlds in the planets came out in 1698, after his death. Its full title calls it conjectures on the folk, plants, and works of other worlds. Huygens works by strict reason, not fancy.

He weighs the size, air, and seas of each planet in turn. He asks how life there might live, build, and watch the sky. Huygens grants those worlds plants, beasts, and wise beings like us. The book is the first full plan of thought on life past Earth.
james-human-immortality-1898:
Human Immortality was James's Ingersoll Lecture at Harvard in 1897, published in 1898. The lecture series required a defense of the doctrine of immortality, and James approached it as a scientist of the mind, answering two supposed objections.

The objections hold that thought is a function of the brain, so death must end it. James replies with his transmission theory: the brain may transmit consciousness rather than produce it, as a prism transmits light. Break the prism and the light is not disproved. The argument is modest and careful, and it shows James keeping a door open that his science could not close.
james-turn-of-the-screw-1898:
Henry James published The Turn of the Screw in 1898, growing it from a ghost story anecdote told by an archbishop. A frame narrator presents it as a young governess's own manuscript, written years after the events. It became the most argued-about novella in English.

The governess takes charge of two beautiful children, Miles and Flora, at a country house called Bly. She begins to see two figures watching the children: the dead valet Quint and the former governess, Miss Jessel. Whether the ghosts are real or her own fevered invention, James never settles. The children may be corrupted innocents or sly conspirators. The screw keeps turning either way.
jastrow-religion-babylonia-assyria-1898:
Morris Jastrow was an American Assyriologist at the University of Pennsylvania who read cuneiform tablets by the thousand. His Religion of Babylonia and Assyria, published in 1898, gives a comprehensive account of Mesopotamian faith. It was the fullest English treatment of its subject for decades.

Jastrow sets out the gods of Babylon and Assyria, their temples, priests, prayers, and omens in ordered detail. He shows how kings read the liver of a sacrificed sheep before battle and how sin was washed by rite. Students of the Bible used his book to grasp the world Israel lived beside.
jenner-inquiry-variolae-vaccinae-1798:
Edward Jenner announced vaccination against smallpox in his Inquiry of 1798. The country doctor had noticed that milkmaids who caught cowpox seemed spared by smallpox. He tested the claim by placing cowpox matter into a boy's arm. The boy later resisted smallpox when Jenner tried the usual inoculation.

Case histories fill the short work, each one adding weight to the claim. Jenner names the cowpox by its Latin label, variolae vaccinae. His paper founded immunology, the science of protecting the body through its own defenses. Smallpox, a killer for centuries, met its match here. The Gutenberg text keeps the cases plain to read. Few short works changed so many lives.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lutzyn-10198:
Lutzyn, a Russian town in the government of Vitebsk, is given a community history in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. The town sits near a chain of mountains, ringed by lakes and streams. It is an old city, fortified by the Livonian Order in the twelfth century. Tradition says Jews began settling there in the fifteenth century.

The article tells a hard story of survival. Under Ivan the Terrible, Jews nearby were killed, though Lutzyn's Jews escaped by tradition. The community stayed unorganized until 1783, when a Jewish tailor named Moses was burned alive after a dispute with priests. His fellow Jews buried his ashes and organized at last. The entry then traces the town's rabbis, father to son, across the next century. It closes with a blood accusation raised in 1883. Few entries show so plainly what small-town Jewish life endured.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-markus-ludwig-1:
Ludwig Markus, a German Orientalist, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906, in an entry by Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar. Born in Dessau on October 31, 1798, he studied medicine at Berlin, gave it up for philosophy and astronomy, and joined the Society for Jewish Culture and Science. He died in Paris on July 15, 1843.

Markus spent his life on a study of foreign colonies in Abyssinia and Senaar, though poverty kept most of it unpublished. The entry follows his work for Cuvier, his years teaching German at Dijon, his deepening melancholy, and the nickname Heine gave him, the King of Abyssinia. It closes with his published books and the asylum where he died.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maurogonato-isa:
Isacco Pesaro Maurogonato was an Italian legislator and finance minister of revolutionary Venice. Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Venice on November 26, 1817, and died at Rome in 1892. He studied law, then finance and political economy, and in the revolution of 1848 he sat in the Venetian assembly. As minister of finance, he found money in an empty treasury to carry on the war, as right hand of Manin and Tommaseo.

Exiled after Austria retook Venice, he returned and did business at Vicenza. He entered Parliament in 1866. Offered the finance portfolio again and again, even by the king in person, he always refused. In 1884 he gave his own claims against the old revolutionary loans, some 16,000 francs, to Venice. They founded a relief fund for the veterans of the revolution there, and King Humbert made him a senator in 1890.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mayhem-10298: Mayhem is handled in a few lines in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906, in a note by Joseph Jacobs and Lewis N. Dembitz. In English law, the entry explains, mayhem is the offense of depriving a person, by violence, of a limb, a member, or an organ. Rather than treat the subject on the spot, the editors send the reader elsewhere: its bearing in rabbinical law, they say, is fully treated under the article on assault and battery. The entry is thus a signpost in the encyclopedia's legal cross-reference system.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-melammed-teache:
Melammed is the Hebrew word for a teacher. Joseph Jacobs and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach anatomize it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In the Bible it meant any instructor. By Talmudic times it had narrowed to the teacher of children, the melammed tinokot. The community appointed him under rules fixing how many pupils he could take and how he might be hired or dismissed.

The article follows the job into the law codes. A melammed might do no other work while teaching. If he fell ill his pay was docked, but if the pupil fell ill he was paid in full. He must not beat children too severely, must teach into the night, be pious, and only a married man could hold the post. It closes with the modern grades of the profession, from the village tutor to the gemara teacher.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-merkabah-lit-ch:
Merkabah, the heavenly Throne-Chariot of Ezekiel's vision, and the secret lore that grew around it, are treated in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Kaufmann Kohler. The picture itself is old and genuinely Hebrew: God rides upon cherubim across the Psalms, His war-chariot thunders in Habakkuk, and the ark itself is called a chariot. Ezekiel's vision of the throne leaving the doomed Temple, likely shaped by Babylonian sculpture, became for a later age a sacred mystery, named Merkabah already in Ben Sira.

The article dwells on the guardedness of the subject. The Mishnah permits teaching the Work of the Chariot only to a sage who can reason his way to knowledge on his own. Kohler retells the famous scene of Johanan ben Zakkai dismounting from his mule, since the Shekinah attends such telling, while his disciple Eleazar discourses and fire comes down from heaven around them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-microcosm-greek:
Microcosm, Greek for small universe, is the old philosophical idea that a human being mirrors the whole cosmos, which writers called the macrocosm. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé trace the doctrine in a Jewish Encyclopedia article of 1906. It runs from Pythagoras, Plato, and Aristotle to the Stoics, who gave it its fullest form.

In the Stoic picture the universe is a living being with body and soul, and man's soul is a piece of the universal soul, so each side can influence the other. The article then follows the idea into Jewish writing, where the Abot de-Rabbi Natan matches parts of the body to things in the world. A section on the four humors and four elements shows the doctrine at work in medicine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moab-hebrew-lxx:
Moab, the nation and district east of the Dead Sea, receives a long Jewish Encyclopedia treatment from Joseph Jacobs and Louis H. Gray, published in 1906. The article starts with the name, whose etymology it calls very uncertain. The Septuagint glosses it from my father, pointing at the Genesis story; Hommel's newest guess reads it as his mother is his father.

Genesis makes Moab the son of Lot by his elder daughter, and Ammon the half-brother by the younger — an origin the article treats as a record of real kinship. Moabites, Ammonites, and Hebrews were close kin, and the language of the Moabite Stone bears the family likeness out. The entry then follows Moab through the biblical narratives, where the two peoples appear bound together again and again.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mordecai-ben-ju:
Mordecai ben Judah, called Mordusch, was a Polish ritualist of Lamkumsh who died in 1584, as Gotthard Deutsch and S. J. Levinson record in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His work was the prayer-book. At Lublin in 1567 he edited the Maḥzor with Abraham Abigdor's commentary, adding notes of his own.

In the year of his death he did the same for Abigdor's seliḥot, the penitential prayers, at Cracow. The books outlived him in his family: his son-in-law Hirsch Sundels revised and enlarged the seliḥot twice more, at Prague in 1587 and Lublin in 1643. A short entry for a liturgical editor whose annotations carried the Polish rite.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-israe:
Moses ben Israel of Landsberg was a German Talmudist and Hebrew scholar of the early eighteenth century. Wilhelm Bacher and M. Seligsohn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. His contemporaries called him the father of those who interpret by gematria, the reading of words by their letter numbers.

Two books carry his name. The Ittur Soferim, printed at Hamburg in 1715, is a Hebrew letter writer for the young, a model book for learning to write letters. The Shomer Emunim, printed at Offenbach in 1724, is a partly cabalistic commentary on the Pentateuch, the Five Scrolls, and the Masorah. The short entry preserves a teacher of Hebrew style and number lore.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mugnon-david-11: David Mugnon was a Spanish scholar and author who died at Venice in 1629. The Jewish Encyclopedia entry, by its editorial committee and M. Seligsohn, records a single work. He wrote in Spanish a treatise on prayer and meditation and on the knowledge of oneself and of God. It was printed at Venice in 1654, twenty-five years after his death, under the title Tratado de la Oracion.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nahum-b-uzziel-:
Nahum ben Uzziel Kaplan, known as Reb Nahum Grodner, was a preacher and philanthropist of Grodno. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia life. Born in 1811, he was a great Talmudist who chose poverty. He took the humble post of sexton in the Hebrah Shas synagogue and kept it for life.

His real work was charity. Kaplan went from house to house collecting money and goods, and gave them where need was greatest. On Sabbath afternoons he preached plain moral truths in words the poor could feel. All Russian Jewry trusted him, and his funeral in 1879 was called the most imposing Grodno had seen.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nose-11598:
Nose treats a feature once read as racial proof. Joseph Jacobs and Maurice Fishberg wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Some classifiers set a Jewish, or Semitic, nose type. They describe it as prominent, arched, and hooked. Old Egyptian monuments show such noses on Semites.

The entry tests that claim against measured heads. Most Jewish noses counted prove straight, or Greek. Over sixty per cent fall in that class. Arched noses stay under a quarter in the tables. In Warsaw only 6.5 per cent showed the type. Luschan blamed such noses on old Hittite mixture. Jacobs lays the Jewish look to the nostrils instead. Cover the nose, his photos show, and it vanishes. Width against length also marks Jews narrow-nosed overall.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-omen-11698:
Omen is a sign thought to foretell good or ill luck. Kaufmann Kohler and Ludwig Blau wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. An omen is a chance event in daily life. It needs no priest and no deep lore to read. That sets it apart from other forms of telling the future.

Belief in omens is the first stage of such telling. Judaism barred the study of stars and bird flight. Yet the lore of omens ran too deep to root out. It lived on in Talmud times in mild forms. The Bible gives signs sought by Eliezer of Damascus. It gives a sign sought by Jonathan, son of Saul. The Talmud calls both of these mere omens. A man's name could be read as an omen too.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ostropoli-samso:
Samson ben Pesah Ostropoli was a Polish rabbi and martyr. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was slain at Polonnoye, in Podolia, in 1648. That was in the great Cossack rising of that year. His death fell on July 15 of that year.

When the Cossacks laid siege to the town, Samson stood firm. He and 300 of his flock went to the synagogue. They wore their shrouds and their prayer shawls there. They stood in prayer till the foe came in on them. The foe slew them all where they stood at prayer. Samson was a noted man of the Cabala too. His notes on a Cabala work were put out in 1709. That was years after his death, by his nephew Pesah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-peltin-samuel-h:
Samuel Hirsh Peltin was a Polish Jewish writer and editor. He was born at Mariampol in 1831 and died at Warsaw in 1896. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He settled in Warsaw in 1855 and stayed.

In 1865 Peltin founded Izraelita, a Polish weekly for Jewish readers. He edited the paper for the rest of his life. In its pages he fought anti-Semitic attacks in print. He also wrote tales of Jewish life. He translated other writers' stories into Polish. A Polish history of the Jews stayed in manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-philip-of-bathy:
Philip of Bathyra was a Jewish commander under Agrippa the Second. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His father and grandfather had governed Bathyra. Agrippa made him leader of the royal troops.

In 66 Rome sent Philip to hold Jerusalem. He brought two thousand horse to keep the city loyal. After Cestius fell, Philip helped the trapped Roman guard. He fled the fallen fort and barely escaped death. Accused later before Vespasian, he was sent to Rome. He never saw Nero, and his end is unknown.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pjurko-abraham-:
Abraham Marcus Pjurko was a Russian Hebrew writer and teacher. Herman Rosenthal and Benzion Eisenstadt wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Lomza on February 15, 1853. He began with Talmud, then turned to modern letters. His books poured out at Warsaw for decades.

Pjurko wrote a Bible poem while still young. His letter-writer gave 150 model letters for learners. He published a hundred stories for the young in 1884. His catechism served teachers of the Bible. In 1899 he launched a weekly, Gan Sha'ashu'im. His son Hayyim shared in his children's tales.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-provence-12398:
Provence is an old province in the south of France. Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn wrote its article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It lies between the Rhône, the sea, and the Maritime Alps. Jewish scholars of old used the name more loosely. They spread it over part of Bas-Languedoc as well.

Jews settled in Provence at a very early date. By the sixth century they formed strong groups at Arles. Marseilles held such a group too. In 1276 Charles the First shielded them from the Inquisition. The article traces their towns, their scholars, and their trials. Provence gave Jewry some of its finest minds in those years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbiner-semina:
The Rabbiner Seminar was a Berlin school for Orthodox rabbis. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Dr. Israel Hildesheimer founded the school in Berlin. In 1869 he took the call as rabbi of Berlin's Orthodox party. He made one firm term for his move north.

Hildesheimer claimed the right to go on with his teaching. He had taught rabbis at Eisenstadt in Hungary before Berlin. His Berlin talks drew a great crowd of pupils at once. He then wrote to ten leading men of the party. From that step the set school grew in due form. The article traces its plan, its staff, and its aims.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-raven-hebrew-or:
The raven is the first bird named in the Old Testament. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Genesis links it to Noah and the ark. Leviticus lists it among unclean birds.

The article says the Hebrew term covers crows and rooks too. Eight kinds lived in Palestine, the writers note. Ravens haunt deep rocky glens and lonely places. Scripture says ravens fed Elijah in the wilderness. Psalms use them to show God's care for creatures. A Talmud part adds other names for the bird. It also tells odd beliefs about young ravens. The entry mixes Bible study with natural history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-retaliation-or-:
Retaliation, or lex talionis, is the law of measure for measure. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Early law put redress of wrongs before contract rights. Rough justice demanded the same loss for the aggressor.

The article says Israel's oldest law included this rule. Talmud sayings picture God punishing in kind as well. The writers then compare Hammurabi's older Babylonian code. Its measure for measure goes far beyond eye for eye. A builder's son could die for the owner's son. A striker's daughter could die for a pregnant victim. The entry uses Babylon to show Israel's rule in context. It sets a harsh law beside still harsher neighbors.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rodrigues-hippo:
Hippolyte Rodrigues was a French banker and writer born at Bordeaux in 1812. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He died at Paris in 1898. He was son of Isaac Rodrigues-Henriques, a Bordeaux banking head.

The article opens with a family tradition he recorded in 1893. His families left Palestine, settled Portugal, then Spain. The Inquisition drove them to refuge in Bordeaux. A Gradis offer of nobility was refused on oath grounds. Rodrigues was educated in Paris and loved literature early. At eighteen he began a romance on the French Revolution. He became a Paris stockbroker in 1840. He retired in 1855 for study and writing. His prolific works treat Bible daughters and early Christians. He also wrote an opera, David Rizzio, himself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rossi-solomon-1:
Solomon Rossi was a rabbi and composer who lived in Mantua around 1600. Gotthard Deutsch and Frank Cramer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. In 1587 the duke of Mantua engaged him as court musician and singer.

Rossi stood so high at court that he needed no yellow badge in public. Other Mantua Jews of the time were forced to wear it. Skilled in counterpoint, he wedded old synagogue melodies to composed part music. His Ha-Shirim Asher li-Shelomoh, printed at Venice in 1622, proves the success. He also wrote madrigals, hymns, and a musical drama, Maddalena.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saint-and-saint:
Saint and saintliness treats hasidut, a piety that goes beyond the Law's demand. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. It sets saintliness apart from holiness, which the Mosaic law commands.

The saint, say the rabbis, acts in front of the law's boundary line. That is, he gives more than strict justice can require of him. Adam counts as a great saint for fasting 130 years in sorrow. David rose at midnight to thank God, unlike other kings who slept late. Even Job is counted a saint among the Gentiles in this reckoning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-of-evreu:
Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Samuel of Evreux, a French tosafist of the thirteenth century. Gross identified him with Samuel ben Shneor. Solomon ben Adret cites his readings of the tractate Nazir. Jonah Gerondi also invokes his authority.

Samuel ran a rabbinical school at Château-Thierry. His pupils included Ḥayyim, Perez, and Isaac of Corbeil. He traded letters on science with Jehiel of Paris. He also wrote to Nathaniel the Elder on points of law. His Talmudic readings appear often in the printed Tosafot. The tosafot to Soṭah seem to be his work too. There his brother, Moses of Evreux, is named.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saratof-13198:
Herman Rosenthal and Julius Gottlieb wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Saratof. The Russian city stands on the right bank of the Volga. It is remembered chiefly for the Saratof affair. That case began in 1853 with the murder of two Christian boys. The killings happened near Passover. Jews were accused at once.

Behind the charge stood a paper of 1844 by Skripitzyn. It claimed that Jews killed Christians to obtain their blood. The paper was later shown to copy a mad priest's treatise of 1740. Still, officials and judges believed it for decades. A Jewish family named Yushkewitzer was arrested, with a soldier and a barber. The chief witness first denied all knowledge. She then told a wild tale of boys starved and stabbed in a synagogue. Her story was full of contradictions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schomberg-ralph:
Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Ralph Schomberg. He was an English physician and author. Schomberg was born at Cologne on August 14, 1714. He died at Reading on June 29, 1792. He was the twin brother of Isaac Schomberg. He studied at Merchant Taylor's School and at Rotterdam.

Schomberg first practiced at Yarmouth. In 1752 he joined the Society of Antiquaries. He then moved to Bath and practiced there with success. Some trouble forced him out of Bath and public practice. He retired to Pangborne and then to Reading. He wrote on a flood of subjects. His list holds odes, medical treatises, burlesques, and satires. One critic called him a scribbler without genius or truth. His works mostly met a cold reception.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-selah-hebrew-13:
Emil G. Hirsch wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the word Selah. Selah is a term of uncertain origin and doubtful meaning. It appears seventy-one times in thirty-nine Psalms. It appears three more times in Habakkuk's third chapter. It usually stands at the end of a verse. Even the ancient translators did not know what it meant.

The Septuagint renders Selah as diapsalma, a Greek word just as dark. Aquila and Jerome give it the sense of always. The Targum mostly reads it as forever. Hippolytus took the Greek term to mark a change of rhythm or melody. Baethgen objected that Selah also ends whole psalms. The article judges the mark a later editor's insertion. Such an editor expected the Psalms to be sung in sequence.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shammai-called-:
Shammai, called the Elder, was a leading scholar of the first century B.C. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He served as vice-president of the Sanhedrin beside Hillel, its president. In legal debate he stood as Hillel's great opponent.

Shammai was quick-tempered where Hillel was patient and gentle. A famous tale has him drive off a would-be convert with hard demands. Hillel, using kindness, won that same man over. Yet Shammai was no hater of people, the entry stresses. His own motto urged study, little speech, and a friendly face for all. Readers meet strictness and warmth in one man.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shkud-13598:
Shkud is a Russian town in Kovno government, where two rivers meet. Isidore Singer and Julius Gottlieb wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. The earliest written record of its Jews is the community register. That register, or pinkes, begins with the year 1725.

The register names no persecutions, yet it honors martyrs. Elders are listed as sons of men called martyr. Central council officers sometimes visited to review local affairs. They even aided the town when help was needed. Once the local chief was jailed over a community debt. Visiting officers ransomed Rabbi Mikel at once, the record says. Shkud Jews also followed outside Jewish affairs with keen interest. The entry works from a town's own memory book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-b-judah-:
Simeon ben Judah was a tanna of the fourth generation, from Kefar Ikos. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He appears almost wholly as a transmitter of others' words. The sentences he passes on come from Simeon ben Yohai.

Two readings of Simeon's own have also been handed down. On Exodus he notes Israel cried out before Moses did. Their cry for aid preceded their leader's prayer, he said. On Deuteronomy he derives a word from a root meaning foundation. God placed Israel upon its foundation, he read it. Another saying of his mentions leprous stones in Galilee. Those were stones from a house struck with leprosy. The entry shows how transmitters keep their own small voice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-slave-trade-137:
The slave trade was allowed by all ancient and medieval laws. Isidore Singer and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Even Christian Europe allowed it into the thirteenth century. Jews were barred from trading in Jewish slaves. No like bar covered the buying and selling of heathen slaves.

Jews in Spain supplied slaves to both Arians and Catholics. Pope Gelasius in 492 let Jews bring heathen slaves into Italy. By the time of Gregory the Great, Jews led this traffic. He objected to Jews holding Christian slaves. With the rise of Islam, Jewish dealers carried slaves both ways. They moved between the Christian and Muslim worlds along set routes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-de-veso: Solomon de Vesoul was the son of Manessier de Vesoul, who died about 1375. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. Charles V appointed Solomon clerk and tax-gatherer for the Jews of France. That decree is dated August 9, 1378. Like his father and brothers, he stood high in royal favor. The king freed him and his family from wearing the Jews' badge.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-steckler-alfred: Alfred Steckler was an American jurist born in New York city in 1856. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T Haneman wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He was born there on December 18 of that year. He was educated in New York public schools and Columbia Law School. He graduated in 1877 and joined the bar that year. In 1881 he became judge of the Fourth District Court. He served in that post until 1893 in New York. In 1900 he filled a vacancy on the Supreme Court.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-succoth-14098:
Succoth names two places in the Bible, one in Egypt and one in Palestine. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. The Egyptian Succoth was Israel's first stop out of Egypt. Scholars link it to the district of Pithom there. The name itself means huts or booths in Hebrew.

The Palestinian Succoth lay east of the Jordan in Gad's territory. Jacob settled there after returning from Aramean country. Gideon reached it while chasing the Midianites west to east. Psalms call its valley the valley of Succoth. Jerome placed it in the territory of Scythopolis. Later writers tie it to a hill north of the Jabbok. The entry sorts two sites that share one name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tahanun-14198:
Tahanun is a prayer for grace said on weekdays. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Worshippers recite it after the Amidah prayer. It comes at morning and afternoon services alike. Its name comes from its opening words of mercy.

The prayer opens with O Merciful and Gracious. Psalm 6 follows in the rite. Verses from Chronicles and Psalms complete the core. On Mondays and Thursdays long poetic verses enter. Those verses plead for rescue from cruel hands. They were likely composed amid Crusade persecutions. After each stanza the congregation answers a refrain. It begs God not to forget his people. Fast days add a Guardian of Israel prayer. The entry lays out a weekday plea step by step.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tiktinski-hayyi:
Hayyim Judah Löb Tiktinski was a Lithuanian Talmudist who led the Mir yeshiva. A. Peiginsky wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was born at Mir in 1823. His father Samuel founded that yeshiva and died in 1835. The boy was left poor at age eleven.

Hard study carried him to a rabbinical pass before twenty. In 1850 he began lecturing at Mir. His clear delivery drew many scholars to his talks. He rejected pilpul, the hair-splitting style then in fashion. In 1867 the whole yeshiva passed into his hands. Fire destroyed the school in 1898, and he raised funds to rebuild. His own writings burned in that fire.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trespass-14498:
Trespass on property under Talmudic law is the focus of this article. Lewis N. Dembitz wrote it with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. A man is always forewarned, the Mishnah says. He pays full damage for his direct acts. Sleep, ignorance, and even unwillingness are no defense.

Scripture gives one model case, killing a domestic animal. Oral law extends it to all direct harm. Blinding an eye or breaking a vessel draws full payment. Tearing clothes or killing a beast works the same way. One exception stands: a sin deserving death cancels money liability. Two potters walking in line illustrate the rule. The first to stumble pays for the second's fall.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-urania-14598: Urania was a woman who led prayer in the women's synagogue at Worms. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. She was the daughter of Abraham the Precentor of Worms. Like her father, she herself acted as precentor. She held that role before the year 1275. The entry cross-refers readers to the article on the Sagerin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vidas-samuel-be:
Samuel ben Habib de Vidas was a Spanish scholar and Bible commentator. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Vidas lived in the fifteenth century. Some say he also worked as a doctor. That claim is not certain. His printed work explains the Book of Lamentations.

That commentary appeared at Salonica in 1595. Its title is Perush Megillat Ekah. Two more works survive in handwriting. One holds sermons on the weekly Torah readings. It runs from Ki Tissa to Nizzabim. The other explains the Song of Songs. In that book his name appears as Samuel Bibas.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wawelberg-hippo:
Hippolite Henrichovich Wawelberg was a Russian banker and philanthropist. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Warsaw in 1844. He died at St. Petersburg on October 20, 1901. He studied at Warsaw and in Germany. He then took over his father's bank.

Wawelberg gave large sums to industrial schools. Warsaw's museum and technical school owe much to him. He also funded cheap lodging houses for workers. Polish science books for common readers gained his support. He directed St. Petersburg's Jewish community. He backed groups that spread culture among Russian Jews. His gifts joined Polish patriotism with Jewish loyalty.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolfner-theodor:
Theodore Wolfner (born 1864) was a Hungarian lawmaker and a leader in leather trade. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Uj-Pest, he schooled there and at Budapest. He learned the leather trade in the tannery of his father.

He then took a long trip through four lands. He saw Germany, Egypt, the Holy Land, and Turkey. Back home he rose in town and county posts. He led the state group of leather makers. He also sat on the trade board at Budapest. Since 1896 he has sat for Godollo in Parliament. That district was a seat of the king and his court. In 1904 the king made him a noble and a hussar chief.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yizhak-ben-hiyy:
Yizhak ben Hiyya the Scribe was a scholar of Palestine in the 300s. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a peer of the scholar Mani in his day. He was well known as a scribe of fine hand.

His one rule treats the skins used for holy books. Torah scrolls may be writ on skins of more than one sort. That free rule does not hold for small scroll cases. It does not hold for door post scrolls as well. In the name of Johanan he passed on a marriage rule. Three tale notes of his live on in the books. One treats the fate of the good and the base. One asks why Saul sought a witch at En-dor. One sets the Torah as a tree of life for all men.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zechariah-15198:
Zechariah was one of the twelve small prophets of the Bible. Emil G. Hirsch wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a son of Berechiah and a grandson of Iddo. In the Book of Ezra he is called the son of Iddo.

He was most like born in the years of the exile. He was brought back to the land at a young age. He began his work in the second year of King Darius. That start came a bit after the start of Haggai. His chief care was the new build of the Temple. God spoke to him most of all in dreams by night. Those dreams woke his keen wish to know their sense. A voice then read each dream for him in plain words. Each dream bore on the state of the returned folk.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zuntz-nathan-15:
Nathan Zuntz was a German physiologist who studied how the body uses food and air. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Bonn on October 6, 1847, he took his medical degree there in 1868. He became an assistant at the university's physiological institute.

Zuntz won the right to lecture in 1871 and became prosector and assistant professor of anatomy three years later. In 1881 he took the chair of animal physiology at Berlin's agricultural college. His many journal papers deal with physiology, nutrition, and respiration. Those topics, the entry notes, fill much of his published work.
knights-of-malta-1523-1798:
Reuben Cohen, a former scholar of Wadham College, Oxford, wrote this history in 1920. It won the Lothian Prize Essay at Oxford that year. Its subject is the Knights of Malta from 1523 to 1798.

The first chapter follows the Order from Rhodes to its settlement in Malta in 1530. The second tells the great siege of 1565, when St. Elmo fell. Later chapters explain the Order's rules, leaders, courts, and hospital. A final part traces decline as the knights slowly became out of step with their age. Cohen keeps the focus on the Order as a working state. Fortresses, fleets, and faith all share the story with battles.
kropotkin-fields-factories-workshops-189:
Peter Kropotkin published Fields, Factories and Workshops in 1898. The book grew from essays on how industry and farming might be joined. Kropotkin argued that small workshops using electric power could match great factories, and that towns could grow much of their own food.

He drew on reports from market gardens near Paris and small industries in Britain and France. His plan mixed mental and hand work for every person and spread production across the land. That vision of decentralized industry, integrated with agriculture, founded a line of anarchist economics. Later planners of garden cities and local production borrowed from it, often without knowing the source.
lancashire-idylls-1898:
Marshall Mather published Lancashire Idylls with Frederick Warne in 1898. Mather had written on Ruskin and on nineteenth-century poets. An introduction explains what he hopes to preserve.

Earlier writers recorded Lancashire's moorland and factory life, he says. Few recorded the stern Puritan faith of its hill sects. Mather finds poetry and simplicity in those small chapels. His tales aim to recall that local character before it fades. Readers get dialect, devotion, and mill-country life in story form. Mather writes with sympathy for plain chapel folk. Their strict faith, in his telling, hides warmth and humor.
landor-gebir-1798:
Walter Savage Landor wrote Gebir while still a young man, and it appeared in 1798 as his first long poem. An Iberian prince named Gebir invades Egypt and falls in love with its queen, in a tale of war and doomed ambition. This printing pairs it with Count Julian, his tragedy on the fall of Christian Spain.

Both works dress old stories in a grand classical style, with dense and musical verse. The 1887 Cassell edition adds a life of Landor, from Rugby and Oxford to his fierce, restless later years. Together the poems show the scale of ambition that marked his long career from the start.
