leibniz-monadology-latta-1898:
G W Leibniz's Monadology appeared in English in Robert Latta's 1898 edition, The Monadology and Other Philosophical Writings. Leibniz, the German philosopher and mathematician, wrote the Monadology in 1714 as a short summary of his system. It runs to just ninety numbered sections.

Leibniz taught that reality is made of monads, simple units each mirroring the whole universe from its own angle. God, the supreme monad, set their harmony in advance, so minds and bodies agree without touching. Latta added related writings and full notes, making the standard English Leibniz for a generation. The volume gives readers the clearest short door into a deep and strange system.
life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld-advo:
Volume Two of Motley's complete Barneveld history covers 1614 to 1623. It opens with Chapter Eleven and Barneveld's alarm in Germany. The Prince Palatine's forces take Aachen, Mulheim, and other towns. Austria and the League answer with increased activity.

Barneveld surveys Europe's condition and strives to avert general war. He seeks help from England and influence through France. King James handles the proposed new treaty in slippery fashion. This half of the work runs from early warnings to Barneveld's fall. Conferences on piracy and the cloth trade fill the later chapters. Barneveld's survey of Europe closes this half's foreign policy account.
malthus-population-1798:
Thomas Robert Malthus was an English clergyman and teacher who set off a lasting public quarrel with one short essay. His Essay on the Principle of Population, published in 1798, warns that people multiply faster than food can grow. The claim cut against the hopeful mood of his age.

Malthus argues that population grows in a fast geometric line while food supply creeps along in a slow arithmetic one. Hunger, disease, and late marriage then act as checks that hold the numbers down. Darwin read the essay and took from it a key push toward natural selection.
marlowe-hero-leander-1598:
Christopher Marlowe left Hero and Leander unfinished when he was killed in 1593. George Chapman completed the poem, and the full version appeared in 1598. The story comes from an ancient Greek poem about two lovers separated by the Hellespont strait.

Leander swims the strait each night to reach Hero, a priestess of Venus in a tower across the water. Marlowe tells their first meeting at a festival with wit, beauty, and bold sensual detail. His couplets sparkle with mythological jokes and rich description. Chapman's ending adds the lovers' deaths. The poem influenced a generation of English poets, including Shakespeare.
marx-brumaire-de-leon-1898:
Karl Marx wrote The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte in the weeks after Louis Napoleon seized power in France in late 1851. Daniel De Leon translated this English edition, published in 1898. Many readers count it as Marx's finest piece of historical writing.

Marx follows the French classes, parties, and factions through the revolutions of 1848 to 1851 with biting wit. His famous opening says history repeats itself, first as tragedy, then as farce. The book shows his method at its most concrete, weighing real interests behind fine phrases. He follows money, land, and class fear behind the slogans of each party. De Leon's version carried the work to American socialists for decades.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-st-cloud-being-s:
Volume seven of the St. Cloud letters opens at letter twenty four. The writer dates it from Paris in October 1805. Russia's firm stand with France leads this letter's argument.

St. Petersburg, he says, kept prudence without weakness through the crisis. It never lost sight of its own dignity in talks. Count Alexander Woronzoff, its chancellor, earns a full portrait here. Catherine the Second chose him young, and courts across Europe trust his word. Fools choose fools as agents, he argues, while genius picks its own kind. That rule frames his praise of Russia's able ministry.
molitor-de-lamiis-latin-1498:
Ulrich Molitor, a lawyer at Constance, wrote his dialogue on witches and pythonesses in the fifteenth century. This edition of 1498 is the first printed demonology with woodcuts, and the pictures are part of its fame. Molitor stages a debate over how much power the devil truly has over witches.

His speakers weigh famous cases and test the claims made for flight, storms, and transformations. Molitor grants the devil much, yet doubts the witches' own powers. The woodcuts show witches at their cauldron in early printed form. Quaint and grim by turns, the book set the new craft of print to serve the old fear. A later reprint also rides inside the library's 1580 Malleus volume.
mooney-calendar-history-of-the-kiowa-ind:
Among the Kiowa of the southern Plains, history was kept in painted calendars, one picture for each season. James Mooney's 1898 report studies the calendar of Set-t'an and others, using their year-by-year images as the frame for a tribal history.

Mooney decodes the pictographs season by season, from early wars and hunts to the years of the sun dance and the reservation. He adds accounts of Kiowa customs, leaders, and relations with other tribes and the United States. The work shows how a people without writing stored their past, and it remains a key source for Kiowa history.
muller-ramakrishna-life-sayings-1898:
Friedrich Max Muller, the Oxford scholar of Eastern religions, published Ramakrishna: His Life and Sayings in 1898. Ramakrishna was a Bengali temple priest whose intense devotion drew disciples across India in the late nineteenth century. Muller never met him, and worked from reports and letters.

The book tells of Ramakrishna's years of prayer, his trials of Hindu, Muslim, and Christian paths, and his teaching by parable. His sayings, short and earthy, fill the second half in Muller's careful rendering. The volume introduced the Bengali mystic to the West and shaped how Europe pictured the Indian saint.
nasa-tm-19690014145-steady-state-interac:
Robert E. Coltrin and David A. Choby of Lewis Research Center studied how a turbojet engine and its inlet interact in this report. Tests covered Mach 1.98 to 2.58 with an axisymmetric inlet having sixty percent internal area contraction. The inlet was a Mach 2.5 mixed-compression design paired with a real engine.

Installing the engine did not grossly change total pressure size or spread at the diffuser exit, versus a choked plug. With large circumferential distortion at the compressor face, the engine reshaped the static pressure field instead. Total pressure profiles stayed largely unaffected in that case. Limited constant-speed data showed large radial distortions cost a slight loss in compressor pressure ratio.
nasa-tm-19710019535-optimization-of-engi:
Gerald A Kraft and John B Whitlow Jr of the Lewis Research Center published this engine study in June 1971, as NASA TM X-67865. It sizes turbofan engines for a fast subsonic transport flying at Mach 0.98. The design assumed a three hundred passenger jet with a supercritical wing, first flying in 1978. Airport noise limits shaped the whole study.

The engine giving the greatest range was also too loud. Adding noise limits changed the best design point. A mid level noise goal could be met with a range loss of five hundred nautical miles. A much stricter goal cost more range still. It also demanded far stronger noise suppression gear than then existed.
openalex-w2058652198:
Margot Bass, Matt Finer, Clinton Jenkins and colleagues assessed the world importance of Yasuni National Park in Ecuador. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2010. The park sits in the western Amazon. The region is one of Earth's richest wild areas. Large untapped oil reserves lie beneath the park.

The authors reviewed the park's species and ecosystems. They set its value in a global context. Yasuni holds exceptional numbers of many species groups. Its forests also store large amounts of carbon. Oil development threatens that richness directly. Roads and settlement bring further harm. The paper argues the park deserves top protection priority. Its case reflects threats across the western Amazon.
openalex-w2103160998:
Carlos Quesada, Jon Lloyd, Michael Schwarz and colleagues compared soils across the Amazon Basin. Their paper appeared in Biogeosciences in 2010. Amazon soils vary with their geological origins. Soil fertility shapes which trees thrive where. The RAINFOR project sampled forests basin-wide for comparison.

Samples came from seventy-one plots in six countries. Labs measured nutrients, carbon, nitrogen and acidity. Phosphorus forms were measured in detail too. Soil properties differed strongly between regions. Young western soils were richer than old eastern ones. Geology explained much of the pattern. The results link soil history to forest composition. They help models of Amazon carbon and growth.
openalex-w2163192098:
Luciano Machado and Marcelo Savi published this review in the Brazilian Journal of Medical and Biological Research in 2003. They explain shape memory alloys, metals that return to a former shape after the right heat and force treatment. These alloys also show rubber-like springiness far beyond ordinary metals, drawing attention from many fields.

The review first walks through how the memory and spring effects behave. It then surveys the most promising medical uses of the alloys. Those include heart and vessel devices, bone and orthopedic hardware, and surgical instruments. Nickel-titanium alloys lead commercial use because they pair strong mechanical performance with the memory effect. Copper-based alloys form the other main family.
openalex-w2918389998:
Joshua Cobb, Roselyne Juma, Partha Biswas, and colleagues wrote this 2019 review in Theoretical and Applied Genetics. It looks at how public-sector plant breeding programs can improve crops faster. Their guide is the breeder's equation, the basic formula of quantitative genetics for predicting response to selection.

The authors argue that new breeding tools can sharply raise the rate of genetic gain when matched to that formula. The most promising steps all cut the time each breeding cycle takes. They include selecting parents from non-inbred offspring, advancing generations quickly, and using genomic selection. The authors stress that these complex changes require breeding organizations to rethink how they run their programs.
openalex-w3015355998:
Mario Herrero, Philip Thornton, Daniel Mason-D'Croz, and colleagues published this article in Nature Food in 2020. It argues that innovation can speed the shift toward a food system that is sustainable. The author list joins many leading research groups on food, farming, and climate.

Today's food system feeds billions but drives emissions, land clearing, and poor diets. The authors survey new ideas across production, processing, and consumption that could cut those harms. Their point is pace: the needed changes are known in outline, but they arrive too slowly on their own. Well-aimed innovation, joined with policy, could compress decades of transition. The paper maps where such speed-ups look most promising.
openalex-w3041007898:
Lydia Scarfò, Thomas Chatzikonstantinou, Gian Rigolin, and colleagues published this study in Leukemia in 2020. It examines how severe COVID-19 runs in patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia, a blood cancer that weakens the immune system. The study joins two European research networks for this disease.

When the pandemic began, doctors lacked data on how this patient group would fare. The joint study gathered cases across many centers to measure severity and death rates in a consistent way. Such figures guide shielding advice, treatment choices during infection, and vaccine planning for people whose cancer already compromises their defenses. The paper gives clinicians an early, shared evidence base for a high-risk group.
openalex-w7125696198:
Yashar Mashayekhi, Nathan Kevin Peter, Sara Baba-Aissa, and colleagues survey problems with body-heat control in metabolic syndrome. Their questionnaire study appeared in the Juntendo Medical Journal in 2026. Metabolic syndrome bundles belly obesity, insulin resistance, and abnormal lipids and blood pressure. It sharply raises cardiovascular risk.

One overlooked feature is faulty thermoregulation. Patients may sense heat and cold in distorted ways. Such odd sensing can signal deeper metabolic and nerve damage. Their multicountry survey asks about felt heat and cold problems alongside heart symptoms. Linking the two could reveal a cheap warning sign. Symptom patterns that patients report themselves may flag those heading for heart attacks and strokes, prompting earlier checks and treatment.
openalex-w7204196198:
Rodrigo Bueno Coimbra and Lucas de Morais Gualtieri released a Portuguese-language paper in Brazil in 2026 debating whether world order is anarchic or hierarchical. Neorealist thinkers such as Morgenthau, Waltz, and Mearsheimer describe a global system with no ruler, where states help themselves and balance power to keep order. Marxist and world-systems writers such as Cox, Arrighi, and Frank describe a system built on hierarchy, production asymmetries, and accumulation that keeps center-periphery inequality in place.

Moving through the balance-of-power concept, systemic accumulation cycles, and systemic chaos, the authors find the two paradigms complementary. Neorealism maps how great powers act on security questions. The Marxist frame supplies the tools to set in history and question the material structures of domination beneath today's order.
openalex-w7204207398:
Eduarda Baranselli Sestito led a Portuguese-language systematic review, published in Brazil in 2026, on blood biomarkers that might reveal early heart remodeling in chronic kidney disease. Cardiovascular disease is the main cause of death in kidney patients, and heart muscle thickening begins early and silently, while imaging is costly and not always available. Following standard guidelines, the team searched two databases and kept only six studies of over six hundred found, covering more than nine thousand patients in early kidney disease stages.

One marker, NT-proBNP, consistently identified remodeling best, linking to tissue scarring and relaxation problems. Troponins instead tracked direct heart injury and cavity size measures. The authors present the blood tests as screening tools where imaging falls short.
openalex-w7204212698:
Jamily Soler do Nascimento Aguiar and Maria do Carmo Monteiro Kobayashi released a Portuguese-language analysis in Brazil in 2026. It looks at children living in care and what broken emotional bonds do to their schooling. The review joins psychology and schooling across three axes. These are the care context and its bond ruptures, the affective bond as a base in Bowlby, Winnicott, and Wallon, and what follows for schooling.

Bond, subjectivity, and growth are intertwined, the authors argue, so a broken bond reaches beyond feelings into a child's readiness to learn. A school that deliberately offers welcome and continuity can act as a repair environment, they conclude, sustaining new bonds and repositioning the child toward learning.
openalex-w7212237598:
Glayson Pereira Vitor, writing alone, reviews the use of smart tech in dentistry. The tools now help dentists spot disease, plan care, and run the clinic day. His review reads work from 2020 to 2026 in five databases. It spans strict trials, watch studies, past reviews, and method work. The aim is to weigh how well the tools work, what blocks their use, and where they may go next.

The tools scored high on spotting tooth decay, root-tip sores, and gum disease. Uses reach all parts of the field, from X-ray work to root care, braces, and mouth surgery. Blocks stay real, the review notes, from cost and training to trust in the screen. Still, the trend is clear. Smart aids are set to sit at the core of the dental chair, with the dentist's hand and eye on top.
openalex-w7213361498:
Maria Fernanda Cardoso and a large team review rusfertide, a new drug approach for polycythemia vera. That illness makes the body produce too many red blood cells and raises clot risk. Standard care relies on removing blood at intervals, which can leave patients short of iron. Their 2026 review asks whether rusfertide can reduce that dependence.

Rusfertide copies hepcidin, a hormone that controls iron use in the body. By limiting iron supply, it slows red cell production in a way the authors liken to chemical blood removal. The review draws on five PubMed papers, including a key phase two trial. Early results look promising, but the evidence base is still small.
openalex-w7213765198:
Antonio Pereira dos Santos studies school climate, work stress, and burnout among public school teachers in São Paulo. His single-author 2026 quantitative study covers eighty teachers in four schools. Standard inventories measured burnout and occupational stress, alongside a climate questionnaire.

Climate was rated moderate, while stress sat moderate to high. About a quarter of teachers showed high emotional exhaustion. Better climate went with lower stress and lower burnout, while stress rose with burnout. Career prospects, recognition, leadership, and working conditions linked most strongly to stress. Stress partly carried the effect of climate onto burnout. Prevention at the level of the single school is offered as the practical route.
openalex-w7214783298:
Samir Codognos led a twelve-author 2026 interdisciplinary review on personalizing mechanical ventilation for patients with acute respiratory failure. A ventilator keeps such patients alive, yet the support itself can injure lungs and the diaphragm. Standard protective settings, based on predicted body weight and fixed pressure tables, ignore how differently each patient's lungs behave.

Reading recent syntheses through an engineering lens, the team organizes personalization into layers: sensing, processing and estimation, decision and control, and actuation with safety. The physiology and the technology are mature, they find. But proof that personalized ventilation beats standard protocols on hard clinical outcomes is still missing, and standards for checking the computer models are lacking. Progress, they conclude, depends on identifying patient subgroups and building credible models more than on new control gadgets.
openalex-w7214800998:
Guilherme Mendes Tomaz dos Santos led a 2026 Spanish-language study of internationalization at the Federal University of Rondônia in Brazil, focused on its pedagogy course. Internationalization means building international links, content, and mobility into university life, and scholars treat it as a strategic dimension of higher education. The team read the course's pedagogical project, institutional documents, and cooperation agreements, and analyzed their content.

What they found was an incipient process: weak institutionalization, no real integration into the curriculum, and partnerships with low effectiveness. Institutional discourse and daily practice did not match. Internationalization at the university is mostly formal, they conclude, with limited effect on teacher formation. They call for rethinking it as a strategic, integrated, and critical policy rather than a set of signed agreements that change little in the classroom.
openalex-w7214996898:
Natália Rosa de Sousa led a 2026 study that built and tested a board game, Rio Abaixo, Rio Arriba, for teaching environmental impacts on Brazil's Parnaíba River. Thirty sixth-grade students at a public school in Teresina played two rounds of the game between an introductory lecture and pre- and post-intervention questionnaires. The game has dozens of spaces mixing river geography, human activities, and rewards and penalties.

Students initially rated waste disposal, sewage discharge, and riverside deforestation as the most critical problems, while underestimating predatory fishing. Most said the game made learning easier, and most rated the method excellent, with nearly all evaluations positive or neutral. A regionalized, playful approach, the authors conclude, can raise both science learning and environmental awareness in basic education, because the river in the game is the river in the students' own region.
openalex-w7218345298: José Cássio de Almeida Magalhães led a seven-author 2026 literature review on surgical treatment of gingival hyperplasia, the overgrowth of gum tissue. It concerns patients wearing orthodontic appliances. Braces and wires make cleaning harder and can irritate the gum, and bacterial film buildup is a main driver of the swelling. The evidence sample for this entry contains only the opening of the abstract, which defines the condition and its causes. It lacks the review's treatment findings, so no specific surgical conclusions are described here.
openalex-w7221020698:
Kaylane Vitória Medeiros do Carmo and four colleagues systematically reviewed studies that combine two management methods: the Plan-Do-Check-Act improvement cycle and Total Productive Maintenance. Their 2026 review asks what the pairing does for industrial performance, and what it could mean for pharmaceutical factories.

Following standard review guidance, they screened nearly two hundred records and kept twenty-one studies. Only six joined the two methods directly, and all of those sat outside the drug industry. Fifteen pharmaceutical studies used one method alone, and most research designs were single cases or simple before-and-after comparisons. The review maps a promising practice whose evidence base, especially in pharmacy, is still thin.
openalex-w7221083398:
Kentaro Shirakura and eight colleagues in Japan examined heart bypass surgery outcomes for patients whose leg arteries are severely diseased, in a 2026 study. They compared three groups among several hundred patients operated between 2014 and 2024. One group had chronic limb-threatening ischemia, the worst stage of leg artery disease. The others had milder disease, or none.

Short-term survival after surgery looked similar across groups. Five years on, the picture split sharply: under forty percent of the most severe group remained alive, against about nine in ten of the others. That group also carried far more diabetes and dialysis treatment. The authors urge individualized plans that weigh full repair against operative risk in these fragile patients.
petrie-religion-conscience-ancient-egypt:
W. M. Flinders Petrie traced the growth of faith in Religion and Conscience in Ancient Egypt, his talks of 1898. The talks were given at a great school in London. Petrie reads the faith from charms and beast gods up to one high God. Graves, hymns, and laws give him his proof at each step of the long climb.

He asks how a sense of right grew by that faith. His frame is of his age, yet his proofs are drawn from the soil. The book shows the dig chief as a thinker on faith. It fed wide thought then.
petrie-syria-egypt-amarna-1898:
W. M. Flinders Petrie gave English fans their first sum of a famed find in Syria and Egypt from the Tell el Amarna Letters, out in 1898. Work men had dug up clay notes at Amarna in Egypt. The notes are mail twixt kings of Egypt and chiefs of the East, writ in wedge script in the age of bronze.

Petrie sorts the mail by king, town, and theme. Plots, pleas, and threats of war crowd the notes. The book threw a new light on state craft of that age. It is the first door most fans took.
philippine-declaration-independence-1898:
On June 12, 1898, at Cavite-Viejo in the province of Cavite, the Philippine Declaration of Independence was proclaimed. Ambrosio Rianzares Bautista, war counsellor and special delegate, read it aloud under a decree of Emilio Aguinaldo, head of the dictatorial government. Military chiefs and town representatives stood witness.

The document rehearses Spain's abuses: arrests without cause, shootings by the Civil Guards, and unjust exile of noted Filipinos. It recalls the revolution of 1896 and the broken pact of Biak-na-Bato, then declares the islands free and independent, with all allegiance to Spain severed. The signers bound themselves to defend it with their lives, fortunes, and honor.
plaw-105-154-1998: Washington National Airport gained a new name under Public Law 105-154. The act was signed on February 6, 1998. The airport sits in the District of Columbia and Virginia. Its name is now the Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport. Named laws are amended to strike the old name. Parts of title 49 of the United States Code are among them. The new name goes in their place. Any other mention of the airport in federal law counts as the new name. Maps, rules, and records are covered too.
plaw-105-155-1998:
The FAA Research, Engineering, and Development Authorization Act of 1998 became Public Law 105-155 on February 11, 1998. It sets aviation research money for two years. The years are fiscal years 1998 and 1999. The money goes to the Federal Aviation Administration.

The first year gets more than two hundred twenty-six million dollars. The act splits the sum by project. System security technology and aircraft safety technology take the largest shares. More money goes to capacity and air traffic management. Human factors and aviation medicine are funded too. So are communications, navigation, weather work, and airport technology. The second year gets a slightly higher flat sum.
plaw-105-156-1998:
The Environmental Policy and Conflict Resolution Act of 1998 became Public Law 105-156 on February 11, 1998. It creates a standing federal center for environmental disputes. The center is the United States Institute for Environmental Conflict Resolution. It runs dispute work and training.

The act amends the Morris K. Udall act of 1992. That act covers scholarships and excellence in environmental policy. It also covers Native American public policy. The act writes new definitions into the Udall act. An environmental dispute is a fight over the environment, public lands, or natural resources. The fund in that act is renamed a trust fund. The institute sits inside the Udall foundation, not on its own.
plaw-105-157-1998: Public Law 105-157 dates from February 11, 1998. It lets one named ship sail in the coastwise trade. The ship is the PRINCE NOVA. Its Canadian registration number is 320804. The Secretary of Transportation may issue its papers. The papers carry the coastwise endorsement. The usual build and ownership rules do not bar the grant. Those rules sit in the Merchant Marine Act and title 46. The papers lapse on one condition. The ship must face work in a United States shipyard. The work may be conversion, repair, or rebuilding.
plaw-105-158-1998:
The Holocaust Victims Redress Act became Public Law 105-158 on February 13, 1998. It revisits assets the United States seized in the Second World War. Some of those assets had belonged to Holocaust victims. Restitution for them had fallen short.

Title I deals with heirless assets. About one hundred ninety-eight million dollars in German assets were seized. The finds included bank accounts, trusts, and securities. They were believed to belong to Jewish victims. About one point two billion dollars in Swiss assets were frozen too. Bank deposits made up over four hundred million of that. Congress had allowed up to three million dollars for survivor relief groups. But proof of ownership proved too hard. A lump-sum settlement followed in 1962.
plaw-105-159-1998:
Public Law 105-159 dates from February 25, 1998. Congress passed it over a presidential veto. It restores military construction projects the President had cut. The cuts came under the line item veto process. The President had sent them on October 6, 1997. They touched Public Law 105-45, the military construction funding act.

The restored items run from 97-4 to 97-41. That is thirty-eight items in all. The text carries the marks of a veto override. The House took up the bill returned with the President's objections. Two thirds of the House agreed to pass it. The Clerk certified the vote. The Speaker and the Senate's President pro tempore signed.
plaw-105-160-1998:
The National Sea Grant College Program Reauthorization Act of 1998 became Public Law 105-160 on March 6, 1998. It renews the Sea Grant program. The program backs university research on coasts and oceans. The act amends the National Sea Grant College Program Act.

The findings gain a new item. It urges work on forecast systems for coastal hazards. The act restates a judgment from the findings. Steady federal support is the most cost-effective way to run the program. Sea grant colleges and institutes do the work. More parts adjust definitions. Some wording for the program's leadership terms is made gender-neutral.
plaw-105-161-1998: Public Law 105-161, approved March 9, 1998, designates the United States Post Office building located at 750 Highway 28 East in Taylorsville, Mississippi, as the Blaine H. Eaton Post Office Building. Any reference in a law, map, regulation, document, paper, or other record of the United States to that post office building is deemed a reference to the Blaine H. Eaton Post Office Building.
plaw-105-162-1998:
A post office in Paterson, New Jersey, was named for a baseball pioneer by Public Law 105-162, approved March 9, 1998. The act designates the post office at 194 Ward Street as the Larry Doby Post Office.

The findings tell Doby's story: born in Camden, South Carolina, in 1923, he moved to Paterson in 1938 and played for the Newark Eagles of the Negro League in 1946. The Cleveland Indians bought his contract on July 3, 1947, and two days later he became the first African-American to play in the American League. Over thirteen seasons he played 1,533 games, batted .283 with 253 home runs, made seven all-star teams, and in 1948 became the first African-American to play in, and homer in, a World Series game.
plaw-105-163-1998: A federal building in Georgia gained a name under Public Law 105-163. The act was signed on March 20, 1998. The building stands at 475 Mulberry Street in Macon. It serves as a federal building and courthouse. Its name is now the William Augustus Bootle Federal Building and United States Courthouse. Any federal record that speaks of the building uses that name.
plaw-105-164-1998:
The Examination Parity and Year 2000 Readiness for Financial Institutions Act became Public Law 105-164 on March 20, 1998. It deals with the Year 2000 computer problem. It also extends exam parity to two regulators. They are the Director of the Office of Thrift Supervision and the National Credit Union Administration.

Congress found the date problem a serious risk to the economy. Thousands of banks and credit unions depend on computers. They use them for check clearing and direct deposit. They use them for accounting, cash machines, and card processing. Outside providers run many of those systems. So regulators needed exam power over the risk. Unready computers could threaten the safety of the whole system.
plaw-105-165-1998: A federal building in Atlanta gained a name under Public Law 105-165. The act was signed on March 20, 1998. The building stands at 61 Forsyth Street SW. Its name is now the Sam Nunn Atlanta Federal Center. Any federal record that speaks of the building uses that name. The act passed as S. 347.
plaw-105-166-1998:
The Lobbying Disclosure Technical Amendments Act of 1998 became Public Law 105-166 on April 6, 1998. It makes technical fixes to the Lobbying Disclosure Act of 1995.

One fix sharpens a cross-reference. It sits in the definition of a covered executive branch official. Another fix clarifies the lobbying contact exception. Contacts forced by a federal contract, grant, loan, permit, or license count. A group of governments acting together counts as a public official too. A later part adjusts estimates. Those estimates rest on the tax reporting system. The act passed as S. 758. It dates from the 105th Congress.
plaw-105-167-1998:
Public Law 105-167 dates from April 13, 1998. It joins scattered oil and gas rights into blocks. The land is the Little Missouri National Grasslands in Billings County, North Dakota. The act swaps federal and private mineral rights. The aim is better land management. It also guards nature and wildlife.

Burlington Resources Oil and Gas Company holds one side of the swap. Within forty-five days, it may convey all its oil and gas rights on the mapped lands. The map is the November 1995 exchange map. The Secretary of Agriculture then conveys the federal rights back to Burlington. Other owners get one hundred eighty days. They may make a like swap for the non-oil and gas rights.
plaw-105-168-1998:
The Birth Defects Prevention Act of 1998 became Public Law 105-168 on April 21, 1998. It backs surveillance, research, and services to prevent birth defects. The work runs through the Public Health Service Act.

Congress found birth defects the top cause of infant deaths. They cause one of every five such deaths. Some 150,000 infants are born with a serious defect each year. Some groups face higher rates. Hispanic-American infants face more neural tube defects. African-American infants face more sickle-cell anemia. The findings blame slow progress on missing facts. Outbreaks can go unseen when surveillance and research are weak and split up.
plaw-105-169-1998: Public Law 105-169 dates from April 24, 1998. It frees a tract of Texas land from a federal claim. The tract runs forty acres. A 1957 law had kept a reversionary interest for the government. The Secretary of State must release that interest. The land goes to two school districts. One is the Clint Independent School District. The other is the Fabens Independent School District. One condition binds the release. Any money from selling the land must serve public education.
plaw-105-170-1998:
The Aviation Medical Assistance Act of 1998 became Public Law 105-170 on April 24, 1998. It puts airline medical gear under review. The Federal Aviation Administration chief must recheck the gear in air carrier medical kits. The chief must also decide one question. Should automatic external defibrillators be required on board?

The review has a one-year deadline. The chief must recheck the rules on kit gear. The rules on flight attendant training in its use are also covered. Changes must be proposed if the review calls for them. Major carriers gain a duty too. For one year, they must try in good faith to collect death reports. The reports are quarterly. They cover deaths on their aircraft, with age and any known cause.
plaw-105-171-1998: Public Law 105-171, approved April 24, 1998, authorizes the Secretary of Agriculture to sell or exchange federal land in Virginia. About 368 acres of administrative sites and other tracts in the George Washington and Jefferson National Forests are covered, including parcels near the Natural Bridge Juvenile Corrections Center and in Alleghany County. The value received must be used to acquire a replacement site and build suitable improvements on it for national forest administrative purposes.
plaw-105-172-1998:
Cloning cell phone numbers to steal service was attacked by the Wireless Telephone Protection Act. Public Law 105-172, approved April 24, 1998, amends title 18 of the United States Code on scanning receivers and similar devices, inside the statute on fraud with counterfeit access devices.

The act makes it a crime, when done knowingly and with intent to defraud, to use, make, traffic in, or possess a scanning receiver. It likewise bans hardware or software known to be configured to insert or change the identifying information in a phone so the phone can obtain telecommunications service without authorization. The section then rewrites the penalties for offenses under the access device statute.
plaw-105-173-1998: Public Law 105-173 dates from April 27, 1998. It changes the visa waiver pilot program. The program sits in the Immigration and Nationality Act. It lets visitors from some states enter without a visa for short stays. The act modifies and extends the program. It also orders data collection. The data counts nonimmigrants who stay past their allowed time. The Attorney General sets that allowed time.
plaw-105-174-1998:
Mid-year military needs were topped up by the 1998 Supplemental Appropriations and Rescissions Act. Public Law 105-174, approved May 1, 1998, makes emergency supplemental appropriations for the fiscal year ending September 30, 1998, paired with rescissions of earlier funds.

Title I covers the Department of Defense. Its first chapter adds military personnel money: one hundred eighty-four million dollars more for the Army, over twenty-two million for the Navy, and about five million for the Marine Corps. Each amount is designated by Congress as an emergency requirement under the Balanced Budget and Emergency Deficit Control Act of 1985, the label that lets the spending bypass normal budget caps.
plaw-105-175-1998:
Public Law 105-175 is a joint resolution from May 11, 1998. It marks fifty years since the founding of the modern State of Israel. It states the sense of Congress on that anniversary. It reaffirms the bonds of friendship between the United States and Israel.

The clauses retell the path to statehood. The United Nations voted on November 29, 1947. It voted to partition the British Mandate of Palestine. Israel proclaimed its establishment on May 14, 1948. The United States granted full diplomatic ties. The clauses trace the wish for a Jewish homeland to the First Zionist Congress. Theodore Herzl led that congress a century before. Statehood followed the murder of more than six million European Jews. The text praises Israel's pluralistic democracy.
plaw-105-176-1998:
Public Law 105-176 dates from May 29, 1998. It gives the Secretary of the Treasury more freedom on coin design. The coins are the state quarters. The act amends title 31. The program is the ten-year 50 States Commemorative Coin Program.

One inscription is normally fixed to one side of the coin. The Secretary may now place it on the reverse instead. Other inscriptions may go on the obverse. The coin's value may go there too. Each state design can thus place its art and lettering where they fit best. The program honors each of the fifty states in turn.
plaw-105-177-1998:
Public Law 105-177 dates from June 1, 1998. It extends some programs under the Energy Policy and Conservation Act. The main move is a date change. The year 1997 becomes 1999 in the funding and end-date rules.

The act also updates the international energy program text. Old references to allocation and information give way to emergency response terms. Small wording fixes appear too. In one response rule, the word shall becomes may. The changes keep the programs alive for two more years. The act passed in the 105th Congress. It is a short extension act.
plaw-105-178-1998:
The big surface transportation law of its era was the Transportation Equity Act for the 21st Century, known as TEA-21. Public Law 105-178, approved June 9, 1998, authorizes funds for federal-aid highways, highway safety programs, and transit programs.

Title I covers federal-aid highways: authorizations and an obligation ceiling, apportionments among the states, a minimum guarantee of funding, revenue aligned budget authority, and the federal-aid systems themselves. Named programs include interstate maintenance, the surface transportation program, the highway bridge program, and the congestion mitigation and air quality improvement program. The act also sets the federal share of project costs and funds recreational trails, emergency relief, and federal lands highways.
plaw-105-179-1998: Public Law 105-179, approved June 16, 1998, redesignates the federal building located at 717 Madison Place, NW, in the District of Columbia. The building, previously known simply as the National Courts Building, becomes the Howard T. Markey National Courts Building. Any reference in a law, map, regulation, document, paper, or other record of the United States to that building is deemed a reference to it by the new name.
plaw-105-180-1998:
The Care for Police Survivors Act of 1998 became Public Law 105-180 on June 16, 1998. It amends the public safety officers' benefits part of a 1968 crime act. That act is the Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act.

The Director must spend at least one hundred fifty thousand dollars. The money comes from the part's funding. It maintains and improves peer support and counseling programs. The programs serve families of officers who died on duty. The Bureau may also spend funds on appeals. Those appeals cover death and disability claims. The act dates from the 105th Congress.
plaw-105-181-1998:
The Bulletproof Vest Partnership Grant Act of 1998 became Public Law 105-181 on June 16, 1998. It helps police buy body armor. The act sets up a matching grant program. State and local bodies get help with the cost of vests for their officers.

The act opens with findings and a statement of purpose. It then builds the grant machinery. The federal government shares the cost with the buyers. It does not pay the whole price. Such a design spreads limited funds across more places. It leaves the choice of gear with the local agencies. They know their officers' needs best.
plaw-105-182-1998: Public Law 105-182 dates from June 19, 1998. It extends the power to build a memorial to George Mason. Mason was a Virginia statesman. The Board of Regents of Gunston Hall holds that power. Under the Commemorative Works Act, such power lapses after a set span. This act sets the end date at August 10, 2000. The standard limit does not apply.
plaw-105-183-1998:
The Religious Liberty and Charitable Donation Protection Act of 1998 became Public Law 105-183 on June 19, 1998. It shields tithes and gifts made before bankruptcy from clawback. The act amends title 11 of the United States Code. That is the bankruptcy code.

The act defines a charitable contribution for this purpose. It is a gift that matches the tax code's definition. A natural person must make it. It must be cash or a financial instrument. The act also defines the groups that may receive one. A later part governs gifts made before the filing. It limits when a trustee can undo them as fraudulent transfers.
plaw-105-184-1998:
The Telemarketing Fraud Prevention Act of 1998 became Public Law 105-184 on June 23, 1998. It strengthens the criminal law on fraud against consumers. Phone scams are the target.

The act adds criminal forfeiture for telemarketing fraud. A court sentences a defendant for mail, wire, or bank fraud that involves telemarketing. The court must then order forfeiture. The property used in the crime is taken. The gross proceeds of the crime are taken too. Another part hardens the penalty rule. The word may becomes shall. The added punishment is now mandatory, not optional. The act works through the fraud and forfeiture parts of title 18.
plaw-105-185-1998:
The Agricultural Research, Extension, and Education Reform Act of 1998 became Public Law 105-185 on June 23, 1998. It refocuses farm research run with federal money. The work should address high-priority concerns. Those concerns may be national or multistate in scope.

Title I sets standards for federal funding. It sets a priority process. It sets tests of relevance and merit for the work. The Agriculture Department funds that work. Title I also covers formula funds. The funds serve the 1862 land-grant schools. They support research and extension work. Support for research facilities is covered too. Title II reforms older authorities. It starts with the Smith-Lever Act and the Hatch Act of 1887. It covers extension work by the 1862, 1890, and 1994 schools.
plaw-105-186-1998:
The U.S. Holocaust Assets Commission Act of 1998 became Public Law 105-186 on June 23, 1998. It creates a presidential panel on Holocaust-era property. The panel studies what became of such assets in the United States. The span runs before, during, and after the Second World War. It then recommends more action to the President.

The panel is the Presidential Advisory Commission on Holocaust Assets in the United States. It has twenty-one members. The President names eight private citizens. He also names four department representatives. The Speaker names two House members. The House minority leader names two more. The Senate majority leader names two senators. The Senate minority leader names two.
plaw-105-188-1998:
Public Law 105-188 dates from July 7, 1998. It allows mineral leasing of some Indian land by majority consent. The land sits in the Fort Berthold Indian Reservation in North Dakota. Such land is often split among many heirs.

The Secretary of the Interior may approve a mineral lease. The lease must touch individually owned Indian land. The owners of a majority of the undivided interest must consent. The Secretary must also find the deal in the owners' best interest. Once approved, the lease binds every owner. It binds even those who did not consent. The rule attacks the problem of parcels split among dozens of heirs.
plaw-105-189-1998:
Public Law 105-189 dates from July 14, 1998. It extends a construction deadline for one hydroelectric project. The project is in Washington. Its Federal Energy Regulatory Commission number is 8864.

The licensee must ask for the extension. The Commission must then grant it. The grant rests on the Federal Power Act tests. They are good faith, due diligence, and the public interest. The extension may run up to three two-year periods in a row. It starts when the earlier extension runs out. Sister acts of the same day did the same for other projects.
plaw-105-190-1998: Public Law 105-190, approved July 14, 1998, extends the construction deadline for a second Washington hydroelectric project, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission project number 9025, in the same form as its companion act. The Commission must allow up to three consecutive two-year extensions for beginning construction. If the project's license already expired before enactment, the Commission must reinstate it as of its expiration date and run the extensions from there.
plaw-105-191-1998: Public Law 105-191, approved July 14, 1998, extends the construction deadline for the AuSable Hydroelectric Project in New York, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission project number 10836-000NY. At the licensee's request and after reasonable notice, the Commission must extend the time to commence construction by up to three consecutive two-year periods under the Federal Power Act standards. An expired license is reinstated as of its expiration date, with the extensions running from that date.
plaw-105-192-1998:
Public Law 105-192 dates from July 14, 1998. It extends a construction deadline for one hydroelectric project. The project is the Bear Creek Hydroelectric Project in Washington. Its Federal Energy Regulatory Commission number is 10371.

The extension may run up to three two-year periods in a row. If the license had expired, it may be reinstated. The act also restores one sentence of the Federal Power Act. A 1996 act had deleted that sentence. The sentence limits how licenses end. They may be revoked only as the act prescribes. They may be altered or surrendered only by mutual agreement. Thirty days of public notice is required.
plaw-105-193-1998: Public Law 105-193, approved July 14, 1998, extends the deadline for a Washington hydroelectric project, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission project number 10359, in different terms from its companion acts. Rather than staged extensions, the Commission must let the licensee complete construction by May 4, 2004. The licensee must report on the project's status to the Commission every December 31 until construction is finished.
plaw-105-194-1998:
Food aid was carved out of nuclear-related sanctions by the Agriculture Export Relief Act of 1998. Public Law 105-194, approved July 14, 1998, amends the Arms Export Control Act, the statute whose sanctions cut off assistance to countries tied to nuclear weapons activity.

The act adds an exemption covering any credit, credit guarantee, or financial assistance from the Department of Agriculture that supports the purchase of food or other agricultural commodities. It also clarifies that agricultural commodities include fertilizer, and widens a neighboring exemption so it reaches medicines and medical equipment as well. The design keeps farm exports and humanitarian goods moving even when sanctions bite elsewhere.
plaw-105-195-1998:
Public Law 105-195 dates from July 16, 1998. It validates some land conveyances in Tulare, California. Tulare sits in Tulare County.

Congress found a title problem in the case. Railroad interests in rights-of-way can cloud local title. A city that wants to develop such land must clear the federal claim too. The Tulare Redevelopment Agency needed clear title. It needed the title to secure financing. The development was meant to bring jobs to an area of high unemployment. The act supplies the validation the agency needed. The validation is narrow and tied to the named conveyances.
plaw-105-196-1998:
The registry that matches bone marrow donors with patients was renewed by the National Bone Marrow Registry Reauthorization Act of 1998. Public Law 105-196, approved July 16, 1998, amends the Public Health Service Act to revise and extend the bone marrow donor program.

The act restates the registry's purpose as increasing the number of transplants for recipients suitably matched to biologically unrelated donors. It rebuilds the board of directors: members serve two-year terms, up to three in a row, with terms staggered so about a third expire each year. The board must include representatives of marrow donor centers and transplant centers, transplant recipients, people who need or have needed a transplant, and their family members.
plaw-105-197-1998:
The Occupational Safety and Health Administration Compliance Assistance Authorization Act of 1998 became Public Law 105-197 on July 16, 1998. It lets employers get safety advice without triggering an inspection.

The Secretary of Labor must set up a consultation program. The program runs with state officials. Employers may consult state staff on safety and health rules. They may also ask about voluntary steps toward safe workplaces. States give on-site advice at the worksite on request. They give other training too. Employee participation is built in. The act stresses one point. Consultation runs apart from enforcement. Asking for help stays separate from being cited.
plaw-105-198-1998:
Public Law 105-198 dates from July 16, 1998. It amends the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970. The act sets one rule about inspections.

The Secretary of Labor may not judge enforcement staff by citation counts. The number of citations issued may not be used. Penalties assessed may not be used either. Quotas or goals on enforcement results are barred. The point is to keep inspector performance judged on other grounds. Citation counts alone do not measure good work. The rule binds reviews by the Secretary's own staff. It dates from the 105th Congress.
plaw-105-199-1998: Public Law 105-199, approved July 16, 1998, establishes an advisory commission on drought, identified in the act's notes with national drought policy. Its stated purpose is to provide advice and recommendations on creating an integrated, coordinated federal policy designed to prepare for and respond to serious drought emergencies. The text sample held for this entry is cut short at the act's opening, so the commission's detailed membership and deadlines are not described here.
plaw-105-200-1998:
How states are rewarded and punished for running child support systems was rebuilt by the Child Support Performance and Incentive Act of 1998. Public Law 105-200, approved July 16, 1998, reforms federal incentive payments for effective child support performance.

Title I gives states an alternative penalty procedure when they miss federal data processing requirements, and lets the single statewide automated system requirement be waived. Title II replaces the incentive system with payments to states based on performance. Title III makes the penalty more flexible for states that violate the rules on adoptions across state lines, and a miscellaneous title follows.
plaw-105-201-1998:
Public Law 105-201 is a joint resolution from July 16, 1998. It approves the site of a Martin Luther King, Jr., Memorial. The memorial will stand in the nation's capital.

A 1996 act had authorized the memorial. The Alpha Phi Alpha Fraternity was to build it. But the chosen spot sits in Area I. That is the capital's most protected monumental zone. A spot there needed its own approval by law. The Secretary of the Interior had recommended the site. This resolution grants the approval. The 1996 act is the Omnibus Parks and Public Lands Management Act.
plaw-105-202-1998:
Public Law 105-202 dates from July 16, 1998. It does two unrelated things.

Part one extends the power to build the National Peace Garden memorial. The new end date is June 30, 2002. The usual Commemorative Works Act deadlines do not apply. Two earlier laws are set aside as well. Part two guards the wild horses of Cape Lookout National Seashore in North Carolina. The Secretary must allow a herd of one hundred free roaming horses there. Within one hundred eighty days, the Secretary must sign a contract. The partner is the Foundation for Shackleford Horses, or another fit nonprofit. The group manages the herd at low cost. It must not harm natural resources. Horses may be removed only on set terms. The group must first fail the deal's terms after notice and ninety days to respond.
plaw-105-203-1998:
The National Underground Railroad Network to Freedom Act of 1998 became Public Law 105-203 on July 21, 1998. It links sites where enslaved people sought freedom. The program sits inside the National Park Service.

Congress found the Underground Railroad a major part of the civil rights story. It flourished from the late eighteenth century to the end of the Civil War. It bridged race, religion, and borders. An earlier study had found gaps in the record. Only a few parts of the story stood in park units or other sites. Many sites faced imminent loss. Many resource types lacked protection.
plaw-105-204-1998:
Public Law 105-204 dates from July 21, 1998. It concerns leftover nuclear material from uranium enrichment. The material is depleted uranium hexafluoride. The Secretary of Energy must send Congress a plan.

The plan guards money on the books of the United States Enrichment Corporation. That money was accrued to dispose of the material. It must be used to treat and recycle the material instead. The plan goes in the President's fiscal year 2000 budget request. It must aim at starting construction by January 31, 2004. A treatment facility is planned at each of two plants. One is at Paducah, Kentucky. The other is at Portsmouth, Ohio. Until a year after the request, none of the money may be withdrawn. That bar holds despite the firm's privatization.
plaw-105-205-1998:
Public Law 105-205 dates from July 22, 1998. It gives divorce decrees power over federal life insurance payouts. The act amends chapter 87 of title 5. That chapter sets the order for paying federal employees' life insurance benefits.

A new part changes the order in one case. A sum may go to another person instead. A court decree must say so in express terms. The decree may be one of divorce, annulment, or legal separation. A court-approved property settlement also counts. The decree must reach the agency or retirement office before the death. The named person's share can change in two ways. The person may consent in writing. Or a court may modify the decree.
plaw-105-206-1998:
The Internal Revenue Service Restructuring and Reform Act of 1998 became Public Law 105-206 on July 22, 1998. It reorganizes the tax collector itself. The act amends the Internal Revenue Code of 1986.

Title I rebuilds the agency's structure and management. It directs a reorganization of the Service. It restates the mission to focus on taxpayers' needs. A subtitle covers executive branch governance and senior management. The act also waives some estimated tax penalties. No addition to tax applies to an underpayment of an installment. The installment must fall due within thirty days after enactment. The underpayment must stem from a rule of this very act.
plaw-105-207-1998:
The National Science Foundation Authorization Act of 1998 became Public Law 105-207 on July 29, 1998. It sets science funding for two years. The years are fiscal years 1998 and 1999. The money goes to the National Science Foundation.

The act first defines its terms. It defines the Director, the Foundation, and the National Science Board. It also defines a national research facility. Such a facility is funded by the Foundation. It is open under fair access rules. Scientists and engineers at research institutions across the country may use it. Title I then states findings and core strategies. The funding figures follow in the act.
plaw-105-208-1998: Public Law 105-208, approved July 29, 1998, facilitates the sale of federal land in the Tahoe National Forest to Placer County, California. The Secretary of Agriculture may sell the county about thirty-five acres, shown on an April 1997 map, so the county can create a community park in Squaw Valley. The county pays fair market value under federal appraisal standards, and the proceeds go into the Sisk Act fund for land acquisition. Existing non-federal uses and improvements on the parcel continue for the rest of their authorized terms.
plaw-105-209-1998:
Public Law 105-209 dates from July 29, 1998. It changes how Guam elects its delegate to the House. The delegate is now elected at large. A majority of the votes cast decides the race. The old separate ballot method is loosened.

A second part extends a program for island communities. The communities sit in the former United States trust territory. The program runs fifteen years instead of ten. The President must make sure the aid reflects population changes. Those changes are counted since the programs began. The act dates from the 105th Congress.
plaw-105-210-1998:
Public Law 105-210 dates from July 29, 1998. It makes a small change to a wilderness border in Missouri. The area is the Devils Backbone Wilderness. It sits in the Mark Twain National Forest.

About two acres leave the wilderness. The land lies in Ozark County. It holds a garage, a well, and a mailbox. It holds a driveway and other improvements too. A June 1996 map shows the new line. The Forest Service keeps the map with its maps and legal descriptions. The public may inspect it there. The change is minor and local in effect.
plaw-105-211-1998: Public Law 105-211, approved July 29, 1998, extends the construction deadline for Federal Energy Regulatory Commission project number 3862 in Iowa. The Commission may allow up to three consecutive two-year extensions of the time to begin construction, under the Federal Power Act's good faith, due diligence, and public interest standards. If the license already expired, it is reinstated as of the expiration date and the extensions run from there.
plaw-105-212-1998: Public Law 105-212, approved July 29, 1998, extends the construction deadline for Federal Energy Regulatory Commission project number 9248 in Colorado. The Commission must extend the time to begin construction until January 30, 2002, at the licensee's request. The act also reinstates the expired license of the Town of Telluride, Colorado, for the project, effective as of the license's expiration date.
plaw-105-213-1998: Public Law 105-213, approved July 29, 1998, extends the time allowed to build a hydroelectric project, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission project number 10395. The Commission must extend the period to commence construction by up to three consecutive two-year periods at the licensee's request, applying the Federal Power Act's standards. The act does not name the project's state in the text shown.
plaw-105-214-1998:
Public Law 105-214 dates from July 29, 1998. It trades debt relief for rainforest protection. The act amends the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961. It adds a part titled the Tropical Forest Conservation Act of 1998. Developing states with tropical forests may cut their debt by guarding those forests.

The findings call forest protection settled United States policy. The forests hold a major share of the Earth's biological wealth. That wealth is the raw material for new medicines and better crops. The forests also serve as carbon sinks. They moderate climate change. They regulate the water cycles that far-off farms and coasts rely on. Yet deforestation went on fast despite a decade of world programs.
plaw-105-215-1998:
Congress's gold medal was presented to Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela under Public Law 105-215, approved July 29, 1998. The act directs the presentation of a congressional gold medal to the South African leader.

The findings honor Mandela for a lifetime spent abolishing apartheid and building democracy in South Africa, at the cost of his own freedom. Imprisoned for nearly thirty years, he never compromised his principles, taught other prisoners, and refused freedom offered in exchange for renouncing his beliefs. After release he was elected and inaugurated as State President on May 10, 1994, at seventy-five, then turned to reconciliation through the Truth and Reconciliation Commission chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu. The act also recognizes American student Amy Biehl, killed in the struggle, and her parents' forgiveness.
plaw-105-216-1998:
The Homeowners Protection Act of 1998 became Public Law 105-216 on July 29, 1998. It lets home buyers drop private mortgage cover once they have paid down enough of the loan. Lenders demand that cover on many home loans.

The act makes the cover end on its own at a set point. It also makes lenders tell buyers of their right to end it sooner. Its parts cover notice at the start of the loan. They cover notice when the cover ends. Lender-paid cover gets special notice rules. Fees for notices are covered. Civil suits and enforcement are covered too. The act also ends the Thrift Depositor Protection Oversight Board.
plaw-105-217-1998: Public Law 105-217 is the African Elephant Conservation Reauthorization Act of 1998. It was signed on August 5, 1998. It renews the African Elephant Conservation Act. The act makes a single change. It extends the funding rule in section 2306 of that act. The old range of years ended in 1998. The new range runs from fiscal year 1997 through fiscal year 2002. Nothing else in the base act changes. The renewal keeps the elephant protection program funded for five more years.
plaw-105-218-1998: Public Law 105-218, approved August 7, 1998, designates the United States courthouse to be constructed at the corner of Superior and Huron Roads in Cleveland, Ohio, as the Carl B. Stokes United States Courthouse. Any reference in a law, map, regulation, document, paper, or other record of the United States to that courthouse is deemed a reference to the Carl B. Stokes United States Courthouse.
plaw-105-219-1998:
The Credit Union Membership Access Act became Public Law 105-219 on August 7, 1998. It widens who may join a credit union. It pairs that wider access with tighter oversight. The act amends the Federal Credit Union Act. Its aims are to clarify membership law and to guard the purpose of federal credit unions.

Title I governs membership itself. It sets fields of membership. It sets tests for wider reach by multiple common-bond credit unions. It sets geographic rules for community credit unions. Title II turns to regulation. It covers audits and financial statements. It covers conversions of insured credit unions. It limits member business loans. It covers the National Credit Union Administration Board. Title III addresses capitalization and net worth. It starts with prompt corrective action.
plaw-105-220-1998:
Enacted on August 7, 1998, the Workforce Investment Act of 1998 is Public Law 105-220 from the 105th Congress. Its stated aim is to consolidate, coordinate, and improve employment, training, literacy, and vocational rehabilitation programs across the United States. The opening titles set up a new workforce investment system built around state and local boards.

Inside, the law defines the programs it covers and requires state workforce investment boards and state plans. It then provides for local workforce investment areas, local boards, and local plans. Readers get the framework Congress chose to replace scattered job training programs with a single state and local system.
plaw-105-221-1998: The Amy Somers Volunteers at Food Banks Act, Public Law 105-221, was approved on August 7, 1998. It makes one narrow change to the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938. People who volunteer solely for humanitarian purposes at a private nonprofit food bank, and who receive groceries from that food bank, are not counted as employees under the act. The whole law is that single added paragraph.
plaw-105-222-1998: Public Law 105-222, approved August 7, 1998, names an auditorium in Albuquerque, New Mexico, for Congressman Steve Schiff. The law first records findings about Schiff, who represented New Mexico's First District from 1988 to 1998 and chaired a science subcommittee. It then designates the auditorium inside the Sandia Technology Transfer Center, known as Building 825, as the Steve Schiff Auditorium, and says later references must use that name.
plaw-105-223-1998: Approved August 7, 1998, Public Law 105-223 creates a memorial fund in the United States Treasury for two fallen Capitol Police officers. Money given to the Capitol Police Board for the United States Capitol Police Memorial Fund is deposited there and paid out in equal halves. Fifty percent goes to the widow and children of Detective John Michael Gibson, and fifty percent to the widow and children of Private First Class Jacob Joseph Chestnut.
plaw-105-224-1998: Land in two New Mexico national forests is the subject of Public Law 105-224, approved August 12, 1998. The Secretary of Agriculture must convey small parcels from the Carson National Forest and the Santa Fe National Forest to the village of El Rito and the town of Jemez Springs. For Jemez Springs the sample describes about one acre in Sandoval County. The exact size is set by a survey the town pays for. Payment terms and an indemnity agreement are also attached.
plaw-105-225-1998:
On August 12, 1998, Congress gathered scattered permanent laws into one title of the United States Code. Public Law 105-225 revises and codifies those laws, without substantive change, as title 36. The full title is Patriotic and National Observances, Ceremonies, and Organizations.

Title 36 opens with rules on the national anthem, motto, floral emblem, and march. It also covers presidential inaugural ceremonies and federal help for the Carl Garner Federal Lands Cleanup Day. Later parts list the chartered groups the title governs. One part covers treaty duty groups, starting at section 300101 in the sample's table. The law makes no new policy. It puts old law in one clear place.
plaw-105-226-1998: The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Authorization Act of 1998 is Public Law 105-226, approved August 12, 1998. It amends the John F. Kennedy Center Act to authorize appropriations for the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts and to further define the criteria for capital repair and operation and maintenance. The center must plan and carry out capital repairs needed to keep its building and site safe, secure, and accessible. It must also handle maintenance, janitorial work, and security to a high standard.
plaw-105-227-1998: A short amendment for the District of Columbia is Public Law 105-227, approved August 12, 1998. It revises the District of Columbia Convention Center and Sports Arena Authorization Act of 1995, changing which revenues and activities that act covers. The new language frees spending of Washington Convention Center Authority revenues from one limit in the District's Home Rule Act, while leaving the Home Rule Act's revenue bond rules untouched. A waiver of congressional review follows.
plaw-105-228-1998: Farmers facing a hard year are the focus of the Emergency Farm Financial Relief Act, Public Law 105-228, approved August 12, 1998. The law amends the Agricultural Market Transition Act with a special rule for fiscal year 1999. At the choice of the owner or producer, the Secretary of Agriculture must pay the full contract payment for that year, or any part the producer names. The producer also specifies the time or times of payment.
plaw-105-229-1998: Wild horses at Cape Lookout National Seashore in North Carolina are protected by Public Law 105-229, approved August 13, 1998. It amends the 1966 law that created the seashore and directs the Secretary to allow a herd of 100 free roaming horses there. Within 180 days the Secretary must reach an agreement with the Foundation for Shackleford Horses, or another qualified nonprofit, to manage the horses in a cost-effective way without harming natural resources.
plaw-105-230-1998:
Congress passed the Biomaterials Access Assurance Act of 1998 as Public Law 105-230, approved August 13, 1998. The law sets rules for product liability cases against suppliers of raw materials and bulk components used by medical device makers. Its findings stress that millions of Americans depend on lifesaving or life-enhancing devices, many of them implanted in the body.

Those findings also note that most device materials move in interstate commerce, were not designed only for medical use, and reach device makers in very small amounts. Sales for medical devices are a tiny share of the overall market for the same materials. The act responds to that supply problem by limiting when a biomaterials supplier can be held liable.
plaw-105-231-1998:
A federal charter for a veterans organization is granted by Public Law 105-231, approved August 13, 1998. The American GI Forum of the United States, a nonprofit corporation organized under Texas law, is recognized and chartered. The forum keeps only the powers given in its own bylaws and articles of incorporation, under Texas law.

The stated purposes include securing the blessings of American democracy for all citizens and upholding the Constitution and the flag. The forum also works for equal educational, economic, and political opportunity and equal justice under the law, regardless of race, color, religion, sex, or national origin. The charter turns those aims into the group's formal federal standing.
plaw-105-232-1998: Public Law 105-232, approved August 13, 1998, gives a new name to a federal building in Columbus, Ohio. The federal building and United States courthouse at 85 Marconi Boulevard must be known as the Joseph P. Kinneary United States Courthouse. The law adds that any reference in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or other record to that building counts as a reference to the Joseph P. Kinneary United States Courthouse.
plaw-105-233-1998: Volunteers at the Supreme Court are covered by Public Law 105-233, approved August 13, 1998. It amends title 28 of the United States Code. With the Chief Justice's approval, the Administrative Assistant to the Chief Justice may accept voluntary personal services to help with public and visitor programs. Volunteers must first waive claims against the United States in writing. Accepting their help must not cut the pay of, or displace, any Supreme Court employee.
plaw-105-234-1998: Aircraft fasteners get a narrow exemption in Public Law 105-234, approved August 14, 1998. It amends the Fastener Quality Act. Its requirements do not apply to fasteners made or altered for use on an aircraft, when the Federal Aviation Administration has approved their quality and suitability. The exemption fails if the maker claims the fasteners meet a consensus or other federal standard. The law also delays Fastener Quality Act regulations until after June 1, 1999, at the earliest.
plaw-105-235-1998:
Iraq's defiance of the United Nations is the subject of a joint resolution enacted as Public Law 105-235 on August 14, 1998. Congress finds the Government of Iraq in unacceptable and material breach of its international obligations. The text recalls that fighting in Operation Desert Storm ended on February 28, 1991, and that cease-fire terms were set by Security Council resolutions.

One resolution required sanctions to stay in place until Iraq disclosed and destroyed its weapons of mass destruction programs and promised never to resume them. A special commission and the International Atomic Energy Agency were charged with finding and removing those weapons. Congress states that Iraq hid its programs, filed false declarations, and obstructed inspectors for seven years.
plaw-105-236-1998:
Consent for a three-state waste agreement is given in the Texas Low-Level Radioactive Waste Disposal Compact Consent Act, Public Law 105-236, approved September 20, 1998. Congress finds that the compact serves the Low-Level Radioactive Waste Policy Act. The sample names Texas in the title and Maine and Vermont in its notes as the states tied to the compact.

Consent takes effect on enactment and lasts only while the regional commission created by the compact follows that policy act. Congress also reserves the right to alter, amend, or repeal its consent after the first ten years, and at intervals the compact allows after that. The full compact text is set out in the law itself.
plaw-105-237-1998:
Money for military building in fiscal year 1999 is provided by the Military Construction Appropriations Act, 1999, Public Law 105-237, approved September 20, 1998. The law funds military construction, family housing, and base realignment and closure work run by the Department of Defense for the year ending September 30, 1999.

For Army military construction alone it provides about eight hundred sixty-nine million dollars, available until September 30, 2003. That money covers buying land, building and equipping permanent and temporary works, and paying Army Corps of Engineers staff. Up to about sixty-four million dollars of it may pay for study, planning, design, and engineering services, unless the Secretary of Defense gives notice that more is needed.
plaw-105-238-1998: Public Law 105-238, approved September 23, 1998, moves about eighty-eight acres in Washington state from one federal manager to another. The boundary of the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area is redrawn to exclude the parcel of land and waters, and the boundary of the Wenatchee National Forest is redrawn to include it. Administrative jurisdiction passes from the Secretary of the Interior to the Secretary of Agriculture. The map behind the change is kept open for public inspection.
plaw-105-239-1998: Two fish facilities in Alabama change owners under Public Law 105-239, approved September 23, 1998. Within 180 days, the Secretary of the Interior must convey the Marion National Fish Hatchery and the Claude Harris National Aquacultural Research Center to the State of Alabama, without payment. The state's Game and Fish Division will use the sites in its fish culture program. As one condition, the division must offer to lease the research center to the Alabama Agriculture Experiment Station.
plaw-105-240-1998: Short-term funding to keep the government running is provided by Public Law 105-240, a joint resolution approved September 25, 1998. It makes continuing appropriations for fiscal year 1999 for departments, agencies, and other units of government. Projects and activities carried on in fiscal year 1998 may continue under the authority and conditions of the 1998 appropriations acts, at the amounts needed, until the regular 1999 acts take over. The sample lists agriculture, commerce, justice, and state programs among those covered.
plaw-105-241-1998: Postal workers gain the same safety law coverage as other workers under the Postal Employees Safety Enhancement Act, Public Law 105-241, approved September 28, 1998. The law makes the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 apply to the United States Postal Service in the same manner as to any other employer. It does so by removing the Postal Service from the federal agency sections and placing it under the general employer rules. Rules on closing post offices are also restated.
plaw-105-242-1998:
Volunteers and local partners for wildlife refuges are encouraged by Public Law 105-242, approved October 5, 1998. Its full name is the National Wildlife Refuge System Volunteer and Community Partnership Enhancement Act of 1998. It amends the Fish and Wildlife Act of 1956 to promote volunteer programs and community partnerships for national wildlife refuges.

Congress found that the refuge system held more than 500 refuges and ninety-three million acres, yet money to run it stayed limited. By drawing in volunteers, donations, and non-federal partners, federal funds could be stretched further. The law also backs refuge education programs, so public awareness of the system and its wildlife could grow alongside the hands-on help.
plaw-105-243-1998:
One of the darkest episodes in Colorado history is examined in the Sand Creek Massacre National Historic Site Study Act of 1998, Public Law 105-243, approved October 6, 1998. The law orders the Secretary of the Interior to study whether the Sand Creek site should become a unit of the National Park System.

Its findings recount November 29, 1864, when Colonel John M Chivington led 700 armed soldiers against a peaceful Cheyenne village on Sand Creek. Several hundred people in Chief Black Kettle's village were killed, most of them women and children. Congress notes the attack was condemned at the time, and that reparations promised in the 1865 Treaty of Little Arkansas were never fulfilled.
plaw-105-244-1998:
Federal college programs are renewed in the Higher Education Amendments of 1998, Public Law 105-244, approved October 7, 1998. The law extends the authorization of programs under the Higher Education Act of 1965. Its table of contents shows titles on general provisions, teacher quality, institutional aid, and student assistance.

Title II creates teacher quality enhancement grants. Title III covers strengthening institutions, aid for historically Black colleges and universities, endowment challenge grants, and capital financing for those schools, plus a minority science and engineering program. Title IV turns to student help, beginning with Federal Pell Grants. Together the titles set the shape of federal higher education aid for the next period.
plaw-105-245-1998:
Rivers, harbors, and energy work for fiscal year 1999 are funded by the Energy and Water Development Appropriations Act, 1999, Public Law 105-245, approved October 7, 1998. Title I covers the civil side of the Department of the Army, where the Corps of Engineers works under the Secretary of the Army and the Chief of Engineers.

For general investigations the law provides more than one hundred sixty-one million dollars, to stay available until spent. That money pays for studies of river and harbor, flood control, and shore protection projects, and for surveys and plans before construction. Small named sums follow for single sites, such as the Delaware Bay coastline and Tampa Harbor in Florida.
plaw-105-246-1998:
Hidden federal files on Nazi war criminals must be opened under the Nazi War Crimes Disclosure Act, Public Law 105-246, approved October 8, 1998. The law amends the Freedom of Information Act rules and the National Security Act of 1947.
