It requires disclosure of records about certain persons, without impairing a Justice Department investigation or prosecution, or certain intelligence matters.

Within sixty days the President must set up a Nazi War Criminal Records Interagency Working Group, to last three years. The President appoints its members, who are chosen under the act's own rules. The group is the engine for finding, reviewing, and releasing the records the law defines, so the public record on Nazi war criminals can be filled in from government files.
plaw-105-247-1998: Only two words change in Public Law 105-247, approved October 9, 1998. The law corrects a provision in title 5 of the United States Code about ending benefits for convicted persons. In section 8148(a) it strikes the phrase a receipt and inserts the phrase or receipt instead. That tiny edit is the entire act, passed after reports from House and Senate committees in the spring and fall of 1998.
plaw-105-248-1998: Breast cancer screening quality is the subject of the Mammography Quality Standards Reauthorization Act of 1998, Public Law 105-248, approved October 9, 1998. It amends the Public Health Service Act to revise and extend the federal mammography quality standards program. Funding authorization dates move from 1997 to 2002, with small wording fixes elsewhere. Later sections deal with which version of appeal regulations applies and with accreditation standards, including a change from practicing physicians to review physicians.
plaw-105-249-1998: Three extra days of stopgap funding are granted by Public Law 105-249, a joint resolution approved October 9, 1998. It makes further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 1999 by editing the earlier stopgap law, Public Law 105-240. In section 106(c) of that law, the date October 9, 1998 is struck and October 12, 1998 is put in its place. The resolution passed the House and Senate on the same day it was approved.
plaw-105-250-1998: In New Haven, Connecticut, a courthouse takes a new name under Public Law 105-250, approved October 9, 1998. The United States courthouse at 141 Church Street must be known and designated as the Richard C Lee United States Courthouse. As with other naming laws, any later reference in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or record to that courthouse counts as a reference under its new Richard C Lee name.
plaw-105-251-1998:
Sharing criminal records across state lines is improved by Public Law 105-251, approved October 9, 1998. The act aims to improve interstate criminal justice identification, information, communications, and forensics. Title I is the Crime Identification Technology Act of 1998, with a state grant program for criminal justice identification, information, and communication.

Title II is the National Criminal History Access and Child Protection Act. Its first subtitle covers exchange of criminal history records for noncriminal justice purposes, with findings, definitions, and federal consent. It also enacts the National Crime Prevention and Privacy Compact, whose opening articles set out definitions and purposes. The structure shows a push to link state systems while guarding privacy.
plaw-105-252-1998: A Commerce Department business report keeps going under Public Law 105-252, approved October 9, 1998. The law extends the quarterly financial report program run by the Secretary of Commerce. That program had been moved from the Federal Trade Commission to the Secretary by a 1983 act. In that act's section 4(b), the end date September 30, 1998 is struck and September 30, 2005 is inserted, giving the program seven more years.
plaw-105-253-1998: Paperwork rules for money bills are waived by Public Law 105-253, a joint resolution approved October 12, 1998. For the rest of the 105th Congress, sections 106 and 107 of title 1 are waived for any bill or joint resolution making general or continuing appropriations for fiscal year 1999. The waiver covers printing the enrollment on parchment or otherwise. Instead, the enrollment counts when the House Oversight Committee certifies it as a true enrollment.
plaw-105-254-1998: Two more days are added to a funding deadline by Public Law 105-254, a joint resolution approved October 12, 1998. It again edits section 106(c) of the stopgap law Public Law 105-240, which first set continuing appropriations for fiscal year 1999. The date October 12, 1998, itself set only days earlier, is struck, and October 14, 1998 takes its place. Both chambers passed the measure on the day it was approved.
plaw-105-255-1998:
Women and minorities in science get a dedicated study body in Public Law 105-255, approved October 14, 1998. The act creates the Commission on the Advancement of Women and Minorities in Science, Engineering, and Technology Development. Its findings draw on a 1996 National Science Foundation report on women, minorities, and persons with disabilities in science and engineering.

Congress found that women had long been underrepresented in science and engineering jobs, even after decades of progress. Female and minority students took fewer advanced math and science courses in high school and earned fewer science degrees. Among degree holders, women were less likely to work full time or in their field, and women with doctorates were far more likely to teach at two-year schools than at research universities.
plaw-105-256-1998: Technical fixes to laws about Native Americans fill Public Law 105-256, approved October 14, 1998. One fix allows ninety-nine year leases for lands held in trust for the Confederated Tribes of the Grand Ronde Community of Oregon. It also adds the Cabazon Indian Reservation to the same long lease language. Another fix raises the Grand Ronde Reservation figure from about ten thousand one hundred twenty acres to about ten thousand three hundred twelve acres. It also rewrites the land table that follows.
plaw-105-257-1998: Public Law 105-257, a joint resolution approved October 14, 1998, pushes a stopgap funding cutoff from October 14 to October 16, 1998. It is the third short edit in a row to section 106(c) of Public Law 105-240, the original continuing appropriations measure for fiscal year 1999. Each edit bought Congress a few more days to finish the regular spending bills. The House and Senate both passed this two-day extension on October 14 itself.
plaw-105-258-1998:
Competition in ocean shipping is the goal of the Ocean Shipping Reform Act of 1998, Public Law 105-258, approved October 14, 1998. The law amends the Shipping Act of 1984 to encourage competition in international shipping and growth of United States exports. Most of it takes effect on May 1, 1999, unless a section says otherwise.

Title I rewrites the 1984 act. Its purpose clause gains a new aim: to promote United States exports through competitive and efficient ocean transportation, with greater reliance on the marketplace. Definitions are then revised, starting with carrier and deferred rebate language. The changes move federal shipping rules away from close rate control and toward market pricing for cargo moving by sea.
plaw-105-259-1998: A deadline for tracking who enters and leaves the country is moved by Public Law 105-259, approved October 15, 1998. The law extends the date by which an automated entry-exit control system must be developed. It amends section 110 of division C of Public Law 104-208, striking the phrase about two years after enactment and inserting the date October 15, 1998 instead. That single substitution is the whole act.
plaw-105-260-1998: Four days, rather than two, are bought by Public Law 105-260, a joint resolution approved October 16, 1998. It makes the fourth short change to the fiscal year 1999 stopgap in Public Law 105-240, moving the date in section 106(c) from October 16, 1998 to October 20, 1998. The series of brief extensions shows Congress and the White House still short of final spending deals well into the new fiscal year.
plaw-105-261-1998:
Defense programs for fiscal year 1999 are authorized by the Strom Thurmond National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 1999, Public Law 105-261, approved October 17, 1998. The law authorizes appropriations for military activities of the Department of Defense, for military construction, and for defense activities of the Department of Energy. It also prescribes personnel strengths for the armed forces for that year.

Unusually, the opening findings honor the senator the act is named for. Congress notes that Strom Thurmond of South Carolina joined the Senate Armed Services Committee on January 19, 1959, and served there for most of its postwar life. It recalls his commission as a reserve infantry officer in 1924 and his distinguished combat service with the First Army in Europe.
plaw-105-262-1998:
Pay and operations for the armed forces in fiscal year 1999 are funded by the Department of Defense Appropriations Act, 1999, Public Law 105-262, approved October 17, 1998. The money comes from the Treasury for military functions run by the Department of Defense for the year ending September 30, 1999. Title I is military personnel.

For Army personnel alone the act gives more than twenty billion dollars. That sum covers pay, allowances, clothing, food, interest on deposits, gratuities, and travel for permanent changes of station and temporary duty. It also pays cadets and aviation cadets, and covers payments owed to the Department of Defense Military Retirement Fund and under the Social Security Act. Navy personnel funding follows.
plaw-105-263-1998:
Federal land around fast-growing Las Vegas is rearranged by the Southern Nevada Public Land Management Act of 1998, Public Law 105-263, approved October 19, 1998. The law provides for the orderly disposal of certain federal lands in Clark County, Nevada, and for buying environmentally sensitive lands elsewhere in the state.

Congress found that the Bureau of Land Management owned many small and large parcels mixed in with private land in the Las Vegas Valley, making them hard to manage. Some should be sold, based on advice from local government and the public, to allow orderly growth. Growth was also pressing on Lake Mead, Red Rock Canyon, and the Spring Mountains recreation areas nearby.
plaw-105-264-1998:
How federal workers pay for official trips changes under the Travel and Transportation Reform Act of 1998, Public Law 105-264, approved October 19, 1998. The law requires federal employees to use federal travel charge cards for all payments for official government travel. It also amends title 31 to require prepayment audits of agency transportation expenses.

Other parts let agencies repay employees for taxes owed on travel or transportation reimbursements, and allow test programs for paying travel and relocation costs. The card rule itself is set by the Administrator of General Services, after consulting the Secretary of the Treasury. The Administrator may exempt a payment, person, or class when an exemption serves the government's best interest.
plaw-105-265-1998:
Restoration work in the Great Lakes Basin is carried forward by the Great Lakes Fish and Wildlife Restoration Act of 1998, Public Law 105-265, approved October 19, 1998. The law amends the 1990 act of the same name. It provides for carrying out recommendations from the United States Fish and Wildlife Service in its Great Lakes Fishery Resources Restoration Study.

Congress found that the study, reported in 1995, was a full review of the status and restoration needs of Great Lakes fishery resources. It was done jointly by the Fish and Wildlife Service, state agencies, Indian tribes, and the Great Lakes Fishery Commission. The study found real progress toward a healthy fish community, but it also called for more action, better coordination, and funding for steps not yet paid for.
plaw-105-266-1998: Unfit health care providers in the federal workers' health plan are targeted by the Federal Employees Health Care Protection Act of 1998, Public Law 105-266, approved October 19, 1998. It amends title 5 to improve sanctions under the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program. The Office of Personnel Management must, not merely may, bar certain providers, including any provider already debarred or suspended from a federal activity. The law also defines should know as acting in deliberate ignorance or reckless disregard, with no proof of intent to defraud required.
plaw-105-267-1998:
North of Yellowstone National Park, land ownership is reshaped by the Gallatin Land Consolidation Act of 1998, Public Law 105-267, approved October 19, 1998. The Secretaries of Agriculture and the Interior are directed to exchange land and other assets with Big Sky Lumber Co. and other entities in Montana.

Congress found that land north of Yellowstone holds outstanding natural features and wildlife habitat worth adding to the National Forest System. A cleaner ownership pattern for the Gallatin National Forest would cut long-term taxpayer costs and improve public access. The definitions describe about two thousand acres of Bureau of Land Management land tied to an option agreement for buying Big Sky Lumber land.
plaw-105-268-1998: Commemorative coins for the Library of Congress bicentennial are ordered by Public Law 105-268, approved October 19, 1998. The Secretary of the Treasury must mint no more than one hundred thousand five-dollar gold coins and no more than five hundred thousand one-dollar silver coins, each ninety percent precious metal. Instead of the gold coins, the Secretary may issue up to two hundred thousand ten-dollar bimetallic coins of gold and platinum. All coins minted under the act are legal tender.
plaw-105-269-1998: Duck stamp money may be spent to sell more duck stamps under the Migratory Bird Hunting and Conservation Stamp Promotion Act, Public Law 105-269, approved October 19, 1998. The Secretary of the Interior may use stamp sale receipts to promote added sales. The cap is one million dollars in each of fiscal years 1999 through 2003. Promotion follows a marketing plan approved by the Migratory Bird Conservation Commission and may include reports and brochures telling the public how stamp sales benefit wildlife.
plaw-105-270-1998:
Agencies must list work that private business could do, under the Federal Activities Inventory Reform Act of 1998, Public Law 105-270, approved October 19, 1998. The act sets a process for finding federal functions that are not inherently governmental. Agency heads do the judging for their own agencies.

By the end of the third quarter of each fiscal year. By then, each agency head must send the Office of Management and Budget a list of activities federal sources perform that are not inherently governmental. Each entry gives the year the activity first appeared and the number of full-time workers needed for it. An entry also names a federal employee who can give more information about the activity. The budget office then reviews the lists.
plaw-105-271-1998:
Fear that computers would fail at the year 2000 sits behind the Year 2000 Information and Readiness Disclosure Act, Public Law 105-271, approved October 19, 1998. The law encourages sharing information about computer problems, solutions, and test practices tied to the changeover. Its findings describe systems that could not read dates in 2000.

Congress found that thousands, possibly millions, of systems, programs, and chips would read a year 2000 date as 1900 or fail to process it at all. Such failures could cripple markets, commerce, utilities, government, and safety and defense systems worldwide. Fixing systems in time was a national and global concern, and prompt, candid sharing of readiness information would help entities judge and solve their own risks.
plaw-105-272-1998:
Spy agencies receive their fiscal year 1999 authority in the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 1999, Public Law 105-272, approved October 20, 1998. It authorizes appropriations for intelligence and intelligence-related activities of the United States Government. The same titles cover the Community Management Account and the Central Intelligence Agency Retirement and Disability System.

Title I authorizes the main intelligence spending, a classified schedule of authorizations, and personnel ceiling adjustments. It also funds the Community Management Account and allows emergency supplemental money for fiscal year 1998. Later titles fund the CIA retirement system and set general rules, including limits on intelligence activities, a one-year extension for sanctions laws, and changes to the national security education program.
plaw-105-273-1998: One single day is added by Public Law 105-273, a joint resolution approved October 20, 1998. It makes a fifth brief change to section 106(c) of Public Law 105-240, the continuing appropriations law for fiscal year 1999. October 20, 1998 is struck and October 21, 1998 is inserted. The House passed the measure on October 19 and the Senate on October 20, showing the funding talks were being extended almost hour by hour.
plaw-105-274-1998: Court pension rules in the District are cleaned up by Public Law 105-274, approved October 21, 1998. Its name is the District of Columbia Courts and Justice Technical Corrections Act of 1998. It fixes the National Capital Revitalization and Self-Government Improvement Act of 1997 for District courts. Early sections fix the judges' pension plan and the fund behind it. Trustees and actuaries chosen by the Secretary may hire help. With approval, they may subcontract with the District government or with others for services.
plaw-105-275-1998:
Congress pays for itself in the Legislative Branch Appropriations Act, 1999, Public Law 105-275, approved October 21, 1998. The text is marked as a corrected print, with the word President added in one section. Title I, called the Congressional Operations Appropriations Act, 1999, funds the Senate and House for the year ending September 30, 1999.

The Senate section opens with expense allowances of ten thousand dollars each for the Vice President, the President Pro Tempore, and the majority and minority leaders. Whips receive five thousand dollars each, and conference committee chairmen three thousand dollars each, for a total of fifty-six thousand dollars. Representation allowances for the two Senate leaders add fifteen thousand dollars each. Salaries for officers and employees follow.
plaw-105-276-1998:
Veterans and housing programs share one spending law in Public Law 105-276, approved October 21, 1998. Its full scope covers the Departments of Veterans Affairs and Housing and Urban Development, plus independent agencies and boards. All funding is for the fiscal year ending September 30, 1999.

Title I is the veterans department. Its benefits office pays compensation to veterans and funds a pilot program for disability exams. The same account covers pensions, burial payments, and officers' retirement pay. It also pays premiums on life policies backed under the Soldiers' and Sailors' Civil Relief Act of 1940. Later titles turn to housing and the other agencies.
plaw-105-277-1998:
A giant package of spending bills was enacted at once as Public Law 105-277, approved October 21, 1998. The sample gives its true short title as the Omnibus Consolidated and Emergency Supplemental Appropriations Act, 1999, for the year ending September 30, 1999. Division A is the omnibus consolidated appropriations part, joining several regular bills into one law.

Section 101 provides money as if each named bill had been enacted on its own. First among them is the Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 1999. Its opening title funds agricultural programs, starting with the Office of the Secretary of Agriculture. That office receives a stated sum for necessary expenses, with a small capped amount for outside employment help.
plaw-105-278-1998:
Charter schools get more federal support from the Charter School Expansion Act of 1998, Public Law 105-278, approved October 22, 1998. The law amends titles VI and X of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965 to improve and expand charter schools. Grants are a central tool in the text.

In title VI, planning, designing, and starting charter schools is added as a supported use, both in the program purposes and in the local uses of funds. Title X then revises the charter school purpose language itself. By naming startup work in two places, the amendments let federal education money flow to new charter schools during their planning and first implementation, not only after they are running.
plaw-105-279-1998:
A volcano monument in Washington state is completed on paper by the Mount St. Helens National Volcanic Monument Completion Act, Public Law 105-279, approved October 23, 1998. The law speeds the buying of private mineral interests inside the monument. That purchase was required by the 1982 act that created the Mount St. Helens National Volcanic Monument.

Congress found that the 1982 act told the Secretary of Agriculture to acquire surface interests and mineral and geothermal interests through separate exchanges. The surface exchange was finished on time, with dates in late 1982 and 1983 named as targets. The mineral and geothermal exchange, by contrast, was still unfinished a decade and a half later. Finishing that stalled exchange is the act's stated purpose.
plaw-105-280-1998: A land swap at Cape Cod National Seashore in Massachusetts is allowed by Public Law 105-280, approved October 26, 1998. The Secretary may convey about seven and six-tenths acres of federal land to the town of Provincetown in exchange for about eleven and two-tenths acres outside the seashore. A map entitled Cape Cod National Seashore Boundary Revision Map, dated May 1997, shows the parcels. Provincetown will use its parcel for a municipal facility limited to solid waste transfer and recycling. The law extends the seashore advisory commission.
plaw-105-281-1998: One contractor will test a new way to care for a California forest under the Granite Watershed Enhancement and Protection Act of 1998, Public Law 105-281, approved October 26, 1998. The Secretary of Agriculture may sign a five-year contract for multiple resource work in the Stanislaus National Forest. The aim is better ecosystem health and water quality in the Granite watershed, with far less risk of catastrophic wildfire, at lower cost. Listed work includes thinning, prescribed burns, and monitoring of ecosystem health, water, and wildlife.
plaw-105-282-1998: An office site for an Oregon forest may be sold under Public Law 105-282, approved October 26, 1998. The Secretary of Agriculture may sell or exchange the Rogue River National Forest administrative site, about five and one-tenth acres shown on an April 1998 map. Proceeds must build or improve offices and support buildings for the Rogue River National Forest and the Bureau of Land Management. In an exchange, the Secretary may accept land for new administrative facilities, and may take a cash equalization payment above the usual limit.
plaw-105-283-1998: More time to build a power project in Arkansas is granted by Public Law 105-283, approved October 26, 1998. It extends a deadline under the Federal Power Act for a hydroelectric project. On the licensee's request, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission may extend the start of construction for Project Number 10455 by up to three straight two-year periods. The extension follows the act's good faith, due diligence, and public interest tests, and it begins when the earlier extension for the project expires.
plaw-105-284-1998: India may build a memorial to Mahatma Gandhi in Washington under Public Law 105-284, approved October 26, 1998. The Government of India is authorized to place the memorial on federal land in the District of Columbia. Federal agency heads may sign cooperative agreements with India to maintain features tied to the memorial. Building must follow the Commemorative Works Act, apart from two sections that are waived. The United States pays nothing toward building or maintaining the memorial.
plaw-105-285-1998:
Three major aid programs are renewed together in Public Law 105-285, approved October 27, 1998. It is called both the Community Opportunities, Accountability, and Training and Educational Services Act of 1998 and the Coats Human Services Reauthorization Act of 1998. The law amends and improves the Head Start Act, the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Act of 1981, and the Community Services Block Grant Act.

Title I covers Head Start programs, including purpose, definitions, financial help, funding authorization, and how funds are divided. It also deals with choosing Head Start agencies, quality standards, agency powers, transition into school, and plans sent to governors. Beyond reauthorization, the act sets up demonstration projects that give people with limited means a chance to build assets, a new savings idea placed beside the older programs.
plaw-105-286-1998: Foreign-plated cars that add to border smog are restricted by the Border Smog Reduction Act of 1998, Public Law 105-286, approved October 27, 1998. It amends the Clean Air Act for ozone nonattainment areas near a border. A noncommercial vehicle registered abroad, driven by a citizen, permanent resident, or work or study visa holder, faces the limit. It may enter the area from the bordering country more than twice in one month only within limits. If state law requires testing, the driver must show proof at the border.
plaw-105-287-1998: Armored car crews may carry their weapons across state lines more clearly under the Armored Car Reciprocity Amendments of 1998, Public Law 105-287, approved October 27, 1998. It rewrites the Armored Car Industry Reciprocity Act of 1993 to clarify rules and improve interstate commerce. A crew member needs a weapons license from the state where the member mainly works, from an agency meeting federal minimum standards. The member must meet all home state requirements. The member may lawfully carry it and work in any state while on duty.
plaw-105-288-1998: Equal parcels swap hands in Colorado under the Miles Land Exchange Act of 1998, Public Law 105-288, approved October 27, 1998. If the non-federal Miles parcel is conveyed to the United States, the Secretary of Agriculture must convey a federal parcel in return. Each side is about eighty-four acres. The federal land lies within the Routt National Forest, and the Miles parcel sits next to it, as shown on a May 1996 map. Title must satisfy the Secretary and federal land standards.
plaw-105-289-1998:
Plant breeders gain stronger patent rights from the Plant Patent Amendments Act of 1998, Public Law 105-289, approved October 27, 1998. The law amends title 35 to protect patent owners against the unauthorized sale of plant parts taken from plants reproduced illegally. Congress ties the change to royalty losses in a changing world farm trade.

Its findings say plant patent protection since 1930 has helped American agriculture and horticulture by rewarding breeders who develop new varieties. An unforeseen gap in the law was now hurting the orderly collection of royalties. Parts from illegally reproduced patented plants were being traded in United States markets, and the lost income was cutting investment in breeding research for many crops.
plaw-105-290-1998:
Help for a trails museum in Casper, Wyoming, is authorized by Public Law 105-290, approved October 27, 1998. The Secretary of the Interior may assist the National Historic Trails Interpretive Center there. Congress begins with findings about why Casper matters to western migration history.

Casper is described as the only place in the western United States where four congressionally recognized trails converged: the Oregon, Mormon, California, and Pony Express trails. The Bridger and Bozeman trails and many Indian routes also passed through. No federal trails center yet existed in Wyoming or a neighboring state. Casper and the National Historic Trails Foundation had signed an understanding with the Bureau of Land Management in 1992 to build one.
plaw-105-291-1998: Guam's top lawyer is redefined by the Guam Organic Act Amendments of 1998, Public Law 105-291, approved October 27, 1998. The Attorney General of Guam is made Chief Legal Officer of the Government of Guam. When the office next falls vacant, the Governor appoints the Attorney General with the legislature's advice and consent, serving at the Governor's pleasure. Instead, the legislature may provide by law for election by Guam voters to a four-year term, with removal by the people or for cause.
plaw-105-292-1998:
Religious persecution abroad becomes a formal concern of United States foreign policy in the International Religious Freedom Act of 1998, Public Law 105-292, approved October 27, 1998. The law strengthens advocacy for people persecuted for religion in foreign countries. It authorizes United States actions when religious freedom is violated abroad.

To carry that policy out, the act creates three posts. An Ambassador at Large for International Religious Freedom leads a new State Department office, a Commission on International Religious Freedom is established, and a Special Adviser serves inside the National Security Council. Title I then covers State Department work, including reports, a religious freedom internet site, training for Foreign Service officers, and programs run by missions abroad.
plaw-105-293-1998: Irrigation contracts tied to Glendo Reservoir are extended by the Irrigation Project Contract Extension Act of 1998, Public Law 105-293, approved October 27, 1998. The Secretary of the Interior must extend water service and repayment contracts for the Glendo Unit of the Missouri River Basin Project, in Wyoming and Nebraska, until December 31, 2000. If a Platte River cooperative agreement on endangered species habitat is extended past that date, the contracts follow it, but no later than December 31, 2001.
plaw-105-294-1998: Extra life for a California Indian advisory body is granted by Public Law 105-294, approved October 27, 1998. The Advisory Council on California Indian Policy had already sent Congress plans for remedial steps for California's terminated and unacknowledged tribes. The plans also covered health, education, and economic self-sufficiency needs. The extension act's purpose is to let the council keep advising Congress as those plans are put into practice. Its duties section is amended to add that advising role.
plaw-105-295-1998: Cold water for fish below a California dam is the aim of Public Law 105-295, approved October 27, 1998. The Secretary of the Interior may build a temperature control device at Folsom Dam, following a draft environmental study and an assessment report. The device and its monitoring facilities will run as part of the Central Valley Project for fall-run chinook salmon and steelhead trout in the American River. The Secretary may also help build such devices on non-federal facilities that deliver project water.
plaw-105-296-1998: Rules for Idaho school land are rewritten by Public Law 105-296, approved October 27, 1998. It replaces section 5 of the Idaho Admission Act of July 3, 1890. Land granted for education must be sold only at public sale. Sale proceeds go to the public school permanent endowment fund, to be spent only for public schools, or to a land bank fund for buying other Idaho land for the fund's beneficiaries. Earnings go to an earnings reserve fund for public schools.
plaw-105-297-1998:
Baseball players win the same antitrust rights as other athletes in the Curt Flood Act of 1998, Public Law 105-297, approved October 27, 1998. The stated purpose is to apply the antitrust laws generally to major league baseball. Congress is careful to say the act changes nothing about antitrust law in any other context, or for any other person.

A new section of the Clayton Act makes conduct in organized professional major league baseball subject to the antitrust laws when it directly relates to employing major league players. The coverage matches what would apply in any other profession. The act is named for Curt Flood, and its text frames the change as equal treatment with football and basketball players, whose employment was already covered.
plaw-105-298-1998:
Copyrights last twenty years longer under Public Law 105-298, approved October 27, 1998. Title I is the Sonny Bono Copyright Term Extension Act, amending title 17 on how long copyright endures. One distant preemption date moves from February 15, 2047 to February 15, 2067.

For works created on or after January 1, 1978, the basic term rises from fifty to seventy years in the sample's amendments. Other terms rise from seventy-five to ninety-five years, and from one hundred to one hundred twenty years. Works created but not published or copyrighted before 1978 are treated in the next section. The pattern is uniform: every stated period grows by twenty years.
plaw-105-299-1998: A federal building in Florence, Alabama, is renamed by Public Law 105-299, approved October 27, 1998. The building at 210 North Seminary Street must be known and designated as the Justice John McKinley Federal Building. Any reference in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or other record to that building counts as a reference to the Justice John McKinley Federal Building. The Senate passed the bill in June 1998 and the House in October.
plaw-105-300-1998: Close relatives may not sit together on the same federal court under Public Law 105-300, approved October 27, 1998. It amends section 458 of title 28 for courts exercising judicial power under article III of the Constitution, other than the Supreme Court. No person may be appointed a judge of a court if that person is related, by blood or marriage, within the degree of first cousin. The relative must be a judge who is a member of the same court. Same court means one district or one circuit.
plaw-105-301-1998:
Victims whom crime statistics had missed are counted in the Crime Victims With Disabilities Awareness Act, Public Law 105-301, approved October 27, 1998. The act aims to raise public awareness of crime victims with developmental disabilities, measure how large the problem is, and build strategies for their safety and justice needs.

Congress found that foreign research showed people with developmental disabilities faced a risk of becoming crime victims four to ten times higher than others. No major United States study existed, and the annual National Crime Victim's Survey did not collect data on crimes against them. Studies in Canada, Australia, and Great Britain showed repeated victimization, in part because crimes went unreported and officials sometimes hesitated to rely on a disabled victim's testimony.
plaw-105-302-1998: Police officers based in schools are encouraged by Public Law 105-302, approved October 27, 1998. It amends part Q of the Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act of 1968. A new grant purpose supports school-based partnerships between local police and school systems, using school resource officers in and around elementary and secondary schools against crime, disorder, gangs, and drugs. A school resource officer is defined as a career officer with sworn authority, working in community-oriented policing with schools and community groups.
plaw-105-303-1998:
Private space business is promoted by the Commercial Space Act of 1998, Public Law 105-303, approved October 28, 1998. Its purpose is to encourage a commercial space industry in the United States. Title I is called Promotion of Commercial Space Opportunities, and Title II covers federal buying of space transportation services.

Title I deals with commercial use of the space station, commercial launch amendments, a launch voucher demonstration program, and promotion of United States Global Positioning System standards. It also covers buying space science data, running Commercial Space Centers, and sources of Earth science data. Title II requires agencies to procure commercial space transportation, revises the Launch Services Purchase Act of 1990, and addresses shuttle privatization and use of excess ballistic missiles.
plaw-105-304-1998:
Copyright law enters the internet age in the Digital Millennium Copyright Act, Public Law 105-304, approved October 28, 1998. The law amends title 17 to carry out two World Intellectual Property Organization treaties, the Copyright Treaty and the Performances and Phonograms Treaty. Its table of contents shows five titles in all.

Title I carries out the WIPO treaties, including rules on protection systems and management information, plus a study of how the law affects electronic commerce. Title II limits liability for online infringement. Title III creates an exemption for computer maintenance or repair. Together the titles set early ground rules for copying, sharing, and fixing digital works and machines.
plaw-105-305-1998:
A faster research network is funded by the Next Generation Internet Research Act of 1998, Public Law 105-305, approved October 28, 1998. The law amends the High-Performance Computing Act of 1991. It authorizes money for fiscal years 1999 and 2000 for the Next Generation Internet program. It also charges a presidential advisory group with watching that program.

Congress found that United States leadership in science and technology had been vital to prosperity, security, and competitiveness. Federal research money had built a science base without peer. Earlier federal work on computer networks had created new industries and new jobs. The President's Information Technology Advisory Committee must track the program, give advice on its growth, and report to the President and Congress.
plaw-105-306-1998: Benefits for some noncitizens are clarified by Public Law 105-306, approved October 28, 1998. Its name is the Noncitizen Benefit Clarification and Other Technical Amendments Act of 1998. One section protects SSI coverage for a nonqualified alien who was receiving benefits on August 22, 1996. That date is when the 1996 welfare law was enacted. The bar in that law does not apply to this person. It also does not apply to programs based on SSI. Other sections deal with jobless benefits, child support, and self-employment help.
plaw-105-307-1998: A Florida park visitor center takes a congressman's name under the Dante Fascell Biscayne National Park Visitor Center Designation Act, Public Law 105-307, approved October 29, 1998. The Biscayne National Park visitor center sits on the shore of Biscayne Bay on Convoy Point, Florida. It is designated as the Dante Fascell Visitor Center. Any reference in a federal law, map, regulation, or other record to that center counts as a reference to the Dante Fascell Visitor Center.
plaw-105-308-1998: Revenue limits for some tribal members are lifted by Public Law 105-308, approved October 30, 1998. It removes a restriction on distributing certain revenues from the Mineral Springs parcel to certain members of the Agua Caliente Band of Cahuilla Indians. The findings trace the Agua Caliente Equalization Act of 1959, passed to equalize allotment values after federal court cases in 1954 and 1956. That act set aside parcels, including two in the Mineral Springs area, whose revenues were held back.
plaw-105-309-1998: Standards and manufacturing help are funded by the Technology Administration Act of 1998, Public Law 105-309, approved October 30, 1998. The law authorizes money for the National Institute of Standards and Technology for fiscal years 1998 and 1999. It also extends Manufacturing Extension Partnership centers: after the sixth year, a center may receive more support after a positive independent review, repeated at least every two years. Later sections add possible awards under the Malcolm Baldrige Quality Award, including a third award at no added federal cost.
plaw-105-310-1998:
A national plan against dirty money is required by the Money Laundering and Financial Crimes Strategy Act of 1998, Public Law 105-310, approved October 30, 1998. The Secretary of the Treasury must develop and carry out a national strategy against money laundering and related financial crimes. A new subchapter is added to chapter 53 of title 31.

That subchapter begins with definitions. Money laundering and related financial crime means moving illicit cash, or cash equivalent proceeds, into, out of, or through the United States, or through United States financial institutions. It also carries a second meaning tied to an equivalent offense named in the text. The strategy must be built on those definitions, so agencies share one picture of the crime they are fighting.
plaw-105-311-1998: New life coverage choices for federal workers are studied under Public Law 105-311, approved October 30, 1998. Its name is the Federal Employees Life Insurance Improvement Act. The Office of Personnel Management must study and report to Congress. The report surveys staff interest in three options. They are group universal life, group variable universal life, and added voluntary accidental death cover. The sample sets the study deadline as July 31, 1998. The report must add the office's comments and advice. A maximum limit on employee coverage is also repealed.
plaw-105-312-1998:
Hunters who did not know bait was present are protected by Public Law 105-312, approved October 30, 1998. Title I is the Migratory Bird Treaty Reform Act of 1998, clarifying baiting rules under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act. It also helps with buying migratory bird habitat.

The reform ends strict liability for baiting. Taking a migratory game bird with bait, or over a baited area, is unlawful only if the person knows, or reasonably should know, the area is baited. Placing bait to cause such a taking is also barred. Criminal penalties rise sharply in the sample's amendment, from five hundred dollars to fifteen thousand dollars for one offense class, with penalty sections rearranged to follow.
plaw-105-313-1998:
Tribal life at the edge of Everglades National Park is recognized in the Miccosukee Reserved Area Act, Public Law 105-313, approved October 30, 1998. The law deems activities of the Miccosukee Tribe on the Miccosukee Reserved Area consistent with the purposes of the park. Florida is the setting throughout.

Congress found that since 1964 the Miccosukee Tribe of Indians of Florida had lived and governed itself on a strip of land on the park's northern edge, under National Park Service permits. The current permit was set to expire in 2014. As membership grew, the tribe needed modern housing, government buildings, schools, and cultural facilities. The area also sits inside a major effort to restore the South Florida ecosystem.
plaw-105-314-1998:
Children are shielded from sexual predators by Public Law 105-314, approved October 30, 1998. Its name is the Protection of Children From Sexual Predators Act of 1998. The law amends title 18 to protect children from sexual abuse and exploitation. Its table of contents splits the work into two titles.

Title I covers sending a minor's identifying facts by interstate means for criminal sexual purposes. It also covers coercion and enticement, and higher penalties for transporting minors for illegal sexual activity. Repeat offenders are treated apart. Title II deals with child pornography. It adds a new basis for prosecuting its production and raises its penalties. It also sets a zero tolerance rule for holding such material.
plaw-105-315-1998:
Settling cases without a full trial is promoted in federal courts by the Alternative Dispute Resolution Act of 1998, Public Law 105-315, approved October 30, 1998. The law amends title 28 on the use of alternative dispute resolution in United States district courts. Congress declares a policy in favor of such programs.

Its findings say that, with support from judges and lawyers and properly trained neutrals, these methods can satisfy the parties, produce new ways to settle disputes, and reach settlements faster. Mediation, early neutral evaluation, minitrials, and voluntary arbitration may cut the large backlog in some federal courts. Growth of mediation in appellate courts suggests trial courts should consider mediation in their local programs as well.
plaw-105-316-1998: A Texas water project may be paid off early under the Canadian River Project Prepayment Act, Public Law 105-316, approved October 30, 1998. The Canadian River Municipal Water Authority, a Texas conservation and reclamation district, may prepay amounts due under its reclamation contract. In return for taking over the federal obligation and paying the set amount within 360 days of enactment, the Secretary of the Interior conveys the project. The project means the pipeline and related facilities built under a 1950 authorization act.
plaw-105-317-1998: Land near Gustavus, Alaska, is swapped under the Glacier Bay National Park Boundary Adjustment Act of 1998, Public Law 105-317, approved October 30, 1998. If Alaska offers state lands chosen by mutual agreement, the Secretary of the Interior must complete an exchange for federal lands described in the act. The exchange must finish no later than six months after the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission licenses the Gustavus Electric Company. Park system exchange laws for Alaska and state land law both apply, and wilderness designation is part of the section heading.
plaw-105-318-1998:
Stealing another person's identity becomes a named federal crime in the Identity Theft and Assumption Deterrence Act of 1998, Public Law 105-318, approved October 30, 1998. The law amends chapter 47 of title 18, which deals with identity fraud. It first states the constitutional commerce power on which Congress rests the act.

A new paragraph in section 1028 makes it an offense to knowingly transfer or use, without lawful authority, a means of identification of another person. The act must be done with intent to commit, or to aid or abet, unlawful activity that breaks federal law or that is a felony under state or local law. Earlier paragraphs are renumbered and an attempts phrase is struck to fit the new offense into the fraud statute.
plaw-105-319-1998:
Young people from Northern Ireland's hardest-hit areas are brought to America by the Irish Peace Process Cultural and Training Program Act of 1998, Public Law 105-319, approved October 30, 1998. The Secretary of State and the Attorney General must set up the program together. It supports the Irish peace process through training and cultural exchange.

Participants come from disadvantaged areas of designated counties suffering sectarian violence and high structural unemployment. In the United States they develop job skills and conflict resolution abilities in a diverse, cooperative, and peaceful setting, then return home better able to aid economic renewal. The program admits not more than four thousand people under a cited visa category, and it promotes cross-community and cross-border work for lasting peaceful coexistence.
plaw-105-320-1998:
Survivors of torture receive a broad support program under the Torture Victims Relief Act of 1998, Public Law 105-320, approved October 30, 1998. The act promises a comprehensive program of support for victims of torture. Its findings open with a plain statement: the American people abhor torture by any government or person.

Congress defines torture as deliberate mental and physical damage by governments to destroy personality and terrorize society, with effects that can last a lifetime and reach later generations. Repressive governments use it to remove opposition leaders and frighten the public. Survivors stay under threat where those responsible escape justice, and even their caregivers face reprisals. A significant number of refugees and asylees entering the United States, the findings add, have been victims of torture.
plaw-105-321-1998: Federal land duties in Oregon are rearranged by the Oregon Public Lands Transfer and Protection Act of 1998, Public Law 105-321, approved October 30, 1998. It transfers administrative jurisdiction over lands in or near the Rogue River National Forest. It clarifies Bureau of Land Management power to sell and exchange other Oregon lands. Later sections protect Oregon and California Railroad grant lands. They transfer jurisdiction at Hart Mountain and expand Bandon Marsh National Wildlife Refuge. They cover the Willow Lake project in Salem and a conveyance to Deschutes County.
plaw-105-322-1998: Marsh-eating rodents in Maryland are the target of Public Law 105-322, approved October 30, 1998. The Secretary of the Interior may give financial help to Maryland for a pilot program to develop ways to eradicate or control nutria and restore marshland nutria damaged. Goals include wiping out nutria in Maryland, controlling them in other states, and restoring damaged marsh. The federal share may not pass seventy-five percent of costs, and administrative spending is capped. Work follows a July 1998 Maryland pilot proposal.
plaw-105-323-1998: Rewards for tips on terrorism and drug crimes are revised by Public Law 105-323, approved October 30, 1998. It rewrites section 36 of the State Department Basic Authorities Act of 1956 to create a Department of State Rewards Program, run by the Secretary of State with the Attorney General. The Secretary may pay a reward for information leading to arrest or conviction in any country for international terrorism. The full title also covers narcotics offenses and serious violations of international humanitarian law tied to the former Yugoslavia.
plaw-105-324-1998: What counts as a pesticide chemical in food law is clarified by Public Law 105-324, approved October 30, 1998. Its name is the Antimicrobial Regulation Technical Corrections Act of 1998. It rewrites the definition in section 201(q) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. The term means a substance that is a pesticide under the federal pesticide law. Active and inert parts of the substance both count. Ethylene oxide and propylene oxide count when used on food. Special rules follow for substances used to kill germs.
plaw-105-325-1998:
Caves get their own research center in the National Cave and Karst Research Institute Act of 1998, Public Law 105-325, approved October 30, 1998. The Secretary of the Interior, through the Director of the National Park Service, must establish the National Cave and Karst Research Institute in New Mexico. It must sit near Carlsbad Caverns National Park, but outside the park boundary.

The stated purposes run to six items. They are to advance the science of speleology, centralize and standardize cave information, and foster joint work across fields in cave and karst research. The institute must also promote public education, support national and international cooperation to protect cave and karst landforms, and develop resource practices that are sound for the environment and sustainable over time.
plaw-105-326-1998:
A federal company town in Utah is handed toward local life by the Dutch John Federal Property Disposition and Assistance Act of 1998, Public Law 105-326, approved October 30, 1998. The law disposes of certain federal properties in Dutch John and helps local government deliver basic services in the interim.

Congress found that the Secretary of the Interior founded Dutch John in 1958 on Bureau of Reclamation land to house workers building and running Flaming Gorge Dam and Reservoir. Houses, offices, storage buildings, and other public facilities were built and stayed federally owned. Land around Flaming Gorge Reservoir, including Dutch John, was placed inside the Flaming Gorge National Recreation Area in 1968, splitting administration duties that the act must now sort out.
plaw-105-327-1998: Parks that cannot charge entry fees may still keep other fees under Public Law 105-327, approved October 30, 1998. It amends the Land and Water Conservation Fund Act of 1965. For a National Park System unit where deed restrictions bar entrance or admission fees, the Secretary of the Interior must withhold all fees and charges collected there from the special account. The unit keeps the money, without a new appropriation, for visitor experience, resource protection, repair, interpretation, signs, and habitat work.
plaw-105-328-1998: Money from selling seized wildlife items may stay with the wildlife agency under the Fish and Wildlife Revenue Enhancement Act of 1998, Public Law 105-328, approved October 30, 1998. Congress found that the Fish and Wildlife Service stores and disposes of fish, wildlife, and plant items, including eagles and eagle parts, gained by abandonment or forfeiture. Many items go to education, science, and Native American religious uses. About ninety percent of items held were abandoned, yet sale revenue was not available to the Service before this act.
plaw-105-329-1998: Arches National Park in Utah grows by Public Law 105-329, approved October 30, 1998. The Arches National Park Expansion Act adds drainages under Bureau of Land Management jurisdiction and part of Fish Seep Draw owned by Utah. The boundary change adds about three thousand one hundred forty acres known as the Lost Spring Canyon Addition, shown on an April 1997 map. The addition takes effect on the date the paragraph is enacted, and the park's establishment section is rewritten to hold both the first and expanded boundaries.
plaw-105-330-1998: Trademark filing is aligned with a treaty by Public Law 105-330, approved October 30, 1998. Title I is the Trademark Law Treaty Implementation Act, carrying out the Trademark Law Treaty. It works through the Trademark Act of 1946. That act is the law for registering and protecting marks used in commerce. The opening amendment rewrites the application for registration. An owner files in the Patent and Trademark Office and pays the fee. The filing gives a verified statement, domicile and citizenship, first use dates, and specimens of the mark.
plaw-105-331-1998: Coins honoring an inventor are ordered by the Thomas Alva Edison Commemorative Coin Act, Public Law 105-331, approved October 31, 1998. Congress found that Edison was born February 11, 1847, in Milan, Ohio, and produced more than one thousand three hundred inventions, including the light bulb and phonograph. The year 2004 marks one hundred twenty-five years since the 1879 light bulb. The Treasury must mint no more than five hundred thousand one-dollar coins, ninety percent silver and ten percent copper.
plaw-105-332-1998:
Job training law is rewritten by Public Law 105-332, approved October 31, 1998. Its name is the Carl D Perkins Vocational and Applied Technology Education Amendments of 1998. It amends the Perkins act in full. Inside the rewritten text, the act takes a new name. That name is the Carl D Perkins Vocational and Technical Education Act of 1998.

The new table of contents opens with purpose, definitions, and transition rules. It also lists privacy, a limit, a special rule, and funding approval. Title I is aid to the states for job training. It begins with allotment and allocation rules for state grants. The structure shows federal money flowing through states to training programs. The 1998 rewrite drops the old applied technology framing from the act's name.
plaw-105-333-1998: Alaska Native land bank protection is clarified by the ANCSA Land Bank Protection Act of 1998, Public Law 105-333, approved October 31, 1998. It amends the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act and a section of the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act. Land conveyed to a Native Corporation in an authorized exchange gains automatic protection. Land exchanged between Native Corporations, or their trusts and ventures, is not treated as developed, leased, or sold to a third party merely because of that exchange.
plaw-105-334-1998: Seventeen-year-olds may drive for work, within strict limits, under the Drive for Teen Employment Act, Public Law 105-334, from 1998. It changes the child labor exemption in the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938. Workers under seventeen may not drive cars or trucks on roads. A seventeen-year-old may drive only in daylight, with a state license and no moving violations at hiring. The driver must have passed a state driver education course. Seat belts must be used, and the vehicle must weigh no more than six thousand pounds gross.
plaw-105-335-1998:
School trust land trapped inside federal monuments is traded out by the Utah Schools and Lands Exchange Act of 1998, Public Law 105-335, approved October 31, 1998. The law provides for exchanging certain lands within Utah. Its findings describe state land run by the Utah School and Institutional Trust Lands Administration.

Utah owned about one hundred seventy-six thousand six hundred acres, plus about twenty-four thousand acres of mineral interests, inside the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument, created by presidential proclamation on September 18, 1996. Another roughly two hundred thousand acres, with seventy-six thousand acres of mineral interests, sat inside national parks, national forests, and Indian reservations. Those lands were granted under the 1894 Utah Enabling Act in trust for public schools and other institutions, and many may hold coal, oil, gas, and tar sands.
plaw-105-336-1998:
School meals for children are renewed by the William F Goodling Child Nutrition Reauthorization Act of 1998, Public Law 105-336, approved October 31, 1998. It amends the National School Lunch Act and the Child Nutrition Act of 1966. The aims are wider access to food and nutrition help, simpler operations, and better management, with authority extended through fiscal year 2003.

Title I covers school lunch and related programs, including commodities, nutrition requirements, special assistance, and the summer food service program. It also covers commodity distribution, the child and adult care food program, meal supplements for children in afterschool care, pilot projects, and training. A section on accommodating special dietary needs of individuals with disabilities closes the title. Title II turns to school breakfast.
plaw-105-337-1998: Two tribal colleges may test their own personnel systems under Public Law 105-337, approved October 31, 1998. Haskell Indian Nations University in Kansas and the Southwestern Indian Polytechnic Institute in New Mexico may each run a demonstration project on new personnel management policies. Congress found that culturally sensitive curricula at both schools fit federal treaty commitments and self-determination. More autonomy, while staying inside the Bureau of Indian Affairs, would help Haskell become a four-year university and improve the polytechnic institute's academic program.
plaw-105-338-1998:
Democracy in Iraq is declared United States policy by the Iraq Liberation Act of 1998, Public Law 105-338, approved October 31, 1998. The act establishes a program to support a transition to democracy in Iraq. It begins with a long list of findings about Iraq's wars and abuses.

Congress found that Iraq invaded Iran on September 22, 1980, starting an eight-year war with chemical weapons and missile attacks on cities. In the 1988 Anfal campaign Iraq forcibly moved Kurdish civilians and killed an estimated fifty thousand to one hundred eighty thousand Kurds. At Halabja that March, chemical weapons killed an estimated five thousand Kurds. Iraq then invaded Kuwait on August 2, 1990, held it for seven months, and set its oil wells ablaze while retreating.
plaw-105-339-1998: Veterans may compete for more federal jobs under the Veterans Employment Opportunities Act of 1998, Public Law 105-339, approved October 31, 1998. It amends title 5 so a preference eligible, or a veteran honorably separated after three or more years of active service, may not be denied a chance to compete for a vacancy. That right applies when the agency accepts applications from outside its own workforce under merit promotion. Announcements must say such veterans are eligible to apply, without creating any new preference entitlement.
plaw-105-340-1998: Women's health research at two federal agencies is extended by Public Law 105-340, approved October 31, 1998. It revises programs at the National Institutes of Health and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention under the Public Health Service Act. Title I covers research on the drug DES, changing a date from 1996 to 2003. It also creates a national education program for health professionals and the public about diethylstilbestrol, commonly called DES, using methods from an earlier demonstration program where fitting.
plaw-105-341-1998:
Sites where women fought for equal rights are to be protected under the Women's Progress Commemoration Act, Public Law 105-341, approved October 31, 1998. The law creates a commission in honor of the one hundred fiftieth anniversary of the Seneca Falls Convention. Its work is to protect places of importance in the long effort to secure equal rights for women.

Congress declares that the first Seneca Falls Convention met in upstate New York in July 1848 to consider women's social conditions and civil rights. It marked the start of a courageous struggle for equal rights, and the anniversary offers a chance to study that history. The Women's Progress Commemoration Commission has fifteen members, with three appointed by each appointing authority named in the text, starting with the President and Congress.
plaw-105-342-1998:
Two presidents' hometown site becomes a national historical park in the Adams National Historical Park Act of 1998, Public Law 105-342, approved November 2, 1998. The park is in Quincy, Massachusetts. Congress builds the new park out of a much older historic site, and its findings trace that growth step by step.

In 1946 Secretary of the Interior J A Krug created the Adams Mansion National Historic Site under the Historic Sites Act. In 1952 the site was enlarged and renamed the Adams National Historic Site. Congress added about three and two-thirds acres in 1972. In 1978 it authorized accepting the birthplaces of John Adams and John Quincy Adams in Quincy, and in 1980 the United First Parish Church, to be managed as part of the site.
plaw-105-343-1998: Land beside a landscape architect's home may be added by donation only, under Public Law 105-343, approved November 2, 1998. It amends the law that created the Frederick Law Olmsted National Historic Site in Massachusetts. To preserve the site's historic setting, the Secretary may acquire lands with easements next to the site, owned by the Brookline Conservation Land Trust, through donation only. The added lands are for education and interpretation, and they will be managed as part of the historic site.
plaw-105-344-1998: A park tract in Arizona may go to only one town, or stay federal, under Public Law 105-344, approved November 2, 1998. The Secretary of Agriculture may not convey the Woodland Lake Park tract in the Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest freely. A conveyance must be made to the town of Pinetop-Lakeside. A later act of Congress may also specifically authorize a conveyance. The tract is a parcel of about five hundred eighty-three acres in that Arizona forest, known by the Woodland Lake Park name.
plaw-105-345-1998: Two more years to build a memorial are granted by Public Law 105-345, approved November 2, 1998. It amends the Omnibus Parks and Public Lands Management Act of 1996, section 506, on the Black Revolutionary War Patriots Memorial. That section gave the Black Patriots Foundation legislative authority to establish a commemorative work. In the cited line, the year 1998 is struck and the year 2000 is inserted. The one-date change is the entire act.
plaw-105-346-1998: A fish research station in Idaho passes to a university under Public Law 105-346, approved November 2, 1998. Within 180 days, the Secretary of the Interior must convey the Tunnison Lab Hagerman Field Station in Gooding County to the University of Idaho, without payment, for fish research. The property is about four acres with the station, improvements, and related personal property, but not federal water rights or needed easements. If the university uses it for another purpose, title reverts to the United States.
plaw-105-347-1998: Job applicants' credit reports get clearer consent rules in the Consumer Reporting Employment Clarification Act of 1998, Public Law 105-347, approved November 2, 1998. It amends the Fair Credit Reporting Act on using consumer reports for employment. A person may not obtain such a report unless a clear written disclosure, in a document consisting solely of that disclosure, tells the consumer a report may be obtained. The consumer must authorize the report in writing, which may be on the same document. Special rules cover applications by mail, phone, or computer.
plaw-105-348-1998: An airport shared by two states receives congressional consent in Public Law 105-348, a joint resolution approved November 2, 1998. Congress consents to the Potomac Highlands Airport Authority Compact between Maryland and West Virginia. The pact lets county leaders in Mineral County, West Virginia, sign deals with Maryland partners. Those partners include Allegany County and the town of Cumberland. The deals cover running and using the Cumberland Municipal Airport. That airport sits in Mineral County. Fees, upkeep, and taxes on aircraft are all covered.
plaw-105-349-1998:
Watchdogs inside federal agencies are honored by Public Law 105-349, a joint resolution approved November 2, 1998. It recognizes what Inspectors General have done since 1978 to prevent and detect waste, fraud, abuse, and mismanagement. The Inspector General Act of 1978 was signed on October 12, 1978, with broad bipartisan support.

Inspectors General now work in the twenty-seven largest executive agencies and in thirty other designated federal bodies. They run and oversee audits and investigations, and they alert Congress and agency heads through semiannual reports. They recommend policies for economy and efficiency, and they take tips from federal workers and citizens about violations, gross waste, abuse of authority, or danger to public health and safety. Their work each year points to billions of dollars that could be spent better.
plaw-105-350-1998: The next Congress gets its starting day from Public Law 105-350, a joint resolution in the sample approved October 31, 1998. It appoints the day for convening the first session of the One Hundred Sixth Congress. That first regular session must begin at noon on Wednesday, January 6, 1999. The House passed the resolution on October 20 and the Senate on October 21, even though the heading date in the sample reads November 3, a mismatch worth noting in the record.
plaw-105-351-1998: Irrigation works in Idaho are handed to the district by Public Law 105-351, approved November 3, 1998. The Secretary of the Interior must convey Minidoka project facilities to the Burley Irrigation District. The transfer is made without payment beyond what the act states, by quitclaim deed or patent. It covers the Southside Pumping Division. The list runs from acquired lands, easements, and pumping plants to canals, drains, laterals, roads, pumps, headgates, transformers, substations, buildings, and transmission lines. The lines deliver water from the Southside Canal headworks, though not the headworks.
plaw-105-352-1998:
Clean drinking water for a dry South Dakota county is authorized by the Fall River Water Users District Rural Water System Act of 1998, Public Law 105-352, approved November 3, 1998. The law allows building the Fall River Water Users District Rural Water System. Federal help may go to the district, a nonprofit corporation, for planning and construction.

Congress found that Fall River County lacked enough water of reasonable quality, and that available supplies were poor and failed minimum health and safety standards. Past severe droughts left residents without a satisfactory supply, and in 1990 many homeowners and ranchers had to haul water. Most district members either hauled bottled water for drinking or used distillers, a hardship the new system is meant to end.
plaw-105-353-1998:
Securities fraud class actions are pulled back into federal court by the Securities Litigation Uniform Standards Act of 1998, Public Law 105-353, approved November 3, 1998. It amends the Securities Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. The aim is to limit securities class actions brought under state law.

Congress found that the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995 tried to stop abuses in private securities fraud suits. Since then, many class actions had shifted from federal to state courts, blocking that reform. National standards for class actions over nationally traded securities would close the detour. State regulation and state enforcement powers stay in place, and the treatment of individual lawsuits does not change.
plaw-105-354-1998: Flag display rules are tidied by Public Law 105-354, approved November 3, 1998. It codifies, without substantive change, laws on patriotic observances, ceremonies, and organizations in title 36, and improves the United States Code. One amendment rewrites rules for the POW/MIA flag. That flag must be displayed at named locations. It stands as a symbol of national commitment to the fullest possible accounting for Americans who were prisoners of war or missing in action. Display days include Armed Forces Day, Memorial Day, Flag Day, Independence Day, and Veterans Day.
plaw-105-355-1998:
Michigan's car industry becomes a heritage area in Public Law 105-355, approved November 6, 1998. Title I is the Automobile National Heritage Area Act. It authorizes the Automobile National Heritage Area in Michigan. Congress finds the car trade's industrial, cultural, and natural legacy to be of national significance.

Around Detroit, Dearborn, Pontiac, Flint, and Lansing, making cars helped build United States industrial power. That strength was vital in two world wars. The trade still touches one out of seven United States jobs. Its past includes the social history and living traditions of several generations of workers. It also includes the United Auto Workers and other unions. Those unions shaped both the labor movement and the car trade itself.
plaw-105-356-1998:
A school at the center of the civil rights struggle becomes a historic site in Public Law 105-356, approved November 6, 1998. The law establishes the Little Rock Central High School National Historic Site in Arkansas as a unit of the National Park System. Its findings start with the Supreme Court's 1954 Brown v Board of Education decision ending school segregation.

Admission of nine African-American students, known as the Little Rock Nine, to Central High was the most prominent national test of Brown, and it pushed integration in other segregated schools. The school building marked seventy years in 1997 and was praised by architects as the most beautiful high school in America. It joined the National Register of Historic Places in 1977 and became a National Historic Landmark in 1982.
plaw-105-357-1998: Prescription drugs carried across a land border are capped by the Controlled Substances Trafficking Prohibition Act, Public Law 105-357, approved November 10, 1998. It amends the Controlled Substances Import and Export Act. A United States resident enters through an international land border with a controlled substance. The substance is not in schedule I, and the resident has no valid prescription or proof of one. That resident may not bring in more than fifty dosage units. The new limit is stated as a federal minimum requirement.
plaw-105-358-1998: Patent office operations are funded from fees by Public Law 105-358, approved November 10, 1998. The United States Patent and Trademark Office Reauthorization Act for fiscal year 1999 makes money available for salaries and necessary expenses, until spent. The amount is sixty-six million dollars from fees collected in fiscal year 1998, plus fees collected in 1999. The act then sets patent fee levels in title 35. It starts with a filing fee of seven hundred sixty dollars for an original patent, with added per-claim charges.
plaw-105-359-1998: Access to the outdoors for people with disabilities must be studied under Public Law 105-359, approved November 10, 1998. The Secretary of Agriculture and the Secretary of the Interior must jointly study how to improve access to public outdoor recreation, such as fishing, hunting, trapping, wildlife viewing, hiking, boating, and camping. Covered lands are national forests, national parks, wildlife refuges, and Bureau of Land Management lands. A report with the results is due to Congress within eighteen months of enactment.
plaw-105-360-1998: Diversity visa applicants stalled by embassy bombings get more time under Public Law 105-360, approved November 10, 1998. Their fiscal year 1998 processing was suspended after the bombings, so the period extends into fiscal year 1999. A qualifying petition is deemed approved for 1999 processing with no added seventy-five dollar filing fee, and the applicant receives the earliest priority rank for that year. Visas issued under the extension are charged to fiscal year 1999. Eligibility turns in part on an interview scheduled on or after August 6, 1998.
plaw-105-361-1998: Native American programs are funded for four more years by the Native American Programs Act Amendments of 1998, Public Law 105-361, approved November 10, 1998. It extends authorizations in the Native American Programs Act of 1974, replacing mid-1990s fiscal years with fiscal years 1999 through 2002 in several places. One funding line becomes such sums as may be necessary for those years. The Native Hawaiian Revolving Loan Fund is also amended, changing grants language to a single grant that carries out the fund.
plaw-105-362-1998:
Paperwork Congress no longer wants is cut by the Federal Reports Elimination Act of 1998, Public Law 105-362, approved November 10, 1998. Its stated aim is to eliminate unnecessary and wasteful federal reports. The table of contents alone fills the sample, organized agency by agency.

Title I eliminates reports at the Department of Agriculture, and Title II does the same for the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Title III removes one education report. The Department of Energy gets reports both eliminated and modified, and the Environmental Protection Agency and the Department of Health and Human Services follow with their own lists. The pattern is a government-wide housecleaning of reports owed to Congress.
plaw-105-363-1998: Room for visitors at an artist's farm is allowed by Public Law 105-363, approved November 10, 1998. It amends the Weir Farm National Historic Site Establishment Act of 1990 in Connecticut. To preserve the site's historic setting and character, the Secretary may acquire not more than fifteen additional acres for visitor and administrative facilities. The land must touch, or sit close to, the existing site, and once acquired it becomes part of the historic site boundary and is managed with it. Development limits follow in the text.
plaw-105-364-1998: Roosevelt family land at Hyde Park, New York, may be bought for the park service under Public Law 105-364, approved November 10, 1998. The Secretary of the Interior may acquire, by purchase with donated or appropriated funds, by donation, or otherwise, lands Franklin D Roosevelt or his family owned when he died. A July 26, 1962 map shows the property. Acquired land joins the Home of Franklin D Roosevelt National Historic Site or the Eleanor Roosevelt National Historic Site, as fitting, with needed sums authorized.
plaw-105-365-1998: A Montana ranch boundary is redrawn by map in the Grant-Kohrs Ranch National Historic Site Boundary Adjustment Act of 1998, Public Law 105-365, approved November 10, 1998. It amends the act of August 25, 1972 that created the site. The old final boundary sentence is replaced: the boundary is as generally described on a map titled Boundary Map, Grant-Kohrs Ranch National Historic Site, numbered 80030-B and dated January 1998. That map stays on file for public inspection in local and Washington park service offices.
plaw-105-366-1998:
Bribing foreign officials is policed more tightly by the International Anti-Bribery and Fair Competition Act of 1998, Public Law 105-366, approved November 10, 1998. The law amends the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act of 1977. Its stated aims are better competitiveness for American business and promotion of foreign commerce.

For issuers, the banned conduct is rewritten in detail. A payment aimed at influencing a foreign official's act or decision, making the official break a lawful duty, or securing an improper advantage is prohibited. The same three aims are then spelled out for payments aimed at a foreign political party, party official, or candidate. The sample shows Congress closing wording gaps so indirect influence counts the same as a direct act.
plaw-105-367-1998: Gas leases signed by surface owners are upheld by Public Law 105-367, approved November 10, 1998. The United States must recognize that a contract or lease for coalbed methane does not infringe federal ownership rights. The protection covers land conveyed under the surface rights act of March 3, 1909, or the agricultural entries on coal lands act of June 22, 1910. The lease must be held by a person with title under those acts, be in effect at enactment, and convey rights to explore for, extract, and sell coalbed methane.
plaw-105-368-1998:
Gulf War veterans' health leads a broad veterans law in the Veterans Programs Enhancement Act of 1998, Public Law 105-368, approved November 11, 1998. The act amends title 38 to improve benefits for Persian Gulf War veterans, give a cost-of-living raise to veterans with service-connected disabilities, and strengthen health care, compensation, education, and insurance programs.

Title I deals with Persian Gulf War and future conflicts. It orders an agreement with the National Academy of Sciences to judge health effects of service in Southwest Asia. It also covers health care for those veterans, a national center on war-related illnesses and post-deployment health, and coordination of the work. Independent advice on research, and a curriculum on caring for Gulf War veterans, are contracted for in later sections of the title.
plaw-105-369-1998:
Payments for people infected through blood products are created by the Ricky Ray Hemophilia Relief Act of 1998, Public Law 105-369, approved November 12, 1998. The act provides compassionate payments to individuals with blood-clotting disorders, such as hemophilia, who contracted HIV from contaminated antihemophilic factor. Title I builds the payment system.

Its sections create the Ricky Ray Hemophilia Relief Fund, define the compassionate payment, and set how claims are decided and paid. Limits cover transfer of rights, number of petitions, filing time, and fees for agents and attorneys. A payment does not disturb certain other claims. Title II then sets how private settlement payments in the hemophilia clotting-factor lawsuit count under the Medicaid and Supplemental Security Income programs.
plaw-105-370-1998: HIV testing in federal prisons is required by the Correction Officers Health and Safety Act of 1998, Public Law 105-370, approved November 12, 1998. The sample heading misspells Safety in one note. A new title 18 section orders the Attorney General to test each person convicted of a federal offense and sentenced to six months or more.
