Testing follows when Bureau of Prisons guidelines find that person at risk. Testing follows when an inmate or detainee may have transmitted the virus to an officer or another person lawfully present.
plaw-105-371-1998: A Medal of Honor a century late is authorized by Public Law 105-371, approved November 12, 1998. The President is authorized and requested to award the congressional Medal of Honor posthumously to Theodore Roosevelt of New York. The honor is for his gallant and heroic actions in the attack on San Juan Heights, Cuba, during the Spanish-American War on July 1, 1898. The award may be made without regard to the time limit in section 3744 of title 10, using the award criteria of Roosevelt's own time.
plaw-105-372-1998:
Saving a shrinking California sea begins with study under the Salton Sea Reclamation Act of 1998, Public Law 105-372, approved November 12, 1998. The Secretary of the Interior, through the Bureau of Reclamation, must run a feasibility study and build a project to reclaim the Salton Sea. Definitions name the congressional committees involved and the Salton Sea Authority, a California joint powers body formed June 2 under state law.

Title I authorizes the feasibility study and parallel wildlife resources studies. It also renames the Salton Sea National Wildlife Refuge as the Sonny Bono Salton Sea National Wildlife Refuge. Title II orders emergency action to improve water quality in the Alamo River and the New River, dealing with irrigation drainage water. The two rivers carry much of the drainage that feeds, and harms, the sea.
plaw-105-373-1998: A television program made for Ukraine may be shared with two archives under Public Law 105-373, approved November 12, 1998. Domestic release rules do not bar the gift. The Director of the United States Information Agency may give copies of Window on America, made by WORLDNET Television, to holders. One is the Ukrainian Museum and Archives in Cleveland, Ohio. The other is the Slavics Collection at Indiana University Libraries. Neither holder may broadcast the material. Both must repay copying costs, and the authority ends five years after enactment.
plaw-105-374-1998: Visitation orders gain the same federal backing as custody orders in Public Law 105-374, approved November 12, 1998. It amends section 1738A of title 28. That section deals with enforcing child custody orders across state lines. Phrases about custody become custody or visitation phrases throughout. The word grandparent is added after parent in one place. A new term is defined. A visitation determination is a court judgment, decree, or order that provides for visiting a child. It includes permanent and temporary orders, first orders, and later changes.
plaw-105-375-1998: Crimes by diplomats must be reported to Congress every year under Public Law 105-375, approved November 12, 1998. It adds section 204B, Crimes Committed by Diplomats, to the Foreign Missions Act. The Secretary of State must send an annual Report on Cases Involving Diplomatic Immunity. It must state how many people in the United States hold immunity from criminal jurisdiction. It must list each case where an authority reported reasonable cause to believe such a person committed a serious criminal offense. The report adds details the act requires.
plaw-105-376-1998:
A New Mexico site gains its watershed in Public Law 105-376, approved November 12, 1998. Its name is the Bandelier National Monument Administrative Improvement and Watershed Protection Act of 1998. The law changes the Bandelier boundary. It adds lands in the headwaters of the Upper Alamo Watershed that drain into the site. Those lands were not under any federal land agency. Buying them, or taking them by gift, is authorized.

Congress found that a presidential order of February 11, 1916 created Bandelier. The aim was to preserve the archeological resources of a vanished people. Land was added as much as protection required. The boundary and purpose were changed several times after that. In 1932 the Otowi Section of the Santa Fe National Forest moved into the site. That transfer covered some four thousand six hundred ninety-nine acres.
plaw-105-377-1998: States and Canadian provinces may fight forest fires together under Public Law 105-377, approved November 12, 1998. Congress consents to an interstate forest fire protection compact, the Northwest Wildland Fire Protection Agreement. Its purpose is better prevention, presuppression, and control of forest fires in the Northwest wildland region and nearby Canada, through mutual aid and shared operating plans. The agreement takes effect for members when two or more ratify it. Named members include Oregon, Washington, Alaska, Idaho, Montana, the Yukon Territory, British Columbia, and Alberta.
plaw-105-378-1998:
Immigrant tenement life in New York is preserved by Public Law 105-378, approved November 12, 1998. The law establishes the Lower East Side Tenement National Historic Site. Congress finds that immigration, and the diversity it brought, is a key part of what defines the United States, and that many citizens trace ancestry to people born in other nations.

Late in the nineteenth century and early in the twentieth, immigrant volume far passed any other era. No neighborhood absorbed more newcomers than Manhattan's Lower East Side. The tenement at 97 Orchard Street survives as a rare example of the humble buildings that housed them. It is run as a museum by the Lower East Side Tenement Museum, dedicated to interpreting immigrant life in that neighborhood.
plaw-105-379-1998:
Food stamps for people who have died are stopped by Public Law 105-379, approved November 12, 1998. It amends the Food Stamp Act of 1977. Each state food stamp agency must work with the Commissioner of Social Security to get information on deceased individuals, and use it to verify that benefits are not issued to the dead.

The Secretary of Agriculture must report progress and effectiveness of those arrangements by September 1, 2000, to House and Senate agriculture committees and others named in the text. The act's full title adds a second job: the Secretary must study options for designing and running a national database. That database would track participation in federal means-tested public assistance programs, linking the death check to a wider eligibility question.
plaw-105-380-1998: Land next to a Hawaii park may be bought under the Hawaii Volcanoes National Park Adjustment Act of 1998, Public Law 105-380, approved November 12, 1998. It removes restrictions on acquiring certain land touching Hawaii Volcanoes National Park. The first section of the Act of June 20, 1938 gains a closing exception: land shown on a map titled NPS-PAC 1997HW may be purchased with donated or appropriated funds. That single inserted clause is the whole change.
plaw-105-381-1998: Cross-border disaster help is approved by Public Law 105-381, a joint resolution approved November 12, 1998. Congress consents to the Pacific Northwest Emergency Management Arrangement. The parties are Alaska, Idaho, Oregon, and Washington, plus British Columbia and the Yukon Territory. They stress shared civil readiness for disasters. The pact covers response and recovery work. It reaches natural and man-made disasters. It also reaches declared or undeclared hostilities, including enemy attack. Working with neighbors, they say, makes each party stronger.
plaw-105-382-1998: State Department agents gain law-enforcement style pensions under the Department of State Special Agents Retirement Act of 1998, Public Law 105-382, approved November 13, 1998. It amends the Foreign Service Act of 1980. Annuities for certain special agents and security staff are computed as for federal law enforcement officers generally. A special agent is a State employee with primary skill code 2501. The duties are chiefly investigating, apprehending, or detaining criminal suspects. They may instead be protecting persons against threats to personal safety.
plaw-105-383-1998:
The Coast Guard is funded and reorganized in small ways by the Coast Guard Authorization Act of 1998, Public Law 105-383, approved November 13, 1998. It authorizes appropriations for fiscal years 1998 and 1999 for the Coast Guard. Title I covers authorization amounts, military strength and training levels, and the LORAN-C navigation system.

Title II turns to management: severance pay, awards programs, use of funds for commercial vehicles at military funerals, and repayment to the Novato, California Reuse Commission. It also gives law enforcement authority to special agents of the Coast Guard Investigative Service, and orders reports on excess property and aids to navigation, plus fees for navigation help. Title III on marine safety begins by extending the territorial sea for certain laws.
plaw-105-384-1998: A fishing agreement with Poland is approved by Public Law 105-384, approved November 13, 1998. A waiting rule in the Magnuson-Stevens fishery law does not block it. The governing international fishery agreement between the United States and the Republic of Poland is approved. The President sent it to Congress on February 5, 1998. It takes effect at enactment. Title II handles other fisheries items. It reauthorizes the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Convention Act of 1995 for each fiscal year through fiscal year 2001. Small technical wording fixes are made too.
plaw-105-385-1998:
Farm development across sub-Saharan Africa is supported by the Africa: Seeds of Hope Act of 1998, Public Law 105-385, approved November 13, 1998. The act backs farm and rural growth there. Title I is assistance for sub-Saharan Africa, and later titles reach worldwide food programs.

Title I sections create an Africa Food Security Initiative and microenterprise assistance. Producer-owned cooperative marketing groups receive support, as do farm and rural activities of the Overseas Private Investment Corporation, and agricultural research and extension work. Title II covers nonemergency food assistance, and one subtitle is the Bill Emerson Humanitarian Trust Act of 1998. Miscellaneous provisions close the act, tying farm aid to a named humanitarian reserve.
plaw-105-386-1998:
Longer prison terms for gun crimes are set by Public Law 105-386, approved November 13, 1998, whose act heading promises to throttle criminal use of guns. It rewrites section 924(c) of title 18 on using a firearm during a crime of violence or drug trafficking crime. The new text covers using, carrying, or possessing a firearm in furtherance of such a crime.

On top of the punishment for the main crime, a person who uses or carries a firearm receives at least five years. Brandishing the firearm raises the floor to seven years, and discharging it raises the floor to ten years. A short-barreled rifle, short-barreled shotgun, or semiautomatic assault weapon also brings at least ten years. Greater minimums elsewhere in the subsection or the law still control where they apply.
plaw-105-387-1998: Judgment money for Sioux tribes is distributed under the Mississippi Sioux Tribes Judgment Fund Distribution Act of 1998, Public Law 105-387, approved November 13, 1998. Definitions name a covered Indian tribe, its governing body, and the Fund Account. That account is the Treasury trust account run by the Secretary of the Interior through the Office of Trust Fund Management. An earlier law, Public Law 92-555, does not bar the plan. Funds from a 1968 law for the Sisseton and Wahpeton Tribes are distributed and used as this act directs.
plaw-105-388-1998: Energy saving programs run five more years under the Energy Conservation Reauthorization Act of 1998, Public Law 105-388, approved November 13, 1998. It extends programs in the Energy Policy and Conservation Act and the Energy Conservation and Production Act. For the state energy conservation program and for the schools and hospitals program, needed sums are authorized for fiscal years 1999 through 2003. The weatherization program receives the same five-year authorization. A sunset section for energy savings performance contracts follows in the text.
plaw-105-389-1998:
The one hundredth birthday of powered flight gets a commission in the Centennial of Flight Commemoration Act, Public Law 105-389, approved November 13, 1998. A commission will help commemorate the centennial and the achievements of the Wright brothers. Section 3 is the establishment section, right after the findings.

Congress found that December 17, 2003 will mark one hundred years since the first successful manned, free, controlled, and sustained flight by a power-driven, heavier-than-air machine. Orville and Wilbur Wright fulfilled the old dream of flying, and the airplane changed transportation, commerce, communication, and warfare worldwide. Their work stands as a triumph of American ingenuity and diligence, worth renewing through local, national, and international observances in the centennial year.
plaw-105-390-1998: College help for families of fallen safety officers is widened by the Police, Fire, and Emergency Officers Educational Assistance Act of 1998, Public Law 105-390, approved November 13, 1998. It gives financial help for college costs of dependents of federal, state, and local public safety officers. The officers must have been killed, or permanently and totally disabled, by a traumatic injury in the line of duty. Headings change from civilian federal law enforcement to public safety. The help is reduced by benefits from other sources named in the text.
plaw-105-391-1998:
Park service management is tightened by the National Parks Omnibus Management Act of 1998, Public Law 105-391, approved November 13, 1998. The law aims at better management and more accountability for National Park Service programs. Its table of contents shows titles on careers, resources, and how new park areas are studied.

Title I covers protection, interpretation, and research in the park system, employee and management training, and park budgets with accountability. Title II sets a resource inventory and management system: a research mandate, cooperative agreements, an inventory and monitoring program, and making resources available for scientific study. It also requires study results to shape management decisions, while keeping certain information confidential. Title III governs studies of adding new areas.
plaw-105-392-1998:
Training health workers is consolidated in the Health Professions Education Partnerships Act of 1998, Public Law 105-392, approved November 13, 1998. It amends the Public Health Service Act to join and reauthorize health professions programs and programs for minority and disadvantaged students. The sample's heading drops an s from Partnerships in one note, a minor defect in the text.

Title I begins with a grant program for under-represented minority health professions, then training in primary care medicine and dentistry. It adds joint, community-based linkages between schools and care sites, workforce information and analysis, and public health workforce development. Preference rules, definitions, and a National Health Service Corps amendment follow. A later subtitle is devoted to nursing workforce development, showing nurses treated as a separate pipeline.
plaw-105-393-1998:
Two regional aid programs are reformed together in Public Law 105-393, approved November 13, 1998. Its full name is the Economic Development Administration and Appalachian Regional Development Reform Act of 1998. The law reauthorizes and reforms programs under two 1965 acts. One is the Public Works and Economic Development Act. The other is the Appalachian Regional Development Act.

Title I reauthorizes the 1965 public works law. It adds conforming changes, transition rules, and an effective date. Title II turns to the Appalachian program. It restates findings and purposes for that region. It then revises how the regional commission meets and pays its office costs and staff. The powers of the commission are spelled out in the last section of the sample. The reform has a housekeeping cast.
plaw-105-394-1998:
Devices that help people with disabilities get state grant support under the Assistive Technology Act of 1998, Public Law 105-394, approved November 13, 1998. The act supports grant programs to states. Those programs address the tech needs of people with disabilities. Findings, purposes, and definitions open the law.

Title I creates the state grant programs. One part gives continuity grants to states that earlier received limited tech help funding. A second part funds state protection and advocacy work tied to such tech. Title II covers national activities. It coordinates federal research and names the National Council on Disability and the barriers compliance board. Other sections back small business incentives, tech transfer, and universal design in products and buildings.
plaw-1998: Nuratu Olarewaju Abeke Kadiri is the person relieved by Private Law 105-9, approved on November 10, 1998 (H.R. 1949). Congress made her eligible for an immigrant visa, or for adjustment of status to lawful permanent resident, despite the caps in the Immigration and Nationality Act. If she entered before the filing deadline, her entry counts as lawful for that adjustment. Her application, with fees, was due within two years, and the State Department then reduces the visa pool for her birth country by one.
plos-pbio-0020098:
György Hutvágner, Martin J. Simard, Craig C. Mello, and their group tested a way to block small RNAs in PLOS Biology in 2004. Small RNAs can silence specific genes, a process called RNA interference. The team used short custom molecules that pair with a chosen small RNA and stop it from working.

A clean off switch lets scientists ask what one small RNA does in a living animal. Without it, they can only add silencing, not remove a natural one. The method targets single RNA sequences with care, so side effects stay low. Tools like this helped turn small RNAs from a curiosity into a standard way to probe gene function across biology.
plos-pbio-0020198:
Kyra Oswald-Richter, Stacy M. Grill, Nikki Shariat, and their team examined regulatory T cells and HIV in PLOS Biology in 2004. Regulatory T cells calm the immune system. HIV can infect them, and can also infect normal T cells that have been reprogrammed to act like regulatory ones.

That dual route matters because regulatory cells sit at a control point of immunity. If HIV hides in them or copies their calming tricks, it may quiet the very response meant to fight it. The study maps both natural and reprogrammed cells as targets. Understanding this niche could help explain why HIV persists despite strong immune attacks, and where new therapies might aim.
plos-pbio-0020398:
Audrey P. Gasch, Alan M. Moses, Derek Y. Chiang, and their team compared gene control systems in fungi in PLOS Biology in 2004. Fungi in the ascomycete group include yeast and molds. Their genes are switched by binding sites near each gene, and those sites change as species evolve.

The team tracked how whole control systems were kept, rewired, or lost across these fungi. Some core systems stayed stable for hundreds of millions of years, while others turned over fast. That contrast shows evolution tinkers with control even when the genes themselves stay much the same. The work is a model for studying regulatory change, the part of evolution many now think drives most new traits.
plos-pone-0000098:
Claudia Arce, Carlos Pérez-Plasencia, Aurora González-Fierro, and their team ran an early clinical test in breast cancer in PLOS ONE in 2006. Epigenetic therapy uses drugs that switch silenced genes back on. The team added such therapy to standard chemotherapy given before surgery for locally advanced tumors.

A proof-of-principle study checks whether an idea works at all in patients, before large trials. The authors report the combined treatment could be given and showed signs of activity against the tumors. That green light is the true product of a small study like this. It justifies the cost and effort of proper trials to learn whether the benefit is real.
plos-pone-0000198:
Graham R. Martin, Kerry-Jayne Wilson, J. Martin Wild, and colleagues published this bird senses paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Kiwi are flightless, nocturnal birds from New Zealand that hunt by smell and touch. The authors report that kiwi forego vision in guiding their night activities, relying on their other senses instead.

Most birds are visual animals, so a bird that largely gives up sight is striking. The paper examines the kiwi's eyes and behavior to support that claim. It reframes the kiwi as a mammal-like bird, feeling its way through the dark forest floor. It also informs how this threatened species should be studied and protected.
plos-pone-0000298:
Tamara Glaser, Steven M. Pollard, Austin Smith, and colleagues published this stem cell paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Neural stem cells, called NS cells here, can be grown stuck to a dish and expanded over time. The authors demonstrate their tripotential differentiation: one cell line can produce all three main neural cell types, neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes.

A stem cell line is only useful if it keeps its full potential while expanding. Showing adherently grown NS cells stay tripotent validates them as a research tool. Such lines support work on brain development and on diseases where specific neural cells are lost.
plos-pone-0000398:
Inês Ribeiro and colleagues studied two genes that pace cell growth in the developing heart, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The genes, Tbx2 and Tbx3, belong to a family of developmental control genes. The team examined how they regulate the dynamics of cell proliferation, the rate at which heart cells multiply, during heart remodeling.

A growing heart must add cells fast enough to build the organ but stop in the right places to shape its chambers. Genes that set the pace of division help draw those boundaries. Understanding their control of heart growth bears on congenital heart defects, which often trace back to errors in these early patterning steps.
plos-pone-0000498:
Joy G. Ghosh, Scott A. Houck, and John I. Clark mapped the working surfaces of a lens chaperone protein, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Human αB crystallin is a molecular chaperone, a helper that keeps other proteins from clumping; in the eye lens it also provides structure. The team identified interactive domains in it that modulate microtubule assembly and disassembly.

Microtubules are the cell's rails and scaffolding, constantly built and taken apart. A chaperone that tunes that cycle connects protein quality control to cell architecture. αB crystallin also appears in brain and muscle. Its mutations cause cataract and muscle disease. So mapping its active regions has reach beyond the eye.
plos-pone-0000598:
Anouk C. Vedder and colleagues compared two replacement enzymes for a rare storage disease, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Fabry disease results from a missing enzyme that leaves fats to accumulate in organs. The comparative trial tested treatment with agalsidase alfa or beta at a dose of 0.2 mg/kg.

Two marketed versions of a therapy invite an obvious question: do they perform alike at the same dose? Head-to-head trials in rare diseases are hard to run because patients are few, making each one valuable. The outcome informs prescribing for a lifelong, expensive treatment.
plos-pone-0000698:
Magalie Lenoir, Fuschia Serre, Lauriane Cantin and colleagues compared the pull of sweetness with the pull of cocaine, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Refined sugars such as sucrose and fructose were absent from most diets until very recently in human history. Today, overconsumption of sugar-rich food helps drive the obesity epidemic. The team asked how strong sugar's reward really is.

Their title states the headline result: intense sweetness surpasses cocaine reward. In plain terms, the sweet option won over the drug option in their tests. A result like that reframes sugar from a soft pleasure to a powerful reward signal. It feeds debate about food design, addiction, and public health.
plos-pone-0000798:
Gerhard Kelter, Daniel Steinbach, Venkata Badireenath Konkimalla and colleagues asked why some tumor cells resist a malaria drug turned cancer drug. Artesunate exerts profound anti-cancer activity, and ferrous iron enhances tumor cells' susceptibility to it. The transferrin receptor, which imports iron by internalizing the carrier protein transferrin, is over-expressed in rapidly growing cells, including many tumors.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE study examines the transferrin receptor and two ABC transporters, ABCB6 and ABCB7, in resistance and differentiation of tumor cells toward artesunate. Transporters can pump drugs out or handle the iron that activates them. Knowing which proteins set sensitivity helps predict which tumors artesunate can treat.
plos-pone-0000898:
Hendrik de Jonge, Rudolf Fehrmann, Eveline de Bont and colleagues set out to choose housekeeping genes on evidence, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Gene studies need steady reference genes to make fair comparisons. The catch is that popular choices such as ACTB and GAPDH can swing widely between samples and conditions.

Unsteady references quietly corrupt results across whole fields. The team weighed candidates against data rather than habit, aiming for references that stay level. Their selection gives labs a safer base for measuring gene activity. The paper is a methods warning as much as a result: check your ruler before you measure.
plos-pone-0000998:
Alexander Sponner, Wolfram Vater, Shamci Monajembashi and colleagues unraveled the layered makeup of spider silk, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Silks are fairly well understood molecule by molecule. How those molecules are organized in layers inside a spun fiber, and what else the fiber contains, was much less clear.

The team linked defined structural elements in dragline silk from the spider Nephila clavipes to their molecular parts. Dragline silk is the famously strong thread spiders use as a lifeline. Mapping its hierarchy helps explain how soft proteins make a fiber tougher than steel by weight. That map also guides attempts to spin artificial silk.
plos-pone-0001098:
Keyue Ding, Samantha McDonough and Iftikhar Kullo found signs of positive selection in part of a cholesterol gene, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Cholesterol balance is kept by tuned control of absorption, liver production and blood clearance. PCSK9, a secreted enzyme, is one of the controllers, and its variants move cholesterol levels strongly.

The team analyzed PCSK9 across fourteen primate species. Positive selection, change favored rather than merely tolerated, showed in the gene's C-terminal domain. Selection on a cholesterol controller hints at dietary pressures in primate history. It also flags which part of the protein evolution could not leave alone.
plos-pone-0001198:
Molecular chaperones help fold proteins inside cells, but they also circulate in the blood and can signal to immune cells. Alireza Shamaei-Tousi and colleagues measured these proteins in patients treated for periodontal disease, gum disease, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Evidence was emerging that chaperones exist in the circulation and can modulate white blood cell function.

The authors report differential regulation of circulating chaperone levels during treatment for periodontal disease. Gum disease is a chronic infection and inflammation, so it offers a window on how local disease affects body-wide signals. Their results connect oral health to the wider immune state.
plos-pone-0001298:
Between 2005 and 2050, the world's population is forecast to grow by 2.7 billion, mostly in low-income countries. Andrew Tatem and colleagues built high-resolution population maps for East Africa to help planners cope, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Census data alone are too coarse: they give totals for districts, not where people actually live.

The authors combined land cover data with census counts to distribute people across the landscape at fine resolution. Growth on that scale has social, economic, and environmental impacts. Maps like these guide where schools, clinics, vaccination campaigns, and aid should go.
plos-pone-0001398:
Daniel Rubio and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on stem cells that changed on their own in the lab. The team had earlier found that human stem cells from fat and marrow could turn into cells with tumor like traits. Here they mapped the gene shifts behind that change. Such maps are vital for safe use of stem cells in care.

By profiling the changed cells, they named the main gene and pathway shifts at work. The findings flag risks that clinics must screen for before transplants. They also show what to watch as cells are grown for long spans. That watch list can make stem cell cures safer for patients.
plos-pone-0001498:
Laura Forsberg White and Marcello Pagano published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on the 1918 flu pandemic. That pandemic was the most deadly outbreak of the last century. With fresh fears of a new pandemic, its spread rate was worth a fresh count. The team used records from towns in Maryland and from two ships with well logged outbreaks.

From those close records they gauged how fast the 1918 virus passed from person to person. A firm rate from real data beats a guess from broad counts. It lets planners test control plans against a proven hard case. The work thus serves both history and future readiness.
plos-pone-0001598:
Sricharan Bandhakavi and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on yeast that resists a key drug. The drug rapamycin blocks the TOR path, a master growth switch in cells. Some yeast shrug the drug off. The team combined protein counts with gene tests to find how. They flagged a heat shock factor as a key player.

Switching that factor on both curbed resistance and dimmed TOR signals. That ties stress reply to growth control in a new way. TOR is a cancer drug target in people, so yeast clues carry weight. They may hint at how tumors dodge TOR drugs too.
plos-pone-0001698:
Jian Fu, Kathryn Fong, Alfonso Bellacosa, and their co-authors studied a tumor suppressor protein lost in lung cancer, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The protein is VILIP-1, part of a family of neuronal calcium sensors. In animal models it acts as a tumor suppressor, slowing cell growth, adhesion, and invasion in squamous cell carcinoma.

The team examined non-small cell lung carcinomas, the commonest lung cancers, to learn how VILIP-1 is turned down and whether its level predicts survival. The full text gives the tumor cell tests, the mechanisms of downregulation they found, and the survival analysis. A protein whose loss marks worse outcomes could guide prognosis, and restoring it is a possible treatment idea.
plos-pone-0001798:
Jonghwan Kim, Ji-hoon Lee, and Vishwanath R. Iyer mapped the target genes of a cancer-linked protein across the genome in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Myc is a transcription factor involved in many human cancers, and its overexpression is tied to malignant transformation. In normal cells Myc rises with growth signals and in turn regulates downstream genes.

Their global identification of Myc targets reveals a direct role in mitochondrial biogenesis, the building of new mitochondria. It also details how Myc uses its DNA binding motif in living cells. The full text gives the target list and validation tests. A growth switch that also orders more power plants explains part of how Myc fuels tumor growth.
plos-pone-0001898:
Branwen Hennig and co-authors asked why genes shape the response to the hepatitis B vaccine, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The vaccine is safe and works well, yet the level of protective proteins it raises fades with time. A high peak right after the shots means a slower fade and a lower risk of infection later.

The team looked for host gene traits that track with that peak level and with how fast it falls. Knowing which traits matter could help spot people who need extra shots. It also shows how much of vaccine success is set by the person, not just the dose. Such work can guide smarter vaccine plans.
plos-pone-0001998:
Pedro Martins, Fernando Rocha, and Ana Damas studied the physics of growing protein crystals, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. To read a protein's shape, labs grow crystals of it, most often by vapor diffusion: a drop loses water slowly until crystals form. The rate at which water leaves the drop sets the quality of the crystals.

Past attempts to solve the math of that evaporation, by formula or by numbers, left gaps. The trio set out the basics of how water balance is reached in the setup. A rational grasp of the step could replace trial and error with design in crystal growth.
plos-pone-0002098:
Kamran Shalchian-Tabrizi and co-authors used many genes to redraw the tree at the root of animals, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Animals are kin to fungi and to Choanozoa, mostly one-celled protozoans, in a great group called opisthokonts. To set the order of events when animals evolved from one-celled ancestors, the branches closest to that split must be right.

The team built a multigene phylogeny of Choanozoa and its kin. Many genes together can settle branches that single genes leave shaky. Knowing which living groups are animals' closest kin shows what the first animals inherited, and what they invented.
plos-pone-0002198:
Jason Rasgon proposed a new way to tell what a mosquito has fed on, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. A mosquito that drinks blood can pass on malaria, dengue fever, and other diseases. Knowing which animals its blood came from helps trace how those diseases spread, but digestion destroys the meal fast. Current tests only work soon after feeding.

Rasgon suggests stable isotope analysis, which reads lasting chemical signatures in the mosquito's tissues. Those signatures can survive complete digestion of the blood meal. If the method holds up, disease teams could learn the feeding habits of caught mosquitoes long after the evidence would once have vanished.
plos-pone-0002298:
Jonathan FitzGerald, Ming Luo, and Abed Chaudhury tested a prediction about parent conflict in plant seeds, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The parental conflict idea says a mother plant restrains embryo growth while the father pushes it up, each serving their own genetic interest. In plants, the enzyme MET1, which places methyl marks on DNA, is a central regulator of the imprinted genes that tune seed growth.

The team asked how DNA methylation links the two parents' opposing pressures to actual embryo size. Their results show methylation causes predominantly maternal control of plant embryo growth. The finding refines how genetic conflict in seeds is understood at the molecular level.
plos-pone-0002398:
A research team led by Martin reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Bronwen Martin, Michele Pearson, Randall Brenneman, and others. Its subject is conserved and Differential Effects of Dietary Energy Intake on the Hippocampal Transcriptomes of Females and Males. The level of dietary energy intake influences metabolism, reproductive function, the development of age-related diseases, and even cognitive behavior.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002498:
Work from Hwang and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Nathaniel S. Hwang, Shyni Varghese, Jennifer Elisseeff, and others. Its subject is derivation of Chondrogenically-Committed Cells from Human Embryonic Cells for Cartilage Tissue Regeneration. Heterogeneous and uncontrolled differentiation of human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) in embryoid bodies (EBs) limits the potential use of hESCs for cell-based therapies.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002598:
In 2008, Valenzuela and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Michael J. Valenzuela, Perminder Sachdev, Wei Wen, and others. Its subject is lifespan Mental Activity Predicts Diminished Rate of Hippocampal Atrophy. Epidemiological studies suggest that complex mental activity may reduce the risk for dementia, however an underlying mechanism remains unclear.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002698:
Published in PLOS ONE in 2008, research by Sun-Chong Wang and colleagues addresses Age-Specific epigenetic drift in Late-Onset alzheimer's disease. The catalog record names Sun-Chong Wang first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Despite an enormous research effort. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002798:
Paolo Facella led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was diurnal and circadian rhythms in the tomato transcriptome and their modulation by cryptochrome photoreceptors. Authorship is credited in the record to Paolo Facella and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Circadian clocks are internal molecular time-keeping mechanisms that provide living organisms with the ability to adjust their growth and physiology and to anticipate diurnal. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002898:
Claudia Rübe, Jan Palm, Michael Erren and colleagues asked in 2008 whether blood cytokine levels can predict lung injury after radiation. Radiation is the main treatment for advanced lung cancer that cannot be removed by surgery. Its most serious dose-limiting harm is radiation pneumonitis, an inflammation of the lung.

Earlier reports had suggested that cytokine signals in plasma might flag who is at risk. The PLOS ONE paper tests that promise with a question in its title and data behind it. If such a test worked, doctors could tailor dose and watch high-risk patients more closely.
plos-pone-0002998:
Veronika Butin-Israeli, Dotan Uzi, Mahmoud Abd-El-Latif and co-authors used empty virus shells to protect mouse kidneys in 2008. Viruses trigger host defense and survival pathways during infection, but using real viruses for therapy is hampered by their harmful effects. SV40 capsids without DNA offer the trigger without the genome.

These DNA-free particles induced stress responses, survival pathways, and a pause in apoptosis, the authors report. Mice were protected from acute renal failure. Published in PLOS ONE, the approach tries to borrow a virus's alarm signals while leaving its dangers behind. Its full text, with tables and references, is openly available to any reader online.
plos-pone-0003098:
Gilberto Paz-Filho, Talin Babikian, Robert Asarnow and co-authors reported leptin treatment improving cognitive development in 2008. Leptin changes brain structure, neuron excitability, and synaptic plasticity, and it regulates feeding circuits. Its effects on how a child's learning and thinking develop were unknown.

Leptin replacement improved cognitive development, the title states, in the case or cases studied. Published in PLOS ONE, leptin deficiency is rare but revealing: a hormone known for satiety also shapes the developing mind. The finding widens what replacement therapy should be assessed for. Its full text, with tables and references, is openly available to any reader online.
plos-pone-0003198: Binh An Diep and colleagues published a PLOS ONE study in 2008 on a toxin in community MRSA, the drug-resistant staph bacterium spread outside hospitals. The title states its subject: what part Panton-Valentine leukocidin plays in how this bacterium causes disease. No abstract text beyond the title was supplied, so this record states no findings.
plos-pone-0003298:
Christopher D. Fiorillo proposes a general theory of neural computation in this single-author 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Although there has been tremendous progress in understanding the mechanics of the nervous system, there has not been a general theory of its computational function. The author presents a theory that relates established biophysical properties of single generic neurons to principles of computation.

The theory is based on prediction by single neurons, as the title states. Readers get an attempt to ground brain computation in what one neuron can do, rather than in abstract networks alone. Single neuron prediction, if right, would simplify many models of learning.
plos-pone-0003398:
Kerry F. Shea and colleagues watched how cancer cells move in this 2008 study. Tumor cells can crawl in two ways inside body tissue. One way is flat and spread out, the other is round with bulging bubbles. The team looked at two proteins, ROCK1 and LIMK2, that help drive this motion.

The two proteins were found working together in the spread-out cells. In the round, bulging cells, that partnership was absent. The split shows each style of movement uses its own machinery. Knowing the machinery may help slow the spread of tumors through tissue.
plos-pone-0003498:
Rami N. Hannoush filmed a key development signal in action for this 2008 study. The Wnt pathway steers growth in embryos across many species. Its signal works by stabilizing a protein called β-catenin. When the pathway fires wrongly, cancer and degenerative disease can follow.

Hannoush used quantitative imaging over time to clock that stabilization. The movies show how fast β-catenin builds after Wnt arrives. Precise timing helps others model the pathway's behavior. Drug hunters can use the same measures to test blockers. Wnt signals also steer gut and skin renewal in adult life.
plos-pone-0003598:
Brian S. Nelson and Terry T. Takahashi studied echo hearing in barn owls in this 2008 paper. Barn owls hunt by sound with remarkable precision. Echoes help animals judge where sounds and surfaces are. Two measures matter: how faint an echo is noticed, and its delay.

The team found echo threshold and echo delay are independent in the owl. One measure can change without dragging the other. That split suggests separate processing for each echo feature. Nature's sonar keeps its channels cleanly divided. Owls hear far better than humans, which is why labs study them.
plos-pone-0003698:
Katsuhiko Nosho, Natsumi Irahara, Kaori Shima, and colleagues published this colorectal cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Some colon tumors carry heavy DNA methylation, a pattern called the CpG island methylator phenotype, or CIMP. Five gene promoters are often used as stand-in markers for it.

Using a large population-based sample, the team ran a broad statistical analysis of CIMP. They examined its links with microsatellite instability and BRAF mutation, both common in colon cancer. The analysis sharpens how this tumor subtype is defined and what it may mean for patients.
plos-pone-0003798:
Giorgio F. Gilestro published this neuroscience study in PLOS ONE in 2008. As the nervous system of the fruit fly Drosophila develops, nerve fibers must cross the body's midline in a controlled way. Crossing too much or too little both cause wiring errors. More than one guidance system watches the process.

Gilestro shows that these systems are redundant: when one mechanism fails, another covers for it. Midline crossing stays regulated because the backup mechanisms overlap. The work shows the developing nervous system refusing to leave a vital wiring step to a single safeguard.
plos-pone-0003898:
Pedro L. Vera, Kenneth A. Iczkowski, Xihai Wang, and co-authors studied bladder inflammation in rats in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article centers on two proteins, MIF and CXCR4. MIF drives inflammation and is known to take part in cystitis, a bladder condition. Lab work had shown MIF can also bind CXCR4, a receptor on cells.

The team asked whether that pairing occurs in real bladder tissue. They used the drug cyclophosphamide to trigger cystitis in twenty male rats. Afterward, bladder CXCR4 levels rose and its pairing with MIF grew. The result links the receptor to bladder inflammation in living tissue.
plos-pone-0003998:
Monika B. Lehmann, Paul J. Funston, Cailey R. Owen, and co-authors tracked lions on a South African reserve in 2008. Managers increasingly intervene in the lives of large carnivores there. Knowing how predators use space is central to that management. Many forces shape where lions range and hold territory.

Their PLOS ONE article reports home range use on Karongwe Game Reserve. It also describes how the lions behaved toward rivals at borders. Such data guide decisions on fencing, releases, and conflict control. Small reserves especially need that spatial knowledge to keep lions safely. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004098:
Judith Helena Prieto, Sasa Koncarevic, Sung Kyu Park, and co-authors compared parasite proteins under drug treatment in 2008. Protein studies illuminate parasite biology and drug action together. For most antimalarial drugs, the mode of action stays partly unclear. Resistance mechanisms are likewise not fully explained.

Their PLOS ONE article runs large-scale proteome analysis on Plasmodium falciparum. Parasites under drug treatment showed which proteins rose or fell. Those shifts can reveal how drugs kill and how resistance begins. The data set serves malaria researchers hunting new drug targets. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004198:
Johanna Kallio and colleagues published this methods study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Growing protein crystals is a slow process of trial and error, and it limits how many protein structures get solved. A universal nucleant, a seed material that starts crystals growing for many proteins, would speed things up.

The team tested polystyrene nanospheres, tiny plastic beads, as such a seed. They measured the contribution the spheres make toward getting proteins to crystallise. If a cheap, general seed works, structural biologists could solve more of the proteins that currently resist crystallisation.
plos-pone-0004298:
Diego Gazzolo and colleagues published this newborn study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Babies who suffer perinatal asphyxia, a lack of oxygen around birth, can die in the newborn period. Yet few tools predict which full-term infants are at risk of that outcome.

The team studied urine testing for S100B, a protein released from damaged brain cells, in full-term asphyxiated newborns. They measured the diagnostic accuracy of the test at birth for predicting neonatal death. A simple urine test that flags the babies in greatest danger could guide intensive care where it is scarce.
plos-pone-0004398:
Carbon nanotubes are tiny tubes with many planned uses in industry and medicine. Their safety depends partly on how immune cells handle them. Nagarjun Konduru, Yulia Tyurina, Weihong Feng, and co-authors studied that handling in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper used single-walled carbon nanotubes. Plain nanotubes are poorly recognized by phagocytes, the cells that eat foreign matter.

The team coated the tubes with phosphatidylserine, a fat found on cell surfaces. Dying cells show this fat as an eat-me signal. The coating targeted the tubes to professional phagocytes. It worked in lab dishes and in living animals. That trick could help control nanotube action in the body. It also sharpens tests of nanotube safety.
plos-pone-0004498:
Fish mothers pass immune protection to their eggs, show Zhiping Wang, Shicui Zhang, Zhou Tong, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009, using zebrafish. Most fish embryos develop outside the mother's body, in water full of germs. Yet embryos have little ability to mount a strong defense of their own. How they survive those first attacks was poorly understood.

The team studied the alternative complement pathway, a fast, always-on arm of immunity. They show that components of this system are transferred from mother to offspring in zebrafish. They also show the transferred parts play a protective role. Maternal gifts like these bridge the gap until the young fish can defend itself, a strategy that may be widespread among egg-laying animals.
plos-pone-0004598:
How many gene regions it takes to barcode a crocus is tested by Ole Seberg and Gitte Petersen in PLOS ONE in 2009. DNA barcoding promises to revolutionize taxonomy: species could be identified from small, standardized portions of the genome instead of by morphology alone. The concept gained momentum in many animal groups, but the higher plant world proved harder.

Plants often need several loci, gene regions, read together before species separate cleanly. Using crocus as the test case, the authors count how many loci a reliable barcode needs. The answer matters for building plant identification systems used in trade, conservation, and customs. A barcode that confuses species is worse than none, so the minimum evidence must be known.
plos-pone-0004698:
Danica Harbaugh and colleagues used gene markers to sort a complex tree group in Hawaii, for PLOS ONE in 2009. Five kinds of Metrosideros trees are named in the islands, led by one wide spread form. The trees vary a lot in shape, leaf, and habitat, yet the forms blend into each other.

That blend made it hard to tell where one kind ends and the next begins. The team used nuclear gene markers to test the splits. Gene data can show if named kinds are real lines or just local forms. The answer guides how Hawaii guards its native forests.
plos-pone-0004798:
Jasper Mullenders and colleagues used a large shRNA barcode screen that identified a clock gene as a putative p53 pathway regulator. In PLOS ONE in 2009. The p53 tumor suppressor gene is mutated in about half of human cancers. Even when intact, its pathway is thought inactivated in the vast majority of tumors, so understanding insensitivity to p53 is of major importance.

The screen tested thousands of gene knockdowns for loss of p53 response. A circadian clock component, ARNTL, emerged as a candidate regulator. The hit links daily rhythms to tumor suppression. It opens a new line of cancer research.
plos-pone-0004898:
Rita Willemssen, Thomas Müller, and Michael Schwarz studied response monitoring in de novo patients with Parkinson disease, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Parkinson disease is accompanied by dysfunctions in cognitive processes including error processing, which depends on phasic decreases of medial prefrontal dopaminergic activity. No study had evaluated these processes in newly diagnosed, untreated patients, prompting electrophysiological assessment before medication confounds brain responses.

Early error monitoring is already altered at diagnosis. Cognitive changes begin alongside motor symptoms. Baseline measures enable treatment monitoring. De novo cohorts are scientifically precious. The results give future studies a clearer base for comparison and follow up. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is. Such work helps guide care, field work, and lab work in the years ahead.
plos-pone-0004998:
Medulloblastoma is a childhood brain tumor. Rare cancer stem cells help drive it and resist treatment. Livia Garzia and colleagues studied a tiny RNA in these tumors. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The RNA is microRNA-199b-5p. MicroRNAs control genes by negative regulation.

They found this microRNA impairs the cancer stem cells. It works by holding down a gene called HES1. Restoring the microRNA weakened the tumor's stem cell core. The work spotlights a small molecule with large potential. It suggests a new angle against a deadly childhood cancer. Treatments that restore lost microRNAs could complement existing therapy.
plos-pone-0005098:
Gene activity over time is noisy and hard to read. Jianfeng Feng and colleagues borrowed a tool from audio engineering. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They analyzed microarray data in the frequency domain. Sound engineers break signals into pitches that way. Gene rhythms can be broken down similarly.

Their approach includes normalization, clustering and network analysis. An error model first cleans the data. The frequency view then reveals rhythms hidden in time. Patterns emerge that time plots obscure. The method gives biologists a new ear for gene data. It suits studies of cycles, like cell division and daily rhythms. Listening to genes turns a metaphor into a working method.
plos-pone-0005198:
Neisseria meningitidis, the germ behind meningitis, must have iron to live. Inside the human host, iron comes bound to different proteins in the throat and in the blood. Jordan and Saunders argued in PLOS ONE in 2009 that those proteins also tell the germ where it is.

When iron is scarce, the bacterium changes which genes it uses so it can grab and spare iron. The mix of iron-binding proteins around it differs by body site, forming a niche signal. Reading that signal may help the germ switch between quiet colonization and invasive disease.
plos-pone-0005298:
Stromatolites are layered rock structures that may hold Earth's earliest signs of life. Reading those signs is risky, since modern microbes can contaminate ancient samples. Gérard and colleagues drilled pristine stromatolite cores in Western Australia and reported their findings in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The fossil samples come from the Fortescue Group and are about 2.7 billion years old. Inside them, the team found modern subsurface bacteria. Their presence is a warning: life found in ancient rock may be a recent guest, and claims about early life must rule that out.
plos-pone-0005398:
Spinocerebellar ataxia type 2 is an inherited disease whose motor deficits define its clinical picture. People who carry the gene but show no symptoms yet had never been characterized for early motor change. Velázquez-Pérez and colleagues studied those presymptomatic carriers in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Measurable motor decline was present before clinical symptoms appeared. Finding decline in the presymptomatic stage extends the known course of the disease backward. It also opens a window for trials that intervene before obvious disability begins. A slow slide that can be felt years ahead of the worst stage gives gene carriers time to plan,. Gives trial teams a way to test drugs while there is still much left to save.
plos-pone-0005498:
Yirui Sun and co-authors challenged a common marker for neural stem cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. A surface protein called CD133 is widely used to find and sort stem cells from brain tissue and tumours. Workers had assumed that all such stem cells carry it at all times.

The team showed that human neural stem cells without CD133 can still copy themselves and make all three main brain cell types. Sorting by CD133 alone would miss those cells. The finding urges care in cancer and stem cell work that relies on this one marker.
plos-pone-0005598:
Agi Deguchi and co-authors characterised toxin-making gut bacteria in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Clostridium perfringens type A is found almost everywhere and is a major cause of food-related gut illness. Only strains that make a certain toxin cause most of that illness.

The toxin gene can sit on the chromosome or on a mobile piece of DNA. The team read the genes of type A strains to see how the toxin gene is carried and spread. That helps track outbreaks and judge the risk from strains found in food.
plos-pone-0005698:
Ali Riazi and co-authors traced how a heart gene shapes two other heart factors in 2009. NKX2-5 is a master gene for building the heart, active early in development. It works in a web with other regulators, among them GATA4 and beta-catenin.

Working in heart muscle cells of the ventricle, the team showed NKX2-5 controls the levels of both factors. That control helps set how heart cells grow and take their final form. Faults in NKX2-5 cause heart defects present at birth. Mapping its targets shows where those defects begin and where future fixes might act.
plos-pone-0005798:
Lasse Evensen and co-authors showed in 2009 that vessel support cells supply a growth signal needed to build proper blood vessels. Vessels are more than tubes of endothelium; mural cells wrap them and steady them. During new vessel growth, these support cells are recruited to sprouts.

The team found the signal VEGF must come from the mural cells themselves for organ-like vessel patterns to form. Without that local supply, vessels form badly. The result reframes VEGF, usually cast as an endothelial signal, as a support-cell duty too. It bears on diseases of leaky, chaotic vessels, including tumors.
plos-pone-0005898:
Shreedhar Natarajan and Eric Jakobsson built a method in 2009 to match proteins with their true counterparts across species. Comparing genomes requires knowing which protein in one species does the same job as a protein in another. Simple similarity searches often pick the wrong match among look-alikes.

Their algorithm, MoLFunCs, finds the most likely functional counterpart using network ideas and trusted sources. Better matches mean better transfer of knowledge from model organisms to humans. Drug and disease research leans on such transfers daily. The paper offers a heuristic that weighs function over raw resemblance.
plos-pone-0005998:
Balancing a pole on a fingertip looks like play, yet it obeys strict math. Tyler Cluff and Ramesh Balasubramaniam tracked learners at that task in 2009. Six people practiced pole balancing over three sessions, sitting and standing, while their PLOS ONE study recorded the speed changes of the fingertip in a sideways plane.

The speed changes follow a heavy-tailed pattern called a Lévy distribution, and its slope fell as skill grew. A changing number thus marks the course of learning itself. The work gives motor learning a compact sign to follow, and it shows how a simple task can expose the deep rules by which people gain control of their own movement.
plos-pone-0006098:
Blood from a lupus patient is a blend, and the blend hides which cells are switched on. Alexander Abbas, Kristen Wolslegel, Dhaya Seshasayee and colleagues unmixed that blend on paper in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper deconvolves blood microarray data from systemic lupus erythematosus, an autoimmune disease with sweeping changes in white blood cell counts and activity.

Working backward from mixed data, the method recovers cellular activation patterns cell type by cell type. That recovery matters because lupus care lacks sharp markers for flares. A tool that reads the immune system's state from one blood sample could guide dosing and warn of worsening disease before symptoms declare it.
plos-pone-0006198:
Feeling sure about a judgment is usually tied to being right, but Eric Fimbel, Rene Michaud, and Mathieu Martin question that link. Their 2009 PLOS ONE study deals with judging sizes and sorting them into classes. From an observer's view, a person who answers the same way each time looks reliably certain.

The authors argue that certainty tracks the consistency of judgments more closely than their accuracy. A steady judge can be steadily wrong, yet still appear sure. That split matters wherever confidence is used as proof, from eyewitness accounts to expert panels. The paper offers a fresh way to test and measure self-confidence.
plos-pone-0006298:
Cells respond to broken DNA with a coordinated alarm and repair program. Maria Quanz and colleagues jammed that alarm in a 2009 PLOS ONE study using molecules that mimic double-strand breaks. The earliest steps of damage recognition in mammal cells are still not fully understood.

The fake breaks hyperactivated DNA-PK, a key damage-sensing enzyme, and disorganised the whole response. Flooding the sensor shows how its tuning shapes downstream choices. The experiment reveals wiring that normal damage levels hide. It may also suggest ways to sensitise cancer cells to DNA-breaking treatments.
plos-pone-0006398:
Dormant bacterial spores wake when nutrients signal that growth is possible again. Tetyana Dodatko and colleagues studied germination of Bacillus cereus spores in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Unlike its close relative Bacillus anthracis, B. cereus spores germinate with a single nutrient germinant, inosine.

The spores release alanine, which synergises with inosine to promote germination, per the title. Self-released signals amplify the wake-up call. Understanding germination helps food safety, since waking spores can spoil food. It also matters for decontamination of spore-forming pathogens. Spore wake-up is the first weak point where food safety work can step in.
plos-pone-0006498:
Rahul Sarugaser, Lorraine Hanoun, Armand Keating, and colleagues described how human mesenchymal stem cells organize themselves in PLOS ONE in 2009. These cells, also called mesenchymal progenitor cells, are isolated from many connective tissues. A stem cell is defined by its ability to renew itself and to produce specialized cells. The team asked how that ability is structured in these human cells.

Their title reports that the cells self-renew and differentiate according to a deterministic hierarchy. In other words, the steps follow a set order rather than chance. A predictable hierarchy helps labs grow the right cell types for therapy. It also frames how tissue repair may work.
plos-pone-0006598:
Michael Treadway and co-authors presented a task to measure drive and pleasure loss in PLOS ONE in 2009. Among the traits proposed for major depression, the anhedonic type has strong support. Anhedonia means loss of pleasure and drive. It is thought to show a fault in motivation. The team assessed a lab task called the Effort Expenditure for Rewards Task, or EEfRT for short.

In the task, people choose between easy work for small rewards and hard work for large ones. Their choices give a plain measure of motivation that does not rely on self-report. Such a measure helps test cures aimed at restoring drive. It gives depression research a tool with clear scores.
plos-pone-0006698:
Shobana Rebecca Dissanayeke and colleagues studied a gene variant and childhood tuberculosis in PLOS ONE in 2009. The gene is TIRAP, which helps pass signals from immune sensors. Those sensors, called toll-like receptors, recognize molecules on mycobacteria. Earlier work had linked TIRAP variants to resistance or risk for several infections. The authors asked whether the same holds for tuberculosis in children.

Their answer was mixed and depended on the group studied. Variation in TIRAP was not linked to general childhood tuberculosis risk. It may, however, affect risk of tuberculous meningitis in some ethnic groups. Meningitis is the most dangerous form of the disease in children. The findings argue for testing genetic risk separately across populations.
plos-pone-0006798:
Luu Thi Lien and colleagues measured tuberculosis infection among hospital workers in Hanoi in PLOS ONE in 2009. TB spreads to health care workers worldwide. Infection control should reduce spread inside hospitals. Yet worker infection is rarely measured in high-burden countries. Vietnam is one such country.

The team ran a cross-sectional study of hospital staff. They estimated prevalence of TB infection among the workers. They also identified risk factors linked to being infected. High infection rates would signal weak points in hospital control. The results give Vietnamese hospitals evidence for protecting their own staff.
plos-pone-0006898:
Zong-Ming Xie and colleagues moved two soybean genes into a model plant to test stress protection in PLOS ONE in 2009. The genes encode trihelix transcription factors, GmGT-2A and GmGT-2B. Trihelix factors guide light responses and development. Their role in abiotic stress was largely unclear. Abiotic stresses include drought, salt, and cold.

Transgenic Arabidopsis carrying the soybean genes tolerated stresses better. Improved tolerance shows the factors do act in stress defense. Soybean is a major world crop facing harsher climates. Genes that protect a model plant may protect crops too. The work nominates two candidates for stress-resistant breeding.
plos-pone-0006998:
Thomas Quack, Jürgen Knobloch, Svenja Beckmann, and colleagues studied parasite reproduction in PLOS ONE in 2009. Schistosomiasis is a major parasitic disease of humans and animals. The worm's eggs drive much of the illness. So the processes that build the worm's gonads are prime targets for intervention.

Working in Schistosoma mansoni, the team characterized a formin protein called SmDia. They showed it interacts with a Src kinase and a small GTPase in the gonads. Those partnerships suggest how egg production is organized. Blocking them might reduce the eggs that cause disease.
plos-pone-0007098:
Silke Schüle, Björn-Philipp Kloke, Julia Kaiser, and colleagues studied HIV's block in monocytes in PLOS ONE in 2009. Human monocytes resist infection by HIV-1. HIV-based gene delivery vectors also fail in them. Yet vectors from a simian virus, SIV of sooty mangabeys, enter monocytes in a single round with ease.

The team traced that difference to a viral protein called Vpx. The version from the strain SIVsmmPBj abolished the restriction. In plain terms, Vpx removes a guard that keeps HIV out. Knowing the guard's identity matters for both cure research and vector design.
plos-pone-0007198:
Martin Pyka, Christian F. Beckmann, Sonja Schöning, and colleagues reported a brain imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their subject is the default-mode network, a set of brain areas active at rest. This network quiets down during hard thinking tasks, and it matters for psychiatric research.

The authors ask whether a demanding working memory task changes later resting brain patterns. They use fMRI scans to compare rest periods that follow different levels of mental load. Their results show that effort can leave a trace in the brain even after the task ends.
plos-pone-0007298:
Caroline V. Palmer, Chintan K. Modi, and Laura D. Mydlarz tested a new role for glowing coral proteins in PLOS ONE in 2009. Anthozoans such as corals carry a wide array of fluorescent proteins. Their biochemical traits and function in host tissue remained to be determined when the study began.

Fluorescent proteins often increase in injured or compromised coral tissue. That pattern suggested a protective role. The authors test whether coral fluorescent proteins act as antioxidants, mopping up damaging oxygen molecules. A confirmed role would recast coral color as part of a stress defense system.
plos-pone-0007398:
Wen-feng Shi, Melanie Leong, Ellen Cho, and colleagues studied a grape compound's effect on prostate cancer signals in 2009. Resveratrol has well established chemopreventive effects on prostate cancer in earlier studies. The androgen receptor plays pivotal roles in prostate tumor growth, because these tumors depend on male hormone signaling to grow.

The exact molecular mechanisms linking resveratrol to the receptor were not fully explained. The authors examine repressive effects of resveratrol on androgen receptor transcriptional activity. Their PLOS ONE work tests whether the compound quiets hormone-driven gene programs. That mechanism could support prevention strategies.
plos-pone-0007498:
Jean Ndjomou and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on hepatitis C virus and the cell signals it lives with. Viruses exploit host machinery to multiply. One signaling chain, called MEK/ERK, helps many RNA viruses copy themselves. Whether it helps or hinders hepatitis C was unclear. The team blocked the pathway and watched what the virus did.

Blocking MEK/ERK boosted hepatitis C replication and virus output, the opposite of the usual pattern. So this virus relates to the host's signaling in its own way. A pathway that restrains hepatitis C is a gift for drug thinking. Strengthening that restraint might slow the virus. The surprise also warns against assuming all RNA viruses treat host signals alike. Each virus negotiates its own deal with the cell.
plos-pone-0007598:
Inna Djagaeva and Sergey Doronkin published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 that follows their earlier work on how neurons shape their branches. The COP9 signalosome is part of the cell's protein degradation system. Its components are altered in patients with several severe syndromes, hinting at a role in neural circuits. The team asked how COP9 controls dendritic branching in fruit fly neurons. Their trail led to a protein called Kelch.

Kelch crosslinks the actin skeleton inside growing branches. COP9 limits branching by ordering Kelch's destruction through a Cullin3-dependent pathway. Controlled removal of a crosslinker prunes growth to the right extent. The mechanism links general protein recycling to precise brain wiring. It also gives the earlier, broader observations a concrete molecular story. One named protein's disposal explains how a neuron keeps its arbor in bounds.
plos-pone-0007698:
Claudia Tortiglione and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns Hydra, a tiny freshwater animal with a simple body. Tiny glowing crystals called fluorescent nanocrystals can be tracked as they move through living tissue. Researchers value them as carriers and probes.

The team watched where the crystals entered Hydra's cells and how they passed between them. Entry turned out to be controlled, through regulated portals rather than random leaks. Knowing how cells take in such particles matters for drug delivery. It also matters for judging the safety of engineered particles.
plos-pone-0007798:
Qunzhou Zhang and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It studies stem-like cells taken from keloids, overgrown scars unique to human skin. Changes in a stem cell's local niche can push growth toward tumors. Whether a niche can drive a benign growth was unexplored.

Keloid cells turned out to be governed by their inflammatory niche. Two signals, IL-17 and IL-6, form the axis that drives them. The keloid thus serves as a model of niche-driven growth without cancer. Understanding that axis could lead to treatments that calm the niche rather than cut the scar out.
plos-pone-0007898:
Paul Bangirana and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks what predicts thinking skills in Ugandan children. Many programs aim to improve cognition in at-risk children. To guide them, researchers must first find the key variables that predict cognitive performance.

The team measured socioeconomic factors alongside children's cognition. Household wealth, schooling and related factors emerged as predictors. The study was designed to point community interventions at what matters most. Its implications reach beyond Uganda. Where resources are scarce, knowing which levers work is the first step to helping children think and learn better.
plos-pone-0007998:
Caroline Bidon and colleagues fed a plant extract to rats losing muscle with age, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The extract, EGb 761, comes from ginkgo leaves and is sold as a supplement. Muscle loss in old age, called sarcopenia, raises the risk of falls and lost independence.

In the rats' worn muscles, the extract woke a gene pattern more like that of young muscle. The shift was broad, across many genes at once, rather than a single change. The result hints that the extract reprograms aging muscle, though proof in people would need its own trials.
plos-pone-0008098:
Lulin Huang and colleagues read the silkworm's whole gene answer to a killer germ in PLOS ONE in 2009. The germ, whose name in the record reads Bacillus bombyseptieus, makes spores and poison crystals and was first found in dead silkworms. Silk farms lose whole batches to it.

Genome-wide reads showed which silkworm genes wake, and which go quiet, as infection takes hold. That full answer sheet reveals the insect's defense plan in detail. Breeders can use it to raise hardier worms, and the plan may echo in other insects facing kindred germs.
plos-pone-0008198:
Jeanette C. Perron and Jane Dodd studied cell movement signals in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Bone morphogenetic proteins, or BMPs, can steer cells toward a source. This steering, called chemotaxis, starts fast at the cell surface. It likely uses paths apart from the slower gene-based responses to BMP. The team focused on BMP7.

They asked which receptor parts BMP7 needs to trigger this movement. Two subunits, ActRIIA and BMPRII, proved selectively required. The response also worked without Smad4, a usual BMP partner. The findings separate rapid steering signals from classic BMP signaling.
plos-pone-0008298:
Orie T. Shafer and Paul H. Taghert studied a clock neuropeptide in fruit flies in PLOS ONE in 2009. Neuropeptide signaling is a key part of circadian timekeeping in animals. Pigment dispersing factor, or PDF, is required for normal daily activity rhythms in Drosophila. Where in the brain PDF acts for each function was unknown. The team used RNA interference to knock it down in neuron subsets.

Silencing PDF in specific neuronal groups separated its various circadian roles. That maps anatomy onto function for this neuropeptide. Knowing which neurons do what sharpens models of the body clock. The approach can be reused for other clock signals.
plos-pone-0008398:
Daniel Shriner and colleagues tested height genetics across populations in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Human height is the classic polygenic trait, shaped by many genes. Recent studies found variants influencing adult height. Those studies mainly involved East Asian or European ancestry groups. Whether the same loci transfer to other populations was open.

The team examined many variants representing over a hundred loci across populations. Fine-mapping can narrow which variant truly drives each signal. Transferability matters for applying genome findings worldwide. The study checks that genome discoveries do not stay confined to one ancestry.
plos-pone-0008498:
Koichi Iijima and co-authors study energy control in fruit flies in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. A factor called CREB helps control sugar and fat stores. In mammals, CREB acts in fat tissue and liver. Flies have a matching factor called dCREB2. Its role in energy metabolism was not fully known. The team switch CREB activity on or off in specific fly tissues.

They find both neuronal and peripheral CREB activity shape energy stores. Activity in the brain and in body tissues affects feeding too. The split shows energy balance is not run from one place. Fly work thus mirrors the multi-tissue control seen in mammals.
plos-pone-0008598:
Xinwei Chen and co-authors analyze barley resistance to leaf rust in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Barley leaf rust is caused by the fungus Puccinia hordei. Genetic resistance involves both major R genes and quantitative trait loci. R genes give higher but less durable resistance. Quantitative loci give partial resistance that lasts longer in the field. Exploring that partial resistance has become a breeding priority. The team use an eQTL analysis, linking gene expression to trait loci.

Their analysis maps expression loci behind partial resistance to the fungus. Genes whose expression varies with resistance become candidates. Breeders can use those markers to select durable resistance. The approach merges genetics and gene expression for crop improvement.
plos-pone-0008698:
Wendy Imlach, Sarah Finch, John Miller, and colleagues tested whether a potassium channel helps set heartbeat pace. Their rodent study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Heart cells fire in rhythm thanks to channels that pass charged particles. Large channels known as BK channels were known in many tissues. Their part in pacing the heart was unclear.

The researchers studied rodents with changes in these channels. They watched heart rate and how it answers bodily demands. The results give BK channels a real share in rate control. That finding adds a piece to the puzzle of rhythm faults and may guide future heart drugs.
plos-pone-0008798:
Mei Qiang, Ashley Denny, Jiguo Chen, and colleagues linked alcohol exposure to a removed chemical tag in brain genes. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The NMDA receptor is a key target of alcohol in the brain. Repeated alcohol bouts raise production of its 2B subunit for a long time. Tag-based gene control, called epigenetic regulation, was suspected. Methyl tags near a gene usually keep it quiet.

After chronic intermittent ethanol, one spot near the 2B gene lost its methyl tag. Gene activity rose at the same time. Site-specific tag loss may lock in alcohol's brain changes. That mechanism could matter for addiction's persistence.
plos-pone-0008898:
Juan Nunez-Iglesias, Chun-Chi Liu, Todd Morgan, and colleagues profiled two RNA layers together in Alzheimer brains. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. MicroRNAs fine-tune how much protein each gene message makes. Their role in Alzheimer disease was little studied. Single-layer studies miss how the tuners and their targets move together. Brain cortex samples from patients offered both layers at once.

Joint profiling showed altered microRNA regulation across the cortex. Some messages rose exactly where their tuner RNAs fell. Paired patterns nominate real regulatory pairs for testing. Dementia research gains a richer map of gene control gone wrong.
plos-pone-0008998:
Frank Curriero and co-authors offered a fix for health records that lack a usable address, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Health research often maps where patients live to spot disease patterns. Mapping needs each record's location pinned down, a step called geocoding. Some addresses cannot be matched to a map, and those records are usually dropped.

The team used imputation, a statistical fill-in method, for the missing locations. Instead of discarding unmatched records, they estimated where those patients likely lived. Keeping the records avoids biasing the map toward easy-to-place addresses. The approach widens the share of health data that mapping studies can honestly use.
plos-pone-0009098:
Lokesh Gakhar and co-authors introduced an airway protein that fights germ films, in PLOS ONE in 2010. PLUNC is a protein poured out by the lining of the human airways. It belongs to a family that handles fats and bacterial toxins. Its exact job in the lung was unsettled.

The team showed PLUNC acts like a surfactant, lowering surface tension. It also attacked biofilms, the slimy cities bacteria build on surfaces. Biofilms protect germs in chronically infected lungs. An airway protein that breaks them up could inspire new lung treatments.
plos-pone-0009198:
Samir Koirala and Gabriel Corfas published this brain study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It profiles Bergmann glial cells, support cells in the cerebellum, the brain region that fine-tunes movement. While young, these cells guide migrating neurons into place. In adults, they help form the cerebellum's outer boundary and support its wiring.

Despite their importance, many genes active in Bergmann glia were unknown. The team read the gene activity of single cells taken from mouse cerebellum. That single-cell profiling turned up glial genes that had not been identified before. The new gene list gives researchers fresh leads on how the cerebellum is built and kept working.
