Yirui Zhu and colleagues ran a 2026 forward-looking study of scleral lenses across eye surface diseases. Scleral lenses are large contact lenses that vault over the cornea, the clear front of the eye. They can restore sight and ease symptoms where standard lenses fail.

Patients with cone-shaped corneas, eye injuries, corneal grafts, or dry eye were fitted with scan-guided custom lenses. Vision improved in all groups after fitting, least in the graft group. Symptom scores fell across groups. The cornea thickened slightly under the lens. About half the patients noted midday fogging of vision. Satisfaction ran high overall, though comfort lagged in the graft group. Tailored fitting is the next focus.
pmc-13198498:
Tadesse Gebrye and colleagues reviewed cost studies of AI tools for spine disorders in a 2026 survey. Spine muscle and joint disorders cause a huge global health burden. AI tools for diagnosis and exercise plans are spreading, yet proof that they save money or add value stays thin.

The team searched seven databases and screened hundreds of papers. Only seven studies from five countries met their bar. Tools ranged from scan-reading aids to back pain apps and decision guides. Study spans ran from weeks in trials to lifetime in models. Three studies found their tools cost-effective. With so few studies, the authors stress that wider economic proof is still needed.
pmc-13210298:
Flea- and mite-borne fevers were long overlooked in Southeast Asia, and a 2026 review authored by Stuart D Blacksell sums up twenty-five years of catching up. The article synthesizes regional research from 2001 to 2025 on rickettsial diseases such as scrub typhus and murine typhus across surveillance, diagnosis, ecology, and treatment trials.

These infections explain a tenth to a quarter of hospitalized fever cases in many endemic settings, the review finds. Sharper antibody cutoffs, rapid tests, and sensitive molecular assays improved detection, while genome work exposed wide strain diversity in the region. Trials confirm doxycycline as first-line therapy for scrub typhus, and the authors offer the integrated program as a model elsewhere.
pmc-13212598:
Ankita Sharma, Shalli Rani, and Mohammad Shabaz are named in a 2026 retraction notice covering their paper on artificial intelligence for guarding electric vehicle charging networks against cyber intrusion. Editors at the journal withdrew the article after its foundations came into question.

Concerns covered the methods, the results, and a dataset that could no longer be found at its stated source, plus odd non-standard wording in the text. Authors supplied code when asked, but their other answers fell short and the data never arrived. Editors therefore lost confidence in the findings. None of the three authors clearly accepted or rejected the withdrawal in the notice.
pmc-13213598:
Syed Saad Ali Chishti and Rimsa Tahir report in 2026 a teenager whose bowel telescoped into itself because a fatty growth inside the colon wall acted as a lead point. Such colo-colic cases are exceedingly rare in adolescents and rarely blamed on a benign lipoma.

The sixteen-year-old arrived with five days of pain, vomiting, and jelly-like bloody stool. Scans confirmed a ten-centimetre telescoped segment anchored by the growth. Attempts to undo it with enema and a scope failed because the lining was swollen and ulcerated. Surgeons removed that colon section, tissue tests confirmed a mature benign lipoma, and the patient went home on day ten after surgery.
pmc-13214298:
Christian Fischer and colleagues review in 2026 outcomes after surgically fusing the elbow, a last-resort operation for joints beyond repair or failed replacements. They compared bone touching bone directly against a gap technique that first grows a membrane to rebuild missing bone.

Twenty adults treated over fourteen years, mostly for infection, trauma, or nonunion, form the cohort. Eighteen fused at the first attempt, and the two failures healed after revision with the gap method. Standard elbow scores, grip strength, and wrist motion showed no clear difference between techniques at about four years. Complications were common, including fractures near implants in seven patients. Twelve of fifteen working-age patients returned to work.
pmc-13214598:
Duygu Zorlu and colleagues test in 2026 whether lavender oil can kill human lung cancer cells grown in dishes. Lung cancer remains among the deadliest cancers worldwide, and plant oils are popular candidates in the search for gentler treatments.

Cells received five oil concentrations, and viability fell steadily as dose rose on a standard assay. Treated cultures thinned out, opened gaps between cells, and showed rounding and detachment, all signs of extensive cell death. The authors rate the effect as moderate antiproliferative activity with good potential. Dish results are only a first hint, since an oil that kills cultured cells must still prove safe and effective in living bodies.
pmc-13215298:
Jinman Zhong and co-authors examine in 2026 a long non-coding RNA that runs high in prostate cancer and may serve as a blood marker for the disease. Such RNAs do not build proteins, yet they can steer cancer behaviour by soaking up smaller regulatory RNAs.

The molecule appeared raised in tumour tissue, patient serum, and cancer cell lines, and its levels carried diagnostic and prognostic value in their analyses. Silencing it in cells slowed growth, blocked a shape-shifting programme linked to spread, and cut migration and invasion. The effect ran through a small RNA partner to a receptor gene that the team tracked with binding and rescue experiments. The axis offers both a marker and a target idea.
pmc-13215398:
Ingrid Elise Oldereid Andersen and colleagues report a 2026 longitudinal study on whether teenage life predicts post-traumatic growth in midlife during the COVID-19 pandemic. The data come from a Norwegian population study that followed people for 28 years.

The analysis covered 2,215 people whose social relationships, mental health, and family background were recorded in 1992, then linked to growth scores measured in 2020. Close friendships and caring parents in adolescence predicted higher growth decades later. Immigrant background predicted stronger appreciation of life, while higher parental education predicted lower personal strength scores. Gender did not change these patterns. The findings point to early support as a lasting resource after collective crises.
pmc-13219498:
Lin Meng and colleagues uncover an epigenetic safety valve that shields growing teeth from stress in a 2026 mouse study. Bones and teeth endure force from walking and chewing, and their progenitor cells must survive loading to keep the tissue renewing. The continuously growing mouse incisor, a front tooth that never stops erupting, offers a window on this balance.

The team identified KDM6B, an enzyme that removes a repressive chemical mark from DNA packaging, as the guardian. Without it, a chain reaction unfolded: the silencing mark accumulated at the Bmi1 gene, Bmi1 fell silent, the channel PIEZO1 was unleashed, calcium flooded the progenitor cells, and they died. Halving the dose of Piezo1 in the deficient mice restored the calcium brake and rescued the cells and the tissue. The authors name the axis a chromatin-based mechanostat and suggest it could be targeted to prevent degeneration in teeth and bone.
pmc-13219798:
Alba González-Lanchas and co-authors reconstruct how ocean algae build limestone shells from Atlantic seafloor sediments in a 2026 study. Coccolithophores, single-celled plankton armored in calcite plates, produce a share of the ocean's calcite and help steer the carbon cycle. What controls how much calcite a species makes, growth or environment, has been hard to settle from cultures.

Using sediments, they measured composition alongside growth and calcification rates to build a framework linking the fossils to the physiology that produced them. The dominant groups related growth to calcification in opposite ways, reflecting carbon budgets. A species group's growth turned out to be the control on its calcite output, and the pattern formed two zones divided near forty degrees north, matching chemistry gradients. North of the line, cells are limited by reaction rates; south of it, by supply. They expect that boundary to shift as ocean carbon changes.
pmc-13222598:
Jiao Tang and co-authors explore why moving patients into palliative care is hard for multidisciplinary teams in China, in a 2026 qualitative study. Thirty-nine team members from six institutions, spanning doctors, nurses, psychologists, social workers, and volunteers, joined semi-structured focus groups. A social-ecological framework organized the analysis of their accounts.

Four layers of difficulty emerged. Individual decision rights got squeezed by protective medical habits and family anguish. Families faced stigma around seeming unfilial, plus clashing views among relatives. Services lacked palliative literacy, skills, and quality control. Society added thin funding, unclear pricing, and missing safeguards for practitioners. Culture and structure, not single actors, hold the transition back.
pmc-13223998:
Omar P Vallejos and a large team report a 2026 microbiology study using friendly gut bacteria to deliver carbon monoxide, a gas the body makes in small amounts to calm inflammation. Certain Escherichia coli strains carry an enzyme called ChuS that releases the gas while breaking down heme. The researchers asked whether such bacteria could soften herpes simplex virus skin infection.

Feeding mice the probiotic strain Nissle 1917 raised a blood marker of carbon monoxide in a ChuS-dependent way. Other gut strains carrying the enzyme, but lacking a known toxin gene, also eased disease. Combined strains lowered viral load significantly, pointing to probiotic bacteria as a natural delivery route.
pmc-13224698:
Mehran Alipour and co-authors conduct a 2026 randomised trial in men with obesity, pairing a plant compound called fisetin with a mixed exercise programme. Obesity involves low-grade inflammation, and a molecule named Maresin-1 helps switch inflammation off, though human intervention data are scarce. Forty-four men spent twelve weeks in one of four arms: supplement alone, training alone, both, or neither.

Training combined resistance intervals with progressive aerobic work, while the supplement dose was 200 milligrams daily. Maresin-1 rose in both training groups, and inflammatory markers fell across the active arms. Blood sugar, insulin, and insulin resistance also improved everywhere except in controls, with the largest gains where training and fisetin were combined.
pmc-13226798:
Anil Tukaram Pawar, S.B. Chandrasekar, and M.P. Venkatesh compare a 2026 set of herbal-medicine regulations across India, China, Europe, the United States, and Japan. Herbal products are booming worldwide, but rules differ so much that quality, safety, and proven effectiveness vary by market. Drawing on official regulator websites and scholarly sources, the study examined licensing, pre-market checks, quality control, and after-sale monitoring.

Europe and Japan lean on evidence demanded before products reach shelves, while the United States relies more on watching the market afterwards. India and China weave traditional practice into modern frameworks. The authors recommend shared manufacturing standards, harmonised pharmacopoeias, and new tools such as artificial intelligence for quality checks and supply-chain transparency.
pmc-13233098:
Sam Sherratt-Mayhew and colleagues published a 2026 systematic review of nicotinamide, a form of vitamin B3, as a protective treatment for glaucoma. The disease slowly kills retinal nerve cells and shrinks the visual field, and pressure-lowering treatment does not always stop it. Nicotinamide feeds a molecule cells need for energy, so researchers hope it can keep nerve cells alive.

Three phase II randomized trials with 152 participants met the review's criteria. None showed a statistically clear preservation of the main visual field measure, although electrical tests of retinal function improved in two crossover trials and one study found more improving test locations. No serious side effects appeared. The reviewers rate the evidence as low certainty and call for larger trials.
pmc-13233298:
Rosemary A Reyneke and colleagues published a 2026 paper describing how they involved farmers and vets while building a guide to encourage preventive care on ruminant farms. Such engagement is routine in human health research but rare in animal care work. The team held in-person and online group discussions plus individual conversations with the framework's future users.

Contributors shaped both what the guide contains and how it is organized, and they influenced the methods used to build it. The authors report that this involvement made the guide more practical and easier to use, raising the chance that farms and practices will adopt it. The paper offers a worked example for veterinary researchers who want engagement to be feasible rather than decorative.
pmc-13233898:
Christopher Troy and colleagues published a 2026 surgical series on giving chemotherapy before operating on pineal region tumors in children. These tumors sit deep in the brain, often block fluid flow, and bleed heavily during removal. The single-center review covered thirty-one children and young adults who received at least two rounds of a three-drug regimen before definitive surgery.

Most tumors were pineoblastomas, with smaller numbers of other embryonal types. Chemotherapy shrank tumor volume by about half on average, and only one tumor grew. No chemotherapy complications occurred. Every operation then achieved a complete or near-complete removal. The authors tracked blood loss as a share of total blood volume, alongside complications, readmissions, and survival, arguing that shrinking and devascularizing the tumor first makes a dangerous operation safer.
pmc-13233998:
Monise F. Petrucelli and colleagues published a 2026 fungus study on how Trichophyton rubrum defends itself against oxidative attack. This dermatophyte causes athlete's foot and similar infections, and immune cells bombard it with reactive oxygen. The team disabled a master switch gene, AP-1, in the fungus and challenged normal and mutant strains with hydrogen peroxide and menadione, two oxidants.

Without AP-1, the fungus produced less catalase, the enzyme that breaks down peroxide, and suffered more membrane damage, especially under menadione. Other stress pathways partly made up the gap, and one catalase gene carried a predicted AP-1 binding site. The mutant also mishandled gene splicing in stress-related genes. The authors conclude AP-1 coordinates both the antioxidant response and parts of the splicing machinery.
pmc-13234098:
Andri Feldmann and colleagues published a 2026 methods paper sorting out two labels in muscle oxygen monitoring. Near-infrared devices shine light into muscle and report oxygen saturation, but makers mix two terms: one claiming a muscle-specific value, the other a vaguer tissue value. The signal always blends skin, fat, and muscle under the probe, so the distinction matters for honest interpretation.

The authors propose calling the measurement regional muscle oxygen saturation, stressing its local, instrument-dependent character. They describe a practical check using arterial occlusion: a truly muscle-weighted signal swings widely, from low values during the block to high values on release, while surface-dominated signals barely move. No commercial device isolates muscle completely, they note, so validated instruments and explicit protocols remain essential.
pmc-13235498:
Neera N. Vora and co-authors described in 2026 a skin vessel inflammation that followed a chest disease in a 36-year-old woman. She first built upper respiratory symptoms, then a fast-spreading purple rash two weeks later across legs, belly, and arms. Joint pain, swollen feet, belly pain, and vomiting accompanied the rash. Chest imaging showed a patchy shadow in one lung area.

Testing of respiratory samples found Chlamydia pneumoniae, an atypical pneumonia bacterium, while other disease and autoimmune checks came back unrevealing. A skin biopsy confirmed the small-vessel inflammation pattern called leukocytoclastic vasculitis. Treatment combined an antibiotic active against the bacterium with steroid drugs for the vessel inflammation. Her condition improved markedly under that combined treatment in the report. The authors caution that cause cannot be proven, yet the timing and exclusions make the bacterium a plausible trigger.
pmc-13236098:
Yun Yun Lee and co-authors studied in 2026 how an Indigenous advisory board shaped a healthy food reward trial for adults with diabetes. The FoodRx trial covered an Indigenous subset of people facing food shortage. Board members and university team members gave interviews, and meeting notes supplied more detail. Analysis ran in rounds with ongoing board input in reading the results.

Four linked themes shaped what people said about the board's work. Culture and ceremony, including Indigenous tongues and naming habits, built belonging and ties in meetings. A trusted, equal-voiced meeting space allowed growth and honest exchange among members. Indigenous ways of knowing tested standard research habits and pushed the trial design toward equity. Themes stressed a shared say in choices and openness from the team. The authors urge teams to work with Indigenous partners early in any such research.
pmc-13236798:
Yun Lin and co-authors reviewed in 2026 how doctors might find hidden neck lymph node spread in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, a cancer of the mouth, throat, and voice box. Patients whose scans show no node disease still face a hard choice between extra surgery and risky watchfulness. The review weighs standard imaging against newer data-driven tools.

Recent work pairs gene-level and tissue data, such as DNA methylation and spatial gene activity maps, with scan features inside deep learning models. These combined systems beat imaging alone at flagging microscopic spread and sorting patients by survival risk. The authors describe a coming noninvasive virtual biopsy, while stressing that validation must come before routine clinical use.
pmc-13237598:
Xunting Wang, Hongxia Wang, and Fuqi Ma used first-principles calculations in 2026 to design nanotube sensors for a toxic gas that forms inside high-voltage switchgear. The eco-friendly insulating gas now replacing SF6 can break down under electrical faults into CF3CN, which operators need to detect quickly. The team coated gallium nitride nanotubes with four metal oxides and simulated how the target gas sticks and changes their electronics.

Every coating shrank the nanotube's band gap, making it more conductive. Zinc oxide bound the gas most strongly through true chemical adsorption, while silver oxide offered a good balance of grip and easy release at room temperature. The authors rank the coatings for real-time monitoring duty. Computational screening of this kind can narrow sensor candidates before bench work begins.
pmc-13239098:
Gillian P. McHugo and a large team merged gene data in 2026 to find the genes behind trypanotolerance, the inherited ability of some African cattle to withstand trypanosome parasites. The disease these parasites cause costs African livestock output billions each year. Hybrid cattle carry mixed taurine and indicine ancestry, so the team combined ancestry mapping across hardy and prone herds with gene activity data from infection experiments over time.

Eight candidate genes surfaced, including several immune and signaling names such as IL1B and NFKB1. The wider gene set leaned toward immune system functions, including the major histocompatibility complex, and cell signaling. The authors present the candidates as signposts for the cell networks that let hardy cattle shrug off infection. Breeding and treatment research can now chase specific mechanisms.
pmc-13239298:
Tian Xia and colleagues combined Mendelian randomization with single-cell sequencing in 2026 to sort out which genetic factors genuinely raise or lower the risk of acute myeloid leukemia. Ten genetic exposures were tested with several statistical methods that use inherited variants as natural experiments. Three genes came out protective, while seven raised risk.

One gene, PDE5A, showed the strongest risk association, with odds more than eight times higher in the analysis. Single-cell data then mapped where the implicated genes switch on, across seventeen cell populations and fourteen cell types in the blood-forming system. The protective trio included a folate-pathway gene and a collagen gene. The authors offer the combined evidence as a guide to disease mechanisms and candidate drug targets at cellular resolution.
pmc-13239498:
Ava McKane and colleagues report a 2026 case where fragile-bone disease and bone cancer appeared together for the first time in a specific genetic form. A 23-year-old woman had osteogenesis imperfecta caused by a rare change in the IFITM5 gene, a variant tied to severe disease without its usual extra bone growth.

She arrived with groin pain that first looked like another fracture from her underlying condition. Closer review raised concern for osteosarcoma, a malignant bone tumour, and chemotherapy plus surgery followed. The team stresses that bone changes from the genetic disease can mimic cancer, so history, genetic results, and tissue findings must be weighed together.
pmc-13240498:
Yuntao Ye and colleagues propose a framework for reading the recurring gene faults of liver cancer in a 2026 review. Hepatocellular carcinoma carries a crowded mutational landscape, and counting how often a variant appears says little about what it does or whether doctors can act on it.

The review organises major alterations by the systems they hit, including telomere upkeep, cell cycle brakes, the WNT growth pathway, and chromatin packaging. Each fault is traced through its effects on gene activity, proteins, metabolism, and immune surroundings. The authors separate firmly supported links from exploratory ones and stress that most variant-guided uses, from liquid biopsy to drug choice, remain investigational.
pmc-13240898:
Alarfaj at King Faisal University tested how well machine learning and deep learning sort legal case documents automatically. Legal files are long, technical, and numerous, making manual review slow. The study drew on thousands of real case documents. Text traits, deep traits, and sentence embeddings each fed competing classifiers.

An ensemble of extremely randomized trees reached eighty-nine percent accuracy. Pairing sentence embeddings with a long short-term memory network did better still, hitting ninety-six percent. Embeddings caught legal meaning and structure that surface traits missed. Alarfaj advises embedding-based pipelines for courts and firms drowning in case paperwork.
pmc-13241398:
Rodgers-Melnick and colleagues in Cleveland asked whether more music therapy sessions ease pain longer for hospitalized cancer and blood patients. Records covered two hundred eighty-three admissions where patients reported notable pain or received opioids. Sessions numbered one, two, or three-plus per stay. Mixed models tracked pain scores and daily opioid doses over time.

No dose-response appeared for either outcome. Extra sessions did not lower pain intensity or opioid use beyond the first session's effect. The null held after adjusting for baseline values and stay length. The team suggests future programs measure stress and anxiety, which may respond better.
pmc-13241498:
Stetza and Kayser at Bielefeld tested whether breathing syncs to inner sight flips. Twenty people watched a Necker cube and reported spontaneous flips. Pupil size and breathing phase were logged throughout. Earlier work showed breathing syncing to outside trial events. No cues told participants when a flip might occur.

Pupils shrank then widened around each flip, proof of arousal at play. Pupil size also moved with breathing phase as foreseen. Yet breathing itself barely aligned to the spontaneous flips. Stetza suggests steady outside timing, not the flip itself, drives breathing alignment.
pmc-13241698:
Thachil and Steensma ask where the 'oma' hides in multiple myeloma and unpack the specialty's vocabulary. Myeloma accounts for roughly a tenth of cancers hematologists manage. The disease was described in the early nineteenth century but named only decades later. The essay traces everyday clinic terms to their origins.

Paraprotein, immunoglobulin, kappa and lambda chains, and plasma cells all receive etymological scrutiny. Older coinages like dysproteinemia have quietly fallen from use. Each term carries limitations the authors bring into the open. The piece invites clinicians to notice the history embedded in their shorthand.
pmc-13242398:
Renner in Zurich and Wolf in Innsbruck settle a quantum foundations puzzle descending from Tsirelson. Two agents share one quantum system, each feeding inputs in and reading outputs out. Their operations commute: the order of access changes nothing observable. Must the shared system then split cleanly into private halves?

For classical inputs and outputs, such factorization can fail in infinite dimensions. The authors prove the fully quantum case behaves identically overall. With finite-dimensional input systems, commuting operations always factorize. The result draws a clean conceptual boundary around shared quantum resources.
pmc-13242698:
Michael Arthur Ofori and colleagues mined Ghana's 2022 Demographic and Health Survey to find what drives low birth weight. Their analysis appeared in Health Science Reports in 2026. Low birth weight, under twenty-five hundred grams, raises the risk of infant illness and death. The study covered 8,581 women of reproductive age and tested social, maternal, and health-care factors together in regression models.

About one baby in six was born underweight. Poverty raised the odds, and the single strongest risk was missing malaria prevention in pregnancy, which nearly tripled them. Skilled antenatal care and iron supplements were protective when present and risky when absent. Secondary schooling, older maternal age, and higher body weight lowered the odds. Young, underweight mothers faced a combined risk greater than either factor alone. The authors call for action on poverty, nutrition, malaria prevention, iron, and skilled care together.
pmc-13242998:
Zhuoyue Shi and a large team present a 2026 vaccine study against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus in mice. Standard alum adjuvants push antibody-heavy immunity, which has repeatedly failed against this bacterium. Their vaccine instead packages a surface protein in biodegradable polymer particles designed to stir cellular immunity.

Compared with the aluminum version, the nano-vaccine produced fewer antibodies but better blocking quality. It raised key immune signals, including one that stayed high for a long period. Every mouse given the vaccine survived a lethal challenge. The vaccine also boosted bacteria-eating cell activity, and blocking the central immune signal erased protection. The authors argue this cellular route is the missing part for staph vaccines.
pmc-13243298:
Wenyue Quan and colleagues review why soil diseases plague herbs grown again and again on the same land in 2026. Demand for natural medicines has pushed farms to plant medicinal crops without rotation. Over time, harmful microbes build up and yields and quality fall.

The review ties together three strands of evidence. Plant roots release chemicals that reshape soil microbe communities and weaken the root barrier. Those same chemicals also disturb defense hormones, leaving plants less able to fight infection. The authors then judge microbe-based fixes, from designed microbe mixes to soils that suppress disease on their own. Their framework gives growers concrete routes toward healthier fields and steadier herb quality.
pmc-13243398:
Yanqiu Chen and co-authors measure adult hesitancy toward the HPV vaccine in China in a 2026 survey. The vaccine guards against cancers tied to a common virus, and supply in China has grown in recent years. Even so, doubt still keeps coverage below what health goals require.

The survey gathered 967 adults in 2024, most of them women. About one in five adults felt hesitant, with men more hesitant than women. Careful modeling tied hesitancy to three factors: a sense that the risk is low, weak trust in the vaccine, and thin knowledge of HPV. The authors urge teaching that speaks to men and older women in particular.
pmc-13243698:
Yingjie Song, Shasha Luo, and Shuang Li fed koi carp diets in which five kinds of duckweed partly replaced fishmeal. Their trial appeared in Aquaculture Nutrition in 2026. Duckweed is a fast-growing water plant rich in protein, but its effects depend on species. In a first phase the team found the best level for each species, then measured color, antioxidant defenses, gut immunity, and gut microbes at those levels.

Two species shone at a fifth of the diet: Lemna minor and Wolffia globosa. Koi on those feeds gained more weight, converted feed better, and digested protein more fully than controls. Their skin reds and yellows deepened as pigment compounds built up in muscle. Antioxidant enzymes rose, oxidative damage fell, and gut immune activity strengthened while inflammatory signals quieted. Other species helped less or needed lower doses. The authors back duckweed, in the right species and dose, as functional feed.
pmc-13246498:
Ekdahl and Lundell wrote this 2026 commentary in the Journal of Research in Nursing, responding to a qualitative study from China on why patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease struggle with self-care. COPD self-care, managing symptoms, monitoring change, and acting early, keeps people out of hospital, yet many patients face real barriers to doing it well.

The commentators read the Chinese findings through the lens of person-centred care, an approach that treats the patient as a partner with their own story, preferences, and resources. They argue the barriers make most sense in that frame, and discuss how digital health tools could support partnership-based care. The piece invites nurses to design support around the person, not the checklist.
pmc-13246698:
Zhongjun Wang and co-authors frame mouth cancer growth around a three-way axis in a 2026 review. Oral squamous cell carcinoma is the most common head and neck cancer. Most research treats microbe shifts, inflammation, and immunity as separate stories.

The review joins them: disturbed mouth microbes can spark inflammation, which then reshapes the immune setting around a tumor. Signal paths switched on by microbe sensing help drive that chain. The authors also gather clinical markers from blood and saliva that reflect each leg of the axis. Such combined markers could aid early detection and choice of care. The axis is offered as a working idea to test.
pmc-13247298:
Nyamira and co-authors described where white-browed sparrow-weavers nest in a dry Kenyan landscape, in this 2026 Ecology and Evolution study. These sociable birds weave communal nests in trees across the semi-arid shrubland of Baringo South, a region losing woody cover to charcoal production, fuelwood cutting, and spreading farms. The team walked five survey transects, recording tree species, trunk size, and nest height.

Umbrella thorn acacia dominated the woody cover, followed by other acacias and desert date. Nesting trees did not differ in trunk diameter across the transects, suggesting the birds select from what the shrinking woodland offers rather than a narrow size class. The authors frame the description as a baseline for conservation: without the acacia woodland, the weavers lose both nest sites and the social colonies they support.
pmc-13247798:
Wang, Huang, Shan, and co-authors scanned the social brain at work in young men with gaming disorder, in this 2026 Psychological Medicine study. Gaming disorder damages social functioning, but its neural basis during live interaction was unclear. Using near-infrared brain imaging, the team recorded one hundred seventy-five male participants, split into gaming disorder, hazardous gaming, and healthy groups, while they cooperated and competed with a partner.

The gaming disorder group reported the worst social and emotional functioning. Their brain patterns differed too: one social-cognition region over-fired during cooperation and under-fired during competition, while a frontal region worked harder overall, as if compensating. Network measures showed disorganized connections in both areas, tracking symptom severity. The hazardous group showed milder versions, suggesting markers for early intervention.
pmc-13248298:
Stepien and an international team studied how young people with Hunter syndrome move to adult care, reported in 2026. Enzyme treatment has helped many patients with this rare disease live into adulthood. Yet the handover from children's to adult services follows no standard path, so the team interviewed patients, caregivers, and clinicians across six countries.

Participants named continuity of care, one key contact person, and early preparation as marks of a good transfer. Practice varied widely within and between countries. The group proposed shared standards, more teaching and support materials, and psychological help, with extra thought for patients whose disease affects the brain.
pmc-13249498:
Huang Tinghua and co-authors launch a web server that mines key transcription factors from gene activity data in a 2026 paper. Transcription factors switch genes on and off by binding near them. Finding which factors drive a gene list's changes is a common, hard task.

Their server, TransPilot, scores binding sites with a neural network trained on binding likelihood patterns. Target gene sets are ranked by those scores and marked as switched up or down. A weighted rank test then matches the ranked sets against a user's changed gene list. Gaps for genes without known sites are filled by imputation. A macrophage dataset served as the benchmark test.
pmc-13249898:
Kuruoglu and an international team built a heat-tunable surface that sniffs molecules with infrared light, in a 2026 study. The silicon membrane carries tiny patterned structures that resonate sharply in the mid-infrared, where molecules leave fingerprints. Warming the silicon slides those resonances across a useful range, turning one fixed device into a scanning sensor.

With no standard machine, the surface picked out the known bands of two common plastics from how they absorb light. When molecules filled its tiny cavities, light and vibration coupled strongly enough to split the resonance in two. The authors see compact chemical sensors and flexible photonics in the platform's future.
pmc-13250198:
Janet Michel and three colleagues wrote a 2026 commentary on menopause care and the wider neglect of women's health. They note that women form half of the world's population and most of its health workforce, yet their own care stays underfunded and understudied. In Europe, an aging population now meets an aging, largely female care workforce.

The authors describe how menopause is often missing from medical training, leaving many women misdiagnosed or unsupported. They trace costs to physical health, mental health, work, and income. Their response is a five-part call for action covering menopause training for clinicians, protected research funding, and research led by women. They also urge menopause-friendly workplace policies and support from allies of all genders. The piece argues that fixing menopause care would strengthen the whole health system that depends on these women.
pmc-13250398:
Verdi and co-authors show how gene sequencing solved the puzzle of a baby girl born with many unrelated problems. Their 2026 Clinical Case Reports paper follows a thirteen-month-old with a small head, weak muscles, hearing and vision loss, hair loss, and underdeveloped kidneys. Standard metabolic and immune workups found no explanation for her condition.

A stepwise genetic evaluation ended with exome sequencing, which reads the protein-coding parts of the genome. It found two uncertain variants, one inherited from each parent, in a gene called ZPR1. Similar variants had been reported in a syndrome matching her features, including growth problems and kidney underdevelopment. The team argues the variants are likely responsible and urges exome testing for such complex childhood cases.
pmc-13250498:
Christine A. Pellegrini and colleagues report a 2026 randomized trial on sitting less after knee replacement surgery. Pain and movement often improve after the operation, yet daily activity levels barely change for most patients. The trial tested a phone-based program called NEAT!2 that prompts patients to break up long sitting spells.

Eighty-three adults who had surgery within the past year were split between the program and a comparison group. The program paired an app that warns after thirty minutes of sitting with five coaching calls on goals and problem solving. Almost everyone stayed in the study for the full five months of follow-up. By then, the program group rose from their chairs more often than the comparison group, a clear gap between the two. Other measures, including total activity and pain, showed no clear benefit from the program.
pmc-13252698:
Hee Yun Lee and co-authors link hot days, drinking, and childhood in this 2026 study of older Americans. Heat waves are growing longer and stronger, older bodies handle heat poorly, and drinking among older adults has climbed for two decades.

Using a national ageing study covering 1996 to 2018 for people over 50, the team found each extra day above 95 degrees Fahrenheit nudged alcohol use up slightly. A warm relationship with one's father in childhood softened that link. Hard early experiences, a parent's substance abuse or run-ins with police, made the heat-drinking link stronger. The authors back support that builds resilience early in life.
pmc-13253098:
Kavanagh and co-authors test whether expressive faces come with richer social lives. Their 2026 iScience study records spontaneous social interaction across five studies with more than one thousand people. Automated facial coding measured how much each person's expressions moved and varied during interaction.

More expressive women had larger, more diverse, and more deeply embedded real-world social networks. The same pattern did not appear in men in these analyses. Across both sexes, though, expressivity predicted more one-to-one close relationships. The authors read this as support for the idea that close bonding needs helped drive the evolution of highly expressive human faces. They note the findings are correlational, not proof of cause.
pmc-13253598:
Hye Guk Ryu and colleagues print human skin in the lab to test a beauty treatment in this 2026 study. Monopolar radiofrequency is used to tighten skin without surgery, but judging its effects fairly needs a standard test bed rather than varied volunteers.

The team bioprinted collagen blocks seeded with human skin cells and treated them with the device. Treated tissue grew denser, better organised collagen, stiffer under pressure, and slightly smaller. Fluid from treated blocks then coaxed skin cells to migrate faster in a wound test, dialled down pigment-making genes in pigment cells, and helped surface cells survive chemical stress. The model offers repeatable checks of skin-tightening claims.
pmc-13254298:
Nagwa El-Bialy and colleagues present a greener way to measure trace copper in a 2026 study. Their method, ionic liquid-assisted cloud point extraction, first binds copper ions to a dye-like compound, then pulls them into a small droplet phase for measurement by light absorption. It was tested on water and food samples.

The method stayed accurate across a wide range, with a detection limit of 0.6 micrograms per liter stated in the paper. Repeat tests varied by only about 2 percent, and certified reference samples confirmed accuracy. Several green chemistry scores rated the method as sustainable and dependable for routine checks.
pmc-13254898:
Lihui Zhang and colleagues report a fifty-three-week trial of velaglucerase alfa for type 1 Gaucher disease in Chinese patients in 2026. The drug replaces the enzyme these patients lack, letting stored fatty material clear from organs, but local data in Chinese children and adults were scarce. Twenty patients, sixteen never treated before, received infusions every two weeks in this open-label, single-arm phase three study.

Safety led the endpoints. Four patients had serious adverse events requiring hospital admission, and none was judged related to the drug. Efficacy measures moved the right way: hemoglobin rose by about a quarter, platelet counts by over eighty percent on average, and spleen and liver volumes shrank substantially. Nineteen of twenty patients reported better quality of life. The authors conclude the drug was well tolerated with no new safety signals.
pmc-13255198:
Wang, Wang, and Xue spoke with esophageal cancer patients on the day before they left hospital after esophagectomy, asking how ready they felt for discharge. Twelve patients at a tertiary hospital in Tianjin took part in guided interviews during mid 2025. The team read the transcripts with Colaizzi's classic seven-step method.

Three themes emerged: mixed feelings about going home, real dilemmas around discharge readiness, and wide-ranging hurdles in home care afterward. The authors argue that nurses should attend to patients' feelings, self-care skills, and confidence in recovery. Better preparation, they conclude, would match support to what each patient truly needs.
pmc-13256098:
Freya Spain and a large team design peptide blockers of a cancer-linked protein pair in a 2026 paper. Protein-protein contacts drive many diseases but are hard to drug because their surfaces are large and flat. The p53 and hDM2 pair is a classic target, since hDM2 restrains the tumor suppressor p53. The team grafted binding features onto a designed coiled-coil peptide scaffold.

The resulting peptides competed with p53 for hDM2 binding with sub-micromolar strength, shown by fluorescence tests. The authors say the work extends their scaffold approach from an earlier target, supporting coiled coils as a general route to block helix-based protein contacts.
pmc-13256298:
Zhang and colleagues developed a greener way to extract polysaccharides from longan shells, a fruit processing byproduct. Their system pairs ultrasound with a hydrophobic deep eutectic solvent made from two fatty acids, inside a three-phase partitioning setup. Conditions were tuned first one variable at a time, then by response surface modeling.

At the optimized settings the process recovered a modest yield of an acidic heteropolysaccharide rich in galacturonic acid and arabinose, with an open fibrous network structure. The solvent survived five reuse cycles without losing performance. The extract strongly scavenged one test radical and reduced iron in a dose-dependent way. The authors pitch the method for sustainable recovery of bioactive plant molecules.
pmc-13256498:
Naruaki Kawasaki leads the authors of a 2026 trial protocol on acupuncture-based treatment for postmastectomy pain syndrome. That syndrome is lasting pain in the chest, neck, or shoulder after breast cancer surgery, and no standard treatment exists for it. Eligible patients are breast cancer survivors at least six months past curative treatment, with a pain score of four or more and no sign that the cancer has returned.

Under the plan, patients get the treatment once a week for twelve sessions, then four weeks of observation. The main measure is change in average pain score from the start to week sixteen. The study began in October 2023, runs to March 31, 2027, and had enrolled 24 patients when the protocol was submitted. Its results will help design larger trials.
pmc-13257698:
Susana González-Suárez and colleagues study shock during liver transplant surgery and later kidney injury in a 2026 cohort paper. Two hundred twenty-six adults were monitored with artery catheters that classified each shock episode by type. Kidney injury was scored by standard criteria during the first week after surgery.

Shock touched about a third of patients, and kidney injury struck about half overall. Shock by itself lost its link to kidney injury after adjustment for other factors. Shock recurring across several surgical phases told a different story, with far higher injury rates, worse severity, and much higher mortality. Mixed-type shock predicted dialysis need and lingering kidney trouble. Transplant anesthetists learn that duration and pattern matter more than a single low-pressure dip. Preventing repeat episodes becomes the practical target.
pmc-13257798:
Nihat Söylemez leads a 2026 study of two simple scores for predicting heart failure soon after heart attack. More than three thousand patients were followed for failure within one month. Models adding the HALP blood score or the AHEAD clinical score were compared with a baseline clinical model.

Every model discriminated extremely well, and accuracy curves overlapped heavily. The AHEAD model edged highest and improved risk reclassification moderately. HALP added little and lost independent significance after adjustment. In patients with preserved pumping function, failure was rarer and models weakened yet held up. Cardiologists get a measured answer: fancy additions barely move an already strong baseline. Reclassification gains from AHEAD may still help borderline decisions at discharge.
pmc-13258498:
Myriam Galfo leads a 2026 pilot survey of weight, food, and daily habits among rural primary school children in Italy. One hundred eighty two pupils aged six to ten took part from two towns in the Lazio region. Height and weight were measured directly, while families answered questions on meals, activity, sleep, and screen time.

About one third of children carried excess weight by international cutoffs. Fewer than one in five scored high on a Mediterranean diet measure. Many skipped daily breakfast, and only a quarter met activity guidance. Weekend screen time ran high for a large share. Wider sampling is planned before local programs are designed from these early figures.
pmc-13258798:
Sumaya Alshatari and Małgorzata Ziarno pool human trials of polyphenol supplements and gut microbes in a 2026 meta analysis. Fifty randomized trials with about two thousand adults met their criteria. Outcomes covered microbe makeup, diversity, and fatty acids made by gut fermentation.

Most trials found total fermentation acids rose with supplements. Butyrate, a key fuel for gut lining cells, rose clearly in pooled results. Helpful genera such as Bifidobacterium increased in most reporting trials. Diversity gains appeared in about two thirds of studies. Effects looked stronger in people with metabolic disorders and in longer trials. Supplement claims gain a measured evidence base here.
pmc-13258898:
Mingkai Leng and colleagues test soil moisture effects on an invasive aquatic plant in a 2026 controlled study. Parrot feather watermilfoil was grown across five moisture bands from near dry to wet. Growth form, biomass split, and stress chemistry were tracked through the trial.

Plants grew best in the wettest band, with more height, branching, and mass. Mid range dryness triggered shorter roots, more dying stem sections, and stress chemical buildup. Plants died in the driest band yet survived the next band with declining mass. Wet substrate below a dry surface still allowed fast recovery growth. Water managers learn that drawdown zones may favor this invader over native plants.
pmc-13259398:
Xiao Liu and coauthors graft glowing quantum dots onto cotton fabric for anion sensing in a 2026 study. The heavy metal free dots shine brightly until certain negative ions touch the fabric. Glow loss scales with ion concentration for each tested anion.

Five anions triggered measurable responses, including fluoride, chloride, and phosphate. Preparation stays simple, repeatable, and cheap according to the authors. The fabric format suits dip and read field checks without instruments beyond a light source. Aquatic life faces real harm from excess anions, which motivates cheap screening. Environmental monitors gain a wearable style sensor for water checks.
pmc-13259998:
Linlin Zhang and co-authors built in 2026 a machine learning model to spot deep infiltrating endometriosis on MRI scans before surgery. In this severe form, tissue much like the womb lining grows deep into nearby organs, and readings vary between doctors. Their study used 330 patients whose diagnoses were confirmed at surgery between 2020 and 2025.

A weighted blend of five learning models beat every single model on held-out test cases. Blood markers, scan brightness, and symptom length were among the strongest inputs. Two radiologists scored lower on the same cases when reading alone. With the model's help, their accuracy rose and reading time fell by about a third. The authors offer the model as decision support rather than a replacement for doctors.
pmc-13260098:
Jiamian Wang and co-authors tested in 2026 a traditional herbal formula against udder inflammation in cow cells grown in the laboratory. Mastitis is a common, costly disease in dairy herds, and antibiotic use brings residue and resistance worries. Their model exposed bovine mammary cells to a bacterial toxin that triggers strong inflammation.

Cells treated with Danggui Buxue decoction showed lower levels of inflammatory signals such as tumor necrosis factor and several interleukins. Damage markers and oxidative stress measures also fell, and fewer cells leaked contents as they died. The formula further lowered two proteins in a key inflammation pathway, toll-like receptor 4 and NF-kB. The authors read the results as support for the formula as a candidate mastitis treatment, pending tests in live animals.
pmc-13260798:
Yuehan Lv and colleagues pooled in 2026 trial evidence on virtual reality for calming anxiety in women facing gynecological exams or surgery. Twelve randomized trials published between 2019 and 2025 met their criteria. Their multi-level analysis combined the results while modeling how sessions, procedures, and measures varied.

Virtual reality cut anxiety during procedures with a small-to-moderate overall effect, and overall quality rated moderate. Effects held up best for non-invasive procedures, for virtual reality used alone, and for sessions in a middle length range. Highly invasive procedures showed no clear benefit in the pooled data. Country, measurement tool, and study quality each shifted the results. The authors see virtual reality as a useful drug-free add-on for gentler settings, pending larger standardized trials.
pmc-13261298:
Brenda Ruvimbo Mutsvairo and colleagues present a 2026 scoping review of tow truck drivers' experiences at roadside events. Tow truck drivers are often first at crash scenes alongside police and ambulance crews. Unlike other first responders, they may not receive similar support. The review asked about their physical and psychological challenges and coping.

The team searched PubMed, Scopus, CINAHL, and EBSCO between February and April 2024, plus Google Scholar. Fourteen studies met the inclusion rules. Drivers were often first on scene because of their well-developed network. They experience physical and psychological trauma, yet support services are limited. Poor coping, such as excessive alcohol intake, was reported. Lack of safety training contributed to occupational hazards. The authors highlight a clear inequity in support and call for deeper study of drivers' lived experience.
pmc-13262098:
Wenzhen Li and co-authors examine blood-fat measures and early artery disease in a 2026 journal article from China. They combined the atherogenic index of plasma, a ratio of two blood fats, with body mass, waist size, or waist-to-height ratio. Then they asked how these combined scores relate to silent thickening and plaque in the neck arteries.

The cross-sectional study drew 59,123 adults from a stroke screening program in Hubei from 2017 to 2020. Higher combined scores were linked to thicker artery walls, more plaque, and more narrowing. The body-mass version sorted cases best for artery disease overall, with a test score of 0.833. The authors say later follow-up studies must test whether these cheap measures help in clinic use.
pmc-13263298:
María F. Beribe and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on what shapes milk output and fertility in Argentine dairy herds kept on pasture. The team analyzed records of 46,588 lactations from 19,936 cows in 16 herds, gathered between 2010 and 2023.

Herd, number of the lactation, and the month and year of calving affected every trait they studied. Milk yield rose with parity, meaning the count of past calvings, and peaked in the third to fifth lactations. Fertility instead declined steadily as parity increased. Cows calving in autumn and winter showed the best overall results, which the authors link to mating decisions and to when cows conceive.
pmc-13263398:
Na Wang and co-authors present a 2026 case report on treating drug-resistant tuberculosis of the brain coverings with a newer antibiotic. The disease, multidrug-resistant tuberculous meningitis, often proves fatal and has few treatment options. A 33-year-old man had taken the standard drug linezolid for six months.

Linezolid damaged his peripheral nerves, causing worsening numbness and pain, so it was stopped. His spinal fluid tests stayed abnormal. Doctors switched him to contezolid, a related drug thought to be gentler. Within three months his headache and blurred vision cleared, and by five months his spinal fluid pressure and chemistry normalized. No side effects appeared, and improvement held through two years of follow-up.
pmc-13263498:
Alex DeBusschere and co-authors report a 2026 qualitative study of communication during dialysis for patients with hearing loss. Hemodialysis centers, where machines clean the blood of people with kidney failure, are noisy places. The team interviewed fourteen patients in Calgary and Edmonton, Canada, about talking with their care teams and about tools that might help.

Views on communication tools differed, and three themes emerged. Some patients wanted tools mainly in transitions or complex situations. Others relied on their own resources and needed center tools less. Awareness of available support, and willingness to ask for it, also varied widely. The authors advise clinicians to ask routinely about communication needs and offer several tool options.
pmc-13264298:
Fenfen Zhang and colleagues evaluate doctor-led virtual reality and medical games for children facing urology surgery in a 2026 retrospective study. One hundred twenty children aged five to twelve treated during 2024 were split between standard preparation and an added program. The program gave an immersive panoramic preview of the surgical journey plus interactive games explaining procedures, led by doctors within a team spanning several specialties and nursing care.

After matching for baseline differences, the program group reported markedly lower fear and anxiety scores. Cooperation with care was higher and parents were more satisfied than in the standard group. All differences reached statistical significance. Playful preview combined with trusted clinician guidance appears to soften the surgical experience for children and families.
pmc-13264898:
Amira Messaoud and colleagues wrote a 2026 study of metabolic syndrome in women with polycystic ovary syndrome in western Algeria. The ovary condition often travels with weight, sugar, and fat problems. The team measured how common the full syndrome is in this group and how affected women differ from unaffected ones.

They studied 313 women aged 16 to 45 who attended clinics in the Oran region. More than half, 57.9 percent, met the syndrome rules. Those women had higher body mass, fasting sugar, and blood fats, and lower good cholesterol. Hormone levels also differed, including lower vitamin D and progesterone. Excess hair growth, irregular periods, and trouble conceiving after prior birth were more common in this group. The authors urge early metabolic screening and whole-person care.
pmc-13264998:
Alberto Leguina-Ruzzi and co-authors wrote a 2026 study of VectorLift, a guided thread-lifting method for the face that avoids full surgery. Thread lifts reposition sagging tissue with shorter recovery, but results vary with design choices. Their method uses anatomy-guided thread paths, ligament support, and refined numbing, and they compared it with two standard thread approaches.

Over three years, 44 women with a mean age of 47 had thread lifts. Eighteen received VectorLift, and the rest received one of two other thread types. The VectorLift group reported less pain during the procedure, shorter downtime, and fewer early problems like dimpling and bruising. Satisfaction scores were similar across groups, and photos showed visible lift without overcorrection. The authors call the findings exploratory, since patients were not assigned by chance.
pmc-13265198:
Xiaomin Wen and colleagues build a risk model for cervical cancer from genes tied to myeloid cell development, in a 2026 study. Myeloid cells inside tumours can suppress immunity and shape treatment response. Their development pathways may hold prognostic clues. Single-cell and bulk gene data were combined.

Four genes formed the final risk score. The score split patients into high-risk and low-risk groups with distinct outcomes. A chart combining the score forecast prognosis accurately. Pathways tied to synapse organisation were enriched in the high-risk group. Eleven immune cell populations differed between groups. Laboratory tests confirmed the gene expression patterns.
pmc-13265698:
Dionysios V Chartoumpekis and Aristea Psilopanagioti review how maternal obesity rewires feeding circuits before birth, published in 2026. Research has centred on the hypothalamus, a brain hub for hunger signals. Damage there raises lifelong obesity risk in offspring. Evidence now points to wider brain networks.

Brainstem circuits sensing body signals and reward-control systems also appear vulnerable. Offspring show weaker white matter, altered connectivity, and changed hunger signals. Inflammation and gene-regulating marks are implicated. Human imaging links maternal body fat with newborn network changes. The authors urge study of how maternal signals reach the developing brain.
pmc-13266398:
Songke Wu, Chengshi Wang, and Shuyun Liu compare first treatments for metastatic bowel cancer without RAS mutations, in a 2026 network meta-analysis. Many targeted regimens exist without head-to-head trials for all pairs. Fifteen randomised trials with about six thousand patients formed the network. Survival, response, and safety were ranked.

Two antibody-plus-chemotherapy regimens beat a third comparator on overall survival. The cetuximab combination ranked highest for survival and time without progression. Benefit concentrated in left-sided tumours, with none seen for right-sided disease. Severe side effects were more frequent with the winning class. Tumour side should guide first choice.
pmc-13267298:
Kyaw Ko Ko Htet leads a 2026 study of hospital returns and survival after lung tuberculosis in Thailand. The team drew on a national database covering all hospital stays from 2017 to 2022. They matched 59,027 patients admitted for drug-sensitive lung TB with the same number of similar patients admitted for other causes.

Former TB patients returned to hospital far more often for chest problems. Risks were about five times higher for fluid around the heart and for collapsed lung. Risks were also higher for widened airways and liver inflammation. The TB group also faced a higher risk of death than matched controls. The authors say care for TB survivors needs to improve after the infection itself is cured.
pmc-13267498:
Dongjie Hou and colleagues report a 2026 method for making glowing dyes used in super-clear cell imaging. The dyes, called silicon-rhodamines, glow far-red and last long under the microscope. A carboxyl-tagged form is needed to attach them to targets, but making that form used to need harsh, costly, or toxic reagents.

The new route uses carbon dioxide, the common gas, as the carbon source. A standard lithium reagent swaps a bromine atom on the dye, and the gas adds the tag in one step. Yields ranged from 60 to 93 percent. The crude product could go straight into the next step without cleaning. Probes built this way let the team film fine cell parts over long periods.
pmc-13267898:
Volodymyr Maksym and colleagues present a 2026 case report on strength training as therapy after war exposure. Their patient was a 32-year-old man, a former combat medic, with six months of severe anxiety and low mood after military service. He also had insomnia, tremor, poor appetite, and widespread pain, and he avoided crowded places.

He joined a supervised gym program of strength-based physical therapy, three times a week for about six months. Loads were adjusted to his daily readiness. Standard questionnaires showed his depression score falling from 27 to 7 and anxiety from 30 to 8. Sleep became normal, pain resolved, and social life improved. No relapse was reported at about twelve months. The authors present the program as a workable add-on within team care.
pmc-13268898:
Jee Ho Kang, Sanghyuk Im, and Seung Yoon Song review in 2026 a rare cause of tongue nerve paralysis: a tear in the neck portion of the carotid artery. The hypoglossal nerve guides tongue movement, and its failure causes slurred speech and swallowing trouble that first suggests stroke. Their systematic review gathered 73 studies covering 87 adult patients.

pmc-13276598:

pmc-13278398:
