Valentin Koch and co-authors present UNICORN in 2026, a learning model that reads several stained versions of the same heart artery tissue slices together to grade fatty plaque severity. Older tools glue stain features together crudely and cope poorly when a stain is missing.

UNICORN first runs a specialist reader for each stain, then a second stage learns how the stain views interact. On a Munich biobank set of slide images it reached classification accuracy the authors report as 0.68, ahead of rival models. The system also highlighted tissue patterns tied to worsening disease. The authors see wider use in multi-stain pathology and treatment decisions.
pmc-13287998:
Daniel Cardona-Cifuentes and colleagues model pregnancy loss in Brahman cattle under heat stress in a 2026 genetics study. Brahman cattle suit tropical farms, yet lost pregnancies still cut herd output. The team used reaction norm models, which track how genetic merit changes across environments. Weather records gave a temperature-humidity index around the time of pregnancy checks in two Bolivian herds.

Genetic variation appeared both in baseline loss risk and in how risk changed as heat rose. Adding DNA data to pedigree data raised the accuracy of breeding value estimates. Heritability estimates for loss stayed modest across heat levels, near one tenth to one eighth. Animals ranked differently under mild and harsh heat, shown by negative genetic correlations between extremes. The authors conclude that selection for heat-resilient reproduction is feasible with genomic reaction norm models.
pmc-13288598: A 2026 retraction notice withdraws a 2010 study of Vinca rosea extracts in diabetic rats, published in the International Journal of Endocrinology. Editors acted after concerns on PubPeer that one figure panel shared repeated regions with a panel in another article. The original authors said the work was done over 17 years earlier and that raw data and files no longer exist, so editors judged the findings unreliable. The notice is brief and gives no new data, only the reason for withdrawal and the parties who agreed to it.
pmc-13288698:
Adela Movaddt and colleagues publish a 2026 trial protocol testing family-focused counseling for first-time mothers in Babol, Iran. Pregnancy often brings anxiety that undermines confidence about giving birth, and the Bowen systemic approach targets family and social dynamics rather than the mother alone.

Seventy-two first-time mothers at prenatal centers will be assigned by chance to counseling or control care, in blocks of four. Counseling means six ninety-minute group sessions, one in person and five online through WhatsApp, in groups of six to ten women. Anxiety, birth confidence, and satisfaction are the main outcomes, with enrollment underway since November 2025 and completion expected by July 2026.
pmc-13288898:
Zong-Yen Wu and colleagues engineer gut bacteria to grow mineral nanomaterials in a 2026 study. Making metal oxide particles usually takes high heat, pressure, or harsh solvents. The team borrowed a urease gene cluster from a mineral-forming bacterium and placed it in E. coli. Urease raises local alkalinity, which coaxes dissolved minerals to crystallize. A gene delivery method called CRAGE-Duet installed the cluster.

The engineered strain produced calcium carbonate and calcium phosphate crystals as expected. Extending the recipe yielded hematite, an iron oxide, and anatase titanium dioxide particles. Microscope images confirmed the crystal forms and tiny sizes. Because growth happens in mild water, the process avoids furnace steps. The authors present E. coli as a flexible green factory for nanomaterials. Such particles serve medicine, electronics, energy, and cleanup technologies.
pmc-13289398:
Annet Onzia led a 2026 community survey on sexually transmitted infections among young women working as domestic workers near Kampala, Uganda. Little was known about infection burden in this group, aged 14 to 24, despite possible high risk. Fieldwork ran from November 2023 to March 2024 in the Kampala Metropolitan Area with self-collected swabs and blood tests.

Among 262 participants with a median age of 20 years, 87 had at least one infection tested. Chlamydia was most common, then syphilis, HIV, and gonorrhea in falling order. About 14.9 percent carried more than one infection at once in testing. Half had gotten symptom-based treatment in the prior year, yet few told partners. Non-cash pay and lower schooling each linked to higher infection rates.
pmc-13289498:
Asmaa S. Taha, Shereen A. Soliman, and Rabab A. Metwally tested a 2026 fungal treatment to shield maize plants from lead stress. Lead is a toxic metal that disrupts plant function, cuts yield, and can enter food chains. The fungus Trichoderma harzianum, isolate Zag-1, can boost plant growth and tolerate metals, so lab and pot trials checked its protective power.

In dishes, the fungus tolerated lead up to 1500 ppm and removed over two thirds at a mid dose as reported. In pots, lead at low and high doses stunted maize shoots and roots and drained leaf pigments sharply. High lead also cut leaf water content by more than a quarter versus clean controls. Fungus-treated plants were then compared for defense and stability gains.
pmc-13290098:
Getting antisense drugs into the brain is the problem taken up by Tatjana Sela and a large team in a 2026 study. Antisense oligonucleotides can tune gene activity with high precision, but they cannot cross the blood-brain barrier on their own, so antibody shuttles that ride the transferrin receptor are used to ferry them.

Sela and colleagues tested how attaching the drug cargo changes shuttle behavior in cell assays and a barrier model. Cargo raised binding for weak transferrin binders yet weakened strong ones, and it slowed passage for high-to-moderate affinity shuttles. Building on that, they engineered adjusted transferrin shuttles and a dual shuttle that also targets CD98hc, which crossed more efficiently. The work argues for design guided by mechanism rather than binding strength alone.
pmc-13290598:
Obesity quiets the skeleton's rebuilding signals, Haiqi Lin and colleagues conclude in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Whether extra weight speeds or slows bone turnover has been murky, so the team pooled studies comparing turnover markers in people with obesity and normal weight.

Fourteen articles with 4,612 subjects met the criteria. Alkaline phosphatase did not differ between groups, but PINP, a marker of bone formation, was significantly lower with obesity. Osteocalcin was also lower overall, though the drop reached significance only in children and adolescents, not adults. Two resorption markers showed no clear difference, a shakier part of the picture. Lin and colleagues read the pattern as suppressed formation and ask for work on the mechanisms.
pmc-13290698:
Wrapping a freed nerve in living fat kept a stubborn nerve disorder from coming back, F. Thuau and colleagues describe in a case report from 2026. Their patient, a 35-year-old woman, had recurrent neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome, where scar tissue re-strangles the brachial plexus after earlier surgery.

The team released the nerves above the collarbone and wrapped the plexus in a free fat flap taken from the abdomen (a DIEP flap). It was the first such use they could find in their own systematic review. Fat flaps protect nerves, feed the area blood, and resist new scarring while sparing muscle and adding little donor harm. At two-year follow-up her pain and function scores (VAS, DASH, and SF-36) had significantly improved. The authors present free perforator fat as a low-morbidity wrapping option for recurrent cases.
pmc-13290998:
Robert Knoerl and colleagues test in a 2026 pilot trial whether young cancer survivors can press their own acupoints at home to ease lasting fatigue. Eligible participants were adolescent and young adult survivors at least three months past treatment whose fatigue scores met a set clinical threshold.

Forty-two survivors joined and were split, two to one, between relaxing acupressure and a sham version, pressing five points daily for six weeks. Recruitment and survey completion met the team’s feasibility aims, though only 38 percent managed three or more sessions in an average week. Fatigue fell in both groups by week six and stayed lower at week ten, with no clear gap between groups. A larger trial would need stronger support for daily practice.
pmc-13291798:
Cortés Sierra's team reports a 2026 cross-sectional analysis of body composition readings from one bioelectrical impedance device in routine outpatients. Because each maker's algorithms differ, values from a single platform need their own reference ranges. The team used the SECA mBCA 514 with about 1,850 adults, charting phase angle and skeletal muscle mass by sex and age.

Men showed higher phase angle and muscle mass than women, and both measures fell across older age groups. Women carried a higher fat-to-muscle ratio, and that ratio tracked moderately with lower phase angle. Its link with the device's visceral fat estimate was weak. The authors present the tables as interpretation aids for clinic use, not proof of biological mechanisms.
pmc-13292298:
Yibo Cheng and co-authors share a 2026 case series on rituximab for children whose kidney disease blends IgA nephropathy with minimal change-like lesions. The combination usually behaves like steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome but relapses often. Eight children who stayed steroid-dependent or kept relapsing despite steroids and second-line drugs received rituximab, then were followed for 12 to 41 months.

Yearly relapses fell by 1.1 episodes per child after treatment, remission stretched by 3.5 months, and the steroid-free stretch grew by 7.4 months on average. Nearly nine in ten children, 87.5 percent of the group, stopped steroids entirely, and half stopped other suppressants. Three relapsed, which the authors link to loose B-cell monitoring and missing booster doses, yet all regained remission. No serious drug harms appeared.
pmc-13292598:
Shorouq Alqannas and colleagues survey a 2026 burnout snapshot among mental healthcare providers in Jordan, where thin resources and public stigma pile onto emotional work. Two hundred twenty-one providers answered the Arabic Maslach Burnout Inventory in February 2025, half online and half on paper. The scale splits burnout into emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and personal accomplishment.

Exhaustion ran high: 42.5 percent of providers scored in the high band, with a mean of 19.06 on that subscale. Depersonalization stayed low for 71.9 percent, and accomplishment looked moderate, with 48.4 percent scoring high. Age and weekly hours shaped the pattern; providers over 45 and those working longer weeks reported stronger accomplishment. The authors prescribe better staffing, workload control, supervision, and well-being programs to keep the workforce intact.
pmc-13292998:
Wei Zhang and co-authors built, in a 2026 study, a battery-free smart dental aligner that can sense and treat chronic mouth disease. Tooth decay and gum disease vary by spot in the mouth, and space for powered devices inside is tight.

The aligner holds a soft two-sided electrode sheet, shaped with butterfly-like design, that tracks acidity and nitrite at matched spots. It can also release germ-killing agents when sensors call for it. Power and commands pass through a near-field link paired with Bluetooth, so no battery sits in the mouth. Tests from lab bench to early human use support the closed-loop design for personal mouth care.
pmc-13293398:
Sangtaek Oh and co-authors ask, in a 2026 study, whether a family history of diabetes speeds up blood sugar drift before any diagnosis. Most past work tracked who gets diabetes, not how fast sugar markers creep up in checkup data.

Korean adult checkup records gave 25,647 people with measures about two years apart and 12,831 with measures about four years apart. After matching and weighting for 49 other factors, those with affected relatives showed slightly faster rises in both long-term and fasting sugar. Gaps grew wider over four years. Family history may flag people for tighter monitoring and earlier prevention.
pmc-13293598:
Zikun Liu and co-authors study, in a 2026 paper, how young Chinese adults with diabetes tell their illness stories on RedNote, a social platform built around diary-style posts. Chronic illness can unsettle identity, above all in youth, and online spaces now host much of that telling.

A total of 303 text and video posts were coded for story patterns and cultural context. Four types stood out: chaos after diagnosis, stigma and hiding, resilience through daily routines, and solidarity through family and peer support online. Together they show illness woven into self-image and social life, not just medical facts. Peer exchange turned isolation into shared experience.
pmc-13293698:
Xinyi Wang and Ruixia Wang review, in a 2026 paper, tools that use future scenarios to plan city green spaces under uncertainty. Green areas give ecological and social gains, yet their future shape depends on climate, land use, and policy shifts.

A total of 157 publications were sorted into two strands: regional ecological planning from land data, and green systems inside built cities. The strands differed in place, focus, and how futures were built and judged. Regional work stressed ecological security and climate, while city work stressed cooling, stormwater, and air quality. Shared judging frameworks and public input stayed thin across both strands.
pmc-13293898:
Einav Levy and Moshe Farchi present a 2026 theory-driven case analysis of psychological first aid given before distress peaks. Their case is a body recovery mission on October 8, 2023, in Kibbutz Be'eri, Israel, after the October 7 attack. A trained commander applied the SIX Cs model before, during, and after exposure to mass death.

Steps covered clear briefings, task rehearsal, role assignment, and a closing review. The six parts stress mental structuring, direct communication, challenge, control, commitment, and continuity. The authors argue that early structure may blunt helplessness and tunnel vision, and they frame proactive aid as a distinct approach needing formal testing.
pmc-13294698:
Baogui Gao and colleagues present a 2026 case report on treating two-level lumbar stenosis through a new endoscopic route. Their patient, a man aged 72, had back pain spreading into his left leg and mild thigh muscle wasting. Scans showed narrowing at two levels plus a far-lateral disc herniation pressing the exiting nerve root.

Surgeons used a contralateral trans-spinous base inclined approach with arthroscopic-assisted uni-portal surgery to free both levels. Pain eased at once after surgery, strength improved, and scans confirmed open canals with no worsening of vertebral slippage. Facet joints were largely preserved, supporting the route as a stability-sparing option for older, frailer patients.
pmc-13294798:
Jingchao Bai and colleagues test a simple blood ratio as a warning sign for intensive care patients with cancer in a 2026 study. The ratio divides lactate by albumin, combining signs of metabolic strain and poor nutrition. Whether it predicts both early and later deaths in this group needed testing.

Records for 1,634 patients were grouped into thirds by the ratio, and deaths climbed steadily across those thirds. Thirty-day deaths rose from 23 percent in the lowest third to 43 percent in the highest third. After adjustment for other factors, a higher ratio still predicted death at both 30 days and 360 days in a straight-line pattern.
pmc-13294998:
Peng Wu and a large team study penicillin allergy labels in lung patients in a 2026 cohort study from China. Labels are often wrong, yet they push doctors toward broader antibiotics during flare-ups of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The team asked whether labelled patients flare more often afterwards.

Among 14,900 patients aged 40 and above, 722 carried an allergy label in their records. Labelled patients received more broad-spectrum antibiotics and faced clearly higher flare risk and flare rates over about four years of follow-up. The authors argue that checking and removing false labels could sharpen antibiotic use and ease the burden of flare-ups.
pmc-13295498:
Chunhao Jiang and co-authors take stock of weakened-virus vaccines against African swine fever, in a 2026 review. The disease devastates pig herds and wild boar, and live-attenuated vaccines, built from tamed virus, remain the leading strategy. Only Vietnam has authorized commercial products so far, and the review explains why wider use has stalled despite decades of effort.

Two problems dominate. New recombinant strains mixing two viral genotypes have completely escaped the protection of current vaccines, which were built on one genotype alone. Every candidate also carries some risk of reverting to a harmful form, a danger regulators cannot ignore. The authors walk through the vaccine family's history, show how viral evolution drives the escapes, and propose design fixes meant to widen protection and lock in safety. Their goal is a vaccine the whole industry can trust.
pmc-13295798:
Erin Hannink and colleagues set out a trial plan on personalised physiotherapy after hip revision surgery in a 2026 protocol. Repeat hip replacement leaves patients worse off than first-time surgery, and no agreed rehabilitation guide exists. Care also scatters because specialist centres sit far from many homes.

Sixty patients from at least four British hospitals will be split evenly between tailored therapy and usual standardised care. The pilot tests whether a full trial can recruit, run, and keep patients, while interviews explore how the tailored approach lands. Functional results and quality of life will be watched to judge whether personal plans deserve a larger test.
pmc-13295998:
Sulaiman Alsaab and colleagues pool evidence in 2026 on how mental illness affects people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Searching five databases, they compare lung function, symptoms, flare-ups and survival between patients with and without mental health conditions.

Fifty-eight studies covering over seven hundred thousand people found worse outcomes nearly across the board: weaker lungs, shorter walking distance, heavier breathlessness and poorer quality of life. Flare-ups, admissions and deaths all ran higher, with depression and anxiety showing the strongest links. The authors argue mental health care should be built into lung disease management.
pmc-13296098:
Jiayin Guo and Jun Liu run, in 2026, a situational experiment on when people say they would trust someone. Earlier work leaned on pure calculation or on closeness alone, so the team vary three things at once in 252 participants. They vary how close the relationship is and how big the sum entrusted is. They also vary whether the trustee seems able and honest.

All three factors shaped trust intentions, and they interacted rather than adding up neatly. Trust with family, acquaintances and general others responded differently as loan sizes grew from small to very large. The authors present trust as a context-bound judgement, not a fixed trait or simple sum.
pmc-13296498:
Ashley J S Scott and colleagues review, in 2026, what registered nurses say after actually using artificial intelligence tools at work, rather than before trying them. Searching five databases to September 2023, they gather twenty studies and sort nurses' accounts by usefulness, ease and workplace support.

Nurses valued help with decisions, smoother workflow and confidence when training, linked systems and technical backing were in place. Clunky design, poor fit with records, privacy worries and unreliable outputs held adoption back. The authors conclude that benefits depend on involving nurses in design and on ready organisations.
pmc-13296598:
Saroj Upreti and a large team used a robotic platform to map how triblock copolymers behave when blended with plain polystyrene, in a 2026 study. Blend behaviour depends on the added polymer's chain length and share, and testing every combination by hand is slow. Robots prepared thin films across a wide grid, which X-ray scattering and microscopy then examined.

Three regimes appeared as chain length grew. Short chains swelled the ordered domains gently before disorder set in at high loadings. Medium chains swelled domains strongly, then disordered earlier, while long chains simply separated out. Computer simulations backed the picture for short chains. The platform could speed design of nanostructured plastics when paired with machine learning.
pmc-13296798:
Jawaher A. Alsubait and colleagues look for immune-gene variants tied to COVID-19 outcomes in Saudi patients in a 2026 prospective study. The HLA genes shape how the immune system presents virus fragments to T cells, so their variants might explain why illness severity varies. A Riyadh hospital typed 123 patients and grouped them by survival and illness stage.

Just over four fifths of the patients recovered, while the rest died, usually after intensive care. Several allele groups appeared more often among patients who died, and one appeared more often among survivors. Severity stages showed their own pattern of differences. Vaccination status did not separate the groups. The authors stress caution, given the small cohort.
pmc-13297298:
In a 2026 study, Yong Sun and co-authors ask whether polyamide 6 microplastics, a common plastic dust, can speed the wearing out of spinal discs. Such particles have been found in human disc tissue, yet direct proof of harm was missing. The team crossed plastic-linked targets drawn from public data banks with genes tied to disc degeneration, then tested the overlap in human disc cells.

Ten shared targets emerged, with four core ones picked out, among them NR3C1 and HDAC1. Computer docking showed the plastic binds these targets firmly. In cell tests, the particles cut cell survival and growth in step with dose. The work links an everyday pollutant to disc decline and names targets for later checks.
pmc-13297698:
Refrigerated mashed potato firms up and weeps water as its starch ages; a plant fiber can slow that decline, report Siyu He and colleagues in a 2026 food science study. They added soluble arabinoxylan to mashed potato and stored it for seven days at 4 °C.

Measurements of stiffness, hardness, and water behavior showed the fiber kept the mash softer and held moisture better. Imaging and diffraction checks found less starch recrystallization, fewer ordered structures, and a physically disrupted starch network, all signs of delayed retrogradation. Tasters also rated the treated product more favorably. The authors pitch arabinoxylan as a clean-label ingredient for longer-lasting starchy convenience foods.
pmc-13297798:
Which glue holds braces on best? Celalettin Noyan Sevindik and his team pooled the trial proof in a 2026 review, setting resin-modified glass ionomer cement next to standard resin glues for fixed braces.

Seven trials made the cut. Fail rates for the glass ionomer ran from 5.95% to 15.0%, and resin showed a wider spread that reached 25.0% at the top. Pooled odds came out even, with no real gap in how often brackets fell off. The trials clashed with each other a lot, and trust in the proof was low. One trial did favor the glass ionomer, but only with a special enamel prep step first. The team calls for bigger, longer trials.
pmc-13297898:
Cláudia Barbosa and co-authors report a 2026 comparison of training teeth used before dental students treat real patients. Learners practised standard root canal work on commercial artificial teeth and on PolyJet 3D-printed teeth, with natural teeth serving as the reference. Questionnaires captured views on shape, feel, X-ray appearance, and usefulness for teaching.

Printed teeth scored better for inner anatomy, radiopacity, canal wall resistance, and feel during instrumentation, while commercial teeth scored better for outer shape. Natural teeth stayed the favourite, printed teeth came second, and printed models also produced higher procedure scores with fewer errors. The authors still call for better material realism.
pmc-13298698:
Prostate cancer tests trade accuracy against cost and invasiveness, and Unathi A Tshoni with colleagues compare the main options in a 2026 review. They weigh cheap screening staples against newer high-technology methods on cost-effectiveness, accuracy, and research value.

PSA blood tests and digital rectal exams are inexpensive and widely available, suiting mass screening, but their weak specificity invites overdiagnosis. Biomarker assays, multiparametric MRI, and liquid biopsies return richer, more accurate information, yet their price and scarcity shut out many settings, especially in less developed countries. The authors frame test choice as matching the tool to the setting's resources and the clinical question at hand.
pmc-13298898:
Plant acids could guard food in place of lab-made guards, but one kin group has far more proof than the next. Zhoujing Li and his team weigh that proof in a 2026 review of phenolic acids and phenolamides.

Phenolic acids kill germs in three ways: they break cell walls, sour the cell core, and spark harsh oxygen forms. They also block rust-like harm in food by giving up hydrogen and by gripping stray metals. For phenolamides, germ claims rest on mere screen models, with near no tests in real food. The team weigh ways to add the guards, from plain mixing to packs that give them off. Low yield and high cleanup cost hold the kin group back.
pmc-13299098:
Sound-wave heat can treat a womb-wall disease with no cut, and the right drug mate makes it hit harder. Qi Qin and her team reach that view in a 2026 pooled study of adenomyosis care. They set high-heat focused sound, HIFU, plus one of six drug mates, next to sound care alone.

Sixteen trials with 1,685 patients made the cut. Sound care plus a shot of ethanol through the skin ranked top on cleared tissue share, energy spent, and time taken. A mate that damps sex hormones led on energy thrift. Each pair beat sound care alone on the marks checked. The team note that pairs win on unlike marks, so the drug pick should fit the aim of care.
pmc-13299598:
A virus RNA structure grabs the cell's protein-making machinery in a pose unlike normal translation, reveal Deepakash Das and co-authors in a 2026 structural study. Using cryo-electron microscopy, they froze the encephalomyocarditis virus's internal ribosome entry site bound to the mammalian 43S initiation complex at the start codon.

The viral RNA touches the initiator tRNA and the small ribosomal subunit's head at their shared interface, holding the tRNA away from its usual position. One viral domain even impersonates a piece of the large subunit's RNA to grip head proteins uS13 and uS19. The structure explains years of biochemical results and may generalize to related viral entry sites.
pmc-13299698:
Lingering concussion symptoms and mood problems travel together in athletes, though the literature measuring them is a patchwork, map MJ Lumb and colleagues in a 2026 scoping review. They gathered five years of studies on adult athletes whose post-concussion symptoms lasted at least four weeks.

Fourteen studies qualified, and nine reported a positive link between persisting symptoms and depression or anxiety symptoms. Methods varied wildly, from single case reports to surveys of 3,406 people, follow-up from twenty-eight days to fifty-five years, and thirteen different screening tools in play. Even the terminology for persisting symptoms was inconsistent. The authors call for shared definitions and standard screening before firm clinical guidance can follow.
pmc-13300398:
F Buoncristiani and colleagues assess alcohol infusion into the vein of Marshall during repeat ablation for persistent atrial fibrillation, in a 2026 study at many centers. Repeat procedures lack a settled best plan, and the infusion is meant to deepen tissue change around a key isthmus. The prospective series covered 263 patients. It set 121 who got the infusion plus a fixed anatomical ablation plan against standard redo approaches, with propensity matching to balance the groups.

In matched follow-up, recurrence of atrial arrhythmias occurred in twenty percent of the infusion group against forty-two percent of controls. After adjustment, the combined strategy was tied to a markedly lower risk of recurrence. That held whatever the age, disease duration, or number of earlier procedures. A three-way weighted comparison also favored the combined approach, most strongly in long-lasting persistent disease. The authors present the pairing as a promising redo template.
pmc-13301498:
M Khan and co-authors mine a Swedish screening cohort for early warnings of atrial fibrillation in a 2026 analysis. Within the STROKESTOP study, 7,165 people aged seventy-five or seventy-six recorded thirty second handheld heart tracings twice daily for two weeks. After exclusions, 6,145 participants without fibrillation at baseline were followed through registries for eight years, and every early beat was classified by pattern and by how premature it was.

About thirteen percent, 772 people, developed fibrillation. Lone early beats appeared in about seventy-two percent of future cases versus fifty-two percent of those who stayed free, and they nearly doubled the risk. The earlier the stray beat fired, the higher the risk climbed. Short runs of beats raised it further. Brief supraventricular tachycardia runs more than doubled it, and they preceded diagnosis within three years. The authors promote prematurity as a susceptibility marker worth acting on.
pmc-13301798:
Kentaro Iwasaki and co-authors report 2026 outcomes for Baerveldt glaucoma implants used as the first drainage operation in eyes that had never had filtering surgery. The implant is a small plate and tube that lets fluid leave the eye to lower pressure. Judging success depends heavily on which pressure ceiling is applied.

The review included 148 eyes treated at one specialist centre, tracked with survival methods over five years. Average eye pressure fell from the mid-thirties before surgery to about fourteen at five years, and daily glaucoma medicines dropped by more than half. Success rates ranged widely across the three pressure criteria, highest under the loosest ceiling. Younger patients failed more often under every definition, a warning for long-term planning in that group.
pmc-13303298:
Feng Zhou and co-authors print, in a 2026 study, a two-layer scaffold designed to regrow the cartilage-and-bone unit inside joints. The two tissues heal at different speeds and bond poorly, which defeats many repairs. Their scaffold pairs a bone-like lower phase with wide pores against a cartilage-guiding upper phase with finer pores.

A gel carrying chondroitin was soaked into the upper region only, leaving a thin bare transition band between layers. In dishes, the gel improved cartilage cell attachment and matrix output, and stem cells switched on both bone and cartilage programmes. In rabbit knee defects, treated scaffolds rebuilt early bone and laid down more cartilage-like matrix than bare scaffolds or no treatment within eight weeks.
pmc-13303798:
Mathew Thomson and co-authors unveil version three of an open data model for wastewater disease surveillance in a 2026 paper. Sewage monitoring boomed during the COVID-19 pandemic, but scattered formats and sloppy metadata block data sharing between programmes. The model standardises how sites, samples, measurements, and populations are recorded.

New features capture richer metadata and link records across places and people, including tables for public health actions taken in response. Mapping tools translate between this model and other standards, and both long and wide data layouts are supported. The authors balance depth against ease of use so small programmes can adopt it too. Wider adoption, they argue, would make sewage data far more useful for decisions.
pmc-13307398:
Xianhong Sun and co-authors measure in 2026 two long lasting pollutants, PFOA and PFOS, in the Henan stretch of the Yellow River in China. They sampled nine sites that covered factory outfalls, sewage plant outflows, busy human areas, and cleaner side streams used as a baseline.

Both chemicals turned up at every site, and PFOA levels ran from 0.45 to 7.46 in nanograms per litre across the survey. Loads were highest near industrial discharge points, which points to factories as the main source. Risk scores for wildlife and for people who drink the water stayed low, yet children faced slightly higher exposure than adults.
pmc-13307798:
Katarina Nenadović, Dejan Bugarski, and Tamara Ilić compare in 2026 sheep welfare and parasite loads in barn kept versus pasture flocks across 26 farms. Their checks covered 1192 ewes from November 2025 to April 2026, scoring fleece, skin, eyes, hooves, udders, and blood signs.

Pasture ewes showed more soiled fleece, skin sores, eye and nose discharge, and itching than barn ewes did in the survey. Barn ewes showed more fleece loss, overgrown hooves, uneven udders, and wool pulling instead. Many worm, fluke, and single cell parasites turned up in both settings. Each system thus needs its own fix list, with parasite control tuned to the risks that setting brings.
pmc-13310198:
Amber Heegers and co-authors compare emotion reading against general thinking across six brain conditions in a 2026 study. Reading faces is a core social skill that brain damage often blunts. Whether social and general thinking fail in the same pattern across diseases was unclear.

Records from four Dutch centers covered 710 patients, spanning head injury, stroke, brain bleeding, a slow brain tumor, Parkinson disease, and a dementia type. Face reading scores fell in every group, with clear gaps between groups in the reported analysis. Memory, processing speed, and mental flexibility were scored beside face reading against healthy norms. The authors chart where emotion reading drops beyond general decline, a pattern that shapes rehab and family guidance.
pmc-13310398:
Tsuyoshi Mino and co-authors measure how lying down changes eye pressure across the day in glaucoma in a 2026 study. Eye pressure rises when patients lie flat, and that posture jump may damage the optic nerve over time. Whether the jump differs between morning and night, and what drives it, was the question.

Records covered 108 eyes of 61 patients with open-angle glaucoma on pressure-lowering medication. Pressure was measured sitting and lying at nine in the morning and nine in the evening, using a rebound device. In the morning the jump averaged 3.5 mmHg across the group, well above the evening average of 2.7 mmHg in the same patients. Morning jumps tied to sitting pressure and tissue thickness behind the retina, while evening jumps tied to body and blood pressure traits.
pmc-13310498:
Dan Yang and co-authors link early pregnancy weight gain to diabetes and large babies in a 2026 study. Weight gained in the first trimester may set metabolic tone for the whole pregnancy. Whether fast early gain alone raises gestational diabetes and oversized newborn risk was the question.

Records for 500 women with single pregnancies at one hospital between 2022 and 2025 were sorted by weekly first-trimester gain into low, fitting, and excessive groups. The excessive group showed gestational diabetes in 63.1 percent and large babies in 69.0 percent of cases in the reported shares. Adjusted odds for both outcomes ran about double in the excessive group. Checks across starting body size groups backed the pattern.
pmc-13311198:
Nicola Rotolo and co-authors report microscopic thymoma found beside a thymic cyst in a 2026 case study. Tiny thymic cell nests under 1 mm wide appear in about 15 percent of myasthenia gravis patients and are seen as early thymoma precursors. Scans cannot spot them, so they surface only under the microscope after surgery.

A woman aged 52 years with drooping lids and weakness had a chest scan showing an enlarged thymus with a cyst. Scope surgery removed the gland with no visible tumor. pmc-13315998:

pmc-13316698:

pmc-13317798:

pmc-13318598:

pmc-13318898:

pmc-13319098:

pmc-13320398:

pmc-13321398:

pmc-13322798:

pmc-13323298:

pmc-13328498:

pmc-13332398:

pmc-13332498:

pmc-13332598:

pmc-13333098:
Hafiza Ateeqa Mubarak and colleagues review 2026 exercise and daily-habit support during and after chemo for ovarian cancer. Ovarian cancer is highly lethal, and chemotherapy toxicity brings fatigue, reduced physical function, and poor quality of life. Activity and daily-habit programs may offer helpful benefits, yet evidence in ovarian cancer has stayed limited and mixed. The review asks how such programs affect clinical outcomes and patient-reported experience in women with ovarian cancer.

Searches of PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library ran from inception through May 2026 under PRISMA reporting rules. Study quality was judged with Cochrane and Newcastle-Ottawa tools. Six studies totaling 724 patients qualified, covering aerobic, resistance, and multimodal exercise routines. Across those studies, the review weighs what activity can and cannot do for patients in active treatment and recovery, guiding clinicians toward realistic helpful prescriptions.
pmc-13333298:
Yining Wang and Ryo Kohsaka study why people sense that local seafood culture in Japan is fading, in a 2026 survey study. Globalization is reshaping diets, and traditional coastal dishes are losing ground in both quantity and quality.

Drawing on 840 online respondents, the team modeled links among seafood eating habits, food-related memory, and the feeling of cultural decline, separately for meals at home and eating out. Habits influenced decline perceptions along two paths: directly, people who ate more seafood felt less decline, and indirectly through memory, which sharpened sensitivity to change. Home dining shaped food memory more strongly than restaurants did. Price, time pressure, and product availability all fed into eating habits themselves. The authors argue food culture change runs through memory and feeling as much as through behavior, with lessons for policy that defends local cuisine.
pmc-13333398:
Hyunho Ryu and colleagues measured every chamber of both atria on CT scans in a 2026 study asking which sizes predict atrial fibrillation returning after catheter ablation. A big left atrium is a known warning sign, but the appendages and the whole right side had rarely been tested together.

The retrospective study included 199 ablation patients who had pre-procedure CT, with volumes cut by AI segmentation software into total, body, and appendage parts for each atrium. Within 12 months, 45 patients, 22.6 percent, had a documented rhythm relapse, and every measured volume ran higher in that group. Using best split points, nearly all large volumes predicted relapse. Two stood independent: a left atrial appendage of at least 15.3 mL, with an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.97, and a right atrial body of at least 82.1 mL, at 2.39. The authors suggest remodeling in those two spots helps drive relapse after ablation.
pmc-13333698:
Megan E. Crawford and co-authors read charts in a 2026 retrospective study of swallowing problems and related complications during acute stroke care. The team examined how documented dysphagia and liquid restrictions relate to aspiration pneumonia and urinary tract infection.

Records covered 1,216 adults admitted after ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke in 2021 through 2023 at a large urban hospital system with two full-service stroke centers. Dysphagia appeared in 31.7 percent of charts, while nothing-by-mouth orders appeared in 23.5 percent and thickened liquids in only 3.5 percent. Aspiration pneumonia occurred in 9.4 percent of patients and urinary infection in 10 percent during the stay. Math models weighed these links against age, how bad the stroke was, and other factors to clarify which restrictions track with harm or protection.
pmc-13334098:
Luman Wang, Ronghua Liu, and Yiwei Chu reviewed regulatory B cells in a 2026 synthesis, focusing on the double-edged nature of these immune cells. Beyond making antibodies, B cells can calm or, when hijacked, worsen immune disease.

Regulatory B cells help hold immune balance, suppressing harmful inflammation in many settings. Yet in autoimmunity, cancer, and allergy they can be co-opted to drive disease forward. Their behavior is steered by metabolic cues, neural signals, and the tissue surroundings they sit in. The review catalogs the molecules that identify these cells and the features that mark their suppressive state. Understanding what flips their role could yield sharper prognostic tools and therapies that tune B cell activity rather than wipe it out.
pmc-13336898:
Yao Fang and a large team free tactile sensors from a classic trade-off in a 2026 study. Flexible touch sensors usually gain sensitivity only by losing their straight, easy-to-read response range. Their design stacks two gradients: a conductivity gradient across layered electrodes and a shape gradient of rough surfaces and arched microstripes.

Pressure switches the layers in sequence, so current grows in a straight line across a huge span. The sensor reached a sensitivity of 5642.02 per kPa with a linear range of 0–1560 kPa in the reported tests, claimed as a first pairing of both extremes. Demos covered health pulse signals, fingertip lighting control, and sorting objects by touch. Wider, truer touch could sharpen robots and wearables.
pmc-13337398:
Xiaohui Yang and Jiaxiang Ni compare two minimally invasive disk procedures for low back pain over 24 months in a 2026 single-center study. Discogenic pain and contained disk herniation drive much chronic back pain, and older needle techniques fade with time. Their cohort held 198 patients: 110 treated with disk percutaneous ablation and extraction, and 88 with Disc-FX nucleoplasty.

At 24 months the ablation group cut pain by a mean of 5.29 points against 4.17 points for Disc-FX on the visual scale used, with better disability scores and a composite success rate of 70.0% versus 51.1% in the matched comparisons. Repeat procedures were rarer after ablation, at 7.3% versus 14.8% of patients in follow-up, while complication rates stayed similar.
pmc-13338698:
Rasheed A. Adeleke and colleagues issued a 2026 correction for a study of microbes living inside traditional food wrapping leaves. The item itself is only a correction notice: the original figures were published in low quality by mistake.

Figures 2 through 13 are replaced with high-quality versions, covering bacterial and fungal diversity in four leaf types used for artisanal wrapping. The corrected charts show diversity scores, community comparisons, and microbe abundance at phylum and genus levels. No new findings are claimed; the notice restores readable evidence for the study's claims about food safety and quality.
pmc-13340698:
Saeed Kargar-Soleimanabad and colleagues reported a missed knee ligament injury in 2026 after a fall from about three metres. Posterior cruciate ligament avulsion fractures are rare after knee trauma and are often missed at first assessment because X ray signs are subtle and pain limits examination. Prompt diagnosis matters to prevent long term knee disability.

A 42 year old woman had foot fracture surgery after the fall and went home stable, yet knee discomfort persisted to the second follow up. Repeat X rays then found an avulsion fracture of the posterior cruciate ligament in the left knee, missed at first assessment. The case urges repeat imaging and a high index of suspicion when knee pain outlasts other injuries.
pmc-13341298:
Stiff arteries and disturbed blood flow jointly drive plaque growth, argue Jin He and Jun Meng in a 2026 narrative review on atherosclerosis. Plaques cluster at branch points and curves, a pattern systemic risk factors alone cannot explain.

The review describes how two sensors, the Piezo1 channel and the 5-HT1B receptor, work as coincidence detectors, merging flow and stiffness signals into hubs such as YAP and c-REL. Downstream effects include deep cell aging, inflammatory cell death, vessel wall cell conversion, and faulty debris clearance by macrophages. New imaging paired with flow modeling now measures wall shear stress in living patients, opening paths toward mechanical risk assessment.
pmc-13341498:
Gene sequencing sharpens diagnosis of early immune defects in a 2026 Brazilian cohort study by Luiza de Mattos and colleagues. The team ran whole-exome sequencing on 100 children up to age 4, drawn from 48 municipalities, whose early symptoms suggested inborn errors of immunity.

A firm molecular diagnosis landed in 17% of cases, covering 21 disease-causing variants, one-third of them new to science. Thirteen more children had suggestive findings, and five turned out to have conditions outside the immune error category. Combined immunodeficiencies led the solved cases. In settings with scarce specialist resources, exome testing can end long diagnostic searches for very young children.
pmc-13341598:
Childhood trauma relates to aggression in prisoners partly through empathy, in a 2026 study by Guiqin Liu's team. Forms from 739 jailed men in Inner Mongolia measured early trauma, empathic concern, perspective-taking, and aggression with standard instruments.

Trauma tracked with more aggression (r = 0.303) and with less of both empathy facets. Mediation analysis found empathic concern carried a real indirect path, making up 25.25% of the total link, while perspective-taking's path was not clear. Feeling for others, more than imagining their viewpoint, appears to be the channel through which early harm echoes into adult aggression in this population.
pmc-13342198:
Raffaella De Santis and colleagues report a 2026 pilot study of allergy patterns in children with eosinophilic esophagitis, a long-term immune condition of the food pipe. The work comes from a single children's hospital in Milan. It asks how often these young patients react to food allergens and to panallergens, a group of proteins shared across pollens and plant foods.

The team reviewed clinical, scope, and tissue data for 24 children and split them by whether acid-blocking drugs kept the disease quiet. Panallergen reactions appeared in 15 of the 24 children, and children who did poorly on acid blockers showed far more panallergen reactions and skin eczema. The authors read the pattern as a possible marker of harder-to-treat disease, while noting that larger studies must confirm it.
pmc-13344598:
SunMin Hwang and co-authors improve an X-ray ionization beam position monitor for soft X-ray free-electron lasers in 2026. Such lasers fire intense, jittery pulses whose position wanders shot to shot, and solid sensors absorb too much soft X-ray light, so gas-based monitors read position from ions the beam knocks loose.

The work evaluates and upgrades the monitor already serving the Pohang Accelerator Laboratory's soft X-ray beamline, where photo-ion patterns on a detector plate reveal beam shifts without touching the beam itself. Running on leftover vacuum gas keeps the device compact, while injected gas can boost signal when needed. Better position data steadies experiments that depend on quantitative pulse readings.
pmc-13345798:
Jacqueline C Saad and Caroline A Brandon review urinary troubles inside the genitourinary syndrome of menopause in 2026. The syndrome, renamed in 2014 to capture its full reach, follows estrogen loss and brings urinary frequency, urgency, night waking, burning, leakage, and repeat infections alongside vaginal symptoms.

Population studies find 45 to 80 percent of postmenopausal women affected, yet the condition stays underdiagnosed and undertreated, and most research chases vaginal complaints instead. Local estrogen therapy anchors care, with vaginal DHEA and ospemifene also easing urinary symptoms, while laser-style energy devices remain experimental. The authors gather worldwide guideline advice so clinicians can treat the urinary side with the same care as the rest.
pmc-13345898:
Xinjuan Zhang, Jiling Zhang, and Yandan Wu test light-scatter blood measures against fatty-sample interference in 2026. Fat particles in lipemic blood fool standard color-based hemoglobin readings upward. The team checked whether a scatter-derived gap measure, Delta-HGB, flags the problem. They also tested whether scatter-based values can correct it without sample cleanup.

Across 471 specimens, scatter readings proved precise and matched standard results in clean samples. For severe lipemia, Delta-HGB and the standard concentration index both discriminated superbly, with accuracy scores near 0.99 and cutoffs catching over 95 percent of cases both ways. Scatter values also agreed with plasma replacement and formula corrections, offering labs a fast, no-pretreatment fix.
pmc-13346598:
Marie Barzen Coors and colleagues evaluated in 2026 SHARE TO CARE, a hospital-wide programme to make shared decision making routine in Germany, asking whether it helps patients clinically and whether it pays. Good conversations are often praised, yet hospitals need proof that system-wide training and support change outcomes and costs.

Using a quasi-experimental difference-in-differences design in a neurology department, the team compared admissions, emergency visits, and imaging rates against implementation costs, viewed from the statutory health insurance perspective. Costs covered design, training, process integration, support, and auditing. The study tests whether investing in better decisions reduces avoidable care enough to justify the effort of changing a whole hospital culture.
pmc-13346698:
Robert Śliwowski and co-authors tested in 2026 whether GPS training data can forecast how hard elite youth soccer players feel they work. Coaches track outside load with care. Yet a player's felt effort, such as leg tiredness, breathlessness, and mental demand, often tells a distinct tale.

Over seventeen weeks in season, the team took 537 training records from fifteen players. GPS measures such as distance, fast running, starts, stops, and impacts were paired with separate effort ratings on a Borg scale. Decision tree models were built for each effort type. Total distance stood out as the top forecast. The models could help coaches tune sessions before tiredness turns to injury or burnout.
pmc-13346998:
Xinyue Qi and co-authors studied in 2026 how nature-inspired packaging shapes the deep flow feel of Generation Z shoppers. Packaging has grown into a key channel for brand links. Biomimetic design draws on living forms. Yet how its sensory traits spark deep engagement was not mapped in full.

Surveying 218 valid replies, the team scored five sense traits, from build function and instant feedback to beauty, story pull, and green values. A hybrid method joined equation modelling, neural nets, and fuzzy-set checks to triangulate which mixes matter most. The findings help designers move past single traits. They can craft packs that hold young shoppers in a focused, rewarding meet with a product.
pmc-13347098:
Yi Ping Sng and colleagues compare keyhole against open liver surgery after a radiation-based bridge treatment for liver cancer, in a matched study published in 2026. Records covered 65 patients treated from 2012 to 2023 at one busy centre, and matching on age, sex, tumour size, and tumour markers produced 18 pairs for fair comparison.

Keyhole patients reached surgery sooner, at 99.7 days against 166.9 days in the reported means, and left hospital sooner at 11.2 days against 15.6 days for open cases. Operating time, blood loss, major complications, recurrence, and survival looked alike across groups, so the authors support keyhole surgery for selected patients after this bridge therapy.
pmc-13347698:
Luca Mazzei and colleagues read enzyme blocking from heat flow alone, in a methods study from 2026. Standard activity tests can miss slow or tight binding, so a single-injection heat method was fitted to raw warming curves to sort fast reversible, slow or tight. Permanent blocking in one format, using the SARS-CoV-2 main protease as the test case.

Four known blockers, including nirmatrelvir and ensitrelvir, gave blocking strengths plus speed and heat values without end-point dyes in the reported fits. Separate binding runs on normal and changed protease forms backed the heat-based calls, each blocker showing its own heat signature. The platform is offered for sharper drug profiling early in design.
pmc-13347898:
Alejandro Rodriguez Bobadilla set out in 2026 a clinical and cost frame for infections after low-key cosmetic work. Fillers, botulinum toxin, mesotherapy, and thread lifts are popular. They are easy to get and heal fast. Yet breaking the skin and placing stuff in it can invite rare but grave infections.

The frame traces how infections show up, from skin redness and abscesses to lasting lumps, granulomas, biofilm ills, and late mycobacterial disease. It links each path to health care use and cost. By splitting avoidable from unavoidable load, it helps clinics, insurers, and regulators aim biosafety rules, training, and checks where they stop the most harm and cost.
pmc-13348298:
Phillip Mawire and colleagues present twenty high-grade genomes from island soils. Their announcement was issued in 2026. The soils come from sub-Antarctic Marion Island. Mud was gathered in April and May 2023. Fern and fellfield sites supplied the mud. Metagenome assemblies were rebuilt from it. Two little-studied Acidobacteriota lines held the genomes. These groups thrive where food is scarce. They also drive carbon and sulfur cycles.

Thirteen genomes fell in one line. Seven fell in the other line. Nutrient cycling genes were common across the set. Carbon breakdown genes were among them. Sulfate use and sulfur burning genes appeared too. The public genomes widen a thin library. This phylum has long outrun its cultured record. Its wild work is only now coming into focus.
pmc-13348898:
Jing Wang, Hong Wang, and Xi Chen ask nursing students how a schizophrenia stigma-cutting program felt to take, in a focus group study from 2026. Thirty students aged 20 to 23 years who had joined a pilot trial in Changsha, China, talked in five online groups in March 2023. Notes and coding were built live alongside each session. The aim was to catch shared themes.

Four themes emerged, covering whether the program could work, how easily students could reach it, whether it seemed to help. How to run it better next time in the grouped accounts. Students rated the program workable, reachable, and helpful overall, and their fixes give trainers a student-tested path for wider rollout.
pmc-13348998:
Rinsila R Hafthar and co-authors told in 2026 of successful outpatient care for severe high triglycerides with eruptive xanthomas, with no pancreatitis. Eruptive xanthomas are raised skin bumps from fat deposits. They most often signal uncontrolled diabetes and a high risk of acute pancreatic inflammation.

A 41-year-old man came in with diffuse papular lesions and nerve symptoms, with no prior diabetes diagnosis. Yet glycated haemoglobin was 13.8 percent and triglycerides were 85.6 millimoles per litre. Despite the extreme level, he had no belly pain, nausea, or tenderness to hint at pancreatitis. Insulin-based outpatient care cut his lipids safely. The case shows that even severe hypertriglyceridaemia can at times be handled outside hospital with close watch.
pmc-13349298:
Ron Sender and colleagues weigh every hormone in human blood, in a quantitative synthesis issued in 2026. Trusted clinic ranges for hormones across the main glands were gathered and cross-checked against published datasets to sum total mass, molecule counts per body cell, sex splits. How much of each hormone floats free to reach its receptor.

Total circulating hormone mass came to about 40 mg, with adiponectin and DHEAS making over 90 percent of both mass and molecule counts in healthy young adults. Roughly a million hormone molecules exist per body cell, women carry about half the male count, and free levels tracked receptor grip strength in class-specific patterns across 56 hormones.
pmc-13349498:
Kazuhisa Tsukamoto and co-authors measured in 2026 how often Japanese patients miss stricter LDL targets set in 2022. They used a nationwide real-world data set of 200,607 adults with dyslipidaemia. LDL cholesterol is a key target for warding off atherosclerotic heart and vessel disease, most of all in high-risk people.

Patients were grouped by Japan Atherosclerosis Society rules into high-risk primary prevention groups, plus familial hypercholesterolaemia, and a secondary prevention group with prior coronary disease or stroke. Miss rates were tallied across risk strata. The large-scale picture shows where drug intensification lags most. It helps clinicians and policy makers close gaps between guideline targets and daily practice.
pmc-13350498:
Harriët Jager-Wittenaar and colleagues built a shared definition of risk of malnutrition in a 2026 consensus study, part one of a GLIM working group project revising how screening should work. Focus groups with nutrition experts and older patient representatives plus a literature scan produced 46 candidate statements.

A panel of 112 experts judged the statements over three questionnaire rounds, accepting those with at least three quarters in agreement. Twenty-six statements survived to shape the definition. Pinning down what risk of malnutrition means, before weight loss or illness strikes, is the foundation for screening tools that hospitals worldwide can apply the same way.
pmc-13350698:
Jingmin Li and colleagues examined sex differences in heart artery flow where a band of muscle bridges over the artery in a 2026 AI-based study. They analysed 300 patients with bridging of the main front artery, 155 with bridging alone and 145 with added plaque, plus 104 controls with normal scans.

Bridging squeezes the artery with each heartbeat, and its impact may differ by sex and by whether plaque coexists, distinctions earlier work blurred. Scan-based flow reserve plus detailed shape measures were compared across groups. Separating these patterns could stop a common, often harmless finding from being either over-treated or wrongly dismissed.
pmc-13351298:
Jair Mauricio Cerón Bohórquez and co-authors told in 2026 of botulinum toxin for lip flip, a technique that subtly everts the upper lip by partly relaxing its marginal muscle part. The short note spells out anatomical rationale, jab path, and early clinical notes in three consecutive patients treated with letybotulinumtoxinA.

Toxin was diluted to 4 units per 0.1 millilitre and jabbed shallowly along the upper lip edge, one unit per site, steering clear of the mouth corners and of deep muscle. Two weeks later, each patient had a gently turned-out upper lip and softer vertical lip lines, rating satisfaction from satisfied to very satisfied, with no speech, movement, asymmetry, or mouth-closure troubles. The authors warn that the tiny, uncontrolled group makes findings preliminary.
pmc-13351698:
Jianming Fang and colleagues assess a two-drug salvage plan for children with solid tumours that returned or resisted treatment, in a 2026 cohort study. Options after relapse are few and outcomes are poor. Records cover 86 children treated at Beijing Jingdu Children's Hospital from March 2021 to March 2025.

Children received irinotecan plus temozolomide in 21-day cycles, with scans every two cycles. Median age was 7 years, 52 children had neuroblastoma, and most had already had three prior drug lines. The response rate was 23.3 percent and disease control reached 52.4 percent. The authors also report survival and safety, while noting real-world data in Chinese children were lacking before.
pmc-13351898:
Lindsay Kate Wanner and colleagues present a 2026 case of nerve stimulation for pain next to a long spinal fusion. Wear at the level beside a fusion is a known late problem with no settled fix. A 71-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis and a prior T11 to S1 fusion had moderately severe pain rated 7 of 10 at the level above.

Therapy, injections, and daily opioids at 30 morphine equivalents had given little relief, and exam showed facet pain at T8 to T10. A stimulator was placed with leads at both T10 medial branches, using motor and sensory settings. The team reasoned that stronger back muscles could ease pain and guard the joint over time.
pmc-13352398:
A Trösch and others at the University Hospital of Bern tracked skin side effects in adults getting cancer immune care. Their 2026 report covers people seen from April 2023 to October 2025. Skin reactions affect a large share of people on these drugs, yet clinic notes often reduce them to a single word such as rash. The team set out to record the full range of skin changes with careful check and lab testing.

Sixty-seven adults treated with PD-1, PD-L1, or CTLA-4 drugs received standard skin checks, with biopsies and immunofluorescence testing when the results called for them. Melanoma and non-small-cell lung cancer were the most common cancers in the group. Eczematous dermatitis showed most often, followed by vitiligo, lichen-like swelling, and psoriasis-like disease. Readers gain a clearer map of which skin problems arise, when they tend to start, and why finding matters for care.
pmc-13352498:
Mohamed A Baghi and co-authors report a 2026 case of relapsed type II lepra reaction with drug-caused blood breakdown. Leprosy, caused by Mycobacterium leprae, spreads through long close contact and mainly harms skin and nerves. A 27-year-old woman had lepromatous leprosy with a severe type two reaction touching several organ systems.

Multi-drug therapy is the standard base, joined by reaction control and rehabilitation. Her course was complicated by haemolysis blamed on dapsone, even though her G6PD enzyme activity tested normal. Baghi and colleagues use the case to show how reaction care and drug harm can collide. Careful monitoring and flexible drug choices are central lessons for similar patients.
pmc-13352598:
Zhixiang Zhong and colleagues build HMGB1 protein in the lab to study how sugar chains change its behaviour in 2026. Adding N-glycans is a common protein modification with wide effects, yet its impact on HMGB1 was unclear. Chemical synthesis plus enzyme-based sugar transfer produced uniform HMGB1 variants carrying a defined two-armed sialylated sugar at set sites.

Routes to the full-length protein were worked out first, then glycosylated forms were assembled the same way. Lab tests measured how the sugar forms bind the RAGE receptor and how they affect cell movement and CXCL12 release. Computer simulations probed the binding shift. Site-exact samples let the team credit effects to the sugar itself rather than mixed natural forms.
pmc-13353098:
Aditya Viswanath and co-authors evaluate a tele-dermatology hub model for epidermolysis bullosa in a 2026 before-and-after study. The rare genetic skin condition needs specialist care that many families cannot reach. At the Centre for Human Genetics in Bangalore, from January 2020 to August 2025, local practitioners or families referred patients for remote specialist consults.

Histories were stored securely, and a multi-specialist team joined when deeper care was needed. A privacy-compliant phone app kept families in contact for follow-up. The team compared reach, assessment quality, and medical costs before and after the model began. Standard care paths for a varied genetic condition were built alongside, aiming for fairer, cheaper access.
pmc-13354998:
Eugenia Piliotis and co-authors describe a 2025 medical degree program at Queen's University with Lakeridge Health that trains doctors only for family medicine. Canada faces a deep shortage of family doctors, with millions lacking a regular doctor. The program, launched in 2023, recruits learners who plan from the start to work in family practice.

The paper walks through six pillars of the program: admissions, curriculum, staff engagement, community ties, facilities and supports, and learner experience. Each pillar aims to keep training rooted in community needs. The authors present the model as one way schools can help rebuild family medicine capacity.
pmc-13355398:
Sun-Hee Cho and co-authors identify a heat shock family protein, Dnajb5, as a brake on muscle formation, first tracing it in the muscle of an Antarctic fish. Their 2026 study screens proteins that bind mTOR, a central growth regulator, then tests Dnajb5 function in mouse muscle cells and in a mouse muscle injury model.

Removing Dnajb5 from muscle precursor cells increased a key growth signal downstream of mTOR without changing another major pathway, and raised genes driving differentiation. In injured mouse muscle, depletion enlarged regenerating fibres by about twenty-six percent five days after injury. The mechanism involved another regulator, HDAC4: without Dnajb5, more of a mitochondrial programme switched on, raising mitochondrial DNA, oxidative enzyme activity, grip strength by fourteen percent, and endurance by thirty-one percent. The interaction with mTOR weakened under oxidative stress, which the authors describe as a redox-sensitive dual-pathway control of regeneration.
pmc-13355498:
Yu-Han Chen and others studied myeloproliferative neoplasms carrying concurrent MPL and JAK2 or CALR changes, in 2026. These blood cancers are usually driven by a single mutation in JAK2, CALR, or MPL, long considered mutually exclusive. JAK2 dominates polycythemia vera, while CALR and MPL appear in subsets of key thrombocythemia and myelofibrosis.

Case reports and small series have told of people carrying two driver changes at once, hard the exclusivity rule. The letter summarises medical traits and results in such concurrent-mutation cases. Haematologists gain a clearer view of a rare pattern that may alter prognosis and care expectations.
pmc-13355798:
Kyung-Gu Chung and Min Kyung Shin report a 2026 case of a 23-year-old woman with stubborn perioral dermatitis, a relapsing rash of red bumps around the mouth and eyes. Her rash had lasted two months and did not improve with steroid cream or a second cream. Later drug mixes, including an antibiotic and immune-calming drugs, gave only brief partial relief over four months.

Care then switched to baricitinib, a drug that blocks a cell signal path called JAK. At four milligrams a day, her itching and rash improved markedly within a month, and the dose was then halved. The authors add a review of past reports and suggest such drugs merit study for hard cases.
pmc-13355898:
Hamza Ahmed and co-authors tested a single teaching session in 2026 on reading common bone X-rays at a major trauma center in the United Kingdom. Junior clinicians often review X-rays before a formal report, and missed fractures are a known risk. Forty-eight early-career clinicians took a 25-image test and rated their confidence before and after a 45-minute senior-led session.

Mean scores jumped from about 59 percent to about 82 percent, and confidence nearly doubled. Critical errors fell by about two-thirds. Six weeks later, scores held at about 77 percent, showing partial retention. The authors suggest short, case-based sessions in induction training, with wider studies to confirm the gains.
pmc-13356798:
Fatih Orhan studied age-related drivers of elder low mood in Turkey, in 2026. Low mood is common in later life, but its risk and guarding factors may differ across age bands from sixty-five to eighty-five and beyond. A single risk profile for all older adults could miss those gaps.

Data from the nationally representative Turkey Elderly Profile Survey 2023 yielded a study sample of 8,370 adults aged sixty-five or older. Low mood was defined by a Geriatric Depression Scale score of eleven or more. Theory-driven logit models with twenty-four factors were estimated apart by age group, with data-driven ways. The study shows which factors matter at which ages, guiding aimed stopping.
pmc-13357098:
Yanqi Sun and co-authors built in 2026 a gene signature to predict glioma recurrence, using genes tied to the complement system, an immune defense network active in the tumor's surroundings. Glioma is the most common malignant brain tumor, and markers for its return are lacking. From public glioma datasets, they picked six core genes and built a risk score, then validated it in a separate cohort.

High-risk patients had shorter survival, more immune-suppressing cells, more drug resistance, and higher immune checkpoint levels. The core genes may act through a complement signaling axis that draws in suppressive macrophages. A combined chart gave strong predictions, offering a tool for tailored care.
pmc-13358498:
Bryant W. Tran and co-authors wrote a 2026 commentary on pain control after pancreas surgery. Open surgery on the pancreas is painful, and opioid drugs bring their own risks. The piece discusses a study that gave patients a quadratus lumborum block, a numbing shot near the back muscles, twice instead of once.

The key question is whether a second block helps more patients leave hospital without opioid drugs, and fewer refill them later. Tran and co-authors trace how this block came into use and weigh its spread and limits. Their take helps anesthesia teams judge if the extra shot earns its place in care plans.
pmc-13358598:
Shenqi Wang and others mapped research trends in lung-guarding ventilation from 2006 to 2025, ran the bibliometric study in 2026. After-op pulmonary harm contribute heavily to perioperative death and illness worldwide, and lung-guarding ventilation reduces ventilator-induced lung injury. Rollout, however, varies widely across doctors and practices.

Publication trends, hot topics, and research focus were studied bibliometrically across two decades of papers. The study highlights which questions drew notice, which faded, and where future research may head. Anaesthetists and intensivists gain an overview of a field whose evidence base is large but unevenly applied.
pmc-13358998:
Xiqiao Sun hunts for new risk genes in sarcoidosis in a 2026 study. Sarcoidosis runs in families in part, and genome scans have found immune-linked regions, but which genes those signals act through is unclear. Sun used a method that joins gene activity across many tissues with genetic risk data to name likely culprit genes.

Candidate genes from that cross-tissue scan were checked with several further methods, including a technique that mimics a natural experiment and maps of gene links to chemicals and diseases. Genes that survive all these filters earn priority for lab follow-up. The work aims to move from broad risk regions to the exact genes that drive the disease.
pmc-13359898:
Longping Chen and co-authors review the fuel choices of immune cells in rheumatoid arthritis in a 2026 paper. In this disease, macrophages in the joint lining switch into states that sustain inflammation, eat cartilage, and erode bone. New single-cell and tissue mapping work shows these cells also rewire how they burn glucose, fats, and amino acids.

That rewiring seems to amplify disease rather than start it, locking in harmful cell states and faulty talk between cells. The review explains the links, notes how current arthritis drugs already shift this metabolism, and appraises early attempts to drug the pathways directly. The authors frame metabolism as a fresh front in treating the disease.
pmc-13360098:
Norhayati Mohd Zain and Wan Azani Mustafa wrote a 2026 review of two breast imaging methods, contrast-enhanced mammography and MRI. Both methods use contrast dye to make breast lumps easier to see than on a standard mammogram. The authors asked how well each method works in real care and how each one shapes doctors' choices.

The pair searched two large databases and kept 20 strong studies for a close read. The authors see a growing role for it before surgery, during treatment checks, and when other scans leave doubts.
