pmc-13400298:
Naomi Murray and Andrew Geddis-Regan present, in 2026, four dental patients who have hereditary angioedema, a rare inherited condition causing sudden swelling. Dental work can trigger attacks, and swelling in the mouth or throat can threaten breathing. The condition looks like allergy but acts through a different pathway, so allergy drugs may not help.

Each case shows planning before, during and after treatment, with input from medical and dental staff. The authors stress that dental teams must know the signs and have a plan ready. Good preparation let routine care proceed while lowering the risk of a severe swelling episode.
pmc-13400998:
Nadège Akissi Kouame and colleagues test, in 2026, whether soil contamination can quickly flag communities at high risk of worm infections in southern Côte d Ivoire. Soil-transmitted helminths remain a major problem where sanitation is limited. Checking stool in every community is slow, while parasite eggs in the environment might serve as a shortcut signal.

In October 2024 the team sampled three villages, collecting stool from schoolchildren and farm animals plus soil and stagnant water. Worm eggs appeared in every material type. Infection prevalence was highest in children at about forty-five percent, with eggs in about a quarter of animal and soil samples and few in water. Only three worm types were found: Ascaris, Trichuris and hookworm.
pmc-13401298:
Anna Rossander, David Wetterbro, and Daniel Karlsson wrote a 2026 feasibility study on whether binding health data terms to SNOMED CT, a standard clinical vocabulary, can bridge different information structures. Safe exchange of health information often forces data to be reshaped between systems, and structured terms might let computers automate that reshaping.

Working in breast cancer pathology, the team had a clinician pick pairs of interface terms with the same meaning from two structures, verified by two informaticians. Each term's bound SNOMED CT concepts were compared and sorted as transformable, partly transformable, or not transformable. Of 73 term pairs, about 70 percent fell on the workable side, and the authors analysed the failing pairs qualitatively to find out why automatic conversion breaks down.
pmc-13401598:
Theresa Hofmann and a large team of co-authors wrote a 2026 heart study on a long non-coding RNA called TRDN-AS. It controls which version of the triadin protein heart muscle makes. Faulty calcium handling in heart cells can trigger cardiomyopathy, and regulatory RNAs are part of that story.

When TRDN-AS falls, the heart switches from its own triadin form, TRISK32, to the skeletal muscle form, TRISK95. The same switch shows in human disease, lab-grown heart cells, and mice lacking the RNA. The RNA's transcription stalls the copying machinery at the right spot, aided by the m6A writer METTL3, forcing proper termination of the cardiac message. The isoform switch reshapes the calcium release complex's partners. It produces abnormal calcium handling and misshapen dyads, the junctions where calcium release happens. A tiny RNA is thus linked to heart failure mechanics.
pmc-13401698:
Ivy Kondowe-Chinangwa, Thokozani Mzumara, and Marie Young studied how coaches and parents judge Special Olympics Malawi's commitment to sport for athletes with intellectual disabilities, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Coaches and parents sit at the heart of these athletes' sporting lives, yet their voices are rarely asked.

Focus group discussions, guided by a structured interview guide, supplied the data for this qualitative descriptive study. Three problem areas surfaced: organizations working alone, institutions not doing their jobs well, and unmotivated employees. Together they mark a gap between what the organization says its goal is and what it actually does. Leaving key people such as teachers and parents out of decisions, participants said, harms the athlete-coach bond, weakens trust, and undermines preparation. The authors urge involving coaches and parents in real decision-making.
pmc-13402598:
Qian and co-authors report, in 2026, the first sighting of singular flat bands on a pentagonal lattice. The bands sit not in a lab-made crystal but on the surface of the ferromagnetic semimetal cobalt disulfide. Flat bands, energy levels where particles barely move, breed exotic behavior, yet they had been seen only on kagome and pyrochlore shapes. The surface of CoS2 arranges its atoms into a flat pentagonal pattern hosting the bands.

Photoemission and scanning tunneling resolved the spin-aligned flat bands alongside the material's Fermi arc states. Coupling between the surface flat bands and the bulk topological bands produced non-Fermi liquid behavior: the particle scattering rate grew linearly with temperature and the particles broadened. The authors propose pyrites as a platform for pentagon flat band physics, opening a lattice geometry that theory predicted but experiment had never reached.
pmc-13402698:
Chang Cheng and colleagues borrow the trick of photosynthesis to run click chemistry with light, using single copper atoms held in an organic framework. The classic click reaction joins azides and alkynes with copper in its plus-one state, normally made by chemical reduction in messy, hard-to-scale mixtures. Their catalyst parks single Cu(II) atoms in a covalent organic framework whose ligand soaks up light like the magnesium ring in chlorophyll.

Light pushes electrons from ligand to metal, briefly turning Cu(II) into the active Cu(I) form for less than a microsecond at a time. In the model pairing of benzylazide and phenylacetylene, the system converted 95 percent of starting material with triazole yields above 90 percent in the reported tests. Because the catalyst is solid and the switch is light, the authors see uses from greener synthesis to photolithography and polymer work.
pmc-13402798:
Çevik Gürel and team tested whether the anesthetic propofol can boost carboplatin against harsh endometrial cancer. Their 2026 work focuses on type II endometrial cancer, which responds poorly to platinum chemo. Propofol has shown anti-tumor hints beyond sleep induction, but its role as a chemo partner in this cancer had been little probed.

In lab and mouse models, propofol alone cut cancer cell life and spread, while the pair beat carboplatin alone on anti-spread effects. Tumors grafted in mice shrank clearly with pair therapy, with hints of less spread to lung and liver. Lab work showed lower cancer-driving small RNAs and growth signals, plus higher tumor-checking small RNAs and guard proteins. The findings back propofol as a possible chemo helper, pending human trials.
pmc-13403098:
Valerio Pedrelli and colleagues build a prediction scale for how many picosecond laser sessions a tattoo will need, replacing a ruler made for older lasers. The Kirby-Desai scale, designed for nanosecond Q-switched machines, overestimates sessions on modern picosecond devices, misleading planning and consent. Their retrospective cohort held 545 patients treated between 2019 and 2024.

The new PT scale scores six features: tattoo type, pigment density, body location, ink color, scarring, and layering. Machine learning and regression models fed PT variables beat Kirby-Desai versions clearly; the best, a ridge regression, missed by only 0.58 sessions on average with an R squared of 0.73 on held-out data. Tattoo type and pigment density drove predictions hardest. The authors offer the scale as a practical counseling tool for contemporary practice.
pmc-13403298:
Gopalakrishnan and colleagues probe why people with complex regional pain syndrome avoid movement until rehabilitation stalls, using a learning game paired with brain recordings. Pain out of proportion to any injury settles in a limb, and fear driven avoidance feeds disability. Their 2026 study seats twenty eight patients and twenty seven volunteers at a task where choices carry odds of a painful stimulus. It fits a reinforcement learning model to play, and records brain waves with magnetoencephalography.

Patients learned faster than controls from pain and safety, yet chose more randomly, and expectations steered choices more weakly. Their threat learning was explained by higher anxiety, a sentimental personality trait, and lower alpha power in the prefrontal cortex, the brain's control center. That alpha signal carried part of pain's effect on threat learning. Avoidance here, the authors argue, is a learning and control problem with named parts, each a treatment target.
pmc-13403598:
Andrew Linkugel and co-authors presented a 2026 case of a toddler whose skull seams fused late after severe vitamin D lack. The 2-year-old boy had rickets from poor vitamin D intake as a baby. By his visit, the lack had been fixed for about a year.

Several skull seams had closed early, and part of his lower brain sagged downward. Pressure inside his head was high, with headaches and swollen eye nerves. Surgery to expand the skull vault and free space at the back eased both signs. Late seam fusion in a young child should prompt checks for bone metabolism faults.
pmc-13404098:
Xiang Zhou, Hongyan Liu, and Zhengdong Hua wrote in 2026 to press a finer question about soda treatment for severe blood acidity. A pooled report found far fewer kidney replacement starts with bicarbonate, a gain of about 16 points. Yet the treatment lifts blood pH, and low pH itself was a trigger for starting replacement in the source trials.

That overlap makes the endpoint slippery, since meeting a pH rule is itself part of the decision. Major kidney harm at 90 days stayed much the same in both arms. The writers ask the trial team to split first replacement starts by whether lasting acidity was a listed reason.
pmc-13404298:
Jae Eun Ha and Ju Young Park surveyed what drives infection control scores among nurses in South Korean national and public hospitals during new disease threats. Their 2026 cross-sectional work covers 193 nurses surveyed in May 2022, gauging burnout, moral sensitivity, prevention climate, and infection control scores. Nurses are central to prevention, yet psychosocial and workplace drivers of scores had been little quantified.

Mean scores hit 4.37 out of 5. Moral sensitivity and a supportive prevention climate clearly predicted scores, together explaining 37 percent of variance, with climate the stronger predictor. Burnout moved in the opposite direction but did not clearly predict scores in the full model. The work urges hospitals to strengthen prevention climates and moral sensitivity teaching for outbreak readiness.
pmc-13404498:
Penelope Markham and colleagues present the ADDRESS-LC protocol, a 2026 phase 2 trial of bezisterim for long COVID. Bezisterim, also called NE3107, is a pill that crosses into the brain and calms inflammation driven by toll-like receptors. The drug is also being developed for diseases where such inflammation dulls thinking.

The triple-blind study will enroll 208 adults aged 18 to 69 with fatigue and thinking problems lasting at least three months after infection. Half receive 20 milligrams of bezisterim twice daily for 12 weeks and half receive placebo. Outcomes cover cognition, fatigue, sleep, post-exertional malaise and quality of life, using a custom Cogstate battery and PROMIS questionnaires. Safety is tracked throughout the treatment period.
pmc-13405298:
Juliana Heitich Brendler and colleagues outline the NUTRI-GUT-PD trial, a 2026 protocol on dietitian care for constipation in Parkinson's disease. Constipation troubles many patients and standard care leans on general advice or laxatives. Diet could help, but Parkinson's makes eating management more complex than simple rules.

Fifty-four outpatients without dementia who meet Rome IV criteria for functional constipation will join the 90-day trial. One group receives personal nutritional counselling from a dietitian, while the other gets usual care. Stool samples will feed gut microbe analysis, and three day-long diet recalls capture eating patterns. Constipation scores, body measures and nerve assessments frame the comparison.
pmc-13407598:
Prasanna T Dahake and Nilima Thosar tested drug pairs against germs from endo-perio lesions in baby teeth. Their 2026 lab work takes on infections that spread fast in baby teeth due to tangled anatomy, where weak care can cause early tooth loss and arch woes. Topical antibiotics could help, but effective pairs had not been weighed.

The team tested clindamycin, metronidazole, doxycycline, and their triple mix against seven lesion germs, gauging lowest blocking and killing doses under standard lab rules. The triple mix proved strongest, followed by clindamycin, doxycycline, and metronidazole, with mix-versus-single gaps clear for both gauges. The work backs the triple mix for topical use, pending medical safety and efficacy trials.
pmc-13407698:
Petra Petranović Ovčariček and co-authors review, in 2026, how inherited multiple endocrine neoplasia syndromes are caught through genes, blood markers, and imaging. These rare disorders seed tumours in several hormone glands, often silently. Such tumours can turn malignant while still symptom-free. That makes early detection decisive.

Genetic testing anchors modern diagnosis: it confirms the syndrome, enables screening of relatives, and sets the intensity of lifelong surveillance. Blood biochemistry adds signals of hormone excess or tumour activity, while specialised imaging locates tumours before they declare themselves. The review synthesises the current state of this three-legged strategy and points toward precision-medicine directions, where a person's exact germline change tailors how hard and how often clinicians look.
pmc-13407798:
Jucier Gonçalves Júnior, Jamily Izabel Alves dos Santos, and Samuel Katsuyuki Shinjo systematically review, in 2026, a form of dermatomyositis that attacks skin while sparing muscle. Clinically amyopathic disease still brings rashes and internal complications, and the team searched seven databases for studies on its frequency, features, causes, treatment, and outlook, keeping 106 studies covering 816 patients.

Women in their fifties and sixties predominated. Signature skin signs included nodules over the knuckles, a violet eyelid rash, and a V-shaped chest rash, while lung disease was the commonest internal complication. Blood tests often showed raised ferritin and inflammatory markers, and antibodies against MDA-5 and Ro-52 appeared most frequently. Treatment usually combined steroid pulses with immune therapies. High ferritin and lung involvement marked a worse prognosis.
pmc-13407898:
Ying-Jie Ma and co-authors present, in 2026, a way to edit ring-shaped ketone molecules by cutting them open with radicals. Doubly decorated chain building blocks are valuable for drugs and materials. They usually demand tedious step-by-step building. The team used simple cyclic ketones instead. A peroxide intermediate turns them into latent two-ended linchpins.

A controlled tandem sequence, one radical cutting the ring and a second stripping a carbon, achieves ring opening, carbon shrinkage, and functionalisation at both ends in one cascade. Sustainable metal catalysis, broad scope, and tolerance of delicate groups are reported, and the method edited complex natural products and drug molecules with precision. Products include chains bearing thiocyanate, azide, or halogen pairs, and mixed thiocyanate-azide versions, all at least four carbons long.
pmc-13408198:
Alexandre Le Moal, Damien Tran, and co-authors tracked the daily and seasonal rhythms of the European flat oyster in a 2026 field study. Flat oysters build reefs that shelter other species, yet their populations have collapsed and restoration projects now depend on understanding when the animals feed, grow, and reproduce. The team worked in the German Bight near Helgoland.

Sensors recorded valve movements and shell growth for well over a year, alongside light, temperature, sound, and food levels, while monthly samples tracked clock-related genes. Oysters showed layered rhythms spanning the day, the tide, the lunar cycle, and the year, governed mainly by daylight and temperature. Restoration planners can use these patterns as health indicators and as a guide to timing reef work.
pmc-13408498:
Mayla Magalhães de Oliveira Alcobaça and team matched preserved anatomy with CT and MRI scans of the crab-eating fox. Their 2026 work takes on a wild South American canid, Cerdocyon thous, often killed on roads in Brazil, whose fine anatomy stays thin for vet diagnosis and surgery. True sectional anatomy is key for reading scans in species with no full atlas.

Four animals had CT and MRI, followed by cold-temperature silicone plastination through fixation, drying, impregnation, and curing, plus 3D rendering and virtual dissection. Crosswise preserved slices detailed head, neck, thorax, abdomen, and pelvis, matched to imaging planes by metamerism, the segmental body plan. The work shows that plastination-imaging matching can lift anatomical knowledge and scan reading for little-studied wild species.
pmc-13408598:
Justin Clark and colleagues spent nearly three years reading HIV genetic material from city wastewater in 2026, across fifteen cities. Sewage monitoring can reveal infections that clinical testing misses, yet HIV is a hard target because people may shed it long before symptoms. A hybrid-capture sequencing method pulled near-complete viral genomes from the flow.

Mixed into the catch was a surprise: many sequences came not from circulating virus but from laboratory retroviral vectors used in research. The team built a mapping method that separates genuine HIV regions from vector look-alikes. Once cleaned, the wastewater signal tracked diagnosed HIV prevalence in communities where clinical figures existed. Public health readers get both a caution about contamination and early evidence that sewage could gauge community HIV burden.
pmc-13408698:
Giulio Aceto, Kexin Liu, and colleagues explain in 2026 how a rare and brutal ovarian cancer grows despite carrying a perfectly normal copy of the guardian protein p53. This small cell carcinoma is driven by losing SMARCA4, a motor subunit of the chromatin-opening SWI/SNF complex, and it carries few other mutations. The puzzle is why p53 fails to restrain it.

Genome-wide mapping showed that losing the remodeler sends the acetyl-writing enzyme p300 wandering to the promoters of cell-cycle genes. There, the chemical marks it leaves switch those genes on and override p53's repression. Healthy repression at the same sites pairs p53 with a deacetylase that strips such marks. Restoring SMARCA4 or drugging p300 stalled tumour growth, unless p53 was also deleted. The findings nominate p300 as a drug target in this cancer.
pmc-13408798:
Olla Sharhan and team synthesized two new sulfonylhydrazinoxamoyl compounds and tested them as preliminary acetylcholinesterase inhibitors. Their 2026 work targets an enzyme relevant to Alzheimer's disease, where blocking acetylcholine breakdown can ease symptoms. New scaffolds with modest activity and low toxicity could seed better drugs.

Both compounds were characterized by spectroscopy and mass spectrometry at high purity, with compound 2 more potent against acetylcholinesterase, at an IC50 of 6.51 micromolar versus 24.05 for compound 1, though both lagged the reference drug donepezil. Cytotoxicity was weak against breast cancer cells and moderate against liver cancer cells, docking favored binding in the enzyme's active gorge, and drug-likeness passed Lipinski rules. The work calls the compounds preliminary scaffolds needing structural optimization.
pmc-13409098:
Zhiwei Zhang and colleagues find in 2026 a mitochondrial gatekeeper whose removal turns a quiet tumour into an immunological bonfire. The protein TOMM40 imports material into mitochondria and, in doing so, restrains the cell's mitochondrial recycling programme. Pan-cancer cell data plus liver cancer models, gene editing, and nanoparticle-delivered RNA were used to test what happens when the gatekeeper falls.

Without it, mitochondria fail catastrophically and recycling runs lethally hot. That chaos is visible to the immune system: reactive oxygen builds up, an inflammatory switch fires, and the machinery that displays tumour fragments to killer T cells is upregulated. Cold tumours became inflamed and infiltrated, and checkpoint immunotherapy worked better in models and patient cohorts. The authors propose TOMM40 as a drug target for sensitising stubborn cancers to immunotherapy.
pmc-13410098:
Zunair Ahsan, Faouzi Haouala, and Mokhtar Rejili propose in 2026 that honeybee hives can serve as early warning posts for nature. Bees roam wide areas and bring back traces of flowers, poisons, and germs in honey, pollen, and hive debris. Watching those traces could flag colony stress and wider harm early.

Their framework joins hive sensors that log weight, warmth, moisture, sound, and flight with DNA tests of hive material. Computer models would read the combined stream and alert keepers before colonies fail. Alerts could also warn officials about pesticide spills, new bee diseases, or loss of flowering plants nearby. The plan is a proposal, so field trials must still prove it works.
pmc-13410598:
Honglin Zheng and colleagues linked two body measures to stroke risk in 2026, using five rounds of a long-running Chinese health survey. Their paper joins an inflammation and blood-sugar index with a frailty index. It then tracks how the combined score at one visit, over time, and as a changing pattern relates to later strokes in people with early heart, kidney, and metabolic disease.

Among 5293 people followed for nearly nine years, 540 strokes occurred, and each one-point rise in the baseline combined score came with about 61 percent higher stroke risk. The paper gives clinicians a combined early-warning signal to test, while noting that prediction still needs checking in other groups before routine use.
pmc-13410698:
Jason Mark Redman leads a team reporting in 2026 a three-part immune therapy trial for stubborn prostate cancer. The cancer had kept growing despite hormone-blocking treatment, a setting where checkpoint drugs alone rarely help. Their mix joined a vaccine, an immune booster, and a two-way blocker of growth and shield signals.

Patients joined three arms in sequence, with a fourth suppressive drug added in the last arm. Side effects in the first two arms stayed manageable, though five people developed a hormone gland shortfall. Lasting drops in the prostate marker PSA appeared in about 29 percent of the middle arm, including men whose tumors usually resist immune therapy. The final arm closed early over skin toxicity.
pmc-13410998:
Thanh Hao Huynh and co-authors report in 2026 new steroid compounds from a soft coral collected off Taiwan. Sea corals brew unusual steroids that drug hunters prize. Extracts of the coral Sclerophytum leptoclados yielded a dozen related steroids for study.

Four proved entirely new, two more appear unreported, and six were known cousins. Spectroscopic detective work mapped each new structure atom by atom. Tested on human white blood cells, three compounds strongly calmed two signs of inflammation, with potency in the low micromolar range. The set was also screened for slowing liver scarring, a second hoped-for use. Marine steroids remain a rich source of anti-inflammatory leads, the results suggest.
pmc-13411298:
Carlton, Antezana, and Richey scan socially anxious teenagers' brains during a rigged social game. They test whether the brain's reward center goes quiet under social stress, and whether bullying history deepens the quiet. Anhedonia, loss of pleasure, travels with social anxiety but its triggers in peer life are unclear. Their 2026 pilot study runs twenty eight adolescents aged thirteen to seventeen through interviews, questionnaires, and an MRI game where peers vote players off an island.

When negative feedback loomed, the ventral striatum, a reward hub, fired less at outcome than during hopeful anticipation. The deeper that dip, the stronger a teenager's anhedonia symptoms. Relational peer victimization, exclusion and manipulation, not physical attack, tracked with the suppressed reward response. The sample is small, and the work is a pilot, but the pattern points at a target. Therapies that rebuild reward response to signals may loosen anhedonia's grip on anxious youth.
pmc-13411798:
Carlotta Marini leads a pilot study in 2026 screening dried chicken feet sold in Europe as dog treats for drug residues and resistant bacteria. Treats are the pet food market's fastest-growing slice, and farm antibiotic use upstream can echo in the bag. Eleven products bought on the European market went through chemical and bacterial testing.

Residues of several farm chemicals turned up in most samples, led by two poultry feed additives and a processing marker. Thirty-seven staph bacteria were grown, several shrugging off multiple antibiotics including key hospital drugs. No resistance appeared in one staph species. Layered residues raise the specter of combined effects over long feeding, which pushes the authors toward a One Health warning.
pmc-13412298:
Qing Yu and co-authors test in 2026 whether plain chest CT scans can flag pulmonary hypertension without dye or invasive testing. Diagnosis of high pressure in the lung arteries still rests on right heart catheterization, an invasive procedure. The team mined radiomic features and vessel shapes from non-contrast scans of patients with two forms of the disease plus controls, all confirmed by catheter readings at two centres.

One feature, the pulmonary arterial surface-to-volume ratio, tracked closely with measured artery pressure, while the vein ratio tracked filling pressure instead. Models built on these features identified the disease in a validation group with strong accuracy. Animal work linked the vein measure to early vessel remodelling before pressures changed, hinting at screening value.
pmc-13412398:
MohamadReza Hashemi and colleagues hunt in 2026 for a circular RNA that could flag breast cancer early and hint at prognosis. Circular RNAs regulate genes partly by soaking up microRNAs, and many remain unexplored in this disease. Mining three public expression datasets turned up 40 circular RNAs differing between tumour and normal tissue, from which the team shortlisted two fresh candidates.

Lab tests on tissue from 24 patients confirmed one candidate, hsa_circ_0000231, runs higher in tumours than in nearby healthy tissue. Network analysis predicted it works through a partner microRNA to free cyclin B1, a cell-division driver. The authors offer the molecule, and their screening-to-validation pipeline, as steps toward a clinically useful marker.
pmc-13413298:
Monica Maier develops in 2026 a conceptual framework for a quiet problem of the AI era: people misjudging their own competence after a tool helps them perform well. Generative assistants can lift task results while leaving users unsure which skill was theirs. Drawing on research about self-monitoring, learning, trust, and mental offloading, the article asks how assisted performance turns into a cue people use to rate themselves.

The proposed framework spans eight axes, from where the AI sits in the task to how success gets credited. AI supports accurate self-judgment when it keeps reflection and checking alive, the argument runs. It distorts judgment when it replaces thinking, cuts effort, or lets users claim the machine's success. The framework is offered as a map for future empirical work.
pmc-13415598:
Pamela Rose V. Samonte and Noelle K. Comolli engineer tiny biodegradable spheres to carry a corticosteroid into joint cartilage, in 2026. Osteoarthritis affects about 240 million people and lacks long acting targeted options. Their PLGA microspheres, made by an oil and water emulsion, varied in size and surface charge, then entered cow cartilage samples for diffusion tests.

Smaller spheres penetrated cartilage further, yet movement proved not truly diffusive, likely blocked by the dense collagen mesh. Surface coatings changed behavior sharply. A polyethylene glycol coating kept about 96 percent of the drug intact at day fourteen, against about 37 percent for plain spheres. Release followed polymer breakdown in a predictable, dose scalable way.
pmc-13416198:
Sabbya Sachi and colleagues dose obese mice with chia seed oil to test protection of blood, liver, and kidneys, in 2026. Mice grew obese on butter fortified feed, then received oil at three doses in custom feed, alongside normal, obese, and chia only control groups. Human equivalent doses were calculated for translation.

Oil treated mice gained less mass, carried less visceral fat, and ate more efficiently per gram gained. Blood counts, hemoglobin, and platelet measures recovered toward normal, while lipid profiles improved. Liver and kidney chemistry markers fell back near healthy levels, and tissue sections confirmed structural repair. Effects grew with dose across most measures.
pmc-13416398:
Ishin Togashi and colleagues randomize athletes with patellar tendinopathy to exercise alone or exercise plus radial pressure wave therapy, in a 2026 trial at Juntendo University in Japan. Thirty-three athletes, average age near twenty, had chronic pain in the tendon below the kneecap. The treatment group received four weekly pressure wave sessions, while both groups stretched and strengthened daily.

A validated knee score started near sixty-eight in both groups. By twenty-eight weeks the therapy group reached about ninety, against about seventy-seven for controls. Adjustment for symptom duration erased the between group significance, however. Both groups gained meaningful relief, and the therapy group reached that threshold sooner.
pmc-13417298:
Pranay Kumar Maitra, Anusmita Rout, and Partha Sarathi Mukherjee build silver cages that harvest light in stages, in a 2026 chemistry study. Two cages differ only in how silver binds: through nitrogen in one, through carbon in the other. The nitrogen cage stays flexible and glows more strongly when clumped, a trait called aggregation induced emission.

That cage passed energy through three dyes in sequence and produced bright near white light with very high efficiency. The rigid carbon bound cage glowed in solution but dimmed when clumped, so it failed at harvesting. Flexibility, the authors conclude, decides whether silver cages can serve in light systems.
pmc-13417598:
Pu and colleagues built in 2026 a fast bead system for tracking immune signals during CAR-T therapy. CAR-T therapy uses a patient's own immune cells, re-engineered to attack cancer, but it can trigger a dangerous cytokine storm. Their method makes coded beads in a 96-well plate, raising output from a few bead types a day to 96 types in eight hours.

The team profiled 136 blood samples from 32 patients with large B-cell lymphoma treated with CD19 CAR-T cells. Cytokine patterns over time differed clearly between patients with mild and severe cytokine release syndrome. One signal, TGF-β1 measured before treatment, was linked to later severe syndrome and to worse event-free survival. The authors present baseline TGF-β1 as a candidate warning marker and the bead system as a practical tool for immune monitoring.
pmc-13418198:
Murat Ay and colleagues report a lung cancer case that triggered extreme hormone excess, in a 2026 case report. A 70 year old man arrived with pneumonia and ketones from high blood sugar, without the classic rounded look of cortisol excess. Blood tests showed very high ACTH and cortisol that suppression drugs could not lower, pointing to the tumour as the hormone source.

Scans found poorly differentiated lung adenocarcinoma, a rare source for this syndrome compared with small cell cancer. The patient declined fast and died three days after biopsy, before cancer treatment could start. Early cortisol checks in stubborn metabolic crises are urged.
pmc-13418698:
Mengnan Liu and colleagues show how past flu immunity steers gene mixing when two flu strains meet in one cell, in a 2026 study. Such mixing, called reassortment, has seeded past pandemics. The team grew two marked test viruses with antibodies of two kinds. Some antibodies hit just one strain. Others hit both strains.

All antibodies cut virus output and changed the mix of offspring. Strain specific antibodies pushed change hardest, favouring mixed viruses that could escape them. Broad antibodies shaped the mix in a way that did not depend on their exact target. Past immunity may thus help decide which new flu types arise.
pmc-13419198:
Thompson and colleagues ran focus groups in 2026 with healthcare providers who treat paediatric feeding disorder. This disorder covers children who cannot eat in a way that meets medical, nutrition, skill, or psychosocial needs. Seven focus groups with 25 providers explored their training paths and practice needs across all four domains of the disorder.

Providers differed widely in how much feeding disorder training their education had given them. Workplace structures and access to specialist services varied and often limited care. Providers wanted comprehensive care but had to balance it against what clinics can feasibly deliver. They also valued the family perspective as central to good treatment. The authors point to fixes: more teaching exposure during training, better mentoring, shared evidence-based resources, and stronger links between research and practice.
pmc-13419298:
I. V. Renuka and colleagues report a 2026 case where a rare muscle cancer in a teenager mimicked a salivary gland tumor. A 19-year-old woman endured a growing, painful left-face swelling for a year, and clinicians first diagnosed a primary parotid tumor with no lymph nodes felt.

Biopsy plus immunostaining revealed embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma instead, chemotherapy followed, and the patient was doing well at six months and one year. The case warns clinicians that this rare tumor can masquerade as gland inflammation or a salivary tumor in young patients where gland swelling is common.
pmc-13422298:
Shen and co-authors built and tested in 2026 an emergency training course for nurses in their first five years on the job. The course runs simulated crises in the real ward, an approach called in situ simulation. Junior nurses must act fast in events they may rarely have seen.

The study enrolled 82 junior nurses at a large hospital in Hubei province in late 2023. It split them into a training group of 37 and a control group of 45 receiving routine teaching. The course held nine themed scenarios, from heart attack and diabetic crisis to unplanned tube removal and a patient suicide attempt. After training, the simulation group scored higher than controls on clinical reasoning and first aid skills. Scores for critical thinking and clinical communication did not differ between groups, which the authors say needs further targeted work.
pmc-13423398:
Cassandra L. Stegall and three co-authors describe a project to improve documentation of lethal means safety counselling for adolescents reaching a children's hospital emergency department with mental health concerns. Counselling families about access to firearms, sharps, and medication is recommended, yet no standard exists for recording it, and baseline records were nearly empty.

Only 3% of charts at baseline noted any access discussion, and 1% covered all three item types. Adding open questions to the social worker's note template lifted those rates to 81% and 68%. A structured electronic form then pushed any-access documentation to 90%, though complete documentation stayed near 66%. The authors track the climb with control charts over six months.
pmc-13423498:
Gen Tsujio and eight colleagues study colorectal cancers containing signet-ring cells, a rare and aggressive cell type found in under 1% of these tumours. Working at the Shizuoka Cancer Center, they reviewed 35 patients operated on between 2002 and 2022, splitting them into pure signet-ring cancers and ordinary adenocarcinomas carrying a signet-ring component.

Most tumours had grown deep, 85.7% reaching stage T3 or beyond, with lymph node spread in 74.3% of cases. Survival did not differ between the pure and mixed groups. What did matter was the makeup of the spread itself: patients whose lymph node deposits contained signet-ring cells fared significantly worse on both survival and relapse. Node histology, the authors argue, deserves a place in prognosis.

pmc-13429898:

The gain was largest against comparable Dalean networks lacking reversal potentials, which the new design beat clearly. Spike patterns also grew more irregular, closer to the near-random firing statistics of real neurons, and network-wide oscillations fell. Rodrigues argues a core feature of biological synapses buys both efficiency and performance in machine systems.
pmc-13469198:
Abdela and colleagues profiled colorectal cancer in patients under 50 in 2026 at Ethiopia's largest referral hospital, where data on early-onset disease were scarce. The team reviewed 630 confirmed cases diagnosed from 2019 to 2024. Early-onset meant diagnosis before age 50. Records covered tumor site, cell type, grade, and stage. Young and older patients were compared statistically.

Nearly half the cases were early-onset: 292 patients, about 46 percent, with a mean age near 36. Their tumors differed in telling ways. Rectal tumors were more common in the young, about 31 percent against 23 percent in older patients. Poorly organized, aggressive-looking tumors were also more frequent, about 22 percent against 13 percent. Yet spread at diagnosis was far less common in the young, about 27 percent against 66 percent. Adjusted analysis kept rectal site and poor grade as young-case markers. The authors urge suspicion of cancer in younger adults with rectal symptoms.
pmc-13469298:
Sheng Sun and colleagues report in a 2026 letter the first complete genome sequences of rabies viruses collected recently in Sierra Leone. Rabies kills an estimated 21,500 people a year in Africa, yet West African virus sequences are scarce, so transmission patterns across the region stay murky. The team sequenced three full viral genomes and placed them on the family tree of African rabies lineages.

All three belonged to the Africa 2H subclade, endemic to the region, and closely matched viruses from neighboring countries, evidence that the virus crosses borders with dogs rather than evolving in isolation. Dog vaccination coverage in Sierra Leone remains low. The authors argue the finding makes rabies control a regional coordination problem: vaccination and surveillance that stop at a national border will keep failing against a virus that does not.
pmc-13469598:
Cao and colleagues investigate a Chinese patient with a combination of delayed puberty, small head size, curved spine, and epilepsy, in a 2026 genetics case study. Suspicion fell on IGSF10, a gene in the immunoglobulin superfamily previously tied to delayed puberty and a skull disorder. The team sequenced the patient's genes, confirmed candidates with a second method, and profiled immune cells from her blood to look for wider effects.

Sequencing revealed a novel IGSF10 variant, a single-letter deletion that shifts the reading frame and truncates the protein. The variant was new in the family, present in the patient but absent from both parents, and her cells produced less IGSF10 message, consistent with the faulty copy being destroyed. Single-cell profiling showed shifts in effector T cells and monocytes, with altered maturation patterns. Cao suggests immune disturbance may contribute to the reproductive, brain, and skeletal features, pending proof.
pmc-13469698:
Kennedy D Agwamba and colleagues reconstruct how the western house mouse colonised the Americas after travelling with European ships. House mice spread from the Fertile Crescent into Europe with early farming and then worldwide through maritime expansion. Their 2026 study uses exome sequences, the protein-coding parts of the genome, from 276 mice.

Samples came from North and South America and Western Europe. Admixture analysis showed mice from Iberia's Atlantic coast are the closest relatives of all American populations, with a secondary contribution from southern Britain into North America. More specific links joined Portugal with Brazil and Spain with Argentina. Modelling dated the split of American populations to roughly the last 500 years, matching post-fifteenth-century European arrival. The authors say commensal mice mirror fine details of human migration.
pmc-13470398:
Xiangyu Dai and colleagues review in 2026 how lactate, long dismissed as waste, steers immune cells inside tumors. Lactate pours out of reprogrammed cancer metabolism and builds up around tumors. Across cancers of the stomach, liver, lung, skin, and pancreas, it blunts killer T cells while favoring regulatory cells, dendritic cells, and checkpoint molecules that calm attack.

The review maps the machinery involved, from the enzyme LDHA that makes lactate to the transporters that move it across membranes. Gaps remain in how each piece changes T cell behavior in real tumors. Early drug work on blocking lactate production or transport is covered, including trials in progress. The authors aim to frame precision immune therapy that targets tumor metabolism rather than the immune cells alone.
pmc-13470698:
Liliane S. de Farias and colleagues report the first synthesis of selenium-bearing dibenzoxepines, ring-shaped molecules of interest for drugs and materials. Their route closes the seven-membered ring in one step using iron chloride and selenium reagents under mild conditions.

The recipe uses 0.6 equivalents of a diselenide and one equivalent of iron chloride in solvent at room temperature. It gave the products in good to excellent yields across many starting variants and tolerated diverse extra chemical groups. The closure runs through a hungry selenium species formed in place, which attacks the carbon chain and seals the ring. Attempts to swap in sulphur or selenium ring cousins failed, de Farias notes, showing how specific the route is.
pmc-13470898:
Bruna L. Kuhn and co-authors show in 2026 that designer solvents can reorganize the working surface of a light driven catalyst and speed dye cleanup. Titanium dioxide photocatalysts degrade pollutants under light, and deep eutectic solvents, cheap mixtures that stay liquid through hydrogen bonding, were added either loose or fixed onto the particles. Five recipes varied the hydrogen bonding partner, from glycerol and ethylene glycol to urea.

Rate measurements followed standard surface kinetics, and the best mixtures ran up to seventeen times faster than bare catalyst. Polyol and acid based partners helped most, likely by easing electron transfer and reactive oxygen formation. Urea and one acid partner seemed to coat the surface too tightly. Surface probes showed the solvent contact is weak and reversible, while magnetic resonance showed the dye kept apart as single molecules rather than stacked clumps.
pmc-13471298:
Seker Gezici and a pediatric team tested in 2026 whether variants of the gene CYP2C19 change how children respond to intravenous diazepam given for seizures. The gene controls how fast the body clears the drug. The prospective study enrolled 100 children up to age 18 at one center. Sequencing checked three gene variants. Doctors recorded whether one or two doses stopped the seizure, and any breathing side effects.

Most seizures stopped: about 76 percent after the first dose and 79 percent overall. Breathing problems appeared in 15 percent of children, and 9 percent needed breathing support. One variant was absent entirely in this Turkish sample, while the other two appeared in 19 and 49 percent of children. A specific combination mattered. Children carrying it faced significantly more treatment failures and significantly more breathing side effects. The authors argue gene profiling before emergency dosing could one day flag children needing different drugs or closer watching.
pmc-13471498:
Topaloğlu and Simsek studied how stress during a high-risk pregnancy affects a mother's emotional bond with her unborn baby. Their 2026 mixed-methods study ran through 2024 at one hospital maternity clinic, pairing stress and attachment questionnaires with open-ended interviews analyzed phenomenologically.

The quantitative stage found a very strong negative correlation of −0.965 between perceived stress and fetal attachment scores, a value the authors themselves say should be read with caution. Interviews filled in the mechanism: coping strategies, partner support, and dread of the postpartum period decided how much stress eroded the bond. The team recommends building psychosocial support, especially partner involvement, into high-risk pregnancy care rather than tracking medical risk alone.
pmc-13471898:
Michael Bernard Barton leads an eleven author retrospective in 2026 on the Australian program that built a combined MRI and linear accelerator for cancer treatment. The device images tumors with magnetic resonance while delivering the beam. It aims at sharper anatomy based targeting and possibly targeting based on body function. Six Australian universities and overseas partners built a one of a kind layout. The layout pairs a split magnet with the beam running along the field, and the patient lying across it.

Work spanned personalized targeting, new device work, and biology discovery. It included AI image sharpening and dose measuring inside magnetic fields. Competitive funding topped twenty seven million dollars. Output passed one hundred twenty papers and twenty five completed doctorates. The authors distill lessons about time, teamwork, and the funding pull of bold engineering in radiation oncology.
pmc-13472498:
Samuel Atiku, Kehinde Owolanke, and Olufisayo Olakotan study in 2026 why artificial intelligence scribes fail in real clinics, using the online talk of clinicians themselves. These tools promise relief from record keeping, and early reports praise saved hours, yet omissions, wrong attributions, and invented content keep surfacing. The team gathered more than two thousand relevant passages from nine hundred fifty two documents across one hundred sixty two Reddit threads posted between 2023 and 2025.

Accounts tied failures to interacting conditions rather than the software alone. Rigid templates, integration gaps, and shaky reliability met billing pressure, governance gaps, and severe time shortage. Individual checking habits decided whether errors reached the record. The authors frame documentation risk as socio technical: fixing the model without fixing its setting will leave the failures in place.
pmc-13472798:
Ueki and colleagues report a 2026 study of early-onset Parkinson's disease using midbrain organoids grown from cells of a patient carrying the 22q11.2 deletion. People with this deletion develop Parkinson's far more often than average, yet the deleted region holds no known Parkinson's gene. The team grew stem cells from a patient into tiny midbrain-like tissues to watch development itself.

The organoids showed defects in neurogenesis, the birth of new neurons: the dopamine neurons that later die in Parkinson's may be too few or flawed from the start. That flips the usual story of neurons dying in old age; here, the disease may begin as a developmental shortfall that aging then exposes. The model may explain why this group falls ill decades early.
pmc-13473498:
Soundariya and Thangaraj built an emotion-reading system for brainwave signals that chains wavelet signal cleaning, reinforcement-learned channel selection, and an ensemble of graph and memory networks. Their 2026 paper tests the pipeline on three public EEG datasets for classifying emotional states.

Reported accuracy was high across the board: 94.5% on the DEAP dataset, 98.5% on the EEG Brainwave dataset, and 97.6% on an emotion EDA dataset, each split 60% training, 20% testing, and 20% validation. The DEAP benchmark itself comes from 32 participants rating 40 music videos on arousal, valence, and dominance. Spectral entropy analysis locates emotional peaks to slice the signal into meaningful epochs before classification, an addition the authors credit for cleaner features.
pmc-13474498:
Yusuke Takei and nine colleagues reported in 2026 early-to-mid-term outcomes for zone 1 total arch replacement with a frozen elephant trunk in acute type A aortic dissection. The zone 1 approach moves the repair closer to the heart and adds a bypass to the left subclavian artery, aiming to balance safety against complexity.

Among 80 patients treated between 2014 and 2025, thirty-day mortality was 8.8 percent and in-hospital mortality 10.0 percent, with stroke in 12.5 percent and spinal cord injury in 5.0 percent. Freedom from aorta-related events fell to 81.5 percent at five years, while bypass-related freedom stayed higher. Most bypass events were silent blockages from technical issues. Bypass durability remains a concern, and careful follow-up matters for selected patients.
pmc-13474698:
Vishesh Khanna and colleagues review HER2-targeted drug results in 2026 for gut cancers treated at one center from 2010 to 2023. HER2 is a growth signal protein that some stomach and bowel tumors carry in excess. Records covered 103 people with advanced disease who got at least one HER2 drug line. Test methods for HER2 status were compared head to head.

Gene sequencing missed about a third of tumors that stain-based tests called HER2 positive, while every gene-positive tumor also stained positive. A two-drug antibody pair gave the longest time before stopping in later lines. A quarter of people who tried a second HER2 drug did better on it than on their first. Layered testing and serial HER2 care both earn support.
pmc-13474798:
Hargitai and colleagues asked why autistic traits and ADHD traits so often come with anxiety and low mood in adults. Their 2026 study surveyed 504 adults drawn to match the United Kingdom population, measuring traits, mood symptoms, and two habits of mind. Those habits were intolerance of uncertainty, meaning distress when outcomes feel unclear, and negative problem orientation, meaning a gloomy view of one's own problem solving.

Together, the two habits of mind fully explained the link between autistic traits and internalising symptoms, the study term for anxiety and depression combined. For ADHD traits the same two habits explained only part of the link, leaving room for other factors the model did not capture in these data. The authors suggest that helping people tolerate uncertainty and view problems more calmly could ease anxiety and low mood, especially for autistic adults in everyday life.
pmc-13474898:
Javier Guerrero-Flores and co-authors launch a web platform in 2026 for genes that control chromatin in brain development disorders. Chromatin is the packaging that decides which genes stay open or shut. Faults in its regulators cause many such disorders, yet data on them sit scattered across tools. The platform, named CRONDEX, merges curated gene sets with function and pathway notes.

Genes were drawn from brain disorder lists and a chromatin factor catalog, with plain gene switches left out. Users can compare genes side by side and hunt shared mechanisms across disorders. General genome tools lack this focused chromatin-only frame. The resource aims to speed hypothesis building for rare disease teams.
pmc-13475998:
Ahn and colleagues compare outcomes for dogs and cats with two kinds of kidney failure treated by dialysis-like therapy at a referral hospital, in 2026 veterinary research. One group had acute kidney injury, a sudden failure; the other had acute-on-chronic disease, a sudden worsening on top of long-term kidney damage. Records covered 136 client-owned animals, 67 dogs and 69 cats, treated between 2017 and 2024 with renal replacement therapy.

Animals with acute-on-chronic disease were older, averaging 10.4 years against 6.3 years for the acute injury group in the reported data. Survival to discharge reached 70 percent for acute injury cases but only 53 percent for acute-on-chronic cases across the cohort. Median survival for the acute-on-chronic group was 57 days overall and just 33 days for dogs. Ahn notes the differences fell short of statistical significance, yet consistently pointed toward worse outcomes when chronic damage underlay the crisis.
pmc-13476398:
Rezvan Asadi and Fatemeh Safari test in 2026 whether fluid from human amniotic stem cells can push breast cancer cells toward death. Fluid and cancer cells shared a divided dish for three days without touching. Death and cell-cycle state were read by protein blots and flow tools. The cancer line used carries a faulty copy of the guard gene p53.

Guard-path proteins rose broadly after fluid exposure, including the p53 family chain and death triggers. A blocker protein that normally restrains p53 fell at the same time. Cells piled up in the DNA-copying phase and death markers climbed. Stem cell fluid may hold a gentler cancer care lead.
pmc-13477598:
Ebru Kübra Taşpolat and Evrim Coşkun wrote a 2026 letter to the editor arguing that stroke recovery education should include caregivers and families, not only patients. Both authors write as clinicians in physical medicine and rehabilitation. Their letter responds to a scoping review on patient education for community-dwelling stroke survivors.

Hands-on caregiver training can cover safe movement, transfers, fall and pressure injury prevention, warning signs, and medicine routines. The letter cites studies linking caregiver preparedness to better patient quality of life, plus reviews showing training improves caregiver skill and confidence. Caregiver teaching today is uneven and often squeezed into discharge day. The authors propose standard modules starting during inpatient rehabilitation, with family doctors reinforcing them and watching for caregiver burden afterward.
pmc-13478198:
Yuki Takakura and seven colleagues showed in 2026 how a small mitochondrial protein helps cancer cells resist DNA-damaging chemotherapy. Such drugs kill fast-dividing cells by breaking DNA, yet acquired resistance limits them, and the mitochondrial side of resistance was little known.

The protein COXFA4L3, formerly C15ORF48, blocks mitochondrial DNA damage and pore opening, stopping damaged mitochondrial DNA from leaking into the cell interior. That leak would otherwise trigger the cGAS-STING immune alarm and cell death. By repressing this damage response, the protein confers resistance. The findings point to mitochondria as a lever for restoring chemosensitivity.
pmc-13478298:
Relangi and colleagues tackled a data problem in 2026: water quality records are too small and lopsided to train good machine learning classifiers for judging whether water is drinkable. They generated synthetic records by oversampling, using a method called SMOTE and a rival approach using generative networks, then checked how closely the fake data matched the real data. Several classifiers were trained on each synthetic set and tested for accuracy.

The SMOTE drinking-water set matched real data closely, with a discrepancy score of 0.0067 where lower means closer to real. Gradient boosting and XGBoost classifiers trained on it hit 99.47 percent test accuracy in the reported experiments. The generative-network data scored worse on closeness despite some strong classifier results. On a second water dataset both methods produced close matches, leading the authors to favor oversampling for dependable synthetic training data.
pmc-13478398:
Hektoen and colleagues used a nationwide Norwegian registry in 2026 to see how other illnesses shape lung cancer care in the immunotherapy era. The study covered 9,178 Norwegians diagnosed with advanced non-small cell lung cancer, stage IIIB to IV, diagnosed before and after immune checkpoint drugs arrived. Trials often exclude such patients, so real-world records fill the gap on who gets treated and who survives.

The commonest added illnesses were chronic lung disease at 22 percent, cardiovascular disease at 21 percent, type 2 diabetes at 10 percent, and rheumatic diseases at 6 percent of patients. Patients with added illnesses received systemic treatment less often, yet after immunotherapy arrived, treatment use rose in every group and two-year survival improved up to threefold. Heart-disease patients fared better on immunotherapy alone than with added chemotherapy, at 38 against 22 percent two-year survival.
pmc-13479198:
Vilert Loving wrote a 2026 article on making doctor-administrator leadership pairs work inside healthcare organizations. Care delivery is too complex for either clinical or business expertise alone, so most organizations now pair a physician leader with an administrative leader. Surveys suggest about 77 percent use this dyad model, yet cross-functional teams often struggle, with one report calling three quarters of them dysfunctional.

Physician leaders bring clinical credibility and quality gains, while administrators bring operations and finance depth. The pairing also breeds cultural friction, since each side can suspect the other of sacrificing care or performance. Loving lays out the benefits and failure modes of the model, then offers practical steps organizations can take to support the partnership and steps the two leaders can take themselves.
pmc-13479598:
Shamshadul Haq and coauthors published a 2026 molecular study of how rice plants respond to nano-sized zinc oxide, a fertilizer form absorbed more efficiently than bulk zinc. Zinc is an essential plant micronutrient, and the bZIP family of gene switches helps manage it. Two contrasting rice varieties, CSR-30 and PB-1, received nano-zinc treatment.

The team first catalogued the structure, control elements, and evolution of the bZIP genes and the small RNAs that target them. They then measured responses of thirty bZIP genes and forty-one partner small RNAs in both varieties. CSR-30 generally switched its bZIP genes in one direction, described in the study's results, showing that varieties deploy the same gene family differently under the same treatment. The work supports breeding and fertilizer strategies tuned by variety.
pmc-13480098:
Niti Mittal and co-authors set out a 2026 trial plan testing a drug called saroglitazar for polycystic ovary syndrome. Faulty insulin response is thought to drive much of the condition; the drug acts on two cell switches tied to fat and sugar handling. About 140 patients will be split evenly between drug plus metformin and metformin alone, with diet and activity advice for everyone.

Treatment runs for 24 weeks, with a further check at 36 weeks. The main outcome is change in a blood protein that carries sex hormones. Other checks cover body measures, hair growth, cycle patterns, blood fats, hormones, liver fat on scans, and quality of life. Safety checks track side effects and blood tests throughout. The trial is open label, so patients and doctors will know who gets the drug, a limit the team notes. Results will show whether the add-on earns a place in care.
pmc-13482098:
Ozbay and co-authors studied 89 teens aged 12 to 17 in 2026, all previously bullied online, to untangle how online bullying connects with depression and gaming problems. The clinical sample completed clinical interviews and standard scales covering victimization, bullying others, internet gaming disorder, depression, and attention and behavior symptoms. Statistical tests then checked which links held on their own.

Depression severity stood on its own with three partners: how badly the teen had been bullied online, older age, and how severe the gaming disorder symptoms were. Bullying others online, by contrast, tracked with defiant behavior symptoms, the hostile, rule-breaking pattern some teens show toward adults. Being victimized related only to depression, not to bullying back, and gaming disorder did not strengthen or weaken either link. The authors urge routine screening for online bullying in depressed or inattentive teens.
pmc-13482298:
Tabrizi and a team in Germany asked in 2026 if a calcium channel called RYR1 is a must for helper T cells in gut disease. These immune cells need calcium rushes to switch on and pick a role. The messenger NAADP was thought to open RYR1 and spark the first tiny calcium puffs. The team bred mice whose T cells lacked the gene, then tested the cells in dishes and in two models of gut swelling.

In dishes, the loss cut the tiny calcium puffs, shrank the peak rush, and slowed its start. In live mice, though, the changed cells drove gut swelling just as well as normal cells. They also grew and picked roles at a normal clip. The authors judge RYR1 a spare part in this setting: its loss dents the signal, but other paths cover for it in real gut disease.
pmc-13482898:
Ivana Kóšiová and co-authors present a 2026 study on stiffening the backbone of DNA strands that wake up an immune sensor. The team built sixteen variants of a known strand, swapping in phosphonate links that are either floppy or locked in shape.

Locked variants mostly beat the parent strand in human reporter cells and in blood immune cells, with the best one near thirty times stronger. Floppy variants matched the parent, while extra sugar tweaks killed activity in two cases. A short six-letter piece with the best lock also boosted the sensor when paired with plain CpG DNA, hinting at a helper binding site. Locked backbones may yield stronger immune stimulants.
pmc-13483398:
Yuxin Pan and co-authors offer a 2026 review of how microbe chatter might rescue oxygen-free treatment of salty factory wastewater. Signal dosing and signal-aware reactor design both show early promise for holding granules together and steadying methane flow. The authors propose a staged framework that matches signal use to reactor stage and measured performance rather than blanket dosing. Most proof still sits at lab scale, so pilot runs under real brine loads form the next test. Chemical talk may become a standard dial for plant operators.
pmc-13483498:
Nicola Cumley and co-authors describe a 2026 study moving gene-hunting scans closer to routine diagnosis of brain and spinal infections. Raw scan output bristled with false leads from stray contamination and sloppy gene matching. Layered filters, kept simple enough for lab staff to apply, stripped most of that noise away. The free-floating fraction gave the cleanest, most trustworthy pathogen calls. The authors package the workflow as a shared framework so other hospitals can judge scan results the same way. Faster, surer naming of the infecting germ could sharpen treatment for a deadly group of illnesses.
pmc-13483698:
Stine Larsen and colleagues test whether hands-on support helps clinics deliver physical health care to people with severe mental illness. Their 2026 multicenter study follows 26 Norwegian specialist sites from 2016 to 2018, half receiving implementation support and half not. Fidelity to a guideline-based care model was scored over 18 months alongside data for 230 patients.

Fidelity started low everywhere, yet supported sites improved their scores far more than unsupported sites. Higher fidelity came with higher odds that patients actually received activity support and general medical interventions. Quit-smoking help rose sharply at supported sites by twelve months. The pattern suggests that publishing guidelines alone changes little, while coaching clinics through delivery steps moves both process scores and patient care.
pmc-13485698:
Skelton and a large consortium pooled genetic data from nearly 700,000 people to find DNA variants that nudge everyday anxiety levels up or down. Their 2026 meta-analysis combined fourteen cohorts of European-ancestry participants who had rated their generalized anxiety symptoms on questionnaires.

The scan found 80 independent variants across 74 genome regions tied to symptom severity. Of those regions, 39 had never been linked to anxiety before this analysis. Common variants together explained only about six percent of symptom differences, so environment still dominates. Scores built from the variants predicted anxiety in African and South Asian ancestry samples too, though more weakly. Skelton says the loci point to brain pathways worth probing for new treatments.
pmc-13486698:
Li and team surveyed surgery patients in a Chinese hospital about postoperative fatigue syndrome, a lingering exhaustion after operations that rest does not fix. Their 2026 study collected 310 valid responses scoring what patients know, how they feel, and what they actually do about the condition. The pattern mattered because self-care drives recovery once patients leave the ward.

Knowledge was strikingly poor, with a median score of only 3 out of 20 on the survey's knowledge scale. Attitudes were much brighter, and self-care practices sat in the middle, leaving a clear knowing-doing gap. Statistical modeling showed knowledge and attitude each independently pushed practice scores upward. Having the syndrome itself, and higher household income, also predicted better practices. Li calls for education that builds both understanding and habits before discharge.
pmc-13486998:
Asmita Gautam reports a 2026 case of leishmaniasis confined to the mouth lining in a young man from an endemic region of Nepal. The patient, aged 28 and living in Surkhet, endured painful mouth lesions for a year that began as lower lip erosion and spread to the upper lip and both palates. No earlier skin or visceral disease preceded the mouth involvement.

Untreated disease can perforate the nasal septum, deform the face, block the airway, and kill. Early recognition matters precisely because the mouth-only presentation invites confusion with common dental and fungal problems. Full case detail on testing and treatment sits in the complete report.
pmc-13487998:
Ikbal Esra Pehlivan, Sema Kaya, and Alaettin Koc measure imaging artifacts from dental filling materials in a 2026 laboratory study. Gray values, a stand-in for artifact strength, differed by material and by tooth surface in the reported tests. Two materials gave the highest values, while one gave the lowest, and the strongest effect appeared on the surface facing the filling rather than beside it. The authors note that filler content may drive the pattern, though no chemical testing was done.
pmc-13490398:
Zhang and team built a shared-control robot that helps surgeons puncture the liver under ultrasound guidance while the patient keeps breathing. Breathing moves the liver, destabilizing images and needle paths, and freehand skill varies widely. Their 2026 system pairs surgeon and robot: the robot positions the probe and holds steady contact force. The surgeon keeps authority over needle angle and insertion, assisted first by pose guidance and then by force regulation.

In a breathing phantom built from medical imaging, the shared system cut average operation time and needle placement error versus manual work, and raised success rates in the trials reported. A feasibility test in a living dog followed the phantom work. The bionic breathing rig itself is offered as a testbed for other motion-plagued procedures. Zhang stresses the design assists rather than replaces the surgeon's judgment.
pmc-13490598:
Yu Ishimoto and a large team untangle a glaucoma-linked gene region with mouse genetics in a 2026 study. The deletion erased the neighbor gene's activity in a specific set of cells around the developing eye, suggesting the cut removed regulatory DNA architecture the neighbor needs. Mice carrying one faulty copy of each gene developed the same eye defects. The authors argue human risk variants likely act through the neighbor's control landscape.
pmc-13491698:
Xu Yan and five co-authors build and test in 2026 a question-answering tool that helps community nurses manage symptoms in palliative care. Nurses working outside hospitals often face scattered guidance when patients near the end of life have complex symptoms. The team used a knowledge graph, a web of linked facts, to organize evidence into a WeChat mini-program that answers plain questions.

Experts first assembled 225 evidence items covering nine common symptoms, and developers converted them into a graph of 442 entities joined by 668 relationships. Nurses and experts then rated the tool over a two-week trial. Scores for usefulness, ease of use, acceptability, and usability were all strong. The authors caution that the trial was small, brief, and based mostly on opinions, so outcome studies come next.
pmc-13493498:
Neslihan Hazel Önür, Vildan Özkocaman, and Fahir Özkalemkaş hunt in 2026 for the blood level of cyclosporine that best shields leukemia patients from graft-versus-host disease after donor stem cell transplants. Too little of this immune-damping drug lets donor cells attack the patient, a frequently fatal complication. Disease struck twenty-eight percent of patients, at a median of about seven weeks. Statistical curve analysis picked a threshold near 274 micrograms per liter during the first two months, catching most future cases while clearing most safe patients. Staying above that line independently predicted lower risk, as did steroid use before transplant. The authors argue the first two months are the critical window for tight level monitoring.
pmc-13493798:
Abulfadhel Amer Saihood Altufaili and Dunya Mohammed Shleej present in 2026 a hybrid artificial intelligence system for sorting patients by heart disease risk. The design reads each patient's record through three separate lenses: background details, clinical signs, and test results. Autoencoders, networks that compress data into its core features, handle each view. A self-tuning weighting step then boosts whichever features carry the most signal for that dataset.

Three different classifiers vote at the end, with their influence weighted by how sure each one is about the individual case. Across five established heart disease datasets the system averaged about ninety-two percent accuracy. It beat classic machine learning tools and several fashionable deep learning models in the authors' comparisons. Explanation analysis spotlighted chest pain type, the count of major vessels involved, and exercise test depression as the decisive inputs.
pmc-13493998:
Jiacheng Wu leads a twelve-author team connecting in 2026 a missing gut bacterium to the anxiety that rides along with irritable bowel syndrome. Feeding the bacterium back calmed the mice, cooled amygdala inflammation, and repaired damaged neuronal branches. Genetic evidence even flagged the microbe as protective against anxiety itself. A live bacterium as anxiety therapy, a psychobiotic, is the proposal.
pmc-13495298:
Danna Wu, Haiwei Bai, Yafei Zhang, and Weina Wang test, in a 2026 randomized study, whether chilling the limbs during chemotherapy shields nerves from damage.
