The trial enrolled 200 patients at a Chinese hospital who were getting paclitaxel with a platinum drug.

Half got standard care, and half wore ice gloves and socks during treatment. From the fourth cycle on, the cold group showed clearly milder nerve harm on grading scales and symptom scores. Their daily living scores three months after chemotherapy also ran higher, and nerve signal tests backed the gains. The authors present limb cooling as a drug-free guard against this side effect, cheap and simple enough for wide use during infusion visits.
pmc-13495498:
Nobuaki Sato and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a hip that slipped out of its socket months after fracture surgery, with no new injury. An 87-year-old woman broke the top of her thigh bone in a fall and was fixed with a long nail down the bone's core, plus cement. Such forward dislocations after this nail surgery had never been reported, the authors say.

She walked with a frame at first and moved to a care home. Four months on, scans found the hip dislocated forward. Review showed the fracture had slowly telescoped, tipped, and failed to heal at its inner edge, draining the tension that holds a hip in place. Attempts to pop it back failed, so the joint was replaced; a year later she had no fresh slip. The authors stress aiming the first repair at solid inner support, not just a neat X-ray line.
pmc-13498598:
Zhang and colleagues investigated in 2026 how citric acid can pull rare earth elements out of roasted coal gangue, a coal mining waste that could become an alternative supply source. Rare earths are vital for electronics and clean energy. The team compared citric acid with hydrochloric acid and studied the chemistry step by step.

At the best settings, citric acid recovered about half of the total rare earths, with light rare earths reaching about 59 percent and heavy ones only about 17 percent. At the same starting acidity, citric acid beat hydrochloric acid on total recovery and held its acidity steadier. Surface and charge analyses showed the citrate binds rare earth ions only weakly. The authors conclude the acid's hydrogen ions do most of the work, which guides greener recovery designs.
pmc-13499398:
Changzheng Guo, Shiyong Liao, and Shourong Shi test in 2026 whether a water-soluble corn protein can replace part of the soybean meal in starter feed for young broiler chickens. Soybean meal is the standard protein source, yet price and supply pressure drive interest in alternatives. A total of 504 day-old male chicks were split among a standard diet and two diets where a small share of soybean meal was swapped for corn protein or cottonseed protein.

Corn protein raised body weight, daily gain, and feed intake by day 14, improved the finger-like gut lining structures that absorb nutrients, and lowered gut acidity without harming the gut barrier. Cottonseed protein instead slowed early growth. Deeper checks tied the corn benefit to reshaped gut microbes and better protein fermentation products, marking it as a promising starter-feed ingredient.
pmc-13499798:
Guo and colleagues measure the placebo effect inside weight-loss drug trials, where even dummy treatment usually sheds some weight. Pooling 182 placebo-controlled trials of anti-obesity medications, their 2026 meta-analysis found placebo groups lost a little over one kilogram on average. The team then asked what makes that phantom effect bigger or smaller, because a strong placebo response can mask or mimic a drug's real benefit.

How the placebo was delivered mattered: people given dummy injections lost noticeably more weight than those given dummy pills, perhaps because injections feel more medical and raise expectations. Diabetes status split the results sharply too, with non-diabetic participants losing the most on placebo and type 1 diabetic participants actually gaining a modest amount on average in the subgroup data. The authors advise trial designers to account for these factors when judging new drugs.
pmc-13500498:
Gianluca Spiteri and co-authors pool in 2026 evidence on obstructive sleep apnea risk among healthcare workers, whose own breathing disorder could endanger patients through impaired alertness. The condition is common yet underdiagnosed, and shift-heavy health work may aggravate it. Their systematic search of two databases for studies published between 2000 and 2026 kept papers that screened risk with structured questionnaires or confirmed diagnosis with validated tools. Prevalence was then combined with random-effects models.

Nine studies covering 8,473 participants entered the meta-analysis. High-risk prevalence estimates swung widely between studies, and the pooled figure landed near a quarter of workers in the reported confidence range. Geography explained part of the spread, since Europe and the Middle East ran higher than South-East Asia and the United States. Only two studies measured diagnosis directly, so the authors call for larger work using home sleep tests and new digital tools.
pmc-13501598:
Xiaokang Luo leads a four-author team reporting a 2026 case of valve surgery in a 59-year-old man with congenital factor VII deficiency. The rare inherited bleeding disorder affects roughly one person in 500,000. He needed a mechanical valve replacement, which demands lifelong blood thinning, yet his clotting tests were already abnormal because of the missing factor. The standard INR measure cannot reflect true anticoagulation in such patients, and no guideline covers the pairing. Perioperative bleeding was controlled with recombinant activated factor VII replacement.

After surgery he suffered a cerebral thrombosis, a clot in the brain, and warfarin began. Instead of the usual INR target, the team steered dosing by factor II and factor X activity, aiming for 30 to 45 percent. No bleeding and no further clotting followed. The authors recommend replacement therapy for operative safety and factor-activity monitoring to balance the twin risks in similar cases.
pmc-13501798:
Haitham Abu Khadija leads a twenty-two-author team with a 2026 study of hallucinations after heart surgery, split by whether patients had hypertension. The multicentre VAACS study followed 1,332 adults having bypass or valve surgery: 517 with hypertension and 815 without. A psychosis questionnaire screened for visual and auditory episodes during the first seven days. Separate Cox models hunted predictors inside each blood-pressure group.

Visual hallucinations struck 12.0 percent of hypertensive and 11.3 percent of non-hypertensive patients, while auditory ones struck 6.2 and 7.4 percent respectively. In the hypertension group, surgical risk score and neutrophil counts predicted visual episodes, and prior antibiotic use stood out for auditory ones, with an adjusted hazard ratio of 2.464 on that link. Oddly, longer breathing support predicted lower risk there. Without hypertension, the overall risk score dominated both hallucination types.
pmc-13503798:
Hamed Dehdashti Jahromi and Ahmad Lotfiani design a methane sensor that powers itself from light, in a 2026 simulation study. Methane leaks are a safety risk and a strong climate threat. Most sensors need wires, power, or lab gear to read them, which limits where they can sit.

The design joins a crystal slab that traps a methane-loving compound with a light detector beneath it. When methane soaks in, the slab's light resonance shifts, and the detector turns that shift into current. Computer models predict a sharp, near-straight response and very low idle current, with no outside power drawn. The build tolerates small flaws in its holes and layers. The authors see it serving leak watch networks and smart sensors.
pmc-13504998:
Jing Sun and others survey orthodontic patients on gum health knowledge, views, and practices. In 2026, the multi-site one-time survey at Jinan Stomatological Hospital collected 2,638 valid questionnaires between December 2024 and May 2025, with mean age about thirty-two years and seventy percent first-time orthodontic patients. Appliances trap plaque and raise gum risk during treatment.

Knowledge averaged 12.54 of 18, views 46.00 of 50, and practices 39.30 of 45, judged insufficient knowledge but mostly positive views and proactive practices. Structural equation model showed knowledge positively linked to attitude and practice, and attitude to practice, with attitude mediating knowledge effects. Patient education should target knowledge gaps to protect gums during orthodontics.
pmc-13507198:
Amy Z. Wang and others link default mode network patterns to event centrality in adult acute trauma survivors. In 2026, the study recruits 215 adults from a Level I trauma center. It scans resting-state brain action two to four weeks after injury and collects surveys at two to four weeks and three, six, and twelve months. Event centrality describes how far a traumatic memory becomes central to personal self.

Centrality at three and twelve months tracked adverse mental results, and twelve-month centrality linked to patterns in two default mode nodes, the lateral top brain cortex and hippocampus. Certain adverse results carried that connectivity-centrality relationship. The findings suggest neural mechanisms behind greater distress and identity-central trauma memories during recovery.
pmc-13508198:
Xiaohan Ai and eight co-authors map the microbes living in red and green snow on an Antarctic peninsula, in work published in 2026. Colored snow is widespread there, yet its tiny communities were poorly known. The team read all the DNA in snow from the Fildes Peninsula to name who lives there and what they do. Bacteria made up most of the community, with eukaryotes next and archaea rare. Community makeup differed clearly between red and green snow.

Green algae groups dominated the plant-like side in both colors, with distinct algae thriving in each. Genes tied to carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and sulfur cycles appeared throughout. Red snow favored breathing and phosphate control pathways, while green snow favored other routes, including gas use and fermentation. The red snow community web looked more complex and stable. Such webs may help colored snow persist and darken the surface, speeding melt.
pmc-13508298:
Tang Zhuo-Dong and six co-authors build a chart-based tool to predict dangerous blood clots after surgery for a broken shinbone top, in 2026 work. The study reviewed 224 patients treated between 2023 and 2025. Thirty-six patients developed both a leg clot and a lung clot after surgery. The team compared traits between groups, then used combined analysis to build a points chart, called a nomogram, and tested how well it sorted patients.

Age and a clot-related blood marker, D-dimer, stood out as the two independent risk factors. The chart built on them sorted patients with fair accuracy. Its check plots showed predicted risks lined up well with real outcomes, and decision analysis suggested real clinical benefit across useful thresholds. The authors give cutoff guideposts for age and the blood marker, so teams can flag high-risk patients early and step up clot prevention.
pmc-13508398:
Keqiang Ma leads a ten-author team mapping immune cell change across the white matter of multiple sclerosis brains, in 2026 work. White matter damage in this disease varies a lot from spot to spot, and the reasons were murky. The team merged two gene-reading methods: one that reads single cell nuclei and one that keeps each reading's place in tissue. Analysis hunted key cell types, control-gene networks, and how cell states shift over time.

That module lived mainly in microglia, the brain's own immune cells, and centered on inflammation pathways. A regulator named IKZF1 emerged as a candidate conductor of the change. Microglia ranged from calm states to inflamed, disease-linked states. In tissue maps, the rim around lesions was the hotspot, rich in those inflamed cells and matching the regulator's altered activity. The authors nominate this regulator network as a target for calming lesion edges.
pmc-13508798:
Kang and colleagues present a 2026 review of how brain MRI scans are de-identified before research sharing. Scans capture the face and skull, so a 'brain' image can reveal who a patient is. The review covers removal methods, from classic defacing, which erases facial features, to refacing with an average face, to deep learning anonymization, and the measures used to check them.

Good de-identification must do two things at once: block re-identification and keep measurements true. The review compares checks such as image similarity and overlap scores that test whether brain analysis still works after faces are altered. Policy frameworks in the United States and Europe set the legal bar. The authors aim at practical guidance, since overly blunt defacing can wreck facial-adjacent data while weak masking leaves patients exposed in data sets shared worldwide.
pmc-13509298:
Stelian Adrian Ritiu leads a ten-author review of the cell and molecular chaos behind hemorrhagic shock, the deadly state after major blood loss, in 2026 work. Shock after trauma kills many who might have been saved, and the damage runs far past lost volume. The review traces the chain: tissue starved of blood triggers the lethal trio of cold, acid buildup, and clotting failure. Immune overreaction, white cell injury, oxygen radical floods, failing cell power units, and a stripped vessel lining all pile in.

Salt fluids shift acid balance and kidney blood flow, gel fluids change vessel pressure and lining integrity, and blood products actively repair power units and vessel walls beyond adding volume. Bedside care therefore needs layered monitoring, the authors argue. Waste markers, dynamic heart measures, and direct views of small vessels can turn molecular targets into live treatment goals.
pmc-13509498:
Ceren Pamukcu and Ahmet Emin Atik compare how sugar attaches to therapeutic antibodies under stress, in a 2026 lab study. Sugar attachment, called glycation, can add unwanted variety to these drugs and matters when firms develop copy versions known as biosimilars. The pair studied one original antibody drug and three biosimilar versions, all aimed at the same inflammation target, after a week in a strong sugar solution.

Mass readings showed a near-identical mass gain in all four products, pointing to three sugar units added to most molecules. Detailed mapping found nine sites where sugar attached, with three hot spots carrying most of the change and the rest barely touched. Total glycation levels sat close together across products despite different making processes. The authors present the paired method as a sound way to compare such drugs.
pmc-13510598:
Delfino and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how the nucleolus, a dense knot inside the cell nucleus, helps drive a wide range of human diseases. The nucleolus builds ribosomes, the machines that make proteins. It also senses stress and can halt cell growth or trigger cell death when its work goes wrong.

The review links faulty nucleolus work to cancer, where cells demand extra ribosomes to grow fast, and to ribosomopathies, a group of disorders caused by too few ribosomes. It also ties the structure to early aging, brain degeneration, and immune faults. The authors map where these fields agree and list open questions. They also point to weak spots drugs might hit, such as small molecules that block ribosome building or gene-based fixes.
pmc-13512498:
Irving A. González-Lara and co-authors review dressings that merge hydrogels with metal-organic frameworks, sponge-like crystals with vast inner surface, for chronic wound care, in 2026 work. Chronic wounds burden patients and health budgets through stalled inflammation, stubborn infection, weak vessel growth, and faulty tissue rebuilding. Modern dressings increasingly stack several jobs into one material.

Hydrogels supply a wet, body-friendly web whose pore size, swelling, and softness can be tuned. Framework crystals add precise pore design and cargo space for drugs and active agents. Together the hybrids can support regeneration while fighting bacteria, calming inflammation, and releasing treatment in a controlled way. The review also weighs a newer idea, antiviral surface functions, and flags it as exploratory rather than proven. Design rules linking structure to performance close the survey.
pmc-13514898:
Wenping Ding and eight co-authors describe three new antibacterial compounds from a coral-reef bacterium in a 2026 natural-products study. The microbe, a Streptomyces strain from reef material, produced molecules the team named strepactones A, B, and C, built on an unusual fused three-ring frame never reported before. Their structures were pinned down through spectroscopy, X-ray crystallography, and computer-checked analyses,.

It froze the cancer cells' division cycle and switched on their death machinery. Ding's team offers the trio as leads for both aquaculture and anticancer research.
pmc-13516198:
Pawel Bakun leads a seventeen-author team building skin-penetrating vesicles for psoriasis care in a 2026 formulation study. Several recipes were made by a film-and-ultrasound method and checked for size, spread, and charge.

The bubbles held a steady size in the one-to-two hundred nanometre band and stayed stable for a month in water and in salt buffer. Tests on normal and psoriasis-derived skin cells looked at survival, and skin microbes were checked for harm. A zebrafish embryo test probed whole-organism toxicity. No harm appeared in the microbe or fish checks. Bakun's team judges the carriers safe and stable enough to merit development as a psoriasis treatment route.
pmc-13517098:
Sato and colleagues explored how knowing an opponent, and how one's skill compares, shapes decisions in kendo. Their 2026 study showed thirty high school kendo experts videos of wrist and head strikes that froze at moments. The strikes were performed by a familiar high-level model and an unfamiliar intermediate model. They were asked to predict the strike and say what cue they used.

Sato found athletes answered uncertain more often for the unfamiliar intermediate model at early stages. At those stages body movement cues had not yet appeared, showing that opponent knowledge fills the gap when motion information is absent. Prediction accuracy was higher for the intermediate model just before the strike landed, suggesting the skill gap between observer and performer alters processing at the decisive moment. Higher-skilled athletes relied more on whole-body movement cues than on intuition, hinting they had built richer internal movement repertoires.
pmc-13518798:
Girish Chandra Gandhi, Payal Mehta, and Ankit Sodha test greener concrete mixes for precast U-shaped drains in 2026 experiments. Ordinary concrete leans heavily on cement, a major source of carbon emissions. Their M40-grade mixes swapped in slag, fly ash, or tiny carbon nanotubes at very low doses.

Four mixes were checked for strength at 3, 7, and 28 days, plus chloride penetration and water permeability. Nanotubes at 0.03 to 0.05 percent raised compressive strength by 56 percent and blocked water passage entirely in testing. Higher doses clumped and helped less. Slag beat fly ash among the mineral swaps. The nanotube mix suits drains needing early strength and long service.
pmc-13518898:
Nazife Çevik, Taner Çevik, and Ahmet Gürhanlı show in 2026 that drug-target binding can be predicted from sequences alone, without any 3D protein structure. Early drug discovery needs to know which molecules bind which proteins, while docking methods depend on structures that are often missing or shaky.

Their framework merges chemical descriptors of proteins, short sequence motifs, and sequence-like drug codes into one feature space. Many model types were trained with imbalance correction, and a stacked ensemble combining three classifiers performed best, passing 0.90 in ROC-AUC with a peak of 0.914. Feature analysis surfaced biologically sensible binding motifs. Docking checks on a subset agreed with the predictions, supporting the sequence-only route.
pmc-13519098:
Rudy and colleagues tested how low thyroid hormone during windows of gestation affects fetal growth and bone development in pigs, in a 2026 animal study. Pregnant gilts received a thyroid-blocking drug for twenty-one days starting at four different gestational stages. Their fetuses were measured, including body and organ weights, body dimensions, X-rays, and bone density scans of the limbs.

Rudy confirmed the drug induced fetal hypothyroidism at every window, with fetal thyroid glands swelling dramatically. Yet body length, girth, weight, and all organ weights grew with gestational age regardless of treatment, showing fetal growth is not driven by thyroid hormone in this period. pmc-13520398:
Zhipeng Zhu and colleagues compare in 2026 two operations for single spinal metastases from lung cancer: complete block removal of the affected vertebra versus a smaller separation operation followed by focused radiation. Records covered 85 patients treated between June 2018 and April 2022.

Block removal controlled local tumour better and lengthened time without progression, yet caused more blood loss and more complications such as fluid leaks. Overall survival did not differ, while quality of life improved under both approaches. The trade-off supports joint decision-making tailored to each patient's fitness.
pmc-13520498:
Yue Liu and colleagues present in 2026 a 10-year-old boy with leukaemia who developed flesh-destroying soft tissue infection without any injury, caused by a usually mild foodborne bacterium. Chemotherapy had wiped out his infection defences, allowing unusually severe spread.

Illness began with gut symptoms after eating, then raced to tissue death and shock. The bacterium grew from both blood and tissue. Immediate radical surgery was judged too risky given low counts and instability, so strong antibiotics and intensive support came first. Staged cleaning surgery followed after stabilisation, and recovery allowed leukaemia treatment to resume. A gut-to-blood route is proposed.
pmc-13522098:
Shaoyang Lu and colleagues build in 2026 a risk score from cell ageing genes for liver cancer, testing whether ageing biology predicts tumour behaviour and treatment response. Gene clustering first defined three ageing-related subtypes with clearly different outlooks.

High scores tracked with advanced stage, poorer survival and a suppressive immune environment rich in regulatory T cells. Mutation load and tumour diversity also ran higher, including frequent TP53 changes. High-risk patients responded poorly to a standard drug and to arterial chemotherapy infusion, with limited expected immunotherapy benefit. Single-cell maps placed score activity mainly in malignant liver cells, tied to stem-like traits.
pmc-13522498:
Xihong Cheng and colleagues map genes for making ergosterol in a wood-decaying fungus in a 2026 genome study. Six members of one gene family were described in detail, differing in structure and in shared sequence motifs. All six carried many light-responsive elements in their control regions. Ergosterol levels in fungal threads rose under white, blue, and green light, peaking under blue light, and levels tracked activity of three family members. The work lays groundwork for breeding strains that produce more ergosterol.
pmc-13523198:
Hristiyanna I Ivanova, Jacqueline A Deurloo, and Caren I Lanting review what helps or hinders the use of healthcare guidelines in public health in a 2026 umbrella review. Barriers, supports, and strategies were sorted with a standard framework for innovation determinants.

Workplace problems were the commonest barriers, including scarce resources, weak teamwork, and limited support from managers. Clinicians' views of relevance and fit with daily practice also mattered. Perceived usefulness, staff engagement, and social support helped uptake. Education was the most used strategy yet worked unevenly alone, and multi-part programs gave mixed results. The authors conclude that strategies must be tailored to local context rather than copied wholesale.
pmc-13524898:
Paige M. Hulls and others explore, in a 2026 qualitative study, how professional stakeholders explain harms and inequalities in the night-time economy of two English towns. Goods and services sold at night, notably alcohol and gambling, are linked with ill health that concentrates in deprived areas and minoritized groups.

17 local authority and third-sector stakeholders in Swindon and Derby were interviewed, and analysis used a framework on sources of power. Participants described years of economic decline creating tension between public health aims and economic priorities, with alcohol licensing revenue often winning. Collaboration and whole-system working were proposed as remedies, alongside frustration at rigid funding rules. Different communities used night spaces differently, and participants wanted future venues designed to serve everyone locally.
pmc-13524998:
Masaki Hatano, Yuya Kimura, Hideo Yasunaga, and Sakae Tanaka offer, in a 2026 methodological guide, target trial emulation as a way to design stronger observational studies in orthopaedics. The approach starts by writing the protocol of the randomized trial one wishes existed, then emulating its pieces in routine data. Their example compares hip replacement types after hip fracture.

The guide shows how conventional designs invite bias. Eligibility rules can include patients who could never receive one option, and treatment labels can blur procedural differences. Follow-up can start at the wrong moment, and exclusions can rest on later information. Emulation forces these choices into the open before analysis. The authors stress the method cannot cure confounding, poor measurement, or biased loss to follow-up, but it improves transparency.
pmc-13525198:
Reid and colleagues ask whether a bone drug works better the longer it is taken. Their 2026 post hoc analysis revisits a six-year Auckland trial in which 2,000 osteopenic women over 65 received zoledronate or placebo every eighteen months. Most trials stop at three years and lose their placebo group, but this one kept both, letting the authors compare fracture protection between the trial's two halves.

In the placebo group, non-vertebral fracture rates stayed roughly flat across both halves. In the zoledronate group, the rate fell from 23 to 13 fractures per thousand women-years between the first and second halves. The relative protection strengthened accordingly, from a rate ratio of 0.83 in years one to three to 0.40 in years four to six, a significant difference between periods. The authors suggest long-term fracture prevention by such drugs has been underestimated.
pmc-13527998:
Biao Li and four colleagues study how thawing permafrost changes the way two trees drink in northeast China. Warming deepens the active layer, the soil band that thaws each summer. The team compared larch and birch growing over layers of different thickness. Stable isotopes in water samples revealed where roots took up water across the season.

Both species shifted their main uptake deeper as the season went on. Where the active layer was thicker, both drank from deeper soil and adjusted more flexibly. Birch moved downward faster and relied more on deep water than larch. Soil traits mattered most near the surface. The authors suggest birch may compete better for deep water as permafrost degrades. The results help explain how northern forests may cope with warming.
pmc-13528098:
Mi-Suk Oh and four colleagues seek blood cutoffs that predict quick recovery after clot-busting treatment for stroke in a 2026 study. Just over half the patients improved early.

The best cutoffs were about 12 micromoles per liter and about 1.16 milligrams per liter. Used alone, each marker sorted patients modestly. Used together, accuracy rose and sensitivity topped ninety percent. Younger age and no diabetes also helped. Oddly, having hypertension helped too. The authors propose the pair as a cheap early guide.
pmc-13528398:
Karol Basta and three colleagues argue AI fairness checks in health care look at too narrow a slice in a 2026 commentary. Most studies split patients by traits like sex, age, or race. Those categories come from anti-discrimination law. A cited review of 467 fairness studies found most stuck to such groups. Another found all twenty record-based studies did the same.

The authors say single traits miss how disadvantage is built. Housing, income, work, and neighborhood shape health before any algorithm runs. A model can look fair per group while deepening structural gaps. Fairness work should start from those social roots, they argue. Data picks, outcome choices, and rollout all carry the bias risk. Their plea is to widen the lens beyond protected traits. Otherwise AI may polish unequal care rather than fix it.
pmc-13529398:
Aulakh and Singh reported a 2026 case of a rare benign vascular growth, called Masson's tumor. It formed inside the inferior vena cava, the large vein returning blood to the heart, and reached into the heart itself. The patient was a 46-year-old woman with chest pain and repeated fainting on exertion. This growth usually appears on skin of the head, neck, or limbs, and heart involvement is exceptionally rare.

Aulakh describes how standard heart ultrasound first showed a mass on the right side of the heart without clarifying its origin. A probe passed down the food pipe traced it to the big vein. Open-heart surgery revealed the full growth, about fourteen centimeters long, and removed it completely. Microscope examination confirmed the benign diagnosis and ruled out a similar-looking cancer, angiosarcoma, which needs very different treatment. Complete removal is the preferred cure, since leftover tissue can regrow.
pmc-13530198:
Mustafizur Rahaman and co-authors present a 2026 vision model that screens eye photos for diabetic retinopathy, a diabetes complication that can blind. The task was simplified to flagging disease presence versus absence for triage. Image cleanup, staged training, and threshold tuning supported the fusion design. On a public contest dataset the hybrid beat four strong image baselines on accuracy and related scores. Visual explanations accompany each call, though lesion-level checking awaits richer data.
pmc-13530498:
Sherman and colleagues present in 2026, as conference paper 53, a five-year analysis of an aragonite-based scaffold implanted for knee cartilage defects. The covariate analysis split 251 trial patients by arthritis grade at entry, none-to-minimal against mild-to-moderate, and tracked the overall KOOS knee score to sixty months. The implant group improved about twice as much as the standard care group in both arthritis strata. It gained near forty points against roughly fourteen to eighteen for standard care among patients in this trial. The probability that the implant was superior exceeded 99.9 percent in both strata, and the treatment advantage did not vary with arthritis grade.
pmc-13531798:
Mohammad Montaseri and colleagues pool in 2026 trial evidence comparing two sedation drugs during heart surgery. Propofol and dexmedetomidine both calm patients around bypass and valve operations, yet their blood pressure and heart rate effects were disputed. Seven databases supplied randomized trials through January 2025 for a guided review.

Dexmedetomidine raised the odds of low blood pressure and slow heart rate compared with propofol, while lowering heart rate overall. Patients on it needed fewer pressure-raising rescue drugs. Fast rhythm problems, bleeding, and a common irregular rhythm showed no clear difference. Clinicians gain a clear trade-off profile for drug choice.
pmc-13536198:
Ruijiao Sun and colleagues modeled how infection load and its uneven spread shape disease in hosts. Published in 2026, the math-based study built math models letting germ load patterns evolve through within- and between-host workings. Most hosts carry light loads while a few carry heavy ones, a pattern called clumping, well studied in large pests but rarely in small germs.

Applied to the amphibian chytrid fungus, a global frog threat, the models showed stronger death that rises with load and faster within-host copying both cut clumping. That cut in turn eased host numbers held down and leveled harm-versus-spread trade-offs, shifting peak spread toward faster copying. The authors argue that similar load workings govern small germs and large pests alike. Readers get a shared model set for disease math across scales.
pmc-13536698:
Sajjad Soofi and co-authors report a 2026 validation of a Persian short scale for measuring stress when patients move from intensive care to a general ward. Statistical checks examined consistency, grouping of items, and fit to the expected structure.

Analysis supported three groups of items that together explained a large share of responses. Fit measures reached accepted levels, and overall consistency was good. The authors conclude that the Persian short form is valid and reliable for Iranian intensive care patients. They recommend its use to guide nursing care that involves families and eases the transfer step.
pmc-13538398:
Jarmon G Lees and colleagues model heart disease in Friedreich ataxia using stem cells in a 2026 study. Patient heart cells beat abnormally with slow tightening and relaxing, swelled in size, mishandled calcium, and showed more stress, splitting power units, and cell death. Added iron worsened the flaws. Gene scans flagged two consistently disturbed genes, and silencing either cut cell death without restoring frataxin. One silencing also calmed stress signals. The authors nominate both genes as early markers and drug leads.
pmc-13538498:
Hyun Woo Jung and colleagues study opposition to neighborhood mental health welfare centers in South Korea in a 2026 multilevel analysis.
