Data combined a 2022 national perception survey with regional statistics in a layered statistical model. Both personal traits and neighborhood conditions were tested as drivers of not-in-my-backyard attitudes.

Older housing shares tracked with stronger opposition, while higher local mortality tracked with weaker opposition. Personally, older age, poor physical health, negative views of mental illness, and seeing center advertisements tracked with stronger opposition. Web information and personal recommendations tracked the other way. The authors urge tailored, trust-based outreach shaped to local context over generic campaigns.
pmc-13538598:
Shahina Pardhan and colleagues examine vision impairment certification patterns across Mid and South Essex in England in a 2026 public data analysis. Certification counts guide service planning, yet local drivers stay murky. Public and board data covered certificates over two years across five sub-areas, set against deprivation shares, eye clinic density, and older population size. Rank correlations probed each pairing.

Certificates rose over the period, with age-related macular degeneration the leading cause. Rates varied widely across sub-areas, the highest zones carrying roughly two and a half times the lowest. The pace of certificate growth tracked deprivation strongly. Links with clinic density and older population share ran moderate. The authors urge targeting support toward deprived and aging areas to cut blindness risk.
pmc-13539798:
Mohammed Saleh Alfawaz and seven colleagues report a 2026 mouse study of astaxanthin, a red pigment from algae with strong antioxidant action, packed into tiny chitosan particles. They tested it against Ehrlich ascites carcinoma, a fast-growing tumor model that also damages the liver and kidneys.

Ninety female mice were split into six groups, some healthy and some carrying the tumor, with plain astaxanthin compared against the particle form. The particle version slowed tumor growth more, lifted survival, restored antioxidant defenses, and lowered inflammatory signals. Tissue slides showed less injury to liver and kidney. The team reads the results as evidence that the packaging improves a poorly absorbed compound.
pmc-13540898:
Omid Mirmosayyeb and colleagues study mood illness in a 2026 survey. They asked how often bipolar disorder appears in two diseases. Both diseases strip insulation from nerves in the brain and spine. One is multiple sclerosis. The other is neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder. Mood disorders are known in the first disease, yet cross-disease data were thin.

Structured interviews covered 4,460 people with sclerosis. They also covered 299 people with the second disease. About three percent had bipolar disorder overall. Rates peaked in secondary progressive sclerosis. Greater disability raised the odds. So did being single, addiction, smoking, and early cerebellar symptoms.
pmc-13541998:
Narges Shakerian and four colleagues examine, in a 2026 gait study, how body mass index shapes the step-to-step variability of walking, and whether age changes that influence. Heavier bodies force walking adjustments, yet most work measured only how large the fluctuations are, not how they pattern over time.

Stride data from 117 young, middle-aged, and older adults in a public dataset were analysed. Higher body mass predicted larger variability in both stride timing and stride length at every age. The temporal pattern told a different story: for stride length, higher mass predicted a less persistent pattern only in older adults. The authors suggest gait checks in ageing should weigh both dimensions.
pmc-13544298:
Raveena Khanna, Justin Morency, and Cheri Frey published a 2026 case series on clearing bruises, called ecchymoses, in patients with skin of colour using a 650-microsecond, 1064-nanometre Nd:YAG laser. Lasers that target blood pigment can misfire on melanin-rich skin and leave discoloration, while this longer wavelength with an unusually short pulse has a safer record in darker skin. Three women, of Fitzpatrick types III, IV, and VI, were treated for bruises on the upper arm, chin, and elbow crease.

Each received a single session at set fluence, in two cross-hatched passes, after simple alcohol cleansing, with photographs taken before treatment and again two days later for judging change. Bruising is a frequent cosmetic complaint after injuries and procedures, and options proven safe on darker skin are scarce. The series adds early clinical experience with a device intended to close that gap.
pmc-13546598:
Junze Chen and a large team built in 2026 a gene-based risk score for liver cancer. The score centers on TRPM4, a gene tied to a recently described form of cell death driven by sodium overload. Starting from nearly 300 genes that move together with TRPM4 in tumor data, they distilled an eleven-gene signature and tested it in two patient cohorts totaling more than 500 people.

Patients the signature rated high risk survived for much shorter times and showed a more immune-suppressed tumor environment. Combining the score with mutation burden sharpened the split, from a median survival near 15 months in the worst group to close to 69 months in the best. Single-cell data pointed to support cells and macrophages as main contributors to the score.
pmc-13547398:
Mahtab Diba and Hossein Naeimi built in 2026 a magnetic, hollow nanocatalyst designed to be fished out of a reaction and reused. They put it to work making bisphenol compounds valued for antioxidant and anti-inflammatory uses. The catalyst pairs a three-metal magnetic core with a carbon shell, made by coating the core in silica and later removing that layer. A full battery of imaging and spectroscopy checks confirmed the yolk-shell structure.

With tiny amounts of catalyst, an aldehyde and a dimethylphenol combined under mild conditions to give bisphenol products in excellent yield, verified by melting point and magnetic resonance spectra. The authors list the practical advantages: simple handling, safety, easy purification, and low catalyst use.
pmc-13548598:
Ning Zhu, Junjie Bi, and Guoxin Tong search gene activity data for diagnostic markers of atherosclerosis tied to the growth of new lymph vessels, in a 2026 computational study. Hardening of the arteries is often caught late, and lymph vessel growth shapes how plaques develop and inflame. The team combined three machine learning screens over public expression datasets to narrow a family of lymphangiogenesis-related genes down to a diagnostic panel.

Three genes survived the screens and anchored a scoring chart that separated patients from controls well in both training and validation data. Each gene connected to immune processes, and diseased tissue showed heavier infiltration by killer T cells, natural killer cells, and neutrophils. Two plant compounds, butein and pimaric acid, surfaced as possible drugs against these targets. Patient samples also split into three molecular subtypes with distinct immune characters.
pmc-13550498:
Phanuwit Paitoon and colleagues spin plastic fibers coated with a Y-chromosome-targeting antibody fragment to sort cattle sperm by sex, in a 2026 proof-of-concept study. Dairy farmers want heifer calves and beef producers want males, and the standard sorting machine is costly. Their mat of electrospun polylactic acid fibers carries an engineered antibody that grabs only Y-bearing sperm, letting the X-bearing fraction flow past.

Trials tuned the fiber recipe, settling on a mat spun from an eight percent solution, and a battery of imaging and chemical tests confirmed the antibody stayed attached after coupling. Packed into a syringe, the mat enriched the flow-through fraction to about seventy-one percent X-sperm and the captured, released fraction to about seventy-six percent Y-sperm. The authors present the biodegradable platform as a cheaper sorting route worth optimizing.
pmc-13551198:
Paul Linsley and John Hurley published a 2026 paper on feelings in clinical supervision for mental health nurses. Supervision backs staff well-being and safe care. Yet few models explain the feelings inside the supervisory bond. The authors join two older models. One sorts ego states, the inner roles people slip into. The other lists three jobs of supervision: support, learning, and standards.

The ego roles are caregiving, caregetting, and standing apart as one's own person. Read together, the models show how trust, need, and growth play out in sessions. The pair say the joined frame can deepen reflection. It may also help services keep skilled nurses and guard their well-being.
pmc-13551498:
Po-Yu Liang, with four colleagues, published a 2026 study building heart organoids whose blood vessel cell share can be dialed up or down. Organoids are tiny lab-grown tissue models, and heart versions need the right mix of muscle and endothelial cells, which line vessels. The team edited human pluripotent stem cells so a gene called SOX17 could be switched on, steering cells toward endothelial identity.

The resulting organoids showed heart-like structure and controllable composition. A chemotherapy drug, doxorubicin, reduced their viability and beating, matching known heart toxicity, while freezing injury mimicked a heart attack and a common drug softened the damage. Another drug raised calcium signals as expected, supporting the model for disease and drug testing.
pmc-13551698:
Ekrem Cakar, leading six colleagues, published a 2026 study proposing a simple index for hidden diaphragm injury after stab wounds to the left chest-abdomen border. Such injuries can stay silent, then allow organs to herniate dangerously. The retrospective study covered 67 adults with single-entry wounds who had surgical exploration between 2010 and 2025, measuring wound-to-diaphragm distance and diaphragm area on CT scans.

Diaphragm injury was confirmed during surgery in about a third of patients. Distance alone did not predict injury significantly, while diaphragm area and the combined index reached significance with only modest discrimination in the reported analysis. Comparing the two showed area drove the index's performance, so the authors present the measure as exploratory rather than decisive.
pmc-13551798:
Jun Wang, Chao Tang, and Zhijie Xie published a 2026 study of a stress blood sugar measure and short-term death risk after spontaneous brain hemorrhage. The stress hyperglycemia ratio compares admission glucose with long-term average sugar, and its value in this stroke type was unclear. Using a large intensive care database, the team analyzed 815 patients grouped in thirds by the ratio, with 28-day mortality as the main outcome.

Survival curves separated the groups clearly, and modeling showed higher ratios tied to higher death risk in a nonlinear pattern in the reported analysis. The link held across patient subgroups, and machine learning models were built to show the measure's predictive contribution. Mean age was near seventy, and just over half the patients were male.
pmc-13554198:
Joshy Jesline and three colleagues study how teens in India felt about their own feelings during COVID stress in a 2026 survey. The work covers 508 high school students aged fourteen to seventeen in Karnataka and Kerala. Three scales measured pandemic stress, distress around the event, and negative meta-emotions, meaning harsh feelings about one's own feelings. Such self-judgement can deepen distress after large crises.

Higher pandemic stress came with stronger distress and more negative meta-emotions. Those harsh self-feelings in turn tied to greater distress as well. The link from stress to distress ran partly through meta-emotions, a path the tests confirmed. The authors urge programmes that teach teens to notice their feelings kindly and steer them with skill.
pmc-13554698:
Kong proposes Lifestyle Medicine 3.0 in this 2026 essay as a new stage for his field. He argues that lifestyle medicine should move beyond preventing and treating disease toward optimizing human health across the whole lifespan.

Kong traces the field's arc. A first phase centered on preventing disease through habits like quitting smoking and exercising, then a second matured into evidence-based clinical practice with defined competencies and multidisciplinary teams. The proposed third phase responds to artificial intelligence, wearables, precision health, and population aging by making interventions more personalized, continuous, and equitable. He cautions that precision must not shrink to genomics or gadgets, insisting the approach stay holistic and person-centered. The framework is offered explicitly as a proposal, not an established classification, for debate about medicine's ultimate goal.
pmc-13555998:
C. Quilliam and eleven colleagues set out in 2026 to define what makes a rural health student placement genuinely good in Australia. Rural communities face uneven access to care, partly because health workers cluster in cities, and student placements are one way to build a rural workforce. Earlier work leaned on stand-ins such as student satisfaction, so the team asked placement staff what quality really consists of.

Eighty-six people across ten cases took part, building mind maps in workshops and refining them in focus groups. Cross-case work produced nine constructs that shape placement quality, starting with placement planning, student selection, and communication among stakeholders. The framework gives universities and health services a shared language for designing placements that serve students and rural communities alike.
pmc-13557798:
Tetsuro Kamiya and three colleagues test a FOXO1-selective inhibitor in triple-negative breast cancer cells. Triple-negative breast cancer is aggressive with few treatment options. FOXO1, a forkhead factor, plays unclear roles in this cancer. Their 2026 study tests AS1842856 on the human cell line MDA-MB-231 and traces its molecular effects.

AS1842856 suppressed cell growth as dose rose and lowered LOXL4 expression. Yet FOXO1 knockdown alone did not lower LOXL4, pointing to a FOXO1-independent route. The team links the LOXL4 drop to ERK activation and reactive oxygen species. Combining ERK pathway blockade with AS1842856 also suppressed cell migration, pointing to the ERK-LOXL4 axis as a treatment target.
pmc-13558698:
Pu Wang and three colleagues present Hip-35, a hip X-ray dataset for orthopedic problems. Scarce labeled data hinders reliable AI for hip joint diagnosis. Their 2026 paper offers 35,000 curated synthetic images in 35 pathology groups plus 76 expert-labeled clinical exams. Its key innovation is a three-stage quality frame for anatomical truth and clinical relevance.

Stage one spots color artifacts via channel thresholding with edge masking. Stage two deblurs with fusion guided by Manhattan distance, cosine similarity, and SSIM. Stage three dedupes via anatomical hashing with U-Net region signatures and temporal checks. Radiologists accepted 92 percent blinded. The public dataset and toolkit set a benchmark for medical images.
pmc-13561598:
Liu and colleagues build a model to judge whether thyroid nodules are cancerous without surgery, in 2026 medical imaging research. The study enrolled 147 patients whose nodules fell into the uncertain C-TIRADS 4a or 4b ultrasound categories. Radiomics, the mining of numeric patterns from images, captured features inside each nodule and in the ring of tissue around it. Three machine learning methods combined those features with clinical signs to estimate cancer risk.

Analysis identified microcalcification, a taller-than-wide shape, and irregular outline as independent predictors of cancer. The joint clinical-radiomics model using logistic regression performed best, reaching an accuracy score, measured as area under the curve, of 0.866. Its accuracy was 84.4 percent, with sensitivity of 91.3 percent and specificity of 77.3 percent in those cases. Features from the tissue around the nodule contributed most.
pmc-13562198:
Jenna Cross and colleagues measure what the guideline-recommended one-year surveillance colonoscopy actually finds after curative colorectal cancer surgery. Their 2026 retrospective study reviews 454 patients resected in Winnipeg between January 2007 and June 2020 whose first check fell within the accepted window. Findings were classed as cancer, advanced adenoma, simple adenoma, or normal.

The harvest was thin. Two patients, 0.44 percent of the group, harbored a new or missed cancer, and three more had advanced adenomas in the reported counts. Simple adenomas appeared in about one in five patients, while nearly eighty percent of examinations were entirely normal. Neither cancer case had been flagged by tumor marker blood tests or imaging beforehand. Missing records of the original examination quality limited judgment about whether lesions were new or overlooked. The authors present the low yield as real-world descriptive evidence.
pmc-13562498:
Andrina Sophia Frank and three colleagues test how well six cleaning methods restore zirconia dental implant surfaces after contamination. Zirconia, a white ceramic, suits visible implants, but saliva or metal particles picked up during handling can spoil how the surface bonds with bone. The 2026 study prepared 90 specimens, left some clean, and fouled others with saliva or metal. Each group then faced one of six protocols, from autoclave steam to an ultrasonic bath, ethanol, chlorhexidine, or hydrogen peroxide.

Both the dirt type and the cleaning method changed how water spread on the surface and what elements remained, measured by X-ray analysis. Chlorhexidine restored the surface best across all conditions. Ethanol and steam also did well, and ultrasound cleared metal debris best through its scrubbing action. Hydrogen peroxide gave uneven results. The authors say cleaner choice should match the contaminant, since peroxide alone may leave a surface unfit.
pmc-13563898:
Zhehan Zheng and five colleagues review how chemical tags on DNA and its packaging proteins reprogram neutrophils during sepsis, turning defenders into sources of damage. In sepsis the body's infection response destroys organs. Neutrophils arrive altered: made in haste, long-lived, poor at migrating, prone to dumping inflammatory signals, and casting traps that snare microbes yet clot vessels and shred tissue. The 2026 review gathers evidence across four layers: DNA methylation, histone modification, non-coding RNAs, and RNA modification.

The same tag can help or harm depending on timing, tissue, and disease stage, a repeated warning. Cohort findings are weighed separately from animal and dish experiments, where the biology looks cleaner than the clinic. Payoffs include fingerprints that flag patients tipping into immune paralysis, and drugs that retune the tags. Timing is the crux: blunting inflammation too early could disarm the defence keeping the infection in check.
pmc-13566398:
Sabina A. Guler and co-authors weigh, in a 2026 review, the benefits and burdens of oxygen therapy for interstitial lung disease, a group of conditions that scar the lungs and lower blood oxygen. Evidence covers home oxygen, portable oxygen during activity, and high-flow oxygen during acute illness.

Observational work hints that home oxygen may cut flare-ups and hospital stays for patients expected to live beyond a year, and portable oxygen helps symptoms for some. Newer portable concentrators, though, may not raise daily oxygen levels or activity as hoped. The authors urge shared decisions that weigh relief against the weight, noise, and limits that oxygen equipment imposes on daily life.
pmc-13571798:
Kristina Nimchenko and co-authors describe, in a 2026 prenatal case, a new variant in the HECW2 gene found in a fetus with severe heart disease. The gene was known mainly for developmental brain disorders, with little tying it to the heart. The parents were healthy and unrelated, and this was their sixth pregnancy.

Scans at twenty-one weeks showed a widened right ventricle and a narrowed lung artery. Later imaging found the right ventricle weakening and, by thirty-three weeks, fluid build-up across the fetus with a slow, irregular heartbeat near one hundred beats a minute. The fetus died a week later. The case strengthens the gene's rare heart picture and argues for heart scans and genetic screening in similar pregnancies.
pmc-13572398:
Amane Sugii and Yoshihiro Hiramatsu present a 2026 method for pinning down slow quakes called tectonic tremor from a single seismic station. Tremor lacks the sharp starts of normal quakes, so locating it has long needed many stations. The work asks how much place data one station's full wave record holds.

Their tool, TremorViT, reads three-part wave records with a vision transformer, a model built for images, and also reports how unsure it is. On the Nankai zone in Japan, one station gave a mean place error of 4.8 kilometres. Pooling calls from several stations cut the error to 2.5 kilometres. The tool placed 68,101 events from January to September 2016, far more than older lists held. The pattern in space and time still matched known tremor behaviour.
pmc-13573598:
Jingyuan Liu, with three colleagues, describes a 2026 study of rising loneliness among older Chinese Americans in one affordable housing community. Loneliness harms health in later life, and immigrant elders face added strain. The team surveyed the same housing complex in 2012 and again in 2025 to see how loneliness moved.

The two rounds covered 120 and 118 residents. Mean loneliness scores rose from just under four to just over five on the scale used, a clear jump. A split method traced most of the rise to weaker social support and to residents having fewer children. Less physical contact with children and trouble with mobile devices tracked the support drop. Health and function did not drive the change. The authors urge peer ties and digital help over health-only fixes.
pmc-13574898:
Desalegn Abebaw leads a twelve-author narrative review, published in 2026, on gut microbes and bowel cancer immunotherapy. Drugs that release the brakes on immune cells help only a minority of colorectal cancer cases, mainly tumours with faulty DNA repair. The review asks whether the gut microbiome helps explain who responds.

The authors gather work linking certain gut bacteria to stronger anti-tumour immune responses, while imbalance in the gut can blunt drug effects. Options covered include probiotics, stool transplants, diet change, and traditional medicines. Early work suggests these steps may restore immune function and slow tumour growth. The review also flags uneven findings and infection risks, and calls for firm trials before routine use.
pmc-13578098:
Nari Yoo studies how often immigrant adults in California are asked for citizenship documents when seeking care or schooling, and whether those requests drive people away from care, in a 2026 paper. The data pool four waves of a state health survey from 2019 to 2022, covering 21,133 foreign-born adults. Such requests are a suspected trigger of the chilling effect that keeps eligible immigrants from services.

Overall, 15.7 percent reported being asked for proof of citizenship or a Social Security number. Noncitizens faced a likelihood 5.3 percentage points higher of being asked than naturalised citizens, and adults with limited English 5.8 points more likely in the adjusted figures. Being asked linked to a 6.1 point rise in delaying or skipping care, with no link to lacking a regular care source. Yoo notes the design cannot prove the requests caused the forgone care.
pmc-13578698:
Renu Kiran Shastri and colleagues fine tune a spark based cutting method for shaping titanium parts used in medicine, in a 2026 study. The alloy is strong and rust proof, yet its hardness defeats normal drills and mills. Reverse spark machining carves pillar arrays into the metal with no tool contact, using three electrode metals for comparison.

Six settings were varied in a planned grid of runs, from pulse length to flushing pressure. The team scored surface roughness, hardness, damaged layer depth, and crack counts under a microscope. A ranking method merged the scores, and a firefly inspired search found the best blend of settings. A confirmation run at those settings improved results by about seven percent over the starting point, giving shops a tested recipe.
pmc-13579798:
Yue Li and colleagues review how worn out T cells shape the fate of stem cell transplants for blood cancers, in a 2026 paper. T cells pushed too long by cancer or infection slide into exhaustion, marked by brake proteins on their surface and fading killing power. After a transplant, that wear can blunt the graft's attack on leftover leukemia and weaken defense against viruses.

The review walks through the signs of exhaustion, how transplant T cells change over time, and where exhaustion feeds complications such as relapse and graft versus host trouble. Fixes under study range from brake blocking drugs to rested cell products grown outside the body. The authors sort what is proven from what is hoped, giving transplant teams a map of a fast moving field.
pmc-13579898:
Nattaporn Phanthaphol and a large team of co-authors upgrade engineered T cells for colorectal cancer and test them on patient grown tumor balls, in a 2026 study. The cells hunt a surface protein common on these tumors. Solid tumors blunt such cells, partly through a brake protein that tumors wear like a shield. Two cell designs were built, one plain and one that also secretes a tiny brake blocker on site.

Both designs killed tumor balls from the same patient at similar strength when the brake ran low. Only the secreting design kept its punch against brake heavy balls at low cell doses, pouring out attack signals all the while. A fourteen day test bed pairing each patient's tumor balls with their own cells is offered as a fast, personal proving ground for cell therapy.
pmc-13579998:
Nan Guo and Guang-Hua Peng sift programmed cell death genes for causal links to retinitis pigmentosa, an inherited blinding disease, in a 2026 genetic study. The method borrows nature's own randomization: gene variants that nudge a gene's activity serve as stand ins for a trial. Public genome, gene activity, and protein data fed several layers of checks, from two sample tests to tissue wide scans.

Eight death related genes carried sturdy links to the disease, one with odds near triple. Their effects held across tissues and after adjusting for smoking and activity habits, and wide scans found no side trait meddling. In real retina data the genes ran off normal and clustered in immune paths. One support cell type in the retina showed the deepest reshaping, a lead for where damage brews.
pmc-13581898: An editorial in the Canadian Medical Education Journal previews the journal's latest issue. It also flags a linked set of abstracts from a French-language forum on health sciences teaching. One study looks at lifestyle medicine teaching in Canadian medical schools. Another looks at how residents learn to care for patients who have several long-term conditions at once. Other pieces cover assessment form design, a review of a wellbeing scale, and hands-on teaching ideas such as remote simulation for rural trainees.
pmc-13583198:
Jozélio Freire de Carvalho, Cezar Augusto Muniz Caldas, and Yehuda Shoenfeld wrote a 2026 review of vaccines meant to prevent autoimmune disease, where the immune system attacks the body's own tissues. Two broad plans are covered. One aims at germs that can set off such disease, such as the Epstein-Barr virus. The other tries to retrain the immune system so it tolerates the body's own proteins again.

The reviewers gathered 68 studies, split between work in people and work in animals or cells. Shots against trigger germs are the closest to real use, with some already in early human trials. The retraining vaccines show promise in illnesses such as multiple sclerosis, yet proof in patients is still thin, and the authors call the field young overall.
pmc-13585398:
Edward Alan Miller and colleagues link Medicaid payment rates to staffing in nursing homes across the United States in this 2026 study. Medicaid pays for most long-stay nursing home care, and staffing is a core part of care quality. The team pulled payment rates straight from the states and matched them with staff records and facility data for 9,510 stand-alone nursing homes.

Higher payment rates went with higher overall staffing, and with more nurse aides and registered nurses on the floor. Pay showed no steady link with practical nurse levels. The pattern held the same in for-profit, nonprofit, and government homes alike. The authors argue that state payment choices shape the care residents get, and they urge lawmakers to weigh staffing when setting those rates.
pmc-13586498:
Ali Omar Abdelaziz and colleagues gauged Toll-like receptor 9, a germ sensor, in chest lining cancer and in lung cancer spread to the chest. The epithelioid form of chest lining cancer is most common but hard to tell from spread lung cancer by eye. Thirty fresh bits were tested for sensor and growth-marker RNA, and sixty old wax blocks were stained for the sensor.

Sensor levels ran far higher in chest lining cancer than in spread lung cancer, both in RNA and in stains. Staining was strong in 90 percent of chest cancers, against just 15 percent of lung cancers. High sensor levels also went with faster cell growth and shorter life. The sensor looks like a good test to tell the two cancers apart and to rank risk.
pmc-13587398:
Mahir Kapmaz and colleagues study a fungal lung infection in patients without HIV at a Turkish hospital. The fungus, Pneumocystis jirovecii, preys on weakened immune systems, above all in cancer care. Gene testing has made it easier to find yet harder to judge, since a positive test can also mean harmless carriage. Their 2026 study reviewed 235 tested patients from 2020 to 2023 and set strict rules for calling a case true disease.

Fifty-nine patients met those rules. They were older, more often had solid tumors, and more often had recent chemotherapy than the rest, and their scans showed widespread cloudy patches in both lungs. A blood enzyme, LDH, climbed far more in true cases unless it already started high. Four-week deaths reached over a third of cases, and catching a second bacterial infection was the strongest death predictor. The authors stress fast sorting of true disease from carriage.
pmc-13587698:
Harry Aricibasi and colleagues teach a camera system to spot mounting behavior in young boars. Mounting in group pens injures pigs and adds stress, and farms raising intact males, a growing practice, need an early warning. Their pilot study filmed eight boars aged four to five months in two pens of four for one week, cutting the footage into 766 short clips.

Their system first outlines each pig with a segmentation network, then hands the shapes to a classifier that judges mounting or not. Scores depended heavily on how the data were split: judging frame by frame flattered the system, while holding out whole days, the honest test, cut balanced accuracy to about three quarters. The team calls it a workable proof of concept running at five frames per second, needing multi-site trials and animal tracking next.
pmc-13588798:
Manisha Bhutani and Peter M Voorhees argue that side-effect reporting in multiple myeloma trials is stuck in the chemotherapy era. Modern myeloma care uses immune drugs, cell therapies, and combinations given until the disease moves, often to older patients whose cancer itself causes symptoms. Their 2026 review finds errors creeping in at every step, from spotting a side effect to naming it, grading it, and judging whether the drug caused it.

The five-tier blame scale yields inconsistent, thin answers, and grading misses slow-building burdens that wax and wane. Their reform plan cuts blame to two tiers and mandates full baseline checks repeated over time. It folds in patient-reported symptoms specific to myeloma, and sets hard rules for when lab values count. Standardized reporting with AI decision support rounds out the plan. The aim is safety data doctors and regulators can trust.
pmc-13590598:
Prithvi Arunachalam and colleagues found that early amyloid loosens the link between brain wiring and brain action in early Alzheimer's disease. Brain wiring usually guides brain action, but how early amyloid disturbs that match, and whether it harms thinking, was unclear. Their 2026 study studied 460 older adults without dementia from the AMYPAD study, mixing brain-action scans, wiring scans, and amyloid scans.

People with amyloid showed higher wiring unlinking, driven by visual areas. Tracing showed amyloid-linked unlinking came from reduced local grouping, meaning less separate work. Oddly, higher unlinking in visual areas eased amyloid's harmful effect on thinking, hinting at backup. Local gene patterns tied the changes to amyloid handling, immune-cell firing, and junction rewiring. The authors propose the unlinking index as a marker for early trials.
pmc-13591698:
Azad Duman and Murat Alay study, in 2026, adrenal lumps found by chance on scans, and whether mild cortisol output below the usual alarm line still matters. The standard test flags cortisol above a set level after a suppression drug. Their records covered 199 patients seen from 2023 to 2025, split by whether results fell below the low band or in a middle band still deemed normal.

The middle band group had far more high blood pressure and diabetes, plus higher blood sugar and more signs of body wide swelling. The link held after age, sex, lump size, and cholesterol were factored in. Duman and Alay suggest these patients merit closer heart and metabolic watch, pending longer studies.
pmc-13592798:
Rosa Sruthy Pereppadan leads a team asking, in 2026, whether double blood thinner therapy guards against very early decline after certain strokes. Worsening within the first day is common and darkens outlook, yet its ties to drug strategy were murky. Their Swiss center records covered 1,207 adults with strokes not caused by heart clots, admitted between 2014 and 2023. Patients were split by single versus double therapy and by whether artery plaque caused the stroke.

About twenty two percent worsened sharply within a day, more often when plaque was not the cause. After statistical balancing, double therapy pointed toward lower risk in plaque caused strokes but higher risk elsewhere. The second pattern likely reflects sicker patients getting stronger treatment, Pereppadan and the team caution, and they call for prospective trials.
pmc-13594598:
Basu Dev Lamichhane and co-authors examined what makes Nepalese microfinance institutions profitable, using annual report data from ten wholesale and retail lenders. Capital adequacy, the cushion of own funds an institution holds against risk, sat at the center of their panel analysis, alongside size, leverage, growth, and inflation.

Capital adequacy and leverage showed significant links with return on assets, as did institution size, economic growth, and lender type, while no variable significantly explained return on equity. Wholesale lenders turned out to be better capitalized yet less profitable than retail ones, showing that a fat capital cushion does not automatically buy earnings. The authors counsel restraint. Piling up capital past a point seems to drag on returns. Managers should balance safety against efficiency. Strategies that work for retail microfinance may not transfer to the wholesale model.
pmc-13596398:
Orly Alter and co-authors introduce a mathematical framework that fuses several kinds of tumor data at once to find predictors that small, noisy patient cohorts usually hide. Their 2026 paper generalizes earlier algorithms into a multitensor method, borrowing the quantum mechanics ideas of superposition and entanglement to describe how measurements in one data type pin down those in another.

Applied to neuroblastoma, a childhood cancer, the framework discovered two predictors. Each appeared simultaneously in the tumor's genome, the blood's genome, and the tumor's gene activity. Reading any one representation therefore roughly determines the others. Together the two predictors beat the standard single-gene clinical test for accuracy in every representation tested. The authors also interpret the signals in terms of known disease machinery and possible drug targets, arguing that interpretability is the point, not a bonus.
pmc-13597298:
Jin Ren and co-authors applied a new inference method, IBI-DT, to whole-exome data from more than eight thousand UK Biobank participants. They hunted Alzheimer's genes that standard association scans miss. Rare variants and gene interactions were the main targets. Their 2026 analysis screened some 790,000 variants and checked findings in an independent cohort of about fifteen hundred people.

The method flagged 178 significant variants across 173 genes, against sixteen variants in four genes from the conventional scan. Its top hits leaned much more heavily toward rare variants, with cleaner, less redundant patterns. Known Alzheimer's genes appeared alongside new candidates. Genetics models built on its picks predicted disease slightly better. Three variants and four genes replicated across cohorts, two of them found only by the new method. The authors present the approach as a complement that rescues signals the standard scan overlooks.
pmc-13601598:
Matteo Ripa and three colleagues review in 2026 how a newer corneal transplant technique, pre-Descemet endothelial keratoplasty, has developed. The surgery replaces the cornea's diseased inner layer while keeping the rest of the eye's window intact. It blends the optical quality of the thinnest existing graft with easier handling, since an extra support layer, Dua's layer, splints the delicate membrane being transplanted.

Published series show fast visual recovery and clear gains in corrected vision. Cell loss stays acceptable, and detachment and re-bubbling rates, the fix for a loose graft, are reasonable in experienced hands. The technique also uses young and even pediatric donor corneas that other methods waste. New clamps, an air-pump method, full-circle scoring, and microscope-linked imaging have made graft preparation more reliable. Wider adoption should follow, the authors expect, as training programs and eye banks build in the method.
pmc-13602498:
Hüseyin Serçe and two colleagues model in 2026 what makes trainee teachers feel ready for the classroom. Readiness rests not only on subject knowledge but on 21st-century skills like critical thinking, collaboration, and technology literacy, plus confidence in the profession. The team surveyed 401 preservice teachers at two public universities in Konya, Türkiye, then tested the links with structural equation modeling.

Stronger 21st-century skills predicted higher self-efficacy, a strong effect, and warmer attitudes toward teaching, a moderate one. The model explained 34 percent of the variation in self-efficacy and 15 percent in attitudes. Because data came from one point in time, the results show association rather than cause. Even so, building modern competencies in teacher training is a direct route to confidence and commitment, the authors argue. Such skills are psychological resources programs should cultivate on purpose, not extras.
pmc-13612198:
Hyunkyun Ahn, Dongyoon Shin, and Deok-Jin Jang study what long-term inclusive dance means to its dancers. Arts research usually counts outcomes like mood or social connection; this team asked how participation is lived and sustained. Their qualitative case study followed three adults with developmental disabilities who had danced nine to thirteen years with an inclusive company in Seoul. The team interviewed them and their caregivers and watched rehearsals and performances.

Through repeated performance, the dancers met their own bodies as capable. Moving with others, taking public roles, and receiving recognition widened their self-expression and sense of self among other people. Staying was its own negotiation, involving body condition, schedules, transport, caregiving ties, and flexible stages. The authors read inclusive dance as embodied agency built inside relationships, not a program effect readable off a wellbeing scale. Their lens, critical phenomenology, attends to how norms make some bodies visible.
pmc-13615498:
Chenxiang Li and colleagues test in 2026 whether fine-tuned large language models, the text systems behind modern chatbots, can forecast flu-like illness better than standard tools. They built a light training method that adds small embedding and prediction layers to models such as Llama2 and GPT2. Then they tested it on seven weekly flu surveillance datasets. Each set held only about 523 time points.

The tuned language models beat a bench of rivals, from classic statistical models to recent time-series networks, on accuracy and steadiness, above all for long-range forecasts. Even with no tuning, the raw models tracked broad epidemic trends about as well as the classic method. Since the setup needs no cloud transfer of data, it suits health agencies that must keep local data private and work with short records.
pmc-13615698:
Thanakrit Visuthikosol and Wit Viseshsindh compare in 2026 two biopsy routes for finding serious prostate cancer in the same men, asking what each route adds at different blood test levels. One route aims needles using MRI scans fused with ultrasound; the other follows a fixed twelve-core pattern through the rectum. The study covered 376 men with confirmed prostate cancer who had both methods in one session for a suspicious scan area.

Overall cancer detection was much the same for the two routes. The interest lies in the cases one route caught and the other missed, sorted by PSA blood level and by PSA density, which adjusts for gland size. Knowing where each method earns its keep helps doctors decide when targeted sampling suffices and when the full pattern is still worth the extra needles.
pmc-13616198:
Dominik Mundt, Kuo-Hui Chiu, Stefan Schillberg, and Che Julius Ngwa test quinoa and peanut extracts as plant-based stand-ins for the animal proteins used to grow cultured meat. Lab-grown meat needs matrix proteins that help animal cells stick, grow, and mature, yet standard ones like gelatin, collagen, and Matrigel come from animals, undercutting the point of the product. Computer screening flagged seed proteins carrying a three-letter motif that cells use as a grip.

Water extracts from peanut and quinoa seeds were then tried on mouse muscle cells and on immortalised cow muscle stem cells. The team watched whether the cells attached, multiplied, and began turning into muscle. A plant extract that does the matrix job would remove a hidden animal input from cultured meat and cut cost, taking the product closer to its promise of meat without slaughter.
pmc-13616398:
Jian Wu and colleagues show that tiny vesicles from the balloon flower plant, Platycodon grandiflorus, soften gastric cancer cells so the immune system's killer T cells can destroy them. Tumour cells often resist such killing outright. The plant vesicles are rich in fats. They rework the cancer cell's fat mix in two moves. First they weaken a protective antioxidant axis. Then they deliver unsaturated fats that rust the cell from inside, a death process called ferroptosis.

Gene readings showed malignant programs quieting alongside the fat changes. Imaging at fine scale confirmed the cell's outer membrane physically changed as the rusting advanced, growing easier for T cells to breach. A plant-made particle that both primes the cancer cell for death and invites immune attack hints at gentler partners for immunotherapy in stomach cancer.
pmc-13616498:
Pedro Cepas-Guillén and colleagues comment in 2026 on same-day discharge after left atrial appendage closure. This catheter procedure seals a heart pouch to prevent strokes. It serves people with atrial fibrillation who cannot take blood thinners for life. The question is whether such patients can safely go home the same day. Same-day discharge frees beds and spares patients an overnight stay. The piece discusses a national analysis of United States hospital data from 2016 to 2020.

That analysis covered 40,564 such procedures where patients stayed zero or one night. Same-day discharge was still rare at 4.1 percent overall, though it climbed from 1.6 percent in 2016 to 7.7 percent in 2020. The question the authors press is patient selection: prime-time readiness depends on naming which patients can leave early without added risk, not on sending everyone home sooner.
pmc-13617598:
Brenda O'Neill and fifteen colleagues, writing for the CLEAR investigator team, explain how flare-ups were judged by an outside panel in a large bronchiectasis trial. Bronchiectasis trials now use pulmonary exacerbations as their main outcome, so counting them well decides whether treatments look effective. The team applied modified EMBARC consensus criteria, requiring at least three symptoms lasting two days plus an antibiotic prescription, using a structured symptom form.

Sites reported four hundred sixty-two exacerbations from two hundred three patients. The independent panel, judging blind and then reaching agreement, classed only about half as fully qualifying under the criteria. A small share were partially qualifying, and over forty percent were not qualifying, despite antibiotics being prescribed. A sensitivity check with older Fuchs criteria matched the main trial results. The authors say careful symptom capture and outside judging are essential for trustworthy trial outcomes.
pmc-13617698:
Zhenyi Xu and six colleagues report a 2026 study of acetylshikonin, a red naphthoquinone compound from the plant Lithospermum erythrorhizon. Its target is Candida albicans, a yeast that causes everything from thrush to deadly bloodstream infections and increasingly resists standard drugs. The team measured killing power in dishes, then tested the compound in mouse models of vaginal and mouth candidiasis.

Acetylshikonin proved active against drug-resistant strains in the laboratory and in the animals. It weakened the yeast's grip on surfaces, damaged its cell membrane and wall, and pushed cells toward an apoptosis-like death. The compound appears to bind and switch down an enzyme called malate synthase 1, choking a metabolic cycle the yeast needs, which unleashes reactive oxygen species that damage DNA. The authors propose the compound as a candidate worth developing for resistant fungal infections.
pmc-13617898:
Tewarit Somkotra and three colleagues report a 2026 analysis of inequality in dental care use among older adults in Thailand, despite the country's near-universal health coverage. They drew on the national Health and Welfare Surveys of 2009, 2015, and 2021, covering fifty-three thousand eight hundred twenty-five adults aged sixty and over. Dental use in the past year was modeled against wealth, education, region, and insurance scheme.

Use fell over the period, from about nine percent in 2009 to about seven percent in 2021. The richest quarter had roughly two and a half times the odds of using care as the poorest. Adults with university-level education had about six times the odds of those with no schooling. Northeastern residents lagged far behind Bangkok, and civil servant scheme members used care at twice the odds of universal scheme members. The authors say coverage alone cannot deliver equity without tackling structural and geographic barriers.
pmc-13619098:
Khaleel Ahmad and six colleagues develop a branch of fixed point theory, the part of mathematics that proves certain equations have a stable solution. They define two new classes of paired mappings in ordered spaces and prove that each class has exactly one coupled fixed point. Their proofs also show that a standard averaging method moves steadily toward that point.

A central trick reduces each paired problem to an ordinary single-variable problem on a combined space, so older theory applies directly. The team then tests the results on a coupled Volterra integral system and on a fractional-order chaotic model of the Thomas attractor. Computer checks matched a period-doubling route to chaos, and the authors note their key condition is sharper than one stated in earlier work.
pmc-13620198:
Jiayi Jiang and five colleagues report real-world results for a color-guided laser routine against the red marks acne leaves behind. Their single-center study screened 147 patients and treated 136 with three sessions spaced four weeks apart. Each visit paired a gentle full-face pass at one wavelength with targeted work: a green-light laser for pink-red marks and a deeper infrared laser for violet ones.

Median redness scores and the share of skin covered by red marks both fell sharply by the end of treatment. Every patient improved at least modestly on the investigator's global scale, and satisfaction ran very high with mild pain. Side effects were mostly brief flushing, with one small blister case and no lasting pigment change or scarring. Scores held steady six months later. The authors call for prospective controlled trials to confirm the routine.
pmc-13620398:
Yoshikazu Ikoma and ten colleagues report two older men whose bulky neck lymphoma threatened to close their airways before treatment could start. Both had diffuse large B-cell lymphoma swelling in the neck, with marked narrowing seen on scope and scan checks. Rather than rushing into radiation or chemotherapy, the team chose a planned tracheostomy first, opening the windpipe below the blockage under controlled conditions.

With breathing secured, doctors confirmed the diagnosis and started full-dose combination therapy about two weeks later in one man and ten days later in the other, with no cuts or delays. Neither patient suffered complications from the tracheostomy. Both finished the planned drug cycles. One later needed extra therapy and cell treatment before clearing the disease fully, while the other stayed under close watch after leftover scan signals proved harmless. The authors argue a planned airway buys calm time for everything else.
pmc-13621598:
Anja Simmet, Janine Ehret, Nana Ama Frimpomaa Agyapong, and Nanette Stroebele-Benschop asked German parents how they use the label formats competing for attention on food packs. The color-coded Nutri-Score grades foods at a glance, the nutrition panel lists numbers, and the ingredients list names contents. Their online survey reached 978 parents who handle most household shopping and live with children.

Large majorities said they understood each format, and around seven in ten reported using each one. Believing healthy eating works went with more understanding and more use, while feeling swamped by nutrition information pushed both down. Men lagged women on the panel and the ingredients list. Plain lack of interest topped the reasons for ignoring labels. Parents rated the Nutri-Score easiest, yet felt they grasped the panel's information better. The authors suggest future label campaigns work on overload and disinterest rather than basic comprehension.
pmc-13623098:
Yu Xiao and colleagues compare treatments for HER2-positive breast cancer that has spread and been treated with trastuzumab-based therapy. Several targeted options exist, and they differ in benefit and harm. The study focuses on one drug pair, trastuzumab deruxtecan, known as T-DXd, and weighs it against the other regimens.

The team combined sixteen reports from seven randomised trial families, covering 3,339 patients, in a network analysis that lets drugs be compared without head-to-head trials. T-DXd came out ahead on tumour shrinkage and showed a favourable survival profile in the networks. One older drug pair lagged well behind on both measures. The balance was not one-sided: T-DXd raised the odds of lung inflammation compared with its closest rival, and its survival ranking could not be tested in some narrower networks. The authors urge care when reading indirect comparisons built on sparse safety data.
pmc-13623298:
Bianca Brandão da Silva, Maria Giovana Borges Saidel, and Maria Helena de Melo Lima explore how people with diabetes make sense of mental healthcare after an amputation. Losing part of a limb to diabetes brings grief, stigma, and lost independence on top of a demanding illness. The study, set in a high-complexity hospital in Brazil, asked patients what mental healthcare means.

Ten patients in follow-up care took part through observation, interviews, and field notes, and the team sorted their accounts into themes. Three themes emerged: the invisible burden of living with diabetes, the ruptures the amputation caused and the meanings patients built afterward, and the value they placed on mental healthcare. Patients singled out the nursing team as central to feeling heard, learning about their condition, and rebuilding a life. The authors argue mental healthcare in this setting is relational work woven into clinical care.
pmc-13623498:
Scarlett R Howard and Kit S Prendergast review what lies ahead for Australia's native bees under human pressure. Australia's isolation has stocked it with more than two thousand native bee species, most found nowhere else, yet basic facts about their lives, ranges, and numbers remain thin. Bees rank among the world's most important pollinators, so the knowledge gap carries economic as well as ecological weight.

The review weighs threats from land clearing, farming, city growth, pesticides, introduced plants and animals, changed fire patterns, pollution, and climate change. Australian native bees are undervalued in farm economics, the authors note, though work on their crop pollination value is growing. Their proposed framework calls for long-term monitoring across species, places, and seasons, and for deeper use of public community science records. They argue the same framework could guide bee protection worldwide, with Australia as a proving ground.
pmc-13627198:
Konstantin Warneke and colleagues introduce an R software package that asks a blunt question of behavioral testing: how much practice is enough before a measurement settles? Test-retest studies lean on correlation scores that hide exactly the warm-up drift that matters for one person. The classic Bland and Altman agreement method, meanwhile, reports limits with no tie to what a clinician would actually accept as close enough.

Their tool lets researchers set content-based limits of acceptance ahead of time, then judges whether repeated scores have steadied within those limits and sizes each source of error. The package wraps the full evaluation into one workflow for psychology and cognitive research. Better reporting of habituation, the authors argue, would stop warm-up effects from masquerading as treatment effects.
pmc-13630098:
Malcolm A. West and fourteen colleagues present the protocol for REMACS, a British observational study of life after extended margin surgery for advanced pelvic cancers. The operation can cure, yet it leaves an empty pelvis prone to collections, abscesses, fistulae, and wound breakdown, a burden affecting over half of patients and known as empty pelvis syndrome.

The multicentre cohort will follow 236 patients who receive perineal reconstruction with tissue flaps or biological meshes. Questionnaires on quality of life, decision regret, and personal costs run before surgery and across the first year, alongside complication records and health economic measures. Thirty purposively chosen patients will also be interviewed, to surface hidden toxicities and guide honest consent conversations.
pmc-13631798:
Veronica Ahlund and three colleagues published this 2026 follow-up study of a nose operation done with radiofrequency energy. The procedure shrinks swollen tissue inside the nose, called the inferior turbinate, to ease blocked breathing. One hundred ninety-eight adults who had the operation filled in a standard symptom questionnaire before surgery and again five to seven years later.

Overall symptom scores improved clearly over that long period. Gains were strongest for nose-related complaints and for sleep. Yet two problems reported before surgery pointed to a weaker result. People who started with thick nasal discharge or poor sleep quality were more likely to stay blocked afterward. The authors suggest the questionnaire can flag patients who may need extra care or different treatment, possibly because other conditions drive their symptoms.
pmc-13633098:
Juan Han led a 2026 study of how fourteen days of extremely low light boosts shoot regeneration in black locust, Robinia pseudoacacia, a woody plant prized for propagation work. Low light is already used to improve regeneration, but the molecular chain behind it was unclear. The team exposed several genotypes to extremely low light and tracked gene activity, hormone levels, and regeneration, then tested candidate genes by overexpression.

Auxin production, transport, and signaling emerged as the core activated pathways, and blocking auxin production or transport largely erased the low-light benefit. A light-sensing protein, RpPHYA, coordinated the response. It raised auxin production through RpAMI1 and steered auxin transport through RpPIN1 by both direct gene control and DNA demethylation. A rival protein, RpHYH, opposed the program under normal light. Overexpressing each key gene boosted regeneration. Plant biotechnologists get a mechanistic lever for improving woody plant propagation.
pmc-13637298:
Thomas Jideofor Ogbu and two colleagues published this 2026 study asking whether the kind of war matters for child hunger in Africa. Armed conflict drives acute malnutrition in young children, yet planners rarely separate state-based wars from fights between non-state groups. The team linked small nutrition surveys from eleven conflict-affected populations, gathered between 1999 and 2015, with a standard conflict database. A Bayesian model compared the two conflict types while holding other factors steady.

Acute malnutrition ran far higher under non-state conflict. Both the general and severe forms struck children at much greater rates than under state-based war. Military spending and dry spells worsened hunger mainly in state-based settings. Foreign aid softened general malnutrition under both types and cut severe malnutrition most where non-state groups fought. The authors argue humanitarian money should follow conflict type, not just conflict presence, when it targets child nutrition.
pmc-13638798:
Lucy A Bartho and nine colleagues report an exploratory cohort study of blood proteins during pregnancy and later health risk. Pregnancies affected by poor fetal growth or preeclampsia, a dangerous blood pressure condition, are linked with higher rates of chronic disease in mothers years later.

The team applied protein signature tests, built earlier in non-pregnant adults, to blood taken at thirty-six weeks from cohorts in Melbourne and Cambridge. Women who later had growth-restricted babies showed signatures tied to weaker heart function, more body fat, and higher dementia risk. The authors say long follow-up studies must confirm whether the signatures truly predict illness.
pmc-13639498:
Fei Zhang and three colleagues wrote a 2026 commentary on the new Asian consensus for diagnosing sarcopenia, the loss of muscle mass and strength with age. The 2025 update from the Asian Working Group lets doctors diagnose the condition when low muscle mass and low strength appear together.

The authors welcome the simpler rule for busy clinics across Asia, yet they ask how it fits the global push for one shared definition. Earlier frameworks mixed mass, strength, and physical performance in different ways. The piece argues that harmonized criteria would help clinicians and researchers compare results across countries.
pmc-13639698:
Sogame and colleagues used a large Japanese insurance claims database in 2026 to ask whether dementia worsens survival for lung cancer patients on targeted pill therapy. The drugs, called EGFR inhibitors, are standard first treatment for a common gene-driven lung cancer, but they demand steady self-management at home. Memory and thinking problems could undermine that routine.

More than thirteen thousand patients who started the drugs between 2018 and 2024 were tracked for three-year survival. About two in a hundred had dementia recorded before treatment. That group died at a rate about a third higher than others, even after adjusting for age, health, and daily function. Among patients with dementia, those who could still manage daily life fully fared better. The authors say dementia marks a group needing close attention at treatment start.
pmc-13642898:
Joshua Strong and eight colleagues present a 2026 scoping review of human collaboration with artificial intelligence in healthcare. As AI enters clinical pathways, how people and systems should work together has become a practical and policy question.

From 17,463 records published between 2015 and late 2025, the review kept 140 empirical studies. Most concerned diagnostic reading, and most reported that mixed teams did better than either side alone. Benefits hinged on task fit, workflow design, training, and well-judged trust. Success was usually measured on short task metrics, and ethics questions were discussed more than tested, which the authors flag as a gap.
pmc-13642998:
Mitsuaki Sawano and nine colleagues present a 2026 review of the PREVENT risk equations and their fit for cardiovascular prevention in East Asia. Older Western risk scores often overestimate danger in East Asian groups, while the American Heart Association's 2025 PREVENT set promises a broader kidney-metabolic view.

The review traces risk prediction history, explains what PREVENT adds, and gathers early validation work from Korea and China suggesting reasonable transport. Evidence from Japan remains thin, and heart failure prediction plus data infrastructure pose challenges. The authors call for local validation and recalibration before routine adoption in the region.
pmc-13645698:
Ruifang Liu and three colleagues link gut microbes to the syndrome patterns used in traditional Chinese medicine for type 2 diabetes. Modern diabetes often shows obesity rather than the wasting described in older texts, which strains the old symptom-based sorting. The team enrolled 154 people across three stages, from prediabetes to diabetes with complications. Stool gene sequencing, syndrome scoring, and machine learning were combined.

Genetic analysis first flagged microbe groups that may play a causal role in diabetes among East Asian populations. Learning models then ranked which microbes mattered most for each syndrome element, and the rankings shifted by disease stage. A fecal transplant check in thirty-four patients partly matched the model's top features. The authors call the study a proof of concept for giving traditional syndrome sorting a measurable biological base.
pmc-13649398:
Yating Lu and eight colleagues searched for a dose range that keeps a key antibiotic both strong and safe in lung infections caught in hospital. The drug, tigecycline, fights germs that resist many other drugs, but high doses can harm blood clotting. The team reviewed 100 patients given standard or high doses.

The high-dose group cleared germs and fared better on most measures of drug action. Yet low platelet counts were more common in that group too. One combined score of drug exposure predicted both good results and clotting harm. The authors propose a narrow target range for that score. They stress it is a first guess from past records, not a firm rule.
pmc-13649698:
Yeong-Il Jeong and six colleagues charted how the soybean genome's packaging shifts as plant tissue turns into callus, the loose cell mass used to regrow whole plants. This switch underlies crop breeding tricks, yet its hidden controls were murky. The team paired maps of open genome zones and two chemical tags with gene activity reads over time.

Early callus growth brought sweeping change, with near sixteen thousand zones shifting their openness. Open zones and one tag tracked closely with genes switching on. Stage-linked DNA motifs pointed to plant hormone and growth switches early on, then stress and upkeep switches later. The authors frame callus growth as a ranked reset of the genome, with tips for better crop regrowth.
pmc-13649998:
Weice Shen and one colleague study how being judged by an algorithm in a job interview shapes what young applicants think of themselves and of the hiring firm. In AI video interviews, students record answers alone while software scores their words, voice, and face, usually with no feedback and little explanation.

Survey data from 520 Chinese university students were modeled along two paths. Skills and attitudes tied to expecting success, such as AI literacy, reflection on one's own thinking, appetite for hard problems, and low technology anxiety, each tracked with confidence in one's own employability. Fairness of the process and openness about how the algorithm works each tracked with how attractive the organization seemed. Past AI use and a habit of comparing oneself with others shifted some of these links. The findings feed debates about fairness and openness in hiring technology.
pmc-13650298:
Peng Ma and three colleagues review how astragaloside IV, the main active compound of the traditional herb Astragalus, may reprogram immune cells inside liver cancer tumors. Liver tumors often shelter suppressor macrophages, a white blood cell type pushed into a state that shields the cancer, feeds blood vessel growth, and blunts treatment.
