At the metabolic layer, it shifts how the cells produce energy, which changes their behavior. At the gene-control layer, it may loosen chemical marks that preserve the suppressor memory. Together these shifts push macrophages toward an attacking state, restoring killer T cell activity and easing the fibrous barrier around tumors. The authors offer the synthesis as groundwork for natural-product immune therapies.
pmc-13651598:
Toufik Mahamdi and seven colleagues solve a dirty-window problem in mass spectrometry imaging. In that technique, laser-based mapping of tissue chemistry is blinded at low masses by the very matrix sprayed on to make molecules fly. Small metabolites, the molecules most worth mapping, hide under that background noise.

Their fix pairs ionic solid matrices, salts built from two classic matrix acids, with gentle low-temperature evaporation instead of wet spraying, which had made the sticky ionic liquids impractical. One pairing detected and annotated sixty-nine small metabolites in mouse brain at fine spatial resolution with cleaner spectra and stronger signals. In mouse pancreas the method achieved a first: pinpointing melatonin and an iodinated tyrosine inside the hormone-producing islets. The authors pitch the approach as opening spatial metabolomics of small molecules to tissues where endocrine questions need exact addresses.
pmc-13652098:
Alexander Muacevic and seven colleagues report a case of throat-area cancer spreading to an armpit lymph node in the middle of treatment. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma normally travels to nodes in the neck, so an axillary node counts as distant, non-regional disease and is exceptionally rare. Their patient, a man in his fifties with advanced undifferentiated disease, had received initial chemotherapy and had just begun combined chemo and radiation.

After only six radiation sessions he reported pain under his left arm. Ultrasound showed enlarged nodes there, and removing one for biopsy confirmed poorly differentiated cancer matching his known primary tumor. A multidisciplinary team kept the planned chemoradiation on course and referred him for systemic treatment afterward. The case warns oncologists to investigate new lumps promptly during therapy, even in places this cancer almost never reaches.
pmc-13653098:
Jason Simpson Spicer and Ruoniu Wang surveyed every known community land trust in North America to test whether community ownership systematically enables fair climate action. The 2026 study covered 355 trusts in the United States and Canada. Land trusts take land out of speculative markets to keep housing affordable for lower-income households, and case studies had suggested they could also advance climate goals. The authors asked whether that promise holds at scale, or whether trusts must trade economic security against climate action.

Most trusts did engage in climate action, with mitigation more common than adaptation, and their action rate exceeded what local climate hazards alone would predict. That supports a just transition story: trusts can tackle precarity and climate together. Yet trusts also acted less often than they wished, held back by finances shaped by policy, a double bind in which economic and climate goals compete.
pmc-13662698:
Robert A. Battaglia led a 2026 study that rewrites the rules for bacterial stop signals that end RNA copying and tune downstream genes. The textbook model, an RNA hairpin followed by a uracil-rich stretch, proved incomplete, since mutations that preserve the hairpin can still abolish termination. The team mapped stop sites precisely across ten thousand sequences to hunt for the missing feature.

They found two-letter units at both edges of the copying bubble, resembling the basic pause signal of RNA polymerase, that are required for stopping. Together, hairpin, uracil tract, and bubble-edge sequences, dubbed HUB, explain most variation in stopping power and pinpoint true stop signals across diverse bacterial groups. Lab biologists get a sharper framework for decoding genomes and engineering gene expression, grounded in a feature the old model missed.
pmc-2265698:
Aziz, Bartels, Best, and co-authors describe the RAST Server for automatic annotation of microbial genomes. Genome sequences from bacteria and their relatives were arriving faster than experts could label them by hand. Annotation means naming each gene and guessing its role.

RAST offers a fully automated service that finds protein-coding genes, RNA genes, and more. It assigns functions using a subsystem approach that groups genes by the cell jobs they serve. Fast, consistent labelling lets small teams start biological analysis at once instead of spending months on setup.  Genome centres used the service to keep pace with sequencing output.
pmc-3772798:
Gupta, Kapoor, Chaudhary, and co-authors present a computational approach for predicting the toxicity of peptides and proteins. Research over past decades had focused on peptide and protein-based therapies for many diseases. Peptides offer advantages over small molecules, including high specificity, good penetration, and ease of manufacture.

A therapy must also be safe, and lab toxicity testing is slow and costly. Their in silico approach predicts harmful peptides before synthesis, guiding design toward safer candidates. Computer screening helps focus animal and cell testing on the most promising molecules.  Virtual screening first lets chemists reserve wet testing for a shortlist of candidates.
pmc-5015598:
The Early Breast Cancer Trialists' Collaborative Group, with McGale, Taylor, and others, analyzed radiotherapy after mastectomy in 2014. Earlier combined analyses showed that radiotherapy after mastectomy cuts recurrence and breast cancer death in women with node-positive disease overall. The benefit was uncertain for women whose cancer had reached just one, two, or three lymph nodes.

The team pooled individual patient data from many randomized trials, covering thousands of women. They measured effects on recurrence over ten years and breast cancer mortality over twenty years. Clear answers for the one-to-three node group matter because radiotherapy has real side effects. The analysis helped oncologists decide which women gain enough to justify treatment.
pmc-5705698:
Kyoko Watanabe, Erdogan Taskesen, Arjen van Bochoven, and colleagues introduced the FUMA web tool in 2017. Genome-wide association studies find DNA regions linked to traits, but most hits sit outside genes. Turning a list of hits into likely causal genes is a hard step.

FUMA lets users upload study results and map them to genes using position, gene activity data, and chromosome shape data. It also annotates the variants and tests which tissues and gene sets stand out. The tool runs in a browser with no coding needed. It has become a routine first step for interpreting association results.
pmc-6467998:
Tian Ge, Chia-Yen Chen, Yang Ni, and coauthors presented PRS-CS for polygenic prediction in 2019. Polygenic scores add up many small genetic effects to estimate disease risk. Better math can sharpen those scores without new data.

PRS-CS infers the true effect of each variant using association summaries plus a reference map of variant correlation. Its Bayesian shrinkage adapts to how heritable and complex a trait is. In tests it beat common rivals across several traits. Sharper scores help research on shared causes and, in time, may guide screening for high-risk groups.
pmc-8546498:
Veronika Skrivankova and colleagues published guidance in 2021 on how to report a kind of study that uses genes to test cause and effect. The method is called Mendelian randomisation. It treats the gene variants a person is born with as a kind of natural trial, which can show whether a habit or trait truly causes a health outcome. Reports of such studies, though, often leave out key facts.

This paper explains a reporting checklist for the method, item by item. It shows what good reporting looks like and warns where authors tend to cut corners. Clear reports matter here, because the results can shape advice on food, drugs, and daily habits. The checklist gives authors and reviewers one shared standard to work from.
rumi-divan-nicholson-1898:
Reynold Nicholson, a Cambridge scholar of Persian, published Selected Poems from the Divani Shamsi Tabriz in 1898. The book draws on the Divan of Rumi, the thirteenth-century Sufi poet of Konya, whose lyrics bear the name of his lost friend Shams. Nicholson's was the first major English translation of Rumi's lyric odes.

The odes burn with longing for the divine beloved, using wine, the tavern, and the reed flute as signs of the soul's exile. Nicholson prints the Persian text beside his English, with notes and an introduction on Rumi's life. Scholars of Sufism still start from this careful, loving edition.
rumi-masnavi-whinfield-1898:
Jalaluddin Rumi, the Persian Sufi master of the 1200s, poured his teaching into the Masnavi, a poem of thousands of couplets. Masnavi I Ma'navi, in the English verse of Edward Whinfield from 1898, gives the poem in a complete abridged form. Whinfield's was the first complete English rendering of the work.

Tale within tale, the poem moves from kings and fools to the soul's hunger for God. Rumi teaches by story: a mouse, a lion, a reed flute each carry a hard truth about love and loss. Sufis call the Masnavi the Quran in Persian dress. Whinfield opened that world to the West.
savonarola-processo-1498:
Florence puts its prophet on trial in the Processo of Girolamo Savonarola, the state record of 1498. Savonarola was a friar whose sermons had ruled the town and burnt its vain goods in a great fire. Caught at last, he is quizzed by the town's chiefs on his claims of God's voice. The Pope's own notes stand in the file by the quiz log of each hard day.

Torture mars the tale the record tells. Weeks past the quiz, the friar was hanged and burnt. The file is the first such trial set in print. It is a grim, prime source.
schiller-camp-wallenstein-1798:
Wallenstein's Camp, in German Wallensteins Lager, is the short opening piece of Schiller's Wallenstein trilogy. Schiller wrote it in 1798, and the text here is the German original. No stand-alone English translation of the piece is in the public domain.

Soldiers, sutlers, peasants, and camp followers crowd the scene outside Pilsen. Their songs, jokes, and complaints paint army life in the Thirty Years' War. Through their talk the great general Wallenstein looms, unseen and much debated. The piece works as a prologue, tuning the ear for the tragedy to come. Schiller wrote it in rough, lively verse quite unlike the high style of the main plays.
scientific-american-supplement-no-1178-j: Scientific American Supplement No. 1178, issued at New York on June 25, 1898, is headed as Volume XLV, Number 1178. A table of contents for the issue follows the masthead lines. Masthead lines give the price of the Supplement as five dollars a year. Scientific American and Supplement together cost seven dollars a year. The lines also note that Scientific American was established in 1845.
shiel-yellow-danger-1898:
M. P. Shiel wrote a tale of war to come in The Yellow Danger, his brisk novel of 1898. A sly foe in China plans to seize the West. Fleets clash, plots race, and Britain fights for its life in his tense plot.

The book helped start a wave of tales of raids to come. Its fears show the bias of its age in plain view. That bias mars the tale now. Yet its pace and reach shaped a whole class of pulp wars and spy tales that came next. Shiel wrote fast, bright prose that drove the plot at a sprint. That speed helped sell a plot that now feels both bold and flawed.
spr-proceedings-vol13-1897-1898:
Volume thirteen holds parts thirty two and thirty three, covering 1897 and 1898. Fifteen years after its founding, the Society for Psychical Research keeps its steady pace. Reports here range from thought reading tests to hauntings with named witnesses. The trance work with Mrs. Piper enters new phases, with proxy sitters tried.

Committees print methods in full so rivals can repeat or attack them. Physical marvels stay at the margin, where fraud had burned the society before. The archive these volumes build became the base for a debate lasting to 1930. Volume thirteen adds its share of cases and caution. It reads as a working journal, not a manifesto.
stanton-womans-bible-vol-2-1898:
Elizabeth Cady Stanton published The Woman's Bible, Part 2 in 1898. It carries her committee's commentary from Joshua to Revelation, completing the project begun with the Pentateuch in Part 1. Stanton was in her eighties and near the end of her public career.

Judges, prophets, psalms, and the New Testament letters all come under the committee's questioning eye. Passages praising strong women are lifted up; passages commanding silence and obedience are disputed. The editors argued that faith and women's equality need not be enemies. The two parts together form a landmark of feminist biblical criticism, still argued over by scholars of religion and of the suffrage movement alike.
strindberg-to-damascus-1898:
August Strindberg wrote The Road to Damascus as a trilogy in 1898, here in Graham Rawson's translation. The great trilogy of the Inferno crisis traces a soul's passage from guilt toward conversion in drama. Critics call it the bridge from naturalism to expressionism in the modern European theatre of experiment and dream.

The Stranger wanders stations of a city that repeat his sins like scenes in a dream. A Lady, a Beggar, and a Confessor mirror his pride, his fall, and his chance of grace. Settings melt and recur, and the dead and living trade places as in a fevered night. Strindberg breaks stage realism to map an inner pilgrimage, guilt to humiliation to a hard peace. Rawson's version carried this landmark of the modern stage to English readers and actors alike.
tao-teh-king-carus-1898:
Lao-Tse is the named author of the Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, rendered into English by James Legge. The work is the root text of Taoist thought from ancient China, set out here in short numbered parts.

Part One opens with a paradox: the Tao that can be trodden is not the lasting Tao. What has no name is the source of heaven and earth, while what has a name is the mother of all things. Legge casts some lines as verse and some as prose. Readers meet core Taoist themes of stillness, soft strength, and pairs of opposites that give rise to each other.
testament-of-solomon-conybeare-1898:
F. C. Conybeare translated the Testament of Solomon into English in 1898. His version appeared in the Jewish Quarterly Review that year. In the text, King Solomon interrogates demons one by one.

Each spirit must give its name, its mischief, and the angel who thwarts it. Solomon then sets the demons to work building the Temple. The dialogue mixes demonology with adventure and practical spell lore. Conybeare introduced Western readers to the fountainhead of Solomonic grimoire literature. Later grimoires borrowed its demon lists and angelic seals for centuries. The translation opened a strange, influential text to English scholarship.
the-library-pg5198:
George Crabbe wrote his poem The Library as a survey of what books do for a troubled mind. An argument printed before the poem promises consolation first. Books, he says, swap a lighter distress for the reader own grief and offer other gains besides.

The poem then walks through a library arrangement by subject. Divinity, controversy, philosophy, medicine, law, history, drama, and old romances each get a searching look. Crabbe warns that friends of religion can harm it more than foes, and he ends with a genius of the place who corrects his fears.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
Number 281 of The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction, dated Saturday, November 3, 1827, continues its series on the manners and customs of all nations. The fourteenth installment illustrates the body guards of the Sheikh of Bornou, copied from Major Denham's recent Travels in Africa. These black chiefs and favourites, raised to rank by deeds of bravery, wear coats of mail. The iron chain covers them from throat to knees and divides behind over the horse.

Helmets and skull-caps of the same metal, with chin-pieces, ward off spear shocks. Their horses' heads carry plates of iron, brass, and silver, leaving room only for the eyes. Charms in little red leather parcels hang about neck, head, and saddle. The article calls their appearance altogether warlike, their evolutions somewhat wild, and the lance formidable in their hands. Readers in London met central African cavalry through a traveler's sketch, armor in detail.

The Mirror's number for Saturday, March 21, 1829, No. 362, illustrates Chester Terrace in Regent's Park. The range of palatial residences stands between the Colosseum and St. Katharine's Church, with the Colosseum's cupola in the engraving's distance. The terrace takes its name from the royal earldom of Chester. Nash designed it, and the article grants the work great genius alongside many irregularities.

Its order is Corinthian, characterized by richness, yet the specimen is weak in detail. The balustrade's form and proportions are called starved and lanky, and the capitals want Corinthian grace. Even so, the composition impresses by powerful conception, and its effect would be extremely beautiful but for the defective details. Corinthian arches close each end of the range, an altogether novel idea. Readers get a terrace praised and faulted in the same breath.

The Mirror's number for Saturday, February 28, 1829, No. 358, illustrates York Terrace in Regent's Park. Readers are invited to start from Waterloo Place and make the architectural tour of the park. Entering by York Gate, they meet York Terrace early: a splendid range of residences with the appearance of a unique palace. All entrances hide in the rear, so the principal front reads as a suite of princely apartments, a little Versailles.

Undvided gardens assist the palace illusion. The architecture is Graeco-Italian: a rusticated ground story with semicircular-headed windows, then balustraded balconies before the principal windows. An Ilissus Ionic colonnade decorates the principal and chamber stories under a well-proportioned entablature. Mr. Elmes, quoted in criticism, finds the attic story too irregular for so chaste a composition. Readers stroll a terrace designed to disguise many houses as one royal residence.

Number 481 of the Mirror, dated Saturday, March 19, 1831, illustrates relics of Ariosto preserved at Ferrara: his arm-chair and his inkstand. Ferrara was the poet's favourite residence though not his birthplace, and the Ferrarese claim him as their own. Byron's notes to Childe Harold are quoted: the author of the Orlando is jealously claimed as the Homer, not of Italy, but of Ferrara. His mother was of Reggio, and his birth house there carries a tablet dated September 8, 1474.

Ferrara answers that birth abroad was an accident. The city possesses his bones, his chair, his inkstand, and his autographs, plus the house where he lived and the room where he died. The library holds his tomb's medallion and an account of his last illness, alongside Tasso's Jerusalem manuscript. Travellers also see the Ferrara hospital cell where Tasso was confined. Readers handle a poet's memory through furniture and bones.
the-revival-of-alchemy-a-rejoinder-1898: Journal pages from Science, volume seven, number 168, page 386, follow a notice for free early journal content in these pages. Visible items concern university posts, a New York school appointment, and Bryn Mawr fellowships in physics and biology. Here only that wrapper notice and general journal news are present, so the rejoinder on alchemy itself does not appear.
tob-10198:
Catherine Benincasa, better known as Saint Catherine of Siena, dictated letters in the fourteenth century despite barely being able to write. Vida Scudder's translation presents correspondence that reached popes, kings, rulers, and prisoners. Catherine wrote as a mystic, but never only about private prayer.

She urged the pope to leave Avignon and return to Rome, demanded reform in the church, and consoled condemned men with talk of Christ's love. Politics and prayer intertwine on every page, in a fierce, affectionate voice. Readers meet a young woman, often ill, steering the affairs of church and city by letter because she believed God required it.
tob-10498:
James Legge opened his monumental Chinese Classics with the Confucian Analects, the Lun Yü, as volume one. Legge printed Confucius's sayings with the Chinese text and extensive notes from the great Chinese commentators. The result is more scholarly apparatus than popular edition, by design.

Sayings on virtue, learning, family duty, and government appear in short exchanges between Confucius and his disciples. Legge's prolegomena and notes explain names, places, and disputed meanings at length. For the nineteenth-century West, the volume was a first serious doorway into the Confucian canon. It remains a foundation stone of Chinese studies in English, demanding but rewarding for patient readers.
tob-10798:
Paul Carus retold the Buddha's life in the manner of a gospel in The Gospel of Buddha, written for Western readers in 1894. Birth, temptation, enlightenment, and teaching follow in narrative order, drawn from the ancient Pali scriptures. Carus shaped episodes into a continuous, readable life.

Buddhism appears here as a religion of reason and compassion, a presentation fitted to Carus's audience of liberal Western seekers. The retelling is beautifully readable, though scholars now prefer the original sources in their own forms. As a historical artifact, the book shows how Buddhism first entered American religious imagination: through a gospel-shaped door built by an admiring editor.
tob-10898:
Scribes in ancient Egypt wrote the Tale of Two Brothers on papyrus more than three thousand years ago. It tells of Anpu and his younger brother Bata, herdsmen in the Nile valley. Many call it the oldest fairy tale that survives.

Anpu's wife falsely accuses Bata, who flees, is aided by gods, and passes through death and strange rebirths, even becoming a bull and then a tree. In the end Bata becomes king and judges those who wronged him. Betrayal, magic, and justice drive a story whose parts echo in folklore worldwide.
tob-14098:
R. H. Charles translated the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, farewell speeches ascribed to the twelve sons of Jacob. Each dying patriarch reviews his life for his children. The work arose in the centuries between the Old and New Testaments.

One son warns against envy, another praises mercy, another confesses lust or anger, each drawing a moral from his own story in Genesis. Prophecies of a coming savior run through the speeches, which Christian copyists preserved and may have enlarged. The testaments form a bridge between the Testaments, showing how moral teaching grew from Bible story.
tob-4098:
J. Armitage Robinson edited three writings from Christianity's second century in one volume: the Epistle of Barnabas, the Shepherd of Hermas, and the Didache. Together they are counted among the Apostolic Fathers, the church's earliest writers after the apostles themselves. Robinson's edition rests on a verified 1919 printing.

Barnabas reads the Hebrew scriptures as Christian allegory. Hermas records visions about sin and forgiveness. The Didache gives rules for baptism, prayer, and testing prophets. Side by side, the three show a young church deciding what it believed and how it would live. Few single volumes open the second century so well.
treatise-on-the-great-art-a-system-of-ph: Treatise on the Great Art, a system of physics according to Hermetic philosophy, 1898. The hermetic physics. This book preserves that work. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
treaty-of-paris-1898:
The Spanish-American War ended with the Treaty of Paris in December 1898. Spain had lost Cuba, Puerto Rico, and its Pacific holdings in a short war with the United States. American and Spanish commissioners met in Paris to settle the terms, with Cuba's own future decided over its head.

Spain gave up Cuba, which became independent under American watch, and ceded Puerto Rico and Guam to the United States. The Philippines also passed to American rule in return for a payment of twenty million dollars. In one summer the United States gained an overseas empire, and a fierce home debate over imperialism began at once.
turgot-reflections-formation-distributio:
Turgot wrote his Reflections on the Formation and the Distribution of Riches in 1766. Macmillan issued the English translation in 1898. Turgot, a French statesman and thinker, belonged to the physiocrats, who saw land as the source of wealth. His short treatise reaches far past that school's limits.

He traces how capital forms, how interest arises, and how wages and profits divide the product. His pages hold some of the first reasoning like later marginal utility theory. Adam Smith read and learned from Turgot's circle. The Reflections pack a whole economics into brief numbered sections. Students still read them as a bridge to Smith.
un-ga-res-998:
Fighting over the Suez Canal forced the UN General Assembly into emergency session in the fall of 1956. Israel had struck deep into Egypt, and British and French forces were attacking Egyptian soil. Resolution 998, adopted on 4 November 1956, builds on the truce call passed two days before, at the height of the Suez Crisis.

The Assembly asks the Secretary-General, as a top priority, to file a plan within 48 hours for an emergency world force. That force, with the consent of the states involved, would guard and oversee the halt to fighting. The plan led within days to the first armed UN peacekeeping force.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: Two days after demanding a cease-fire in the Suez crisis, the General Assembly went further in resolution 998 (ES-I) of 4 November 1956. As a matter of priority, it asks the Secretary-General to submit a plan within forty-eight hours. The plan is for an emergency international United Nations Force. The force would be set up with the consent of the countries concerned. It would secure and supervise the end of hostilities, on the terms the Assembly had already laid down.
un-sc-res-1298:
War between Eritrea and Ethiopia brought an arms embargo on 17 May 2000. Fighting had flared again days earlier, after proximity talks in Algiers from 29 April to 5 May failed to settle the border war. The Council deplored the loss of life and the diversion of food-crisis funds into arms. Its own mission to the region had just returned.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council strongly condemned the continued fighting. It demanded that both parties stop all military action at once and pull their forces back from engagement. Substantive peace talks under the African body had to restart at the earliest date, without preconditions, on the basis of the framework agreement. All states were barred from selling or supplying arms, ammunition, and related goods to either side. The embargo would run for twelve months, with a sanctions committee to watch it. Humanitarian and non-lethal supplies were exempt.
un-sc-res-1398: Among the formal acts of the United Nations Security Council sits Resolution 1398, which the catalog dates to 2002. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later.
un-sc-res-1498: The Security Council's Resolution 1498, issued in 2003, survives in this collection as a Wikisource copy of the official record. Its structure is the familiar one: context and prior steps first, then the voted decisions in numbered order. Together with its neighbors in the 1400s sequence, it forms part of the Council's continuous written output.
un-sc-res-1598: In 2005 the Council adopted Resolution 1598, preserved in this collection from the official record via English Wikisource. Such texts are the UN's working law on peace and security while they stand. The entry holds the full decision, preamble and operative paragraphs alike, in the form governments received it and were expected to answer.
un-sc-res-1698:
The Democratic Republic of the Congo faced the Security Council in Resolution 1698, adopted on 31 July 2006. The parties had failed to meet the Council's earlier demands. Armed groups still operated across Ituri and the Kivus. Children kept being recruited and attacked, and stolen resources kept paying for guns.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the sanctions package until 31 July 2007. It then widens the travel and money measures to a new class of targets. Leaders who recruit or use child soldiers now face listing. So do people who commit grave crimes against children in war. The Group of Experts also serves to 31 July 2007, and must weigh how far resource theft funds the armed groups.
un-sc-res-1798: Security Council Resolution 1798 survives as part of the body's official record, held here through a transcription by English Wikisource. A reader finds the expected architecture: the situation as the members stated it, then the response they voted. Because later practice builds on earlier texts, preserving each one keeps the whole structure of precedent standing.
un-sc-res-1898: Resolution 1898 is preserved here as part of the Security Council's official record, in a transcription from English Wikisource. The Council's numbered output is the closest thing world politics has to a statute book on peace and security. This entry is one page of that book, kept complete: findings, decisions, and follow-up instructions included.
un-sc-res-198: Resolution 198 stands in the official record of the United Nations Security Council, catalogued here with a 1965 date. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-1998: Kept as Resolution 1998, a Security Council act survives in official-record form in this collection. The source transcription comes from English Wikisource. The document shows the Council's habit of building by layers. One more decision is laid on a base of earlier ones, all of them citable by number, and this one is kept whole at its number.
un-sc-res-298:
Jerusalem's occupied sector was the subject of the Council's clearest wording yet in 1971. Jordan had written about new Israeli measures in the city. On 25 September 1971 the Council restated its resolutions of 1968 and 1969. It deplored Israel's failure to respect them. Land taken by force, it repeated, gives no valid claim. The Secretary-General's reports fed the debate.

All Israeli acts meant to change Jerusalem's status were declared invalid. The Council listed land seizures, population transfers, and laws aimed at absorbing the occupied part. Israel had to cancel every such measure at once. It had to take no further steps of the kind. The vote was fourteen to none. Syria abstained.
un-sc-res-398:
Six more months for the Golan observer force were granted by the Security Council on 30 November 1976. The Secretary-General had reported on the United Nations Disengagement Observer Force between Israel and Syria. Efforts toward a durable and just peace in the Middle East were noted, along with the urgent need to press them harder. Tension in the area still worried the Council.

The Council called on the parties to apply resolution 338 (1973) without delay. It renewed the observer force's mandate to 31 May 1977. The Secretary-General was asked to report at the end of the period on developments and on steps taken to apply resolution 338. That text had demanded a cease-fire in the October 1973 war and a negotiated settlement. The renewal kept United Nations observers on the Golan separation line while the wider peace effort remained stuck.
un-sc-res-598:
The Iran-Iraq War had ground on for nearly seven years by 1987. On 20 July 1987 the Security Council demanded an immediate ceasefire. It deplored the bombing of civilian areas and attacks on neutral shipping. It condemned the use of chemical weapons, against the 1925 Geneva Protocol. Both states had to stop all military action on land, at sea, and in the air. Their forces had to pull back to the recognized borders without delay.

The Secretary-General had to send observers to verify the halt. Prisoners of war were to be freed and sent home after fighting stopped. The Council backed his mediation efforts. It warned it would meet again to weigh further steps. Iran accepted the text only a year later, as the war turned against it.
un-sc-res-798: The catalog's entries for 1992 include Resolution 798 of the United Nations Security Council. Year by year, these decisions build the written history of how the world body handled the crises of its time. The transcription keeps the preamble and numbered clauses in their official order, as the Council adopted them. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-98:
Kashmir's stalled demilitarization drew fresh numbers from the Council on 23 December 1952. The United Nations Representative for India and Pakistan had sent his third and fourth reports that year. India and Pakistan had accepted all but two points of his twelve-point plan. The block sat in paragraph 7, on how many troops would stay on each side of the cease-fire line.

The Council backed the representative's general principles and thanked him for his efforts. It urged India and Pakistan to open talks at once under his guidance. The goal was a firm figure for forces left after demilitarization. His suggested bands were 3,000 to 6,000 troops on the Pakistan side and 12,000 to 18,000 on the India side. Both governments had to report back within thirty days. The representative would keep the Council posted on any progress toward the plebiscite the plan served.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Resolution 1298, adopted on 17 May 2000, imposes an arms embargo on both Eritrea and Ethiopia as their border war flares again. Fighting had resumed days earlier despite proximity talks in Algiers at the end of April, where the African Union tried to broker a final implementation plan. The Council deplored the loss of life and the resources the war was diverting from a humanitarian food crisis in the region.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council barred the sale or supply of arms and related material to either country, along with technical help for making weapons. The embargo ran for twelve months and came with a sanctions committee to monitor it. Both states were, unusually, treated with identical restrictions.

Ethiopia and Eritrea's peacekeeping mission, UNMEE, is extended on 15 March 2002, until 15 September 2002. A Council mission had just visited both countries. The December 2000 Algiers peace deal was in place, and a Boundary Commission was set to rule on the disputed border.

UNMEE stays at the strength set in 2000, and both parties are called on to cooperate fully with it. They are pressed to respect their agreements and to do the demining needed before the border can be marked out. Eritrea is again told to give the mission full freedom of movement and to conclude a status-of-forces agreement without delay.

West African and French forces keeping the peace in Côte d'Ivoire are renewed on 4 August 2003. The country had split during civil war, and a national reconciliation government was meant to reunite it. A small United Nations political mission, MINUCI, was already at work under an earlier resolution.

The authorization for states taking part in the ECOWAS force, together with the French forces supporting them, is extended for six months. Both are to report regularly through the Secretary-General on how their mandates are being carried out. Redeploying state administration across the whole country and completing disarmament, demobilization, and reintegration of fighters are stressed.

Western Sahara's referendum mission, MINURSO, is extended until 31 October 2005 on 28 April 2005. The political impasse held firm. The call for a mutually acceptable solution providing for the self-determination of the people of Western Sahara is repeated.

The POLISARIO Front is urged to release all remaining prisoners of war without further delay, as humanitarian law requires. Morocco and POLISARIO are called on to keep working with the Red Cross to settle the fate of people still unaccounted for since the conflict began. States are again asked to fund confidence-building measures, and a report on the situation is requested before the mandate expires.

Congo's sanctions are extended and widened to child abusers in Resolution 1698, adopted on 31 July 2006. The parties had failed to meet the Council's demands. Armed groups still held Ituri and the Kivus. The Group of Experts' July 2006 report traced how illegal resource exploitation financed the fighting.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the arms embargo and the travel and financial measures until 31 July 2007, and extends the Group of Experts to the same date. It extends the targeted measures to two new classes. The first is leaders who recruit or use children in armed conflict. The second is individuals who commit serious violations against children. Those violations include killing, maiming, sexual violence, abduction, and forced displacement. The Group must also propose, by 20 December 2006, ways to cut off resource financing of armed groups.

Ethiopia and Eritrea's mission, UNMEE, is extended for six months on 30 January 2008. The Boundary Commission had restated its ruling in November 2006 after the parties failed to mark the border on the ground. Both countries, it is repeated, had accepted the ruling as final and binding when they signed the peace agreements.

The extension kept the mission in place while the demarcation dispute festered. Support for the Boundary Commission's efforts is expressed, and member states are called on to keep funding the trust fund for demarcation. Within weeks, Eritrea's restrictions on fuel and movement would force the mission to pull back from the border zone, a crisis this renewal did not foresee in its text.

Cyprus's peacekeeping force, UNFICYP, is extended on 14 December 2009. The Secretary-General's November reports covered both the operation and his good-offices work on a settlement. The duty to find a solution, it is repeated, lies first with the Cypriots themselves, and a rare chance for decisive progress still exists in the leaders' talks.

The force's mandate is extended for a further period, and the leaders are urged to quicken the negotiations, build goodwill, and engage openly. Confidence-building steps, including new crossing points, are pressed for. Both sides are told to agree the buffer zone's demarcation with UNFICYP urgently. The force would keep watching the ceasefire lines while the settlement talks it underpins continue into 2010.

By December 1964 the fighting in Cyprus had eased, and the island's government wanted the United Nations peacekeeping force to stay. The force had been created in March 1964, after fighting broke out between Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots. Resolution 198, adopted unanimously on 18 December 1964, deals with that force.

The Council noted that the situation on the island had improved and that real progress had been made. It reaffirmed its earlier resolutions on Cyprus. The force would stay for three more months, ending on 26 March 1965. Short renewals like this one kept the peacekeepers in place while talks went on. They set the pattern for a mission that would last for decades.

Children caught up in war are the subject of Resolution 1998, adopted on 12 July 2011. Earlier Council resolutions had built a system for naming armed groups that recruit child soldiers. Groups that kill or abuse children could also be named. Once named, a group was pressed to sign an action plan to stop.

The Council strongly condemned the continuing harm done to children in wars. It kept the monitoring and reporting system in place. It also widened the rules for naming groups. Parties that repeatedly attacked schools or hospitals could now be named in the Secretary-General's reports. So could parties that attacked the people protected inside them. Armed groups were urged to let children reach schools, hospitals, and aid without obstruction.

Jordan brought Jerusalem back to the fore in 1971. Israel held the city's east since 1967. Fresh laws there aimed to fuse the seized half to the state. Land was being taken. Folk were being moved in. Past UN texts had banned all such steps. Resolution 298 passed on 25 September 1971 by fourteen votes to none. Syria held back.

The Council stood by its 1968 and 1969 texts in full. It voiced grief at Israel's cold shrug to those calls. Then the key line: all such laws and acts were void, in the most clear terms the Council could find. Seized land, moved folk, and merger laws changed naught in law. Israel had to scrap the lot and take no new steps. Word on its reply was due in sixty days.

Resolution 398, adopted on 30 November 1976 by twelve votes to none, is a routine but necessary renewal of the observer force between Israel and Syria. The Secretary-General's report on the United Nations Disengagement Observer Force was before the Council. Members noted work toward a lasting, fair peace in the region, and the urgent need to keep at it, alongside concern over tension in the area.

The Council called on the parties to carry out resolution 338 of 1973, the war-ending ceasefire text, immediately. It then renewed the observer force's mandate for six months, until 31 May 1977. A closing request asked the Secretary-General to report at the end of the period on developments and on measures taken to apply resolution 338.

Seven years of war had ground Iran and Iraq down by 1987. The Council had called for quiet before, in vain. This time it spoke with one voice and with legal force. Resolution 598 passed with no dissent on 20 July 1987. It found a breach of the peace. It acted under the Charter's tough enforcement clauses.

Both states had to halt fire at once. All troops had to pull back to the known borders. UN teams would watch the truce and the pullback. Captives had to go home fast, as the Geneva rules demand. The text also raised blame for the war's start. It asked for a fair probe of who began the fight. A year later, Iran at last said yes. The guns fell silent.

Reports of mass rape in detention camps in Bosnia appalled the Council at the end of 1992. Women, in particular Muslim women, were being held and raped in a massive, organized, and systematic way. The reports came from the war then tearing Bosnia and Herzegovina apart. Resolution 798 was adopted unanimously on 18 December 1992.

The Council demanded that all the detention camps be closed at once. The camps holding women were named above all. The acts reported were strongly condemned as unspeakable brutality. The Council backed a European plan to send a delegation to investigate the facts. The Secretary-General was asked to give that delegation support. He also had to secure its access to the places of detention. A report on the matter was requested within fifteen days.

Resolution 98, adopted on 23 December 1952 by nine votes to none with one abstention, measures how close India and Pakistan came to a Kashmir deal. The UN representative for the two countries, Frank Graham, had tabled twelve-point proposals. Both governments, he reported, had accepted all but two paragraphs; the sticking point was paragraph seven, the heart of the plan to demilitarize the state before a plebiscite.

The Council endorsed the general principles behind the representative's work. It noted with satisfaction the near-agreement he had built. It then urged both governments to enter immediate negotiations under his auspices to settle the remaining differences, above all the numbers of troops to remain on each side after demilitarization.
vancouver-voyage-discovery-vol3-1798:
George Vancouver commanded a great survey of the Pacific coast of North America from 1791 to 1795. Volume Three of the official account, published in 1798, carries the voyage to its close. Vancouver had sailed as a young man with Captain Cook.

This volume covers the later seasons of charting, the meetings with Spanish officers, and the long sail home by way of South America. Vancouver's charts of the northwest coast stayed standard for decades. He died young, soon after finishing his account, and his brother saw it through the press. The set remains the founding record of the coast's modern mapping.
waverley-or-tis-sixty-years-since-pg5998: Sir Walter Scott's Waverley, or 'Tis Sixty Years Since, appears here in the edition of 1893, with an introductory essay and notes by Andrew Lang, and with illustrations. The publishers dedicated this new edition of the Waverley Novels to the Hon. Mrs. Maxwell Scott of Abbotsford and her children. Pages present here hold front matter only: the title page, that dedication, and the start of Scott's own dedication of his works to the king, by royal permission. The novel itself, and Lang's essay, are not shown.
wells-war-worlds-1898:
H. G. Wells wrote The War of the Worlds in 1898. The tale tells of a Martian raid on Earth, told by a man who lived through it. Vast war craft land in the fields of Surrey, south of London. Their heat rays and black smoke lay waste to towns.

Men flee, guns fail, and the great city stands bare in days. The Martians fall at last not to arms but to Earth's germs. Wells made the tale a sharp jab at empire and its pride. The book set the mold for a whole age of alien raid tales.
white-desire-of-ages-1898:
Ellen White's Desire of Ages, published in 1898, is her life of Christ and the Adventist devotional classic on the incarnation. White retells the Gospel story from Bethlehem to the ascension in warm, flowing prose. Seventh-day Adventists rank the book among her finest works.

She dwells on Christ's childhood, his healings, his parables, and his patience with slow and doubting followers. Each scene closes with a lesson for the reader's own prayer and conduct at home and work. Generations of Adventist families have read the book aloud as their chief picture of Jesus. Her portrait stresses Christ's sympathy for the poor, the sick, and the outcast.
wordsworth-coleridge-lyrical-ballads-179:
William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge were close neighbors in Somerset when they planned Lyrical Ballads together. The small anonymous volume appeared in 1798. The two young poets split the task oddly: Coleridge would make the supernatural feel real, Wordsworth would find wonder in common life.

Coleridge contributed The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, his eerie tale of a sailor cursed for killing an albatross. Wordsworth closed the book with Tintern Abbey, a deep meditation on memory and nature. Between them sit ballads of peasants, mad mothers, and convicts, written in plain speech. The volume quietly started the Romantic movement in English poetry. This text is the 1798 first edition as first published.
zola-trial-1898:
January 1898 brought Zola's great stand for justice in the Dreyfus affair. His open letter J'accuse charged the French state with framing Alfred Dreyfus. Dreyfus, a Jewish officer, sat in prison for a crime he did not commit.

The state answered by putting Zola himself on trial for libel. Court records of that trial fill this volume, scene by scene. France's greatest living writer faced prison for telling the truth in print. The drama plays out with a whole nation in the dock beside him. It endures as a landmark in the history of conscience and of the writer's duty to speak.
